units.la: ILLVSTRISSIMO FLORENTISSIMOQVE PRINCIPI AC DOMINO, DOMINO FRIDERICO IV. Comiti Palatino ad Renum, Duci Bauariæ, Sacri Rom. Imperij Archidapifero & Electori, Domino ac Principi suo clementissimo:
units.tr: TO THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS AND MOST FLOURISHING PRINCE AND LORD, LORD FREDERICK IV, Count Palatine of the Rhine, Duke of Bavaria, Archsteward of the Holy Roman Empire and Elector, my most gracious Lord and Prince:

units.la: ILLVSTRISSIME PRINCEPS ELECTOR, Domine clementissime, Multa requiruntur in bono Principe, Dei inter homines vicario: inter alia, singulare eius ornamentum & præsidium longè optimum est sapientia, quæ diuinarum & humanarum rerum cognitionem complectitur. Hinc Plato Resp. tum demum felices fore censebat, si aut Principes philosopharetur, aut Philosophi Respubl. administrarent. Et, ut teste vtar graviore, sapientum multitudo est mundi salus, & rex prudens stabilimentum populi, inquit Sapiens. Quocirca etiam mortalium ille sapientissimus rex Salomon, filius Dauid, cum tenella ætate, regni gubernacula accepisset, oblata à Deo optione petendi quod à y vellet, vellet, sapientiam unice in votis habuit. Refert etiam Plato institutum Persarum in regum filiis primogenitis, qui in regnum succedebant, educadis, atque a teneris ad sapientia & virtutis studiu assuefaciendis, quo regno aliquando cum honore praeesset. Erat hoc eiusmodi. Anno aetatis XIV, illos suscipiebat regy (vt appellabatur) paedagogi, qui ex omnib. Persis eligebantur quatuor, sapientissimus, iustissimus, temperatissimus atq; fortissimus aliquis vir. Quorum primus deorum cultum docebat, idemq; regia tradebat instituta. Secundus admonebat, vt in omni vita veritati studerent. Tertius, ne vlla cupiditate superaretur, & libere viuere cosuescerent, ac reuera reges, imperantes sibi ipsis ante omnia, nec vllis servientes cupiditatibus. Quartus denique impavidos illos reddebat, ne quid metu alienum a dignitate committerent, & serui fierent. Haec apud Persas futuri Principis vigebat institutio. Et sane rectissime iudicabant, ante omnia sapientia, id est, religionis & regni praeceptis imbuendum: nisi quod diuina veritatis ignari falsam religionem amplexabantur, ex magica Zoroastri disciplina. Non absimilis, quanquam modis omnibus praefereda, vtpote ex
units.tr: MOST ILLUSTRIOUS PRINCE ELECTOR, most gracious Lord, Many qualities are required in a good prince, who is God's vicar among men. Among them, his singular adornment and by far the best safeguard is wisdom, which embraces the knowledge of divine and human things. Hence Plato held in his Republic that states would at last be happy only if either princes philosophised or philosophers governed the state. And, to use a weightier witness, the multitude of the wise is the salvation of the world, and a prudent king is the stability of the people, says the Wise Man. For this reason also that most wise of mortal kings, Solomon the son of David, when he had received the reins of the kingdom at a tender age, and God had offered him the choice of asking for whatever he wished, kept wisdom alone in his prayers. Plato also reports the custom of the Persians, by which the eldest sons of their kings, who were to succeed to the throne, were educated and trained from tender years in the pursuit of wisdom and virtue, so that they might one day preside over the kingdom with honour. It was of this kind. In the fourteenth year of his age, the king's (as they called him) tutors took the boy in hand. Four were chosen from all the Persians: a man most wise, most just, most temperate and most brave. The first of these taught the worship of the gods, and at the same time handed down the precepts of kingship. The second urged them to pursue truth in every part of life. The third trained them not to be overcome by any desire, and to live freely, truly as kings, ruling themselves above all and serving no appetite. The fourth, finally, made them fearless, so that they would commit nothing unworthy of their rank out of fear, and would not become slaves. Such was the training of the future prince among the Persians. And indeed they judged very rightly that before all things he must be imbued with wisdom, that is, with the precepts of religion and of kingship; except that, ignorant of the divine truth, they embraced a false religion from the magical teaching of Zoroaster. Not unlike this, though in every way to be preferred, since it is drawn from the most limpid fountains of heavenly wisdom, is the training that has fallen to your Highness, most gracious Prince.

units.la: ex limpidissimis cœlestis sapientiæ fontibus hausta, Cels. V. cõtigit institutio, Princeps clementissime. Nec defuerunt vota Salomonica, cum V. Cels. quæ ab ineunte ætate vtilium & bonarum rerum cognitione delectata, quotidianis apud Deum precibus institit, & indesinenter instat, ab illo donari se cupiens corde intelligete; tum bonorum omnium, quibus publicè priuatimq; id ipsum cõmendatissimum est, nõ abs re. Quantum vero ijs reb. adhuc effectum sit, documenta testantur nõ obscura, eaq; in honorem Dei gratis animis ad posteritatē prædicãda. Primùm, quòd Inclito Heroë & Domino, Dn. Johanne Casimiro, Cels. V. tutore & altero veluti parente, rebus humanis nuper erepto, in tam acerbo casu perfugiũ & solatium præbuerit, tua, Friderice Illustrissime, floretissima & iã iam principatui matura ætas, & ætate iudiciũ maturius. Tu, quòd suscepto iam regimine amplißimorum principatuũ, ea læti vidimus specimina summæ virtutis tuæ, eaq; fundamenta bonæ gubernationis iacta sunt, quantumuis luctuoso & iniquo tempore, vt omniũ animos in præclaram exspectationem erexerint.
units.tr: Nor have the prayers of Solomon been wanting in your Highness's case, for from earliest youth, delighting in the knowledge of useful and good things, you have daily persisted in prayer to God and never cease to persist, desiring to be granted by him an understanding heart; and this, not without reason, is most commended both publicly and privately for all good things. How much has been achieved in these matters so far, unclear proofs bear witness, and these, to the honour of God, are gladly to be proclaimed to posterity. First, that under the illustrious hero and lord, Lord John Casimir, your Highness's guardian and, as it were, second father, recently taken from human affairs, in so bitter a misfortune you found refuge and comfort, you, Frederick most illustrious, in your most flourishing youth, already ripe for government, and of an age more mature in judgement than your years. Second, that since you have now taken up the rule of the most ample principalities, we have happily seen the signs of your supreme virtue, and the foundations of good government have been laid, so that, however sorrowful and unfavourable the times, they have raised the minds of all to a splendid expectation.

units.la: Macte igitur animo & virtute ista, Illustrissime... strissime princeps Elector, corroborare per Domi-num & forte ipsius robur, memor exhortationis Domini olim ad Josuam, Ero tecum, quemadmodum fui cū Mose. Non derelinquā te, neque deseram te. Confortare, vt facias secundum legem. Non recedat liber legis ab ore tuo. Tunc intelligenter, & prosperè ages in omnibus. In quam sententiam & sanctissimus Dauid filium Salomonem, cum tenellus adhuc regno iam inauguratus esset, sedulò hortatus fuisse legitur. Dominus Deus, qui aufert & constituit Principes, & à cuius facie est sapientia & fortitudo, Cels. V. magis magisq; induat virtute ex alto.
units.tr: Be brave, then, in spirit and in that virtue, most illustrious Prince Elector, and be strengthened by the Lord and in his own strength, mindful of the Lord's exhortation once given to Joshua: "I will be with you, as I was with Moses. I will not leave you nor forsake you. Be strong, that you may do according to the law. Let not the book of the law depart from your mouth. Then you shall act wisely and prosperously in all things." To this same effect we read that the most holy David earnestly exhorted his son Solomon, when he was still tender and already anointed to the kingdom. May the Lord God, who takes away and sets up princes, and from whose face come wisdom and strength, clothe your Highness with virtue more and more from on high.

units.la: Ceterum, Illustrissime Princeps Elector, Domine clementissime, cum hi quatuor libri de redemtione generis humani & diuina prædestinatione, anno superiore à me conscripti, nunc sub ipsa auspicia gubernationis vestræ in lucem prodirent, Cels. V. non ingratum fore officium hoc meum arbitrabar, si eidem illos inscriberem & offerrem humiliter: idq; pro ea gratitudine, ad quam Palatinatui multis nominibus obstrictus sum. Sat scio, hac ratione exsoluere eam potis haud sum, attamen profiteri hominis quoque est non ingrati. Accedit, quod
units.tr: Moreover, most illustrious Prince Elector, most gracious Lord, since these four books on the redemption of mankind and on divine predestination, which I wrote last year, now come forth into the light under the very auspices of your government, I thought this duty of mine would not be unwelcome to your Highness, if I inscribed them to you and humbly offered them: and this for that gratitude which, on many grounds, I owe to the Palatinate. I know well that by this means I am by no means able to repay it, yet to acknowledge it is also the part of a man who is not ungrateful. Add to this that
1 Kings 1.

units.la: DEDICATORIA.
units.tr: DEDICATION.

units.la: quod in huiusmodi & similibus controuersiis ecclesiasticis, quæ subinde ab irrequietis ingeniis noua existunt, viros principes in primis decet cognitio & custodia veritatis, quo calumniatores & deprauatores minus noceant rei Christianæ.
units.tr: In controversies of this kind and similar ecclesiastical ones, which from time to time arise as novelties from restless minds, a knowledge and guarding of the truth befits princes above all, so that slanderers and distorters may do less harm to the Christian cause.

units.la: Sic hodie nouo in nos consisto crimine traducimur à maleuolis, quasi negemus Christu mortuum pro omnibus. Impudens calumnia. Id enim secundum scripturas fatemur & nos sed inficiamur inde sequi, morte Christi omnes in genere humano, sine cuiusquam exceptione, re ipsa iustificatos, saluatos, & accepta remissione peccatorum in sinum gratia restitutos, siue scilicet illi credant, siue non. Homi-num hoc sigmentum est, eoque repudiandum, retento consensu Prophetarum & Apostolorum, remissionem videlicet peccatorum accipere per nomen Iesu quemuis qui crediderit in eum, manenteira Dei super incredulos.
units.tr: Thus today I am accused by malicious people of a new crime laid against us, as if we denied that Christ died for all. Shameless calumny. For we confess this according to the Scriptures, but we deny that it follows from this that by the death of Christ all in the human race, without any exception, are in fact justified and saved, and, having received the forgiveness of sins, are restored to the bosom of grace, whether or not they believe. This is a human fiction and must be rejected, while we hold to the consensus of the Prophets and Apostles: that whoever believes in Jesus receives the forgiveness of sins through his name, while the wrath of God remains upon unbelievers.

units.la: Iam doctrina prædestinatiouis, secundum quam ex damnabili massa generis humani aliospisericorditer Deus seruat, aliòs iuste in eadem derelictos, ob peccata punit: per se plana est, si diuini Spiritus magisterium quàm stulta rationis consequentias sequi malimus.
units.tr: Now the doctrine of predestination, according to which God mercifully saves some from the condemned mass of the human race, while others left in that same mass he justly punishes for their sins, is plain in itself, if we prefer to follow the teaching of the divine Spirit rather than the foolish consequences of reason.

units.tr: Epistle of Dedication

units.la: Sed altitudine gratiæ & iudicij diuini obturbata ratio nihil hic intentatum relinquit, exemplo Pelagianorum veterum & recentium: quorum illos Augustinus olim, hos Lutherus, solidissime confutarunt. Viderint igitur qui Lutherani audire volunt, & contra Lutherum & veritatem ipsam, cum Pelagianis sentiunt. Sed finem facio, Deumque oro, ut sub Cels. vestra pacis, literarum & pietatis studia semper floreant. Amen. Heidelbergæ xij. Mart. Anno MDXCII.
units.tr: But reason, troubled by the height of grace and the judgment of God, leaves nothing here unattempted, following the example of the ancient and recent Pelagians; of whom the former were refuted most thoroughly by Augustine long ago, and the latter by Luther. Let them see to it, then, who wish to hear Lutherans, and who side with the Pelagians against Luther and against the truth itself. But I make an end, and I pray God that the studies of peace, of letters and of piety may always flourish under your Excellency's protection. Amen. Heidelberg, 12 March, in the year 1592.

units.la: DE REDEMTIONE HVMANI GENERIS PER CHRISTVM. Liber Primus. CAPVT I,
units.tr: ON THE REDEMPTION OF THE HUMAN RACE THROUGH CHRIST. Book One. Chapter I.

units.la: Quo summa & partitio doctrinæ huius proponitur.
units.tr: Which sets out the sum and the division of this doctrine.

units.la: MYSTERIVM redemtionis generis humani per vnigenitum Dei Filium, Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, fideliter & quàm simplicissimè Apostoli, primùm quidem viua voce, deinde verò & scriptis, Iudæis simul & gentibus, testificati sunt plenissimè; quod scilicet verbum æternum (quod æternus Dei filius lius est) vt confirmaret promissiones patrum, & vt gentes pro misericordia glorificaret Deum, postremis diebus, posteaquam temporis veniflet plenitudo, naturam vere humanam ex Maria Virgine Deipara, operatione Spiritus sancti affumferit, atque in affumta fertui forma obediens patri fuerit, vsque ad mortem, mortem autem crucis: vt preciofo suo sanguine, tanquam agni immaculati, & incoraminati nos redimeret, ab omni iniquitate, & purificaret sibi ipsi populum peculiarem, studiosum bonorum operum.
units.tr: The mystery of the redemption of the human race through the only-begotten Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, was attested most fully, faithfully and as simply as possible by the Apostles, first indeed by the living voice and afterwards also in writing, to Jews and Gentiles alike. Namely, the eternal Word (who is the eternal Son of God) in the last days, after the fullness of time had come, took up a truly human nature from the Virgin Mary, the Mother of God, by the working of the Holy Spirit. In the assumed form of a servant he was obedient to the Father even unto death, the death of the cross, so that by his precious blood, as of a spotless and undefiled Lamb, he might redeem us from all iniquity and cleanse for himself a peculiar people, zealous for good works.

units.la: Testificati quoque sunt iidem illi, vt redemtionis huius confortes euadamus, veram in Christum fidem requiri a nobis, qua ipsum, ceu manu quadam apprehendamus, nobisque cum omni suo merito atque beneficiis applicemus.
units.tr: The same Apostles also attested that, if we are to escape along with the partakers of this redemption, a true faith in Christ is required of us. By it we lay hold of him, as it were by a hand, and apply him to ourselves with all his merit and benefits.

units.la: Hæc est fides & confessio Catholica, quam Apostoli tradiderunt, Martyres roborauerunt, & fideles nunc vsque custodiunt. Sic enim D. Apostolus Paulus totum hoc mysterium paupaucis, sed luculetis verbis describens, inquit: Omnes peccauerunt, ac destituuntur gloria Dei; iustificantur autem gratis, id est, eius gratia, per redemtionem factam in Iesu Christo: quem Deus proposuit, ut esset propitiatio per fidem, in sanguine ipsius, ad declarandam iustitiam suam per remissionem peccatorum praecedentium, ut sit ipse iustus, & iustificans eum, qui est ex fide Iesu.
units.tr: This is the faith and the Catholic confession which the Apostles delivered, the Martyrs confirmed, and the faithful have kept until now. For the holy Apostle Paul, describing this whole mystery in few but clear words, says: All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God; they are justified freely, that is, by his grace, through the redemption that is in Jesus Christ, whom God set forth to be a propitiation through faith in his blood, to declare his righteousness through the remission of sins that are past, that he might be just and the justifier of him who is of the faith of Jesus.

units.la: Et autor ad Hebr. ad hunc modum scribit: Aduéniens autem Christus, pontifex futurorum bonorum, per proprium sanguinem ingressus est semel in sacrarium, aeternam redemtionem nactus. Nam si sanguis taurorum & hircorum inquinatos sanctificat ad carnis puritatem, quanto magis sanguis Christi, qui per Spiritum aeternum semetipsum obtulit inculpatum Deo, purgabit conscientiam vestram a mortuis operibus, ad seruiendum Deo viuo? Itaque ob id noui foederis mediator est, ut morte intercedente ad redemtionem earum praeuaricationum, quae fuerant sub priori Testamento, ij qui vocati sunt, promissionem accipiant aeternae hereditatis. Vbi animaduertendum est obiter, per praecedentia peccata in dicto Apostoli ad Romanos, conuenienter intelligi peccata sub Veteri Testamento commissa: quae non poterant expiari sanguine hircorum, & vitulorum, sed exspectabant iusti iis temporibus meliorem oblationem, consecraturam in perpetuum eos, qui sanctificantur. Unde & Petrus dicebat: Per gratiam Domini nostri Iesu Christi credimus nos seruatum iri, quem admodum & patres nostri.
units.tr: And the author of Hebrews writes in this manner: But Christ, coming as high priest of the good things to come, entered once for all into the sanctuary through his own blood, having obtained eternal redemption. For if the blood of bulls and goats sanctifies the defiled to the cleanness of the flesh, how much more shall the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, cleanse your conscience from dead works to serve the living God? Therefore he is the mediator of a new covenant, so that, death intervening for the redemption of the transgressions that were under the first testament, those who are called may receive the promise of the eternal inheritance. Here it should be noted in passing that by the "former sins" in the aforesaid words of the Apostle to the Romans are rightly understood the sins committed under the Old Testament. These could not be expiated by the blood of goats and calves, but the righteous of those times awaited a better sacrifice which would consecrate for ever those who are sanctified. Hence also Peter said: We believe that we shall be saved through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, just as our fathers also were.

units.la: Est vero totus hic locus de redemtione amplus, & multae considerationis: Unde nempe, per quem, quomodo, quando, qua de causa, ad quid, & quinam redemti sint. Haec sane omnia vtilem & necessariam habent considerationem, & passim in scripturis traduntur. Nos propositarum quaestionum priores breuibus perstringemus: septimam, eamque vltimam, cuius gratia potissimum labor hic a nobis suscipitur, plenius explicaturi, quantum Dominus largietur.
units.tr: This whole topic of redemption is indeed broad and deserving of much consideration: from whence, by whom, how, when, for what cause, to what end, and who have been redeemed. All these questions certainly merit a useful and necessary consideration, and they are handed down throughout the Scriptures. We shall treat the first of the proposed questions briefly, and we shall explain the seventh, which is the last and for whose sake this labour is chiefly undertaken by us, more fully, as far as the Lord shall grant.

units.tr: Heb. 1o.

units.la: CAPVT II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: Vnde namsimus redemti.
units.tr: From what we have been redeemed.

units.la: Quod igitur ad quæstionem atti- net, Vnde redemti simus; abunde nos docent sacræ literæ, redemtionem, de qua loquimur, non esse temporalem à seruitute, aut tyrannide aliqua corporali, qualis fuit redemtio Israëlis ex Ægypto, e domo seruitutis, & e manu Pharaonis per Moisen: & postea e manu Chananæorum, & Midianitarum, aliorumque inimicorum suorum per Gideonem, aliósque Iudices, & præsertim e tristissima & septuagenaria captiuitate Babylonica, per Cyrum Persarum regem, & Monarcham: sed est redemtio hæc spiritualis atque æterna, corporalibus illis liberationibus olim adumbrata: e potestate videlicet tenebrarum, & seruitute peccati & mortis, & eius, qui mortis habebat imperium, hoc est, Diaboli. Atqui hi sunt inimici & osores, quorum Zacharias, pater Baptistæ, in Cantico suo meminit hanc ipsam redemtionē celebrans:
units.tr: As to the question, from what we have been redeemed, the holy letters teach us amply that the redemption we are speaking of is not temporal, a deliverance from servitude or some bodily tyranny, such as the redemption of Israel from Egypt, out of the house of bondage and from the hand of Pharaoh through Moses; or afterwards from the hand of the Canaanites, the Midianites and their other enemies through Gideon and the other judges, and above all from the most sorrowful captivity of seventy years in Babylon, through Cyrus, king and monarch of the Persians. This redemption is spiritual and eternal, and those bodily deliverances foreshadowed it. It is a deliverance from the power of darkness, from the servitude of sin and death, and from him who held the power of death, that is, the Devil. And these are the enemies and haters of whom Zacharias, the father of the Baptist, makes mention in his canticle, celebrating this very redemption:

units.la: Benedictus, inquit, Dominus noster Deus Israel, quod inuiserit, & redemerit populum suum, & erexerit cornu salutis nobis in domo Dauid pueri sui, prout locutus est per os sanctorum prophetarum, fore vt nos seruaret ex inimicis nostris, & e manu omnium qui oderunt nos: vt sine metu, e manu inimicorum nostrorum liberati, seruiremus ipsi cum sanctitate & iustitia, in conspectu eius, cunctos dies vitæ nostræ.
units.tr: "Blessed," he says, "be the Lord our God, the God of Israel, because he has visited and redeemed his people, and has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of David his servant, as he spoke through the mouth of his holy prophets, that he would save us from our enemies and from the hand of all who hate us; so that, freed from the hand of our enemies, we might serve him without fear, in holiness and righteousness before him, all the days of our life."

units.la: Etsi vero carnalibus hominibus beneficium hoc spirituale & æternæ redemptionis sordere solet, vtpote qui nihil nisi quæ carnis sunt sapiunt, quibusque suauis adeo est peccati & mundi seruitus, prout Satan Deus seculi huius, mentes eorum excæcauit: tamen tanta magnitudo, tamque inæstimabilis eius est dignitas, vt qui redemtionem Christi, qua captiuis libertas, perditis salus, mortuis vita reparatur, reste gustarint, vel totius mundi opes, regna, voluptates, præ ea pro nihilo ducenda facile intelligant. Quid enim prodest cuiquam, si totum mundum lucretur, animæ vero suæ dispendium fa-
units.tr: Although this spiritual benefit of eternal redemption is wont to be despised by carnal men, who savour only the things of the flesh, and for whom the servitude of sin and the world is so pleasant that Satan, the god of this age, has blinded their minds, nevertheless its greatness is so great and its worth so inestimable that those who have truly tasted the redemption of Christ, by which freedom is restored to captives, salvation to the lost and life to the dead, easily understand that all the riches, kingdoms and pleasures of the whole world are to be counted as nothing in comparison with it. For what does it profit anyone, if he gains the whole world and suffers the loss of his soul? Or what will anyone give in exchange for his soul?

units.la: Luc. 1. Benedictus... (marginal reference) faciat? aut quam dabit quispiam compensationem animae suae?
units.tr: Luc. 1. Blessed... (marginal reference) ...should he do? Or what will anyone give in exchange for his soul?

units.la: CAPVT III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: Per quem redemptio hæc contigerit.
units.tr: Through whom this redemption came about.

units.la: I A M vero liberator, qui nos à seruitute peccati, & mortis ac dominatu Satanæ vindicauit, non est alius, praeterquam mediator Dei & hominum, Dominus noster Iesus Christus, verus Deus, & verus homo, nobis per omnia similis factus, demto peccato.
units.tr: Now the Liberator, who has delivered us from the slavery of sin, and from death and the dominion of Satan, is none other than the Mediator between God and men, our Lord Jesus Christ, true God and true man, made like us in all things, apart from sin.

units.la: Vnus enim Deus, inquit Apostolus, 1. Timoth. 2, Vnus etiam mediator Dei & hominum, homo Christus Iesus, qui semetipsum redemtionis dedit pretium omnibus. Et ad Romanos 3 iustificari nos docet per redemtionem factam in Christo Iesu. Alibi idem pronunciat, Christum nobis factum à Deo sapientiam, iustitiam, sanctificationem, ac redemtionem, vt sicut scriptum est, qui gloriatur, glorietur in Domino. Iohannes, qui de pectore Domini secretum biberat mysteriorum, similiter testatur, si quis peccarit, aduocatum nos habehabere apud Deum, Iesum Christum, iustum, & ipsum esse propitiationem pro peccatis nostris, nec pro nostris solum, sed etiam pro totius mundi. Sed nusquam non huiusmodi testimonia occurrunt in scripturis diuinis. Totius enim scripturæ Propheticæ,& Apostolicæ fundamentum est Iesus Christus, nec est in alio quoquam salus,nec aliud nomen sub cœlo datum est inter homines, per quod oporteat nos seruari.
units.tr: For there is one God, says the Apostle, 1 Tim. 2: there is also one Mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all. And to the Romans, chapter 3, he teaches that we are justified through the redemption made in Christ Jesus. Elsewhere the same writer declares that Christ was made for us by God wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption, so that, as it is written, "he who glories, let him glory in the Lord." John, who had drunk the secret of the mysteries from the Lord's breast, likewise testifies that if anyone sins, we have an advocate with God, Jesus Christ the righteous, and that he himself is the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only but also for the sins of the whole world. Such testimonies are found everywhere in the divine Scriptures. For Jesus Christ is the foundation of the whole prophetic and apostolic Scripture, nor is there salvation in anyone else, nor is there any other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved.

units.la: Vnde merito detestabilis est eorum error,qui vnico & perfecto redemtore Christo non contenti, partem redemtionis atque salutis alibi, apud se, vel apud sanctos,quærunt: cum tamen sanctissimi quique nisi Christi gratia iis redimedis succurrilet, ne pro semetipsis quidem satisfacere vnquam potuissent. Idcirco etiam Iohannes, vt recte Augustinus expendit,non dixit: si quis peccârit,habetis aduocatum: nec dixit, me habetis, nec ipsum Christum habetis,dixit,sed & Christum poluit,nō se, & habemus, dixit, non, habetis. Maluit se poponere in numero peccatorum, vt haberet aduocatum Christum, quàm ponere se pro Christo aduocatum, & inueniri inter damnandos superbos. Fratres, inquit, Iesum Christum iustum ipsum habemus aduocatū apud patrem: ipse propitiatio est peccatorum nostrorum. Hactenus Augustinus, tractatu primo in 1. Epist. Ioh.
units.tr: Hence the error of those is rightly detestable who, not content with the one and perfect Redeemer Christ, seek a part of redemption and salvation elsewhere, in themselves or in the saints; yet the holiest of all could never have made satisfaction even for themselves, had not the grace of Christ come to help them in that redemption. Therefore John too, as Augustine rightly observes, did not say, "If anyone sins, you have an advocate"; nor did he say "me, you have," nor did he say that you have Christ himself; he said "Christ," not himself, and he said "we have," not "you have." He preferred to put himself among the number of sinners, so as to have Christ as advocate, rather than to put himself forward as advocate in place of Christ and be found among the proud who are to be condemned. "Brethren," he says, "we have Jesus Christ the righteous himself as advocate with the Father; he himself is the propitiation for our sins." Thus far Augustine, tractate first on the First Epistle of John.

units.la: CAPVT IIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER 4.

units.la: De modo peracta redemtionis.
units.tr: On the manner in which the redemption was accomplished.

units.la: MODVM porrò nostri per Christum redemtionis, arcanum plane & admirabilem, sed diuinæ iustitiæ & veritati per omnia congruentem, assignat scriptura, videlicet, quod filius Dei æternus, propter nos & salutem nostram ipse se exinaniuerit forma serui accepta, similis hominibus factus, & habitu compertus vt homo: & submiserit sese, factus obediens víque ad mortem, mortem autem crucis, vt sua passione & morte, & sacratissimi sanguinis effusione, tanquam vnico sacrificio propitiatorio, corpus & animam mam nostram ab æterna damnatione redimeret, nobísque gratiam Dei, iustitiam ac vitam æternam acquireret.
units.tr: Scripture sets forth the manner of our redemption through Christ. It is plainly a hidden and wonderful thing, yet in every respect it agrees with divine justice and truth. The eternal Son of God, for us and for our salvation, emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, made like unto men and found in fashion as a man. He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even the death of the cross, so that by his suffering and death, and by the shedding of his most holy blood, as by one propitiatory sacrifice, he might redeem our body and soul from eternal damnation, and might obtain for us the grace of God, justification, and eternal life.

units.la: Hinc Apostolus 1.Corinth.6. Nonnestis vestri iuris, pretio emti estis, nolite fieri ser-ui hominum. Quo autem pretio? Respondet diuus Petrus, non argento vel auro, aliisue rebus caducis (quæ ad æternam redemtionem animarum, nec minimum conferunt) sed pretioso sanguine vtpote agni immaculati, nem pe Christi, qui peccatum non fecit, neç inuentus est dolus in ore ipsius: pertulit autem peccata nostra in corpore suo super lignum: & passus est iustus pro iniustis, vt nos ad Deum adduceret: mortificatus quidem carne, viuificatus autem spiritu.
units.tr: Hence the Apostle says: 1 Corinthians 6: Ye are not your own, for ye were bought with a price; do not become the servants of men. But with what price? The divine Peter answers: not with silver or gold or other perishable things, which contribute nothing, or next to nothing, to the eternal redemption of souls, but with the precious blood of a lamb without blemish, namely of Christ, who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth. He bore our sins in his own body on the tree, and suffered, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God, being put to death indeed in the flesh but made alive in the Spirit.

units.la: Quam sententiam & hæc dicta confirmant: Tradidit semetipsum pro nobis, oblationem & hostiā Deo, in odorem suauitatis. In ipso habemus redemtionem per sanguinem ipsius, remissionem inquam peccatorum ex diuite ipsius gratia. Dedit semetipsum pro nobis, vt redimeret nos ab omni pec-
units.tr: This statement is confirmed by these words also: He gave himself up for us, an offering and sacrifice to God, for a sweet-smelling savour. In him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, I say, according to the riches of his grace. He gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from every

units.la: 1.Pet.1. 1.Pet.2. 1.Pet.3. Eph.5. Eph.1. Tit.2. peccato, & purificaret sibi populum peculiarem, sectatorem honorū operarum. Item, per Spiritum æternum se- ipsum obtulit inculpatum Deo, vt purgati à mortuis operibus, seruiremus Deo viuo. Et eodem capite, Semel in cōsummatione seculorum, ad abolendum peccatum, per sui ipsius immolationem patefactus est. Multaque alia huc eodem pertinentia, accuratè ibidem disserit Apostolus: veluti quod à proprietate & natura testamenti colligit mortis Christi interuentu opus fuisse, eò quòd mors requiratur testatoris, vt testamentum ratum esse possit. Et confirmans id ipsum à ritu Veteris Testameti, subiicit, ne illud quidem absque sanguine dedicatum fuisse, & omnia fere secundum legem sanguine purificata: & exemplaria quidem eorum quæ sunt in cœlis, sanguine victimarum purificata, ipsa verò cœlestia potiorem Victimam, potiorem sanguinem desiderasse, eum videlicet, de quo Christus ipse iam iam impleturus nouum Testamentum testa-babatur, Hoc est sanguis meus noui Testamenti, qui pro multis effunditur in remissionem peccatorum. Similiter dilectus discipulus: Sanguis filij Dei, inquit, mundat nos ab omni peccato.
units.tr: 1 Pet. 1; 1 Pet. 2; 1 Pet. 3; Eph. 5; Eph. 1; Tit. 2. sin, and might purify for himself a peculiar people, zealous of good works. Likewise, through the eternal Spirit he offered himself without blemish to God, so that we, purged from dead works, might serve the living God. And in the same chapter, once, in the consummation of the ages, he was manifested to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself. The Apostle discusses many other things pertaining to this in the same place with care. For example, from the nature and character of a testament he infers that the death of Christ was necessary, since the death of the testator is required for a testament to be valid. Confirming the same point from the rite of the Old Testament, he adds that not even that was dedicated without blood, and that almost all things are purified with blood according to the law; and that the copies of heavenly things were purified with the blood of victims, but the heavenly things themselves required a better sacrifice and better blood, namely that of which Christ himself, about to fulfil the New Testament, was saying: This is my blood of the New Testament, which is shed for many for the remission of sins. Similarly the beloved disciple: The blood of the Son of God, he says, cleanses us from all sin.

units.la: Loquimur autem nunc de modo redemtionis in priori aduentu Christi peractæ. Est enim & alia quaedam, posteriore peragenda aduentu. De qua dicitur Luc.21: Attollite capita vestra, quoniam appropinquat redemtio vestra. Et de eadem loquitur Paulus ad Rom.8.23. & 1.Cor.1.30. Hæc prioris erit quasi impletio, atque consummatio. Nunc enim spe, & nondum re salui facti sumus, vt scribit Apostolus Rom.8.
units.tr: We are now speaking, however, of the manner of redemption accomplished at the first coming of Christ. For there is also another, to be accomplished at his later coming. Of this it is said in Luke 21: Lift up your heads, for your redemption draws near. Paul also speaks of the same in Romans 8:23 and 1 Corinthians 1:30. The latter will be, as it were, the fulfilment and completion of the former. For now we have been saved in hope, and not yet in reality, as the Apostle writes in Romans 8.

units.la: CAPVT V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: Solutio quarundam quaestionum circa modum redemtionis.
units.tr: Solution of certain questions concerning the manner of redemption.

units.la: VERVM enim quaeritur hoc loco, quid opus fuerit pretij persolutione à filio Dei nos redimi, qui captiui eramus Diaboli? Conuenientius enim videtur, vt, qui violenter & iniuste ab alio dedetinetur, per superiorem potentiam ei eripiatur, etiam sine pretio. Diabolus autem iniuste nos inuaserat.
units.tr: But the question is raised here: why was it necessary for us to be redeemed by the payment of a price by the Son of God, since we were captives of the Diabolus? For it seems more fitting that one who is held violently and unjustly by another should be snatched from him by a higher power, even without a price. The Diabolus, however, had unjustly invaded us.

units.la: Respondeo, precium hoc non Diabolo, sed Deo persolutum, qui ius damnationis in nos habebat, & Diaboli potestati iusto suo iudicio nos obnoxios reddiderat. Nam quatum ad Diabolum, iniuste hominem tenebat; sed homo interim iuste tenebatur, sic praevaricatione ipsius & iusto Dei iudicio postulantibus, vt Satanæ mancipare-tur. Deo itaque satisfecit, & reconciliauit nos Christus ei sese offerens per Spiritum æternum; atque ita iam nobis Deo reconciliatis, cui peccaueramus, regnum Satanæ necessario destructum fuit.
units.tr: I answer that this price was paid not to the Devil but to God, who had the right of condemnation over us and, by his just judgment, had made us liable to the power of the Devil. As far as the Devil was concerned, he held man unjustly; but man was meanwhile justly held, since his own transgression and God's just judgment required that he be handed over to Satan. Christ therefore satisfied God and reconciled us to him, offering himself through the eternal Spirit. And so, now that we were reconciled to God, against whom we had sinned, the kingdom of Satan was necessarily destroyed.

units.la: Ambrosius tamen lib. 9 epist. 77 scribit pretium liberationis nostræ sanguine Domini Iesu solutum fuisse ei, cui peccatis nostris venditi eramus, id est, Diabolo. Sed sententia ista durior est. Nam cum sacrificium offerre non licuerit, nisi soli Deo, quato magis hoc singulare sacrificium, quod æternus Pon-
units.tr: Ambrose, however, in book 9, letter 77, writes that the price of our liberation was paid with the blood of the Lord Jesus to him to whom we had been sold by our sins, that is, to the Devil. But that opinion is harsher. For if it was not lawful to offer sacrifice except to God alone, how much more was it fitting that this unique sacrifice, which the eternal

units.la: Pontifex altari crucis per immolationem sua carnis, & effusionem sui sanguinis, impolsuit, quodq; solum est propitiatio pro peccatis mundi, nemini prěterquam soli Deo offerri oportuit?
units.tr: High Priest offered on the altar of the cross by the immolation of his flesh and the effusion of his blood, and which alone is the propitiation for the sins of the world, should be offered to no one except God alone?

units.la: Quaeritur praeterea, Vndenam dignitas illa passionis, & mortis Christi existat, vt sit precium sufficiens pro redemtione generis humani?
units.tr: It is further asked: whence does that dignity of the passion and death of Christ arise, so that it is a sufficient price for the redemption of the human race?

units.la: Sut autem plures causae ad effectum illum concurrentes. I. Spontanea obedientia filij ad mortem vsque crucis. Phil.2. Satisfactoria enim non fuisset Christi passio, nisi fuisset voluntaria. Hinc Apostolus ad Rom.5. ait, sicut per inobedientiam vnius peccatores constituti sunt multi, ita per vnius obedientiam iusti constituuntur multi. Loquitur autem, vt recte exponit Theophylactus, de obedientia mortis Christi, per quam obedientiam morte contrita, ex mortis fumus erepti condemnatione. Atque hac de causa Euangelistae etiam vnanimiter passionis Christi historiam describentes, diligenter annotarunt complures circumstantias, quæ vltrò passim ostendunt. Oblatus enim est, quia ipse voluit, dicente Iesu.
units.tr: There are several causes concurring to that effect. I. The voluntary obedience of the Son unto death, even the death of the cross (Phil.2.). For Christ's passion would not have been satisfactory unless it had been voluntary. Hence the Apostle says in ad Rom.5. that as through the disobedience of one many were made sinners, so through the obedience of one many are made righteous. He speaks, as Theophylact rightly explains, of the obedience of Christ's death, by which obedience, death having been crushed, we were rescued from the condemnation of death. For this reason the Evangelists also, describing the history of the passion, unanimously and carefully noted many circumstances which everywhere show this of their own accord. For he was offered because he himself willed it, as Jesus said.

units.la: §3. II. non solùm voluntaria fuit mors, & tota humiliatio Christi, sed etiam summè innocens passus est, tanquam qui peccatum non fecit, & in cuius ore dolus inuentus non est. Talis enim decebat nos pontifex, pius, innocens, impollutus, segregatus à peccatoribus, cui non esset necesse primum pro propriis peccatis, deinde pro populi peccatis offerre. Quoniam itaque passus est iustus pro iniustis, iure preciosus ad redemptionem censetur sanguis eius, tanquam agni incontaminati, & immaculati, vt est apud Petrum 1.Epist.1.
units.tr: §3. II. Not only was the death and the whole humiliation of Christ voluntary, but he also suffered while most innocent, as one who had done no sin, and in whose mouth no guile was found. For such a high priest became us: holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, who had no need to offer first for his own sins and then for the sins of the people. Since therefore the just one suffered for the unjust, his blood is rightly reckoned precious for redemption, as the blood of a lamb unspotted and without blemish, as is said in Peter, 1 Epist. 1.

units.la: Multis hanc causam vrget Augustinus De trinitate lib.13.c.14: Qui solus, inquit liber erat à debito mortis, mortuus est. Proinde iustum est, vt debitores liberi dimittantur, credentes in eum, qui sine vllo debito occisus est. Idem cap.15: Sanguis Christi, quoniam eius erat, qui nullum habuit omnino peccatum, fusus est ad remissionem peccatorum. Et capite sequenti; peccata nostra Diabolus tenebat, & pro illis nos nos merito figebat in morte: dimisit ea ille, qui sua non habebat, & ab illo immerito per- ductus est ad mortem.
units.tr: Augustine urges this cause in many places. In De Trinitate, book 13, chapter 14, he says: He alone, who was free from the debt of death, died. Therefore it is just that debtors be set free, believing in him who was killed without any debt. The same, chapter 15: The blood of Christ, since it was his who had no sin at all, was poured out for the forgiveness of sins. And in the following chapter: The Devil held our sins, and rightly fixed us to death on account of them; he dismissed them, he who had none of his own, and was led to death by him undeservedly.

units.la: Præclarè etiam Leo Papa epist. 97: Mortis vinculum unius prævaricatione contractum, unius morte, qui solus nihil mortis debuit, solutum est. III. Quod omnium maximum est, mors Christi non fuit meri hominis, quam uis innocentis & iusti, sed fuit eius, qui simul est verus Deus, & homo in una eademque persona. Atque hæc immensa personæ huius dignitas facit ut ἀντίλυτρον hoc sanguinis, & mortis ipsius licet temporarium, si duratio spectetur, immensi tamen vigoris sit ad seruandum in perpetuum eos, qui per ipsum accedunt ad Deum.Quod docens autor ad Heb.cap.9 inquit; si sanguis taurorum & hircorum, & cinis iuuencæ aspergens inquinatos sanctificat ad carnis puritatem; quanto magis sanguis Christi, qui per Spiritum æternum seipsum obtulit inculpatum Deo, purgabit conscientiam vestram a mortuis operibus, ad seruiendum Deo viuo? Et Actorum 20
units.tr: Leo the Pope also writes admirably, letter 97: The chain of death, contracted through the transgression of one, was loosed by the death of one alone, who owed nothing to death. III. What is greatest of all: the death of Christ was not that of a mere man, however innocent and just, but of him who is at once true God and man in one and the same person. And this immense dignity of the person makes this ransom [ἀντίλυτρον] of blood and of death itself, though temporary if its duration is considered, nevertheless of immense power to preserve forever those who through him come to God. The author of Hebrews teaches this in chapter 9, saying: if the blood of bulls and goats, and the ashes of a heifer sprinkled on the unclean, sanctify them to the purity of the flesh, how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, purge your conscience from dead works, to serve the living God? And in Acts 20

units.la: Paulus testis est, Deum proprio fan-guine Ecclesiam suam redemisse: non quòd Deitas carnem aut sanguinem habeat (quippe Deus Spiritus est) sed persona ista, quæ morte pro nobis oppetiit, simul Deus & homo est; atque itasanguis hic vere dicitur atq; est sanguis Dei: cuius proinde summa præstantia atque dignitas est.
units.tr: Paul is a witness that God redeemed his Church with his own blood: not that the Godhead has flesh or blood (for God is Spirit), but that person who faced death for us is at once God and man; and so this blood is truly called, and is, the blood of God, and its surpassing excellence and dignity is therefore supreme.

units.la: His accedit, quòd præter virtutem diuinam, & abundè sufficientem ad liberandum, communis noster Redemtor etiam ius redemtionis plenum atque perfectum habuit; cùm, quia vniuersorum Dominus est, tum quia sanguine nobis propinquus. Nam iure dominij cōueniens est, a Domino seruum, à principe subditum redimi. Iure autem propinquitatis rectè redimit pater filium, frater fratrem, cognatus cognatum. Atque huc referre licet, quod Leu.25.vers.25. speciatim de iure propinquitatis cautum legimus.
units.tr: To this is added that, besides the divine power, which is abundantly sufficient for liberating, our common Redeemer also had the full and perfect right of redemption, both because he is the Lord of all and because he is near to us by blood. For by right of lordship it is fitting that a slave be redeemed by his master, and a subject by his prince. By right of kinship, a father redeems a son, a brother a brother, a kinsman a kinsman. To this we may refer what we read in Lev. 25:25, where the right of kinship is specifically provided for.

units.la: Quæsitum & illud fuit, quod ad modum redemtionis attinet, an non alio modo possibilis fuerit liberatio nostri B quàm qu am per mortem filij Dei?
units.tr: It was also asked, concerning the manner of redemption, whether our liberation could have been possible in some other way than through the death of the Son of God.

units.la: Respondemus cū Augustino, lib.13.de Trinit. alium modum possibilem Deo non defuisse, cuius potestati cūcta subiacent: sed fanandę nostræ miseriæ modum hunc couenientissimum, & congruum plane Deo fuisse: Seu, vt Thomas parte 3. q. 46. quæstionem hanc decidit, distinguimus inter possibile vel impossibile simpliciter, & ex hypothesi. Simpliciter & absolute loquendo possibile fuit Deo alio modo liberare homine quàm per mortem Christi, quia non est impossibile apud Deum vllum verbum, vt dicitur Luc. 1. Sed ex hypothesi suppositione, prætscientiæ vi-delicet & prædordinationis diuinæ, fuit impossibile; quemadmodum Domini verba aperte indicant Matth. 26. Pater si non potest hic calix transfire, nisi bibam eum, fiat voluntas tua. Vnde & Hilarius dicit, Ideo transfire calix non poterat, nisi illú bibat: quia reparari nisi ex eius passione non possumus; ob dis-positionem nempe voluntatis diuinæ. Cæterùm Deo inprimis congruum, & nostræ sanandæ miseriæ conuenientisfimum modum fuisse eum, quo Deus vsus est per passionem filij fui, perfpi- cuum est. Iustum enim erat, vt pro pec catis generis humani per poena iudicio Dei fatisfieret, atque eade natura, quae peccarat, etiam pro peccato depende- ret. Veritati etiam & bonitati diuinae confentaneu id erat. Veritati quidem, quia comminatio praecesserat. Quo- cunque die comederis de ligno scientia boni & mali morte morieris: promissumque erat, & continuis semper teftificationibus annunciatum, variisque ceremoniis adumbratum, fore vt filius Dei, natus de muliere mortem pro nobis obiret, atque ita nouum Testamentum fan- guine suo sanciret. Bonitati vero, quia cum homo per fe satisfacere non pof- set pro peccatis, Deus ex immensa mi- fericordia fatisfactorem ei dedit, filium suum vnigenitum. Vnde a Christo ipso dictum est Ioh.3. Sic Deus dilexit mun- dum, vt filium suum dederit. Et Paulo testante, commendat Deus suam erga nos caritatem, quod cum adhuc esse- mus peccatores, Christus pro nobis mor-
units.tr: We answer with Augustine, De Trinitate, book 13, that no other possible way was lacking to God, to whose power all things are subject; but this way was most fitting and altogether suitable to God for healing our misery. Or, as Thomas decides this question in part 3, q. 46, we distinguish between the possible or impossible simply, and the possible or impossible from hypothesis. Speaking simply and absolutely, it was possible for God to free man in another way than by the death of Christ, since no word is impossible with God, as is said in Luke 1. But by hypothetical supposition, namely of divine foreknowledge and predestination, it was impossible; as the Lord's words in Matt. 26 clearly indicate: Father, if this cup cannot pass away unless I drink it, let your will be done. Hence Hilary also says: the cup could not pass away unless he drank it, because we could not be restored except through his passion, on account of the disposition of the divine will. Moreover, that the manner in which God used the passion of his Son was, above all, suitable to God and most convenient for healing our misery, is plain. For it was just that satisfaction for the sins of the human race should be made through the punishment of God's judgment, and that the same nature which had sinned should also pay for the sin. This was also consonant with the truth and goodness of God. With truth, indeed, because the threat had gone before: On whatever day you eat of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, you will die the death; and it had been promised, continually announced by repeated testimonies and foreshadowed by various ceremonies, that the Son of God, born of a woman, would die for us, and so ratify the new Testament with his blood. With goodness, because since man could not satisfy for sins by himself, God out of immense mercy gave him a satisfier, his only-begotten Son. Hence Christ himself said in John 3: So God loved the world that he gave his Son. And, as Paul testifies, God commends his love toward us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.

units.la: Ifa 53. Luc. 24. Heb. 9. Ioh. 3. Ioh. 1. Rom. 5. mortuus fit. Et sane longe abundantioris misericordiæ hoc fuit, quod filio proprio nō pepercerit pro nobis, quàm si peccata abíque satisfactione remi-sisset; vt nunc merito dicamus cum eodem ad Eph.2: Deus qui diues est miseri-cordia, propter multam caritatem suam, qua dilexit nos, etiam cum per offensas mortui es-semus, vna viuificauit nos per Christum, cu-ius gratia sumus seruati.
units.tr: Isa. 53. Luke 24. Heb. 9. John 3. John 1. Rom. 5. He died. Indeed this was a far more abundant mercy, that he did not spare his own Son for us, than if he had forgiven sins without satisfaction; so that we may rightly say with the same apostle in Eph. 2: God, who is rich in mercy, because of his great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead through our offences, made us alive together in Christ, by whose grace we have been saved.

units.la: Noftrę etiam saluti expedientissima fuit ea ipsa liberationis ratio. Sic enim experimento omnium maximo cognoscimus, quantum Deus nos diligat, & prouocamur ad Deum vicissim diligendum. Deinde exemplum nobis datum est obedientiæ, caritatis, humilitatis, passionum, & gloriæ, quam superatis passionibus exspectamus; quemadmodum apud Petrum 1. Epist. 2. Christus pro nobis passus dicitur, & reliquisse nobis exemplar, vt sequamur vestigia eius. Similiter Paulus Philip. 2. f. & 2. Cor. 5. g. & alibi, propósito Christi exemplo hortatur ad dilectionis & aliarum virtutum officia. Adhæc quod morte filij Dei
units.tr: This manner of deliverance was also most expedient for our salvation. For by the greatest of all proofs we know how much God loves us, and we are stirred to love God in return. Next, an example has been given us of obedience, love, humility, suffering, and of the glory which we look for after the sufferings are overcome; just as in 1 Peter 2 Christ is said to have suffered for us and to have left us an example, that we should follow in his steps. Likewise Paul, in Phil. 2 and 2 Cor. 5, and elsewhere, holds up the example of Christ to urge us to the duties of love and of the other virtues. Moreover, since we have been redeemed by the death of the Son of God

units.la: Rom. 8. Dei iumus redemti, & sanguine eius mundati à peccatis, maior nobis incumbit necessitas, vt immaculatos, corpore & Spiritu Deo nos seruemus, quemadmodum ait Apostolus: Precio emti estis; glorificate igitur Deum in corpore vestro, & spiritu vestro, quæ sunt Dei.
units.tr: Rom. 8. ...and cleansed from our sins by his blood, a greater necessity lies upon us to keep ourselves unspotted, in body and spirit, for God, as the Apostle says: You were bought with a price; therefore glorify God in your body and in your spirit, which are God's.

units.la: Atque hæc de modo redemtionis prorsus mirabili & ineffabilis mysterij, quem autor Meditat. apud Augustinum capite 7. pulcre celebrat his verbis: O mirabilis censura conditio, & ineffabilis mysterij dispositio. Peccat iniquus, & punitur iustus: delinquit reus, & vapulat innocens: offendit impius, & damnatur pius, quod meretur malus, patitur bonus; quod perpetrat seruus, exsoluit Dominus; quod committit homo, sustinet Deus. Hæc cœlestis medicina est, bone Iesu, hoc tui antidotum amoris.
units.tr: So much concerning the manner of redemption, altogether wonderful and of an unspeakable mystery, which the author of the Meditations, in chapter 7, cited under Augustine's name, celebrates finely in these words: O wonderful condition of judgment, and unspeakable arrangement of the mystery! The unrighteous sins, and the just is punished; the guilty offends, and the innocent is scourged; the impious offends, and the pious is condemned; what the wicked deserves, the good suffers; what the servant does, the Lord pays; what man commits, God endures. This is the heavenly medicine, good Jesus, this is your antidote of love.

units.la: CAPVT VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: Visus superioris doctrinæ ad errorum quorundam redargutionem.
units.tr: The sense of the preceding doctrine, for the refutation of certain errors.

units.la: REFELLVNTVR exposita iam doctrina trina ij, qui in Christo negarunt humanæ substantiæ veritatem: vt Eutyches, Apollinaris, Manichæus, Marcio, & alij olim hæretici, & hodie Anabaptistarum quidam per impios veterum hæreticorum volutati errores. Hos Leo Papa vrgens inquit; Dicant, quo sacrificio reconciliati, dicant, quo sanguine ne sint redemti: quis est, qui tradidit semetipsum oblationem Deo & hostiam in odorem suauitatis?
units.tr: The doctrine now set out is also used to refute those who denied the truth of human substance in Christ: such as Eutyches, Apollinaris, Manichaeus, Marcion, and other heretics of old, and some of the Anabaptists today, who wallow in the impious errors of the ancient heretics. Pope Leo, pressing these men, says: Let them say by what sacrifice they have been reconciled, let them say by what blood they have been redeemed; who is it that gave himself up as an offering to God and a sacrifice of sweet odour?

units.la: Refelluntur etiam hac eadem doctrina Pontificij, qui sanctorum pressu-ras passionibus Christi adiungūt, fictium thesaurum suum indulgetiarum promiscue inde confiantes: nec pudet istos superabundantiam meritorum & satisfactionum humanarum iactare, sanctos plus passos quam pro peccatis suis pati debuerunt; & errorem errore cumulantes, fingunt superabundatiam iam non ad vivos solum, verum etiam ad mortuos in purgatorio pertinere.
units.tr: The same doctrine also refutes the Papists, who attach the sufferings of the saints to the passion of Christ, and from these they promiscuously compound their fictitious treasury of indulgences. They are not ashamed to boast of an excess of human merits and satisfactions, claiming that the saints suffered more than they were bound to suffer for their own sins. Heaping error upon error, they imagine that this surplus pertains not only to the living but also to the dead in purgatory.

units.la: Merum hoc est Satanæ ludibrium & sanguinis Christi profanatio, vt præclare Leo Papa epistolis memoratis aduersus horum temporum Papistas oftenoftedit:cuius hæc totidem verba sunt: Quamuis, inquit, multorum sanctorum in conspectu Domini preciosa mors fuerit, nullius tamen insontis occisio propitiatio fuit mundi. Accepere iusti, non dedere coronas: & de fortitudine fidelium, exempla nata sunt patientiæ, non dona iustitiæ. Singulares quippe in singulis mortes fuere, nec alterius debitum quisquam suo fine persoluit, cum inter filios hominum unus solus Dominus noster Iesus Christus exstiterit, in quo omnes crucifixi, omnes mortui, omnes sepulti, omnes etiam sunt suscitati. Atque id ipsum ante Leonem Gaius Papa, natione Dalmata, qui sedit circa annum 284 scripsit elegantissima ad Felice Episcopum: quorum veterum pontificum doctrinam, utinam Romanensis Ecclesia inuiolatam custodiuisset.
units.tr: This is sheer mockery by Satan and a profanation of the blood of Christ, as Pope Leo admirably showed in the letters already mentioned, against the Papists of our own times. His words are these: "Although the death of many saints has been precious in the sight of the Lord, yet the slaying of no innocent man has been the propitiation of the world. The righteous have received crowns; they have not given them. From the courage of the faithful have arisen examples of patience, not gifts of righteousness. For deaths have been singular in each case, and none has paid the debt of another by his end, since among the sons of men there has been one only Lord Jesus Christ, in whom all were crucified, all dead, all buried, and all also raised." Before Leo, Pope Gaius, a Dalmatian by birth, who held the see about the year 284, wrote most elegantly to Bishop Felix the same thing. Would that the Roman Church had kept the teaching of these ancient pontiffs inviolate.

units.la: In eandem sententiam Augustinus scribit tractatu 84 in Iohan. Et si fratres pro fratribus morimur, nullius tamen sanguis martyris in peccatorum remissionem funditur: quod fecit Christus pro nobis, neque in hoc quod imitaremur, sed quod gratularemur, contulit nobis.
units.tr: Augustine writes to the same effect in tractate 84 on John: "Even if brothers die for brothers, the blood of no martyr is poured out for the remission of sins. What Christ did for us, he bestowed on us not so that we might imitate it, but so that we might rejoice in it."

units.la: Obiiciunt indulgentiarij nugatores, aut verius impostores & sacrilegi, verba Apostoli ad Coloff. Gaudeo in iis, quae patior pro vobis, & reliquias afflictionum Christi vicissim expleo in carne mea, pro corpore ipsius, id est Ecclesia. Sed genuinum eius loci sensum vel ab Aquinate suo didicisse debebant, qui parte 3. Summa, quaestione 48. articulo penult. dispu-tas solum Christum esse redemptionem nostram, locum istum obiicit, & sic exponit: Passiones sanctorum, inquit, proficiunt Ecclesiae, non quidem per modum redemtionis, sed per modum exempli & exhortationis, secundum illud 2. Cor. 1. Sive tribulamur, pro vestra exhortatione & salute id fit. Recte omnino, nisi quod Graece ibi ὑπὲρ τῆς ὑμῶν παρακλήσεως: quod eo loci rectius consolationem, quam exhortationem verteris. Quod autem afflictiones sanctorum vocantur ἀντιπλήρωματα, reliquia afflictionum Christi, non significat imperfectam eius fuisse passionem (absit tata blasphemia) sed ideo id dictum est, quia Christus quotidie adhuc in suis membris patitur, sed fine & modo valde diuerso. Verum qua sunt improbitate, non pudet istos superabundantiam, ut dixi, meritorum, & satisfactionum humanarum venditare, quae viuos & mortuos adeo redundet. Quid vero? An non diserte scriptura testatum voluit, ea quae praesenti tempore perpetimur, minime esse paria gloriae in filiis Dei retegendae? Quid, quod frustra rem redimendo non redimit quisquam, nec dabit Deo precium redemtionis eius? Nam preciosa est redemtio animae, vt canit Psaltes. In quem locum Basilius in scholiis notat, ne mundum quidem vniuersum precium essanimae. Et tom.1. in eundem Psalmum, Ne in vniuersum quidem, inquit, homo ergo Deum pro peccatore propitiationem offerre facultatem habet, quod & ipse peccati reus sit. Omnes enim peccauerunt, & destituuntur gloria Dei; iustificantur autem gratis per redemtionem quae est in Christo Iesu. Non ergo Deo quis dabit placationem suam & precium animae suae: neque fratrem redemtionem quaerit, sed aliquem, qui nostram superet naturam, nempe non hominem tantum, sed hominem Deum Iesum Christum, qui solus pro nobis omnibus Deo propitiationem se dare potest. Hæc ille.
units.tr: The indulgence-mongers, or rather impostors and sacrilegious men, object the words of the Apostle to the Colossians: "I rejoice in my sufferings for you, and in my flesh I fill up what is lacking of the afflictions of Christ, for his body, which is the Church." But they ought to have learned the true sense of that passage at least from their Aquinas, who, in Summa 3, question 48, penultimate article, disputes that Christ alone is our redemption, cites this passage as an objection, and explains it thus: "The sufferings of the saints, he says, profit the Church, not by way of redemption, but by way of example and exhortation, according to that passage of 2 Corinthians 1: Whether we are afflicted, it is for your exhortation and salvation." Quite right, except that there the Greek reads ὑπὲρ τῆς ὑμῶν παρακλήσεως [for your consolation], which you translate more correctly there as consolation rather than exhortation. But that the afflictions of the saints are called ἀντιπλήρωματα [fillings-up], the remnants of Christ's afflictions, does not mean that his passion was incomplete (far be such blasphemy). It was said because Christ still suffers daily in his members, though in a very different end and manner. But with what shamelessness, as I said, they are not ashamed to peddle an excess of merits and human satisfactions, which overflows so much for the living and the dead! What then? Has not Scripture plainly testified that the things we now suffer are not at all comparable to the glory to be revealed in the sons of God? And what of this: that no one redeems a thing by redeeming it in vain, nor will he give God the price of his redemption? For the redemption of the soul is precious, as the Psalmist sings. On this verse Basil notes in his scholia that not even the whole world is the price of a soul. And in his first volume on the same Psalm, he says: "Not even at all, he says. Man therefore has no power to offer God propitiation for a sinner, since he himself is also guilty of sin. For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God; but they are justified freely through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus. Therefore no one will give God his own placation and the price of his soul; nor does he seek a brother as redemption, but one who surpasses our nature, namely not merely a man, but the God-man Jesus Christ, who alone can give himself to God as propitiation for us all." So he.

units.la: In ipso igitur cunctis sperandum est vnice, qui solus est Mediator Dei & hominum, Redemtio, propitiatio, & salus omnium. Ipsi dicat cor nostrum, Diligam te Domine fortitudo mea, petra mea, arx mea, liberator meus, scutum meum, & cornu salutis meæ. Sperabo in te, & non pudebiam in æternum. Habentes, inquit Apostolus ad Heb. Pontificem misericordem, & fidelem in iis quæ apud Deum agenda sunt, ad expiandum peccata populi, Iesum filium Dei, accedamus cum fiducia ad throinum gratiæ, vt consequamur misericordiam. Accedamus vero corde & certa persuasione fidei, vtpote habentes libertatem ingrediendi Sacrarium per sanguinem Iesu, ea via quam dedicauit nobis recentem & viuam, per velum, hoc est, per carnem suam. Non est, non est, inquam, quod hæsitemus peripsum accedere ad Deum. Si gra- uia deliquimus, magnum medicum in- uenimus, magnam medicinam gratiæ eius accipimus. Neque id tantum, ve- rum cõfidimus quoque, quod qui pro-prio filio non pepercit, sed dedit eum pro nobis omnibus, etiam cum ipso omnia nobis gratificabitur.
units.tr: Therefore in him alone, who alone is the Mediator between God and men, must all hope be placed: the redemption, the propitiation and the salvation of all. Let our heart say to him: "I will love you, O Lord, my strength, my rock, my fortress, my deliverer, my shield, and the horn of my salvation. I will hope in you, and I shall never be put to shame." Says the Apostle to the Hebrews: "Since we have a merciful and faithful high priest in the things that pertain to God, to make expiation for the sins of the people, Jesus the Son of God, let us draw near with confidence to the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy. Let us draw near indeed with a true heart and in the assurance of faith, having freedom to enter the sanctuary by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way which he has opened for us through the veil, that is, through his flesh. There is no reason, I say, there is no reason for us to hesitate to approach God through him. If we have sinned against grace, we have found a great physician and receive the great remedy of his grace. Nor is this all; we are also confident that he who did not spare his own Son, but gave him up for us all, will with him also grant us all things graciously."

units.la: CAPVT VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.

units.la: De tempore parta Redemtionis.
units.tr: On the time at which redemption was obtained.

units.la: SEQVITVR, vt de tempore quo-que disp̄iciamus acquisitæ nobis per Christum redemtionis. Est autem no-tissimum ex historia Euangelica, Do-minum, & redemtorem nostrum Ie-sum Christum Regem, & Pontificem æternũ in mundum venisse, factum ex semine Dauid secundum carnem, re-gnante Octauio Augusto, anno impe-rij eius XLII. qui mundi fuit, vt Func-cius supputat, ter millesimus nongen-tesimus sexagesimus tertius. Non me latet tamen alios ab ista supputatione discordare, quibusdam veterum lati-norum & Græcorum, ad quintum vsq; milmillenarium adscendentibus, sed manifesto errore calculi, orto ex discrepantia inter codices Hebraeos & 70. interpretum apud Graecos. Sed ut pergam in instituto, a tempore aduentus, & apparitionis suae in carne, iram Dei aduersus peccatum vniuersi generis humani corpore & anima Dominus sustinuit in tota sua vita; praecipue vero in eius extremo, cum peccata nostra pertulit in corpore super lignum, & mortis contra nos chirographum cruci affixum e medio sustulit. Id factum traditur anno incarnationis Christi xxxiv. Tiberij autem Caesaris xviii. Epiphanius tamen contra Alogos haereses 51. omnes annos praesentiae Christi in carne a natiuitate ad passionem, quam factam scribit die ante decimum tertium Calendas Aprilis, vult tantum fuisse annorum triginta duorum & dierum septuaginta quatuor, vno anno a praecedenti sententia discrepans. Ac diligenter idem refutat peruersam aliorum suppurationem, qui finiftre intelligentes propheticum illud Isai. 61: Ut praprædicem annum Domini acceptum, arbitrabantur Dominum peracto duntaxat vnius anni ministerio posse percep-tum à Iohane Baptisma, mortem per-pessum, anno ætatis trigesimo iâ com-pleto. In qua sententia fuit Seuerus Sulpitius, qui annotat Dominum cru-cifixum duobus Geminis, Fusio & Re-bellio Coss. Incidit autem horum con-sulatus in annum Christi tricesimum primum, teste Epiphanio.
units.tr: Next we must also consider the time of the redemption acquired for us through Christ. It is very well known from the Gospel history that our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, the eternal King and High Priest, came into the world, made from the seed of David according to the flesh, in the forty-second year of the reign of Octavian Augustus. By Funccius's reckoning, this was the year 3963 of the world. I am not unaware that others disagree with this calculation, since some of the older Latin and Greek writers put it as late as the five-thousandth year. But that is a plain error of computation, arising from the disagreement between the Hebrew manuscripts and the Seventy interpreters among the Greeks. To return to my purpose: from the time of his coming and appearing in the flesh, the Lord bore God's wrath against the sin of the whole human race in body and soul throughout his whole life, but especially at its end, when he bore our sins in his body upon the wood and, nailing to the cross the handwriting that stood against us, took it out of the way. This is said to have happened in the thirty-fourth year of Christ's incarnation, the eighteenth of Tiberius Caesar. Epiphanius, however, in his book against the Alogi heresy (51), holds that all the years of Christ's presence in the flesh, from his birth to his passion, which he writes took place on the day before the thirteenth of the Kalends of April, amounted to thirty-two years and seventy-four days. In this he differs from the previous opinion by one year. The same writer carefully refutes the mistaken calculation of others who, misunderstanding that prophecy of Isaiah 61, "to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord," supposed that the Lord had received baptism from John and suffered death, in the thirtieth year of his age, after a ministry of only one year. Severus Sulpitius held this opinion. He notes that the Lord was crucified in the consulship of the two Gemini, Fusius and Rebellius. Epiphanius says that this consulship fell in the thirty-first year of Christ.

units.la: Verum vt ista nunc non excutiamus scrupulosius, ne quis miretur, quod Christus tot iam elapsis annorum mil-libus sub Tiberio demum, quasi sub mundi vesperam, &, vt scriptura loqui-tur, in consummatione seculorum, ad abolendum peccatum per immolatio-nem sui patefactus sit; cogitandum est id minimè casu aut fortuito ita euenis-se, sed æterno consilio atque prouiden-tia Dei: quæ, vt ait Sapiens, ab extremo ad extremum pertingit fortiter, & om-nia disponit suauiter; omniaq; in nu-mero, pondere, & mensura temperat. Hinc Petrus 1. Epist. cap. 2, ait, agnum il-lum
units.tr: But, so that we do not examine these matters too closely, let no one be surprised that Christ was revealed only under Tiberius, after so many thousands of years had passed, as it were towards the evening of the world, and, as Scripture says, "in the consummation of the ages," to abolish sin by the sacrifice of himself. We must reflect that this happened by no chance or accident, but by the eternal counsel and providence of God. As the Wise Man says, this providence reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly, and it arranges all things in number, weight, and measure. Hence Peter, in 1 Peter 2, says that that Lamb, by whose precious blood we have been redeemed, was indeed revealed in the last times for our sake, but was foreordained before the foundation of the world. [Heb.* — Sap. 8. &c.] And, as Paul bears witness in Galatians 4, God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, when the fullness of time had come. The passage means the time of the Son's incarnation, and of our redemption through him, which the heavenly Father had appointed beforehand. The comparison used in that place shows this. For Paul had said that the heir, as a child, is under guardians until the time the father has appointed. Likewise in Ephesians 1 he speaks of the fullness of the times for the restoration of all things through Christ.

units.la: Heb.* — Sap. 8. &c. lum, cuius precio so sanguine redemti fumus, patefactu quidem vltimis temporibus propter nos, praeordinatum vero ante iacta mundi fundamenta. Et Paulo teste ad Galat.4. emisit Deus filium suu factum ex muliere, postquam temporis venisset plenitudo. Significat autem tempus incarnationis filij,& nostrae per eu redemtionis a patre coelesti praefinitum : quod similitudo eo loci adhibita ostendit. Dixerat enim haeredem infantem sub curatoribus esse, vsque ad tempus quod pater praefinierit. Sic ad Eph.1. meminit plenitudinis temporum, ad instaurationem omnium per Christum.
units.tr: And so that we may understand more certainly that this time of the restoration of all things was appointed by God from eternity, the same was not obscurely foretold by divine instruction through the mouths of the holy prophets. As Peter reminds us, they prophesied of the grace that would come to us, searching into what time or what kind of time that Spirit of Christ, which was in them, was indicating, when it testified beforehand the sufferings of Christ and the glory that would follow.

units.la: Atque vt certius intelligamus, diuinitus tempus hoc instaurationis omnium ab aeterno praefinitum fuisse, non obscure id ipsum instructu diuino praenunciatum fuit per os sanctorum Prophetarum, qui, vt Petrus admonet, veruam in nos gratiam praedixerunt, scrutantes, in quê, aut cuiusmodi temporis articulum praenuncius ille, qui in ipsis erat, Spiritus Christi, declararet euen-
units.tr: 1 Peter 1. It was revealed to them that they were ministering these things not to themselves but to us. We have examples in the prophecy of Jacob, Genesis 49, and in the seventy weeks in Daniel 9. And throughout, when the prophets prophesy about the kingdom of Christ, they mention the latter days.

units.la: 1.Pet.1. euenturas Christo passiones, & sequu-turam gloriam. Quibus patefactum est, eos non sibi, sed nobis ea administrare. Exempla habemus in vaticinio Iacobi: Genes. 49. & de LXX. hebdomadibus apud Danielem cap. 9. Et passim Prophetæ, cum de regno Christi vaticinantur, nouissimorum dierum meminerunt.
units.tr: 1 Pet. 1. that the sufferings of Christ and the glory that would follow were to come. It was revealed to them that they were ministering these things not to themselves but to us. We have examples in Jacob's prophecy, Gen. 49, and in the seventy weeks in Daniel ch. 9. Throughout, when the Prophets speak of the kingdom of Christ, they mention the last days.

units.la: Sed enim quærat aliquis cur sene-scenti demum, & iam occideti mundo Deus filium suum miserit redemtorem, & non potius post lapsum ilico generis humani? Etsi vero nostrum non est curiosius in consilium Dei inquirere: & curiosis ingenuis respondere sufficit, quod Christus discipulis respondebat, Vestrum non est nosse tempus, seu opportunitates, quas pater in sua ipsius autoritate posuit: rationes tamen non contemnendæ à doctis afferuntur, dilatæ tam diu redemtionis, seu missionis filij.
units.tr: But someone may ask why God sent his Son as Redeemer only when the world was now growing old and already declining, and not immediately after the fall of the human race. Yet it is not for us to inquire too curiously into the counsel of God, and it is enough to answer curious people as Christ answered his disciples: "It is not for you to know the times or seasons, which the Father has placed under his own authority." Still, learned writers offer reasons, not to be despised, for why the redemption, or the sending of the Son, was deferred for so long.

units.la: I. Vtile erat non vnius tantùm sensus, sed multorum exemplis magis magisque sentiri, & patefieri magnitudinem dinem morbi & corruptionis humanæ.Propterea reliquit Deus hominem prius in statu naturæ: vt vires seu infirmitatem potius naturæ suæ cognosceret, vbi cum deficeret, legem accepit, qua data inualuit morbus, non legis, sed naturæ vitio;vt ita cognita sua infirmitate ad medicum clamaret, & gratiæ quæreret auxilium.
units.tr: I. It was useful that the greatness of the disease and corruption of humankind should be felt and made plain, not by the experience of one or two, but more and more by the examples of many. Therefore God first left man in the state of nature, so that he might come to know the strength, or rather the weakness, of his nature. When nature failed, he received the law. Through the law the disease grew worse, not because of any fault in the law, but because of the fault of nature. Thus, having recognized his weakness, he would cry out to the physician and seek the help of grace.

units.la: II. Lex & Prophetæ,figuræ atque vmbræ legales, & promissiones veteri, Christi,suü quoq; cursum habere debebant: & quanto maior iudex seu dominus veniebat, tanto præconum series longior præcedere debebat, vt dicit glossa in illud Galat. 4. vbi venit temporis plenitudo.
units.tr: II. The Law and the Prophets, the legal figures and shadows, and the promises to the old covenant also had to run their course, as did Christ's. And as a greater judge or lord was coming, a longer series of heralds had to go before him, as the gloss says on that passage of Galatians 4: when the fullness of time came.

units.la: III. Ordinis est,vt prius sit imperfectum, prius quod animale est, deinde quod spirituale est, 1.Cor. 15. Ergo status naturæ, & legis,tanquam imperfectiores,rectè præcessisse statum gratiæ, & iusto quidem interuallo.
units.tr: III. It is the order of things that the imperfect comes first, that which is natural comes before that which is spiritual (1 Cor. 15). Therefore the state of nature and the state of the law, as more imperfect, rightly preceded the state of grace, and with a fitting interval.

units.la: IV. Ea ratione exercebantur pij in fide,& expectatione futuræ redemptionis, quam eminus conspicati cum essent, per fidem mortui sunt, non adepti promissa: quatenus nempe exhibitio Messiae in ipsorum tempora non incidebat. Hinc fidem & tolerantiam eorum autor ad Hebraeos praeclaris encomiis ornat, nobisque ad imitationem proponit. Heb.11.&7.v.12.
units.tr: IV. In this way the godly were exercised in faith and in expectation of the future redemption. Having seen it from afar, they died in faith without having received the promises, namely because the manifestation of the Messiah did not fall within their times. Hence the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews adorns their faith and endurance with notable praises and sets them before us for imitation. Heb. 11 and 7 v. 12.

units.la: Augustinus contra Porphyrium disputans de tempore religionis Christianae, lib. de sex paganorum quaestionibus, scripsit, Christum tum venisse, cum sciret homines credituros. Sed inimici gratiae dictum hoc torquentes, occasionem Augustino dederunt, partim interpretatione, partim retractatione id corrigendi.
units.tr: Augustine, disputing against Porphyry about the time of the Christian religion, wrote in his book on the six questions of the pagans that Christ came at the time when he knew that men would believe. But enemies of grace twisted this statement, and gave Augustine occasion to correct it, partly by interpretation and partly by retraction.

units.la: CAPVT VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: Agitatur quaestio de redemtione veterum: & duplex circa eam opinio refellitur.
units.tr: The question of the redemption of the ancients is discussed, and two opinions about it are refuted.

units.la: HINC vero altera quaedam quaestio emergit de patribus, qui ante Christum natum ex hac vita excesserunt, ecquid redemtio ad eos quoque pertinuerit?
units.tr: From this arises another question, about the fathers who departed this life before Christ was born: whether redemption also pertained to them.

units.la: C Ne-
units.tr: C Ne-

units.la: Negarunt olim Marcionitæ, & eorum similes Manichæi: qui contendebant, neminem ferè ruantum ante decimum quintum annum Tiberij, vt refert Epiphanius. Quos imitati sunt impurissimus ille Seruetus, & alij nonnulli ex sectâ Anabaptistarum, qui Israelitieum populum, non aliter ac gregem aliquem porcorum in terra Canaan saginatu à Domino nugantur, citra ipsam vllam cœlestis immortalitatis. Sed prodigiosus iste error multis è Scriptura facilè refellitur: ex quibus nos pauca dutaxat delibabimus.
