Certè autor ad Heb. longam texit seriem priscorum, qui Deo placuerunt ante Christum mudo exhibitu, & eius, quæ ex fide est, iustitiæ, facti sunt hæredes. Quid forma illa fœderis, Ero Deus tuus & semini tui? Et quod dictu fuit, Ego sum Deus Abraham, Deus Isaac, Deus Iacob? Nonne ostendunt gratiæ eos fuisse participes, cuius unicum fundamentum est Christus? Quò etiā spectat insignis Domini sententia Iohan. 8: Abraham desiderauit videre diem meum, & vidit illum, ac gauisus est.
units.tr: Marcionites long ago denied this, and their like the Manichaeans, who contended that almost no one was saved before the fifteenth year of Tiberius, as Epiphanius reports. The most impure Servetus imitated them, and some others from the sect of the Anabaptists, who babble that the Israelite people were fattened by the Lord like a herd of pigs in the land of Canaan, with no hope of heavenly immortality at all. But this monstrous error is easily refuted from Scripture in many places, of which we will touch on only a few. Certainly the author of Hebrews wove a long series of the ancients who pleased God before Christ was revealed in the flesh, and who became heirs of the righteousness that is by faith. What of that formula of the covenant, I will be your God and the God of your seed? And what was said, I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob? Do they not show that they were partakers of grace, whose sole foundation is Christ? To this also pertains the notable saying of the Lord, John 8: Abraham desired to see my day, and he saw it and rejoiced.

units.la: Nec aliud in Euangelio regnum nobis promittitur, quàm in quo recumbamus cum Abraham,Isaac, & Iacob, & omnibus ab Oriente & Occidente venientibus,electis Dei.
units.tr: Nor does the Gospel promise us any other kingdom than one in which we recline with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and with all the elect of God who come from east and west.

units.la: At patres illi mortui sunt ante adventum Christi in carnem. Quid tum? Promissionem interim habebant venturi Christi, spei & fiduciæ suæ fundamentum: nec vis mortis Christi ad nostratantùm, verùm etiam ad patrum tempora, iam inde ab origine mundi, se extendit. Nam Iesus Christus heri & hodie & in secula, ait Apostolus Heb.13. Sentit Christum non tantùm exstitisse præteritis temporibus, quod ad diuinitatem, sicut alibi ab ipso dictum est, antequam Abraham esset, ego sum: sed qua lis nunc sit, talem olim fuisse & nunc permanere & permansurum in secula, ad suos clementer seruandos, protegendósque. Quo sensu etiam locus Apoc.13. rectè legitur, de agno occiso ante iacta mundi fundamenta, nempe quod ad consilium Dei & virtutem perpetuâ huius victimæ: quomodo etiam
units.tr: But those fathers died before Christ came in the flesh. So what? Meanwhile they had the promise of the coming Christ, the foundation of their hope and trust; and the power of Christ's death extends not only to us but also to the times of the fathers, from the very beginning of the world. For Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today and forever, says the Apostle, Heb. 13. He means that Christ did not merely exist in past times, as to his divinity, as he himself said elsewhere, before Abraham was, I am: but that he who is now such a one was also such a one of old, and remains and will remain forever, to save and protect his own with mercy. In this sense also the passage Rev. 13 is rightly read, concerning the Lamb slain before the foundation of the world, namely with respect to the counsel of God and the perpetual efficacy of this sacrifice. So also among the ancients Ambrose takes that saying in his commentary on Romans 5.

units.la: ex veteribus Ambrosius dictum illud accipit super epist.ad Rom. 5. Non inficior tamen Græca eo loci etiam sic posse construi, ἐν ᾧ γίγραπται τὰ ὀνόματα ὑπὸ καταβολῆς τοῦ κόσμου: propter similē prorsus locum Apoc.17. Concludimus ergo cum Augustino, eandem fidem iustos fanauisse antiquos, quę sanat & nos: fidem mediatoris Dei & hominum Iesu Christi, fidem sanguinis eius, fidem crucis eius. Et alibi, regnum mortis, ait, sola in quolibet homine gratia destruit saluatoris, quæ operata est etiam in antiquis sanctis, quicunque, antequam in carne Christus veniret, ad eius tamen adiuuantem gratiam, non ad legis literam, quæ iubere tantum, non adiuuare poterat, pertinebant.
units.tr: I do not deny, however, that the Greek there can also be construed thus: in whom the names have been written from the foundation of the world [ἐν ᾧ γέγραπται τὰ ὀνόματα ὑπὸ καταβολῆς τοῦ κόσμου], on account of the entirely similar passage in Rev. 17. We conclude therefore with Augustine that the same faith saved the righteous of old as saves us too: faith in the Mediator between God and men, Jesus Christ, faith in his blood, faith in his cross. And elsewhere, he says: only grace, which works in each man, destroys the kingdom of death of the Saviour; and this grace also worked in the ancient saints, whoever, before Christ came in the flesh, nevertheless belonged to his helping grace, not to the letter of the law, which could command only, not help.

units.la: Non prætereundum tamen hoc loco, redemtionis beneficium ad antiquos iustos ficè extendi à multis, vt negent interim patuisse cuiquam introitum regni cœlestis ante mortem Christi, qua cœli ianuam apertam demum intelligi volunt. Et si quæras, quò igitur piorum animæ prisci temporibus reccereceptæ fuerunt? respondent; ad inferos, in limbum patrum scilicet. Hinc liber de Ecclesiasticis dogmatibus, qui Augustino inscribitur cap.78. & 79. ita definit: Ante passionem Domini omnes animæ sanctorum sub debito præuaricationis Adæ in inferno tenebantur, donec per indebitam Domini mortem a seruili conditione liberarentur: post ascensionem autem ad cœlos, omnes sanctorum animæ excedentes e corpore, ad Christum vadunt, sicut & peccatorum animæ ad infernum. Et Hieronymus super Ecclesiast. cap.3. scribit, quod ante aduentum Christi omnes ad inferos ducebantur, in tenebris detinendi; clausaque fuerint cœlestia, donec Paradisi fores Christus cum latrone reseraret. Meminit huius opinionis & Basilius in Psal.48: aliique veterum complures. Atque hæc communisferè scholasticorum sententia est. Et declarationem hi addunt, sanctos patres nullam pœnam sensus, sed tantum pœnam damni passos in inferno, exclusionem videlicet à vita gloriæ. Causam autem dedetentionis illius patrum apud inferos assignant, reatum vniuersæ naturæ humanæ ex peccato originali, quem nullius sanctorum fides vel iustitia potuerit remouere, sed remoueri demum potuerit pretio sanguinis Christi. Thomas parte 3. q. 49. art. 5.
units.tr: It must not be passed over here, however, that many extend the benefit of redemption to the ancient righteous in such a way that they deny that anyone entered the heavenly kingdom before the death of Christ, since they want the gate of heaven to be understood as opened only then. And if you ask where, then, the souls of the pious were received in earlier times, they answer: into hell, namely into the limbo of the fathers. Hence the book On Ecclesiastical Dogmas, ascribed to Augustine, chapters 78 and 79, defines thus: Before the passion of the Lord, all the souls of the saints were held in hell under the debt of Adam's transgression, until through the undeserved death of the Lord they were freed from their servile condition; but after the ascension to heaven, all the souls of the saints, on leaving the body, go to Christ, just as the souls of sinners go to hell. And Jerome on Ecclesiastes, ch. 3, writes that before the coming of Christ all were led down to hell, to be kept in darkness, and the heavenly things were shut until Christ unlocked the gates of Paradise with the thief. Basil in his commentary on Psalm 48 also mentions this opinion, and many other ancients. And this is almost the common view of the schoolmen. They add an explanation: the holy fathers suffered no pain of sense but only the pain of loss in hell, namely exclusion from the life of glory. They assign as the cause of that detention of the fathers in the underworld the guilt of the whole of human nature from original sin, which no faith or righteousness of any saint could remove, but which could be removed at last by the price of Christ's blood. Thomas, part 3, q. 49, art. 5.

units.la: Sed commentum hoc de limbo patrum etsi magnos habet autores, nil tamen nisi commetum est. Nam eadem est ratio solutionis reatus in omni peccato tam actuali quam originali: quoniam sanguis Christi mundat nos ab omni peccato, inquit Ioh. Non igitur ab originali dūtaxat. Quemadmodum & Paulus vniuersè loquitur ad Titum, dedit semetipsum, vt nos redimeret ab omni iniquitate. Nec diffitetur id Thomas loco citato: quod notandum est aduersus horribilem blasphemiam Cathari-ni, & similium Papistarum, qui contendunt passionem Christi expiare tātum originale peccatum, & ea actualia, quæ ante baptismum ab homine admissa sunt: reliqua vero omnia, quæ sequuntur, non iam per illud sacrificiū, sed per Mis-
units.tr: But this fiction about the limbo of the fathers, although it has great authors, is nothing but a fiction. For the manner of releasing guilt is the same in every sin, actual as well as original, since the blood of Christ cleanses us from every sin, says John; not from original sin alone. Just as Paul also speaks generally to Titus: he gave himself, that he might redeem us from all iniquity. Thomas does not deny this in the passage cited. This must be noted against the horrible blasphemy of Catharinus and similar Papists, who contend that Christ's passion expiates only original sin and those actual sins committed by a man before baptism, but that all the rest which follow are not expiated through that sacrifice but through the Mis-

units.la: Cathar. Archiepisc. libro Romae edito, cum priuilegio Papæ anno 1552. Missam expianda esse. Enimuero Thomas ingenuè scribit, per passionem Christi nos liberari no solum à peccato communi totius humanæ naturæ, & quantum ad culpam, & quantum ad reatum pœnæ, ipso soluente pretium pro nobis : sed etiam à peccatis proprijs singulorum, qui passioni eius per fidem, & caritatem & fidei sacramenta communicamus.
units.tr: Catharinus, archbishop, in a book published at Rome with the Pope's privilege in the year 1552: the Mass is to be expiated. Indeed Thomas candidly writes that through Christ's passion we are freed not only from the sin common to all human nature, both as to guilt and as to the penalty owed, the Lord himself having paid the price for us, but also from the proper sins of individuals, who share in his passion through faith and charity and the sacraments of faith.

units.la: Atsanêti patres, vt eûdem Thomam confitentem habemus, olim dum ad-huc viuerent, à reatu pœnæ actualium peccatorum per fidem Christi liberati fuerunt. Ergo per eandem fidem liberati quoque fuerint à reatu pœnæ originalis peccati, necesse est: aut si in inferno detinebantur à gloria exclusi, & pœnam patiebantur damni, vt loquuntur, ob peccatum originis, similiter fatendum erit etiam pœna sensus punitos ob peccata sua actualia.
units.tr: But holy fathers, as we have Thomas confessing, while they were still alive were freed from the guilt of the penalty of actual sins through faith in Christ. Therefore they must necessarily have been freed from the guilt of the penalty of original sin through the same faith. Or if they were detained in hell, excluded from glory and suffering the pain of loss, as they say, on account of original sin, then it must similarly be admitted that they were also punished with the pain of sense for their actual sins.

units.la: Deinde. Quis illis reuelauit peccatum originale apud inferos puniri tantum pœna damni, & non sensus, id est sola exclusione à vita gloriæ citra dolorem aliquem sensibilem?
units.tr: Next: who revealed to them that original sin is punished in hell only with the pain of loss, and not of sense, that is, by exclusion alone from the life of glory without any sensible pain?

units.la: Adhæc legimus Luca 16. pauperem La-
units.tr: Moreover we read in Luke 16 that the poor man La-

units.la: Lazarum ab angelis deportatum fuisse in sinum Abrahæ, vbi gaudio frueba-tur: diuitem apud inferos, sublatis oculis Lazarum vidisse {Greek} de longinquo: itemque dixisse Abrahamum. Inter nos & vos chaos magnum firmatum est. Solos autem duos, id est, Abraha-mum & Lazarum in illo memorabilis quietis sinu tum fuisse, absurdum est, vt notat Augustinus ad Euodium epistola 99.
units.tr: Lazarus was carried by angels into the bosom of Abraham, where he enjoyed delight; the rich man in hell, lifting up his eyes, saw Lazarus from afar [ἀπὸ μακρόθεν]; and Abraham said: between us and you a great chasm has been fixed. But that only two, that is Abraham and Lazarus, were then in that memorable bosom of rest is absurd, as Augustine notes in his letter 99 to Evodius.

units.la: Quod si autem plures, inquit, quàm duo ibi erant, quis auderet dicere ibi non fuisse Patriarchas & Prophetas? Hinc ita colligo: Patriarchæ & Prophetæ & cæteri iusti antiquitus recepti fuerunt in sinum Abrahæ. Ergo non in infernum. Probatur consequentia; quia nusquam in scriptura inferi in bono appellantur. At sinus ille Abrahæ in bono sumitur, tanquam sinus memorabilis quietis, & secretæ cuiusdam quietis habitatio. Sinum igitur illum credere non debemus partem aliquam fuisse inferorum. Probatio hæc tota Augustini est ad Euodium. Idémque probat verbis illis summi magistri, cùm ait, di-xisse xiffe Abraham, inter nos & vos chaos magnum firmatum est. ex quo satis appa-ret, inquit Augustinus, non esse quandam partem, & quasi membrum inferorum tantæ felicitatis sinum. Addit & hanc probationem: Quòd si, inquit, in illum Abrahæ sinû Christum mortuum venisse sancta scriptura dixisset, non no-minato inferno eiusque doloribus, nemo idcirco ad inferos eum descendisse afferere auderet.
units.tr: But if, he says, more than two were there, who would dare to say that the Patriarchs and Prophets were not there? Hence I conclude thus: the Patriarchs, the Prophets and the other righteous of old were received into the bosom of Abraham; therefore not into hell. The consequence is proved, because nowhere in Scripture are the underworld and hell called good. But that bosom of Abraham is taken in a good sense, as a bosom of memorable rest and the dwelling of a certain secret quiet. We ought not, therefore, to believe that bosom was any part of hell. This whole proof is Augustine's, in his letter to Evodius. He proves the same by those words of the supreme Master, when he says that Abraham said: between us and you a great chasm has been fixed; from which it sufficiently appears, says Augustine, that the bosom of such happiness was not some part, or as it were a member, of hell. He adds this proof too: but if, he says, holy Scripture had said that Christ came dead into that bosom of Abraham, without naming hell and its pains, no one would therefore dare to assert that he descended into hell.

units.la: Expendant autem lectores, an non hæ rationes ab Augustino è scriptura depromtæ, plus fidei mereantur quàm Scholasticorum næniæ, qui quadruplicé fabricant infernum; scilicet damnatorum, puerorum, purgandorum, & sanctorum patrum : seu Gehennam, & limbum puerorum, purgatorium, & limbum patrum; quem manifeste statuunt partem & quasi membrum inferorum, contra rationes ex Augustino excerptas.
units.tr: Let the readers consider whether these arguments drawn by Augustine from Scripture do not deserve more trust than the trifles of the Scholastics, who build hell in fourfold form: namely the hell of the damned, of the children, of those to be purged, and of the holy fathers; or Gehenna, and the limbo of children, purgatory, and the limbo of the fathers. They plainly set up this as a part, and as it were a member, of the lower regions, against the arguments taken from Augustine.

units.la: Huc accedit, quod autores qui limbum patrum commenti sunt, hærere videas in assignanda piarum animarum ex carcere isto liberatione. Modò enim passioni Christi eam tribuunt, qua reatum poenæ peccati originalis, quo patres secundum ipsos apud inferos detinebantur, dissoluerit, & ianuam regni cœlestis aperuerit: modò animæ Christi ad infernum patrum descensu opus fuisse, tradunt, vt omnes qui originali peccato adstricti tenebantur sanctos, ibidem absolueret: vbi parum abest, quin descensum illum Christo poenalem statuant, sicut philosophatur Aquinas part.3.q.52.art.1. conueniens fuisse Christum ad inferos descendere, quia venerit poenam nostram portare, poena autem nostra erat, inquit, non tantum mors corporis, sed etiam descensus ad inferos. Modò rursum decernunt magistraliter, licet animæ illæ in Christi descensu factæ sunt beatæ, & sic statim eis cœlum patuerit, quantum ad præmium beatitudinis; non tamen patuisse quantum ad locum, donec Christo adscendente simul in cœlum traductæ fuerint.
units.tr: To this must be added that the authors who invented the limbo of the fathers are seen to waver in explaining the liberation of pious souls from that prison. For at one time they attribute it to the passion of Christ, which dissolved the guilt of punishment of original sin, on account of which the fathers were held in the lower regions according to them, and opened the gate of the heavenly kingdom; at another time they teach that Christ's descent to the fathers' hell was needed so that he might absolve there the saints who were bound and held by original sin. Here they come close to making that descent a penal thing for Christ, as Aquinas philosophises in Part 3, question 52, article 1, that it was fitting for Christ to descend to hell because he came to bear our punishment, and our punishment, he says, was not only the death of the body but also the descent to hell. Again, at another time they decree authoritatively that although those souls were made blessed at Christ's descent, and so heaven was at once open to them as regards the reward of blessedness, nevertheless it was not open as regards place, until they were carried up into heaven together with Christ's ascension.

units.la: Sed cur à veteribus dissentiunt, quorum rum videri volùt sequi sententia? Hieron.enim,vt citabamus, clausa tantum voluit cœlestia,donec Christus cum latrone paradisi fores referârit. Pręterea, fifecretorum cœlestium peritiores sibi videntur, explicent nobis, vbi igitur sanctorum animæ spacio illo quadraginta dierum inter resurrectionem & afcefionem Domini, commoratæ sint? Solutæ enim nexu originalis peccati, quo apud inferos adstringebantur,diu-tius ibidem, nisi sua & sanguis Christi, per quem libertas ingrediendi facrariu acquisita est iniuria, detineri non potuerunt:nec tamen, vt volunt, erant in cœlo. Vbi ergo peregrinabantur? Idem obiici potest de spiritibus piorû, quotquot dicto spatio quadraginta dierum obdormiuerunt.
units.tr: But why do they dissent from the ancients, whose opinion they wish to seem to follow? For Jerome, as we quoted, wanted the heavenly things to be closed until Christ, with the thief, unbarred the gates of paradise. Moreover, let those who seem to themselves more skilled in the heavenly mysteries explain to us where, then, the souls of the saints dwelt during that space of forty days between the resurrection and ascension of the Lord. For, freed from the bond of original sin by which they were bound in the lower regions, they could not have been detained there longer, except by the injury done to his own blood, through which freedom of entrance into the sanctuary was won; yet, as they hold, they were not in heaven. Where then were they wandering? The same can be objected concerning the spirits of the pious, as many as fell asleep during the said space of forty days.

units.la: Caput IX. De causa impulsiua redemtionis humanæ.
units.tr: Chapter 9. On the impelling cause of the redemption of mankind.

units.la: S E D vt ad alia nostra sese vertat oratio,in considerationem & illud venit, qua de causa filius Dei, Dominus no-ster Iesus Christus, generis humani redemtionem susceperit? Quaerimus autem nunc non de causa finali, de qua sequenti capite aliquid dicemus, sed de causa, vt vocat, impulsiua: quid eum mouerit nempe, vt ipse opifex & Dominus, pro suo plasmate, plasmatione suscepta, ad humilimam, & ignominiofiffimam pariter mortem crucis sese propter nos & salutem nostram demitteret.
units.tr: But to turn our discussion to other matters, the question arises: for what cause did the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, undertake the redemption of mankind? We are asking now not about the final cause, of which we will say something in the next chapter, but about what is called the impelling cause: what moved him, as the Maker and Lord himself, to submit to the formation of his own creature, and so to lower himself, for us and for our salvation, to the most humble and most ignominious death of the cross.

units.la: Refponfio expedita & plana est, id factum ob Seruatoris nostri erga nos amorem, & spontaneam erga patrem obedientiam.
units.tr: The answer is ready and plain: he did this out of love for us, our Saviour, and out of his willing obedience to the Father.

units.la: De filij erga nos amore in toto opere humiliationis loquitur Paulus tum alibi, tum ad Phil.2. vbi hortatur ad caritatem proximi, ne sua quisque spectemus, sed etiam ea, quae aliorum sunt: & hortationem propositam exemplo Christi confirmat iubens, vt is fit affectus in nobis, qui etiam fuit in Christo Iesu, qui, cum effet in forma Dei, exinaniuerit fe nostra causa, ex mera videli-cet cet erga nos caritate, quandoquidem ad eius imitationem Apostolus ibi hortatur.
units.tr: Paul speaks of the Son's love for us throughout the whole work of humiliation, both elsewhere and in Phil. 2., where he urges love of neighbour, that each of us should look not only to his own interests but also to the interests of others. He confirms this exhortation by the example of Christ, bidding that the same mind be in us which was also in Christ Jesus, who, though he was in the form of God, emptied himself for our sake, out of pure love for us, since the Apostle there exhorts us to imitate him.

units.la: De obedientia verò sua erga patrem Christus ipse testatur Iohan.5. Non quaero voluntatem meam, sed eius qui misit me, patris, Et clarius capite 6. Descendi de coelo, ut faciam, non voluntatem meam, sed voluntatem eius, qui misit me, patris, ut, quicquid mihi dederit, non perdam ex eo, sed suscitem illud in die novissimo.
units.tr: Christ himself testifies to his obedience to the Father in John 5. I do not seek my own will, but the will of him who sent me, the Father. And more clearly in chapter 6: I came down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me, the Father, that of all he has given me I should lose nothing, but raise it up on the last day.

units.la: Quod autem patri visum est per filij sui immolationem nos seruare, id totum est diuinae dignationis, dilectionis, bonitatis, & φιλανθρωπίας, testante Domino Iohan.3. Sic Deus dilexit mundum, ut filium suum dederit. Unde & Paulus Rom. 5.ait, Commendat Deus suam erga nos caritatem, quod cum essemus peccatores, Christus pro nobis mortuus sit. Idem Ephes.2. Deus inquit, qui dives est misericordia, propter multam caritatem suam, qua dilexit nos, etiam cum per offensas mortui essemus, viuificauit nos per Christum. Et luculentissime omnium ad Titum 3. Apparuit bonitas, & amor erga homines seruatoris nostri Dei, & ferseruauit nos, non ex operibus iustis, quae nos fecerimus, sed ex sua misericordia. Consentiunt & Prophetarum dicta: In momento irae abscondi ad momentum faciem meam a te, sed misericordia sempiterna misertus sum tui, dixit redemptor tuus Iehoua. Ego, ego sum, qui deleo praeuaricationes tuas propter me, & peccatorum tuorum no recordabor. Propter me, autem dicit: id est, non propter vos, sed propter nomen sanctum meum: vt explicatur Ezech.36. Neque alio spectat quod Iesaias cap.9. Vaticinans de incarnatione filij & Ecclesiae per ipsum redemtione a iugo peccati & mortis, rem totam pulcerrimo hoc Epiphonemate concludit: Zelus Iehouae exercituum faciet istud: quasi dicat, Magna quidem, sed vera, cano: Pater ipse potest Perficiet dextra, aeterno succensus amore, Seruatosque voles caeli quibus annuit arcem Vide etiam quid de causa redemtionis populi Israel ex Aegypto, quae typus erat aeternae huius, concionetur Moses Deuter.7.
units.tr: That it pleased the Father to save us through the sacrifice of his Son is wholly a matter of divine condescension, love, goodness, and love of mankind [φιλανθρωπίας], as the Lord testifies in John 3. God so loved the world that he gave his Son. Hence Paul also says in Rom. 5.: God commends his love toward us, in that while we were sinners, Christ died for us. The same in Eph. 2.: God, who is rich in mercy, because of his great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead in our offences, made us alive together with Christ. And most splendidly of all, in Titus 3.: The kindness and love of God our Saviour toward men appeared, and he saved us, not by works of righteousness that we had done, but according to his mercy. The sayings of the prophets agree: In a moment of wrath I hid my face from you for a moment, but with everlasting mercy I have had compassion on you, says the Lord your Redeemer. I, I am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake, and I will not remember your sins. He says "for my own sake," that is, not for your sake but for the sake of my holy name, as is explained in Ezek. 36. Isaiah, prophesying in chapter 9 about the incarnation of the Son and the redemption of the Church through him from the yoke of sin and death, concludes the whole matter with this most beautiful exclamation: The zeal of the Lord of hosts will do this. It is as if he said: "I sing great things, but true: the Father himself can do it; his right hand will accomplish it, kindled with eternal love, and will save those for whom he has promised the heights of heaven." See also what Moses preaches in Deut. 7. about the cause of the redemption of the people of Israel out of Egypt, which was a type of this eternal redemption.

units.la: Vtus porro huius considerationis est, vt nos ex animo corā Deo humilie-mus, mus, & qui gloriatur, in Domino glorietur, non in suis operibus, aut dignitate propria. Obseruanda enim, & vrgenda semper est antithesis illa misericordiæ Dei, & operum iustitiæ, quod ad causam salutis attinet: sicut Paulus ista opponebat: non ex operibus iustitiæ quæ nos fecerimus, sed ex misericordia sua seruauit nos. Et inculcatur eadem antithesis 2.Tim.1.v.9.& Danielis 9.v.18.
units.tr: The use of this consideration is that we should in our hearts humble ourselves before God, and that he who glories should glory in the Lord, not in his own works or his own dignity. For that antithesis between the mercy of God and the works of righteousness, as far as the cause of salvation is concerned, must always be observed and pressed. Paul set these against each other: not by works of righteousness that we had done, but according to his mercy he saved us. The same antithesis is pressed in 2 Tim. 1:9 and Dan. 9:18.

units.la: Alter vsus est, vt nos quoque diuinæ erga nos caritatis immensum, vt Damascenus loquitur, pelagus, animo pendentes, Deum redamemus, idque non verbo neque lingua solum, sed opere & veritate; sicut ipse dilexit nos, & posuit animam suam pro nobis 1.Ioh.3. Et ca.4. eiusdem epist. utrumque vsum coniungens pulcerrimis verbis ita scribit; per hoc patefacta est caritas Dei in nobis, quod filium suum unigenitum misit Deus in mundum, vt viuamus per eum. In hoc est caritas, non quod dilexerimus eum, sed quod ipse dilexerit nos, & miserit filium suum, vt esset propitiatio pro peccatis nostris. Et continenter subiungit: dilecti, si Deus nos ita dile-
units.tr: Another use is that we too, hanging in spirit upon the immense sea (as Damascene puts it) of divine love toward us, should love God in return, and not with word and tongue only, but in deed and truth, as he loved us and laid down his life for us, 1 John 3. In chapter 4 of the same epistle, joining both uses together, he writes in most beautiful words: In this the love of God was made manifest among us, that God sent his only begotten Son into the world, that we might live through him. In this is love, not that we loved him, but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins. And immediately he adds: Beloved, if God so loved us, we also ought to love one another.

units.la: Damasc. lib.3. orth. fid. cap.1. dilexit, debemus & nos alij alios diligere. Et sub finem; nos diligimus eum, quia ipse prior dilexit nos. Si quis autem dixerit, diligo Deum, & fratrem oderit, mendax est.
units.tr: Damascene, Orthodox Faith book 3, chapter 1 (as above). Ought to love one another. And near the end: We love him, because he first loved us. If anyone says, "I love God," and hates his brother, he is a liar.

units.la: Verum enim, cum per mortem Christi Deo reconciliati simus, sicut ait Apostolus, Reconciliauit nos Deo per crucem, interemptis inimicitiis per eam: alienum videtur, quod diximus, ex dilectione Dei traditum pro nobis in mortem. Nam si antea diligebamur a Deo, quorsum reconciliatio? Si quis dicat opus fuisse reconciliatione respectu nostri, ut nos definieremus inimicitias exercere erga Deum, & nos invicem; Iudei ergaGentiles, & Gentiles erga Iudaeos: is neque nihil dicit, teste Paulo, nequeatotum dicit. In primis enim reconciliatoris erat placare irā Dei adversus nos propter peccata, eumque nobis fauentem ac propitium reddere. Quomodo igitur conuenit, quod gratuito fauore, & dilectione sua Deus praevenerit reconciliationem, dato nobis filio? Argumentum tale fit:
units.tr: But since we have been reconciled to God through the death of Christ, as the Apostle says, He reconciled us to God through the cross, having killed the enmities by it, it seems out of place to say what we have said, that God, out of love for us, delivered his Son to death for us. For if we were loved by God before, why was reconciliation needed? If someone says that reconciliation was needed on our side, so that we might cease to be hostile to God and to one another, the Jews to the Gentiles and the Gentiles to the Jews, he is not wrong, as Paul bears witness, but he does not say everything. For it was chiefly the task of the reconciler to appease the wrath of God against us on account of our sins, and to make him favourable and propitious toward us. How then does it agree that God, by his free favour and his love, went before the reconciliation by giving us his Son? The argument runs thus:

units.la: Idem non est causa & effectus. Dilectio Dei est effectus reconciliationis. Ergo non est eius causa.
units.tr: The same thing cannot be both cause and effect. The love of God is an effect of reconciliation. Therefore it is not its cause.

units.la: Sed maior vera est respectu eiusdem. Dilectio autem Dei effectus est reconciliationis, non simpliciter, quasi tum demum ceperit nos diligere, sed secundum quid; quatenus reconciliatio per sanguinem filij ipsius remouet peccatum, per quod inimici Dei & filij irae constituti eramus, secundum illud Sap. 14. perque odio Deo sunt impius & impietas eius: Et Psalm. 5. Odisti omnes, qui operantur iniquitatem: Iesaia etiam clamante, iniquitas nostra diuidit inter nos, & Deum nostrum, & peccata nostra faciunt ut abscondat faciem suam a nobis, ne exaudiat. Ies. 59.
units.tr: The major premise is true as regards the same thing. But the love of God is an effect of reconciliation not simply, as though God had only then begun to love us, but in a certain respect: insofar as reconciliation through the blood of his Son removes the sin by which we were made enemies of God and children of wrath, according to Wisdom 14: The impious and his impiety are equally hateful to God, and Psalm 5: You hate all who work iniquity. Isaiah also cries out: Your iniquity separates you and your God, and your sins make him hide his face from you, so that he does not hear. Isa. 59.

units.la: Optime rem totam Augustinus explicat tractatu 110. in Iohannem: Miro, inquit, & diuino modo, quando nos oderat Deus, diligebat. Oderat enim nos, quales ipse non fecerat (id est propter peccata) & quia, inquit, iniquitas nostra opus eius non omni ex parte consumserat, nouerat simul in vnoquoque nostrum, & odisse quod feceramus, & amare quod fecerat: & hoc quidem in omnibus bus intelligi potest, fecundum illud: nihil odi- sti eorum quæ fecisti. Nam in eo, quod odit, est etiam quod amet. Odit enim, & velut à regula suæ artis alienum improbat vitium: amat tamen quod suum est, etiam in vitiosis.
units.tr: Augustine explains the whole matter best in tractate 110 on John: In a wonderful and divine way, God loved us while he hated us. For he hated us as we were, not as he had made us, that is, on account of our sins; and because, he says, our iniquity had not wholly destroyed his work in every part, he knew at the same time in each of us both to hate what we had done and to love what he had made. This can be understood in all of us according to the words: you hate nothing of what you have made. For in what he hates there is also something he loves. He hates, and as something alien to the rule of his art he disapproves of the fault; yet he loves what is his own, even in those who are faulty.

units.la: Adhæc cùm eorum quę fecerit, nihil oderit: peculiariter, vt ibidem Augustinus docet, diligit membra vnigeniti sui. Qui enim, ait, membra filij non diligeret, qui diligit filium? quia non alia causa est diligendi membra eius: nisi quia diligit eu. Nos igitur diligit, quia sumus eius membra, quem diligit: & hoc vt essemus, propter hoc nos dilexit antequam essemus. Ex quo ei reconciliati sumus per sanguinem filij eius, cœpit nos diligere, sed ante mundi constitutionem dilexit nos, vt cum eius vnigenito etiam nos filij eius essemus, priusquam omnino aliquid essemus. Quod ergo reconciliati sumus Deo per mortem filij eius, non sic audiatur, non sic accipiatur, quasi ideò nos reconciliauerit filius, vt iâ inciperet amare, quos oderat, sicut reconciliatur inimicus inimico: sed iam nos diligenti reconciliati sumus, cum quo propter peccata inimicitias habebamus: & tamen ei verissime dictum est, odisti omnes, qui opeoperantur iniquitatem. Hactenus Augustinus. Summa est, cum Deus nos tanquam opus suum, praecipue vero tanquam membra filij sui ante iacta mundi fundamenta diligeret, mera & gratuita dilectione excitatum, dedisse nobis filiu, ut redemti ipsius gratia a peccato, quo a conspectu & fruitione Dei arceba-mur, haeredes efficeremur vitae aeternae.
units.tr: Moreover, since he hates nothing of what he has made, he loves especially, as Augustine teaches in the same place, the members of his only begotten Son. For who, he says, would not love the members of his Son, if he loves the Son? There is no other reason for loving his members than that he loves him. So he loves us, because we are members of him whom he loves; and he loved us before we were, so that we might be his sons together with his only begotten, before we were anything at all. Therefore, when we are said to have been reconciled to God through the death of his Son, let it not be heard or understood as if the Son reconciled us so that God might then begin to love those whom he hated, as an enemy is reconciled to an enemy; rather, we were reconciled to him whom we had enmity against because of our sins, while he already loved us. And yet it is most truly said of him: you hate all who work iniquity. Thus far Augustine. The sum is this: since God loved us as his work, and especially as the members of his Son, before the foundations of the world were laid, moved by pure and free love, he gave us his Son, so that by his grace we might be redeemed from the sin by which we were shut out from the sight and enjoyment of God, and become heirs of eternal life.

units.la: Scite Bernardus Sermone 20. de verf. 9. Psalmi, Qui habitat, &c. Christus secundum tempus quidem pro impiis mortuus est, secundum praedestinationem autem pro fratribus & amicis.
units.tr: Bernard well says in Sermon 20 on Psalm 90, verse 9, "He who dwells": Christ died for the wicked according to time, but for his brothers and friends according to predestination.

units.la: CAPVT X. De redemptionis causa finali.
units.tr: CHAPTER X. On the final cause of redemption.

units.la: SEQVITVR quaestio illa, Ad quid simus redemti? qua de fine iam redemptionis nostri quaeritur. Est autem finis ille duplex: nempe gloria Dei, & salus nostra. Priorem finem celebrat Apostolus Eph. 1. vbi ait, quod Deus nos elegerit in Christo ante iacta mundi fundamenta, & praeordinarit, quos adopta-
units.tr: THE next question follows: For what purpose were we redeemed? This asks about the end of our redemption. That end is twofold: the glory of God and our salvation. The Apostle celebrates the first end in Eph. 1, where he says that God chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world, and predestined those whom he would adopt

units.la: D ij ret in filios per eundem Iesum Christum in sese, pro beneuolo affectu voluntatis suæ, idque ad laudem gloriosæ suæ gratiæ, qua nos sibi gratos effecit in illo dilecto, in quo habemus redemtionem, per sanguinem ipsius, remissionem peccatorum. Quibus verbis non tantum docet finem æternæ atque gratuitæ electionis Dei, esse laudem gloriosæ & diuitiis gratiæ ipsius, sed ad eundem etiam finem subordinatam ostendit nostri per Christum redemtionem. Omnia enim fecit Deus propter semetipsum, etiam impium ad diem malum; vt & salvationis beneficiū in his, qui liberatur, & damnationis iudicium in pœna debita pereuntiū, gloriæ ipsius proficiat.
units.tr: as sons through the same Jesus Christ to himself, according to the good pleasure of his will, and this to the praise of the glory of his grace, by which he made us acceptable to himself in the Beloved, in whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins. In these words he teaches not only that the end of God's eternal and free election is the praise of the glory and riches of his grace, but also shows that our redemption through Christ is subordinated to that same end. For God made all things for himself, even the wicked for the day of evil, so that both the benefit of salvation in those who are set free and the judgment of damnation in the due punishment of those who perish might serve his glory.

units.la: Proinde admonemur hic, vt cum Paulo indesinenter gratias agamus patri, qui idoneos nos fecit ad participandam sortem sanctorum in luce, & liberauit nos è potestate tenebrarum, transduxitque in regnum filij dilecti, in quo habemus redemtionem per sanguinem ipsius. Quemadmodum & Petrus officij nos hac in parte admonet, vt virtutes
units.tr: Therefore we are reminded here to give thanks without ceasing to the Father, with Paul, who has made us fit to share in the lot of the saints in light, and has delivered us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of his beloved Son, in whom we have redemption through his blood. Peter likewise reminds us of our duty in this matter, that we should proclaim the virtues

units.la: Prou. 16. tes prædicemus illius, qui nos vocauit e tenebris in admirabilem suam lucem. Notum est quid Moses, quid filij Israël fecerint, cùm mare peruium toti populo iter expeditum præbuisset: quomodo diuina protecti manu, & stupendam conspicati redemtionē, more agnorum exultauerint, te liberatorem, ô Domine, te fortitudinē, & laudem suam decantantes. Sed quid veterem populum, quid vetus canticum dico? Nouum habemus canticum, cantici agni: id statesad mare vitreum mundi huius, & citharas Dei habetes, indefessē cum vniuersa Ecclesia canamus sedenti in throno & Agno; quoniam mactatus est, & redemit nos Deo per sanguinem suum, ex omni tribu & lingua, & populo, & natione: & fecit nos Deo nostro reges & sacerdotes, & regnabimus super terram.
units.tr: Prov. 16. of him who called us out of darkness into his marvellous light. It is well known what Moses and the children of Israel did when the sea, having been crossed, opened a passage for the whole people: how, protected by the divine hand and beholding a wonderful redemption, they exulted like lambs, singing of you, O Lord, as their liberator and their strength and their praise. But why do I speak of the old people, of the old song? We have a new song, the song of the Lamb. Standing by the glassy sea of this world, and holding the harps of God, let us sing without ceasing, with the whole Church, to him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb, because he was slain and has redeemed us to God by his blood, out of every tribe and tongue and people and nation, and has made us kings and priests to our God, and we shall reign upon the earth.

units.la: Tibi, O fili Dei, mortalium amator, & bone domine, ô pacificator, ô opulente saluator, & reuera rex, creator & conditor omnium, verbum & sapientia patris, lumen & iubar patris, virtus, bra-chium, chiū, & dextera patris; tibi fit benedi-ctio, & honor & gloria & robur in fecu-la seculorum. Tu nos captiuos redemi-fti, & seruientes peccato,tua propria morte liberafti. Tu nobis filiorum ado-ptionem reddidisti. Tu pauper fuisti, vt nos tua paupertate ditares. Tu nobis regnum cœlorum largitus es. Tu nos denuò formafti, in tenebris illumina-fti, mortuos viuificafti:dolores mortis soluisti, ianuas æreas, & vectes ferreos confregisti, iugúmque peccatorum contriuisti.
units.tr: To you, O Son of God, lover of mortals, good Lord, O peacemaker, O bountiful Saviour, and truly King, creator and maker of all things, Word and wisdom of the Father, light and radiance of the Father, power, arm, and right hand of the Father: to you be blessing, honour, glory and strength for ever and ever. You have redeemed us when we were captives and slaves to sin, and you have freed us by your own death. You have restored to us the adoption of sons. You became poor, that by your poverty you might enrich us. You have bestowed on us the kingdom of heaven. You have formed us anew, enlightened us in darkness, made us alive when we were dead; you have loosed the pains of death, broken the brazen gates and iron bars, and crushed the yoke of sins.

units.la: Quoniam vero indecens est laus in ore stultorum,& non tam verbis quàm factis ipsis mirifica & diuina prorsus redemtio ifthæc prædicanda nobis est agedum,sic affecti fimus,sic vitam,mores,actiones,consilia, omniáque nostra componamus, ne communi liberatori nostro, cuius gloriæ toti dicati, consecratique esse debemus,turpiter ingrati reperiamur, nih ilo meliores, imò modis omnibus deteriores,Iudæis illis perui cacibus, propter quos nomen Dei blasphemabatur inter gētes, sicut scriptum ptum est. Verùm nunquam animo nostro excidat Mosaica illa exprobratio in cantico Deuteronomij: Nunquid Iehoua retribuetis istud, populus stulte & insipiens? Nonne ipse est pater tuus, qui possedit te? Nonne ipse fecit, & præparauit te? Deuteron.32.
units.tr: Since indeed praise is unseemly in the mouth of fools, and this wonderful and altogether divine redemption must be proclaimed to us not so much in words as in deeds, let us be so disposed, and let us so order our life, morals, actions, counsels, and all that is ours, that we are not found shamefully ungrateful to our common Liberator, to whose glory we ought to be wholly devoted and consecrated, no better, but in every way worse, than those perverse Jews, on whose account the name of God was blasphemed among the nations, as it is written. Yet let that reproach from the Mosaic song in Deuteronomy never fall from our minds: Do you thus repay Jehovah, foolish and senseless people? Is he not your father who possessed you? Did he not make you and prepare you? Deut. 32.

units.la: Alter redemtionis finis est salus nostra, quæ quidem varia beneficia, licet uno eodemque nexu inter se colligata, copulectitur: cuiusmodi in primis sunt; Iustificatio, quæ in gratuita peccatorum remissione sita est: Sanctificatio, & novitas vitæ, consolatio, imò gloriatio in aduersis sub spe gloriæ Dei. Denique introitus in æternum regnum Dei nostri ac seruatoris Iesu Christi, & perennia gaudia in vita æterna.
units.tr: The other end of redemption is our salvation, which embraces various benefits, though they are bound together by one and the same tie. Of these the chief are: justification, which lies in the free forgiveness of sins; sanctification and newness of life; consolation, and indeed glorying in adversities under the hope of the glory of God; and finally, entrance into the eternal kingdom of our God and Saviour Jesus Christ, and everlasting joys in eternal life.

units.la: Hæc tot tantaque Dei munera, acquisita nobis sunt largitate gratiæ mortis Christi, vt Scripturæ dicta ostendūt. Rom.3. Iustificamur gratis per redemtionem factam in Christo Iesu, quem proposuit Deus vt esset placamentum per fidem in sanguine ipsius per remissionem peccatorum. In eadem epistola cap.5. Cùm adhuc peccatores tores effemus, Christus pro nobis mortuus est. Iustificati igitur sanguine eius, seruabimur nunc multò magis per eum ab ira. Nam si cum inimici essemus reconciliati sumus Deo per mortem filij eius, multo magis reconciliati seruabimur per vitam ipsius. Et mox: Neque solum id, verum etiam gloriamur in Deo per Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, per quem nunc reconciliationem consecuti sumus. Item, si per vnam offensam mors regnauit, multò magis ij, qui redundantem illam gratiam & donum iustitiæ accipiunt, in vita regnabunt.
units.tr: These many and great gifts of God have been won for us by the largess of grace in the death of Christ, as the words of Scripture show. Rom. 3: We are justified freely through the redemption made in Christ Jesus, whom God set forth to be a propitiation through faith in his blood, for the remission of sins. In the same letter, chapter 5: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us. Therefore, justified by his blood, we shall now be saved much more through him from wrath. For if, while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, being reconciled, we shall be saved through his life. And soon after: Not only that, but we also glory in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now obtained reconciliation. Likewise: If by the one offence death reigned, much more shall those who receive the abundant grace and the gift of righteousness reign in life.

units.la: Ad Titum 2: dedit se pro nobis, vt redime- ret nos ab omni peccato, & purificaret sibi ipsi populum peculiarem, studiosum bonorum operum. Coniungit isthæc Petrus quoque 1. Epist. 2, cum ait, Dominum pertulit se peccata nostra in corpore super lignum, vt peccatis mortui, iustitiæ viuerémus.
units.tr: Titus 2: He gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity, and purify for himself a peculiar people, zealous of good works. Peter also joins these things in 1 Epist. 2, when he says: The Lord bore our sins himself in his body upon the tree, so that, being dead to sins, we might live to righteousness.

units.la: Horum assidua consideratio esse debet, vt magnitudinem doni Christi intelligamus, & gratias eidem sine intermissione agamus: apud animum expedentes, quæ sit latitudo, & longitudo, & profunditas, vt Paulus loquitur, gratiæ Dei; & quæ sit spes vocationis ipsius, & quae opes gloriae ipsius in sanctis. Deinde vtilis & necessaria est meditatio horum assidua, partim ad alendā in nobis fidem, & spem, partim ad vitae noui-tatem magis magisque in nobis excitandam & corroborandam. Habentes, inquit Apostolus Heb.10. libertatem ingrediendi sacrarium per sanguinem Iesu, & habentes sacerdotem magnum praefectum domui Dei; accedamus cum vero corde & certa perfuasione fidei, & teneamus confessionem spei non vacillantem. Quod vero ad vitae institutionem attinet, iubemur incede re sicut dignum est Domino, qui nos, cum peccati serui essemus ad mortem, liberauit a peccato, & mancipauit iustitiae. Hinc Pauli illae exhortationes: Non regnet peccatum in mortali corpore vestro: nec sistite membra vestra arma iniustitiae peccato; sed sistite vos Deo, vt ex mortuis viuos, & membra vestra arma iustitiae Deo. Item, sicut stitistis membra vestra serua impuritati, & iniquitati ad iniquitatem: ita nunc sistite membra vestra serua iustitiae ad sanctimoniam. Certe cum liberti Christi simus, ei viuendum est, qui nos redemit, & peculium suum bonorumque operum sectatores esse voluit: nec committendum est, ut redemptoris obliti ad hostilia mundi, & Satanæ ipsius castra recurramus, & pristinæ seruitutis iugo, unde sanguine filij Dei redemti eramus, corpora & animas nostras denuò subiiciamus. O amentes, ô nequissimos transfugas & mortalium omnium improbissimos, qui tantam contumeliam nomini Christiano, imò redemtori Christo irrogant, & tantum non sanguinem fœderis pedibus suis concul-cant.
units.tr: Our constant consideration of these things ought to be so that we understand the greatness of Christ's gift and give thanks to him without intermission, weighing in our minds what is the breadth, and length, and depth, as Paul puts it, of the grace of God; and what is the hope of his calling, and what the riches of his glory in the saints. Then the constant meditation on these things is useful and necessary, partly to nourish faith and hope in us, and partly to stir up and strengthen in us more and more newness of life. Having, says the Apostle in Heb. 10, boldness to enter the sanctuary by the blood of Jesus, and having a great priest set over the house of God, let us draw near with a true heart and in the assurance of faith, and hold fast the confession of our hope without wavering. As for the ordering of life, we are commanded to walk worthily of the Lord, who, when we were slaves of sin unto death, has freed us from sin and made us servants of righteousness. Hence those exhortations of Paul: Let not sin reign in your mortal body, nor yield your members as weapons of unrighteousness to sin; but yield yourselves to God, as those alive from the dead, and your members as weapons of righteousness to God. Likewise: As you once yielded your members as slaves to uncleanness and iniquity, leading to iniquity, so now yield your members as slaves to righteousness, leading to holiness. Certainly, since we are the freed people of Christ, we must live for him who redeemed us, and he wished us to be zealous followers of good works, his own possession. Nor must we commit the fault of forgetting our Redeemer and running back to the hostile camps of the world and of Satan himself, and subjecting again our bodies and souls to the yoke of our former slavery, from which we were redeemed by the blood of the Son of God. O madmen, O most wicked deserters and most shameless of all mortals, who heap such insult upon the Christian name, and indeed upon Christ the Redeemer, and trample underfoot, as it were, the blood of the covenant!

units.la: CAPVT XI. QVINAM A CHRISTO REDEMTI SINT.
units.tr: CHAPTER XI. WHICH MEN HAVE BEEN REDEEMED BY CHRIST.

units.la: Recitatur controuersia de propositaque-stione, & explicatur summatim.
units.tr: The controversy and the question put are set out and briefly explained.

units.la: His declaratis, veniamus ad quæstionem vltimo loco reseruatam: Quinam sint, quos Christus mediator Dei & hominum, morte sua redemerit: seu pro quibusnam mortuus sit? Erit autem negotium hoc (quantum Dominus dederit) in gratiam studiosorum, & ad veritatis Euangelicæ defensionem, fusius aliquanto, quàm præcedentibus quæstionibus factum est, tractandum; cùm non ita pridem occasione colloquij Mompelgartensis, res in contentionem gravem adducta sit, & quidam iracundia æstuans, & rabiem vbique præse ferens, nimium sane acerbè & maledicè scriptis suis, quæ Latinè & Germanicè sparsit, quasi flabello contentionis eam ventilauerit: ac si non antea hoc nostro exulcerato seculo certaminum ac dissidiorum plus satis in Ecclesia Christi existeret, cum crebris & grauissimis infirmorum offendiculis.
units.tr: With these matters made clear, let us come to the question reserved for the last place: Who are those whom Christ, the mediator between God and men, has redeemed by his death; or for whom, in other words, did he die? This matter will be treated, God willing, somewhat more fully than the earlier questions, for the sake of students and in defence of the Gospel truth. The reason is that not long ago, at the colloquy of Mömpelgard, the question was brought into serious dispute, and a certain man, seething with anger and showing his rage everywhere, has stirred it up in his writings, in Latin and German, far too bitterly and abusively, as if he were fanning the flames of strife. As if our age, already so full of wrangling and division, did not have enough of them in the Church of Christ, with its frequent and very grave stumbling-blocks for the weak.

units.la: Adobruit ille à se dissentientes quibuslibet contumeliis, & maledictis, prout in buccam venit; quòd Alcorano, quòd Paganismo accedant; quòd Satanicam foueat blasphemiam, phrenesi laborent, nomen Christi exstinguere cupiant, & in hoc intenti sint, vt Christum primum ex cordibus, deinde ex Scriptura, denique ex Ecclesia ipsa.
units.tr: He pours every kind of insult and abuse on those who differ from him, whatever comes into his mouth: that they go over to the Koran, that they go over to paganism, that they foster Satanic blasphemy, that they are frenzied, that they wish to extinguish the name of Christ, and that they are intent on this, that they destroy Christ first from hearts, then from Scripture, and finally from the Church itself.

units.la: Colloq. Mompelgart. Huberus. ipsa profligent: Et nuncupat eos seductores, Pharisaeos, Scribas, genus hominum veriutum, venenatum, salsissimum; aliisque verborum suorum faxis, quoties ita ipsi visum est, pro egregio illo suo in Ecclesiam Dei Christi Zelo, lapidat innoxios; ex frontis, opinor, duritia fidem arbitratus facere se posse lectori, ut quod impudenter scriberet, vere scribere existimaretur: immemor prorsus admonitionis Apostolicae: Servum Domini non oportet esse litigiosum, sed placidum erga omnes, aptum ad docendum, tolerantem malos, cum lenitate erudientem eos qui contrario animo affecti sunt.
units.tr: Colloquy of Mömpelgard. Huber. He calls them seducers, Pharisees, scribes, a race of men that is poisonous, venomous and most salty. With other darts of his words, whenever it seems good to him, in his notable zeal for the Church of Christ, he stones the innocent. He thinks, I suppose, from the hardness of his forehead, that he can make the reader believe, so that what he writes shamelessly may be taken to be written truly. He is wholly forgetful of the apostolic admonition: The servant of the Lord must not be quarrelsome, but gentle towards all, apt to teach, patient with the wicked, instructing with gentleness those who are opposed to him.

units.la: Hoc Theologi officium est. Conuicia autem, maledicta, sannas, Sarcasmos, obtrectationes, & quicquid caninae loquentiae est, βωμολόχοι & scurrae sibi habeat. Collatio, inquit Ambrosius inter Dei servos esse debet, non altercatio. Necesse est enim ut contentio extorqueat aliquid, imo multa, quae dicuntur contra conscientiam, ut intus in animo perdat, foris victor abscedat. Nemo enim patitur se vinci, licet sciat vera quae audit.
units.tr: This is the office of a theologian. As for insults, curses, sneers, sarcasms, slanders, and whatever belongs to dog-like talk, let the buffoons [βωμολόχοι] and the jesters keep them to themselves. A conference, says Ambrose, ought to be among the servants of God, not a wrangle. For it is necessary that contention wrings something out, indeed many things that are said against one's conscience, so that a man loses inwardly and leaves outwardly as the victor. For no one suffers himself to be beaten, even when he knows that what he hears is true.

units.la: Ambrof. in 2. cap. poster ad Timoth.
units.tr: Ambrose, on the second chapter of the second letter to Timothy.
1 Tim. 2.

units.la: Nos igitur de re ipsa dicamus. Maledictis enim & conuiciis respondebit qui dixit, Mea est vltio, ego rependam: quem eundem propter Christum, qui nobis nostra condonauit peccata, ex animo precamur, vt grauissimas illas iniurias quibus aduersarij nos afficiùt, ipsis condonet, dissidia tollat, caritatem autem & pacem in veritate inter Ecclesias sarciat, vt vno ore glorificemus Deum, ac patrem Domini nostri Iesu Christi, & alij alios assumamus, sicut nos Christus assumsit in gloriam Dei.
units.tr: Let us therefore speak about the matter itself. For he who said, Vengeance is mine, I will repay, will answer insults and abuse with abuse. We pray from the heart, for the sake of Christ who forgave us our sins, that this same God would forgive our opponents the very grave injuries they inflict on us, would remove the divisions, and would restore charity and peace in truth among the Churches, so that with one mouth we may glorify God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, and that we may receive one another, as Christ received us to the glory of God.
Rom. 15.

units.la: Rem ergo cum re, causam cum causa collaturi, a statu controuersiae ordiamur. Quaeritur, An Christus pro omniu redemtione passus sit nec ne?
units.tr: Let us therefore set matter against matter and cause against cause, and begin from the state of the controversy. The question is: Did Christ suffer for the redemption of all, or not?

units.la: Hic statim clamitant isti, Caluinistas (sic nos in odium veritatis vocant) in passionem Domini Iesu Christi furentes, palam negare Iesum Christum mortuum pro peccatis totius mundi. Item, Caluinistas tum dissimulanter, tu aperte negare Christum passum & mortuum pro omnibus hominibus.
units.tr: At once they cry out that we Calvinists (for so they call us, in hatred of the truth) rage against the passion of the Lord Jesus Christ, and openly deny that Jesus Christ died for the sins of the whole world. Likewise, they charge that we Calvinists, some covertly and some openly, deny that Christ suffered and died for all men.

units.la: Verum in ipso, quod dicitur, limine impingunt, talsam nobis sententiam affingentes, contra quam postea Anda-batarum more perpetuo luctantur. Etenim nos libenter locutiones istas agnoscimus, quod Christus propitiatio sit pro peccatis totius mundi, & semetipsum dederit redemtionis pretium pro omnibus. Quis enim neget, quod totidem verbis scriptura expressum esse voluit? Sed de sensu dictorum quaeritur. Ut enim impudentiae notam non effugerit, qui, quod scriptura exprimit, inficietur: ita videndum, ne non intelligentes quod scribitur, repugnantiam aliquam scripturae inesse arbitremur. Nam eadem scriptura canonica, quae Christum pro omnibus mortuum perhibet, atque ita omnibus communem quadantenus redemtionem facit, restringit aliis locis proprietatem redemtionis ad Ecclesiam. Pauli verba sunt Eph.5. Christus dilexit Ecclesiam, & semetipsum exposuit pro ea, ut eam sanctificaret, ac sisteret eam sibi gloriosam. Ibidem, Christus est caput Ecclesiae, & servator corporis. Et 1.Tim.4. Servator omnium hominum ... dicitur omnium hominum, at maxime fide- lium. Item ad Heb.9. Ob id noui fœderis mediator est, vt morte intercedente ad redem- tionem prauaricationum, vocati promissio- nem accipiant æternæ hæreditatis. De qui-bus etiam vocatis recte accipitur, quod in fine eiusde capitis legitur Christus semel oblatus, vt multorum peccata tol-leret. Quid quod Christus in solemni sua intercessione nominatim pro suis, & non pro mundo rogauit? Non pro mundo rogo, inquit, sed pro iis, quos dedisti mihi. Intercessio autem & oblatio Christi pro nobis, partes sunt Pontificatus ipsius inter se inseparabiles. Taceo alia id genus testimonia suo loco proferenda.
units.tr: But they stumble at the very threshold of what they say, attributing to us an opinion that is false, and afterwards they struggle against it perpetually, like the Andabatae. For we gladly acknowledge those phrases: that Christ is the propitiation for the sins of the whole world, and that he gave himself as the price of redemption for all. For who would deny what Scripture has expressed in so many words? But the question is about the sense of these statements. Just as he will not escape the mark of shamelessness who denies what Scripture expresses, so we must take care that, not understanding what is written, we do not suppose there is some contradiction in Scripture. For the same canonical Scripture which declares that Christ died for all, and so makes redemption in some measure common to all, restricts the particular character of redemption to the Church in other places. The words of Paul in Ephesians 5: Christ loved the Church and gave himself up for her, that he might sanctify her and present her to himself in glory. And in the same place: Christ is the head of the Church and the Saviour of the body. And in 1 Timothy 4: the Saviour of all men ... it is said of all men, but especially of the faithful. Likewise in Hebrews 9: For this reason he is the mediator of a new covenant, so that, death having intervened for the redemption of transgressions, those who are called may receive the promise of the eternal inheritance. And it is rightly understood of these called ones what is read at the end of the same chapter, that Christ, once offered, bore the sins of many. What of the fact that in his solemn intercession Christ prayed by name for his own, and not for the world? I do not pray for the world, he says, but for those whom you have given me. Now the intercession and the offering of Christ for us are inseparable parts of his priesthood. I pass over other testimonies of this kind, which will be brought forward in their proper place.

units.la: Cum igitur scriptura diuina hic, quæ-admodum & alibi, non rixosos disputatores, sed intelligentes lectores requirat: veteres pro horum explicatione adhibuerunt distinctionem sufficientiæ, & efficientiæ.
units.tr: Since, then, the divine Scripture here, as elsewhere, requires not quarrelsome disputants but intelligent readers, the ancients, for the explanation of these matters, made use of the distinction between sufficiency and efficacy.

units.la: Thomas Aquinas doctrinæ scholasticæ princeps, qui floruit ab hinc annis cccc. super 5. caput Apocalypseos ea de
units.tr: Thomas Aquinas, the prince of scholastic teaching, who flourished about four hundred years ago, on the fifth chapter of the Apocalypse, writes on this matter as follows:

units.la: {i} Ioh.17. ea de re in hunc modum scribit: Depaf- fione Domini, inquit, loqui est duplicitèr: Aut fecundum fufficientiam, & sic passio redemit omnes. Omnibus enim redimendis & saluandis sufficiens est, etiamsi plures effent mundi: vt dicit Anfelmus lib.2. cur Deus homo, cap.14. Aut fecundum efficientiam, & sic non omnes redemti sunt per passionem, quia non omnes adhærent redemtori, & ideo non omnes habent efficaciam redemtionis. Idem parte 3. summæ quæst. 1. art. 3. cum dixisset Christum venille in hunc mundu ad deletione omniu peccatoru, fele explicans subiecit hæc verba: non quod omnium pec deleantur, quod est propter defectum homi-nu, qui Christo non inhærent: Sed quia ipse exhibuit, quod sufficiens fuit ad omnium peccatorum deletionem. Quo referantur etiam quæ scribit quæstione 49. articulis 1.3.5. Christus liberauit nos, inquit, tanquam membra sua à peccatis, & effectum suum in illis sortitur passio, qui ei incorporantur, vt membra corpori, & sic passioni ipsius communicant. Qui autem passioni Christi non coniunguntur, effectum eius percipere non possunt.
units.tr: {i} John 17. Speaking of the passion of the Lord, he says, is twofold: either according to sufficiency, and in this way the passion redeemed all. For it is sufficient for the redemption and salvation of all, even if there were more worlds, as Anselm says in book 2 of Why God Became Man, chapter 14. Or according to efficacy, and in this way not all have been redeemed by the passion, because not all cling to the Redeemer, and therefore not all have the efficacy of redemption. The same, in part 3 of the Summa, question 1, article 3, after saying that Christ came into this world to blot out the sins of all, explaining himself, added these words: not that the sins of all are blotted out, which is due to the defect of men who do not cling to Christ; but because he himself offered what was sufficient for the blotting out of the sins of all. To this also belongs what he writes in question 49, articles 1, 3 and 5: Christ freed us, he says, as his members from sins, and his passion produces its effect in those who are incorporated into him, as members into a body, and so they share in his passion. But those who are not joined to the passion of Christ cannot receive its effect.

units.la: Sed
units.tr: But

units.la: Sed audiamus & alios Thoma antiquiores. Innocentius III. qui sedit anno Domini ducentesimo supra mille–simum, eandem distinctionem inculcans, inquit lib.2. de officio Missæ cap. 41. Sanguis Christi pro solis prædestinatis effusus est, quantum ad efficientiam; sed pro cunctis hominibus effusus est, quantum ad sufficientiam. Effusio quippe sanguinis iusti tam fuit dives ad pretium, ut, si universitas captivorum in redemptorem suum crederet, nullum tyrannica vincula retinerent, quia, sicut Apostolus ait, ubi abundavit peccatum, superabundavit & gratia. Est autem posterior ista sententia tota Leonis Papæ epistola 83 & 97, quam cum Innocentius adducat, satis innuit eandem Leonis fuisse sententiam.
units.tr: Let us hear others too, older than Thomas. Innocent III, who held the papacy in the year of the Lord 1200, insisting on the same distinction, says in book 2 of On the Office of the Mass, chapter 41: The blood of Christ was poured out for the predestined alone, as to its efficacy; but it was poured out for all men, as to its sufficiency. The effusion of the blood of the just was so rich in its price that, if the whole multitude of captives had believed in their redeemer, no tyrannical chains would have held them, because, as the Apostle says, where sin abounded, grace did much more abound. That latter opinion is the whole of Pope Leo's letters 83 and 97, which Innocent cites; and by citing it, he sufficiently indicates that this was also Leo's view.

units.la: His non absimile est, quod apud Basilium scribitur in Psalm. 48. Non dabit homo Deo propitiationem pro se ipso. Unum tamen inventum est pro omnibus simul hominibus dignum precium, sanguis Domini nostri Iesu Christi, quem pro nobis omnibus effudit. Quod de sufficientia & dignitate precij loquatur, ex verbis ipsis patet, & ex eo, quòd alibi làpiffimè ad ef-ficientiam relpicies, definit, sanguinem Christi nō pro omnibus sine exceptio-ne hominibus, sed pro multis, nempe credentibus effusum.
units.tr: Not unlike this is what is written in Basil on Psalm 48: A man cannot give God a propitiation for himself. Yet one price has been found, worthy for all men together: the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, which he poured out for us all. That he is speaking of sufficiency and worth of price is clear from these very words, and from the fact that elsewhere, plainly looking to efficacy, he states that the blood of Christ was poured out not for all men without exception, but for many, namely those who believe.

units.la: Chrysoft. quoque, & huius abbre-uiator Theophylactus, distinctionem eandem agnoscunt, vt in progressu vi-debimus.
units.tr: Chrysostom too, and his abridger Theophylact, acknowledge the same distinction, as we shall see as we go on.

units.la: Porrò Augustinus, veterum Orthodoxorum facile princeps, distinctione illam non agnoscit solum, verumetiam multis explicat, Tom. 7. ad articulos falsò ipsi impositos: quorum sane primus erat, quòd dicebatur astruere, Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum non pro omnium hominum redemtione esse passum. Verum distinguit ille in hunc modum: Quod, inquit, ad magnitudinem & potentiam pretij, & quod ad unam perti-net causam generis humani, sanguis Christi redemtio est totius mundi, & sic omnes recte redemti dicuntur. Quoniam tamen non omnes captivitate eruti sunt, multique redemtionis alieni sunt, redemtionis proprietas haud dubie penes illos est, de quibus princeps mundi emissus. emissus est foras, & iam non vasa Diaboli, sed membra sunt Christi, cuius mors non impensa est humano generi, ut ad redemptionem eius etiam qui regenerandi non erant pertinerent, sed ita ut quod per unicum exemplum gestum est pro universis, per singulare sacramentum celebraretur in singulis. Hoc idem est, ac si dixisset, Quod ad sufficientiam precij, redemptionem esse omnium, quod ad effectum vero, non omnium, sed membrorum dumtaxat Christi. Et mox simili rem illustrat, inquiens: poculum quippe immortalitatis, quod confectum est de infirmitate nostra & virtute divina, habet quidem in se ut omnibus prosit: sed si non bibitur, non proficit.
units.tr: Moreover Augustine, the easy chief of the ancient orthodox writers, not only acknowledges that distinction but explains it in many places, in volume 7, against the articles falsely imputed to him; of which the first, surely, was that he was said to assert that our Lord Jesus Christ did not suffer for the redemption of all men. But he distinguishes in this way: As to the magnitude and power of the price, and as far as it concerns the one cause of the human race, the blood of Christ is the redemption of the whole world, and so all are rightly said to be redeemed. Yet since not all have been snatched from captivity, and many are strangers to redemption, the proper benefit of redemption undoubtedly belongs to those of whom the prince of the world has been cast out. He has been cast out, and they are no longer vessels of the devil but members of Christ, whose death was not intended for the human race in such a way that those who were not to be regenerated also belonged to its redemption; rather, what was done once for all by a unique example was to be celebrated in each individual by a particular sacrament. This is the same as if he had said: as to the sufficiency of the price, it is the redemption of all; but as to the effect, it is not of all, but only of the members of Christ. And soon after he illustrates the matter with a similar image, saying: The cup of immortality, which is made from our weakness and divine power, indeed has in itself the power to benefit all; but if it is not drunk, it does not profit.

units.la: Atque hanc distinctionem, tritam sane, peruetustam, atque vtilem, & hoc nomine diligenter retinendam, neoterici quoque probarunt.
units.tr: This distinction, certainly well worn, very ancient, and useful, and on that account to be carefully retained, the moderns too have approved.

units.la: Stapulensis in epist. ad Rom. 5. adhibita quoque simili tudine rem declarans, sicut lux, inquit, infinitas potis est propulsare tenebras, licet non omnium oculi illuminentur: ita Christus apud se habet omnium redemptionem, non solum nobis, sed & innu-
units.tr: Stapulensis, in his commentary on Romans 5, also declaring the matter by a similar comparison: As light, though infinite, is able to drive out darkness, although not all eyes are illumined, so Christ has in himself the redemption of all, not only for us but also for innumerable

units.la: E ij memeris etiam mundis redimendis sufficietem, licet propria quadam peruersitate non omnes eius fiant participes. Nec aliter Caluinus, Beza, Grynæus, aliijq; nostræ confessionis Theologi, qui ab aduersariis odiosè iactantur, quasi simpliciter, & absque omni distinctione statuant, Christum nō esse mortuum pro omnibus. Quod falsò iis impingi, latebitur, quisquis loca autorum, quorum nunc metio facta est, expenderit: Calu.in 1.Ioh.2. Beza in 2. Corin.5.verf.15. & pluribus ad acta colloquij Mompelgar. parte altera sol. 217 & 221. Gryn.in thesauro thesium, classis 1. thesi 13. Tossanus thesi 31. in disput. de loco Pauli 1.Cor.15. sicut in Adam omnes moriuntur &c. Zanch. lib.2. Miscell.pag.312. & Pet. Mart. loco de praedestinatione ad Rom.9. Iis locis nominati scriptores, quèadmodū & aliis nostrorum complures in suis scriptis, vnanimiter retinent vulgatam distinctionem sufficientiæ & efficientiæ, minimè certè in hac disputatione repudiadam.
units.tr: other worlds to be redeemed, sufficient, although by some perversity of their own not all become partakers of it. Nor do Calvin, Beza, Grynaeus, and the other theologians of our confession differ from this, though they are odiously bandied about by our adversaries, as if they simply and without any distinction maintained that Christ did not die for all. That this is falsely imputed to them will become clear to anyone who weighs the passages of the authors just mentioned: Calvin on 1 John 2; Beza on 2 Cor. 5:15, and more in the Acts of the Montbéliard colloquy, part two, pages 217 and 221; Grynaeus, Thesaurus thesium, class 1, thesis 13; Tossanus, thesis 31, in his disputation on 1 Cor. 15, "as in Adam all die," etc.; Zanchi, book 2 of Miscellanea, page 312; and Peter Martyr, on predestination, on Romans 9. In these places the named writers, as well as many others of ours in their writings, unanimously retain the common distinction between sufficiency and efficiency, which is by no means to be rejected in this dispute.

units.la: Tantùm candidè & sine Sophistica accipiantur vocabula sufficienter, & efficienter. Sufficienter, id est, Augustino interprete,quod ad magnitudinem & po tentiam pretij attinet, seu, vt Thomas declarat,quatenus ipse exhibuit, quod erat sufficiens ad omnium peccatorum deletionem. Efficienter vero, seu vt alij loquuntur, efficaciter intelligatur respe-ctu effectus, qui in solis Christi membris reperitur, ceteris qui sine fide & regeneratione seculum hoc pertransi-eunt, redemtionis alienis exi stetibus, vt Augustinus etiam diserte scriptum reliquit.
units.tr: Let the words "sufficiently" and "efficiently" be taken candidly and without sophistry. "Sufficiently," that is, in Augustine's sense, refers to the magnitude and power of the price; or, as Thomas explains, insofar as he offered what was sufficient for the blotting out of all sins. Efficiently, or, as others put it, effectively, is to be understood with respect to the effect, which is found only in the members of Christ, while the rest, who pass through this age without faith and regeneration, remain strangers to redemption, as Augustine too plainly left written.

units.la: Hic vero aduersariorum sententia est, Christum sine discrimine pro omnium hominum peccatis esse mortuum, & omnia omnium hominum peccata, non modo sufficienter, verum etiam sufficienter expiasse. Quod sic declarant, patrem in coelis cum omnibus & singulis hominibus, absque vllo fidei vel incredulitatis respectu, ipso facto reconciliationem instituisse. Ceterum qui fide recipiant istam reconciliationem cum Deo per hostiâ Christi sancitam, in iis efficacem manere : qui vero per incredulitatem respuant, in his aboleri,& tolli, non aliter quàm si pro multis ægrotis commune sit balneum instru- ctum, in quo omnes ipso facto sanitati restituatur, & horum alij per intempe- rantiam recuperata sanitate rursus excidant, quæ in aliis temperanter viuen- tibus permaneat. Quod simile non parum profecto senserunt ab iis, qui- bus Augustinus & Stapulensis supra vtebantur.
units.tr: But the opinion of our adversaries is this: that Christ died without distinction for the sins of all men, and that he has expiated all the sins of all men, not only sufficiently but also effectively. They explain this by saying that the Father in heaven, with all and each of men, established reconciliation by the very fact, without any regard to faith or unbelief. But those who receive this reconciliation with God, sanctioned by the sacrifice of Christ, through faith, in them it remains effective; but those who reject it through unbelief, in them it is abolished and taken away. It is like a common bath prepared for many sick people, in which all are restored to health by the very fact; yet some of them, through intemperance, lose their recovered health again, while it remains in others who live temperately. Those from whom Augustine and Stapulensis were quoted above have certainly not thought very differently from this.

units.la: Quin etiam profitentur & scribunt aperte Christum non minus pro omnibus iam tum damnatis & in posterum damnandis, esse passum, crucifixu, mortuum, & pro peccatis illorum satisfecisse, quàm pro peccatis Petri, Pauli & omnium sanctorum: id est, Christum non tantum dedisse, quod sufficies erat pro omnium peccatorum deletione, sed etiam re ipsa non minus damnatorum, & damnandorum, quàm seruatorum & seruandorum peccata sanguine ipsius deleta. Quod autem illi nihilominus condemnentur, fieri statuunt, non propter illorum peccata, utpote à Christo re ipsa expiata, sed propter solam incredulitatem dulidulitatem, qua factam & praestitam reconciliationem denuò euertant & inefficacem reddant.
units.tr: Indeed they even profess and openly write that Christ suffered, was crucified, and died no less for all those already condemned and to be condemned in the future, and satisfied for their sins, than for the sins of Peter, Paul, and all the saints. That is, Christ gave not only what was sufficient for the blotting out of all sins, but also, in fact, the sins of the damned and those to be damned were blotted out by his blood no less than those of the saved and those to be saved. Yet they maintain that those others are nevertheless condemned, not on account of their sins, as these were in fact expiated by Christ, but on account of unbelief alone, by which they again overturn the reconciliation made and offered and render it ineffective.

units.la: Haec sententia fuit Iacobi Andreae in colloquio Mompelgart: quam eandem Huberus thesi 19. hunc in modum proponit: Christum videlicet passum & mortuum esse non pro aliquibus tantum hominibus, sed pro omnibus Adami posteris, nullo, &c, vt clarissime dicatur, nullo penitus ex tota humani generis vniuersitate excepto, siue salutem per fidem sibi vendicet, atque in salute accepta maneat, seu per incredulitatem, salutem sibi praestitam respuat, atque ea propter denuò in aeternum pereat. Videmus, vt audacter statuat, indifferenter omnes & singulos, credentes & incredulos, salutem re ipsa in Christo consequutos, sed alios in salute accepta manere credendo, alios ea denuò priuari non credendo. Idem in compendio thes.19. Asseueramus, inquit, Christum sua morte omnium re ipsa & opere ipso esse misertum, & se ipsum non minus, pro quouis infideli, quàm
units.tr: This was the view of Jacob Andreae at the Montbéliard colloquy; and Huber proposes the same in thesis 19 in this manner: that Christ, namely, suffered and died not for some men only, but for all the posterity of Adam, with no one excepted, as it may be stated most clearly, with no one at all excepted from the whole of the human race, whether he claims salvation for himself through faith and remains in the salvation received, or through unbelief rejects the salvation offered to him and therefore perishes again forever. We see how boldly he asserts that all and each, believers and unbelievers alike, have in fact obtained salvation in Christ, but that some remain in the salvation received by believing, and others, by not believing, are again deprived of it. In the summary of thesis 19 he likewise says: "We assert that Christ by his death has in fact and in deed had mercy on all of them, and has given himself up as a sacrifice for sins, no less for any unbeliever than for any believer,

units.la: pro quouis fideli, tradidisse victimam pro peccatis, nimirum vt omnes quot-quot sunt homines, liberaret a morte, Diabolo & inferno: intelligit re ipsa & opere ipso, vt loqui solet, & non suffi-cienter duntaxat.
units.tr: namely that he might free all who are men from death, the devil and hell. He means this in fact and in deed, as they habitually say, and not merely sufficiently."
