units.la: Et vt nihil sit obscurum, contendit in omnes peccatores pertinere operationem salutis per Christum, & quibus peccatum per Adam, eis etiam iustitiam per Christum adscribendam: omne item iudicium, iramque diuinam in vniuersis hominibus esse sublatam atque deletam re ipsa & proprie: omnesque simul per mortem Christi vere & indubitanter ab omni peccato & condemnatione liberatos, & re ipsa totum genus humanum in gratiam & finum patris receptum: omnes ad salutis communionem, & regnum gratiae pertinere: denique omnes, reprobos & electos, aeque per Christum saluatos: siue scilicet credant, siue non: & quae alia huiusmodi plane cruda atque ἀσέβημα pasim apud eum occurrunt.
units.tr: And so that nothing may be unclear, he contends that the working of salvation through Christ extends to all sinners, and that righteousness through Christ must be ascribed to all those to whom sin came through Adam. He holds likewise that all judgment and divine wrath has been removed and blotted out from all men, in very fact and properly, and that all have together been truly and beyond doubt freed from all sin and condemnation through the death of Christ, and that the whole human race has in very fact been received into grace and the Father's favour. All, he says, belong to the communion of salvation and the kingdom of grace. Finally, all, reprobate and elect alike, are saved through Christ, whether they believe or not. And there are other things of this kind, plainly crude and impious (ἀσέβημα), which occur everywhere in him.

units.la: Huic nos opinioni, vt novae & inaudi-tae &c tæ,& multis,vt patebit,modis erroneæ, subscribere non possumus: sed veterem sequentes distinctione afferimus,Christum sane exhibuisse quod sufficiens erat ad omnium peccatorum deletionem, & sic deleta omnia peccata; omnésque redemtos,quod attinet ad sufficientiam,seu magnitudinem,& potentia pretij,vt Augustinus exponit. Quod ad efficientiam vero, dicimus morte Christi deleta solû peccata electorum, qui in ipsum credunt,ipsíque tanquam membra capiti inhærent: qui autem Christo non incorporantur, effectum passionis ipsius percipere non possunt. Nam dicente Domino, Sic Deus dilexit mundum, vt filium suum dederit, vt omnis qui credit in eum, non pereat, sed habeat vitam æternam. Qui credit non condemnatur, qui vero non credit, iam condemnatus est. Ioh.3. Quæ ibidem Baptista confirmans testatur: Qui credit in filium,habet vitam æternam :qui vero non credit filio, non videbit vitam,sed ira Dei manet super eum.
units.tr: We cannot subscribe to this opinion, which is new and unheard of and, as will appear, erroneous in many respects. Following the old distinction, we instead maintain that Christ indeed offered what was sufficient for the blotting out of all sins, and so all sins have been blotted out, and all are redeemed as far as sufficiency, that is, the magnitude and power of the price, is concerned, as Augustine explains. As to efficacy, however, we say that by the death of Christ only the sins of the elect have been blotted out, those who believe in him and cleave to him as members to their head. Those who are not incorporated into Christ cannot receive the effect of his passion. For the Lord says: God so loved the world that he gave his Son, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life. He who believes is not condemned, but he who does not believe is already condemned. John 3. The Baptist also confirms this and testifies: He who believes in the Son has eternal life; but he who does not believe the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him.

units.la: Atque hoc sensu,non autem absolute,& sine restrictione,accipiendum est, si quandoque apud nostros legitur, Christum non esse passum pro omnibus. quod nempe ad passionis effectum, qui non est damnandorum, sed seruandorum; fidelium, non infidelium. Et sic Beza etiam se declarat coll. Mompelgart. pag. 217. Atque in eo nihil est, quod non totidem verbis, & eodem sensu a veteribus scriptum sit.
units.tr: And this is the sense in which it must be understood, not absolutely and without qualification, whenever it is read among our people that Christ did not suffer for all. That is, it concerns the effect of the passion, which belongs not to the damned but to the saved, that is, to believers and not unbelievers. Beza also explains himself in this way in the Colloquy of Mompelgard, p. 217. And there is nothing in this that the ancients have not written in just the same words and with the same meaning.

units.la: Neque vero audiendi sunt cavillatores: Quid opus est, inquiunt, dicere, Christi precium esse sufficiens toti mundo? Quid fascinatis mortales istis vocabulis? Respondeo, non isthaec fascinatio est, sed controversiae huius vetusta & commoda explicatio contra eos, qui mudum novus opinionibus fascinare studeant.
units.tr: Nor indeed should the scoffers be listened to. "What need is there," they say, "to say that the price of Christ is sufficient for the whole world? Why do you bewitch mortals with these words?" I reply that this is not bewitching, but an old and useful explanation of this controversy, directed against those who strive to bewitch the world with new opinions.

units.la: At, inquiunt, vocabulum Sufficienter in ea significatione acceptum, in qua pia antiquitas accepit: non auersamur, sed probamus potius. Verum Calvinistae, aiunt, fabricantes sinistram & aequivocam vocabuli significationem, fucum eo simplicioribus faciunt. Hoc enim volunt, Christi mor-
units.tr: "But," they say, "we do not object to the word sufficiently taken in the sense in which pious antiquity took it; rather we approve of it. Yet the Calvinists, they say, fabricate a sinister and equivocal meaning of the word, and so make a veil of it for the simpler folk. For this is what they want: that the death of Christ"

units.la: Hub. cop. th. 5. & 6. mortem adeò esse potentem, vt, si ea vellet omnibus hominibus succurrere, perfacile id posset. Quod si vocabulo sufficientiæ in alia vterentur significatione, veluti cùm dicimus contra Papistas, mortem Christi sufficere pro omnibus hominibus, id est, nullo egere subsidio operum hominum ad redimendum nos: Vel etiam tali, cùm dicimus, mortem Christi sufficere pro omnibus, siue homines credant, & salui fiat, siue non credant, & pereant, Christum tamen satisfecisse pro omnibus, non recusaremus vocis istius vsum in tali significatione.
units.tr: Hub. cop. th. 5. & 6. is so powerful that, if it wished to help all men, it could very easily do so. But if they used the word sufficiency in another sense, as when we say against the Papists that the death of Christ suffices for all men, that is, that it needs no help from the works of men to redeem us; or again in such a sense as when we say that the death of Christ suffices for all, whether men believe and are saved or do not believe and perish, and that Christ nonetheless made satisfaction for all, we would not refuse the use of the word in that sense.

units.la: Sed satis liquere arbitror ex iis, quæ ante recitata sunt, quomodo antiquitas vocabulis istis sufficientiæ & efficientiæ vsa sit, nec quicquam nos in sensu mutare, aut fucum facere cuiquam æquivocatione. Interim res ipsa probat, fucũ hic fieri simplicioribus ab Antagonista, qui cùm videri velit vocabulum sufficientiæ in ea significatione, qua antiquitas illud accepit, probare; significationes tamen ex cerebro suo affingit antiquitati prorsus ignotas, in proposita quidem antithesi: Alioquin defendimus & nos contra Papistas, meritum Christi nullo egere subsidio operum humanorum; nec inficiamur, eum pro omnibus siue salui fiant, siue pereat, satisfecisse, quantum nempe ad sufficientiam & magnitudinem pretij, tam potentis atque diuitis ad redemtionem, vt si vniuersitas captiuorum in ipsum crederet, nullum diabolica vincula detinerent.
units.tr: But I think it is clear enough from what has been recited before how antiquity used these words of sufficiency and efficacy, and that we change nothing in the meaning or make a veil of equivocation for anyone. Meanwhile the thing itself shows that the veil is being made for the simpler folk by the Antagonist. Though he wishes to seem to prove the word sufficiency in the sense in which antiquity took it, he nevertheless invents meanings entirely unknown to antiquity, in the antithesis proposed. Otherwise we too defend against the Papists that the merit of Christ needs no help from human works, and we do not deny that he made satisfaction for all, whether they are saved or perish, as far as sufficiency and the magnitude of the price are concerned. That price is so powerful and rich for redemption that, if the whole multitude of captives believed in him, no diabolical chains would hold any of them.

units.la: CAPVT XII.
units.tr: CAPUT XII.

units.la: Alter modus vniuersalis redemtionis.
units.tr: The second way of universal redemption.

units.la: Asserimus & illud, quod licet non omnes, quotquot ex Adamo nascuntur, morte Christi efficaciter renascantur, redimantur, iustificentur; recte nihilominus dicatur, Christum pro omnibus mortuo, etiam quod ad effectum mortis, iustificationem, regenerationem, & similia beneficia. Non quod ad omnes & singulos homines illa redundent, sed ad omnes qui Christi sunt: sicut Apostolus dicit, si Deus pro nobis, quis contra nos? Qui etiam filio proprio non pepercit, sed pro nobis omnibus tradidit eum. Qui sunt illi omnes, quorum vox ea in ore est, & fiducia in corde, Si Deus pro nobis, quis cōtra nos? Nimirum ij quos praescidiuit, & praedestinauit, quos etiam vocat, iustificat, glorificat: electi Dei, quorum est salus & vita æterna, quibus nulla creatura separare potest à dilectione Dei in Christo, sicut ibidem dicitur. Quis intentabit crimina aduersus electos Dei?
units.tr: We assert also this: although not all who are born of Adam are effectually reborn, redeemed and justified by the death of Christ, it may nevertheless rightly be said that Christ died for all, even as regards the effect of his death: justification, regeneration and similar benefits. Not that these benefits flow out to all and each of men, but to all who belong to Christ. As the Apostle says: "If God is for us, who is against us? He who did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all." Who are those all, whose voice is this in the mouth and confidence in the heart: "If God is for us, who is against us?" Surely those whom he foreknew and predestined, whom he also calls, justifies and glorifies: the elect of God, whose is salvation and eternal life, from whom no creature can separate them from the love of God in Christ, as is said in the same place. "Who shall bring any charge against God's elect?"

units.la: Præclare autor librorum De vocatione gentium, homo iane pulcre doctus, & disertus, siue is fit Ambrosius, seu potius Prosper Aquitanicus, libro primo ca. 3. in hunc modum scribit: Habet ergo, inquit, populus Dei plenitudinem suam, & quamuis magna pars hominum saluantis gratiam aut repellat aut negligat: in electis tamen & præscitis, atque ab omnium generalitate discretis, specialis quædam censetur vniuersitas, vt de toto mundo totus mundus liberatus, & de omnibus hominibus omnes homines videantur assumti. Vbi notemus duplicem, imò triplicem vniuersitatem: nempe vniuersitatem, seu generalita- tem omnium hominum: vniuersitate item electorum qui seruantur: & vice versa, vniuersitatem reproborum, qui pereunt. De his tam electis quàm re- probis, vt idem autor probè obseruat, diuinus stylus locutionem suam ita or- dinat, vt & ea quæ de parte quadam ho- minum dicuntur, ad omnes pertinere vi- deatur: & cum alij sint qui pereunt, alij qui seruantur, neutra tamè pars nuncu- patione omnium hominum priuetur, habere quidem salutis suę damnum re- bellium portione, sed obtinente pleni- tudinis censum fidelium dignitate.
units.tr: The author of the books On the Calling of the Gentiles, a man excellently learned and eloquent, whether he is Ambrose or rather Prosper of Aquitaine, writes in book one, chapter 3, in this manner: "The people of God therefore has its fullness, and although a great part of mankind either rejects or neglects the grace that saves, yet among the elect and foreknown, and distinguished from the general mass of all, a certain special universality is reckoned, so that from the whole world the whole world is seen to be set free, and from all men all men are seen to be taken up." Here we should note a twofold, indeed a threefold, universality: namely, the universality or generality of all men; the universality of the elect who are saved; and conversely, the universality of the reprobate who perish. Concerning both these elect and reprobate, as the same author rightly observes, the divine style so orders its speech that what is said of a certain part of men seems to pertain to all; and although some perish and others are saved, neither part is deprived of the name of all men, the one possessing the loss of its own salvation in the portion of the rebellious, the other holding the estimate of fullness by the dignity of the faithful.

units.la: Sed exemplorum appositione res fiet illustrior. Dicente Domino Ioh.12. Cum exaltatus fuero à terra, omnia (seu se- cundum alteram lectionem, omnes) traham ad me: nonne vniuersorum vide- tur promissa conuersio? Et tamè multa ad huc hominum millia dæmoniis, & mundo seruiunt. Sed rectè cum Augu- stino intelligimus, Omnia, id est, omnes prædestinatos ad salutem, ex quibus omomnibus nihil est periturum.
units.tr: But the matter will become clearer by the adducing of examples. The Lord says in John 12: "When I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all (or, according to another reading, all men) to me." Does not this seem to be a promise of the conversion of all? And yet many thousands of men still serve demons and the world. But we rightly understand with Augustine that "all" means all the predestined to salvation, of whom none will perish.

units.la: Ita quod scriptum est in Prophetis, Erunt omnes ἅγιοι τοῦ θεοῦ, docti à Deo: & omnes cognoscent me à minimo vsque ad maximum: similiter utrumque verum est de hominibus regni illius, secundum limitationem Augustini Tract. 26. Vide etiam Athanasium de tribus his dictis iam allegatis in Evangelio de passione & cruce Domini. Quid, cum dicitur, Et veniet omnis caro in conspectum meum, vt adorent in Hierusalem, dicit Dominus, Aut illud, Et erit in diebus novissimis effundam de Spiritu meo super omnem carne: Aut illud Alleuat Dominus omnes qui corruunt, & erigit omnes elisos, nūquid non ita hęc pronunciantur, quasi ab hoc Dei munere nemo discretus sit? Eiusmodi & illa sunt: Donec occurramus omnes in vnitatem fidei, & agnitionis filii Dei in virum perfectū: Vetera transierunt, & ecce omnia facta sunt noua: Bibite ex eo omnes &c. nunquid etiā incredūli, & palam scelerati?
units.tr: So too what is written in the Prophets, "They shall all be holy ἅγιοι τοῦ θεοῦ, taught of God," and "they shall all know me, from the least to the greatest," both are true in the same way of the men of that kingdom, according to the limitation of Augustine in Tractate 26. See also Athanasius on these three sayings already cited, in his work on the passion and cross of the Lord. What of when it is said, "All flesh shall come before me to worship in Jerusalem, says the Lord," or that other, "And it shall come to pass in the last days that I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh," or that, "The Lord lifts up all who fall and raises up all who are bowed down"? Are not these statements made as though no one were excluded from this gift of God? Such also are these: "Until we all come to the unity of faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to a perfect man"; "Old things have passed away, and behold, all things have become new"; "Drink of it, all of you," etc. Are not these also said of unbelievers and openly wicked men?

units.la: De impiorum vniuersitate ad eundem modum sacrę loquuntur literę: vt ad Philip.2. Omnes quæ sua sunt quærunt. Ioh.3. Testimonium eius nemo accipit. Si nemo, vt quid de cœlo venit? Quorūdam ergo nemo, quia est quidam populus præparatus ad iram Dei, damnandus cum diabolis: horum nemo accipit testimonium Christi, ait Augusti. Tract. 14.
units.tr: The sacred letters speak in the same way of the universality of the wicked: as in Philippians 2, "All seek their own things"; John 3, "No one receives his testimony." If no one, why did he come from heaven? Therefore "no one" refers to certain people: since there is a certain people prepared for the wrath of God, to be damned with the devils, none of these receives the testimony of Christ, says Augustine in Tractate 14.

units.la: Plura alia exempla autor de vocatione gentium adducit. Quibus omnibus demonstratur pro parte hominum omnes homines sæpissime in scripturis nominari, quorum tamen discretionem scriptura cito aperit, vt sensus legentis ab vniuersitatis appellatione ad parte, quę intelligenda est, transferatur. Hinc Dialectici quoque præcipiunt de restringendo signo vniuersali ad subiectum, fecundum regulam: Talia sunt prædicata, qualia permittuntur esse à suis subiectis. Quæ præceptio non in hoc tantum proposito de electis atque reprobis, credentibus, atque incredulis; locum habet, sed passim quoque alias, vt cum dicitur, omnia munda mundis: omnia mihi licent, &c.
units.tr: The author of On the Calling of the Gentiles adduces many other examples. By all of these it is shown that for a part of men, all men are very often named in the Scriptures, yet Scripture quickly reveals their distinction, so that the reader's sense is transferred from the name of universality to the part that is to be understood. Hence the dialecticians also teach the restriction of a universal sign to its subject, according to the rule: "Predicates are such as their subjects allow them to be." This rule holds not only in this matter of the elect and reprobate, believers and unbelievers, but also elsewhere everywhere, as when it is said, "To the pure all things are pure"; "All things are lawful for me," etc.

units.la: CAP.
units.tr: CAP.

units.la: CAPVT XIII. Alij aliquot modi de vniuersalitate redemtionis.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIII. Several other ways of understanding the universality of redemption.

units.la: Asserimus porrò, ex vsu scriptu-rarum, & piæ antiquitatis rectè dici Christum pro omnibus mortuum, omnesque morte ipsius redimi & seruari: per distributionem commodam, vt loquuntur, quatenus videlicet omnes, qui redimuntur, & seruantur, redemtionem & salutem non nisi in Christo assequuntur, per sanguinem ipsius. Omnis enim redemtio (vt loquitur Cyrillus) in Christo est, & per ipsum omne donum bonum.
units.tr: We further assert that, from the usage of Scripture and of pious antiquity, it is rightly said that Christ died for all, and that all are redeemed and saved by his death: by a convenient distribution, as they say, namely inasmuch as all who are redeemed and saved obtain redemption and salvation only in Christ, through his blood. For all redemption (as Cyril says) is in Christ, and through him every good gift.

units.la: In hunc sensum Apostolica dicta, omnes in Christo viuificari & iustificari, Augustinus passim explicat, vt pluribus post videbimus: quia, inquit, sicut omnes, qui moriuntur, non nisi in Adam moriuntur, ita omnes, qui viuificantur, non nisi in Christo viuificabuntur. Et hoc eodem locutionis genere idem de peccatorum meritis, & remissione lib.1. ca.25.
units.tr: Augustine explains the apostolic sayings that all are made alive and justified in Christ in this sense, in many places, as we shall see later. Because, he says, just as all who die die only in Adam, so all who are made alive will be made alive only in Christ. The same author, by this same manner of speaking, On the merits and remission of sins, bk. 1, ch. 25.

units.la: F exexponit illud apud Iohannem 1. Illuminat omnem hominem venientem in hunc mundum. Ideo nempe id dictum est, inquit, quia nullus hominum illuminatur, nisi illo lumine veritatis. Scio Theophylactum & alios quosdam dictum illud ad lumen rationis, tanquam interioris oculi, referre: cuius expositionis & Augustinus meminit. Sed nobis hic satis est, cum etiam altero modo verba Euangelistæ recte accipiantur, locutionis huius vsum ostendisse.
units.tr: Augustine expounds that passage of John 1, He enlightens every man coming into this world. That was said, he says, because no man is enlightened except by that light of truth. I know that Theophylact and some others refer that saying to the light of reason, as of the inner eye, and Augustine also mentions this explanation. But for us it is enough here that, since the words of the evangelist are also rightly taken in the other way, we have shown the usage of this manner of speaking.

units.la: Manifestius exemplum habemus 1. Corint. 12. Omnia operatur in omnibus. Vbi duplici adeo limitatione opus; Omnia, id est, facultates & dona quæcunque in quibuscunque efficit. Nemini enim largitur omnia, nedum omnia omnibus: sed quicquid gratiæ aut facultatis spiritualis est in quocunque, ab ipso est. Philippus in paruis logicalibus exemplum adfert ex Ioh. 1. Ex plenitudine eius omnes accepimus, & monet exclusiue id dictū: contrahi enim vniuersalem ad certam speciem, & significari aliorum exclusionem: Quotquot accepimus gratia, à solo Christo omnes accepimus. Tanquam si dicamus de vno literarum magistro in ciuitate aliqua, Omnes iste literas hic docet : aut de vna aliqua obstetrice in ciuitate: obstetrix illa omnes excipit: aut sicut dicere possumus, In aliquam domum omnes per vnam ianuam intrare. Ifthæc omnia, & similia recte dicuntur: nec tamen intelligere possumus omnes, nisi qui literas discunt, & qui in ciuitate illa nascuntur: aut in domum eandem intrant. Similiter omnes Christus iustificat, quatenus nemo iustificatur, nisi per ipsum. Ac diligenter Augustinus hoc vrget contra Pelagianos, sentientes non omnes, sed multos per Christum liberari: siquidem aliquos etiā extra Christum per naturam & liberum arbitrium, & legem; siue naturalem, siue per Mosen datam, seruari volebant, licet interim fatentur commodiorem esse salutis viam per Christum.
units.tr: We have a clearer example in 1 Cor. 12: He works all things in all. Here a double limitation is needed: All things means whatever faculties and gifts he produces in whomever. For he does not bestow all things on anyone, much less all things on all; but whatever grace or spiritual ability there is in anyone, it is from him. Philip, in his small logical works, gives an example from John 1, From his fullness we have all received, and notes that the statement is exclusive: the universal is restricted to a certain kind, and the exclusion of others is signified. (As many as received grace, we all received from Christ alone.) It is as if we say of one teacher of letters in some city, This man teaches all these letters here; or of one midwife in a city, that midwife delivers all; or as we can say, All enter one house through one door. These and similar things are rightly said, yet we can understand all only of those who learn letters, and who are born in that city, or who enter that same house. Similarly, Christ justifies all, inasmuch as no one is justified except through him. Augustine presses this carefully against the Pelagians, who held that not all but many are freed through Christ, since they wanted some to be saved even outside Christ, through nature, free will and the law, whether natural or given through Moses, although they meanwhile admitted that the way of salvation through Christ is more convenient.

units.la: In hunc sensum etiam Hilarius scribit Commentariis in Matth. Canone 7. Salus gentium omnis ex fide est, & in præceptis DomiDomini vita est vniuersorum. Sed clarius aliquanto Ambrosius lib.9.Epift.71. Ve-niens, inquit, Dominus Iesus, peccatum omnibus, quod nemo poterat vitare, donauit, & totius mundi peccatum abstulit, testificante Ioanne. Ideo nemo glorietur in operibus: quia nemo fastis suis iustificatur: sed qui iustus est, donatum habet: quia post lauacrum iustificatus est: Fides ergo est, ait, qua liberat per sanguinem Iesu Christi. Dicit expresse Christum omnibus donaffe peccatum: sed seipsum declarans, non vult quod omnes & singuli per sanguinem Christi ipso actu liberati sint, absque respectu fidei, vel incredulitatis (manifeste enim redemtionis proprietatem ad credentes restringit) sed hoc vult, quod, qui liberatur a peccato, ex dono Christi & non operibus suis liberentur.
units.tr: In this sense Hilary also writes in his Commentary on Matthew, canon 7: The salvation of all the nations is from faith, and in the precepts of the Lord is the life of all. But Ambrose, somewhat more clearly, in book 9, letter 71: The Lord Jesus, coming, gave forgiveness of sin to all, which no one could avoid, and took away the sin of the whole world, as John bears witness. Therefore let no one glory in works, because no one is justified by his own deeds; but he who is just has it as a gift, because he has been justified after the washing. Faith, therefore, is that by which we are freed through the blood of Jesus Christ. He says expressly that Christ has granted sin to all. But in explaining himself he does not mean that all and each have actually been freed through the blood of Christ, without regard to faith or unbelief (for he clearly restricts the property of redemption to believers). He means this: whoever is freed from sin is freed by the gift of Christ, and not by his own works.

units.la: E recentioribus VVolfgangus Muf-culus in locis hoc plane sensu explicat, redemtionem Iesu Christi recte dici vniuersalem, quod extra eam nemo redimatur neque redimi queat: quoniam non est in alio salus, neque aliud nome sub coelo datu est hominibus, per quod feruemur. Idem hac quoque rationem assignat vniuersalis redemtionis, quod nimirum parata sit cunctis, & omnes ad eam vocentur: hoc est, vt ipse titulo de remissione peccatorum quaest.2. explicat: quod licet gratia redemtionis non omnibus contingat, omnibus tamen annuncianda, atque proponenda sit, & communiter ad eam inuitandi omnes; sicut in Euangelio nuptiae regiae omnibus paratae erant, omnesque inuitabantur, licet no omnes peraeque nuptiarum consortes fierent: quia nuptiae quidem paratae erant omnibus, sed vocati non erant digni: multi quippe vocati, pauci electi. Quod igitur ad vocationem externam, Christus cum omnibus suis beneficiis, omnibus proponitur, hoc annexo, vt omnes in ipsum credant: & Domino praecipiente Euangelium omni creaturae annunciatur, & praedicatur in nomine ipsius resipiscentia ac remissio peccatorum apud omnes gentes, vt omnis qui credit in filium non pereat, sed habeat vitam aeternam. Hac praeceptione nullarum nationum, nullorum homi-num
units.tr: Among more recent writers, Wolfgang Musculus, in his Loci, explains in plainly this sense that the redemption of Jesus Christ is rightly called universal, because outside it no one is redeemed or can be redeemed: for there is no salvation in another, nor is any other name given under heaven to men by which we are saved. He gives the same reason for universal redemption, namely that it is prepared for all and all are called to it. That is, as he explains in the title on the remission of sins, question 2: although the grace of redemption does not come to all, it must nevertheless be announced and proposed to all, and all must in common be invited to it. Just as in the Gospel the royal marriage was prepared for all and all were invited, although not all equally became partakers of the marriage: for the marriage was indeed prepared for all, but those called were not worthy; many are called, few are chosen. Therefore, as to the external calling, Christ with all his benefits is proposed to all, with this attached: that all believe in him. And by the Lord's command the Gospel is announced to every creature, and repentance and remission of sins are preached in his name among all nations, so that everyone who believes in the Son should not perish but have eternal life. By this command no distinction has been made of any nations or any men.

units.la: Matth.22. Marci 16. Luc.24. Ioh.3. nů facta est discretio. Ad omnes prophetas mittitur Euangelium crucis Christi, qui neminem excepit, neminem separauit genere, neminem conditione distinxit, inquiens, Prædicate Euangelium vniuersæ creaturæ. Qui crediderit & baptizatus fuerit, saluabitur, qui non crediderit, condemnabitur. Hinc & Dominus per Euangelium clamat: Venite ad me omnes, qui defatigati estis, ego vos refi-ciam. In quibus verbis aliud est, quod iussit, aliud quod promisit. Nos faciamus quod iussit: accedamus omnes ad Dominum, sequamur eum, ita habituri quod promisit. Non enim eiicit foras, sed suscipit, & refocillat, qui ad ipsum accedunt. Interim qui sint venturi, qui non venturi, nouit ille de quo filius tc-statur, Nemo venit ad me, nisi pater traxerit eum, sicut scriptum est in Prophetis: Erunt omnes docti a Deo. Quisquis ergo audiuit a patre, & didicit, venit ad me. Homines siquidem, vt Augustinus locum istum edisserit, forinsecus annunciant, & stre-pitum verborum auribus ingerunt: & sic homines ab hominibus audiunt. Sed quòd intelligunt, intus datur, intus coruìcat, intus reuelatur ab eo, qui incrementum dat. Aug. tract. 26. in Ioh. & pluribus Tract. 3. in primam Ioh. Et dicente Prosper lib. 2. cap. 9. de vocatione gentium: qui veniunt, Dei auxilio diriguntur; qui non veniunt, sua pertinacia relucantur.
units.tr: Matth. 22. Marc. 16. Luc. 24. Ioh. 3. No distinction has been made. The Gospel of the cross of Christ is sent to all nations, and it excepts no one, separates no one by kind, distinguishes no one by condition, saying: Preach the Gospel to every creature. He who believes and is baptized will be saved; he who does not believe will be condemned. Hence the Lord also cries out through the Gospel: Come to me, all you who are weary, and I will refresh you. In these words one thing is what he commanded, another what he promised. Let us do what he commanded: let us all come to the Lord and follow him, so that we shall have what he promised. For he does not cast out, but receives and refreshes those who come to him. Meanwhile, who will come and who will not, he knows, of whom the Son testifies: No one comes to me unless the Father draws him, as it is written in the Prophets: They shall all be taught by God. Everyone therefore who has heard from the Father and learned comes to me. For men, as Augustine expounds that passage, announce outwardly and pour the noise of words into the ears; and so men hear from men. But what they understand is given inwardly, shines inwardly, is revealed inwardly by him who gives the increase. Aug. tract. 26 on John, and more fully tract 3 on the first epistle of John. And Prosper says, book 2, ch. 9, on the calling of the Gentiles: those who come are directed by God's help; those who do not come are resisted by their own obstinacy.

units.la: Postremò docti interpretes admonèt, & exempla locutionum in scriptu-ris confirmant, particulam O M N E S & O M N I A saepenumero non pro simpliciter vniuersali, sed pro indefinita expo-ni oportere, vt omnia notet quaevis, & genera potiùs omnia, quàm omnia genera-rum indiuidua.
units.tr: Finally, learned interpreters warn, and examples of expression in Scripture confirm, that the words all (omnes, omnia) must often be understood not as simply universal but as indefinite, so that omnia means any things, and means kinds of all things rather than all the individuals of the kinds.

units.la: Sic Augustinus Tractatu 53. in Ioh: explicans illud, omnia traham ad me, cum exaltatus fuero, per omnia, inquit, rectè possunt intelligi omnes praedestinati ad salutem, ex quibus omnibus nihil peritu-rum est. Aut certè, inquit, omnia, id est, omnia hominum genera; siue in linguis omnibus, siue in aetatibus omnibus, siue in gradibus hominum omnibus: & quicquid aliud dici potest secundùm
units.tr: So Augustine, in Tractate 53 on John, explaining I will draw all things to me, when I have been lifted up, says: By all things, he says, all the predestined to salvation can rightly be understood, of whom none will perish. Or certainly, he says, all things, that is, all kinds of men: whether in all tongues, or in all ages, or in all ranks of men; and whatever else can be said according to

units.la: F iiij ininnumerabiles differetias, quibus praeter sola peccata homines inter se distat: ab excelsissimis ad humilimos, a rege vsq; ad mendicum, omnia traham ad me.
units.tr: countless differences, by which men differ from one another apart from sins alone: from the highest to the lowest, from the king to the beggar, I will draw all things to me.

units.la: Hunc locutionis modum pluribus idem docet Enchir: ad Laurent: cap. 103.
units.tr: The same author teaches this manner of speaking in many places, in the Enchiridion to Laurentius, chapter 103.

units.la: Et de correptione & gratia cap. 14, Vtrobiq; illud adducit, Decimatis mentham & rutam, & omne olus. Neq; enim, inquit, Pharisaei, & quaecunque aliena, & omnium per omnes terras alienigenarum omnia olera decimabat, sed omne olus, omne olerum genus intelligere debemus. Et multa secundum istum locutionis modum in sacris occurrunt: vt quod Christus & Apostoli sanauerint {a}omnem morbum & languorem in populo, & omnes sub Diaboli potestatem redactos. Quod idem Petro{b} omnia quadrupedia terrae & reptilia ostensa fuerint in linteo coelitus demissio. Quod Paulus{c} omne consilium Dei Ephesiis annunciauerit. Quod{d} Iudaeos omnes vbique gentium docuerit filios non circumcidere: & quod amplius est,{e} omnes illuilluminârit: nec non quod omnem leni-tatem erga omnes, id est, quosuis homi-nes exhibere iubemur: & infinita huius-modi alia, quæ sacras literas scrutanti-bus passim obuia sunt.
units.tr: And in On Correction and Grace, chapter 14, he cites in both places the verse, "You tithe mint and rue and every herb." For, he says, we must understand not that the Pharisees tithed the herbs of strangers and all the vegetables of foreigners through all the lands of the world, but every herb, every kind of herb. And many things in the Sacred Writings occur according to this manner of speaking: for example, that Christ and the Apostles healed every disease and every infirmity among the people, and all who had been brought under the power of the Devil. The same holds for Peter, to whom all the four-footed beasts of the earth and the creeping things were shown in a sheet let down from heaven. And that Paul declared to the Ephesians the whole counsel of God; that he taught the Jews everywhere among the Gentiles not to circumcise their sons; and, what is more, that he enlightened all men; likewise that we are commanded to show all gentleness toward all, that is, toward whatever men; and countless other things of this kind, which lie open on every page to those who search the sacred letters.

units.la: Quid tam absonum, & inconueni-ens, quàm si quis Vniuersalem talibus in locis præcise vrgeat? Et ne quis mi-retur id à nobis dici, perpendat & has locutiones: Exibat ad Baptistam omnis Iudæa, & baptizabantur omnes in Iordane. Eritis exosi omnibus hominibus propter no-men meum. omnes qui interficient vos, puta-bunt se cultum præstare Deo. Omnes in Asia Paulum auersati sunt.
units.tr: What could be so absurd and out of place as to press the universal term strictly in such passages? So that no one may wonder that we say this, let him weigh also these expressions: "All Judea went out to John the Baptist, and all were baptized in the Jordan." "You will be hated by all men for my name's sake." "All who kill you will think they are offering worship to God." "All in Asia turned away from Paul."

units.la: Hic neutiquam sensus est, omnes Iudæos, nullo excepto, accessisse ad Iohannem, & ab eo baptizatos: sed multos passim ex Iudæa tota. Et nisi eadem Synecdoche aliis dictis adhibeatur, pro digiosæ nascentur interpretationes. Eas euitabimus seruato scripturæ more, de quo Augustus: epist: 59. Scriptura mos est, ait, ita loqui de parte, tanquam de toto: quam diuina scriptura consuetudinem per omne corpus literarum eius creberrime spar-sam, sam, quisque diligenter aduerterit, multa dissoluit qua inter se videntur esse contraria.
units.tr: Here the sense is by no means that all the Jews, without exception, came to John and were baptized by him, but many from all over Judea. Unless the same synecdoche is applied to the other sayings, monstrous interpretations will arise. We shall avoid them by keeping to the manner of Scripture, of which Augustine says in Epistle 59: "It is the custom of Scripture," he says, "to speak of a part as of the whole; and whoever carefully notices this custom of divine Scripture, scattered very frequently throughout its whole body of writings, will resolve many things that seem to be contrary to one another."

units.la: Quid ergò vetat, quò minus & hîc secundum receptam scripturarum consuetudinem, vniuersalem pari ratione quis exponat? Christum nempe mortuū esse pro omnibus, id est, de efficacia redemtionis loquendo, pro quibusvis? vt non tam ad singulos homines, quàm ad omnia hominum genera, quibus vniuersitatem illam electorum constare dubium non est, rectè & sine piaculo referatur.
units.tr: What, then, prevents us from explaining the universal term in the same way here, according to the accepted custom of the Scriptures? Namely, that Christ died for all, that is, speaking of the efficacy of redemption, for whatever persons? So that it may be rightly and without offence referred not so much to single men as to all kinds of men, of which that universal body of the elect plainly consists beyond doubt.

units.la: Sed de re tota nouo sumto principio diligentius tractandum videtur.
units.tr: But the whole matter seems to need to be treated more carefully, from a newly taken starting point.

units.la: LIBER SECVNDVS. DE REDEMTIONE CHRISTIANA, Ἀπολυτρωτικός. CAPVT I. Transitio ad examen argumentorum aduersæ partis & eorundem in classes distributio.
units.tr: BOOK TWO. ON CHRISTIAN REDEMPTION, Apolytrōtikos. CHAPTER I. Transition to the examination of the arguments of the opposing side, and their distribution into classes.

units.la: IS quæ de summa controuersiæ præmittere visum fuit, breuiter explicatis, nunc ad argumenta, quibus aduersa pars pro defensione suæ sententiæ nititur, particulatim examinanda nos cōferamus: postmodum nostram quoque sententiam idoneis sacrarum literarum testimoniis & argumentis confirmaturi.
units.tr: Having briefly explained the matters which I thought it right to set out before the main point of the controversy, we now proceed to examine one by one the arguments on which the opposing side relies in defence of its view; afterwards we shall also confirm our own position by fitting testimonies and arguments from Holy Scripture.

units.la: Pro omnibus igitur Adami posteris nullo penitus ex tota humani generis univniuersitate excepto, Christum esse mortuum, & ita quidem vt peccata omnium efficienter, vt loquuntur, & non sufficienter duntaxat expiarit, omnefq; adeo, fiue credant, fiue non credant, nec credituri vnquam sint, æqualiter morte Christi à peccato & damnatione redemti, in gratiæ finum restituti, iustificati, viuificati, saluati denique sint, triplici argumetorum classe euincere conantur.
units.tr: So, for all the posterity of Adam, without exception from the whole of mankind, they try to prove by a threefold class of arguments that Christ died, and indeed that he so expiated the sins of all, as they put it, efficiently, and not merely sufficiently; and that all alike, whether they believe or not, and whether or not they will ever believe, have been redeemed from sin and damnation by the death of Christ, restored to the bosom of grace, justified, made alive, and finally saved.

units.la: Prima classis eorum argumentorum est, in quibus vniuerfalitas expresse continetur.
units.tr: The first class of these arguments is that in which universality is expressly contained.

units.la: Altera classis ea argumenta profert, quæ nominatim loquuntur de reprobis, & non minus efficaciter pro his quâ pro Petro, Paulo & quouis fanéto, Christum testantur mortuum, fi ipsis credimus.
units.tr: The second class offers those arguments which speak by name of the reprobate, and bear witness to Christ's death for them no less effectively than for Peter, Paul, or any saint, if we believe them.

units.la: Tertia classis habet stupenda, vt loquuntur, absurda, quę ex contraria sententia sequi volunt.
units.tr: The third class contains what they call amazing absurdities, which they claim follow from the opposing view.

units.la: Hac triplici classe confisus certaminis istius Antesignanus & Pyrgopolinices, nihilo modeftius agit nec minus fese iactat, & triumphum canit ante vi-ctoria, quàm vel immanis ille Goliath, gladio & lancea & clypeo suo ferocies, vel superbus ille Sanherib, gloriosulve Benhadad, in equis & curribus fidentes, in opprobrium Israelis. Gloriatur enim intrepidè, classibus illis euerten-dis omnem conatum esse irritum, nisi prius qui hoc tentant, scripturam falsitatis arguant & conuincant.
units.tr: Confident in this threefold class, the champion and braggart of this contest acts with no less arrogance and boasts no less, and sings his triumph before the victory, fiercer than that huge Goliath with his sword, spear and shield, or than that proud Sennacherib or boastful Ben-hadad, trusting in horses and chariots, to the reproach of Israel. For he boldly boasts that every effort to overthrow those classes is in vain, unless first those who attempt it prove and convict Scripture of falsehood.

units.la: Sed heus tu sodes, <bl>μὴ πρὸ νίκης ἐγκωμίων</bl>: Et quemadmodum nostris, hoc est sacris, literis proditum est, ne gloriatur qui induit arma, velut qui exuit: uti Achabum olim Benhadado sapienter respondisse accepimus.
units.tr: But, my friend, pray, [Do not praise before victory]: and as it has been declared in our sacred writings, "let not him who puts on his armour boast as one who takes it off"; just as we have heard that Ahab once wisely answered Ben-hadad.

units.la: Scripturæ apud nos indubitata fides est, & incócusa autoritas. Verùm quæstio non est de veritate scripturarum, quà qui non credit, paganus non Christianus est: sed de veritate opinionis humanæ, quam nimium sane confidenter obtentu diuinorum sermonum defendis, vt videbimus: Quare tam exercitus quàm triumphos tuos nil moramur.
units.tr: For us the faith of Scripture is beyond doubt, and its authority unshaken. But the question is not about the truth of the Scriptures, for whoever does not believe that is a pagan, not a Christian; the question is about the truth of a human opinion, which you defend, with far too much confidence and under the pretext of divine words, as we shall see. Therefore we do not concern ourselves with your armies or your triumphs.

units.la: AD ARGVMENTA PRIMAE CLASIS. CAPVT II.
units.tr: AD ARGVMENTA PRIMAE CLASIS. CAPVT II.

units.la: Responsio generalis ad testimonia de morte Christi pro omnibus.
units.tr: A general reply to the testimonies that Christ died for all.

units.la: PRIMA classis, quantum obseruo, quadruplici constat testimoniorum genere tanquam quadripartitis copijs auxiliaribus. Afferuntur enim scripturæ loca, noui & vet. Testamenti, quibus aut Christus pro omnibus dicitur mortuus: aut fructus mortis eius ad omnes sine exceptione videntur extendi: aut mundi mentio fit in negotio salutis: aut denique Euangelium ad omnes perhibetur pertinere. De omnibus ordine agemus.
units.tr: The first class, as far as I observe, consists of four kinds of testimony, like four auxiliary forces. For they cite passages of the Old and New Testament in which either Christ is said to have died for all, or the fruit of his death seems to be extended to all without exception, or the world is mentioned in the matter of salvation, or finally the Gospel is said to pertain to all. We shall take them up in order.

units.la: Principio quantum ad testimonia de morte Christi pro omnibus, suo modo concedimus & nos, Christum passum & mortuum pro omnibus omnino hominibus, quotquot fuerunt, sunt & futuri sunt. Quid tum? An inde sequetur, omnes & singulos, siue credât, siue non credant, ipso facto reconciliatos, iustificatos, viuificatos, renouatos, saluatos, & omne iudicium iramque diuinam in vniuersis hominibus veré & proprié sublatam, & indubitanter omnes simul ab omni peccato & condemnatione liberatos, inque gratiam & sinum patris tanquam filios receptos? Idassertor peruicax in Thesibus suis totidem quidem verbis contendit: sed nos consequentias istas negamus, & pernegamus. Nam vt eæ admitti possint, necesse est hæc sit maior Syllogismi:
units.tr: First, as regards the testimonies that Christ died for all, we too concede in our own way that Christ suffered and died for absolutely all men, whoever have been, are, or will be. So what follows? Does it follow from this that all and each, whether they believe or not, are by that very fact reconciled, justified, made alive, renewed, saved, and that all judgment and divine wrath has been truly and properly removed from all men, and that without doubt all have been freed at once from every sin and condemnation and received into grace and into the Father's bosom as sons? The stubborn champion [Idassertor] asserts this in his Theses in just so many words, but we deny these consequences, and utterly deny them. For that they may be admitted, it is necessary that this be the major premise of the syllogism:

units.la: Pro quibuscunque Christus passus & mortuus est, ij indubitanter ab omni peccato & condemnatione liberati, & salutis, reconciliationis, iustificationis, renouationis, aliorumque beneficiorum morte Christi acquisitorum, re ipsa participes facti sunt, absque vllo prorsus respectu fidei & incredulitatis.
units.tr: For whomever Christ suffered and died, those men have without doubt been freed from every sin and condemnation, and have in fact become partakers of salvation, reconciliation, justification, renewal, and the other benefits acquired by the death of Christ, with absolutely no regard to faith or unbelief.

units.la: Sequitur assumtio; Christum esse mortuum pro omnibus. Ergo &c.
units.tr: The minor follows: Christ died for all. Therefore etc.

units.la: At maior ita absolute sumta salsissima est, & in omnem veritatem religionis nis Christianæ, atque in ipsam passionē & mortem filij Dei modis omnibus contumeliosa est. Vera autem est conditionaliter; participes esse bonorum enumeratorum, pro quibus Christus mortuus est, si nempe in Christum credant, eique obediant. Impossibile enim est, vt qui sine fide est Deo placeat. Et Christus aperte ita distinguit: provt Moses serpentem extulit in deserto, ita extolli oportet filium hominis, vt omnis qui credit, habeat vitam aternam. Et mox, Ita enim dilexit Deus mundum, vt filium suum vnigenitum dederit, vt quisquis credit in eum, non pereat, sed habeat vitam æternam. Rursum ibidem; Non enim misit Deus filium suum in mundum vt condemnet mundum, sed vt seruetur mundus per eum: qui crediderit non condemnatur : qui vero non credit condemnatus est. Et sub finem cap. verba sunt Ioh. Baptistæ: Qui credit in filium habet vitam, qui non credit filio non videbit vitam, sed ira Dei manet super eum. Nec alios Paulus agnoscit iustificatos per redemtionem Christi, nisi qui credunt: Omnes, inquit, peccarunt, & destituuntur gloria Dei, iustificantur autem gratis per redemtionem factam in Iesu Christo, quem proposuit Deus, ut esset propitiatio per fidem, in sanguine ipsius.
units.tr: But the major, taken absolutely like this, is most false, and in every way contrary to all the truth of the Christian religion and insulting to the very passion and death of the Son of God. It is true only conditionally: that they become partakers of the enumerated benefits for whom Christ died, if indeed they believe in Christ and obey him. For it is impossible that one without faith should please God. And Christ plainly makes this distinction: just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the desert, so the Son of man must be lifted up, that everyone who believes may have eternal life. And soon after: For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life. Again in the same place: For God did not send his Son into the world to condemn the world, but that the world might be saved through him: he who believes is not condemned; but he who does not believe is condemned already. And near the end of the chapter are the words of John the Baptist: He who believes in the Son has life; he who does not believe the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God abides on him. Nor does Paul acknowledge as justified through the redemption of Christ any others than those who believe: All, he says, have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, but they are justified freely by the redemption that is in Jesus Christ, whom God set forth to be a propitiation through faith, in his blood.

units.la: Hac responsione vtitur Theoph. ad Heb. 2. quem Anselmus ibidem secutus videtur. Verba eius haec sunt: Gustavit mortem non pro fidelibus solum, sed pro vniuerso terrarum orbe. Nam etsi haudquicquam omnes sunt salui effecti, ipse tamen pergit quod sua intererat: Vide ut non sequatur, si Christus pro omnibus mortuus sit, omnes statim saluos effectos: quae Hub. est Theologia, Thes. 270. In nonum cap. ad Heb. idem interpres ita scriptum reliquit: Multum exhausit peccata: Cur multorum dixit, non omnium? Quia nequaquam cuncti credidere mortales: Christi quidem mors omnium aequauit perditionem, id est, sat valuit ne omnes perderentur, & pro cunctorum salute depensa est, & quantum in eo fuit, pro cunctis est mortuus: nec tamen omnium peccata exhausit, quia qui ipsi reluctatur, inutilem sibi prorsus Christi mortem reddunt. Haec ille.
units.tr: Theophylact, on Hebrews 2, uses this answer, and Anselm seems to have followed him there. His words are these: He tasted death not only for the faithful, but for the whole world. For although not all have been made saved at all, he nonetheless went on to do what was his part. See that it does not follow, if Christ died for all, that all are at once made saved: this is from Hub.'s Theology, Thes. 270. On the ninth chapter of Hebrews the same interpreter left this written: He poured out his sins greatly. Why did he say of many, not of all? Because not all mortals at all believed. The death of Christ indeed equalled the perdition of all, that is, it was sufficient that all should not perish, and it was paid out for the salvation of all, and insofar as it lay in him, he died for all; yet he did not pour out the sins of all, because those who struggle against him render Christ's death utterly useless to themselves. So he.

units.la: Dictam solutionem è Neotericis confirmat Stapulensis, non aspernandus interpres in 2. cap. ad Heb. his verbis, Passius quidem est Christus pro omnibus hominibus, & mors eius valida est pro redemtione omnium, sed tum mors eius nos a metu mortis liberauit, & ex seruitutis metu asseruit in libertatem vitae, si eum sequi velimus. Et in cap. 10. scribit, oblatione Christi superplenissime satisfactum pro omnibus mundi peccatis, quae fuerunt, sunt & futura sunt: remitti autem ijs peccata, qui ad Christum venientes, gratiam, quam a patre pro ipsis obtinere dignatus est, petunt: non remitti, qui gratiam ipsius repudiant, & vniuersalem fontem lotionis peccatorum contemnunt, nescientes aut nolentes se in illo abluere.
units.tr: Stapulensis, no contemptible interpreter, confirms this solution from the moderns, on Hebrews 2, in these words: Christ indeed suffered for all men, and his death is powerful for the redemption of all; but his death freed us from the fear of death, and rescued us from the fear of slavery into the liberty of life, if we are willing to follow him. And on chapter 10 he writes that by the offering of Christ satisfaction has been made most abundantly for all the sins of the world, which have been, are, and will be; but sins are remitted to those who come to Christ and seek the grace which he has deigned to obtain for them from the Father; they are not remitted to those who reject his grace and despise the universal fountain of the washing of sins, not knowing or not willing to be washed in him.

units.la: Nec aliter Brentius explicat. Catech. articulo de remissione peccatorum: iustificamur, ait, mera Dei clementia, tantum propter redemtionem qua Christus humanum genus a peccatis redemit, & propter reconciliationem quam ipse impetrauit, nequaquam autem propter meritum aliquod humanum. Sed hoc hoc beneficium Dei non accipimus nisi per fidem, ex praedicatione Euangelij. Etsi enim Christus redemit humanum genus à peccatis, & reconciliauit cum Deo, tamen hoc beneficium nihil prodesset humano generi, nisi ei annunciaretur Euangelio. Euangelium autem fidem exigit, & accipiendum est fide. Qui enim non crediderit, condemnabitur: qui autem crediderit, saluus erit. Quare remissio peccatorum à Christo parta & Euangelio annunciata, accipitur à nobis, & applicatur nobis NON NISI per fidem. Huic contraria est assertio, reconciliationem & salutem accepisse omnes, siue credant, siue non credant.
units.tr: Brentius likewise explains it in his Catechism, in the article on the remission of sins: we are justified, he says, by the mere clemency of God, only on account of the redemption by which Christ redeemed the human race from sins, and on account of the reconciliation which he himself obtained, and by no means on account of any human merit. But we do not receive this benefit of God except through faith, from the preaching of the Gospel. For although Christ redeemed the human race from sins and reconciled it to God, yet this benefit would profit the human race nothing unless it were announced to them in the Gospel. The Gospel, however, demands faith and must be received by faith. For he who does not believe will be condemned; but he who believes will be saved. Therefore the remission of sins, obtained by Christ and announced in the Gospel, is received by us and applied to us NOT EXCEPT through faith. Opposed to this is the assertion that all have received reconciliation and salvation, whether they believe or not.

units.la: CAPVT III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: Speciales solutiones ad scripturæ illa dicta, quæ Christum pro omnibus mortuum perhibent.
units.tr: Particular solutions to those passages of Scripture which state that Christ died for all.

units.la: PRÆMISSA solutio generalis plana & sana est, & sola sufficere poterat. Lubet tamen speciatim examinare dicta sacrarum literarum de morte Christi pro omnibus.
units.tr: The general solution is plain and sound, and could alone have been sufficient. Still, it is worth examining in particular the passages of Holy Scripture about Christ's death for all.

units.la: Primus igitur in hoc ordine esto locus 1. Timoth.2. Vult Deus omnes homines saluos fieri, & ad agnitionem veritatis venire. Vnus enim Deus, & vnus mediator Dei & hominum, homo Christus Iesus, qui semetipsum dedit pretium redemtionis pro omnibus.
units.tr: The first passage in this order, then, is 1 Tim. 2. God wills all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. For there is one God and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all.

units.la: Hic primũ vrgent verba,quod Deus omnes velit saluos fieri. Ex quo colligi volunt, semel igitur omnes homines, nullo excepto, re ipsa saluos factos per redemtionem Christi,absque respectu fidei vel incredulitatis, licet multi recuperatam salutem postea per incredulitatem amittant denuo.
units.tr: Here the words that God wills all to be saved are pressed first. From them they want to conclude that all men, without exception, have once for all actually been saved through Christ's redemption, without any regard to faith or unbelief, although many afterwards lose the salvation they regained through unbelief.

units.la: Atqui Apostolus de salute agit quæ per fidem est, vt recte interpretatur Theophyl. & res ipsa loquitur:non autem de salute quapiam vniuersali, credentium & non credentium. Præterea Apostolus, vt res inter se coniunctiffimas, conectit salutem & veritatis agnitionem. Vult, inquit, omnes homines saluos fieri, & ad cognitionem veritatis venire. Pari ergo modo inferant,etiam omnes homines, nullo excepto, ad veritatis cognitionem, id est, fidem; & per consequens, ad vitam ęternam, quę in Dei & Christi cognitione posita est, perurenire. Ita argumentum abunde solutū est.
units.tr: But the Apostle is speaking of the salvation that comes through faith, as Theophylact rightly interprets, and the matter itself makes this plain; he is not speaking of some universal salvation of believers and unbelievers. Moreover, the Apostle joins salvation and knowledge of the truth, as things most closely connected: He wills, he says, all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. By the same reasoning they could infer that all men without exception come to the knowledge of the truth, that is, to faith, and consequently to eternal life, which consists in the knowledge of God and of Christ. So the argument is fully answered.

units.la: Quod tamen ad mentem Pauli attinet, locus interpretatione indiget: vt Ambrosius quoque admonet. Quod si enim Deus (qui vtique omnipotens dicitur, atque in coelo ac in terra quæcūque vult, facit) omnes homines vult salvos fieri, & ad veritatis cognitionem venire, cur non impletur eius voluntas? Nec dicas, vt Pelagiani soliti erant excipere, teste Augustino, ideo nō impleri Dei istam voluntatem, quia homines nolint. Deo enim volenti salvum facere, vt idem de corrept. & gratia cap.14. docet, nullum resistit liberum arbitrium. Sic enim velle vel nolle, in volentis aut nolentis est potestate, vt diuinam voluntatem nō impediat, nec superet potestatem. De iis enim qui non faciunt quæ vult, facit ipse quæ vult: quandoquidem etiam de ipsis hominum voluntatibus, quod vult facit. Ne igitur ipsum fidei nostræ principium, quo nos in Deum Patrem omnipotentem credere profitemur, vacillet, multis sanè modis Apostolica & diuina sententia rectè intelligi potest. Ex quibus vnum & alterum recitabimus.
units.tr: As far as the mind of Paul is concerned, however, the passage needs interpretation, as Ambrose also warns. For if God (who is surely called almighty, and who does whatever he wills in heaven and on earth) wills all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, why is his will not fulfilled? Nor should you say, as the Pelagians were accustomed to except, according to Augustine, that God's will is not fulfilled because men are unwilling. For, as the same writer teaches in de corrept. & gratia cap. 14, no free will resists God when he wills to save. For to will or not to will lies in the power of the one who wills or does not will, so that it does not hinder the divine will or overcome its power. He does what he wills even with those who do not do what he wills, since he also does what he wills with the very wills of men. So that the very principle of our faith, by which we profess that we believe in God the Father almighty, may not waver, the apostolic and divine saying can be rightly understood in many ways. We shall recite one or two of them.

units.la: Primùm, etsi ad salutem non perueniunt nisi electi, eóque per Spiritum sanctum efficaciter vocati, vocatione illa quæ est secúdum Dei propositum: tamen verbo suo Deus omnes iubet credere & conuerti vt seruentur, neq; seipsos regno Dei indignos iudicent. Hæc enim est voluntas Dei illa bona, accepta ac perfecta, vt omnes filiu audiant, pœnitentiam agant, & credant Euangelio ad salutem. Sicut etiam te-statur Ezech. 18. vt quid moriemini domus Israel? Conuertimini ab omnibus iniquitatibus vestris: quia nolo mortem peccatoris. conuertimini & viuetis. Et cap. 33. Viuo ego, inquit Dominus, non volo mortem impij, sed vt couertatur impius à via sua, & viuat. Neque enim in perditione pereuntium Deus lætatur, nec approbat cor incredulum & impœnitens: sed, Paulo teste, denuntiat omnibus hominibus, nibus,vt resipiscant. Cur autem hoc donum gratię,puta conuersio,sine qua nemo saluus esse potest, ab eo, qui omnes saluos esse vult, non omnibus conferatur, ad occulta diuinæ iustitiæ iudicia referendum est. Quis enim cognouit metem Domini? aut quis prior dedit ei vt retribuat ei?
units.tr: First, although none come to salvation except the elect, and these are efficaciously called through the Holy Spirit, by that calling which is according to God's purpose, nevertheless by his word God commands all to believe and be converted so that they may be saved, and not to judge themselves unworthy of the kingdom of God. For this is God's good, acceptable and perfect will, that all should hear the Son, repent, and believe the gospel unto salvation. As he also testifies in Ezek. 18: Why will you die, house of Israel? Turn from all your iniquities, for I do not desire the death of the sinner; turn and live. And in chapter 33: As I live, says the Lord, I do not wish the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live. For God does not rejoice in the destruction of those who perish, nor does he approve of an unbelieving and unrepentant heart; but, as Paul testifies, he commands all men everywhere to repent. Why this gift of grace, namely conversion, without which no one can be saved, is not bestowed on all by him who wills that all be saved, must be referred to the hidden judgments of divine justice. For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has first given to him, that he should repay him?

units.la: Hæc expositio Luthero probatur De seruo arbitrio, ad locū Ezech.18. Illo verbo, inquit ille, Nolo mortem peccatoris, nihil aliud agi videmus, quàm prædicari & offerri diuinam gratiam in mundo, quam illi solum suscipiunt, in quibus iam lex suum officium, id est, cognitionem peccati compleuit. Reliqui misericordiam eo verbo promissam contemnunt. Caterum cur alij lege tangantur alij non tangantur, vt illi suscipiant, hi contemnant gratiam oblatam, alia quaestio est, nec hoc loco tractatur ab Ezechiele, qui de prædicata & oblata Dei misericordia loquitur, non de occulta illa & metuenda voluntate Dei, ordinantis suo consilio, quos & quales prædicatæ & oblatæ misericordiæ capaces & participes esse velit. Quæ voluntas non requirenda, sed cum reuerentia adorandaest, ut secretum maiestatis diuinæ, ipsi soli reser-vatum ac nobis prohibitum. Et mox, Multa facit Deus quæ verbo suo non ostendit nobis. Multa quoque vult, quæ verbo suo non ostendit fieri velle. Sic non vult mortem peccatoris; verbo scilicet: vult autem illam, voluntate illa imperscrutabili. Nobis autem verbum spectandum est, relicta voluntate illa imperscrutabili. Rursum, conferens cum loco Prophetæ præsentem locum Apostoli, subdit: Si de Deo prædicato dixeris, ille vult omnes homines salvos fieri, dum verbo salutis ad omnes venit, vitiumque est voluntatis quæ non admittit eum: sicut dicitur Matth. 23: Quoties volui congregare filios tuos, & noluisti? Verum quare maiestas diuina vitium hoc voluntatis nostræ non tollat aut mutet in omnibus, cum non sit in potestate hominis; aut cur ei illud imputet, cum non possit homo eo carere, quærere non licet: ac si multum quæras, nunquam tamen invenies. Hæc non piguit pluribus ex Luthero proferre propter aduersarios.
units.tr: This interpretation is approved by Luther in De servo arbitrio, on the passage of Ezekiel 18. "In that word," he says, "I do not desire the death of the sinner, we see nothing else being done than that the divine grace is preached and offered in the world, which those alone receive in whom the law has already fulfilled its office, that is, the knowledge of sin. The rest despise the mercy promised in that word. But why some are touched by the law and others are not, so that the former accept and the latter despise the offered grace, is another question, and it is not treated in this place by Ezekiel, who speaks of the preached and offered mercy of God, not of that hidden and fearful will of God, by which he, by his counsel, ordains who and what kind of people he wills to be capable of and to share in the preached and offered mercy. That will is not to be searched into, but adored with reverence, as the secret of the divine majesty, reserved to himself alone and forbidden to us." And soon after: "God does many things which he does not show us in his word. He also wills many things which he does not show by his word that he wills. So he does not will the death of the sinner, by his word; but he wills it by that inscrutable will. For us, the word must be regarded, leaving aside that inscrutable will." Again, comparing the present passage of the Apostle with the passage of the Prophet, he adds: "If you say of God as preached, that he wills all men to be saved, since by the word of salvation he comes to all, and the fault lies in the will which does not admit him, as it is said in Matt. 23: How often would I have gathered your children, and you would not? But why the divine majesty does not remove or change this fault of our will in all, since it is not in man's power, or why it imputes it to him, since man cannot be free of it, it is not permitted to ask; and if you ask much, you will never find out." I have not been reluctant to cite these many words from Luther on account of our opponents.

units.la: Secundo, potest esse sensus, & sic Augustinus Ench. ad Laurent. cap. 103. expo-nit, nit, Vult omnes homines saluos fieri, id est, omne genus hominū, per quascunque differetias distributum, reges, priuatos, nobiles, sublimes, humiles, doctos, indoctos, ingeniosos, fatuos, diuites, pauperes, mares, foeminas, pueros, infantes: in aetatibus omnibus, in professionibus omnibus, & si quid aliud differentiarum est in hominibus. Et satis quadrat expositio ista instituto Pauli. Sic enim colligit: Quos Deus vult seruari, pro eorum salute Ecclesia precari debet. At Deus omnes, id est, quotvis vult seruari; sublato gentis, sexus, aetatis, ordinis, atque dignitatis discrimine: Ergo pro omnibus, id est, quibusuis, vtpote regibus & aliis hominū generibus, fidelibus & infidelibus Ecclesia precari debet. Sic recte sane explicatur, quod dicit orandum pro omnibus. Etenim si simpliciter & sine cuiuspiam exceptione orandum esset pro omnibus, frustra dixisset Iohannes, Est peccatum ad mortem: non pro illo dico vt rogetis.1.Ioh.5.
units.tr: Second, there may be another sense, and Augustine explains it thus in Ench. ad Laurent. cap. 103: God wills all men to be saved, that is, every kind of men, distributed through whatever differences: kings, private persons, nobles, the exalted, the humble, the learned, the unlearned, the gifted, the foolish, the rich, the poor, males, females, boys, infants; in all ages, in all callings, and whatever other differences there are among men. This explanation fits well with Paul's purpose. For he infers thus: Those whom God wills to be preserved, for their salvation the Church ought to pray. But God wills all, that is, as many as he wills to be preserved, with distinctions of nation, sex, age, rank and dignity set aside. Therefore the Church ought to pray for all, that is, for whomever, namely for kings and other classes of men, for believers and unbelievers. So what he says, that prayer should be made for all, is rightly explained. For if prayer were to be made simply and without any exception for all, John would have spoken in vain: There is a sin unto death; I do not say that you should ask for it. 1 John 5.

units.la: Alibi Augustinus exponit, vult omnes saluos fieri, vt intelligantur omnes praedestinati. Quia omne genus homimum in eis est, inquit de corrept. & gratia cap.14. Sed de iis verbis satis: quibus si abuti pergant aduersarij, recolant etiam expositionem Heerbrandi, Disput. de praedest. th.93. itemque Bidenbacchij & Ofiandri, Responsione ad assertiones Iesuitarum Dillingensium: vbi & receptam scholasticorum distinctionem duplicis voluntatis Dei, quam Schmidlinus ipsorum postea explodere conatus est, probat: & verba Pauli cum Augustin. interpretantur, quòd videlicet non de singulis hominum personis, sed de omnibus hominum ordinibus, seu non de singulis generum, sed de generibus singulorum loquatur. Deinde, quod alterum argumentum est aduersariorum ex loco illo Apostoli, captiose arripiunt, quod dicit, vnus Mediator Dei & hominum: quicquid nempe hominum ab Adamo propagatum est, inquiut: quia etiam per vocem Dei quicquid in Deo est, intelligitur.
units.tr: Elsewhere Augustine explains, "He wills all to be saved," so that all the predestined may be understood, because every kind of men is among them, as he says in de corrept. & gratia cap. 14. But enough on these words. If our opponents persist in abusing them, let them also recall the exposition of Heerbrand in Disput. de praedest. th. 93, and likewise that of Bidembach and Osiander in Responsio ad assertiones Iesuitarum Dillingensium, where they also approve the scholastic distinction between a twofold will of God, which Schmidlin later tried to explode, and interpret the words of Paul together with Augustine, namely that he speaks not of single persons of men but of all orders of men, or not of single members of kinds but of kinds of single individuals. Next, what is the opponents' second argument from that passage of the Apostle, they seize on captiously, namely that he says, one Mediator between God and men: whatever is propagated from Adam, they say, since by the voice of God whatever is in God is also understood.

units.la: Sed mera est cauillatio. Paulus indefinifinitè dicit, Christum mediatorem es- se Dei & hominū, non addit, omnium: & si addidisset, eadem locum haberet restrictio de qua ante dictum est. Mediatoris quippe est, obseruante Ambrosio in explic. prioris ad Tim. vt sit arbiter inter eum qui peccauit, & eum cui peccatum est, vt hic ignoscat, & homo de cætero in fide Dei maneat: quod sane Christus pro mundo reprobo non spopondit, pro quo ne rogare quidem patrem dignatus est. Ioh.17. Quem locum Cyrillus quoque edisserens perspicuè testatur, Christum non mundi, sed suorum esse Mediatorem atque Pontificem, & ipsis tantummodo Mediatoris bonum non iniuria attribui.
units.tr: But this is mere quibbling. Paul says indefinitely that Christ is the mediator of God and of men; he does not add "of all." Even if he had added it, the same restriction would apply that was mentioned before. For a mediator, as Ambrose observes In explanation of the first Epistle to Timothy, is one who stands between the offender and the one offended, so that the latter may forgive and the man may remain in God's faith from then on. Christ certainly did not undertake this for the reprobate world, for whom he did not even deign to pray (John 17). Cyril, expounding this same passage, clearly testifies that Christ is the Mediator and High Priest not of the world but of his own, and that the good of the Mediator is rightly attributed to them alone.

units.la: Sed vide acumen. Per vocem Dei procul dubio intelligitur quicquid in Deo est: Ergo & per homines, quicquid ab Adamo natum est, intelligi debet.
units.tr: But see how sharp they are! By the voice of God is undoubtedly meant whatever is in God. Therefore, by men, whatever has been born from Adam must also be understood.

units.la: Nego consequentiam: tantùm sunt scopæ dissolutæ, & funiculi ex arena contexti, nec magis cohærentes quàm si dicam: Deus cum hominibus pepepigit fœdus gratiæ & vitæ æternæ. Ergo sicut per vocem Dei intelligitur quicquid Dei est, ita per homines etiam intelligi debet quicquid vbique hominū est aut erit, & sic omnes æternum seruabuntur. Hoc argutandi seu potius ineptiendi genere, multa abfurdiffima colligerentur. Inter Deum & femen Abrahæ pactum fuit circumcisionis. Iam fi quicquid feminis Abrahæ erit, accipias, quod per vocem Dei, quicquid Dei est accipiatur, tam fœmellæ quàm mares circumcidi debuissent in Israël. Quid ineptius?
units.tr: I deny the inference. These are loose brooms and ropes woven from sand, holding together no more than if I said: God made a covenant of grace and eternal life with men. Therefore, just as by the voice of God is understood whatever belongs to God, so by men must be understood whatever men there are or will be anywhere, and so all will be saved eternally. By this kind of arguing, or rather babbling, many absurdities would follow. Between God and the seed of Abraham there was a covenant of circumcision. Now if you take whatever will be the seed of Abraham, and by the voice of God take whatever belongs to God, then both females and males should have been circumcised in Israel. What could be more absurd?

units.la: Sed quid dicemus ad id quod sequitur, qui dedit seipsum ἀντίλυτρον pro omnibus?
units.tr: But what shall we say to what follows: "who gave himself as a ransom [ἀντίλυτρον] for all"?

units.la: Refponfio ex superioribus liquet. Verè enim pretium redemtionis seipsum dedit sufficiens pro omnibus, nemine penitus ex tota vniuersitate hominum excepto: sed quia increduli redemtionem sibi non applicant, ira Dei manet super eos. Item, reconciliationis pretium dedit semetipsum pro omnibus pertinentibus ad vniuersitatem
units.tr: The answer is clear from what was said above. He truly gave himself as a sufficient ransom price for all, excluding no one at all from the whole human race. But because unbelievers do not apply the redemption to themselves, the wrath of God remains upon them. Likewise, he gave himself as the price of reconciliation for all belonging to the whole body

units.la: Note: the Greek phrase ἀντίλυτρον is printed in the italic line above. tem electorum, & corpus ipsius. Item, pro omnibus indefinite, hoc est, pro quibusuis, Iudæis & gentibus, sublimi-bus, humilibus, dominis & seruis, vt sæpe iam dictum est. In quam sententiam & Theophilactus inclinat.
units.tr: of the elect, and of his body. Likewise, he died for all indefinitely, that is, for whomever, Jews and Gentiles, high and low, masters and servants, as has often been said already. The Greek commentator Theophylact also inclines to this view.

units.la: Alter locus habetur 2. Corinth. 5. Si vnus pro omnibus mortuus fuit, nempe omnes mortui sunt: & ille pro omnibus mortuus est, vt qui viuunt, posthac sibi non viuant, sed ei qui pro ipsis mortuus est, & resurrexit. Itaque nos posthac neminem nouimus secundum carnem. Quod si etiam nouimus Christum secundum carnem, nunc tamen non amplius nouimus. Si quis igitur in Christo noua creatura est, vetera praeterierunt, ecce noua facta sunt omnia. Bis dicitur hic Christum esse mortuum pro omnibus.
units.tr: Another passage is found in 2 Corinthians 5: If one died for all, then all died; and he died for all, so that those who live should no longer live for themselves, but for him who died for them and rose again. Therefore from now on we know no one according to the flesh. And even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him so. If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation; the old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new. Here it is said twice that Christ died for all.

units.la: Recte: quis negat? dicimus & nos: sed de sensu laboratur. Efficaciter pro omnibus mortuum esse Christum, sic vt pater coelestis re ipsa totum genus humanum in gratiam receperit, & nemo non a morte ad vitam, a peccato ad iustitiam, a vetustate ad nouitatē transierit, aduersarius dicit, Paulus non dicit: cit: imò verbis Pauli manifestè repu- gnat. Reconciliationem enim in se-quentibus, definit per id, quòd Deus peccata non imputet, &, quod iustitia Dei fiamus in Christo. Id autem fide fit. Etenim peccata non imputari, & fi-dem pro iustitia imputari, Paulus pro eodem vsurpat, nec aliam intelligi vult iustitiam Dei, nisi quæ per fidem Jesu Christi est in omnes &super omnes qui credunt, & non in omnes simpliciter, siue credant siue non credant.
units.tr: Quite right: who denies it? We also say so. But the dispute is about the meaning. That Christ died effectively for all, so that the heavenly Father has in fact received the whole human race into favour, and everyone has passed from death to life, from sin to righteousness, from the old to the new, the opponent says Paul does not say. Indeed, he clearly contradicts the words of Paul. For in what follows Paul defines reconciliation by this: that God does not impute sins, and that we become the righteousness of God in Christ. This happens through faith. For Paul uses the same thing for both: that sins are not imputed and that faith is imputed for righteousness. Nor does he wish the righteousness of God to be understood as anything other than that which is through faith in Jesus Christ, upon all and over all who believe, and not upon all simply, whether they believe or not.

units.la: Quid vox illa ministrorum reconci-liationis, hoc ipso cap. nonne idem euincit? Legatione fungentes Christi nomi-ne, oramus Christi nomine, reconciliamini Deo. Quod quid aliud est, quàm, resipi-scite & conuertimini, vt deleantur peccata vestra, & sic re ipsa participes euadatis peractæ reconciliationis?
units.tr: Does not that phrase about the ministers of reconciliation prove the same thing in this very chapter? "We are ambassadors for Christ, we beseech you in Christ's name: be reconciled to God." What is this other than: repent and be converted, so that your sins may be blotted out, and so that you may in fact become partakers of the completed reconciliation?

units.la: Nouum item & inauditum est, nullum non hominem nouam factum creaturam per Christum: cùm Apostolus tam distinctè scribat, Si quis in Christo est (hoc est, Christi fidem admisit, & in ipsum credit, vt Hieron: Theophylactus, stus, & alij vetusti notant interpretes) i noua creatura est.Et Augustinus inquit: omnis ergo noua creatura, id est, populus renouatus per fidem in Christo, habet iam quod in sesperat. Extra Christum igitur existentes & manentes, nec sunt, nec fuerunt vnquam noua creatura.
units.tr: It is also new and unheard of that every single man has been made a new creature through Christ, since the Apostle writes so distinctly: If anyone is in Christ (that is, has admitted faith in Christ and believes in him, as Jerome, Theophylact and other ancient interpreters note) is a new creature. And Augustine says: Therefore every new creature, that is, the people renewed through faith in Christ, already has what it hopes for. Those, then, who exist and remain outside Christ, neither are nor ever were a new creature.

units.la: Quod autem ait Paulus, neminem nouimus posthac secundum carnem: non est sensus, neminem non renouatum beneficio Christi, vt dictum hoc ab aduersario torquetur: sed sentit omnes non renatos, sibi esse tanquam nondum natos, nihil se in quoquam spectare aut laudare carnale, sed eum demum approbare, qui noua factus sit creatura per fidem Christi, vt ipsi deinceps, & non mundo viuat. August: & Theophil: illud Neminem restringunt ad credentes, sensu nonnihil diuerso ab eo qui nunc dictus est. Ex his liquet, opinionem de vniuersali omnium, credentium & non credentium, redemtione & renouatione, verbis Apostoli e diametro repugnare.
units.tr: As for what Paul says, "we know no one from now on according to the flesh," the sense is not that no one is renewed by the benefit of Christ, as the opponent twists the saying; rather, Paul means that all the unregenerate are to him as if not yet born, and that he regards nothing carnal in anyone or praises it, but approves only the one who has become a new creature through faith in Christ, so that he may live from then on for them and not for the world. Augustine and Theophylact restrict that "no one" to believers, in a sense somewhat different from the one just given.
