From this it is clear that the opinion of a universal redemption and renewal of all, believers and unbelievers alike, is diametrically opposed to the words of the Apostle.

units.la: Age inquies, Quomodo igitur Christum stum mortuum dicit pro omnibus? Respondeo: quia beneficium Christi per se sufficit seruandis omnibus, licet effectum duntaxat sortiatur in ijs, qui Christo tanquam membra capiti per Spiritum sanctum inhærent. Augustinus loco citato, & Theophilactus in comment. ad efficientiam respicientes, τὸ καθόλου, consuetudine scripturæ restringūt ad credentes. Nam etiam ij soli peccato mortui sunt, & Christo viuunt, qui pro ipsis mortuus est & resurrexit. Et adducit Augustinus locum Ephes. 2. huic sententiæ attestantem, dicente Apostolo, cum per offensas mortui essemus, vna viuificauit nos per Christum, cuius gratia estis seruati, vnaque excitauit, vnaque collocauit in cœlis, vt ostenderet futuris seculis summas opes gratiæ erga nos: Gratia enim estis seruati per fidem, & opus Dei estis, conditi in Iesu Christo ad opera bona.
units.tr: Come, you will say, how then does he say that Christ died for all? I answer: because the benefit of Christ is in itself sufficient to save all, although it produces its effect only in those who cling to Christ as members to the head through the Holy Spirit. Augustine in the passage cited, and Theophylact in his commentary, looking to the efficacy, restrict the universal [τὸ καθόλου] to believers by the custom of Scripture. For those alone are dead to sin and live to Christ who died for them and rose again. Augustine also cites Ephesians 2 as attesting this view, where the Apostle says: When we were dead through trespasses, he made us alive together with Christ, by whose grace you have been saved, and raised us up together and seated us together in the heavenly places, so that he might show in the ages to come the surpassing riches of his grace toward us. For by grace you have been saved through faith, and you are God's workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works.

units.la: Tertiò obiicitur locus Rom. 8. Si Deus pro nobis, quis contra nos? qui filio proprio non pepercit, sed tradidit eum pro nobis omnibus, &c.
units.tr: Thirdly, the passage of Romans 8 is objected: "If God is for us, who is against us? He who did not spare his own Son, but gave him up for us all, etc."

units.la: Verùm hic nihil probatur degeneraliralitate hominum simpliciter, sed de vniuersitate fidelium atq; electorum: cum manifeste τὸ καθόλου ad eiusmodi restringatur: sicut cum idem Apostolus de Abrahamo scribit, quod sit pater omnium nostrum, & de sublimi illa Hierusalem, quod sit mater omnium nostrum, non vtique omnium hominum, sed omnium fidelium intelligi vult. Eadem hic est restrictio, pro omnibus nobis. Et multa concurrunt spectatis antecedentibus & consequentibus, quae sententiam istam apertissime confirmant. Certè credentium, & mundo quem per fidem vincunt, insultantium, voces ex sunt, Si Deus pro nobis, quis contra nos? Quomodo non omnia nobis gratificabitur, qui filio proprio non pepercit pro nobis? Quis nos separabit à caritate Christi? In omnibus plus quàm victores sumus per eum qui dilexit nos. Item, Quis intentabit crimina aduersus electos Dei? Deus est qui iustificat. Hinc Augustinus de correpţ. & grat. c.7. scribit, vocem esse ad regnum electorum, Si Deus pro nobis, quis contra nos? & H quæ sequuntur.
units.tr: But here nothing is proved concerning the generality of men simply, but concerning the whole body of believers and the elect, since the universal [τὸ καθόλου] is clearly restricted in this way. Just as when the same Apostle writes that Abraham is "the father of us all," and that the heavenly Jerusalem is "the mother of us all," he certainly means not all men but all believers. The restriction is the same here: "for us all." And many things, when the preceding and following context is considered, confirm this view most plainly. Surely these are the words of believers who triumph over the world which they conquer through faith: "If God is for us, who is against us? How will he not graciously give us all things, he who did not spare his own Son for us? Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? In all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us." Likewise: "Who will bring charges against God's elect? It is God who justifies." Hence Augustine (On Rebuke and Grace, ch. 7) writes that the voice of the kingdom of the elect is: "If God is for us, who is against us?" and what follows.

units.la: Obiicitur, Paulum loqui cum omnibus quibus epistolam scripsit, inter quos fuerint aliqui non electi, sed excidendi cum incredulis.
units.tr: It is objected that Paul speaks to all those to whom he wrote his letter, among whom there may have been some who were not elect but were to be cut off along with the unbelievers.

units.la: Verisimile id quidem est, sed pro ingenio caritatis æquum & iustum erat, vt Paulus de omnibus Ecclesiæ filiis Romæ & alibi, quamdiu contrarium non apparebat, tanquam de dilectis & electis Dei sentiret: quëadmodum ipse de se ipso testatur Phil. 1. 7. Et 1 Thess. 1. 4. Exemplo sunt ea ipsa dicta modò citata, ad Gal. 4. 26. Rom. 4. 16. item cap. 8. 18.
units.tr: That is indeed likely, but out of charity it was fair and right that Paul, while the contrary did not appear, should regard all the children of the Church at Rome and elsewhere as beloved and chosen of God, just as he himself testifies of himself: Phil. 1. 7. And 1 Thess. 1. 4. The very passages just cited are examples: Gal. 4. 26. Rom. 4. 16. Likewise chap. 8. 18.

units.la: Quarto habetur ad Heb. 2. Omnia subiecisti sub pedibus eius. Enimvero per hoc quod ei subiecit omnia, nihil omisit quod ei non sit subiectum. At nunc nondum videmus ei omnia subiecta, sed Iesum illum cernimus gloria & honore coronatum, qui paulisper fuit inferior angelis factus, propter mortis perpessionem, vt beneficio Dei pro omnibus mortem gustaret: decebat enim vt ipse propter quem sunt hæc omnia, & per quem sunt hæc omnia, multos filios in gloriam adducendo, principem salutis ipsorum per afflictiones con-
units.tr: Fourthly, it is cited from Heb. 2.: You have put all things under his feet. For in that he put all things under him, he left nothing that is not subject to him. But now we do not yet see all things subjected to him, but we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, crowned with glory and honour, because of the suffering of death, so that by the grace of God he might taste death for all. For it was fitting that he, for whom and by whom all things exist, in bringing many sons to glory, should make perfect through sufferings the author of their salvation.

units.la: secra seraret. Nam & qui sanctificat, & qui sanctificantur, ex uno sunt omnes. Quam ob causam non erubescit fratres ipsos vocare, dicens, Annunciabo nomen tuum fratribus meis, in medio Ecclesiæ tibi hymnos canam. Et rursum, Ego fretus ero ipso. Et iterum, Ecce ego & pueri quos mihi dedit Deus. Quoniam igitur pueri participes sunt carnis & sanguinis, ipse quoque consimiliter particeps factus est eorundem, ut per mortem aboleret eum, qui mortis imperium habet, hoc est, diabolum. & liberos redderet quotquot metu mortis, per omnem vitam obnoxii erant seruituti. Non enim utique angelos assumpsit, sed semen Abrahæ assumpsit.
units.tr: For both he who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all of one. For this reason he is not ashamed to call them brothers, saying, I will declare your name to my brothers; in the midst of the Church I will sing hymns to you. And again, I will put my trust in him. And again, Behold, I and the children whom God has given me. Since therefore the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he himself likewise was made a partaker of the same, so that through death he might destroy him who has the power of death, that is, the devil, and might free all those who through fear of death were all their life subject to bondage. For he did not take hold of angels, but he took hold of the seed of Abraham.

units.la: Ex his verbis Huberus aliquot nectit argumenta, quæ lector mecum iudicet atque trutinet. Primo sic infert: Christo omnia subiecta sunt sine exceptione. Ergo etiam reprobi: & per consequens, ad salutis communionem & regnum gratiæ, ipsi quoque peruenire debuerunt.
units.tr: From these words Huber draws several arguments, which the reader may weigh and examine along with me. First he infers thus: all things are subject to Christ without exception. Therefore the reprobate also; and consequently they too ought to come to the fellowship of salvation and the kingdom of grace.

units.la: Respondeo, Christo omnia subiecta sunt, sed non ad salutis communionem: alioquin etiam Diabolus cum angelis suis, peccatum, mors, & infernus ipse,
units.tr: I answer: all things are subject to Christ, but not to the fellowship of salvation. Otherwise, according to this disputant, the devil with his angels, sin, death, and hell itself,

units.la: ad salutis atque gratiæ communionem adsciscenda eílent, secundum hunc disputatorem. Sed omnia ei subiecta sunt; quia in omnia habet imperium, & omnibus dominatur, sive fidelibus, sive infidelibus; his ad mortem, illis ad vitam, ut recte in hunc locum Faber Stapulensis scriptum reliquit.
units.tr: would also have to be admitted to the fellowship of salvation and grace. But all things are subject to him because he has dominion over all things and rules over all, whether faithful or unfaithful: the one to death, the others to life. So Faber Stapulensis rightly left written on this passage.

units.la: Quod excipit, reprobos Christo subiectos ut saluatori, id est, ad saluandum; tum assentiemur, cum omnia docuerit Christo subiecta ad saluandum, etiam oues & boues & ipsa dæmonia. Saluatori quidem Christo omnia subiecta sunt; sed no ut saluatori ad saluandum;
units.tr: As for the objection that the reprobate are subject to Christ as Saviour, that is, for the purpose of saving: we will agree only when he has taught that all things, including sheep, oxen, and the demons themselves, are subject to Christ for the purpose of saving. Indeed all things are subject to Christ as Saviour, but not as Saviour for the purpose of saving;

units.la: verum ut ei, qui potestatem omnem accepit in cœlo & in terra.
units.tr: rather as the one who has received all power in heaven and on earth.

units.la: Deinde vrget verba, sanctificantem & qui sanctificantur, omnes dici ex vno, id est, eiusdem naturæ participes. ex quo infert, Christum pro tota humana natura & quotquot eius participes sunt, esse passum; intellige semper efficaciter.
units.tr: Next he presses the words: he who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all said to be of one, that is, partakers of the same nature. From this he infers that Christ suffered for the whole human nature and for as many as are partakers of it; understand, always effectively.

units.la: Verum consequutio nulla omnino est. Et audet ille scribere, hoc ita esse clarum ut nihil posset esse clarius. Nu-gæ. gæ.Neque enim dicit Apostolus, Christum omnes sanctificare qui eiusdem naturæ humanæ cum ipso participes sunt: nec ex verbis eius inferri hoc potest, nisi quis Dialecticæ prorsus rudis, putet affirmatiuam illam, qui sanctificat & sanctificantur, ex uno sunt omnes, simpliciter posseconuerti. Rectius scriptor de votatione Gent: extremo lib. primo, Natura, inquit, in omnibus hominibus ante reconciliationem mala, in omnibus misera, non in omnibus iustificatur, & a pereuntibus in quada parte discernitur ab eo qui venit quærere & salvare quod perierat.
units.tr: But there is no consequence at all. And he dares to write that this is so clear that nothing could be clearer. Trifles. For the Apostle does not say that Christ sanctifies all who are partakers with him of the same human nature, nor can this be inferred from his words, unless someone wholly unskilled in dialectic thinks that the affirmative proposition, he who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all of one, can simply be converted. The writer On the Calling of the Gentiles, at the end of the first book, more correctly says: "Nature, in all men before reconciliation, is evil, in all miserable; it is not justified in all, and it is distinguished in a certain part from those who are perishing by him who came to seek and to save what had perished."

units.la: Tertio argumentatur: Christus aboleuit eum, qui mortis habebat imperium, diabolum. Ergo moriendo omnes & singulos ex potestate eius eruit.
units.tr: Thirdly he argues: Christ destroyed him who had the power of death, the devil. Therefore by dying he rescued all and each from his power.

units.la: Respondeo, abolitu diabolum morte Christi credentibus, quibus omnis diaboli conatus inanis atque irritus reddicitur, donec Deus pacis tandem aliquando Satanam sub pedes ipsorum prorsus conterat. Super incredulos autem manet ira Dei, & per consequens potestas diaboli, qui velut carnifex quidam est irae diuinae ad irrogandum supplicia. Interim fatemur cum Leone, mortem Christi tam esse diuitem ad pretium, vt si vniuersitas captiuorum in Christum crederet, nullum Satanae vincula retinerent.
units.tr: I answer: the devil was destroyed by the death of Christ for those who believe, for whom every attempt of the devil is rendered empty and void, until the God of peace at last crushes Satan completely under their feet. But upon unbelievers the wrath of God remains, and consequently the power of the devil, who is in a way the executioner of divine wrath for inflicting punishments. Meanwhile we agree with Leo that the death of Christ is so rich in its price that, if the whole multitude of captives believed in Christ, no chains of Satan would hold them.

units.la: At sic Diabolus non erit katargēthēsetai, abolitus: manente nimirum ipsius imperio erga plurimos. Ad hoc dico, esse fallaciam a dicto secundum quid. Sicut enim recte dicimus Christum abolere & dissoluere peccata, opera videlicet diaboli, suos iustificando & regendo, licet interim peccatum in plurimos non desinat regnare; ita morte Christi non iniuria diabolus dicitur abolitus, licet ipsius potestas non cessauerit in filios contumaciae. Conferantur & alia loca, quibus Graeca vox occurrit, vt 1.Cor.1. v.28. Rom.6.6. & 2.Tim.1.10.
units.tr: But in this way the devil will not be katargēthēsetai [destroyed], that is, abolished, since his dominion certainly remains over very many. To this I say that this is a fallacy from a statement made with qualification. For just as we rightly say that Christ abolishes and dissolves sins, the works of the devil, by justifying and governing his own, although meanwhile sin does not cease to reign over very many, so too the devil is rightly said to be abolished by the death of Christ, although his power has not ceased over the sons of disobedience. Let other passages also be compared, in which the Greek word occurs, such as 1 Cor. 1. 28. Rom. 6. 6. and 2 Tim. 1. 10.

units.la: Quarto, expressa Apostoli verba sunt, Christum mortem gustasse pro omnibus, vt liberos redderet, quotquot per omnem vitam obnoxij erant seruituti. Ad id respondemus: si dictum hoc de efficacia mortis tis Christi accipiatur, particulam vni-uersalem non complecti omnes & singulos homines, sed omnes qui sanctificantur: sicut hic & infra autor ipse declarat. Cum enim meminisset mortis pro omnibus gustatæ, confestim declarationem adiecit de filiis Dei, velut chorum aut exercitum quendam eorum depingés, quibus in veram terram promissionis, & gloriam regni cœlestis ex hoc Pharaonis infernalis regno adducendis, primogenitus ille Dei filius, princeps & autor salutis eorum, pro omnibus ipsis mortuus, excitatusque, & gloria & honore coronatus, velut crucem pro vexillo præferendo, alacriter præcat, viámque aperiat præmuniatque. Et paulo post, qui sanctificantur, inquit, & qui sanctificat, ex vno sunt omnes. Vbi per eos qui sanctificantur, denotat illos qui saluti animæ destinantur, & in gloriam adducendi sunt, vt prius dixerat. In his vtique mortis Christi efficacia exstat, nō in iis qui non sanctificantur: sicut infra etiam cap.10. ait, Christum vnica oblatione,
units.tr: Fourthly, the Apostle's words are express: that Christ tasted death for all, so that he might set free all who through all their life were subject to bondage. To this we reply: if this statement is taken of the efficacy of the death of Christ, the universal particle does not embrace all and each of men, but all who are sanctified, as the author himself also explains here and below. For when he had mentioned death tasted for all, he immediately added a declaration about the sons of God, depicting them as a kind of choir or army, to whom that firstborn Son of God, their prince and author of salvation, who died and was raised for all of them and was crowned with glory and honour, goes before them eagerly, bearing the cross as a standard, to lead them into the true land of promise and the glory of the heavenly kingdom out of this infernal kingdom of Pharaoh, and opens the way and prepares it. And a little later he says: those who are sanctified and he who sanctifies are all of one. Here by "those who are sanctified" he denotes those who are destined for the salvation of their souls and are to be brought into glory, as he had said before. In these, certainly, the efficacy of Christ's death exists, not in those who are not sanctified; as also below, in chap. 10, he says that by one offering Christ has perfected for ever those who are sanctified.

units.la: H iiij concōsummare in perpetuum eos qui sanctificantur. Atque hi sunt de quibus Christus ipse inquit Ioh. 17. Pater pro eis sanctifico, id est, offero me ipsum, vt sint & ipsi sanctificati per veritatem: ij nempe qui filio à patre dati, & populus ipsius sunt, sicut Apostolus quoque dicit ver. penult. huius cap. ad Heb. Christum per omnia fratribus similem factum, vt misericors esset, & fidelis Pontifex in iis quæ apud Deum agenda forent, ad expiandum peccata populi.
units.tr: These are the ones of whom Christ himself says in John 17: For them I sanctify myself, that is, I offer myself, that they also may be sanctified in truth: namely those who have been given to the Son by the Father and are his people, just as the Apostle also says in the second-last verse of this chapter of Hebrews, that Christ was made like his brothers in all things, so that he might be a merciful and faithful high priest in those things which had to be done before God, to make expiation for the sins of the people.

units.la: Quod autem commemoratur de liberatione à seruitute & horrore mortis per Christi mortem, hunc quoque effectum in piis demum reperire est, qui aduersus corporalem & spiritualem mortem, Christi morte, velut alexicaco, instructi, à morte ad vitam transierunt. Et sic Brentius ipse in Expli. Catech. dictum hoc exprimit pag. 164. Christus, inquit, aboleuit mortem sua mortē, non, vt non moriamur corporaliter, sed nē corporalis mors sit interitus eius qui in Christum credit: Hic enim conseruatur in mortē ad æternam vitam. Quanquam ad pofterius hoc membrum quod attinet, sciendum est, textum indefinite legi posse, quomodo & vetus reddidit, & posteum Lutherus versione Germ. vt liberaret eos, qui timore mortis per totam vitam obnoxij erant seruituti. Græcis enim, vt Stephanus etiam in thesauro monet, ὀσοι frequenter accipitur pro οι.
units.tr: As for what is mentioned about deliverance from bondage and the dread of death through the death of Christ, this effect too is found in the pious only, who, armed against bodily and spiritual death by the death of Christ as with an antidote, have passed from death to life. And so Brenz himself, in his Explanation of the Catechism, p. 164, expresses this saying: Christ abolished death by his death, not so that we do not die bodily, but so that bodily death may not be the ruin of him who believes in Christ: for he is kept in death for eternal life. Yet as far as this latter clause is concerned, it must be noted that the text can be read indefinitely, as both the old translator rendered it and Luther later in the German version: so that he might free those who through fear of death were all their life subject to bondage. For among the Greeks, as Stephanus also warns in his Thesaurus, [hosoi] is often taken for [hoi].

units.la: Atque hæc dicta sunto de hoc genere testimoniorum, quæ Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum pro omnibus mortuum prædicant, additis simul responsionibus ad argumenta ex eorundem testimoniorum circumstantiis. Sequuntur ea loca quibus fructus mortis & passionis Christi ad omnes sine exceptione extendi videntur.
units.tr: Let these things be said about this kind of testimony, which proclaims that our Lord Jesus Christ died for all, together with the replies to the arguments drawn from the circumstances of these same testimonies. There follow the passages in which the fruit of the death and passion of Christ seems to be extended to all without exception.

units.la: Caput IIII.
units.tr: Chapter 4.

units.la: Hic primum obijciuntur verba Apostoli comparantis lapsum Adæ, & redemtionem per Christum, Rom. 5. vbi inter alia scribit, quod sicut per vnam offensam reatus venerit in omnes homines ad condemnationem, ita per vnam iustificationem beneficium Christi redundet ad omnes homines ad iustificationem vitæ.
units.tr: Here the words of the Apostle are first brought forward, comparing the fall of Adam with redemption through Christ, in Rom. 5. where, among other things, he writes that as through one offence guilt came upon all men to condemnation, so through one act of justification the benefit of Christ overflows to all men to the justification of life.

units.la: Et ibi omnes, & hïc omnes :
units.tr: And there "all," and here "all":

units.la: Ergo quotquot in Adamo perierút, per Christum iustificantur. Nec obstat, inquiùnt, quòd statim sequitur, pervnius obedientiam iustos constitui multos : per multos enim non intelligi aliquot duntaxat, sed omnes, eo quòd similiter dictum sit, in Adamo multos constitutos esse peccatores.
units.tr: Therefore, as many as perished in Adam are justified through Christ. They say that it is no objection that there immediately follows, "through one man's obedience many are made righteous," for "many" is not to be understood as only some, but as all, since it is similarly said that "in Adam many were made sinners."

units.la: Respondeo. Non plane eo testimonio probant quod volunt, etiam concesso (vt cum August. libenter concedimus) eosdem multos debere omnes intelligi. Solutio enim duplex est. Primò Augustinus verba ista læpissimè tractans, constanter exponit omnes iustificari in Christo, non quòd omnes qui nascuntur peccatores ex Adam, per Christum iustificati intelligantur: sed quia omnes qui iustificatur, non aliter possùt iustificari, quàm per ipsum, perinde atque omnes qui moriuntur, in Adamo moriuntur. August. de natura & gratia cap. 40. contra Iulianum lib. 6. cap. 12. De
units.tr: I reply: they do not prove what they want by that testimony, even granting (as we gladly grant with Augustine) that the same "many" must be understood as all. For the solution is twofold. First, Augustine, who treats these words very often, consistently explains that all are justified in Christ, not in the sense that all who are born sinners from Adam are understood to be justified through Christ, but because all who are justified cannot be justified otherwise than through him, just as all who die die in Adam. Augustine, On Nature and Grace, ch. 40; Against Julian, bk. 6, ch. 12; On the Merits of Sins, bk. 1, ch. 28; Letter 57; Enchiridion, ch. 51.

units.la: 12. De peccatorum meritis lib.1. cap.28. Epist. 57. In Enchir. cap.51.
units.tr: 12. On the Merits of Sins, bk. 1, ch. 28. Letter 57. In the Enchiridion, ch. 51.

units.la: Deinde, quòd dicit omnes & omnes, aduersriusque partis multitudinem pertinet: atque ita omnium est iustificatio per Christum, nempe eorum omnium qui ad Christi posteritatem, per spiritualem regenerationem pertinent. Hanc expositionem probat Hieron. in comment: & è Scholasticis Thomas Aquinas Expos̄it: ad Romanos. Quos si disputatores Tubingenses minoris faciunt, videant ne amicum & collegam suum Heerbrandum arguant falsæ expositionis. Sic enim ille Disput: de iusti-ficat: thes. 148. antithesin primi & secundi Adæ explicans; vterque, inquit, aliquid suis meruit. Adam ex se natis, peccatum & mortem. Christus in se credentibus iustitiam & vitam. Exuberat autem gratia Christi supra peccatum, quia Christus non vnius tantum peccati, sed omninò omnium remissionē nobis peperit, sicut verba Apostoli tenentur. Hæc ille, pie & orthodoxè. Falsissimum verò est, & à Pauli mente alienissinissimum, quod quibuscunque peccatum adscribitur, ijs etiam iustitia ab Apostolo tribuatur. Loquitur enim Apostolus diserte non de iustitia aliqua quae post denuo reddatur inefficax, & quam consequuti nihilominus postea in aeternum damnari possint; sed de ea agit iustitia, quam qui habent, in aeternum regnaturi sunt. Ait enim, per unum offensam mors regnavit per unum, multo magis ij, qui redundantem illam gratiam & donum iustitiae accipiunt, in vita regnabunt per unum. Unde etiam iustificationem vitae appellat. Atqui non omnes quotquot in Adamo mortui sunt, in vita caelesti regnabunt. Ergo neque omnes simpliciter donum iustitiae per Christum accipiunt. Expendit hoc Hieron. inquiens, Cum omnes iustificari dicit, non generaliter dicit, sed vniuscuiusque partis significat multitudinem. Alioquin si inveniuntur omnes homines in Christo iustificati, sicut in Adamo condemnati sunt, non erit vltro qui puniatur.
units.tr: Second, that he says "all" and "all" refers to a multitude of the other part; and so the justification through Christ belongs to all, namely to all those who pertain to the posterity of Christ through spiritual regeneration. Jerome, in his commentary, proves this interpretation, and among the Scholastics Thomas Aquinas, in his exposition of Romans. If the Tübingen disputants think little of these, let them see that they do not charge their friend and colleague Heerbrand with a false exposition. For he, in his Disputation on Justification, thesis 148, explaining the antithesis between the first and second Adam, says: each of them, he says, merited something for his own. Adam, for those born of him, sin and death; Christ, for those believing in him, righteousness and life. The grace of Christ, moreover, abounds above sin, because Christ has obtained for us not merely the forgiveness of one sin, but absolutely of all, as the words of the Apostle hold. So he; piously and orthodoxly. But it is most false, and most alien to the mind of Paul, that righteousness should be ascribed by the Apostle to those to whom sin is ascribed. For the Apostle speaks expressly not of some righteousness which afterwards is rendered ineffective again, and which those who have obtained it might nevertheless be damned for eternity; but he speaks of that righteousness which those who have it are going to reign with eternally. For he says: through one offence death reigned through one; much more those who receive the abundance of grace and the gift of righteousness will reign in life through one. Hence he also calls it the justification of life. But not all who died in Adam will reign in heavenly life. Therefore not all simply receive the gift of righteousness through Christ. Jerome weighs this, saying: "When he says that all are justified, he does not speak generally, but signifies the multitude of each part. Otherwise, if all men are found justified in Christ, as they were condemned in Adam, there would be no one left to be punished."

units.la: At, inquis, si plures perierunt in Adamo, quam in Christo servantur, huius ius igitur gratia debilior erit peccato Adæ: quod est contra Apostolum in ista comparatione.
units.tr: But, you say, if more have perished in Adam than are saved in Christ, then the grace of this one will be weaker than the sin of Adam; which is contrary to the Apostle in this comparison.

units.la: Negatur consequentia: quia magnitudo & potentia gratiæ supra peccatum, non debet æstimari secundum multitudinem in Adamo condemnatorum, & in Christo iustificatorum atque glorificatorum: sic enim pari dun-taxat, & nihilo adhuc validior esset gratia peccato, etiam si in Christo iusti constituerentur, quotquot in Adamo peccatores nascuntur. Iam autem gratia Seruatoris in infinitum est potentior peccato protoplasti, & tanto plus potest, quanto plus Deus homine potest. Sed in his consistit amplitudo illa gratiæ super peccatum.
units.tr: The consequence is denied: because the greatness and power of grace above sin ought not to be measured by the number of those condemned in Adam and of those justified and glorified in Christ. For thus grace would be only equal to sin, and no stronger at all, even if as many as are born sinners in Adam were made righteous in Christ. But now the grace of the Saviour is infinitely more powerful than the sin of the first man, and it can do as much more as God is more powerful than man. But that greatness of grace above sin consists in these things.

units.la: I. Peccatum mortem peperit; gratia iustitiam & vitam. Facilius autem est innumeros perdere & condemnare, quàm vnicum viuificare & saluare: quandoquidé hoc ne omnes quidem homines in vnum conflati possunt; illud solius Adæ noxa potuit.
units.tr: First, sin brought forth death; grace brings righteousness and life. It is easier to destroy and condemn countless people than to quicken and save one; since not even all men together could be fused into one, whereas the harm of Adam alone was able to do the former.

units.la: II. In Adamo omnes ad condem-nationationem inuoluimur vno tantum de- licto ; at Christus non tantum ab illo vno originali, verum etiam ab omni- bus actualibus peccatis suos liberat. Neq; enim aliqua iustitia praeter Chri- ftum, sicut aliqua peccata praeter Ada, ait Augustinus, de peccatorum meritis lib. 1. cap. 15. Quàm potens vero hoc donum est, cui innumera resistere non valent peccata? Atque id Apostolus praecipue spectat, abundantiam gratiae praedicans supra peccatum. Ait enim: Non vt offensa, ita etiam est quod gratificatur Deus. Nam reatus quidem ex vna offensa introijt ad condemnationem. quod autem gratificatur Deus, datur ex multis offensis ad iustificationem. Et alia ratione abundantiā gratiae ostendens, ilico subdit: Etenim si pervnam offensam mors regnauit per vnum, multo magis ij, qui redundantem illam gratiam & donum iustitiae accipiunt, in vita regnabunt per vnum Iesum Christum. Quasi dicat, si peccatum tam est efficax ad mortem, quanto magis gratia ad vitā, imò regnum in vita coelesti? Quæ quidem comparatio enerwatur, & gratia peccapeccato iam superatur, fi statuitur eos etiam redundantem illam gratiam & donum iustitiæ accepisse, qui in æter-num cum Diabolis cruciabuntur.
units.tr: Second, in Adam we are all involved in condemnation by one transgression alone; but Christ frees his own not only from that one original sin, but also from all actual sins. For, as Augustine says, there is no righteousness apart from Christ, just as there are no sins apart from Adam. On the Merits of Sins, bk. 1, ch. 15. How powerful indeed is this gift, which countless sins cannot resist? And this the Apostle especially has in view, when he proclaims the abundance of grace above sin. For he says: The gift is not like the offence. For the judgment indeed came from one offence to condemnation; but the gift of grace comes from many offences to justification. And, showing the abundance of grace by another argument, he immediately adds: For if through one offence death reigned through one, much more those who receive the abundance of grace and the gift of righteousness will reign in life through the one Jesus Christ. As if he said: if sin is so effective for death, how much more is grace for life, indeed for reigning in heavenly life? This comparison is indeed weakened, and grace is already overcome by sin, if it is maintained that even those who are to be tormented eternally with the devils have received that abounding grace and gift of righteousness.

units.la: In his igitur gratiæ Christi amplitu-do & dominatus proprie cernitur, non autem in collatione iecundum numerum, eorum qui perierunt & qui seruantur. Accedit quòd non inopia redemtionis, aut infufficietia aliqua gratiæ & obedientiæ Christi fit, quòd multinon seruantur, sed propria ipsorum incredulitate. Effusio quippe sanguinis iusti, vt supra ex Leone retuli, tam est dies ad pretium, vt si vniuersitas captiuorum in Christum crederet, nullum diaboli vincula retinerent.
units.tr: In these things, therefore, the greatness and dominion of the grace of Christ is properly seen, and not in a comparison according to the number of those who perished and those who are saved. Moreover, it is not from any lack of redemption, or from some insufficiency of the grace and obedience of Christ, that many are not saved, but from their own unbelief. For the shedding of the blood of the righteous One, as I related above from Leo, is so sufficient for the price, that if the whole multitude of captives believed in Christ, the chains of the devil would hold none of them.

units.la: Similis locus profertur ex 1.Cor.15.Per hominem mors, per hominem resurrectio mortuorum: quia sicut in Adam omnes moriuntur, ita & in Christo omnes viuificabuntur. Ergo omnes, nullo excepto, per mortem Christi redemti, semelque seruati sunt.
units.tr: A similar passage is cited from 1 Cor. 15: By man came death, by man came the resurrection of the dead; for as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive. Therefore all, with none excepted, have been redeemed through the death of Christ and have been saved once for all.

units.la: Respondeo hoc argumentum facilè dissolui, & ne speciem quidem veri habere: bere: quoniam Paulus non loquitur de viuificatione iā facta in cruce Christi; sed futura in die nouissimo: & intelligitur isthæc viuificatio, secundum probatos interpretes, vel de communi resurrectione, aliorum quidem ad vitam, aliorum autem ad condemnationem, vel (quod magis placet) de beatitudine & glorificatione piorum. Si prior sensus probatur, nullum inde argumentū est pro vniuersali omnium hominum redemtione & salute. Si posterior, certum est, eam viuificationem non fore omnium simpliciter hominū, sed omnium electorum duntaxat.
units.tr: I reply that this argument is easily dissolved and does not even have the appearance of truth: because Paul is not speaking of a quickening already accomplished on the cross of Christ, but of one to come on the last day; and this quickening is understood, according to the approved interpreters, either of the common resurrection, of some indeed to life, of others to condemnation, or (which pleases me more) of the blessedness and glorification of the pious. If the former sense is accepted, there is no argument from it for the universal redemption and salvation of all men. If the latter, it is certain that this quickening will not be of all men simply, but of the elect only.

units.la: Augustus: posteriore sensu intelligit viuificationem eo loci, & exponit ideo dictum esse & hic omnes, & ibi omnes, quia sicut omnes qui moriuntur non nisi in Adam moriuntur, ita omnes qui viuificabuntur, non nisi in Christo viuificabuntur.
units.tr: Augustine understands the quickening in the latter sense in this place, and explains that therefore it is said "all" here and "all" there, because just as all who die die only in Adam, so all who will be made alive will be made alive only in Christ.

units.la: Ambrosius in commēt: illud omnes refert ad vniuersitatem electorum. Sicut mors, inquit, omnes tenuit qui ex Adami origine sunt, ita & Christus vitam acquisiuit omnibus, qui videlicet ex eius corpore sunt. Cui & Hieronymus subscribit in loci huius explicatione. Imo haec aperte Pauli ipsius declaratio est, qui cum dixisset, omnes viuificatum iri in Christo, immediatè addidit haec verba, vnusquisque autem in ordine suo : primitiæ Christus, postea qui sunt Christi, in aduentu ipsius: Loquitur ergo de viuificatione omnium ad Christum pertinentium.
units.tr: Ambrose, in his commentary, refers the word "all" to the whole body of the elect. As death, he says, held all who are from the origin of Adam, so also Christ has acquired life for all who are, of course, from his body. Jerome also agrees with this in his explanation of this passage. Indeed, this is a plain declaration of Paul himself, who, after saying that all will be made alive in Christ, immediately added these words: but each in his own order: Christ the firstfruits, afterwards those who are Christ's, at his coming. He therefore speaks of the quickening of all who belong to Christ.

units.la: Tertius locus allegatur ex 1. c. ad Eph. vbi legitur patris beneuolu fuisse propositu ἀνακεφαλαιώσασθαι, id est, recolligere seu instaurare omnia in Christo, tum quæ in cœlis sunt, tum quæ in terra. Quam eandem sententiam Paulus repetit & vberius inculcat, ad Coloss. 1. Hoc patris beneplacitum fuisse, inquiens, vt in Christo omnis plenitudo inhabitaret, vtq; per eum omnia sibi reconciliaret, in cœlo & in terra, pace nimirum per sanguinem crucis eius facta. Et generalem doctrinam Colossensibus, qui iam Christi fidem admiserant, applicas Apostolus, porrò ait: Itaque vos quondam abalienatos & hostes, mente operibus malis intenta, nunc sane reconciliauit, in corpore illo I. carcarnis suæ, per mortem, ut sisteret vos sanctos & irreprehensos & inculpatos coram se: si quidem permanetis in fide fundati & firmi, nec dimouemini ab spe Euangelij quod audistis, Euangelij, inquam, prædicati omni creaturæ quæ sub cælo est: cuius factus sum ego Paulus minister: qui nunc gaudeo in iis quæ patior pro vobis, & reliquias afflictionum Christi vicissim expleo in carne mea, pro corpore ipsius, id est, Ecclesia.
units.tr: The third passage cited is from 1. c. ad Eph., where we read that it was the Father's good pleasure to sum up all things [ἀνακεφαλαιώσασθαι], that is, to gather together and restore all things in Christ, both those in heaven and those on earth. Paul repeats this same teaching and presses it more fully in Col. 1: It was the Father's good pleasure that in Christ all fullness should dwell, and that through him he should reconcile all things to himself, both in heaven and on earth, making peace through the blood of his cross. Then, applying this general doctrine to the Colossians, who had already received faith in Christ, the Apostle goes on: And you, who were once estranged and enemies in mind, engaged in evil works, he has now reconciled in the body of his flesh, through death, so that he might present you holy, blameless and irreproachable before him, if indeed you continue in the faith, grounded and steadfast, and are not moved away from the hope of the gospel that you have heard, the gospel, I say, which has been preached to every creature under heaven, of which I, Paul, have become a minister. I now rejoice in my sufferings for you, and in my flesh I fill up what is lacking in the afflictions of Christ, for his body, which is the Church.

units.la: Vrget aduersarius vniuersalem, Omnia. Quia omnia reconciliata & instaurata sunt, nihil penitus esse omissum inter homines, quod non sit reconciliatum & instauratum per mortem Christi.
units.tr: The opponent presses the universal word, all things: because all things have been reconciled and restored, nothing whatever among men has been left out that has not been reconciled and restored through the death of Christ.

units.la: Sed suo se gladio iugulat. Si enim vniuersalitati inhærendum est sine vlla restrictione, cur ad vnam speciem humanam restringit τὰ καθόλου, & exponit omnia, id est, homines omnes? Ante verba illa de omnium reconciliatione, præcesserat sane, omnia quę in cœlis & quę in terra sunt per Christum esse condita: omniaque per ipsum consistere; & ipsum ante omnia esse: & in omnibus priprimas tenere. Cur ab ista vniuersa-litate rerum omnium, tam paucis verbis toties inculcata, nunc recedit, & de sola humana natura exponit, quod omnia per Christum dicuntur reconciliata? Agnoscit tandem particulam vniuersalem pro circumstantia loci & materiae, de qua agitur, determinationem subinde efflagitare?
units.tr: But he cuts his own throat with his own sword. For if we must hold to the universal without any restriction, why does he restrict τὰ καθόλου to the one human species and explain all things as all men? Just before those words about the reconciliation of all things, the text had said that all things in heaven and on earth were created through Christ, that all things consist through him, that he is before all things, and that he holds the first place among all things. Why does he now depart from this universality of all things, so often stressed in so few words, and explain only of human nature that all things are said to be reconciled through Christ? Does he at last admit that the universal particle, by the circumstances of place and subject matter under discussion, keeps calling for qualification?

units.la: Quod autem ad sensum huius loci attinet, de recollectione & reconciliatione omnium per Christum, multi diuersa dixerunt super hac re: nemo tamen veterum interpretum, quod sciam, in eum sensum verba Apostoli accepit, in quem ab aduersario proferuntur. Tres autem expositiones alicuius momenti adferuntur, vt alias leuiores omittam.
units.tr: As for the meaning of this passage, concerning the recollecting and reconciling of all things through Christ, many have said various things about this matter. Yet, so far as I know, none of the older interpreters has taken the Apostle's words in the sense in which the opponent puts them forward. Three explanations of some weight are offered, and I will pass over the lighter ones.

units.la: Prima est, vniuersam simpliciter creaturam eguisse remedio mortis Christi: homines quidem, vt peccato & morte destructis, salutem sempiternam ex fide consequerentur: Angelos vero, vt reparatione hominum, & terrenorum cum coelestibus coniunctione, plena laetilætitia fruerentur: Elementa denique & creaturam quę videtur, propter vin-dicationem sui ab interitu & corru-ptione; si quidem ipsa etiam creatura, teste Paulo, liberabitur à seruitute cor-ruptionis, in libertatem gloriæ filiorum Dei. Hæc expositio est Theodoriti in comment. ad Eph.1. Col.1. & Heb.2.
units.tr: The first is that the whole creation, simply, needed the remedy of Christ's death: men indeed so that, with sin and death destroyed, they might obtain eternal salvation through faith; the angels so that, by the restoration of men and the joining of earthly things with heavenly, they might enjoy full gladness; and finally the elements and visible creation, for their own deliverance from destruction and corruption, since, as Paul testifies, the creature itself will be set free from the bondage of corruption into the liberty of the glory of the sons of God. This is the explanation of Theodoret in his commentaries on Ephesians 1, Colossians 1 and Hebrews 2.

units.la: Alij autem de angelis & hominibus exponunt. Hinc Aug. Enchir. ad Laur. cap.62. In Christo, inquit, instaurantur quæ in cœlis sunt, cum id quod inde in angelis la-psum est, ex hominibus redditur. Instauran-tur autem quæ in terris sunt, cum ipsi homi-nes, qui prædestinati sunt ad vitam æternam, à corruptionis vetustate renouatur. Ibidem exponens verba ad Coloss.1: Quomodo, inquit pacificantur cœlestia nisi in nobis, id est, concordando nobiscum? Terrena quip-pe à cœlestibus propter contrarietatem vitæ separata erant; vt in eum locum Hieronymus annotauit.
units.tr: Others, however, explain it of angels and men. Hence Augustine, in the Enchiridion to Laurentius, chapter 62: In Christ, he says, the things in heaven are restored, when that which fell from there among the angels is returned from men. The things on earth are restored when men themselves, who are predestined to eternal life, are renewed from the old state of corruption. Explaining the words of Colossians 1 in the same place, he asks: How are heavenly things made peaceful, except in us, that is, by being brought into harmony with us? For earthly things had been separated from heavenly ones because of their contrariety of life, as Jerome noted on that passage.

units.la: Tertiò, per ea quæ in cœlis sunt alij intelligunt animas sanctorum, quę iam sunt in regno cœlorum: per ea autem quæ in terra sunt, electos qui adhuc pe-regriregrinantur in exilio vitæ præsentis: vti Anselmus totidem verbis interpretatur. Appositè equidem. Neque enim dicit Paulus pacem factam inter cœlestia & terrestria, inter angelos & homines; sed Deum sibi reconciliasse, tum quæ in cœlis, tum quæ in terra sunt. Sic enim rectè ista construi, Græcus textus euincit, licet alij construant cum verbo ἀποκαταλλάξας. Applicatio etiam quæ additur, Itaque nos quondam abalienatos & hostes, nunc sane reconciliauit, satis declarat, reconciliationis proprietatem esse penes credentes: infideles autem, quantisper tales sunt, reconciliationis alienos & hostes Dei existere.
units.tr: Thirdly, by the things in heaven some understand the souls of the saints who are already in the kingdom of heaven, and by the things on earth the elect who are still wandering in exile in the present life, as Anselm interprets it in just these words. And this is fitting. For Paul does not say that peace was made between heavenly and earthly things, between angels and men, but that God reconciled to himself both the things in heaven and the things on earth. For the Greek text shows that this is the correct construction, although others construe it with the verb [ἀποκαταλλάξας]. The application that follows, you who were once estranged and enemies he has now reconciled, sufficiently shows that the proper reconciliation belongs to believers, while unbelievers, as long as they are such, are strangers to reconciliation and enemies of God.

units.la: Ceterum aduersarius, vt nullum non moueat lapidem, suam de vniuersalitate reconciliationis sententiam eo quoque stabilire vult, quod Paulus Colossenses omnes hortetur vt perseuerent firmi in spe Euangelij, & sic innuat, eos quoque reconciliatos esse qui à spe & fide deficiant aut deficere possint.
units.tr: Moreover, the opponent, leaving no stone unturned, wishes to confirm his view of the universality of reconciliation also by the fact that Paul exhorts all the Colossians to persevere firm in the hope of the gospel, and so hints that those also are reconciled who fall away, or can fall away, from hope and faith.

units.la: Respondeo. Cum nobis ex caritate de aliis iudicandum sit, pro fidelibus electis,& proinde pro reconcilitatis & hæredibus iustitiæ & vitæ æternæ habentur, talésque appellantur, quicunque Christi fidem nobiscum profitentur: sed tunc verè sunt id quod appellantur, si manserint in eo propter quod sic appellantur. Si autem perseueran-tiam non habent,non verè appellantur quod appellantur. vt scribit Augustus: de correpț. & gratia cap. 9. Sed de hoc pluribus infrà in secundę classis argumentis.
units.tr: I answer: since we must judge others by charity, those who profess the faith of Christ with us are regarded as faithful elect, and therefore as reconciled and heirs of righteousness and eternal life, and are called such. But they truly are what they are called only if they remain in that by which they are so called. If they do not have perseverance, they are not truly what they are called, as Augustine writes in On Correction and Grace, chapter 9. But of this more below, in the arguments of the second class.

units.la: Monet etiam aduersarius,probè notandū in verbis Apostoli ad Col.1. quod non solum dixerit, Euangelium omnibus Colossensibus esse prædicatum,sed ipsem Euangelij. In textu tamen est, nec dimoueamini à spe Euangelij,quod audiuistis. Mira igitur hominis attentio, qui nos notare hic iubet,quod in textu nusquam reperitur, nec si reperiretur, ad rem quicquā faceret. Neque enim spes Euangelij audientium est, sed credentium: & dicente Hieronymo, spem Euangelij contra Euangelium viuentes, sperare non possunt. Illud potiùs notandum hîc fuerat, quod Paulus Coloss.
units.tr: The opponent also warns that we should carefully note, in the Apostle's words to Colossians 1, that he says not only that the gospel was preached to all the Colossians, but the hope of the gospel itself. Yet the text reads: and do not be moved away from the hope of the gospel that you have heard. So it is a remarkable carelessness on the man's part to bid us note here something that is found nowhere in the text, and even if it were found, it would have no bearing on the matter. For the hope of the gospel belongs not to hearers but to believers; and, as Jerome says, those who live against the gospel cannot hope in the hope of the gospel. Rather, what should have been noted here is that Paul preaches reconciliation to God only to those already converted and believing.

units.la: Hieron. in com. lofs.non nisi conuersos iam & credentes, Deo reconciliatos prædicat. Vos quondam alienatos, inquit, nunc sane reconciliauit. Est enim in his verbis manifesta antithesis duplicis ipsorum status, fidei nempe & incredulitatis. Prius alienati & hostes, nunc reconciliati erant in corpore illo carnis Christi. Vbi igitur generalis illa reconciliatio, etiam non credentium, nec credituroruũ vnquam?
units.tr: Jerome, on Joshua, likewise. Once you were estranged, he says, but now he has reconciled you. For in these words there is a clear antithesis between their two states, namely of faith and of unbelief. Formerly they were estranged and enemies; now they were reconciled in the body of Christ's flesh. Where, then, is that general reconciliation, of those who do not believe, nor ever will believe?

units.la: Colloquio Mompelgart. citatur & locus ad Rom. 11. Conclusit Deus omnes sub incredulitate, vt omnium misereatur.
units.tr: At the Colloquy of Montbéliard the passage Romans 11: God has shut up all under unbelief, that he may have mercy on all is also cited.

units.la: Sed sermo ibi est de duobus populis, gentium & Iudaeorum, quos alterna contentione Deo visum sit ad fidem adducere: Nimirum, quod sicut Iudaeorum contumacia occasionem dederit conuersionis gentilium, ita Iudaei postmodū misericordiae gentibus factae æmulatione impulsi, & ipsi in Christum credituri sint, & sic omnes misericordiae diuinae futuri sint participes, id est, vterque populus, Iudaeorum & gentilium. Ad singulas personas in vtrovtroque populo referre hoc non possumus, cùm extra omnem dubitationem positum sit, fidem & conuersionem, quæ voce misericordiæ Paulus hîc denotat, non esse cunctorum & singulorum.
units.tr: But the discussion there concerns two peoples, the Gentiles and the Jews, whom God, by a mutual rivalry, was pleased to bring to faith: namely, that just as the obstinacy of the Jews gave occasion for the conversion of the Gentiles, so the Jews, moved afterwards by emulation of the mercy shown to the Gentiles, will themselves believe in Christ, and thus all will become partakers of divine mercy, that is, both peoples, of Jews and Gentiles. We cannot refer this to each single person in either people, since it is beyond all doubt that faith and conversion, which Paul here denotes by the word mercy, do not belong to all and to each.

units.la: Restat huius ordinis locus vnicus Ioh.17.Dedisti, inquit Christus, mihi potestatem omnis carnis, vt quicquid dedisti mihi dem eis vitam æternam. Hinc infert Huberus, nihil esse certius, quâ Deum omnibus esse reconciliatum.
units.tr: There remains the one passage of this kind, John 17: You have given me, says Christ, power over all flesh, so that whatever you have given me, I may give them eternal life. From this Huber infers that nothing is more certain than that God is reconciled to all.

units.la: Imò nihil incertius. Fiat syllogismus, & statim apparebit vitiosa consecutio. Nam maior falsa est vniuersè sumpta, vt sumi debet: quòd quorumcunque potestas Christo data est, ij Deo sint reconciliati. Siquidem & boum & asinorum, & omniù in cœlo & in terra creaturarum, etiam dæmoniorum, potestas ipsi data est.
units.tr: Indeed nothing is less certain. Let us make a syllogism, and at once the faulty inference will appear. For the major premise is false when taken universally, as it must be taken: that to whomever power has been given by Christ, those are reconciled to God. For power has been given to him over oxen and asses, and over all creatures in heaven and on earth, even the demons.

units.la: Quid verò si in specie duntaxat humana maneamus? hoc modo: Quicunque homines Christo dati sunt à patre, ideo dati sunt vt illis det vitam æternā. Iam autem omnes homines Christo dati sunt à patre: quia dedit ei potestatem omnis carnis, humanæ scilicet. Ergo omnes homines ideo ipsi dati sunt, vt illis det vitam æternam.
units.tr: But what if we remain within the human species alone? Put this way: whoever has been given to Christ by the Father has been given so that he may give them eternal life. Now all men have been given to Christ by the Father, since he has given him power over all flesh, that is, human flesh. Therefore all men have been given to him so that he may give them eternal life.

units.la: Nego minorem, eo quidem sensu quo hîc & alibi sæpissime locutio ea accipitur, Christo datum ⁂ esse. Ad probationem respondeo, aliud esse quod Christo dicitur data potestas omnis carnis, quàm omnes homines ipsi datos esse. Quæ quoniam à disputatore hoc confunduntur, audiamus Augustinum. super Ioh.tract.iii. Qui sunt isti quos ait à patre datos sibi? Nonne illi de quibus alio loco dicitur, Nemo venit ad me, nisi pater, qui misit me, traxerit eum? Ipsi sunt ergo quos à patre accepit, quos & ipse elegit de mundo, vt iam non sint de mundo: & sint tamen etiam ipsi mundus credes & cognoscens quod Christus à Deo patre missus sit. Sic enim ait, dedisti ei potestatem omnis carnis, id est, omnis hominis, vt omne quod dedisti ei det eis vitam æternam. Vbi ostendit, potestatem se quidem omnis hominis accepisse, vt liberet quos voluerit, damnet quos voluerit: sed eos sibi esse datos quibus omnibus det vitam æternam. Sic enim ait, ut omne quod dedisti ei, det eis vitam æternam. Proinde non ei dati sunt, quibus vitam non dabit æternam: quamuis & ipsorum potestas ipsi data sit, cui potestas data est omnis carnis. Hæc ille, veterum facile probatissimus. Et sane verba textus tam perspicua sunt, ut hallucinatio sit manifesta, & plus quam hallucinatio, omnes indifferenter Christo datos. Ait enim veritas, patefeci nomen tuum hominibus quos dedisti mihi e mundo: Ego pro eis rogo, non pro mundo rogo, sed pro ijs quos dedisti mihi: pater sancte, serua eos quos dedisti mihi, ut sint unum prout & nos. Pater quos dedisti mihi, volim ut ubi sum ego, & illi sint mecum. Item, quicquid dat mihi pater, ad me veniet, & hæc est voluntas eius, qui misit me, ut quicquid mihi dederit, non perdam ex eo quicquam, sed suscitem illud die nouissimo. Quis hic, nisi sponte cæcus, non cernit, Dominum ea locutione, suos à non suis, seruandos à damnandis discretos voluisse?
units.tr: I deny the minor premise, in the sense in which this expression is most often used here and elsewhere, namely that they have been given to Christ. As for the proof, I answer that it is one thing for power over all flesh to be said to have been given to Christ, and another for all men to have been given to him. Since the opponent confuses these, let us hear Augustine: "Who are those whom he says were given to him by the Father? Are they not those of whom it is said in another place, 'No one comes to me unless the Father who sent me draws him' (John 6:44)? They, then, are the ones whom he received from the Father, whom he himself chose out of the world, so that they are no longer of the world; yet they are still the world, believing and knowing that Christ was sent by God the Father. For he says, 'You have given him power over all flesh,' that is, over every man, 'so that he may give eternal life to all whom you have given him.' Here he shows that he has indeed received power over every man, to free whom he will and condemn whom he will; but that those are given to him to whom he gives eternal life." For he says, "so that to all whom you have given him he may give eternal life." Therefore those are not given to him to whom he will not give eternal life, although their power too has been given to him to whom power over all flesh has been given. So far Augustine, the most approved of the ancients. And indeed the words of the text are so plain that the error is manifest, and more than an error, to say that all men without distinction have been given to Christ. For the truth says: "I have manifested your name to the men whom you gave me out of the world. I pray for them; I do not pray for the world, but for those whom you have given me. Holy Father, keep those whom you have given me, that they may be one, as we are. Father, those whom you have given me, I desire that where I am, they also may be with me" (John 17:6, 9, 11, 24). Likewise: "All that the Father gives me will come to me, and this is the will of him who sent me, that of all he has given me I should lose nothing, but raise it up at the last day" (John 6:37, 39). Who here, unless he is wilfully blind, does not see that the Lord by this way of speaking meant to distinguish his own from those who are not his, and those to be saved from those to be condemned?

units.la: Nec obest, quod de filio perditionis obiicitur: Quos dedisti mihi ego custodiui, & nemo ex eis periit, nisi filius ille perditionis. nis, vt scriptura impleretur. Illud enim recte accipitur de electione ad Apostolatum, & sic August. quoque explicat tract. 106. Hic igitur phrasis in alia accipitur significatione: quemadmodum & tertia reperitur significatio, eaque generalissima, Omnia filio data a patre Ioh.3.& Matth.11.
units.tr: Nor is it an objection that concerning the son of perdition it is said: "Those whom you gave me I have kept, and none of them has perished, except the son of perdition, that the Scripture might be fulfilled" (John 17:12). For that is rightly understood of his election to the apostleship, and Augustine also explains it thus in tractate 106. Here, then, the phrase is taken in another sense, just as a third sense is also found, and that a most general one: "All things have been given to the Son by the Father" (John 3:35; Matt. 11:27).

units.la: CAPUT V. Examen locorum quibus mundi fit mentio in hoc negotio.
units.tr: CHAPTER V. An examination of the passages in which the world is mentioned in this matter.

units.la: PROGREDIOR ad testimonia quibus mundi fit mentio in scripturis in negotio salutis: quae similiter ab adversariis in confirmationem erroris trahuntur de vniversalitate gratiae, quod ad singulas personas in genere humano: Talia sunt, a Sic Deus dilexit mundum. Ecce agnus Dei qui tollit peccata mundi: Panis quem daturus sum, est caro mea, quam dabo pro mundi vita. Non veni vt condemnem mundum, sed vt saluem eum. Et apud Paulum, Deus erat in Christo mundum reconcilians sibi. Quomodo etiam salvator uator mundi & propitiatio pro peccatis to-tius mundi appellatur.
units.tr: I now turn to the testimonies in which Scripture mentions the world in the matter of salvation. Our opponents likewise draw these into support of their error about the universality of grace, that it extends to each individual person in the human race. Such are: God so loved the world (John 3:16). Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world (John 1:29). The bread that I will give is my flesh, which I will give for the life of the world (John 6:51). I did not come to condemn the world, but to save it (John 3:17). And in Paul: God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself (2 Cor. 5:19). Likewise he is called the Saviour of the world and the propitiation for the sins of the whole world.

units.la: In his & similibus locis, vbicunq; mündus commemoratur, cui gratiam suam contulerit Christus, contendunt non posse vocem illam aliter accipi, quàm promiscue pro omnibus hominibus, credentibus & non credentibus. Ex pluribus enim mundi significationibus tres praecipuas tantum agnoscunt, in quibus reliquas aiut facile posse includi: vt, quòd mundus accipiatur pro opificio, seu vniuerso systemate coeli & terrae: tum pro promiscua omnium hominum multitudine, bonorum & malorum: denique, pro parte ea hominū quae reprobos & incredulos complectitur. Ex his significationibus autem prima & tertia locis iis non quadrant. Superest igitur vt secunda significatione omnia illa loca accipiantur.
units.tr: In these and similar passages, wherever the world is mentioned as the world for which Christ has conferred his grace, they contend that the word cannot be understood otherwise than as referring indiscriminately to all men, believers and unbelievers alike. For they acknowledge only three principal meanings of the world out of many, and they say the rest can easily be included in these: namely, that the world is taken for the workmanship, or the whole system of heaven and earth; or for the indiscriminate multitude of all men, good and bad; and finally, for that part of men which embraces the reprobate and unbelieving. Of these meanings, however, the first and third do not fit these passages. It remains, therefore, that all those passages be taken in the second sense.

units.la: Respondeo, in sufficientem esse enumeratione in maiore. Sicut enim mundus in sacris literis pro reprobis & incredulis tantum, ita etiam pro electis & credentibus per totum mundum di-fpersperfis frequenter vsurpatur. Testimonia ad hoc probandum perspicua suppetunt. Iohannes cap. 14. vtramque significationem illam coniungit, verbis illis Christi, Venit princeps mundi, & in me non habet quicquam, sed vt cognoscat mundus quod diligam patrem, & facia sicut praecepit pater, surgite eamus hinc. De hoc mundo etiam est, Ioh. 17. vt credat mundus me a te missum esse. Quis est ille mundus, qui Christum cogniturus & in eum creditururus erat, nisi qui a mundo reproborum discernuntur? De his enim circa finem eiusdem capitis inquit, Pater iuste, mundus te non cognouit; ego autem te noui, & hi nouerunt me a te missum esse, & notum feci eis nomen tuum, & notum faciam: vtique illis, de quibus dixerat, vt credat mundus me a te missum esse. Sic ad Rom.4. Abrahae facta dicitur promissio, vt haeres esset mundi, id est, patet omnium credentium, circumcisorum & incircumcisorum, vt Paulus ipse explicat. Et cap. 11. ait, ruinam Iudaeorum opulentiam esse mundi, & abiectione eorum, reconciliationem mundi: id est, gentium, tium, quibus salutem dicit ex ruina Judæorū obtigisse, vt ij ad æmulationem prouocarentur. Vbi videmus mundi vocabulū etiam restrictius sumptum, pro pertinentibus ad plenitudinem illam gentium, quæ destinata est in locum Judæorum introire.
units.tr: I answer that this enumeration is too large. For just as in the sacred writings the world means only the reprobate and unbelieving, so also it is often used for the elect and believers scattered throughout the whole world. Clear testimonies are available to prove this. John in chapter 14 joins both meanings in the words of Christ: The prince of the world comes, and he has nothing in me; but that the world may know that I love the Father, and do as the Father commanded me, arise, let us go hence (John 14:30–31). Of this world also is the saying in John 17: that the world may believe that you sent me. What is that world which was going to know Christ and believe in him, if not the one distinguished from the world of the reprobate? For about the end of the same chapter he says of these: Righteous Father, the world has not known you; but I have known you, and these have known that you sent me; and I have made your name known to them, and will make it known (John 17:25–26). Clearly these are the ones of whom he had said, that the world may believe that you sent me. So in Romans 4 the promise made to Abraham is said to be that he should be heir of the world, that is, the father of all believers, circumcised and uncircumcised, as Paul himself explains. And in chapter 11 he says that the fall of the Jews is the riches of the world, and their rejection is the reconciliation of the world (Rom. 11:12, 15): that is, of the Gentiles, to whom he says salvation came from the fall of the Jews, so that they might be provoked to emulation. Here we see the word world taken in a more restricted sense, for the fullness of the Gentiles, which is destined to enter into the place of the Jews.

units.la: Otiosa igitur & impudens est tergiuersatio, vbinam in vniuersa scriptura inuenire & demóstrare possimus, mundum pro certo tantum hominum genere, quos Deus saluandos elegerit, accipi?
units.tr: Is it not therefore an idle and shameless evasion, when we cannot find and demonstrate anywhere in the whole of Scripture that the world is taken for a certain kind of men only, whom God has chosen to save?

units.la: Sed agedum istis subiiciamus testimonia August. principis facile veterum Theologorū, & in eiusmodi quæstionibus contra Pelagianos exercitatissimi. Is tractatu in Ioh. 110. in dictum, vt mundus credat, in hunc modum scribit: Ecce qui dixerat, non pro mundo rogo, pro mundo rogat, vt credat, quoniam est mundus, de quo scriptum est, ne cum mundo hoc damnemur. Pro isto mundo non rogat, neque enim quò sit prædestinatus, ignorat. Et est mundus de quo scriptum est, non venit filius hominis vt iudicet mundum, sed vt saluetur munmundus per ipsum. Unde & Apostolus, Deus, inquit, erat in Christo mundum reconciliàs sibi. Pro ipso mundo rogat, dicens, ut mundus credat, quia tu me misisti. Idem tractatu sequenti, Qui sunt isti, quos ait à patre datos sibi? Ipsi sunt, quos à patre accepit, quos & ipse è mundo elegit, ut non sint de mundo: & sunt tamen ipsi mundus credens & cognoscens quòd Christus à Deo patre fit missus, ut mundus ex mundo liberaretur, nec mundus Deo reconciliandus, cum mundo inimicissimo damnaretur. Et sub finem eiusdem tractatus, in illud, mundus te non cognouit. Mundus quippe ille damnationi praedestinatus, merito non cognouit, mundus autem quem per Christum reconciliat sibi, non merito sed gratia cognouit. Rursum tractat. 53. Mundus appellatur in malis hominibus, qui tota terrarum orbe diffusi sunt: appellatur etiam mundus in bonus, qui similiter toto terrarum orbe diffusi sunt. Unde dicit Apostolus, Deus erat in Christo mundum reconcilians sibi. Atque hoc sensu ibidem exponit dictum, Nunc iudicium est mundi, iudicium videlicet non damnationis, sed discretionis, quo futurum erat, ut longè latèque que peccata dimitterentur, & millia millium à dominatu diaboli per fidem liberata Deo reconciliarentur.
units.tr: But come, let us add to these the testimonies of Augustine, the chief of the ancient theologians, and most practised in questions of this kind against the Pelagians. In his tractate 110 on John, on the words that the world may believe, he writes in this way: Behold, he who had said, I do not pray for the world, now prays for the world, that it may believe, because it is the world of which it is written that we should not be condemned with this world. He does not pray for that world, for he does not fail to know to what it is predestined. And it is the world of which it is written that the Son of man did not come to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him. Hence also the Apostle says, God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself. He prays for that very world, saying, that the world may believe, because you sent me. In the following tractate he says: Who are those whom he says were given to him by the Father? They are those whom he received from the Father, whom he himself chose out of the world, that they might not be of the world; and yet they are the very world that believes and knows that Christ was sent by God the Father, so that the world might be freed from the world, and the world be reconciled to God, and not be condemned with the world, which is most hostile. And near the end of the same tractate, on the words the world has not known you: That world, predestined to damnation, rightly did not know him; but the world which he reconciles to himself through Christ knew him, not by merit but by grace. Again, in tractate 53: The world is called the wicked men who are spread throughout the whole orb of the earth; the world is also called the good, who are likewise spread throughout the whole orb of the earth. Hence the Apostle says, God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself. And in this same sense he explains in the same place the saying, Now is the judgment of the world (John 12:31): a judgment, namely, not of condemnation but of discernment, by which it was to come about that sins should be forgiven far and wide, and thousands upon thousands, liberated through faith from the dominion of the devil, should be reconciled to God.

units.la: Similiter Ambrosius ait in Psalm 118. ferm.12. Vere orbis terrarum in Ecclesia est, in qua non Iudæus tantummodo aut Græcus, non Barbarus aut Scytha, non seruus aut liber, sed omnes in Christo vnum sumus.
units.tr: Similarly Ambrose says, on Psalm 118, sermon 12: Truly the orb of the earth is in the Church, in which there is not only Jew or Greek, not barbarian or Scythian, not slave or free, but we are all one in Christ.

units.la: Ex his apparet, nimis ruinosum esse fundamentum, quod mundi vocabulum, vbicunque in scriptura exprimatur in negotio gratiæ, totius humani generis vniuersitatem designet, nemine prorsus excepto.
units.tr: From these things it appears that it is a far too ruinous foundation to hold that the word world, wherever it occurs in Scripture in the matter of grace, designates the totality of the whole human race, with no one at all excepted.

units.la: Nunc loca ipsa sigillatim consideremus. Quod ad verba Ioh.3. Sic Deus dilexit mundum, dicimus appellatione mundi indefinitè humanum genus intelligi, dicente Christo Ioh. 17. Se non orare pro mundo, id est pro reprobis, sed tantum pro iis quos dedit ei pater, & in ipsum crediturí erant. Paulus etiam ad Rom. declarat, tantam esse vim dilectionis Dei in Christo, vt aduersus praesentia & futura, & omnes mundi tentationes dilecti Dei reddantur insuperabiles.
units.tr: Now let us consider the passages themselves one by one. As to the words God so loved the world (John 3:16), we say that by the name world the human race is understood indefinitely, Christ saying in John 17 that he does not pray for the world, that is, for the reprobate, but only for those whom the Father gave him, and who were going to believe in him. Paul also declares in Romans that the power of God's love in Christ is so great that, against present and future things, and all the temptations of the world, the beloved of God are made invincible.

units.la: Hyphenated line end "in-"/"supera-" continues: insuperabiles. superabiles : quod certè de omnibus hominibus dici nequit. Non igitur omnium est ea dilectio, licet in genere Deus nihil oderit eorum quæ fecit, vt suprà vidimus.
units.tr: But this cannot certainly be said of all men: insuperable, not superable. Therefore that love is not of all, although in general God hates nothing of what he has made, as we have seen above.

units.la: Age vero, contrarias rationes dissoluamus, quibus probare conantur vocem mundi, quę in scriptura valdè ambigua est, hìc pro vniuersa massa generis humani accipi necessariò, prorsus inquiunt vt accipitur Rom.f. Per vnum hominem peccatum in mundum intrøjt, & per peccatum mors. D. Iacobus Colloquio Mompelgart. prouocat ad iudicium & vnanimem consensum omnium scriptorum & interpretum, veterum & neotericorum. Magna sanè temeritas, ad quam retundendam vnum è multis producam, Rupertum Tuitiesem, qui ab hinc annos plus minus CD. floruit.
units.tr: Come now, let us dissolve the contrary arguments by which they try to prove that the word world, which in Scripture is very ambiguous, must necessarily be taken here for the whole mass of the human race. They say flatly that it is so taken in Romans 5: Through one man sin entered into the world, and through sin death. Dr. James, at the Colloquy of Mömpelgard, appeals to the judgment and unanimous consent of all writers and interpreters, both ancient and modern. It is indeed great rashness; and to beat it back I will bring forward one out of many, Rupert of Deutz, who flourished some 500 years ago.

units.la: Is commentariis suis in Ioh. quibus Augustinum strenuè imitari solet, in præsentem locum ita scribit, Mundum sanè quem dilexit Deus, humanum genus accipimus, id est, viuos & mortuos; mortuos scilicet, qui venturum in fide expestauerunt, viuos, qui in illum, siue ex Iudaeis, siue ex gentibus, crediturierant. Sic enim ait absque distinctione Gentilis aut Iudaei vniuersaliter, vt omnis qui credit in eum non pereat, sed habeat vitam æternam.
units.tr: In his commentaries on John, which he usually imitates vigorously after Augustine, he writes on the present passage as follows: By the world that God loved we understand the human race, that is, the living and the dead: the dead, namely, who waited in faith for him who was to come; the living, who were going to believe in him, whether from the Jews or from the Gentiles. For he says without distinction of Gentile or Jew, universally, that everyone who believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life.

units.la: Secundum August. expositio hæc confirmatur ex sententia à Christo immediatè subiecta, cùm ait; non enim misit Deus filium suum in mundum, vt iudicet mundum, sed vt mundus saluetur. Idem nempe mundus haud dubiè est, quem pater dilexit, & quem Christus venit saluare. Mundus autè is, cuius saluandi gratia Christus venit, August. teste, vt ante citauimus, sunt electi & credetes.
units.tr: According to Augustine, this interpretation is confirmed by the sentence Christ adds immediately after: "For God did not send his Son into the world to judge the world, but that the world might be saved." Surely the world that the Father loved is the same world that Christ came to save. Yet, as Augustine testifies, as we cited above, the world for whose salvation Christ came is the elect and believers.

units.la: Audi Huberè, & stomachari desine, si & nobis interpretatio ista non displiceat; aut si eam improbas, rationibus, non conuitijs memineris certandum ad veritatis inquisitionem. Ecquam verò rationem habetis? D. Jacobus pro ratione adfert, quòd Christus eodem loco subiecerit, hoc est iudicium quod lux venit in mundum, & mundus plus amauit tenebras. Hîc vocabulum mundus, inquit, non potest intelligi de electis tantum.
units.tr: Hear, Huber, and stop fuming, if this interpretation does not displease us too. If you reject it, let your objections be reasoned, not abusive, since we must contend in the search for truth. What reason do you have? Saint James offers as his reason that Christ added in the same place, this is the judgment, that the light has come into the world, and men loved darkness more than light. Here, he says, the word world cannot be understood of the elect only.

units.la: Tract. no. gratia Christus venit
units.tr: Tract. no. Gratia, Christus venit.

units.la: Colloq. Mom. venit in mundum tům, sed maxime de illis qui reijciuntur & damnantur. Sed ósciter textum allegauit: quia textus habet, & homines plus dilexerunt tenebras. Mundi hic nulla mentio.
units.tr: Colloq. Mom.: he came into the world then, but chiefly concerning those who are rejected and condemned. But he quoted the text carelessly, because the text says men loved darkness more than light. There is no mention of the world here.

units.la: Nihilo solidior est Huberiana probatio. Mundum, inquit, Christus in duo diuidit genera, accipientiū & aduersantium lucem: seu, credentium & non credentium. Vtrique igitur hominum parti Deus filium suū misit. Respondeo, Negatur antecedens. Hominum quidem alij credunt, alij non, alij lucem amant, alij oderunt: sed quod Christus mundū illum, de quo dixerat, Sic Deus dilexit mundū, in duo genera diuidat, ex contextu haberi nequit.
units.tr: Huber's proof is no more solid. Christ, he says, divides the world into two kinds: those who receive the light and those who oppose it, or believers and unbelievers. God therefore sent his Son to both parts of humankind. I answer: the premise is denied. Some people believe and some do not; some love the light and some hate it. But that Christ divides into two kinds the world of which he had said, "God so loved the world," cannot be derived from the context.

units.la: Ita patet nullum hic esse argumentum ex vocabulo mundi. Deinde, etiamsi admitteretur, per mundum ibi omnes homines designari, nondum sequeretur, Christum eiusque beneficia propterea esse omnium, siue credant sine non; cum ad credentium vniuersitatem exprese restringantur, dum additur, vt omnis qui credit, non pereat, sed K ij hahabeat vitam aeternam. Quid clarius?
units.tr: So it is plain that there is no argument here from the word world. Moreover, even if it were granted that by world all humans are meant there, it would still not follow that Christ and his benefits belong to all, whether they believe or not, since the verse explicitly restricts them to the whole body of believers, when it adds that everyone who believes should not perish, but have eternal life. What could be clearer?

units.la: Quod ad locum Ioh.1. Ecce agnus Dei qui tollit peccatum mundi, libenter concedimus, immolationem agni huius pro omnibus omnium peccatis sufficientem esse, sed quod ad effectum, tollit Christus peccata confitentibus & credentibus, ipso Iohanne 1. Epist.1. dicente, Si confiteamur peccata nostra, fidelis est & iustus, ut remittat nobis peccata nostra, & purget nos ab omni iniquitate. Item, si in luce incedimus, sicut ipse lux est, communionem cum eo habemus, & sanguis filij eius purgat nos ab omni peccato. Peccatum autem singulari numero dixit pro quavis iniquitate. Et cum dicit mundi, promiscue efficaciam sacrificij huius ad redemtionem, gentibus & Judaeis vendicat, ne solis Judaei redemtorem missum putarent. Hinc sancti in cantico agni canunt Apoc.5. Mactatus es & redemisti nos Deo per sanguinem tuum, ex omni tribu & lingua, & populo, & natione, & fecisti nos Deo nostro reges & sacerdotes, & regnabimus super terram.
units.tr: As for the passage in John 1, "Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world," we gladly grant that the sacrifice of this Lamb is sufficient for the sins of all, but as to its effect, Christ takes away the sins of those who confess and believe, as John himself says in 1 John 1: If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just, to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness. Likewise: if we walk in the light, as he himself is in the light, we have fellowship with him, and the blood of his Son cleanses us from every sin. He used the singular sin to mean any unrighteousness whatever. And when he says of the world, he claims the efficacy of this sacrifice for redemption indiscriminately for Gentiles and Jews, so that the Jews alone would not suppose that the Redeemer had been sent for them only. Hence the saints sing to the Lamb in Revelation 5: You were slain and by your blood you redeemed us for God from every tribe and tongue and people and nation, and you have made us kings and priests to our God, and we shall reign on the earth.

units.la: Quod ad verba Christi attinet Ioh. 6. Panis quem ego dabo, caro mea est, quam da-bo pro mundi vita, ex tota illa concione meridiana luce clarius est, vitæ huius spiritualis & æternæ, atque etiam panis illius verè cœlestis, re ipsa non fieri participes quoliibet, sed qui credendo ad Christum veniunt, & carnem eius manducantes, bibentesque sanguinem eius ipsi incorporantur, quales demum sunt ij, quos pater filio dedit.
