Ait enim veritas, Amen dico vobis, nisi ederitis carnem filij hominis, & sanguinem biberitis, non habebitis vitam in vobis. Qui edit meam carnem, & sanguinem meum bibit, habet vitam æternam. Caro enim mea vere est cibus. Sicut misit me viuens ille pater, & ego viuo per patrem, ita etiam qui ederit me, viuit ipse quoque per me. Quibus quid dici poterit clarius pro nostræ sententiæ confirmatione, effectum videlicet huius sacrificij, quo Christus patri se obtulit in odore bonæ fragrantiæ pro mundi vita, nō esse omnium absque discrimine fidei vel incrédulitatis, sed eorum qui Christo incorporentur ad Spiritus participationem? Etenim ut propter Christum quis vi-uat, uat, ait Augustus, participatio facit, qua manducat ipsum: nec potest quis viure re de Spiritu Christi, nisi qui de corpore eius fuerit, sicut corpus meum viuit de Spiritu meo, & tuum de tuo.
units.tr: As for the words of Christ in John 6, "The bread that I will give is my flesh, which I will give for the life of the world," it is clearer than midday from that whole discourse that the participants in this spiritual and eternal life, and in that truly heavenly bread, are not anyone at all in fact, but those who come to Christ by believing, and who, eating his flesh and drinking his blood, are themselves incorporated into him. Such, in the end, are those whom the Father gave to the Son. For the truth says: Amen, I say to you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in you. He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life. For my flesh is truly food. As the living Father sent me, and I live through the Father, so also he who eats me will live through me. What could be said more clearly, to confirm our view, than that the effect of this sacrifice, by which Christ offered himself to the Father as a fragrant odour for the life of the world, is not shared by all without regard to faith or unbelief, but by those who are incorporated into Christ for participation in the Spirit? For, as Augustine says, it is participation by which one eats him that makes someone live because of Christ; nor can anyone live by the Spirit of Christ unless he is of his body, just as my body lives by my Spirit, and yours by yours.

units.la: Quomodo igitur Christus mundi vita est? Testatur enim quòd mundo det vitam, & quòd pro mundi vita se- ipsum daturus sit. Deinde Christus ad omnes dicebat, quibus concionabatur, Pater meus dat vobis verum panem e coelo: eorum tamen multi postea retrocesserunt. Ergo panis iste vitae aequè est omnium, retrocedentium & perse- uerantium: seruandorum & damnan- dorum.
units.tr: How, then, is Christ the life of the world? For he testifies that he gives life to the world, and that he will give himself for the life of the world. Further, Christ spoke to all those to whom he preached: "My Father gives you the true bread from heaven." Yet many of them afterwards drew back. Therefore that bread is equally for all: for those who draw back and for those who persevere, for those who are to be saved and for those who are to be condemned.

units.la: Ad primam obiectionem dico, sicut de Abrahamo scribit Apostolus, quod per promissionem factus sit haeres mundi, id est, pater omnium credentium, sic multo magis Christi iure appellari vitam mundi, quatenus toto terrarum orbe dispersos Abrahae filios vita donat aeterna. Secundò mundi etiam vita est, sumendo iam mundum pro omnibus hominibus, qui sunt, fuerunt, & futuri sunt, in quantum nemo omnium mortalium viuificari potest nisi per ipsum, quamuis interim non omnes re ipsa viuificentur. Neque enim est in alio quoquam salus aut vita, nec aliud nomen est sub coelo, quod datum sit inter homines, per quod oporteat nos seruari.
units.tr: To the first objection I say: just as the Apostle writes of Abraham that through the promise he became heir of the world, that is, the father of all believers, so much more can Christ rightly be called the life of the world, insofar as he gives eternal life to the sons of Abraham scattered throughout the whole earth. Secondly, he is also the life of the world, if we now take world for all humans who are, who have been, and who will be, inasmuch as no mortal at all can be made alive except through him, although in the meantime not all are in fact made alive. For there is no salvation or life in anyone else, nor is there any other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved.

units.la: Tertio fecit ipse quod in se erat, tale offerens sacrificium, quod ad omnium exhauriendam perditionem, & vitam omnibus restituendam sat erat. verum quod infideles vitam non accipiunt, ipsi in culpa sunt Christum repudiando: vti in hunc ipsum locum & 9. ad Heb. tradit Theophylactus. Idem annotat & mundi vitam pro generali resurrectione posse intelligi, vt pro mundi vita se dederit, quatenus mors eius generalem resurrectionem toti hominum generi procurauit. Sed hoc videtur coactius.
units.tr: Thirdly, he did what was in him to do, offering such a sacrifice as was enough to exhaust the destruction of all and to restore life to all. But because unbelievers do not receive life, they are themselves to blame for rejecting Christ, as Theophylact teaches on this passage and on Hebrews 9. The same writer notes that the life of the world may also be understood of the general resurrection, in that he gave himself for the life of the world inasmuch as his death procured the general resurrection for the whole human race. But this seems too forced.

units.la: Ad posterius obiectum, Pater dat vobis panem caelestem; respondeo bifariam id exponi: Dat vobis, id est, offert vobis, (erat enim Christus in medio ipsorum) tantum restat vt accipiatis: vel potius, vt illud vobis accipiatur de corpore populi indefinitè, non de singulis personis in populo; similí prorsus locutione & antithesi in re ipsa, qualis est in sententia Baptistæ, Ego quidem baptizo vos aqua, sed venit qui validior me est, ipse baptizabit vos Spiritu sancto & igni. Id quod Iohannes, Luca teste, dicebat ad omnes, etiam ad Pharisæos & Sadducæos, vt elit apud alium Euangelistam. Quis tamen hic, nisi extremè insci tus & impudens, ex vocabulo Vos, contendat, omnes Spiritu & igni à Christo baptizatos fuisse, quotquot vocem istam ex Ioh. audierant? Sed qui simpliciter intelligere vult, sensus patet, Iohannem nimirum, vt seruum exterioris operis, aqua baptizasse; Christum, vt Dominum, spiritu ipsum largiri. Virtus quippe baptismi solius Dei, non ministri est, ait Ambrosius epist.217. Sic sensus hoc loco est, non Mosis, sed Dei esse dare panem illum verum è cœlo: Mosen vt famulum in domo Dei, manna ipsis dedisse, panem corporalé & figuram spiritualis illius quem Deus dat, & non homo.
units.tr: To the later objection, "The Father gives you the bread from heaven": I answer that it can be explained in two ways. Gives you means offers you (for Christ was in their midst); there remains only that you receive it. Or rather, let the word you be taken indefinitely of the body of the people, not of single persons within the people: a expression and antithesis entirely similar in substance to the saying of the Baptist, I indeed baptize you with water, but he who is mightier than I is coming, and he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire. John said this, as Luke testifies, to all, even to the Pharisees and Sadducees, as it is recorded in another Evangelist. Yet who here, unless utterly ignorant and shameless, would argue from the word you that all who had heard that voice from John were baptized by Christ with the Spirit and with fire? But whoever wishes to understand simply, the sense is plain: John, as a servant of the outward work, baptized with water; Christ, as Lord, bestows the Spirit himself. For the power of baptism belongs to God alone, not to the minister, says Ambrose, Epistle 217. So the sense here is that it is not Moses but God who gives that true bread from heaven: Moses, as a servant in God's house, gave them manna, a bodily bread and a figure of that spiritual bread which God gives, and not man.

units.la: Luc. 3. Matth. 3. homo. Vnde & Dei panis à Christo nuncupatur. Hunc sensum & Augustinus reddidit,& verba exigunt: & confirmatur eo quod eodem cap. ait Christus, Operamini cibo qui permanet in vitâ æternam, quem filius hominis dabit vobis: si nempe in me credideritis. Nam cùm cibus ille in vitam æternam permaneat,non vtique damnandorum est, qui esurient sitientque æternum.
units.tr: Luke 3. Matt. 3. man. Hence also the bread of God is named by Christ. Augustine too gave this sense, and the words require it. It is confirmed by what Christ says in the same chapter: Work for the food that endures to eternal life, which the Son of Man will give you, namely if you believe in me. For since that food endures to eternal life, it is certainly not for those who will hunger and thirst eternally to be condemned.

units.la: De dictis, no veni vt iudicem mundum, sed vt saluem mundum: Item, Deus erat in Christo, mundum sibi reconcilians, liquet ex testimonijs Augustini suprà adductis, orthodoxè ea accipi de credentibus per totum mundum. Vt enim peccata nobis non imputentur, sed fiamus iustitia Dei in Christo(quomodo mundi ista reconciliatio à Paulo describitur) vera in Christum fides requiritur: super incredulos autem manet ira Dei.
units.tr: As for the words, I did not come to judge the world but to save the world, and likewise, God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself: it is clear from the testimonies of Augustine cited above that these are rightly understood, in the orthodox sense, of believers throughout the whole world. For that our sins are not imputed to us, but that we become the righteousness of God in Christ (this is how Paul describes that reconciliation of the world), requires true faith in Christ; but the wrath of God remains upon unbelievers.

units.la: Sic ex eo quod Christum dicimus mundi seruatorem, non sequitur omnes & singulos in genere humano, siue credant siue non, propterea ab omni peccato & condemnatione redemtos, salutisque in Christo factos participes: sed seruat Dominus Iesus populum suum a peccatis suis, omnes nimirum qui sperant in ipsum. Quoniam vero illi toto orbe dispersi sunt, ob hanc & alias causas, ante expositas, sicut mundi vita, ita etiam mundi seruator merito nuncupatur. Quemadmodum etiam lux mundi vocatur, nec tamen omnes absque discrimine tenebris per ipsum eximuntur. Interim quia omnes in ipsum credentes habent lumen vitae aeternae, & nemo nisi per ipsum lumen vllum gratiae cofequi potest: elogiu hoc iure in ipsum competit: prorsus vt solifte aspectibilis mundi lux est, & quotidie mundum illuminare iure dicitur, licet interim tam multa in mundo luminis maneant expertia, vel quia eius capacia non fut, vel quia in tenebris manentia, ad lucem non veniunt vt ea frui possint.
units.tr: So from the fact that we call Christ the Saviour of the world, it does not follow that all and each person in the human race, whether they believe or not, have on that account been redeemed from all sin and condemnation and made partakers of salvation in Christ. Rather, the Lord Jesus saves his people from their sins, namely all who hope in him. Yet since they are scattered throughout the whole earth, for this reason and the other causes set out above, he is rightly called the Saviour of the world, just as he is called the light of the world, though not all are freed from darkness through him without distinction. Moreover, since all who believe in him have the light of eternal life, and no one can obtain any light of grace except through him, this title belongs to him by right. Just as the light of the visible sun alone is the light of the world, and it is rightly said to illuminate the world every day, although in the meantime many things in the world remain without its light, either because they are not capable of it, or because, remaining in darkness, they do not come to the light so that they may enjoy it.

units.la: Supersunt verba ex r.Ioh.2. Filioli, quod si quis peccarit, aduocatum habemus apud patrem, & ipse est propitiatio pro peccatis nostris, nec pro nostris solum, sed etiam pro totius mundi. Hic effertur Hub. locum esse illustrem
units.tr: There remain the words from 1 John 2: Little children, if anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, and he himself is the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only, but also for the sins of the whole world. Here Huber declares that this passage is illustrious

units.la: Matth.1. / Thef.ij. strem & inexstinguibilem. Omninò: sed non eo sensu, pro quo ipse propugnat. Aitque, si locum e scripturis proferamus, Christū esse propitiationem pro aliquibus tantum hominibus, puta pro credentibus, tum se acquieturum.
units.tr: Matt. 1. / 1 Thess. 2. and inextinguishable. Certainly; but not in the sense for which he himself contends. And he says that if we bring forward a passage from Scripture, Christ is the propitiation only for some men, namely believers, and that then he will be satisfied.

units.la: Verum solutio duplex est. Si de sufficientia locum placet intelligi, libenter admittimus, pro omnium hominū peccatis sufficere sanguinem Christi ad propitiationem, vt alia expiatione aut victima opus non esset ad omnium emundationem & salutem, dummodo omnes expiationem istam fide sibi applicaret. Et sic locum istum e Neoteri-cis Illyricus quoque, quem aduersarij magni facere solent, edidderit in Glossa. Quid quod ipsummet Iacobum Andreæ Coll. Mompelg. pag. 514. & 546. eo tandem delabi videas? Extra oleas tamen: quia ipsi probandum erat Christum non sufficienter tantum, sed etiam efficiēter omnium peccata expiasse, nemine penitus excepto. Id cum instituisset probare præsenti testimonio, nio,& aqua, quod dicitur, ipsi hæreret, confugit ad vulgare dictum scholasti-corum, Christum mortuum esse pro omnium hominum peccatis sufficien-ter,licet nō efficienter. Singularis dex-teritas summi scilicet disputatoris.
units.tr: But the answer is twofold. If it is agreed that the passage speaks of sufficiency, we gladly admit that the blood of Christ is sufficient as a propitiation for the sins of all men, so that no other expiation or sacrifice would be needed for the cleansing and salvation of everyone, provided that all apply that expiation to themselves by faith. And so Illyricus too, among the more recent writers, whom our opponents are wont to hold in high regard, has set forth this passage in his Gloss. What of the fact that you may see Jacob Andreae himself (Colloquy of Montbéliard, pp. 514 and 546) slide at last into this view? Yet he is off the mark, because he had to prove that Christ expiated the sins of all, not merely sufficiently but also efficaciously, with no one at all excepted. When he undertook to prove this by the present testimony, and (as they say) water was in his way, he took refuge in the common saying of the schoolmen, that Christ died for the sins of all men sufficiently, though not efficaciously. Singular dexterity of that great disputant!

units.la: Hoc igitur concesso de sufficientia aut potentia huius propitiationis, dico secundum propositam distinctionem, re ipsa interim sanguinem Christi ad propitiationem prodesse credentibus, non autem incredulis:sicut disertè scri-bitur Rom.3. Iustificamur gratis per redem-tionem factam in Iesu Christo, quem propo-suit Deus propitiationem per fidem, in san-guine ipsius. Et ipse Iohannes; Si in luce, inquit, incedimus, communionem habemus cum Deo, & sanguis Iesu Christi purgat nos ab omni peccato. Quo pacto etiam Ecclesia ex omni tribu & lingua ab eo describi-tur, tanquam ad quam proprietas re-demtionis per sanguinem agni mactati pertineat. Videsne Hubere, Christum effectiuè, (de quo inter nos quæritur) propitiationem esse credentium, non incredulorum? Ac in credentium illam vniuersitatem optime quadrant verba Joh.Ipse est propitiatio pro peccatis nostris, nec pro nostris solum (qui nimirum iam credimus) sed etiam pro peccatis totius mundi, id est, iam credentium & deinceps crediturorum in nomen ipsius, ad finem vsque seculi. Quemadmodum & Christus pontifex professionis nostrae (cuius verba Johannes de industria videtur sequutus) in extrema sua ardentissima precatione, non tantum pro tum credentibus, verum etiam pro iis qui postmodum credituri erant, patrem rogabat, quos etiam, vt supra ex Augustino obseruauimus, mundum ibidem appellat, cum ait, vt mundus credat quod a te misisti sim.
units.tr: Granting therefore this point about the sufficiency or power of this propitiation, I say, according to the distinction proposed, that in fact the blood of Christ benefits believers as a propitiation, but not unbelievers, just as is plainly written in Romans 3: We are justified freely through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus, whom God set forth as a propitiation through faith, in his blood. And John himself says: If we walk in the light, he says, we have fellowship with God, and the blood of Jesus Christ cleanses us from all sin. In this way too the Church, out of every tribe and tongue, is described by him as the one to whom the benefit of redemption through the blood of the slain Lamb belongs. Do you see, Huber, that Christ is the propitiation of believers, not of unbelievers, in an effective sense (which is the matter in dispute between us)? And the words of John fit very well this universality of believers: He himself is the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only (that is, we who now believe), but also for the sins of the whole world, that is, of those who now believe and who will believe in his name from now until the end of the age. Likewise Christ, the high priest of our profession (whose words John seems to have followed deliberately), in his final most fervent prayer asked the Father not only for those who then believed but also for those who were afterwards to believe; these he also calls the world there, as we noted above from Augustine, when he says: that the world may believe that you sent me.

units.la: Et de hoc ipso mundo credentium, ex omnibus gentibus & omnibus temporibus, hoc est, de Ecclesia per totum mundum, hunc ipsum locum Iohannis Augustinus exponit, tractatu primo. Epistola item 48. his verbis: Totus mundus in maligno positus est, propter zizania quae sunt per totum mundum: Et Christus propitiatio est peccatorum nostrorum, nec tantum no-
units.tr: And Augustine explains this very passage of John concerning this same world of believers, out of all nations and all times, that is, concerning the Church throughout the whole world, in his first tractate and in Epistle 48, in these words: The whole world lies in evil, on account of the tares that are throughout the whole world. And Christ is the propitiation for our sins, and not only for ours,

units.la: Ioh.17. Tract. 110. nostrorum, sed totius mundi propter tritícum quod est per totum mundum. Et plenius Tract. 87. in Ioh: Vniuersa Ecclesia, inquit, mundi nomine plerunque appellatur: sicut est illud, Deus erat in Christo mundum reconcilians sibi, Itemque illud. Non venit filius hominis vt iudicet mundũ, sed vt saluetur mundus per ipsum. Et in Epist: sua Iohannes ait: Aduocatum habemus apud patrem, Iesum Christum, iustum, & ipse est propitiator peccatorum nostrorum: nec tantum nostrorum, sed totius mundi. Totus ergo mundus Ecclesia est, & totus mundus perditionis, odit mundum redemtionis. Hæc August:
units.tr: John 17. Tractate 110. but for the sins of the whole world, on account of the wheat which is throughout the whole world. And more fully, in Tractate 87 on John: The whole Church, he says, is often called by the name of the world, as in that saying, God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself; and likewise that saying: The Son of Man did not come to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him. And in his Epistle John says: We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, and he is the propitiation for our sins, and not only for ours, but for the sins of the whole world. Therefore the whole world is the Church, and the whole world of perdition hates the world of redemption. So Augustine.

units.la: Cyrillus quoque in Iohannem lib.11. cap. 19. Christi verba, Non pro mundo rogo, cum dicto Ioh. concilians, scribitad hunc modum: Iohannes videtur discrepare à saluatore. Saluator enim pro mundo hic rogare abnuit: Iohannes autem no pro nostris solum peccatis propitiationem & paracletum illum esse, sed pro vniuerso affirmat mundo. Verum Beatus Iohannes, quoniam erat Iudæus, ne pro Iudæis tantum paracletus esse Dominus apud patrem videretur, non autem etiam pro aliis gentibus, quæ vocatæ obsecutæ sunt, sunt, necessario, pro toto mundo, adiecit. Dominus autem Iesus suos a non suis separans, pro eis inquit tantummodo, qui verba mea seruant, & iugum meum acceperint, rogo. Nam quorum Mediator atque pontifex est , ipsis tantummodo mediationis bonum non iniuria attribuit. Hæc Cyrillus.
units.tr: Cyril too, in his commentary on John, book 11, chapter 19, setting the words of Christ, I do not pray for the world, alongside the saying of John, writes in this way: John seems to differ from the Saviour. For the Saviour here refuses to pray for the world, but John affirms that he is the propitiation and the Paraclete not only for our sins, but for the whole world. Yet Blessed John, since he was a Jew, added of necessity "for the whole world," lest the Lord seem to be a Paraclete before the Father only for the Jews, and not also for the other nations, which were called and obeyed. But the Lord Jesus, separating his own from those who are not his, says: I pray only for those who keep my words and have received my yoke. For to those for whom he is Mediator and High Priest, he rightly attributes the good of mediation only to them. So Cyril.

units.la: Similiter autor de vocatione gentium lib.2.cap.1. dictum Ioh: non nisi de fidelium plenitudine exponit, quorum speciális quædam censetur vniuersitas, vt de toto mundo totus mundus liberatus, & de omnibus hominibus omnes homines videantur assumti; idque consuetudine quadam scripturarum, pro parte terræ omnem terram, & pro parte mundi totum mundum, & pro parte hominum omnes homines nominantium, vt copiose idem ostendit lib.1.cap.3. Adhæc Ecclesia Smyrnensis in epist: de vita Polycarpi, quam recitat Eusebius, de Christo loquens ait, eum pro totius seruandorum mundi salute passum. Hinc rursum apparet summa temeritas Iacobi Andreæ, non dubitaneis affirmare, hoc certissimum esse, & apud
units.tr: Likewise the author concerning the calling of the Gentiles, book 2, chapter 1, explains the saying of John as referring only to the fullness of believers, which is regarded as a certain particular universality, so that the whole world is considered set free out of the whole world, and all men are seen to be taken up out of all men. This is by a certain custom of the Scriptures, which name the whole earth for a part of the earth, the whole world for a part of the world, and all men for a part of men; as the same author shows at length in book 1, chapter 3. Further, the Church of Smyrna, in its letter on the life of Polycarp, which Eusebius recites, speaks of Christ, saying that he suffered for the salvation of the whole world of those who are to be saved. From this again appears the great rashness of Jacob Andreae, who does not hesitate to affirm that this is most certain, and among

units.la: Eusseb. hist. Eccles. lib. 4. cap. 15. apud omnes vere pios & sinceros doctores indubitatum, verba Iohannis de hominibus omnibus, nemine excluso, intelligi debere. Falsissimum id esse, apparet ex ijs quos protuli, sine controversia pijs & sinceris Ecclesiæ doctoribus.
units.tr: Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, book 4, chapter 15. The claim that John's words must be understood of all men without exception is, according to all truly pious and sincere teachers, beyond doubt. That this is most false appears from those whom I have cited, who are without controversy pious and sincere teachers of the Church.

units.la: At Iohannes particulam posuit universale, totius mundi. Quasi vero non & suam vniuersitatem habeat bonorum ille mundus. Certe idem Apostolus non metuit dicere, totum mundū in malo iacere, propter zizania videlicet, quæ sunt per totum mundum. Et in Euangelio secundum Iohannem, Pharisæi dicunt, videtis vos nihil proficere. Ecce mundus eum sequitur. Vbi adeo vetus interpres, atque Nonnus Græcus paraphrastes, & Germanica versio Lutheri, legunt cum particula vniuersali, totus mundus eum sequitur. Dicemusne igitur istorum more, omnes homines, nemine excepto, Christum sequutos? Quid stolidius? Sic Matth. 8. v. 34. tota ciuitas Christo exijt obuiam: & Luc. 7. v. 29. totus populus & publicani iustificarunt Deum. Deum. Totius mundi reges congregantur ab impuris spiritibus ad praelium: Apocal.16.14. & cap.19. ibidem, vniuersa terra dicitur sequi bestiam. Hanc visitatam scripturis loquendi rationem interpretes passim imitantur. Sic Aug. tract.4. in primam Ioh. scribit totum mundum esse Christianum, & totum mundum esse impium; eo quod per totum mundum impij, per totum mundum etiam pij sint. Idem in Psalm.21. in illud, In Ecclesia magna confitebor tibi: Ecclesia magna, ait, totus orbis est: & pro hoc toto orbe terrarum, hoc est, Ecclesia vbique diffusa, dicit sanguinem Christi effusum, totumque redemtum, & non solum Aphricam: vti Donatistae Ecclesiam in Aphricae parte concludebant.
units.tr: But John has used the universal particle, "of the whole world." As if that world did not have its own universality of good things! Certainly the same Apostle did not fear to say, "the whole world lies in evil," surely on account of the tares, which are throughout the whole world. And in the Gospel according to John, the Pharisees say, "You see that you accomplish nothing; behold, the world has gone after him." Here the old translator, the Greek paraphrast Nonnus, and Luther's German version all read with the universal particle, "the whole world has gone after him." Shall we then say, after their manner, that all men, without exception, followed Christ? What could be more foolish? So in Matthew 8:34, "the whole city went out to meet Christ," and in Luke 7:29, "all the people and the tax collectors justified God." The kings of the whole world are gathered by unclean spirits to battle (Rev. 16:14, and ibid. chapter 19), and the whole earth is said to follow the beast. Interpreters everywhere imitate this manner of speaking, which is familiar in Scripture. Thus Augustine, in his tractate 4 on the first epistle of John, writes that "the whole world is Christian, and the whole world is impious," because through the whole world there are impious, and through the whole world also there are pious. The same Augustine, in Psalm 21, on the words "In the great Church I will confess to you," says: "the great Church," he says, "is the whole globe; and for this whole globe of the earth," that is, the Church spread everywhere, he says that the blood of Christ was poured out, "and the whole world was redeemed, and not only Africa," as the Donatists confined the Church to a part of Africa.

units.la: Omitto alios, & ad scripturae exempla reuertor, illud superioribus adiiciens, quod Luc.2. legitur, exiisse edictum a Caesare Augusto, vt vniuersus orbis describeretur. Cum hae nationes diuersissimae iure vnius sociae imperij Romani, vniuersi orbis sortiantur appellationem: quid mirum,
units.tr: I pass over others, and return to examples from Scripture, adding to the above what is read in Luke 2, that a decree went out from Caesar Augustus "that the whole world should be enrolled." Since these most diverse nations, by right of being one allied empire of Rome, obtain the name of the whole world, what wonder is it

units.la: L pœnitudinem gentium ad vnitatem fi- dei & corporis Christi vocatarum, vni- uersi orbis censum obtinere? Gratia quippe Christiana non contenta est eoldem limites habere quos Roma, sed multos iam populorum sceptro crucis Christi illa subdidit, quos armis suis ista non domuit. Quapropter vniuersalis vocula expositioni prius allata nihil officit: sicut nec quicquam ei prę- iudicat, quod Hub. scribit de argumento a genere ad speciem, seu a specie ad indiuidua. Nempe a genere fidelium vniuersaliter, argumentum procedit ad te & me; quod si quis peccauerit, crediderit autem in Christum, partam ei expiationem per fidem in sanguine ipsius.
units.tr: that the multitude of the nations called to the unity of the faith and the body of Christ should hold the census of the whole world? For Christian grace is not content to have the same limits as Rome, but it has already subjected to the scepter of the cross of Christ many peoples whom Rome's arms did not subdue. Wherefore the little word "universal" does nothing to hinder the explanation given earlier; nor does what Hub. writes about the argument from genus to species, or from species to individuals, prejudice it in any way. Indeed, from the universal genus of believers the argument proceeds to you and me: if anyone has sinned, but believes in Christ, expiation has been obtained for him through faith in his blood.

units.la: Atque hæc hactenus de testimoniis quibus mundi mentio in causa gratia facta est.
units.tr: And so much for the testimonies by which mention of the world has been made in the cause of grace.

units.la: CAPVT VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: Responsiones ad Scripturæ dicta de vniuersalitate prædicationis Euangelicæ.
units.tr: Replies to the Scriptural passages on the universality of the Gospel preaching.

units.la: CITANTVR & alia quædam Scripturæ pturæ loca, quæ docent Euangelium ad omnes pertinere: vt, quod Paulus ad Rom. vltimo testatur, mysterium illud tacitum ab æternis temporibus, suo tempore ex decreto æterni Dei omnibus gentibus fuisse declaratum. Et Col.1. de eodem mysterio recondito à seculis & ætatibus, ait, illud tum patefactum fuisse à Deo sanctis ipsius, quibus ille voluerit notum facere quæ sint diuitiæ gloriæ huius inter gentes. Tale etiá est quod ex Act.17. allegatur. Temporibus quidem ignorantiæ dissimulatis, nunc annunciari omnibus omnino hominibus, vt resipiscant. Et ad Tit.2. Illuxit gratia Dei salutifera omnibus hominibus. Item Luc.24. Sic scriptum est, & sic oportuit Christum pati, & prædicari in nomine eius pœnitentiam & remissionem peccatorum in omnes gentes.
units.tr: Other passages of Scripture are also cited which teach that the Gospel pertains to all. Thus Paul testifies at the end of Romans that the mystery, hidden from eternal times, was in its own time, by the decree of the eternal God, declared to all nations. And in Colossians 1, speaking of the same mystery hidden from ages and generations, he says that it was then revealed by God to his saints, to whom he willed to make known what are the riches of the glory of this mystery among the Gentiles. Of a similar kind is what is alleged from Acts 17: "The times of ignorance having been overlooked, he now announces to all men everywhere that they should repent." And Titus 2: "The saving grace of God has dawned on all men." Likewise Luke 24: "Thus it is written, and thus it behoved Christ to suffer and to be preached in his name, repentance and remission of sins among all nations."

units.la: Adferuntur autem talia, non tam ad probandam vniuersalem redemtionem omnium hominum, quotquot ex Adamo propagatur, quàm ad arrodendam tantum & cauillis eludendam doctrinam prædestinationis diuinæ, quæ passim in verbo Dei tradita, & perspicuis testimoniis ita communita est, vt pre-
units.tr: Such passages are adduced not so much to prove a universal redemption of all men, as many as are propagated from Adam, as to gnaw at and mock away only the doctrine of divine predestination, which is handed down everywhere in the Word of God and is so fortified by clear testimonies that it can be pre-

units.la: L. ij premi possit, opprimi non possit.
units.tr: L. ij can be pressed, but it cannot be overpowered.

units.la: Sed de prædestinatione tractatio alius loci atque instituti est, nec temere hic commiscenda. Tria tamen breuiter admonebo. Primum, vt dixi, ex eo quod Euangelium omnibus prædicatur, non potest colligi redemtionem & iustitiam, aliaque gratiæ Christi diuitias, idcirco esse omnium, proprietate & fruitione; sed diuitiæ Euangelicæ propriæ demum sunt eorum, qui Euangelio obtemperant. Beati enim à Christo prædicantur, qui audiut sermonem Dei & eum obseruant. At in quibus sermo Euangelij fidei mixtus non est, iis nihil prodest auditus: sicut exemplo veteris populi ad Hebræos copiose ostenditur.
units.tr: But the treatment of predestination belongs to another place and plan, and is not to be rashly mixed in here. Still, I will briefly admonish about three things. First, as I have said, from the fact that the Gospel is preached to all it cannot be inferred that redemption and righteousness, and the other riches of Christ's grace, are therefore the property and enjoyment of all. Rather, the riches of the Gospel belong at last only to those who obey the Gospel. For those are called blessed by Christ who hear the word of God and keep it. But for those in whom the word of the Gospel is not mixed with faith, hearing profits nothing, as is abundantly shown by the example of the ancient people in the Epistle to the Hebrews.

units.la: Secundo, ineptum & falsum esse aio, quod isti volunt Euangelium salutis præcise ad omnes & singulos pertinere, & inter omnes gentes singulis, nemine hominum excluso, ex æquo diuitias gratiæ Christi exhiberi, falsè quod ad externa prædicationem. Probant, quia Apostolus testetur mysterium EuanEuangelicum suo iam tempore inter omnes gentes fuisse praedicatum, & declaratum vniuersæ creaturæ sub cœlo. Quia item Christus in nomine suo praedicari coepit praedicari poenitentiam & remissionem peccatorum in omnes gentes. In his autem locis (quæ valde mirabilis glossa est) per omnes getes intelligi volunt singulos in omnibus getibus.
units.tr: Second, I say it is absurd and false that these men want the Gospel of salvation to pertain precisely to all and each, and that the riches of Christ's grace are offered equally to each individual among all nations, no one excluded, falsely so as to refer to external preaching. They prove it because the Apostle testifies that the Gospel mystery was already in his time preached among all nations and declared to every creature under heaven; and likewise because Christ began to have repentance and remission of sins preached in his name among all nations. But in these passages (what a wonderfully strange gloss!) they want "all nations" to be understood as each individual in all nations.

units.la: Respondeo, ex collatione similium phraseon & re ipsa facile redargui falsitatem glossæ istius, nimium sane crassæ & intolerabilis. Legimus 1. Paral.14. verf. vlt. exijsse nomen Dauidis in vniuersam terram & pauorem eius iniectum fuisse omnibus populis. Et Psalm. 118. queritur idem, circumdatum se fuisse ab omnibus gentibus. Nebucadnezari item legimus omnes gentes subditas fuisse ut ei seruirent, Ier. 27. v. 7. ac dominium eius fuisse in omni loco, & in omnibus filijs hominum & iumentis. Dan.2.v.38. Quomodo etiam illa dicta sunt, Eritis odio omnibus gentibus, Matth.10. Docete omnes gentes & baptizate eas Matth.28. Sciunt omnes gentes suis ipsarum vias incedere Act.14. Et de Paulo Rom.1. verf.5. quòd datus ei fuerit Apostolatus ad obedientiam fidei inter omnes gentes. Similiter de meretrica Babylonica Apoc. 18. verf.3. & 23. quòd ex vino fcortationis ipsius biberint omnes gentes,& veneficio eius seductæ sint omnes gentes. Quam prodigiosæ existent absurditates, fi in his & similibus locis per omnes gentes intelligantur singulí in omnibus gentibus?
units.tr: I answer that the falsity of this gloss, which is certainly too crude and intolerable, is easily refuted by comparing similar phrases and by the thing itself. We read at the end of 1 Chronicles 14 that the name of David went out into all lands and that dread of him was put on all peoples. The same man complains in Psalm 118 that he was surrounded by all nations. We read likewise that all nations were made subject to Nebuchadnezzar so that they served him (Jer. 27:7), and that his dominion extended "in every place, and over all the sons of men and beasts" (Dan. 2:38). So too are those sayings: "You will be hated by all nations" (Matt. 10); "Teach all nations and baptize them" (Matt. 28); "All nations walk in their own ways" (Acts 14). And of Paul, Rom. 1:5, that the apostleship was given him to bring about the obedience of faith among all nations. Similarly of the Babylonian harlot, Rev. 18:3 and 23: all nations drank of the wine of her fornication, and all nations were seduced by her sorcery. How monstrous would the absurdities be if in these and similar passages "all nations" were understood as individuals in all nations!

units.la: Res quoque ipsa multis modis expositioni reclamat, qua omnes gentes pro singulis omnium gentium hominibus dictas volunt. Etenim dicit Apostolus suo iam tempore Euangelium declaratum fuisse omnibus gentibus. Etenim certissimum est, etiam diu post Apostolorum tempora, innumerabiles fuisse gentes, in quibus nondum prædicatum erat Euangelium, nedum vt singulis omnium gentium hominibus, Apostolis adhuc viuentibus, prædicatum illud fuerit. Testis Auguft. epift.80. de innumerabilibus gentibus barbaris in Aphrica: vt tacea de tot gentibus aliis sub cœlo, fero tandem ad fidem dem Christi conuersis.
units.tr: The thing itself also objects in many ways to that exposition, by which they want "all nations" to mean each individual of all the nations. For the Apostle says that the Gospel was already in his time declared to all nations. It is most certain that even long after the times of the Apostles there were countless nations in which the Gospel had not yet been preached, much less that it was preached to each individual of all nations while the Apostles were still living. Augustine bears witness in Letter 80 to countless barbarian nations in Africa; to say nothing of so many other nations under heaven, which were at last converted to the faith of Christ.

units.la: At Paulus dicit Euagelium illo iam suo omnibus gentibus,& vniuersæ sub cœlo creaturæ fuisse prædicatum.
units.tr: But Paul says that the Gospel was already in his time preached to all nations and to every creature under heaven.

units.la: Verum illud est, sed eo locutionis genere, quo superiora in sacris literis dicuntur,& quo vniuersa Iudæa perhibetur exiisse ad Iohannem,& ab eo baptizata esse. Quomodo etiam Hieronymus explicat à Paulo dictum, quod omnes docuerit in omni sapientia, id est, Iudæos & Græcos. Amentis enim esset cogitare, Apostolum quicquid tum hominum vbique locorum erat, doctrina Euangelica conuenisse.
units.tr: That is true, but it is in the manner of speaking by which the things above are described in the sacred writings, and by which all Judea is said to have gone out to John and been baptized by him. So Jerome also explains what Paul said, that he taught "everyone" in all wisdom (Col. 1:28), namely Jews and Greeks. For it would be madness to think that the Apostle reached with Gospel teaching everyone, whatever men there were anywhere in the world at that time.

units.la: Quantum vero ad hoc, quod gratia Dei salutifera omnibus dicitur illuxisse hominibus, optime apud Hieron. explanatur in comment: omnibus dictum, quod nulla excipiatur conditio, nec differetia aliqua sit liberi & serui, Græci & Barbari, circucisi & præputium habentis, sed cuncti in Christo vnu fimus, & vniuersi ad regnum Dei vocemur, post offensam reconciliandi non per merita nostra, sed per gratiam saluatoris.
units.tr: As for the statement that the saving grace of God "has dawned on all men," Jerome explains it excellently in his commentary: "all" is said because no condition is excepted, and there is no difference between free and slave, Greek and barbarian, circumcised and uncircumcised; but we are all one in Christ, and all are called to the kingdom of God, to be reconciled after offence not through our merits but through the grace of the Saviour.

units.la: Atque vt magis etiam elucescat, vel externa Euangelij prædicatione Deum non omnes sigillatim dignari, quid dicemus de tot millibus paruulorum, qui quotidie è viuis excedunt & excefcerunt hactenus, priusquàm ratione vti possint, & vel minimum de gratia Euangelica audierint? Quid, quod inter eos qui adultiore iam ætate, iudicio veritatis rationis, innumeri omnibus ætatibus existunt, quibus lux Euangelij nō affulget, sed in tenebris suis iusto Dei iudicio versari sinuntur? Qua de re lector videat Augustinum ad Euodium epist. 99.
units.tr: And so that it may shine out even more clearly that God does not deign to bring all individually even by the external preaching of the Gospel, what shall we say of so many thousands of infants who daily depart from the living, and have hitherto departed, before they can use reason and have heard even the least of the Gospel grace? What of the countless people who, at a more mature age, come to the judgment of truth and reason, in every age, and to whom the light of the Gospel does not shine, but who are allowed by the just judgment of God to remain in their darkness? On this matter let the reader see Augustine, to Euodius, Letter 99.

units.la: Adhæc, si maximè verum esset, nunc tempore gratiæ, singulis inter omnes gentes ex æquo exhiberi gratiam audiendi Euangelium; quid de anterioribus sæculis, de temporibus ignorantiæ dicemus, quibus dimissæ sunt omnes gentes suis ipsarum viis incedere? Non quidem passus est Deus se testimonij expertem esse inter gētes, benefaciendo, dando cœlitus pluuias ac tempora fructifera, & implendo corda ho-
units.tr: Moreover, even if it were most true that now, in the time of grace, the grace of hearing the Gospel is offered equally to each individual among all nations, what shall we say of earlier ages, of the times of ignorance, when all nations were allowed to walk in their own ways? God indeed did not suffer himself to be without witness among the nations, doing good, giving rain from heaven and fruitful seasons, and filling men's hearts

units.la: Act. 14. v. 16. hominum cibo & lætitia, quæ omnia prædicatione continua clementiam loquebantur largitoris : Veruntamen mysterium illud de quo loquimur,præteritis seculis & generationibus abscônditū fuisse Apostolus clamat. Olim siquidè misericordia, Domini,quę nullis generationibus defuit,naturę testimonijs gentes omnes conueniebat: doctrina autem legis & Prophetarum, non nisi domui Iacob,& paucis quibusdam, secuturæ aliquando gentium vocationis candidatis, vt ita dicam, consulebat.
units.tr: Act. 14. v. 16. with food and gladness, which all by continual preaching spoke of the clemency of the giver. Nevertheless, the mystery we are speaking of, the Apostle cries out, was hidden in past ages and generations. For formerly the mercy of the Lord, which never failed in any generation, gathered all nations by the testimonies of nature; but the teaching of the law and the Prophets provided, so to speak, only for the house of Jacob and for a few candidates for the calling of the Gentiles that was to follow at some time.

units.la: Tertium quod hic monendum videtur,illud est, quòd quamuis per ministros verbi & gratiæ Dei,eadem cunctis veritas, eadem gratia prædicetur, eadem cohortatio adhibeatur, non idè tamè profectus apud omnes sequatur. Siquidem alij ex Euangelij auditione proficiunt,alij non proficiunt, imò indurantur; & qui proficiunt, non ad eundem modum incrementi omnes proficiunt. Vnde tanta disparitas, nisi ex disparitate gratiæ vocantis? Nemo venit, nit ad me,ait Dominus, nisi pater traxe-rit eum. Omnis qui audiuit & didicit a patre, venit ad me. Si autem omnis qui audiuit & didicit a patre, venit, colligi-mus cum Augustt: de praedest. sanct. cap. 8. omne profecto qui non venit, non audire, nec didicisse a patre. Valde aute vt pulchre idem ait, remota est a carnis sensibus haec schola, in qua pater audi-tur & docet, vt veniatur ad filium. Ibi est & ipse filius, quia ipse est verbum eius, per quod sic docet, nec agit cum carnis aure, sed cordis.
units.tr: A third point that seems worth noting here is this: although through the ministers of the Word and the grace of God the same truth is preached to all, the same grace is proclaimed and the same exhortation applied, yet progress does not follow equally among all. For some profit from hearing the Gospel, others do not profit but are rather hardened; and those who do profit do not all advance at the same rate. Whence such great disparity, unless from a disparity in the calling grace? "No one comes to me," says the Lord, "unless the Father draws him" (John 6:44). "Everyone who has heard and learned from the Father comes to me" (John 6:45). If, then, everyone who has heard and learned from the Father comes, we conclude with Augustine, On the Predestination of the Saints, ch. 8, that surely whoever does not come has not heard nor learned from the Father. And, as the same author beautifully says, this school in which the Father is heard and teaches, so that one may come to the Son, is far removed from the senses of the flesh. There too is the Son himself, for he is his Word, through which he teaches in this way; and he does not work with the ear of the flesh but with that of the heart.

units.la: Sed & Apostolum audimus dicen-tem, Dei agricultura, Dei aedificatio sumus, Et, plantat Paulus, rigat Apollos, sed neque qui plantat neque qui rigat, est aliquid, sed Deus qui dat incrementum. Ab eo est initium & progressus, & consummatio omnis boni operis, sicut ait Apostolus, Qui incepit in vobis bonum opus, perficiet usque ad diem Iesu Christi. Item, Deus est qui efficit in vobis velle & efficere. Et ne forsan roges, cur specialia isthaec gratiae beneficia aliis dentur, aliis negentur; addit eo loci, sic eum facere pro beneplacito. Cui sententiæ etiam verba ad Col. 1. di-ferte attestantur, dicente Paulo, abscõditum à seculis mysterium nunc patefactum esse sanctis eius, quibus voluerit Deus notum facere. Quasi dicat, ne in præsentia quidem vniuersis & singulis mysterium hoc palàm esse factum, sed sanctis Dei, hoc est, Apostolis, & qui per eos crediderunt. Et ne roges cur sanctis eius & non cæteris patefactum sit & patefiat quotidie, subiecit statim, quibus voluit: sicut recte Theodoritus & Theophyl. in loci huius enarratione ista expedÿt.
units.tr: But we also hear the Apostle saying, "You are God's husbandry, God's building," and, "Paul plants, Apollos waters, but neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but God who gives the increase." From God comes the beginning and the progress, and the completion of every good work, as the Apostle says: "He who began a good work in you will perfect it until the day of Jesus Christ." Likewise: "It is God who works in you both to will and to work." And lest you perhaps ask why these special benefits of grace are given to some and denied to others, he adds in that place that God works thus "according to his good pleasure." The sentence is also clearly confirmed by the words of Colossians 1, where Paul says that the mystery hidden from the ages is "now made manifest to his saints, to whom God willed to make it known." As if he said that not even now is this mystery made plain to all and each, but to "the saints of God," that is, the Apostles and those who believed through them. And lest you ask why it was made known to his saints and not to others, and why it is made known daily, he immediately added "to whom he willed": as Theodoret and Theophylact rightly set out in their explanations of this passage.

units.la: Ex his omnibus perspicuum est, diuinæ gratiæ opera ac dona nunquam eadem omnibus aut paria conferri, sed multis magnisque differentijs variata esse. Videmus enim triplicem vocationem. Vnam generalem omnium, per vocem naturæ, quæ nunquam quiescit; alteram specialem, per vocem Euangelij, quæ & ipsa iam vniuersis est facta communis, ex quo omni genti Euangelium annunciatur in nouo testamento; tertiam denique, qua vocantur electi, de qua dicitur, Quos prædestinauit, eos etiâ voetiam vocauit, non vtique illa vocatione, inquit Augustinus, De perseu.sanct. lib.1. cap. 16. de qua dictum est, Multi vocati, pauci electi, sed illa ad quam qui pertinent omnes sunt docibiles Dei, nec potest quisquam dicere, credidi vt sic vocarer, quia praeueniente eum misericordia Dei, sic vocatus est vt crederet: & istorum nemo perit: omne enim quod dat mihi pater, ait filius, venit ad me, & non perdam ex eo quicquam.
units.tr: From all these things it is clear that the works and gifts of divine grace are never the same or equal for all, but are varied by many and great differences. For we see a threefold calling. One is general to all, through the voice of nature, which never ceases; another is special, through the voice of the Gospel, which has now also become common to all, since the Gospel is announced to every nation in the New Testament; and the third is that by which the elect are called, of which it is said, "Whom he predestined, them he also called," not indeed by that calling, says Augustine (On the Perseverance of the Saints, book 1, chapter 16), of which it was said, "Many are called, few are chosen." Rather, by that calling to which those who belong to it are all taught of God, and no one can say, "I believed so that I might be called," since the mercy of God went before him, so that he was called in such a way that he believed; and none of these perishes, for "everything that the Father gives me," says the Son, "comes to me, and I will lose none of it."

units.la: De hac varietate gratiae & donorum Dei, solidissime & vberrime tractat auctor librorum de vocat. gentium: cuius haec inter alia sunt verba lib.2.cap.3. Altitudo diuitiarum sapientiae & scientiae Dei, cuius inscrutabilia sunt iudicia, & inuestigabiles viae, sic semper misericordiam & iudicium temperauit, vt secretissima aeterni consilij voluntate noluerit in omnibus super omnes generationes, aut super omnes homines, aequales donorum suorum esse mensuras. Siquidem aliter eos iuuerit, quos ad cognoscendum se & caeli & terrae testimonijs conueniebat, aliter illos, quibus non solum elementorum famulatu, sed etiam doctrina legis, Prophetarum oraoraculis, miraculorum signis, & angelorum cooperationibus consulebat. Qua autem cau- sa sint harum sub eadem gratia diffimilitudi- num, quae rationes, sanctis scripturis non loquentibus, quis loquetur, inquit ? patienter & aequanimiter ignoretur tam remotum ab humana cogitatione secretum, in quo scientia Pauli Apostoli a disputatione transiit ad stu- pore. Plenior tractatio huius argumen- ti de vocatione (quae sive in singulis ho- minibus, sive in populis atque ipso genere humano operatur) altae ordinatio- nis, & profundae considerationis est ab eodem petatur autore, homine, vt res ipsa loquitur, & Erasmus in praef. iudi- cat, in sacris literis diligenter exercita- to, ingenio sano & acuto.
units.tr: Concerning this variety of grace and of God's gifts, the author of the books On the Calling of the Gentiles treats the matter most solidly and copiously. Among other things, these are his words (book 2, chapter 3): "The height of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God, whose judgments are unsearchable and whose ways past finding out, has so tempered mercy and judgment that, by the most secret will of his eternal counsel, he has not wished the measures of his gifts to be equal in all, over all generations or over all men. For he has helped in one way those whom it was fitting to bring to know himself by the testimonies of heaven and earth, and in another way those whom he provided for not only by the service of the elements but also by the teaching of the law, the oracles of the prophets, the signs of miracles and the cooperation of angels. But what the causes are of these dissimilarities under the same grace, and what reasons there are, since the holy Scriptures do not speak of them, who will speak? Let it be patiently and calmly left unknown, a secret so remote from human thought, at which the knowledge of the Apostle Paul passed from disputation into wonder." A fuller treatment of this subject of calling (which works either in single men or in peoples and the human race itself) of deep ordering and profound consideration is to be sought from the same author, a man, as the matter itself speaks, and Erasmus in his preface judges him to be one practised diligently in the sacred letters, of sound and sharp wit.

units.la: CAPVT VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.

units.la: Examinantur testimonia ex veteri testamento.
units.tr: The testimonies from the Old Testament are examined.

units.la: PROGREDIAMVR ad loca vete- ris testamenti. Primum citatur promis- sio Gen. 3. Semen mulieris conteret caput ser- pentis. Promissio haec accipienda est, ait dispudisputator, de toto genere humano, & tota totius generis reparatione. thes.33.
units.tr: Let us proceed to the passages of the Old Testament. First, the promise in Gen. 3. The seed of the woman shall crush the head of the serpent. The disputant says this promise must be understood of the whole human race and the whole restoration of the entire race thes.33.

units.la: Imo vero toto coelo aberrat disputator, benedictionem quae Ecclesiae propria est, ad alienos extendendo. Promittitur enim filius virginis, Iesus Christus, qui destrueret opera Diaboli, & eo victo Christianos suos ex eius ditione liberaret, secum perpetuo regnaturos in sorte sanctorum.
units.tr: On the contrary, the disputant is wholly mistaken in extending to outsiders a blessing that belongs to the Church. For the promise is of the Son of the Virgin, Jesus Christ, who would destroy the works of the devil and, having overcome him, would free his Christians from his power, to reign with him forever in the inheritance of the saints.

units.la: Hinc Paulus ad Rom. 16. v. 20. Deus pacis conteret Satanam sub pedibus vestris cito. Vbi victoriam contra Satanam ad fideles sine controversia restringit, de quibus etiam ad Col. 1. ait, Idoneos nos fecit ad participandam sortem sanctorum in luce, & liberavit nos a potestate tenebrarum, ac transtulit in regnum filii sui dilecti, utique per fidem: sine qua, inquit Ambrosius, non est egressus ex inferno, aut potestate tenebrarum, in qua captivi a Diabolo tenebamur.
units.tr: Hence Paul, in Rom. 16. v. 20. The God of peace will crush Satan under your feet shortly. Here he undoubtedly restricts the victory over Satan to the faithful, of whom he also says in Col. 1.: He has made us fit to share in the inheritance of the saints in light, and has delivered us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of his beloved Son, and that surely through faith. Without faith, says Ambrose, there is no going out from hell or from the power of darkness, in which we were held captive by the devil.

units.la: Adhaec, reparatio illa & victoria contra Satanam, qualis promittitur, non solum meritum, verum & efficaciam Christi respicit, qua partam nobis bis salutem tuetur, & conseruat in hu- ius vitæ certaminibus, contraq; diabo- lum, mundum & propriam nostram carnem, nos spiritus sui robore firmat, donec plenam tandem victoriam obti- neamus. Est enim id Saluatoris opus, ut Athanasius, vt non solum nos à ser- uitute vindicet, sed autorem seruitutis conficiat, ne rursum inualescens nos supplantet, victoriamque liberatoris irritam faciat. Iam vero experientia & scriptura docent multum abesse, vt hoc modo supra Diabolum victores emergant omnes filij Adæ: sed victo- riam illam sanctis suis Deus demum largitur.
units.tr: Moreover, that restoration and victory over Satan, as it is promised, looks not only to the merit but also to the efficacy of Christ, by which he guards and preserves the salvation once obtained for us amid the struggles of this life, against the devil, the world and our own flesh, strengthening us by the power of his Spirit until at last we obtain full victory. For it is the work of the Saviour, as Athanasius says, not only to free us from slavery but to destroy the author of slavery, lest he rise again, supplant us and render the Liberator's victory void. Indeed, experience and Scripture teach that it is far from the case that all the sons of Adam emerge in this way victorious over the devil; God grants that victory to his saints only at the last.

units.la: Sed & verbis illis apud Mosen, Pone nam inimicitias inter te & inter mulierem, inter semen tuum, & inter semen eius; aperte reprobi à promissione excluduntur. Adiunguntur enim Diabolo, qui reproborum caput & pater est: & contra hoc regnum Satanæ, id est, contra diabolum & membra eius, Ecclesiæ promittitur victoria per Christum. In femine enim mulieris, prorsus vt in femi-ne ne Abrahæ, filij cœnsentur promissio-nis. Rom.9.v.8.& cap.4. v.16.
units.tr: But also by those words in Moses, I will put enmity between you and the woman, between your seed and her seed, the reprobate are plainly excluded from the promise. For they are joined to the devil, who is the head and father of the reprobate; and against this kingdom of Satan, that is, against the devil and his members, victory through Christ is promised to the Church. For in the seed of the woman, just as in the seed of Abraham, the children of the promise are reckoned. Rom. 9. v. 8. and chap. 4. v. 16.

units.la: Sed videamus ratiunculas aduersa-rij. Primò, locum istum de tota totius generis humani reparatione intelligi vult, eo quòd non tàtum pars corporis Diaboli, sed caput eius conterendum fuerit.
units.tr: But let us look at the little arguments of our opponent. First, he wants that passage to be understood of the restoration of the whole human race, because not only a part of the body of the devil but its head was to be crushed.

units.la: Bella ratio : quasi non caput etiam pars sit corporis. Tu quia caput diaboli per Christum conculcandum fuit, ne-cesse est intelligamus, ita Diabolum conteri, vt in eos quibus contritus est, potestatem mortis non amplius exer-ceat. Hoc autem in ijs locum tantùm habet, qui Christi membra sunt,
units.tr: A fine argument, as if the head were not also a part of the body! Since the head of the devil was to be trampled by Christ, we must understand that the devil is so crushed that he no longer exercises the power of death over those by whom he has been crushed. But this holds only for those who are members of Christ.

units.la: Adfert etiam pro declaratione, di-sta illa : quod princeps mundi dicitur eiectus foras : quod filius Dei venerit destruere opera Diaboli : quod per mortem aboleuerit Diabo-lum : quod Diabolus & omnis eius potestas in triumpho ostentanda fuerit : item, quod in aulam fortis armati superueniens, vincit eum & totam eius armaturam aufert & spolia eius distribuit, &c. Ex his inferre cona-tur, non excipi quenquam sub potesta-tem tem Diaboli redactum, quem Christus à Diabolo non liberârit, seu cui caput eius non sit contritum.
units.tr: To confirm this he also cites those sayings: that the prince of this world is said to be cast out; that the Son of God came to destroy the works of the devil; that by his death he abolished the devil; that the devil and all his power were to be displayed in triumph; likewise, that coming into the house of the strong armed man he overcomes him, takes away all his armour and distributes his spoils, and so on. From these he tries to infer that no one who has been brought under the power of the devil is excluded, whom Christ has not freed from the devil, or on whom his head has not been crushed.

units.la: Verba isthæc sunt & voces, non rationum momenta. Sic enim Augustinus noster accuratius illa edisserens tractat. 53. in Iohannem: Possidebat Diabolus genus humanum & reos suppliciorum tenebat chirographo peccatorum: dominabatur in cordibus infidelium. Per Christi autem fidem, per eius sanguinem, qui in remissionem fusus est peccatorum, millia credentium à dominatu liberantur Diaboli. Hoc vocabat iudicium: hanc discretionem: hanc à suis redemtis Diaboli expulsionem. Idem paulo post, Præuidebat Deus quod sciebat, post passionem & glorificationem suam, multos populos per vniuersum mundum credituros, in quorum cordibus Diabolus intus erat, cui quando ex fide renunciant, eicitur foràs, de credentium videlicet cordibus. Augustinum secutus Magister sententiarum similiter ista explicat, lib.3. dist.19.
units.tr: These are words and phrases, not weighty arguments. For our Augustine, explaining them more carefully, says in tractate 53 on John: The devil possessed the human race and held those guilty of punishment by the bond of sins; he ruled in the hearts of unbelievers. But through faith in Christ, through his blood, which was poured out for the remission of sins, thousands of believers are freed from the dominion of the devil. This he called judgment, this separation, this expulsion of the devil from his redeemed. The same, a little later: God foresaw what he knew, that after his passion and glorification many peoples throughout the world would believe, in whose hearts the devil was within, and when they renounce him by faith, he is cast out, namely from the hearts of believers. Following Augustine, the Master of the Sentences explains these things in the same way, book 3, distinction 19.

units.la: Credentes ergo sunt ex quibus ille eicitur foras. His abolitus, deuictus, triumphatusque est, operaque eius de-struit structa: In incredulis autem, in quibus princeps huius seculi etiamnum efficax est, luctuosum non definit agere triumphum, donec & ipsi fide, quæ victoria nostra est, ex diaboli laqueo elabantur, à quo captiui tenentur. Atque id verba Iohānis perspicuè confirmat. Si enim qui committit peccatū ex Diabolo est, & verò qui ex Deo natus est, peccatū nō committit; nō vtiq; nisi renatis opera Diaboli reipsa destructa sunt.
units.tr: Those who believe, therefore, are those from whom he is cast out. Over these he has been abolished, defeated and triumphed over, and the works he built are destroyed. But among unbelievers, in whom the prince of this age is still active, he does not cease to carry on his baleful triumph, until they too, by the faith which is our victory, escape the snare of the devil by which they are held captive. And the words of John clearly confirm this. For if he who commits sin is of the devil, and he who is born of God does not commit sin, then surely the works of the devil are actually destroyed only in the reborn.

units.la: At, si abolitus est & triumphatus Satanas, omnibus simul & semel abolitus est. Minimè gentium. Nam & vltimus hostis, mors, abolebitur: & erit omnium illustrissimus triumphus ille diei nouissimi de Satana. Quantus tamen eorum futurus est numerus, quibus mors, & qui mortis potestatem habet, Diabolus, æternum dominabuntur? Erunt nihilominus tunc verè omnia Christo subiecta, teste Apostolo, vti & nunc omnia subiecta ei sunt, suo modo; contra quam inscitè excipit Hub: non omnia posse dici Christo subiecta, si magna pars regni Satanici per ipsum non sit contrita. Imò verò totum regnum Satanicum ab ipso conteretur, die præsertim nouissimo : sed idcirco haud opus est Christum omnes, nemine excepto, in regnum suum gratiæ aut gloriæ coöptare. Interim reprobi omnes cum Diabolo & angelis eius pedibus Domini subiecti sunt & erunt in perpetuū, vlcifceturq; eos flama inextinguibili, tanquā subditos contumaces, quod ad regnum potentiæ. Norūt enim qui scripturas, harūq; interpretes antiquos legerūt, regnū Dei aliud esse quod gratiæ, aliud quod gloriæ dicitur, aliud quod potentiæ vulgò vocatur, in quo sunt cū Diabolis impij quoque ad vnū omnes. Sed regnum illud gratiæ, quod hic est ad finem vsque seculi, licet non hinc, quia peregrinamur in mundo, sunt credentes, habetque admixta zizania vsque ad messem, inquit Augustinus Tract.11s. in Ioh.
units.tr: But, it is said, if Satan has been abolished and triumphed over, he has been abolished for all at once and at a single stroke. By no means! For death, the last enemy, will also be abolished, and that triumph of the last day over Satan will be the most illustrious of all. Yet how great will be the number of those over whom death and the devil, who has the power of death, will rule forever? Nevertheless, then truly all things will be subjected to Christ, as the Apostle witnesses, just as now too all things are subjected to him in their own way. Against this Hub. foolishly objects that all things cannot be said to be subjected to Christ if a large part of the Satanic kingdom has not been crushed by him. Indeed, the whole Satanic kingdom will be crushed by him, especially on the last day. But for this it is not necessary that Christ should gather all, without exception, into his kingdom of grace or of glory. Meanwhile all the reprobate, with the devil and his angels, are and will be forever subject to the feet of the Lord, and he will punish them with unquenchable fire as stubborn subjects, so far as the kingdom of power is concerned. For those who have read the Scriptures and the ancient interpreters of them know that the kingdom of God is one thing called the kingdom of grace, another the kingdom of glory, and another commonly called the kingdom of power, in which the impious are also included, all of them together with the devils. But that kingdom of grace, which exists here until the end of the age, although believers are not there yet, since we are pilgrims in the world, nevertheless has believers, and has tares mixed in with the wheat until the harvest, says Augustine, Tractate 11 on John.

units.la: Quod ad parabolam de forti armato, quanquam non refragor vt etiam mundo eiectus dicatur, quatenus post passionem Christi, per vniuersum mundo dum populi crediderunt, vt ante Augustinus explicabat: tamen non describitur ille vt atrio, id est mundo, plane eiectus, sed vt in eo vinctus potius. Nec vniuersa arma sunt vniuersi homines, sed πάνυGræce est, qua ita a forti illo superueniente exuitur Satanas, vt sine eius nutu ne mouere quidem se possit. Quod autem Spiritus impurus reuerti dicitur in eum vnde exiuit, id fit quia multi ore magis quam corde & ex vera fide, Diabolo renunciant, & sub velamine religionis occulte mali sunt, quos non mirum est relabi, & vltima eorum fieri deteriora prioribus. Vide Augustin. in Psal. 48.
units.tr: As for the parable of the strong armed man, although I do not object that he may be said to be cast out even of the world, in so far as after Christ's passion the peoples throughout the world have believed, as Augustine explained earlier, nevertheless he is not described as being plainly cast out of the court, that is, the world, but rather as being bound in it. Nor are all the arms all men, but the Greek is [πάνυ], by which Satan is so stripped by that stronger one who comes upon him that he cannot even move himself without his nod. As for the statement that the unclean spirit returns to the place from which he came, this happens because many renounce the devil with the mouth rather than the heart and not from true faith, and under the cover of religion are secretly evil; it is no wonder that they relapse and that their last state becomes worse than the first. See Augustine on Psalm 48.

units.la: Alter locus est Isai. 53. Omnes nos quasi oues errauimus: & vnusquisque declinauit in viam suam, & posuit Dominus in eo iniquitates omnium nostrum. Ergo peccata omnium hominum, siue credant siue non credant, re ipsa sacrificio Christi expiata sunt.
units.tr: The other passage is Isa. 53. We all like sheep have gone astray, and each has turned to his own way, and the Lord has laid on him the iniquities of us all. Therefore the sins of all men, whether they believe or not, have in fact been expiated by the sacrifice of Christ.

units.la: Respondetur ad antecedens, verba nempe textus; posse ea accipi tanquam vocem fidelium, in sua & sui similium perpersona dicente Propheta, omnium no-stFrum: Quemadmodum & apud Paulu Abraham dicitur pater omnium nostrum, & Hierusalem mater omnium nostrum.
units.tr: The reply to the antecedent, namely the words of the text, is that they can be taken as the voice of the faithful, the prophet speaking in his own person and that of those like him, "all of us" (omnium nostrum). In the same way Paul also says that Abraham is "the father of us all" and Jerusalem "the mother of us all."

units.la: Augustinus certe de peccatorum meri-tis & remiss.lib.1.cap.27. ita scribit; Omniū membrorum Christi vox est, omnes vt oues errauimus, & ipse traditus est pro peccatis nostris. Similiter beatus Petrus locum Propheticum credentibus applicat, inquiens 1.Epist.2. Eratis velut oues erran-tes, sed conuersi estis ad pastorem, & curato-rem animarum vestrarum. Et certe con-sessio ista, Omnes quasi oues errauimus, nō est hominum perseuerantium & ma-nentium in peccatis; vt taceam, quod in præterito dicitur, errauimus, tāquam de conuersis iam ad pastorem animarum suarum.
units.tr: Augustine, certainly, in On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins, book 1, chapter 27, writes thus: "It is the voice of all the members of Christ: 'We all like sheep have gone astray, and he was delivered up for our sins.'" Likewise the blessed Peter applies the prophetic passage to believers, saying (1 Pet. 2): "You were like sheep going astray, but you have now returned to the shepherd and guardian of your souls." And indeed this confession, "We have all gone astray like sheep," is not the confession of people who persist and remain in their sins; not to mention that it is said in the past tense, "we have gone astray," as of those already converted to the shepherd of their souls.

units.la: Mere autem puerilis cauillatio est, quod vult aduersarius non de fidelium vniuersalitate tantum verba esse, quia Iefaiæ auditores non omnes fuerint fideles. Nihil enim id vetabat, quo minus Propheta verbis istis beneficium gratiæ exprimeret, quod in fidelium vniuersitatem competit. Quid Paulus? an fideles tantum circa se habebat, aut ab electis duntaxat auditur vel legitur hodie? Et tamen tendiculas istas nihil veritus, scribit tanquam de fidelibus & electis, pater omnium nostrum, mater omnium nostrum.
units.tr: But it is a purely childish cavil when the opponent wants the words to refer not to the whole body of the faithful, on the ground that the hearers of Isaiah were not all believers. For nothing forbade the prophet from expressing in these words the benefit of grace, which belongs to the whole body of the faithful. What of Paul? Did he have only believers around him, or is only the elect read or heard today? Yet he, fearing those snares not at all, writes as of believers and the elect: "the father of us all, the mother of us all."

units.la: Secundò, vt demus in Christum omnium hominum coniectas fuisse iniquitates; negamus consequentiam, Christi igitur sacrificio re ipsa omnium peccata expiata, omnésque iustificatos & in gratiam receptos. Vt enim victima & meritum Christi nobis prosit ad iustitiam & gratiam coram Deo, applicatione opus est per fidem. Iustificati enim fide pacem habemus erga Deum: & sine fide impossibile est Deo placere. Hinc & apud Iesaiam additur, Seruus meus iustus cognitione sui iustificabit multos, & iniquitates eorum ipse portabit. Tametsi ergo omnium peccata portauerit sufficientia: proprie tamen redemti eius censentur, in quibus viget vera Christi cognitio siue fides. Sed de hoc loco plura libro sequenti.
units.tr: Second, grant that the iniquities of all human beings were laid upon Christ; we deny the consequence that therefore by the sacrifice of Christ the sins of all have in fact been expiated, and all are justified and received into grace. For that the victim and merit of Christ should benefit us for righteousness and grace before God, application is needed through faith. For "being justified by faith we have peace with God, and without faith it is impossible to please God." Hence in Isaiah it is also added: "My righteous servant, by his knowledge, will justify many, and he himself will bear their iniquities." Although, therefore, he bore the sins of all, sufficiently, yet properly those are counted his redeemed in whom the true knowledge of Christ, or faith, flourishes. But of this passage more in the following book.

units.la: Obiicitur praeterea, quod Zachariæ 3. ait Dominus, Auferam iniquitatem terræ illius die vna.
units.tr: It is further objected that the Lord says in Zechariah 3: "I will remove the iniquity of that land in one day."

units.la: Sed sensus esse potest de Iudæa, quod populo suo placatus, tandem liberaturus eum esset à vexationibus & molestiis hostium, quas hactenus, Deo irato ipsorum peccatis, perpessi erant. Cui expositioni fauet restrictio addita, terræ illius. Deinde, si de vniuersa terra malimus exponere, idem erit sensus qui antea in dictis de redemtione & propitiatione mundi. Certè Apoc. 13. legimus quod vniuersa terra secuta sit bestiam. Neque tamen inferri inde potest de vniuersis & singulis hominibus toto orbe, quòd à Deo defecerint, necChristus Ecclesiam reliquam in genere humano habuerit.
units.tr: But the sense can be that concerning Judea: that, appeased toward his people, he would at last deliver them from the vexations and troubles of their enemies, which hitherto, with God angry at their sins, they had suffered. The restriction added, "of that land," favours this exposition. Then, if we prefer to explain it of the whole earth, the sense will be the same as before in the sayings about the redemption and propitiation of the world. Certainly in Revelation 13 we read that "the whole earth followed the beast." Yet it cannot be inferred from this that all and each of the human beings throughout the world have fallen away from God, nor that Christ had no Church left in the human race.

units.la: Affertur dehinc promissio Abrahæ facta Gen.12. & 23. In semine tuo benedicentur omnes gentes terræ. Vbi semen illud benedictum aduersarius intelligi vult omnes homines sine exceptione. Hoc vt extorqueat, omnes gentes interpretatur singulos omnium gentium.
units.tr: Next is brought the promise made to Abraham in Genesis 12 and 22: "In your seed all the nations of the earth shall be blessed." Here the opponent wants that blessed seed to be understood as all human beings without exception. To extort this, he interprets "all nations" as each individual of all nations.

units.la: Cui vero potius credamus; Hubero, an Paulo Apostolo Iesu Christi? propter- ea ex fide est hereditas, inquit Paulus Rom.4. ut firma sit promissio toti semini, non solum ei quod est ex lege, verum etiam ei quod est ex fide Abraham, qui est pater omnium nostrum, sicut scriptum est: patrem multarum gentium constitui te. Idem Rom. 9. Non qui filii carnis, ii filii Dei sunt, sed qui filii promissionis, censentur in semine. Eadem que explicationem multis inculcat Gal: 3. Providens scriptura, Deum ex fide iustificaturum gentes, ante Evangelizavit Abrahae: benedicetur, inquiens, in te omnes gentes. Quae igitur sive infscitia sive malitia est, Apostolo lice expositioni ta aperte contradicere, & tanquam hostes benedicti illius feminis contumeliose proscindere, qui per semen hoc fideles ubique gentium & terrarum cum Paulo intelligunt? Hostis igitur feminis istius Paulus. Vah. Hostis Augustinus tract.1. in prima Ioh. hostis Ambrosius in Luc. lib.3. & universus patrum chorus.
units.tr: But whom should we rather believe: Huber, or Paul the Apostle of Jesus Christ? "Therefore," says Paul in Romans 4, "the inheritance is of faith, so that the promise may be firm to the whole seed, not only to that which is of the law, but also to that which is of the faith of Abraham, who is the father of us all, as it is written: I have made you a father of many nations." Likewise in Romans 9: "Not those who are children of the flesh are children of God, but those who are children of the promise are counted in the seed." And Galatians 3 inculcates the same explanation to many: "Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the nations by faith, preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham: 'In you,' it says, 'all the nations shall be blessed.'" What ignorance or malice, then, is it that allows him to contradict the Apostle so openly, and, as enemies of that blessed seed, to tear it to pieces insolently, when with Paul they understand by this seed the faithful everywhere in all the nations and lands? Paul is therefore an enemy of this seed. Woe! Augustine is an enemy (Tractate 1 on the First Epistle of John), Ambrose is an enemy (On Luke, book 3), and the whole chorus of the Fathers.

units.la: At per omnes gentes singuli omnium gentium veniut vniuersaliter. No femsemper, sed fallit sepissime glossa isthec. Praeter exempla superius allata, hic & illa considerentur.Psal.22.Reminiscentur & conuertentur ad Iehouam omnes fines terra, & inclinabunt se coram te vniuersa familia gentium.Psal.72.Incuruabunt se ei omnes reges, omnes getes seruiet ei: Et Psal.86.Omnes gentes venient & adorabunt coram te Domine, glorificabunt nomen tuum. Haec vaticinia, Augustinus & Basilio interpretibus, impleta sunt in conuersione gentium, dum ex omnibus gentibus aliqui splendore diuinae cognitionis admirtunt.
units.tr: But "through all the nations" singular individuals of all nations come in universally. No, it does not always, and this gloss very often deceives. Besides the examples cited above, let these also be considered: Psalm 22: "All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to Jehovah, and the whole family of the nations shall bow down before you." Psalm 72: "All kings shall bow down to him, all nations shall serve him." And Psalm 86: "All nations shall come and worship before you, O Lord, and they shall glorify your name." These prophecies, according to the interpretations of Augustine and Basil, were fulfilled in the conversion of the nations, when from all nations some are admitted by the splendour of divine knowledge.

units.la: Sic apud Iesaiam praedicitur diebus nouissimis omnes gentes venturas ad montem Domini, & populos ambulaturos in lege ipsius. Vbi rursum Basilius putidam istorum glossam reijciens, admonet, quod res ipsa quoque clamat, haud quaquam id accipiendum de integro numero in terra viuentium, seu de omnibus hominibus, quos vndique vnaquaeque gens complectitur.
units.tr: So in Isaiah it is foretold that "in the last days all nations will come to the mountain of the Lord," and peoples will walk in his law. There again Basil, rejecting the stinking gloss of these men, admonishes what the thing itself also cries out: that it is by no means to be taken of the whole number of living things on the earth, or of all human beings whom each nation embraces from every side.

units.la: Hinc iam responsio quoque liquet ad dictum Psal. 2.Postula a me & dabo tibi gentes hereditatem tuam, & possessionem terminos... nos terræ. Promittitur igitur, inquit Hub:omnium gentium adoptio in hæreditatem Christi.
units.tr: Hence the answer also becomes clear to the saying in Psalm 2: "Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession." It is promised, therefore, says Huber, that all nations will be adopted into the inheritance of Christ.

units.la: Concedo: sed non omnium hominum quos vnaquæque gens continet. Apostolica enim disciplina, inquit Augustinus lib.1. de sermone Domini in monte, adoptionem appellat, qua in æternam hæreditate vocamur, vt cohæredes Christi simus, & cum Deo, tanquam filij, æterna vita fruamur, reformati in agnitione eius ad imaginem Dei. Id verò non est omnium. Vnde, vt idem exponit, sensus est, Postula à me, vt scilicet gentes nomini Christiano copulentur, atque ita à morte redimantur, & possideantur à Deo: & dabo tibi gentes hæreditatem tuam, quas possideas nimirum ad earum salutem, vt tibi fructificent spiritualia.
