It follows, therefore, that since salvation comes to such children also, faith is given to many infants everywhere, even before they are baptized; and Jakob Andreae denied that he could affirm this. The same objection could be raised about the girls among the Jews, who, because they were the seed of Abraham, were not excluded from Abraham's righteousness, but obtained it through faith, according to Luther in the place cited, even in infancy.

units.la: Quapropter opinio de fide infantum facilius affirmatur quàm defenditur.
units.tr: Therefore the opinion about the faith of infants is more easily asserted than defended.

units.la: Hinc Doctor Heerbrandus Defens. contra Gotthardum Canonicum, sententiam Lutheri sic mitigat, cum, cum dicit infantes habere fidem aut credere, non id velle, quod intelligant, aut motus fidei sentiant; sed reijci, ita errorem illorum, rum, qui imaginetur infantes baptiza-tos Deo placere & saluos fieri sine actione aliqua spiritus Sancti. Si hoc tantum volunt, qui de fide paruulorum statuunt, plane assentior. Sed quia verendum est, vt plerique ipsorum interpretationem istam velint agnoscere, non dubito interim sentire & loqui cū veteribus, infantes non credere. Quam veterum simplicitatem è neotericis, Musculo, Martyri, aliisque doctissimis & diligentissimis Theologis probatam quoque fuisse, scripta ipsorum loquuntur.
units.tr: Hence Doctor Heerbrand, in his Defence against Gotthard the Canon, softens Luther's view in this way: when he says that infants have faith or believe, he does not mean that they understand what they believe or feel the motions of faith; he rejects instead the error of those who imagine that baptized infants please God and are saved without some action of the Holy Spirit. "If this alone is what those who make statements about the faith of little children mean, I plainly agree." But since it is to be feared that most of them will not wish to accept this interpretation, I do not hesitate meanwhile to think and speak with the ancients, that infants do not believe. The writings of these men show that this simplicity of the ancients was also approved by modern and most learned and diligent theologians, such as Musculus, Martyr and others.

units.la: Nec obstant verba Matth. 18. Quiofenderit vnum ex pueris istis qui in me credunt. Id enim August. quastionibus Euangelicis lib. 1. cap. 24. nec non Theophyl. Hilarius & alii potiùs accipiunt de humilibus & pueris malitiâ, non ætate.
units.tr: Nor do the words of Matthew 18: Whoever offends one of these little ones who believe in me stand in the way. For Augustine, in Questions on the Gospels, book 1, chapter 24, and also Theophylact, Hilary and others, take them rather of the humble and of those who are little in malice, not in age.

units.la: Fatemur nihilominus, infantes nostros corpori fidelium, hoc est, populo Dei rectè accenseri, cum ob promissionem fœderis, tum suscepto iam baptismo, ob initiationis & fidei sacramentū, vt Augustino placet Epist. 23. At enim si infantes destituuntur fide, quomodo gratiæ baptismi & salutis fiunt participes? Qui enim non crediderit condemnabitur. Corde creditur ad iustitiam: & sine fide impossibile est Deo placere.
units.tr: Nevertheless we confess that our infants are rightly counted among the body of the faithful, that is, the people of God, both because of the promise of the covenant and, now that baptism has been received, because of the sacrament of initiation and of faith, as Augustine pleases to hold in Letter 23. But, it will be said, if infants lack faith, how do they become partakers of the grace of baptism and of salvation? For "whoever does not believe will be condemned"; "with the heart one believes unto righteousness"; and "without faith it is impossible to please God."

units.la: Respondeo, aliam esse rationem infantum, aliam adultorum. Eiusmodi sententiæ, quæ de fidei, confessionis, spei, dilectionis, mortificationis carnis, & similium necessitate ad salutem in sacris literis traduntur, ad infantes non pertinet, sed ad adultos, qui talium per ætatem capaces sunt. Hac distinctione neglecta necessario sequuntur multi errores, sicut Augustinus lib. de hæresibus probat de Hierachitis: & Bernardus ad Hugonem Epist. 77. itemque Homilia 66. in Canticum canticorum, de alia quadam sententia eius temporis per Galliam.
units.tr: I answer that the reasoning for infants is one thing, and for adults another. Those statements which Scripture delivers about the necessity of faith, confession, hope, love and the mortification of the flesh for salvation do not pertain to infants, but to adults, who are capable of such things by their age. If this distinction is neglected, many errors necessarily follow, as Augustine proves in his book on heresies concerning the Hieracites, and Bernard, to Hugh, in Letter 77, and likewise in Sermon 66 on the Song of Songs, concerning a certain other opinion of his time held throughout Gaul.

units.la: Quod ad infantes Christianorum, satis est eos in promissione fœderis comprehendi. Etsi enim adoptio in filios Dei non est ex carnali natiuitate, secundum quam liberi fidelium non minus quam infidelium, filij sunt iræ, conceconcepti & nati in peccato, vti & reliqui: tamen, quæ gratiæ diuinæ largitas est, infantes Christianis nati parentibus, in numero populi Dei habentur, æquè ac olim infates posteritatis Abrahæ, secundum promissionem: Ero Deus tuus & feminis tui post te. Et Matth.19. Dominus inquit, Sinite parvulos, & ne prohibete eos venire ad me: talium enim est regnum cœlorum. Atque ea de causa Christianorum liberos baptizamus in signum divini fœderis: Turcarum autem liberos non baptizamus, nisi de fide iam respondere valentes. Ac si infantes nostri morte præuenti baptizari non potuerint, regulâ sequimur Bernardi ad Hugonem Epist.77. Non priuatio, sed contemptus baptismi damnat. Durior hic est Augustinus: sed præterquàm quod Scholastici communiter ab eius rigore non nihil recesserunt, vt qui pueros huiusmodi in proprio limbo extra omnem cruciatum posuerint, etiam alij magni nominis in medio Papatu, Gerson, Cardinalis Caietanus, Biel, aliique, mitiorem sententiam de talium salute approbarunt.
units.tr: As for the infants of Christians, it is enough that they are included in the promise of the covenant. For although adoption into the sons of God does not come from carnal birth, by which the children of believers are no less than those of unbelievers sons of wrath, conceived and born in sin, as are the rest; yet, by the generosity of divine grace, infants born to Christian parents are counted among the people of God, just as in former times the infants of the posterity of Abraham were, according to the promise: I will be your God and the God of your seed after you. And in Matthew 19 the Lord says: "Suffer the little children, and do not forbid them to come to me; for of such is the kingdom of heaven." And for this reason we baptize the children of Christians as a sign of the divine covenant; but we do not baptize the children of the Turks, unless they are able to answer for their faith. And if our infants, prevented by death, could not be baptized, we follow the rule of Bernard in Letter 77 to Hugh: "It is not the lack, but the contempt of baptism that condemns." Augustine is harder here; but apart from the fact that the Scholastics in general have departed somewhat from his rigour, placing such children in their own limbo outside all torment, other men of great name in the midst of Papacy, Gerson, Cardinal Cajetan, Biel and others, have approved a milder opinion about the salvation of such children.

units.la: De infantibus nostris mortem præuenti baptismi. Dictum Bernardi. runt. Verum de his plura non addam.
units.tr: Concerning our infants prevented by death before baptism: the saying of Bernard. But I will not add more about these matters.

units.la: Restat cauillatio de Coena Domini, quam pari quoque futilitate sublatum iri criminatur aduerlarius, negata vni-uerfalitate redemtionis, qualem ipse tutatur. Quinam vero Hubere? Reperio equidem á Thesi tua 437. quo le-ctorem remittis, multa tuo more, idest, impudenter & acerbè confiͤta, atque ad propositæ criminationis probatio-nem parum speͤtantia: nisi quod tandem ad hunc modum videris voluisse ratiocinari (Quippe absurditatibus tuis sic implicaris, vt hic & alias sæpè non facilè intelligi possit quid volueris)
units.tr: There remains the cavil about the Lord's Supper, which our adversary accuses us of abolishing with equal futility, since we deny the universality of redemption, which he himself defends. But where indeed does he find this? I find, to be sure, that you send the reader to your Thesis 437, where, in your usual manner, that is, shamelessly and bitterly, you have cobbled together many things that bear little on the proof of the charge you have made; except that at last you seem to have wished to reason in this way (for you are so entangled in your absurdities that it is often not easy to understand here or elsewhere what you intend).

units.la: Tantum pro quibus Christus efficaciter mortuus est, adcoenam debet accedere, opinione nostra, vt tu dicis.
units.tr: Only those for whom Christ has efficaciously died ought to approach the Supper, in our opinion, as you say.

units.la: Sed num Christus pro nobis efficaciter mortuus fit, singulis ignotum est.
units.tr: But whether Christ has died effectively for us is unknown to individuals.

units.la: Ergo nemo penitus sciet, quis Domini conuiua esse debeat, Atque ita coena Dominica omnibus vnà surripietur.
units.tr: Therefore no one at all will know who ought to be a guest at the Lord's table, and so the Lord's Supper will be snatched away from everyone at once.

units.la: Nugæ. Primùm enim in deductione ad absurdum alterutra præmissarum dedebet esse hypothesis, seu ea ipsa antagonistae sententia quae oppugnatur, quod hic non fit. Quaestio enim de eo est, Sitne Christus pro omnibus mortuus efficaciter? Ipse ait: Nos negamus.
units.tr: Trifles. First, in a reduction to absurdity, one of the premises must be the hypothesis, that is, the very opinion of the opponent that is being attacked. That does not happen here. For the question is this: Did Christ die effectively for all? He himself says: We deny it.

units.la: Secundò ad Maiorem: In nostris Ecclesiis dum sacra coena administranda est, haud moris est, si nescis, ut dicatur eos accedere debere pro quibus Christus mortuus sit, reliquos abesse, ut tu nugaris: verùm hoc dicitur, ut nostro commodo & solatio Coenam Domini celebremus, ante omnia requiri, ut prius nos ipsos probemus, expendendo unusquisque apud se sua peccata & maledictionem: & explorando cor suum, an credat promissioni gratiae & remissionis peccatorum, propter solius Christi meritum, & an nova obedientia gratitudinem Deo exhibere ex animo cogitet. Tales enim convivas mensa Domini requirit; hypocritis autem & qui in flagitiis perseuerant, ab hoc cibo, quem Christus fidelibus suis instituit & adornauit, abstinendum est, ne iudicium ipsorum tanto reddatur grauius.
units.tr: Second, as to the major premise: in our churches, when the holy supper is to be administered, it is not our custom (if you did not know) to say that those for whom Christ died should come and the rest stay away, as you trifle. Rather, it is said that, for our own benefit and comfort, we celebrate the Lord's Supper, and that above all each one must first examine himself, weighing his own sins and their curse before himself, and testing his heart whether he believes the promise of grace and the forgiveness of sins for the sake of Christ's merit alone, and whether he sincerely intends to show gratitude to God by new obedience. For the Lord's table calls for such guests. Hypocrites, however, and those who persist in wickedness, must abstain from this food which Christ has instituted and prepared for his faithful people, so that their judgment may not be made the heavier.

units.la: Tertiò, Minor argumenti fàlsa est. Sciens enim scit se credere, vt supra quoque ostensum est. Quisquis verò credit, particeps est meritorum mortis & humiliationis Domini nostri Iesu Christi, dicente ipso; Hoc est corpus meum, quod pro vobis datur: &, Hoc est sanguis meus, sanguis noui testamenti, qui pro vobis effunditur: vt habet Lucas; seu, vt verba illa Matth. recitat, qui pro multis effunditur in remissionem peccatorum. Quare pro multis dicit? Quia licet Christi sanguis pro omnibus suus sit, quantum ad suf-ficientiam: tamen pro solis renatis su-sus est, quantum ad efficientiam, vt su-prà ex Innocentio retuli. Vnde & Basi-lius, Exhortatione ad Baptismum: Omnes quotquot credimus, gratia Dei, quæ est per v-nigenitum ipsius filium Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, à peccatis redempti sumus: qui dixit; Hic est sanguis meus, sanguis N. T. qui pro multis in remissionem peccatorum effunditur. Quæ explicatio & sequenti Serm. de Baptismo, apud eundem bis reperitur: pro multis, hoc est, pro omnibus credentibus, sisum Christi sanguinem.
units.tr: Third, the minor premise of the argument is false. For one who knows, knows that he believes, as was also shown above. Whoever believes is a partaker of the merits of the death and humiliation of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord himself saying: This is my body, which is given for you; and This is my blood, the blood of the new covenant, which is shed for you, as Luke has it; or, as Matthew recites those words, which is shed for many for the remission of sins. Why does he say "for many"? Because although the blood of Christ is his for all, as to sufficiency, yet it is shed only for the reborn, as to efficacy, as I related above from Innocent. Hence also Basil, in his Exhortation to Baptism: All of us who believe have been redeemed from sins by the grace of God, which is through his only-begotten Son our Lord Jesus Christ, who said: This is my blood, the blood of the New Testament, which is shed for many in the remission of sins. This explanation is found twice more in the following sermon on Baptism, in the same author: for many, that is, for all believers, the shed blood of Christ.

units.la: CAPVT XVI. Responsio ad reliqua absurda.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVI. Reply to the remaining absurdities.

units.la: PROGREDITVR Hub. & vt opinionem suam quoquo modo tueatur, alias etiam absurditates obiicit, ita horrendas, vt pia mens non possit non ad cogitationem earum contremiscere: vt, quod Deus accusetur fraudis & medacii. Fraudis, quod aliud dicat & aliud sentiat. Mendacii, quod verbo offerat & iubeat accipere, quae interim irreuocabili suo iudicio accipere vetet. Quod ite Christus passione sua Deo & hominibus illuserit: quodq; immesus & sanctus Deus Zebaoth merito accusetur crudelitatis, <bl>ἐπιχαιρεκακίας</bl> iniustitiae, & aliorum scelerum, saeuissimo potius Tyranno quam Deo competentium. Totidem enim verbis loquituraut, fremit potius os durum & impudens.
units.tr: Huber goes on, and to defend his opinion in some way or other he raises other absurdities, so monstrous that a pious mind cannot help shuddering at the thought of them. He charges God with fraud and lying: with fraud, because he says one thing and means another; with lying, because he offers something in his word and commands us to accept it, while in his irrevocable judgement he forbids us to accept it. He charges that Christ by his passion has mocked God and men in this way, and that the immense and holy God of Sabaoth is rightly accused of cruelty, malice [ἐπιχαιρεκακίας], injustice and other crimes that belong more to the most savage tyrant than to God. For he speaks in just these words, or rather a hard and shameless mouth rages.

units.la: Sed artes istae sunt aduersarii, ex eademprofectae officina, qua reliqua ipsius mendacia & calumniae, nimium sane audaces. Quoniam vero obiecta illa & subsannationes, excepta tantum penultima, non tam redemtionis, quam prae-
units.tr: But these are the tricks of our opponent, come from the same workshop that produced his other lies and calumnies, which are certainly far too bold. Since, however, those objections and taunts, except the next to last, concern not so much the doctrine of redemption as that of predestination,

units.la: Blasphemiae Hubiriana. prædestinationis doctrinam respiciunt (quos tractatus passim Huberus ἀμεθί- σεως inter se miscet) & vero iam pridem multis à Doctore Luthero de servo arbitrio refutatæ sunt, non patiar me iis refellendis hoc loco extra institutum abripi. Vnum & alterum duntaxat Lutheri locum in medium adducam, propter eos qui à viri istius autoritate pendent, vt per nostrum latus doctrinam Lutheri confodi intelligant.
units.tr: Huber's blasphemies. (which Huber everywhere mixes up indiscriminately [ἀμεθίσεως] with one another) and have already long since been refuted by many, by Doctor Luther in On the Bondage of the Will, I will not allow myself to be dragged off outside my purpose here to refute them. I will bring forward only one or two passages of Luther, for the sake of those who depend on that man's authority, so that they may understand that the doctrine of Luther is stabbed through our side.

units.la: Is igitur de servo arbitrio, in responsione ad locum Ezech. 18. Nolo mortem peccatoris, confirmat distinctionem receptam duplicis in Deo voluntatis, quæ quidem ita distingui solet pro nostro captu. Et vnam voluntatem, modò vocat occultam ac metuendam atque imperscrutabilem, modò reuerendissimum diuinæ maiestatis secretum, modò Deum abscônditum: alteram vero vocat, modò reuelatam voluntatem, modò verbum prædicatum, modò Deum prædicatum & cultum: Et subiicit in hunc modum: Multa facit Deus quæ verbo suo non ostendit nobis: multa quoque vult
units.tr: Luther, then, in On the Bondage of the Will, in his reply to the passage of Ezekiel 18, "I do not desire the death of the sinner," confirms the received distinction of a twofold will in God, which is commonly drawn in this way to suit our understanding. Now he calls the one will hidden, dreaded and unsearchable, now the most reverend secret of the divine majesty, now the hidden God; but the other he calls now the revealed will, now the preached word, now God preached and worshipped. And he adds in this manner: God does many things that he does not show us in his word; he also wills many things

units.la: p. 167. seq. -vult quæ verbo non ostendit se velle. Sic non vult mortem peccatoris verbo, id est, voluntate in verbo reuelata: vult autem illam voluntate imperscrutabili.
units.tr: (p. 167 and following) that he does not show in his word that he wills. Thus he does not will the death of the sinner by his word, that is, by his will revealed in the word; but he does will it by his unsearchable will.

units.la: Igitur recte dicitur: Si Deus non vult mortem peccatoris, nostræ voluntati imputandum esse quod perimus, recte, inquam, si de Deo prædicato intelligatur. Nam ille vult omnes homines salvos fieri: dum verbo salutis ad omnes venit: vitiumque est voluntatis, quæ non admittit Deum: sicut Matth. 23. dicitur: Quoties volui congregare pullos tuos & noluisti? Verum quare maiestas diuina vitium hoc voluntatis nostræ non tollat, aut mutet in omnibus, aut cur id homini imputet, cum carere eo non possit, quærere non licet, ac si multum quæras, nunquam tamen inuenies, ut Paulus Rom. 9. dicit. Tu igitur quis es qui respondes Deo? Rursum, satis est, inquit Lutherus, nosse quod Deus ita velit, & hac voluntatem reuereri, diligere, & adorare decet, coërcita rationis temeritate.
units.tr: Therefore it is rightly said: if God does not will the death of the sinner, the fact that we perish must be imputed to our will. Rightly, I say, if this is understood of God as preached. For he wills that all men be saved, since he comes to all by the word of salvation; and the fault lies in the will, which does not admit God, as it is said in Matthew 23: "How often would I have gathered your chicks, and you would not?" But why the divine majesty does not remove this fault of our will in all, or change it, or why it imputes it to man when he cannot be free of it, we are not allowed to ask; and if you ask much, you will never find out, as Paul says in Romans 9: "But who are you, O man, to answer back to God?" Again, says Luther, it is enough to know that God so wills, and we ought to revere, love and adore this will, with the rashness of reason restrained.

units.la: His satis ostendit Lutherus, quòd
units.tr: By these things Luther sufficiently shows that

units.la: Deus vult conuersionem & salutem omnium, voluntatis esse ipsius reuelatæ: occultæ autem, quod conuersionem & salutem neque dat neque dare constituit omnibus : sed quibus vult, pro mero suo beneplacito. Nec pugnant ista inter se, quasi aliud loquatur, aliud sentiat Deus, cùm dicimus ipsum velle, id est, iubere vt omnes resipiscant & credant Euangelio ad salutem, & tamen nö in omnibus velle operari fidem & pœnitentiâ. Vel pueri intelligât hic nullam esse contradictionē, propter diuersam significationē verbi volendi. ·
units.tr: God's willing the conversion and salvation of all belongs to his revealed will; but his hidden will is that he neither gives nor has determined to give conversion and salvation to all, but to those whom he wills, by his mere good pleasure. Nor do these things conflict with one another, as if God said one thing and meant another, when we say that he wills, that is, commands, that all should repent and believe the gospel unto salvation, and yet does not will to work faith and repentance in all. Even a boy can understand that there is no contradiction here, on account of the different meaning of the verb "to will."

units.la: Idem cap. 160. Hoc scilicet offendit sensum illum communem seu rationē naturalem, quod Deus mera voluntate sua homines deserat, induret, damnet: quasi delectetur pœnis & cruciatibus miserorum tantis & æternis, qui prædicatur tantæ misericordiæ & bonitatis. Hoc iniquum, hoc crudele, hoc intolerabile de Deo visum est sentire. Sed hîc honorandus & reuerendus est Deus clementissimus, donandumque est nonnihil diuinæ eius sapientiæ, vt iuftus esse credatur,vbi nobis iniquus ei- se videtur. Si enim talis esset eius iusti- tia, quæ humano captu posset iudicari esse iusta,plane non esset diuina, & ni- hil differret à iustitia humana. At cum sit Deus verus & vnus, deinde totus in- comprehensibilis & inaccessibilis hu- mana ratione, par est, imo necesse est, vt & iustitia eius incoprehensibilis sit, &c. Quæ igitur ista est peruersitas, vt iustitiam & iudiciū Dei vexemus? Hæc & multa alia eiusmodi Lutherus con- tra contendentes cum plasmatore suo.
units.tr: The same, chapter 160. Clearly this offends that common sense, or natural reason, that God by his mere will deserts, hardens and condemns men, as if he took pleasure in such great and eternal punishments and torments of the wretched, when he is proclaimed as of such great mercy and goodness. This seems unjust, cruel, intolerable to think of God. But here God, most merciful, must be honoured and revered, and some concession must be made to his divine wisdom, so that he is believed to be just where he seems unjust to us. For if his justice were of such a kind that it could be judged just by human understanding, it would plainly not be divine and would differ in nothing from human justice. But since God is true and one, and moreover wholly incomprehensible and inaccessible to human reason, it is fitting, nay necessary, that his justice too be incomprehensible, and so on. What then is this perversity, that we should vex the justice and judgement of God? These and many other things of this kind Luther urges against those who contend with their Maker.

units.la: Sed & Brentius in 1. Sam. 2. in ea verba defiliis Eli, v.25. Non audierūt vocem patris sui, quia volebat Ichoua occidere eos, subscribit huic doctrinæ, & totam hanc quæstionem his verbis concludit. Itaque vt pro meritorum suorum dignitate pu- nirentur, occulta sua potentia Domi- nus effecit, vt ad patris monitione non resipiscerent, & perirent: nimirum in- tus operas, quod foris verbo prohibet, & potentia intus impediens quod ma- nifesta sua voluntate foris fieri madabat. Atque hoc non est autore seu causam V iij esse malitiæ, sed est iustum inferre supplicium propter malitiam. Ceterum qui fiat, quod Dominus occulta sua potentia intus operetur, aut impediat, quod foris manifesto verbo prohibet aut mandat, altius est, quàm vt humano captu inuestigari queat. Hæc Brentius.
units.tr: But Brenz too, on 1 Samuel 2, on the words concerning the sons of Eli, verse 25, "They did not listen to the voice of their father, because the Lord willed to kill them," subscribes to this doctrine and concludes the whole question in these words: "So that they might be punished in accordance with the worth of their merits, the Lord by his hidden power brought it about that they did not repent at their father's admonition and perished. Clearly he works inwardly what he outwardly forbids by his word, and by an impeding power inwardly prevents what he commanded to be done outwardly by his manifest will. And this does not make him the author or cause of wickedness, but it is just to inflict punishment for wickedness. But how it happens that the Lord by his hidden power works within, or prevents, what he outwardly forbids or commands by his manifest word, is too deep to be searched out by human understanding." Thus Brenz.

units.la: Quod porrò obiicitur, nisi morte Christi omnes, fideles & infideles, re ipsa & proprie, condonatis peccatis gratiæ & saluti restituti sint, Christum accusari, quod falsa pastione Deo & hominibus illuserit; commentum est vanum atque insipidum. Mera est enim petitio principii in antecedente, cum adversarius sic argumentatur;
units.tr: As for what is further objected, that unless all, faithful and unfaithful alike, were in very fact and properly restored to grace and salvation by the death of Christ, with their sins forgiven, Christ is accused of having mocked God and men by a false pretence: this is an empty and foolish invention. For there is a mere begging of the question in the premise, since the opponent argues in this way:

units.la: Christus ipse fatetur se non pro paucis tantum esse mortuum, sed pro toto mundo, toto mimirum genere humano. Quare si patris consilium fuit, vt pro electis tantùm moreretur, Christus Deo in primis, deinde & hominibus illuserit, tanta ipse ora hominum suspendendo, quasi pro omnibus moreretur.
units.tr: Christ himself confesses that he died not only for a few, but for the whole world, that is, for the whole human race. Therefore, if it was the Father's plan that he should die only for the elect, Christ mocked God first and then men, holding the mouths of men in suspense as if he had died for all.

units.la: Comp. Thel. 17.
units.tr: Compare Thelesius, 17.

units.la: Vbi quæso fatetur Dominus, quòd pro omnibus efficaciter mortuus sit aut mori voluerit? seu quòdeffectu mortis suæ nepe reconciliationem iustitiam & salutem voluerit esse omnium, nullo penitus ex tota humani generis vniuersitate excepto, siue ille Seruatorem fide amplestatur, siue incredulitate repuat? Contrarium Christus Ioh. 17. testatur, Non pro mundo rogo, sed pro eis quos dedisti mihi. Pro quibus autem ne rogare quidem dignatus est, mirum si iudicii iramq; Patris ijs placauit. Et eodem cap. Pro eis ego sanctifico me ipsum, vt & ipsi sint sanctificati. Pro quibus igitur orauit, pro ijs etiam efficaciter à peccato & morte redimendis, & in perpetuū sanctificandis, sanctificauit, id est, sacrificium obtulit se ipsum, & contrà.
units.tr: Where, I ask, does the Lord confess that he died effectually for all, or that he willed, by the effect of his death, that reconciliation, righteousness and salvation should belong to all, with no one at all excepted from the whole universe of the human race, whether that man embraces the Saviour in faith or rejects him in unbelief? Christ testifies the contrary in John 17: "I do not pray for the world, but for those whom you have given me." And for those for whom he did not even deign to pray, it would be strange if he appeased the Father's wrath and judgement for them. And in the same chapter: "For them I sanctify myself, that they also may be sanctified." For whom therefore he prayed, for them he also sanctified himself, that is, offered himself as a sacrifice, so as to redeem them effectually from sin and death and sanctify them for ever, and conversely.

units.la: V iiij
units.tr: V iiij

units.la: CAPVT XVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVII.

units.la: De eo quod sola incredulitas damnet, ac non alia peccata: sed propter solam incredulitatem damnetur, quisquis damnetur.
units.tr: That unbelief alone condemns, and not other sins; rather, whoever is condemned is condemned on account of unbelief alone.

units.la: His omnibus ad hunc modum explicatis, actum nunc est de opinione Huberi, dissesta triplici eius classe, cui nequicquam confisus, & numero magis quàm robore argumentorum instructus, certamen hoc veritati indixit.
units.tr: Having set out all these matters in this way, we now turn to the opinion of Huber. We have divided it into three parts, and we have taken it on in this contest against the truth, relying on it in vain, and supported more by numbers than by the strength of its arguments.

units.la: Antequâ tamen huic parti, qua noui & erronei dogmatis de redemtione confutatio suscepta nobis est, fine imponamus, non prætereundum est, quid à nouis dogmatistis de causa damnationis tradatur; qui nimirum fiat, quòd cum omnessine exceptione à iudicio iraque Dei absolutos, inque gratiam & sinum patris receptos, & reprobos æque ac electos saluatos esse contendant passione Christi, non omnes tamen æternum seruentur.
units.tr: Before we bring to an end this part, in which we have undertaken the refutation of the new and erroneous doctrine of redemption, we must not pass over what the new dogmatists teach about the cause of damnation. They maintain, namely, that although all men without exception have been absolved by Christ's passion from the judgment and wrath of God, and received into grace and the bosom of the Father, and that both the reprobate and the elect have been saved alike, yet not all are kept for eternity.

units.la: Causam igitur aiunt esse hanc, quod alii per fidem in accepta salute permaneant, neant, alij per incredulitatem salutem sibi præstitam respuant, contemnant, abiiciant,atque ita negligendo & spernendo salutem suam, reprobos se ipsos faciant,& idcirco tantum damnentur, qnod gratiam fastidiant, atque incredulitate omnium peccatorum reatu se denuo obstringat. Hæc totidem verbis apud Hub. exstant thesi. 19. 69. 155. 245. Thesi quoque 187. scribit, non credentes conculare suam redemtionem, & expiationem peccatorum suorum, per incredulitatem sibimet excutere: atque sic incredulitatem vnicam ipsis causam fieri damnationis. Similiter Coll. Momp. pag. 548. Iacobus Andreæ inquit, non ideo damnari homines, quod peccarint, sed quod nolint vera fide ampleCti Iesum Christum, qui nō minus pro damnatorum peccatis passus,crucifixus & mortuus sit,quam pro peccatis Petri, Pauli, & omnium sanctorum: annotatis in margine ibidem his verbis: sola incredulitas damnat homines.
units.tr: They say the cause of this is that some remain in the salvation they have received through faith, while others, through unbelief, reject, despise and cast away the salvation offered to them; and so, by neglecting and scorning their salvation, they make themselves reprobate, and are therefore damned only because they loathe grace and by unbelief bind themselves again to the guilt of all their sins. These very words stand in Huber, thesis 19, 69, 155, 245. In thesis 187 too he writes that those who do not believe trample underfoot their redemption and the expiation of their sins, and by unbelief shake off from themselves the atonement; and so unbelief alone becomes the cause of their damnation. Similarly, James Andreae says in the Colloquium of Montbéliard, p. 548, that men are not damned because they have sinned, but because they are unwilling to embrace Jesus Christ with true faith, who suffered, was crucified and died no less for the sins of the damned than for the sins of Peter, Paul and all the saints; and in the margin there he noted these words: unbelief alone condemns men.

units.la: Ad hanc doctrinam quod attinet, in V confesso sane est, si quis vere in Christũ credat, totius mundi peccata eum in infernum deprimere non posse: & contrà, si quis fidem nõ habeat, damnatum iri etiâsi totius mundi iustitia eius propria esset. Qui enim crediderit seruabitur, qui non crediderit condemnabitur, dicit testis ille fidelis & verax. Et scribente Augustino, vno incredulitatis peccato aducrsus cetera peccata clauditur, ne per Dei gratiam relaxentur: sicut credendo cuncta soluuntur peccata. Aug. de verbis Domini secundum Ioh. serm. 6o. Et enarrat. Psal. 109.
units.tr: As for this doctrine, it is certainly admitted that if anyone truly believes in Christ, the sins of the whole world cannot drag him down into hell; and conversely, if anyone lacks faith, he will be condemned even if the whole righteousness of the world were his own. For he who believes will be saved, he who does not believe will be condemned, says that faithful and true witness. And Augustine writes that by the one sin of unbelief the way is closed against all other sins, so that they are not forgiven by the grace of God; just as, by believing, all sins are loosed. Augustine, On the words of the Lord according to John, sermon 60; and in the exposition of Psalm 109.

units.la: Duo tamen in dicta iam opinione merito displicêt. Vnum est, quod cum opinio hæc cogatur agnoscere salutem regni cœlestis non contingere nisi per fidem, ausit tamen remissionem peccatorum, & liberationem à iudicio atque ira Dei & potestate Diaboli, adoptionemq; in filios Dei, & ipsam adeo salutem statuere sine fide. Vult enim omnibus omnia ista contigisse communiter morte Christi: siue credant siue nõ, contra atque omnes Prophetæ & Apostoli
units.tr: Yet there are two points in the opinion just stated which rightly displease. The first is that, while this opinion is forced to acknowledge that salvation in the heavenly kingdom comes only through faith, it nevertheless dares to set down the forgiveness of sins, deliverance from the judgment and wrath of God and the power of the devil, adoption as sons of God, and salvation itself, as existing without faith. For it holds that all these things have come to all men alike through the death of Christ, whether they believe or not; contrary to what all the prophets and apostles testify,

units.la: Marc. 16. stoli testificantur, quod qui crediderit in Christum, per nomen eius remissionem accipiat peccatorū; manente super incredulos ira Dei. Hæc longè alia sententia est, ac si dicas, quemadmodū Huberus, omnes simul ab omni pecca- to liberatos, & omne iudicium iram-que diuinam in vniuersis hominibus sublatam atque deletam, etiam in non credentibus: Tantùm per incredulitatem eos denuò obstringi peccatorum suorum reatu, & recidere sub iram Dei. Bene Augustinus, loco prius citato, Medicina animæ omnium vulnerum, & vna propitiatio pro delictis hominum, est credere in Christum, & credendo nascimur ex Deo & filij Dei simus, sicut scriptum est; his qui credunt in nomen eius, dedit potestatem vt filij Dei sierent.
units.tr: Mark 16: that whoever believes in Christ receives forgiveness of sins through his name, while the wrath of God remains upon the unbelieving. This is a very different sentence from saying, as Huber does, that all men together have been freed from all sin, and that all judgment and the wrath of God have been taken away and wiped out in all men, even in those who do not believe; and only that through unbelief they are bound again to the guilt of their sins and fall back under the wrath of God. Augustine rightly says in the passage cited above: The medicine of the soul for all wounds, and the one propitiation for the sins of men, is to believe in Christ; and by believing we are born of God and become sons of God, as it is written: to those who believe in his name he gave the power to become sons of God.

units.la: Alterum quod in opinione allata merito reprehenditur, illud est, quod damnationis causam præcisè statuit contemtum vel fastidium gratiæ Euangelij per incredulitatem. Primò enim sententia hæc præsupponit oblationè gratiæ Euangelij, respectu cunctorum & singulorū qui vnquam fuerunt, sunt, aut erunt: Quod quàm vanum sit, multis scriptu-rarum testimoniis docetur: Act. 14. v.16. & cap.17. v.30. Eph.2. v.12. Psal. 147. v. 19. & 20. Vide praeterea quae hoc libro diximus cap. 6.
units.tr: The second point in the opinion quoted, which is rightly censured, is that it sets down contempt or loathing of the grace of the gospel through unbelief as the sole cause of damnation. For first, this view presupposes that the gospel grace is offered to all and each of those who have ever been, are now, or will be; how false this is is taught by many testimonies of Scripture: Acts 14:16; Acts 17:30; Eph. 2:12; Ps. 147:19–20. See also what we have said in this book, chapter 6.

units.la: Secundò, Apostolus inquiens, qui sine lege peccarunt, etiam sine lege peribunt, & qui in lege peccarunt, per legem damnabuntur; non tantum concedit, gentes maiori ex parte caruisse notitia legis scriptae, multò magis notitia promissionum gratiae Euangelii per Mosen & Prophetas annunciatarum: verùm etiam iustae gentilium damnationis rationem adfert ex violata lege naturae, nullam contemtae Euangelii gratiae mentionem faciens.
units.tr: Second, the Apostle, saying those who have sinned without the law will also perish without the law, and those who have sinned under the law will be judged by the law, not only concedes that the Gentiles for the most part lacked knowledge of the written law, and much more knowledge of the promises of the gospel grace announced through Moses and the prophets; but he also gives the just reason for the damnation of the Gentiles from the violated law of nature, making no mention at all of contempt for the grace of the gospel.

units.la: Tertiò, quid dicemus de tot myrtidibus infantum extra Ecclesiam, qui iam inde à condito mundo vitae huius fine praeueti sunt, & praeueniuntur quotidie, priusquam vel minimum de Euangelij gratia audire possunt? Quae ibi salutis conclucatio? quod gratiae fastidium?
units.tr: Third, what shall we say of the countless infants outside the Church, who from the beginning of the world have been seized by the end of this life, and are seized every day, before they can hear even the smallest thing about the grace of the gospel? What salvation is there for them? What contempt of grace?

units.la: Quarto
units.tr: Fourthly

units.la: Quartò, Dominus in Euangelio ait, Si non venissem & non loquutus essem eis, peccatum non haberent, nunc autem non habent quod prætexant peccatis. Hunc locum Augustus.. tract. 89. accipiendum monet non de omni, sed de magno infidelitatis peccato: & mota quæstione, utrum ij ad quos non venit Christus, nec locutus est eis, habeant excusationem de peccato suo? respondet, non quidem de omni peccato suo, sed de hoc peccato, quod in Christum non crediderunt, habere plane excusationem, nec posse tamen ideo damnationem effugere, secundum illud, Quicunque sine lege peccarunt, etiam sine lege peribunt: quicunque autem in lege peccarunt, etiam in lege iudicabuntur. Atque tales dicit esse, qui cum audiunt, contemnunt, aut etiam resistunt contradicentes, aut eos à quibus audiunt, odiis persequentes. Epist item pp. ad Euodiu, agens de constitutis apud inferos, tam ex sua quàm communi aliorum sententia, discernit illos, qui Euangelio hic annunciato credere noluerunt, ab his qui non hic contemserunt, inquit, quod audire minimè potuerunt, & sine vllo reatu contemti Euangelij ad inferos deuenerunt. Similia scribit lib. de Natura & gratia cap. 4. Cum his veterum dictis si conferantur phrases Nouatorum, videbimus pugnantiam è diametro. Atque hęc pro refutatione eorum, quatum instituti nostri ratio visa fuit exigere, dicta sunto.
units.tr: Fourth, the Lord says in the Gospel: If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin. Augustine, Tractate 89, advises that this passage is to be understood not of every sin but of the great sin of unbelief; and raising the question whether those to whom Christ did not come, and to whom he did not speak, have an excuse for their sin, he answers: not indeed for every sin of theirs, but for this sin, that they did not believe in Christ, they plainly have an excuse; yet they cannot on that account escape condemnation, according to that saying: whoever have sinned without the law will also perish without the law; but whoever have sinned under the law will also be judged by the law. And he says that such are those who, when they hear, despise, or even resist those who contradict them, or persecute with hatred those from whom they hear. In his letter to Euodius, Epistle 1, discussing the condition of those in hell, both from his own opinion and from the common opinion of others, he distinguishes those who were unwilling to believe the gospel announced here from those who did not despise it here, he says, because they could not hear it at all, and went down to hell without any guilt of despising the gospel. He writes similar things in On Nature and Grace, chapter 4. If the phrases of the Novatians are compared with these sayings of the ancients, we shall see a direct contradiction. And let these things be said in refutation of them, as far as the plan of our undertaking seemed to require.

units.la: LIBER
units.tr: BOOK

units.la: LIBER TERTIVS DE REDEMTIONE CHRISTIANA, κατασκευαστικὸς: Seu assertio verae sententiae, Quinam redemtionis sint participes.
units.tr: THE THIRD BOOK ON CHRISTIAN REDEMPTION, constructive: or an assertion of the true opinion, who are the partakers of redemption.

units.la: CAPVT I.
units.tr: CHAPTER I.

units.la: Propositio & partitio.
units.tr: Proposition and division.

units.la: VENTVM nunc est ad verae doctrinae confirmationem. Ea vero est, quod licet mors filij Dei, Domini nostri Iesu Christi, quantum ad magnitudinem pretij attinet, sit redemtio totius generis humani, nullo penitus excepto, redemtionis tamen proprietas penes illos sit, qui non iam vasa Diaboli, sed membra sunt Christi, per fidem & gratiam regenerationis: reliquis, qui seculum hoc sine fide & regeneratione transeunt, ad redemtionem hanc a peccato & morte non pertinentibus. Et quoniam fides & regeneratio non omnium, sed electorum rum rum sunt, recte quoque eorundem perhibetur esse redemtio, & non reproborum.
units.tr: WE have now come to the confirmation of the true doctrine. It is this: although the death of the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, as far as the greatness of the price is concerned, is the redemption of the whole human race, without any exception at all, nevertheless the proper benefit of redemption belongs to those who are no longer vessels of the Devil but members of Christ, through faith and the grace of regeneration; it does not pertain to the rest, who pass through this age without faith and regeneration, to this redemption from sin and death. And since faith and regeneration belong not to all but to the elect, it is rightly said that redemption belongs to them, and not to the reprobate.

units.la: Sententiam hanc confirmaturi: vte- mur & nos triplici probationum classe.
units.tr: In confirming this opinion, we too shall use a threefold class of proofs.

units.la: Prima erit quorundam scripturæ te- stimoniorum, veteris & noui testamen- ti, quibus spiritualis redemtio per Chri- stum parta restringitur ad Ecclesiam: quæ certè non est totius humani gene- ris vniuersitas, sed cœtus quidam ex genere humano, ex omni tribu, lingua, natione & populo, ad vitam æternam electus.
units.tr: The first will be a class of certain testimonies of Scripture, both Old and New Testament, by which spiritual redemption obtained through Christ is restricted to the Church: which is certainly not the whole universality of the human race, but a certain assembly drawn from the human race, from every tribe, tongue, nation and people, chosen to eternal life.

units.la: Altera classe proferemus diuersa argumenta, hausta ex analogia fidei, seu apostolica & catholica fidei regula, cui expositio omnis Ecclesiastica, & quarumlibet fidei controuersiarum decisio, adaptari debet.
units.tr: In the second class we shall set forth various arguments drawn from the analogy of faith, that is, the apostolic and catholic rule of faith, to which all ecclesiastical exposition, and the decision of whatever controversies of faith, ought to be fitted.

units.la: Denique tertia classis habebit testimonia piæ antiquitatis, ex quibus luce clarius apparebit, nihil hic tradi aut proferri à nobis, quod non optimi & laudatissimi quique scriptores olim magno consensu secundum scripturas tradiderint.
units.tr: Finally, the third class will contain testimonies of pious antiquity, from which it will appear more clearly than light that nothing is taught or put forward here by us which the best and most highly praised writers of old did not hand down, with great agreement, in accordance with the Scriptures.

units.la: Cap.II.
units.tr: Chapter II.

units.la: CAPVT II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: Loca quaedam noui testamenti, cum admonitione de Huberiana disputandi ratione.
units.tr: Some passages of the New Testament, with a warning about Huber's method of disputing.

units.la: INSTITVTAM confirmationem ab expressis Scripturae testimoniis eò ordimur libentius, quod aduersarius non dubitauit effutire, quasi sententiae nostrae nullum habeamus τὸ ἐντὸν in Scripturis, & consequetiis tatum elicere & exprimere ea conemur. Ac quo magis mirêre Christiane lector, hominis oscitantia atque ineptias in re rata, appareat eum de controuersia ista scribentem & meditantem quotidie, diu tamen (quoad nimirum Doctoris Toffani thesibus commonefactus, appendice sibi opus esse vidit) in ea fuisse opinione, ac si omnis sententiae nostrae probatio recideret ad hoc Enthymema: Est praedestinatio Dei aeterna, qua aliorum statuit in Christo misericordiam salutè, aliorum non: Ergo Christus non est mortuus pro omnibus. Quo errore postea abreptus, nec iam curru audiente habenas, magnū ciet puluere ad infuscandā ve-
units.tr: We undertake the confirmation of our position from express testimonies of Scripture more willingly, because our opponent did not hesitate to blurt out that we have no explicit basis for our view in the Scriptures [τὸ ἐνδον], and that we try to draw out and express only what follows by inference. And, Christian reader, so that you may see more clearly the drowsiness and silliness of this man, who wrote and meditated on this controversy every day, yet for a long time (until, that is, he was reminded by the theses of Doctor Toffanus that he needed an appendix) remained under the impression that the whole proof of our position came down to this enthymeme: "The eternal predestination of God is that by which he has decided to grant mercy and salvation in Christ to some and not to others; therefore Christ did not die for all." Carried off by this error, and no longer keeping the reins of his chariot, he raises a great dust to darken the truth of the doctrine of predestination,

units.la: X ritaritate doctrinę de prędestinatione: idqꝫ non solùm loco prorsus alieno & explicationibus plane prodigiosis : verùm etiam errore tam multiloquo, ut pro vnica pagella locorum Scripturæ à M. Pareo citatorum de prædestinatione, ipse euagetur in pag. C. theses autem CCCL. In qua tota disputatione perpetuum ipsius artificium est, quod argumenta nostrorum de prædestinatione (huic enim ut dixi vnicè immoratur, cū de redemtione agere debuisset) mala fide & ingenio Sycophatico proponit, & pro solutionibus vbique occinit Coccysmum suum, de repetitione principij, quam Dialecticorum scholis non repetitionem, sed petitionem dicere moris est. Eiusdem, imò crassioris rudi-tatis est, quod in appendice ad D. Tossani argumenta, vehementer sibi placet in altero Coccysmo suo, Nego Consequens: Semper negamus consequens. O miserum disputatorem, æquè infeliciter in Dialecticis, atqꝫ in Theologicis versatum! Nondum tenet, propositaargumentatione, quam Enthymema vocamus, mus, nunquam responderi oportere negatione consequentis: Sed vel antecedentis distinctione, negationeve, vel consequentiæ inficiatione. Nam consequês velle negare in Enthymemate, tam est ineptum, quàm si quis ad Syllogismum respondsurus, velit negare conclusionem. Quo genere solutionum nihil nō posset solui facilimè à quouis, nisi Dialectica refragaretur.
units.tr: and that not only in a place wholly foreign to the subject and with explanations plainly monstrous, but also with an error so wordy that, from a single little page of Scripture passages cited by M. Pareus on predestination, he wanders across page C and into 350 theses. In this whole disputation his method is constant: he presents the arguments of our side on predestination (for on this alone he lingers, as I said, when he ought to have been treating of redemption) with bad faith and a sycophantic cleverness, and for his solutions he everywhere sings his own cuckoo-refrain, "a repetition of the principle," which the schools of the dialecticians are accustomed to call not a "repetition" but a "petition of principle." It is of the same, or rather of a cruder, rudeness that in the appendix to the arguments of Doctor Toffanus he takes great pleasure in his other cuckoo-refrain: "I deny the consequent: we always deny the consequent." O wretched disputant, equally unhappy in dialectic and in theology! He does not yet grasp that in a proposed argument, which we call an enthymeme, one should never answer by denying the consequent, but either by distinguishing or denying the antecedent, or by disputing the consequence. For to wish to deny the consequent in an enthymeme is as foolish as if someone, about to answer a syllogism, wished to deny the conclusion. With this kind of solution anything could be refuted most easily by anyone, were dialectic not opposed to it.

units.la: Verùm his omissis, pauca è multis Scripturæ testimonia proferamus ad ostendendum inftitutū nostrum, quod redemtio à peccatis iustitia & salus, beneficia sint Ecclesiæ propria, & nequaquam communia omnibus, siue credant, siue non credat, vt noua vult opinio. Hic causæ status est proprie, quod diligenter notandum est. Nam Christum pro omnibus mortuum esse concedimus & nos: sed negamus beneficiorū mortis Christi ideo omnes reddi participes absque respectu fidei vel incredulitatis, seu quod idem est, Christum pro omnibus mortuum efficaciter negamus, idque causa inefficacitatis tis illius non in Christo, sed in hominibus ipsis considerata. Ad hoc enim ut Christi mors nobis efficax sit ad redemptionem, non solum merito ipsius, sed etiam eiusdem applicatione & perceptione opus est, quae per fidem fit minime simulatam.
units.tr: But setting these aside, let us put forward a few of the many testimonies of Scripture to show our purpose, namely that redemption from sins, righteousness and salvation are the proper benefits of the Church, and by no means common to all, whether they believe or do not believe, as the new opinion wishes. Here the state of the question is properly this, and it must be carefully noted. For we too grant that Christ died for all; but we deny that all are made partakers of the benefits of Christ's death without regard to faith or unbelief; or, which is the same thing, we deny that Christ died for all effectively, and this because of the ineffectiveness which is to be considered not in Christ but in men themselves. For in order that Christ's death may be effective for us unto redemption, not only his merit but also its application and reception are needed, and this comes about through a faith that is not feigned.

units.la: Primum igitur testimonium habemus Matth.1. in verbis Angeli ad Ioseph-um: vocabis nomen eius Iesum: Ipse enim salvabit populum suum a peccatis eorum. Hic videmus redemptionem peculiariter attribui populo Christi. Populus autem Christi est Ecclesia ipsius omnium locorum & aetatum. Ecclesiae igitur peculiaris est redemptio: & tamen universalis, eo modo quo & Ecclesiam universalem confitemur.
units.tr: The first testimony, then, we have in Matthew 1, in the words of the angel to Joseph: "You shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins." Here we see redemption attributed peculiarly to the people of Christ. But the people of Christ is his Church in all places and ages. Redemption, therefore, is peculiar to the Church; and yet it is universal, in the same way that we also confess a universal Church.

units.la: Obstrepit Hub. & quae ipsius Theologia est, per populum Christi denotari ait, universam Adami progeniem & omnes vere vocatos ad regnum Dei dicit, ut sint populus ipsius.
units.tr: Huber objects, and, as is his own theology, says that by the people of Christ is meant the whole offspring of Adam and all who are truly called to the kingdom of God, so that they may be his people.

units.la: Sed contrarium facile probatur. Primum, appellatione populi Dei Scriptura non solet omnes homines complecti, sed certum duntaxat coetum in quo agnoscitur & inuocatur Deus, quémque ipse pro suo peculio vicissim agnoscit,& cuius sunt pacta &promissiones, dicente Domino. Ambulabo in medio vestri, eróque vobis in Deum & vos eritis mihi in populum. Et ero vobis pater, & vos eritis mihi filij, ac filiæ, dicit Deus omnipotes. Vt etiam in Osea dicit, vocabo populum qui meus non erat, populum meum, & eam quæ dilecta non erat, dilectam: & erit in loco vbi dictum fuerat eis, Nō populus meus vos, illic vocabuntur filij Dei viuentis. Quę omnia Paulus ad Rom. de gentium vocatione declarat; quæ cum quódam alienæ fuissent à republica Israelis, & extraneæ à pactis promissionis, spem non habentes, & expertes Dei in mundo; postmodum in regno Christi adoptionem gratiæ consequutæ sunt. Sic ad Tit.legimus, Christum purificasse sibi populum peculiarem, sectatorē bonorum operum. Quem & Petrus vocat λαὸν εἰς περιποίησιν, gentem sanctam, regale sacerdotium. Cuius igitur insolentiæ est comminisci, omnes homines esse po-
units.tr: But the contrary is easily proved. First, by the name "people of God" Scripture does not usually embrace all men, but only a certain assembly in which God is acknowledged and invoked, and which in turn he acknowledges as his own possession, and to which belong his covenants and promises; as the Lord says: "I will walk among you, and I will be your God, and you shall be my people. And I will be a father to you, and you shall be my sons and daughters, says the Almighty God." As he also says in Hosea: "I will call that which was not my people, my people, and her who was not beloved, beloved; and in the place where it was said to them, 'You are not my people,' there they shall be called sons of the living God." Paul declares all these things in Romans concerning the calling of the Gentiles; who, though they were once aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in the world, afterwards in the kingdom of Christ obtained the adoption of grace. So in Titus we read that Christ purified for himself a peculiar people, zealous for good works. Peter also calls them "a people for possession" [λαὸν εἰς περιποίησιν], a holy nation, a royal priesthood. What insolence, then, is it to invent that all men are the people of God?

units.la: Rom.9. Tit.2. 1.Pet.2. pulum Dei? Hoc nihil aliud est, quàm fideles cum infidelibus, iustitiam cum iniustitia, lucè cum tenebris, Christum cum Belial, templum Dei cum simulacris coniungere, & miscere sacra profanis.
units.tr: (Romans 9; Titus 2; 1 Peter 2.) This is nothing other than joining believers with unbelievers, righteousness with unrighteousness, light with darkness, Christ with Belial, the temple of God with idols, and mixing holy things with profane.

units.la: Secundò, si omnes essent populus Christi, non tantum sequeretur omnes etiam appellandos Christianos, sed etiam iuxta figmentum Origenis, omnes tandem seruaretur ad vitam æternam; cùm salus, quam Christus populo suo impertit, vitam æternam, tàquam praecipuum complementum, includat.
units.tr: Secondly, if all were the people of Christ, it would follow not only that all must be called Christians, but also, according to the fiction of Origen, that all would at last be saved unto eternal life; since the salvation which Christ bestows on his people includes eternal life as its chief completion.

units.la: Tertiò, Theophylactus in eũ ipsum locum ita scribit: Ipse, inquit, saluabit populum suum, nõ solùm Iudaicum, sed & Gentilem, qui credet & fieri populus eius non dubitauerit.
units.tr: Thirdly, Theophylact, on that very passage, writes thus: "He, he says, will save his people, not only the Jewish but also the Gentile, who believe and have not doubted to become his people."

units.la: Lutherus quoque in Genes. 31. multis testatur, nõ omnes esse populum Dei, sed qui ipsi grati & accepti sunt, & non possunt rapi ex manibus eius. In primis autem Brentium suum audiat Huberus ita scribentem in Expos. Cat. Exponito nobis, inquit, quibus Iesus sit Iesus, id est Saluator à peccatis ipsorum. Euangelista dicit: Saluum faciet populum suum: Non facit sal-uos alienos, sed suum populum. Alieni sunt, quotquot non credunt in ipsum, siue illi sint Iudæi, siue Gentes. Sui autem sunt, siue & ipsi fuerint Iudæi, siue Gentes, quotquot eü agno-scunt & amplectuntur fide. Quare qualicun-que Gente fueris, si credideris Euangelio Christi, efficeris per fidem membrum populi eius: & vere Iesus tibi fit Iesus. Hæc ille, cuius aliud quoque dictum infra citabitur cap. 7. Viderint vero Tubingenses, Brentium an Huberum potius erroris hic damnare velint.
units.tr: Luther also, on Genesis 31, bears witness in many places that not all are the people of God, but those who are pleasing and acceptable to him, and who cannot be snatched from his hands. But above all let Huber listen to his Brenz writing thus in the Exposition of the Catechism: "Tell us, he says, to whom Jesus is Jesus, that is, the Saviour from their sins. The evangelist says: 'He will save his people.' He does not save strangers, but his own people. Strangers are all who do not believe in him, whether they be Jews or Gentiles. His own are all, whether they were Jews or Gentiles, who acknowledge and embrace him by faith. Therefore, of whatever nation you may be, if you have believed the gospel of Christ, you become by faith a member of his people, and Jesus truly becomes Jesus to you." So he; and another saying of his will be cited below in chapter 7. But let the Tübingen men see whether Brenz or rather Huber they wish to condemn here as in error.

units.la: Alterum testimonium apud eúdem Euangelistam habemus Cap. 26. Accepto poculo dedit eis dicens, bibite ex eo omnes. Hoc est enim sanguis noui testamenti qui PRO MVLTIS effunditur in remissionem peccatorum.
units.tr: We have another testimony in the same evangelist, chapter 26: "Taking the cup, he gave it to them, saying: Drink of it, all of you. For this is my blood of the new covenant, which is shed FOR MANY for the remission of sins."

units.la: Scio quidem veterum nonnullos, ad sufficientiam respicientes exponere, pro multis, id est pro omnibus sanguinem illum fusum, cum & omnes multi sint. sed sensus magis quadrat, seruata vsitata significatione multorum, ad distinctionem credetium ab incredulis: quorum illi accepta peccatorum, condonatione per gratiam Christi redemti sunt, hi redemtionis adhuc alieni sunt, vt suprà à Basilio frequenter exponi diximus. Et commentarij in Marcum, qui Hieronymo adscribuntur, expresse habet, sanguinem noui testamenti pro multis dici effusum, quia non omnes emundet: vel in ipsa Ecclesia esse, quos nullum sacrificium emundet. Multo igitur magis extra Ecclesiam. Quid, quod é neotericis Brentius non aliter exponit in Catechismo? Christus, inquit, cum de sanguine suo diceret, qui pro vobis effunditur, addidit & hoc, pro multis, vt significaret non pro Iudaeis tantum, sed etiam pro Gentibus, ex quibus Ecclesia colligenda erat, effundi. Ac probare ibi instituit ea allegatione & explicatione, id ipsum quod & nobis propositum est, Christum videlicet morte sua expiare peccata suorum, vt habeant remissionem peccatorum, & reputentur iusti coram Deo, fiant caro & sanguis Christi, adoptentur in filios & haeredes Dei: & haec beneficia ad vniuersam perti-nere
units.tr: I know indeed that some of the ancients, looking to sufficiency, explain "for many" as "for all, that is, that blood was shed for all," since all are indeed many. But the sense fits better, keeping the usual meaning of "many," in distinction from believers and unbelievers: of whom the former have been redeemed by the grace of Christ through the reception of the forgiveness of sins, while the latter are still strangers to redemption, as we said Basil often explains above. And the commentaries on Mark, which are ascribed to Jerome, expressly say that "the blood of the new covenant is said to be shed for many, because it does not cleanse all; or because there are in the Church itself those whom no sacrifice cleanses." Much more, therefore, outside the Church. Moreover, does not Brenz, among the modern writers, explain it in no other way in his Catechism? "Christ," he says, "when he spoke of his blood, which is shed for you, added this also, 'for many,' to signify that he was shed not for the Jews only, but also for the Gentiles, from whom the Church was to be gathered." And there he undertakes to prove, by that allegation and explanation, the very thing that is also our purpose, namely that Christ by his death expiates the sins of his own, so that they may have the remission of sins and be reckoned righteous before God, become flesh and blood of Christ, be adopted as sons and heirs of God; and that these benefits pertain to the whole Church, not to strangers.

units.la: Christus inquit, cum de sanguine suo diceret, nere Ecclesiam, non ad alienos. Nam eadem hic valet antithesis suorum & alienorum, quæ prius ex Bretio notata fuit.
units.tr: Christ, he says, when speaking of his blood, pertains to the Church, not to strangers. For the same antithesis holds here, of his own and of aliens, which was noted earlier from Bretius.

units.la: Adhæc Lutherus hunc ipsum locum expendens de capt. Babyl. inquit: Pro vobis, & pro multis dixit, id est, qui acceptât & credunt promissioni testatoris. Fides enim hic hæredes facit.
units.tr: Luther too, expounding this very passage in On the Babylonian Captivity, says: He said "for you and for many," that is, for those who accept and believe the promise of the testator. For faith makes heirs here.

units.la: Tertius locus est in cantico Zachariæ, Luc. 1. Benedictus Dominus Deus Israël: Quia visitavit & redemit populum suum, & erexit cornu salutis in domo David pueri sui, prout locutus est per os sanctorum prophetarum, salutem ex inimicis nostris, & e manu omnium, qui oderunt nos: ut e manibus inimicorum nostrorum liberati, sine metu serviamus ipsi in sanctitate & iustitia coram ipso, omnibus diebus vitæ nostræ.
units.tr: The third passage is in the canticle of Zechariah, Luke 1. "Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, for he has visited and redeemed his people, and has raised up a horn of salvation in the house of David his servant, as he spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets, that we should be saved from our enemies and from the hand of all who hate us, so that, freed from the hands of our enemies, we might serve him without fear, in holiness and righteousness before him, all the days of our life."

units.la: Primum & hic videmus redemtionem Christi peculiariter tribui populo Dei, qui est populus fidelium seu verorum Israelitarum, teste Theophylacto, ex omni populo & natione.
units.tr: First, here too we see that the redemption of Christ is attributed especially to the people of God, who are the people of believers, or true Israelites, according to Theophylact, out of every people and nation.

units.la: Secundo, quod meminit cornu salutis in domo Dauid, respicit vaticinium Psal. 132. Ibi autem regis & triumphato-
units.tr: Second, the mention of the horn of salvation in the house of David points to the prophecy of Psalm 132. There, however, the grace of the king and triumphant

units.la: XVIII ris Christi gratia tantum promittitur sanctis & pauperibus spiritu: inimicis vero ipsius nihil nisi perditio & confusio annunciatur, attestante & beata Virgine in suo cantico: detraxit potentes de sede, & exaltauit humiles, esurientes implevit bonis, & divites dimisit inanes.
units.tr: XVIII Christ is promised only to the holy and to the poor in spirit, while nothing but destruction and confusion is announced to his enemies, as the blessed Virgin also attests in her canticle: He has put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted the humble; he has filled the hungry with good things, and sent the rich away empty.

units.la: Tertio, redemtionis per Zachariam celebratæ, non solum finis sed etiam pars est seruire Deo in sanctitate & iustitia vera. Ait enim Deum iure iurando promisisse Abrahamo, daturum se nobis ut sine metu ab inimicis nostris liberati ipsi seruiremus. At plane constat plurimos non seruire Deo, sed ventri & mundo potius. Non igitur omnibus sine discrimine, promissa vel praestita est redemtio isthæc spiritualis per Christum.
units.tr: Third, the redemption celebrated through Zechariah is not only its end but also a part of it, namely to serve God in holiness and true righteousness. For he says that God promised Abraham by an oath that he would give us that, being freed from our enemies, we might serve him without fear. But it is plain that very many do not serve God, but rather the belly and the world. Therefore this spiritual redemption through Christ has not been promised or granted to all without distinction.

units.la: Quarto, inuisit, inquit, nos oriens ex alto, ut appareat iis qui in tenebris & umbra mortis positi sunt, ad dirigendos pedes nostros in viam pacis. Non autem quicquid vspiam est mortalium a tenebris ad lucem convertitur, directis pedibus in viam pacis, hoc est iustitiæ.
units.tr: Fourth, he has visited us, a rising sun from on high, to shine on those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the way of peace. But not everyone anywhere among mortals is turned from darkness to light, with his feet directed into the way of peace, that is, of righteousness.

units.la: Quartus locus Luc. 2. Ne timete, inquit angelus ad pastores: Ecce enim annuncio vobis gaudium magnum, quod erit toti populo: nempe natum esse vobis hodie seruatorem, qui est Christus Dominus in urbe Dauid.
units.tr: The fourth passage is Luke 2. "Fear not," the angel said to the shepherds, "for behold, I bring you good news of great joy, which will be for all the people: that today there has been born to you in the city of David a Saviour, who is Christ the Lord."

units.la: Hæc prima fuit Euangelii annunciatio de nato mundi seruatore. Clamat autem res ipsa, ne quidem Iudæis omnibus, nedum aliis vniuersis per orbem terrarum, incarnationem Dominicam fuisse vel esse gaudio. Sicut de Herode refert Matthæus, quod ad percunctationem Magorum de nato rege Iudeorum, turbatus sit cum tota Hierosolyma. Ceterum gaudium hoc, ac proinde etiam eius materia, nempe Christus cum tota humiliatione & merito suo, eorum est, qui proprie populus Dei sunt. Non enim omnes Iudæi populus Dei, multo minus omnes homines: sed qui ex Iudæis & gentibus omnibus congregantur fideles, vt Theophylactus & Zacharias Chrysopolitanus hoc loco annotarunt.
units.tr: This was the first announcement of the Gospel about the birth of the Saviour of the world. The thing itself declares that the Lord's incarnation was a joy not even to all the Jews, much less to all people throughout the world. Matthew reports of Herod that, when the Magi asked about the newborn king of the Jews, he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him. But this joy, and therefore also its matter, namely Christ with all his humiliation and merit, belongs to those who are properly the people of God. For not all Jews are the people of God, much less all men; rather, it is the believers gathered from Jews and from all nations, as Theophylact and Zacharias of Chrysopolis noted in this place.

units.la: Quintus locus esto prophetia Simeonis ibidem: Viderunt oculi mei salutem tem tuam, quam parasti in oculis omnium populorum: Lumen ad revelationem gentium, et gloriam populi tui Israel.
units.tr: The fifth passage is the prophecy of Simeon in the same place: "Mine eyes have seen your salvation, which you have prepared before the face of all peoples, a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and the glory of your people Israel."

units.la: Quomodo illuminator, ita etiam seruator omnium est Christus. Falsum vero est omnes homines, sine cuiusquam exceptione, actu & re ipsa per Christum illuminari, reuelatis oculis mentis ipsorum & accepta veritatis cognitione. Ergo similiter falsum est, ex aequo omnes, nullo penitus excepto, vere & re ipsa per Christum salvatos. Sed hoc verum est, testimonium Iesu, unici omnium Seruatoris, in omne terram exijsse, & ad fines orbis terrarum populis omnibus praedicatum & etiamnum praedicari, colligendis atque seruandis filiis Dei dispersis.
units.tr: As he is the illuminator, so also Christ is the Saviour of all. But it is false that all men, without exception, are in fact and in reality enlightened through Christ, with the eyes of their minds opened and the knowledge of the truth received. Therefore it is likewise false that all equally, none excepted, are truly and really saved through Christ. But this is true: the testimony of Jesus, the one Saviour of all, has gone out into all the earth and has been, and is still being, preached to all peoples to the ends of the world, for the gathering and saving of the scattered children of God.

units.la: His & illud suffragatur, quod porro dixit Simeon de puero: Ecce positus est puer iste in casum & resurrectionem multorum in Israel. Id Simeon non dixisset, si omnino omnes beneficio ipsius surgerent ex morte in vitam, a peccato ad iustitiam.
units.tr: This is also supported by what Simeon further said about the child: "Behold, this child is set for the fall and the rising again of many in Israel." Simeon would not have said this if all, by his benefit, rose altogether from death to life, from sin to righteousness.

units.la: Sextus locus est terribile & expressum dictum Iohannis Baptistae, quo inter
units.tr: The sixth passage is the terrible and explicit saying of John the Baptist, by which

units.la: ter
units.tr: among

units.la: Ioh. ii. ter natos mulierum maior est nemo, Qui credit filium, habet vitam aeternam: Qui vero non credit filio, non videbit vitā, sed ira Dei manet super ipsum.
units.tr: (among those born of women there is none greater), John 3: "He who believes in the Son has eternal life; but he who does not believe the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him."

units.la: Emphasis est in verbo manendi: Non dicit omnibus sine exceptione, credentibus & non credentibus, omne iudicium iramque Dei sublatam re ipsa, & incredulitate iram Dei redire dunta-xat super non credentes: sed ira Dei manet, inquit, super incredulum. vrget Emphasin iltam Augustinus tract. 14. in Ioh. Non dixit ira Dei venit super eum: sed ira Dei manet super ipso. Et quae est ista ira Dei? Quam omnes qui nascuntur mortales secum habent, quam excepit primus Adam, de qua dicit Apostolus, sumus natura filii irae ut & ceteri. Quomodo & autor de vocatione gentium lib.1.c.5. dictum hoc allegat, sive Iudaeus, inquit, sive Gentilis, priusquam iustificetur per fidem, conclusus est sub peccatum, & si in infidelitate perstiterit, ira Dei manet super eum: illa scilicet in Adae praevaricatione contracta, de qua loquitur Apostolus: Eramus & nos filii irae, ut & ceteri. Falsum igitur est, ira Dei vniuersa-liter liter sublata, omnes in sinum gratiæ re-ceptos siue credant, siue non: sed gratia isthæc eorum demum est, qui credunt in Christum, qui attulit gratiam Dei, abstulit iram Dei.
units.tr: The emphasis lies on the word remains. He does not say, to all without exception, believers and unbelievers alike, that all judgement and wrath of God is in fact removed, and that by unbelief the wrath of God returns only upon unbelievers; rather, the wrath of God remains, he says, upon the unbeliever. Augustine presses this emphasis in tract. 14 on John: "He did not say, 'the wrath of God comes upon him,' but 'the wrath of God remains upon him.' And what is this wrath of God? All who are born mortal have it with them; the first Adam incurred it, and of it the Apostle says: 'we too were by nature children of wrath, as the rest.'" In the same way the author, in On the Calling of the Gentiles, book 1, ch. 5, cites this saying: "Whether Jew or Gentile, before he is justified by faith, is shut up under sin, and if he persists in unbelief, the wrath of God remains upon him: that wrath, namely, which was contracted in Adam's transgression, of which the Apostle speaks: 'we too were children of wrath, as the rest.'" It is therefore false that the wrath of God is universally taken away, and that all are received into the bosom of grace whether they believe or not. This grace belongs only to those who believe in Christ, who brought the grace of God and took away the wrath of God.

units.la: Septimus locus est Ioh.10. vbi ait pastor ille bonus: animam meam pono pro ouibus: oues meæ vocem meam audiunt, & ego eas agnosco & sequuntur me, & ego vitam æternam do eis, nec peribunt in æternum: neque rapiet eas quisquam e manu mea. Ex his apparet, vtcunque pro omnibus suo modo Christus mortuus sit: specialiter tamen mortuum pro seruandis: Quia pro ouibus mortuus est.
units.tr: The seventh passage is John 10, where the good shepherd says: "I lay down my life for the sheep. My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me; and I give them eternal life, and they shall never perish, nor shall anyone snatch them out of my hand." From these words it appears that, however Christ died for all in his own way, yet he died specially for the saving of those who are his: because he died for the sheep.

units.la: Exceptio Huberiana, quod omnes homines facti sint oues, hæreditas & populus Dei, nullo labore ex textu refellitur. Ouium enim Christi propria sunt, vocem eius audire & nosse, ipsum sequi, alienum refugere, vitam æternam consequi, non perire in æternum, nec posse rapi e manu Christi pastoris sui. His notis cum magna hominum pars destituatur, salsissimum est, omnes esse oues Christi & gregem pascuorum Dei.
units.tr: The Huberian objection, that all men have been made sheep, heirs and people of God, is refuted from the text without any difficulty. For the proper marks of Christ's sheep are: to hear and know his voice, to follow him, to flee from a stranger, to obtain eternal life, not to perish for ever, and not to be able to be snatched out of the hand of Christ their shepherd. Since a great part of mankind lacks these marks, it is most absurd to say that all are sheep of Christ and the flock of God's pasture.

units.la: Ineptissima vero est probatio; pro ouibus agnoscuntur etiam illi, qui dispersi, lacerati & devorati sunt à pastoribus improbis & bestiis agri : seducti denique & perditi, Ier. 23. Ezech. 34. Ergo quicunque homines oves sunt Christi. Nam uterque, Ieremias & Ezechiel, tantum loquuntur de Iudaico populo, qui tum temporis à gentibus distinctus erat, tanquam peculium, grex & hæreditas Domini, ut loca ista contrarium plane euincant.
units.tr: The proof, however, is most inept: those too are recognised as sheep who are scattered, torn and devoured by wicked shepherds and the beasts of the field, and finally led astray and lost (Jer. 23, Ezek. 34). Therefore, whoever men are, they are sheep of Christ. For both Jeremiah and Ezekiel speak only of the Jewish people, who at that time were distinguished from the Gentiles as the peculiar possession, flock and inheritance of the Lord; so these places clearly prove the opposite.

units.la: Ac notandum, Scripturam loquii dupliciter de ouibus Dei, secundum vocationem & secundum prædestinationem. Secundum vocationem oves dicuntur, quicunque externè ad censum populi Dei, seu ad Ecclesiam pertinent: sed secundum præscientiam Dei & prædestinationem, quàm multæ oves foris, quàm multi lupi intus, & quàm multæ oves intus, & quàm multi lupi foris? inquit Augustinus. Multi enim modò luxuriantes, casti futuri sunt, multi blasphemates Christum, in ipsum credituri sunt. Et contra, multi nunc ipsum laulaudantes, blasphematuri eum sunt, & fornicaturi qui casti sunt. Non enim de ouibus iunt, loquendo de praedestinatis. Haec ille tract. 46. in Euangelium Ioh. Et confirmantur haec omnia Ierem. 23. vbi taxatis pastoribus, qui perdiderant & dispersérat oues Domini, statim promissio additur de residuo ouium seruando. Residuum autem hoc sunt electi, vt Paulus interpretatur Rom. 9. 27. ca. 11. ver. 2. 5. Similiter apud Ezech. 34. salutem firmā & stabilem ouibus suis policetur Dominus, pastore Christo, vero illo Dauide. Quia tamen multi extrinsecus oues, intrinsecus haedi & lupi sunt; dicit se iudicaturum inter pecudem & pecudem, inter arietes & hircos: vt perditas quidem oues requirat, abiectas reducat, confractas obliget, pingues vero & petulcas disperdat.
units.tr: It must be noted that Scripture speaks of the sheep of God in two ways: according to calling and according to predestination. According to calling, those are called sheep who belong outwardly to the roll of God's people, or to the Church; but according to God's foreknowledge and predestination, "how many sheep are outside, how many wolves inside; and how many sheep inside, how many wolves outside?" says Augustine. For many who now live in luxury will be chaste, and many who now blaspheme Christ will believe in him; and conversely, many who now praise him will blaspheme him, and those who are chaste will fornicate. For these are not sheep, if we speak of the predestined. Thus he in tract. 46 on the Gospel of John. All these things are confirmed by Jer. 23, where, after the shepherds who had lost and scattered the Lord's sheep are censured, a promise is at once added about preserving the remnant of the sheep. This remnant, however, are the elect, as Paul interprets it, Rom. 9:27; ch. 11, vv. 2, 5. Similarly in Ezek. 34 the Lord promises firm and stable salvation to his sheep through the shepherd Christ, the true David. Yet since many are sheep outwardly but goats and wolves inwardly, he says that he will judge between sheep and sheep, between rams and he-goats: that he will indeed seek out the lost sheep, bring back those cast out, bind up the broken, but destroy the fat and the wanton.

units.la: Octauus locus est Ioh. 11. vbi recitata prophetia Caiphae Pontificis maximi: Expedit nobis vt vnus moriatur pro populo & non tota gens pereat, subiungit Euangelista, id eum ex se ipso non dixisse, sed cum esset Pontifex Max. anni illius, proprophetasse, fore vt Iesus moreretur pro gente: nec tantum pro ea gente, sed vt etiam filios Dei dispersos in vnum congeret.
units.tr: The eighth place is John 11, where, after the prophecy of Caiaphas the high priest is quoted, It is expedient for us that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation should not perish, the Evangelist adds that he did not say this on his own account, but, since he was high priest that year, he prophesied that Jesus would die for the nation: and not only for that nation, but so that he might also gather together into one the children of God who are scattered.
