Et mox, Donatistas Africæ includentes Ecclesiam refellēs, ait: Quid mihi dicis ô hæretice? Non est pretium orbis terrarum? Africa sola redempta est? Non audes dicere, Totus orbis redemptus est, sed periit. Quem inuasorem passus est Christus, ut perderet rem suam? Ecce Christus passus est: sanguis eius fusus est: Ecce redemptor noster: Ecce pretium nostrum. Quid emit? Conuertentur ad Dominum vniuersi fines terræ, & adorabunt in conspectu eius vniuersæ Gentes. Ecce Ecclesiam quam ostendo: Ecce quid emerit „Christus: Ecce quid redemerit, Ecce pro quo „sanguinem dederit.
units.tr: In his commentary on Psalm 21 he writes the same, that Christ suffered on account of the Church, and that the Church is the whole great world for which he poured out his blood. And soon after, refuting the Donatists who confine the Church to Africa, he says: What do you say to me, O heretic? Is the world not worth the price? Has Africa alone been redeemed? Do you not dare to say, "The whole world has been redeemed, but has perished"? What invader did Christ suffer, that he should lose his own property? Behold, Christ suffered; his blood was shed. Behold our redeemer; behold our price. What did he buy? "All the ends of the earth shall turn to the Lord, and all the nations shall worship before him." Behold the Church which I point to; behold what he bought; behold what he redeemed; behold for whom he gave his blood.

units.la: Sic Enchiridio ad Laureutium cap. 6. ait, Ecclesiam quæ in hominibus est, sanguine Mediatoris nullum habentis peccatum, ab omni redemtâ peccato: eiusque vocem esse, Si Deus pro nobis, quis contra nos? Qui etiam filio proprio non pepercit, sed pro nobis omnibus tradidit eum. Et cap. sequenti: Ait Apostolus in Christo instaurari quæ in cœlis & terris sunt. In ipso quippe instaurantur quæ in cœlis sunt, cum id quod inde in angelisladitur: Instauran-
units.tr: So too in the Enchiridion to Laurentius, chapter 6, he says that the Church which is among men has been redeemed from all sin by the blood of the Mediator, who had no sin; and that its voice is: "If God is for us, who can be against us? He who did not spare his own Son, but gave him up for us all." And in the following chapter: the Apostle says that all things in heaven and on earth are restored in Christ. For in him are restored the things that are in heaven, when that which is there is fallen from the angels and is replaced by men; and the things that are on earth are restored when men themselves, who are predestined to eternal life, are renewed from the old corruption. The same writer, in chapter 30, testifies that God promised liberation and an eternal kingdom to that part of the human race, namely the elect.

units.la: pfum est, ex hominibus redditur: Instauran- tur autem quæ in terris sunt, cum ipsi homines, qui prædestinati sunt ad vitam æternam à corruptionis vetustate renouantur. Idem cap. 30. testatur, quod parti generis humani, nempe electis, Deus promiserit liberationem regnumque æternum.
units.tr: Again, in On the Trinity, book 13, chapter 12 and the following chapters, after saying that men are rescued from the Devil by the forgiveness of sins through God's gracious reconciliation, he at once explains at length that not all men, but only all believers and the predestined, are freed from the dominion of the Devil. All who are born of Adam according to the flesh are indeed held under the power of the Devil on account of that one man; yet they are not released on account of the one Christ, except all those who are regenerated by spiritual grace.

units.la: Rursum, de trinitate lib. 13. cap. 12. & sequentibus, cùm dixisset, remissione peccatorum per reconciliationem Dei benignam, erui homines à Diabolo, multis statim exponit, à Diaboli dominatu non homines omnes, sed credentes & prædestinatos omnes liberari: Omnes quiquidem carnaliter ex Adamo natos sub potestate Diaboli teneri propter vnum illum: nō dimitti tamen propter vnum Christum, nisi omnes illos qui per spiritualem gratiam regenerentur.
units.tr: In the same book, chapter 18, he says that the conqueror of the first Adam, who held the human race, was conquered by the second Adam, and that the Christian race is lost, while the human race is freed from the human crime, through him who was not in crime, though he was of the race. In his fifty-third tractate on John he says: The Devil therefore held the human race in bondage and kept those liable to punishment under the bond of their sins. But through faith in Christ, which was confirmed by his death and resurrection, through his blood, which was poured out for the remission of sins, thousands of believers are freed from the Devil and joined to the body of Christ.

units.la: Eodem libro cap.18.ait, Victorem primi Adami, tenetem genus humanum, victum à secundo Adam, & amittere genus Christianum, liberatum ex humano genere ab humano crimine, per eum qui non erat in crimine, quamuis esset ex genere. Idem tract.53.super Iohan. inquit: Poliidebat ergo Diabolus genus humanum, & reos iuppliciorum tenebat chirographo peccatorum: Per Christi autem fidem, quæ morte eius & resurrectione firmata est, per eius sanguinē, qui in remissionem fusus est peccatorum, millia credentium liberantur à Diabolo Christique corpori copulantur.
units.tr: In all these passages the argument runs thus. Redemption is liberation from the dominion of the Devil, and indeed of such a kind that the Devil cannot drag anyone of those whom Christ redeemed with his blood, entangled in the nets of sin, to the ruin of eternal death. But liberation from the dominion of the Devil does not belong to all. Therefore neither does redemption. But, according to Augustine and the truth of the matter, just as that liberation, so this redemption belongs to believers and the predestined alone.

units.la: In his omnibus tale est argumentum. Redemtio est libertas à dominatu Diaboli, & quidem talis, quâ fit ne Diabolus quenquā secum eorum, quos Christus sanguine suo redemit, peccatorum retibus inuolutum ad sempiternas mortis tis trahere possit exitium. Non autem omnium est libertas à dominatu Diaboli. Ergo nec redemtio: sed quemadmodum illa, ita hæc credentium & prædestinatorum propria est, secundum Augustinum & rei veritatem.
units.tr: In all these matters the argument runs thus. Redemption is liberty from the dominion of the Devil, and indeed such liberty that the Devil cannot drag anyone of those whom Christ has redeemed with his blood, entangled in the nets of sins, down to the eternal destruction of death. But liberty from the dominion of the Devil is not the possession of all. Therefore neither is redemption. Rather, just as the former belongs to believers and the predestined alone, so too does the latter, according to Augustine and the truth of the matter.

units.la: Huc eodem spectat quod iam memorato tractatu, quemadmodum etiam tractatibus iio. & iii. idem scriptor Mundum, quem Christus venerit salvare & reconciliare Deo, constanter exponit, de bonis & ad vitam æternam prædestinatis, toto terrarum orbe diffusis. Hunc mundu ex inimico amicum effectum. Mudum autem danationi prædestinatum, manere inimicum: nec de eo intelligendu, quod Deus erat in Christo mundum sibi reconcilians. Sic Tract. 48. in illud, Vos non creditis, non enim estis ex ovibus meis. Hoc dixit, inquit, quia videbat eos ad sempiternum interitum prædestinatos, non ad vitam æternam sui sanguinis precio comparatos. Et paulo post, securus est de numero ovium, quia pro eis nouit quid dederit. Et alibi, de corrept. nimirum & gratia, cap. 11. Quos MeMediatoris sanguine Deus redemit, facit deinceps in aeternum bonos. Sed satis testimoniorum ex Augustino. Singula enim autoris huius quis recensent?
units.tr: To this same point belongs what the same writer, in the tractate already mentioned, and also in tractates 2 and 3, constantly explains: the world which Christ came to save and reconcile to God is to be understood of the good and those predestined to eternal life, scattered throughout the whole earth. This world has been made a friend from an enemy. But the world predestined to damnation remains an enemy, and it is not to be understood of that world which God was in Christ reconciling to himself. So in Tractate 48, on the words "You do not believe, for you are not of my sheep." He said this, he says, because he saw them predestined to eternal perdition, not purchased with the price of his blood for eternal life. And a little after, he is certain of the number of the sheep, because he knows what he has given for them. And elsewhere, in On Rebuke and Grace, chapter 11: Those whom God has redeemed by the blood of the Mediator he makes good forever after. But there are enough testimonies from Augustine. For who could enumerate each single one of this author's passages?

units.la: Porro commentarij in Marcum Hieronymo adscripti, expresse habent, sanguinem noui testamenti pro multis dici ef fusum, quoniam non omnes emundet: esse vel in ipsa Ecclesia quos nullum emu- detsacrificium. Quemadmodum & Re- migius (citante Thoma Cat: aurea) su- per hoc ipso loco notandum monet, quod non ait, pro paucis, aut pro omnibus, sed pro multis sanguis meus effundetur, quia non veneritunam tantum gentem redimere, sed multos de omnibus gentibus. Hilarius in Matth. canone 7. Salus gentium, inquit, omnis ex fide est, & in praeceptis Domini vita est vniuersorum. Non dicit reprobos atque incredulos aeque per Christum saluatos ac quoslibet alios: sicut nouis visum est Dogmatistis.
units.tr: Moreover, the commentaries on Mark ascribed to Jerome expressly state that the blood of the New Testament is said to be poured out "for many," because it does not cleanse everyone; there are some, even within the Church itself, whom the sacrifice does not cleanse. Likewise Remigius (cited by Thomas in the Catena aurea) notes on this very passage that Christ did not say "for a few" or "for all," but "for many": my blood will be poured out, because he came to redeem not only one nation but "many from all nations." Hilary, on Matthew, canon 7: "The salvation of the nations," he says, "is wholly from faith, and life is in the Lord's precepts for all." He does not say that the reprobate and unbelieving are saved through Christ in the same way as any others, as the new Dogmatists have thought fit.

units.la: Chrysostomus Hom. 39. in 1. ad Cor. explicans dictum Apostoli de vivificatione omnium „ omnium per Christum, negat id accipien-„ dum de iustitia omnium, quasi quicun-„ que in Adamo peccatores facti sunt, in Christo iusti constituantur: quod tamē volunt aduersarij. Idem hom. 17. ad Hebr. 4. os confirmat distinctionem, Christum mortuum pro omnibus quod ad sufficientiam, non pro omnibus, quod ad effectum. Verba eius haec sunt. Quare oblatus dicitur ad multorum, & non omnium peccata auferenda? Quia non omnes credunt. Pro omnibus quidem mortuus est, quantum in ipso est, hoc est, mors illa eius momenti est, cuius est omnium perditio, & sat valet ne quisquam pereat.
units.tr: Chrysostom, Homily 39 on 1 Corinthians, explaining the Apostle's words about the making alive of all "all in Christ," denies that this is to be taken of the justification of all, as if everyone who became a sinner in Adam were made righteous in Christ; yet our opponents want it so. The same writer, Homily 17 on Hebrews 4, confirms the distinction: Christ died for all as regards sufficiency, but not for all as regards effect. His words are these: "Why is he said to have been offered to take away the sins of many, and not of all? Because not all believe. He indeed died for all, so far as lies in him: that is, that death of his has such weight that it is the destruction of all, and it is quite enough that no one perish."

units.la: Abbreuiator eius Theophylactus eandem distinctionem vsurpat in 2. & 9. ad Heb. nec non in dictum Ioh. 6. panis quem ego dabo, caro mea est, quam ego dabo pro mundi vita: vbi scribit, quamuis non omnes acceperint sanctificationem & vitam in spiritu: posse tamen intelligi Christum pro omnium satisfactione mortuum, quantum ad virtutem mortis eius attinet.
units.tr: Theophylact, his abridger, uses the same distinction on Hebrews 2 and 9, and on John 6, "the bread which I will give is my flesh, which I will give for the life of the world," where he writes that although not all have received sanctification and life in the Spirit, it may nevertheless be understood that Christ died as the satisfaction for all, so far as the power of his death is concerned.

units.la: Eiusdem sententiae est Basilius, referente rente Theophylacto in 9. ad Heb. Sic enim ille scribit, Exhortatione ad Baptismum: omnes quotquot credimus, gratia Dei quæ est per unigenitum eius filium, à peccatis redemti sumus: qui dixit, Hic est sanguis meus, sanguis noui Testamenti, qui pro multis effunditur in remissionem peccatorum. Hæc explicatio & sequenti sermone de Baptismo bis repetitur: Pro multis, id est, credentibus, fusum esse Christi sanguinem. Interim spectata sufficientia meriti, verum est, quod alibi dicit in psal. 48. Pro omnibus simul hominibus unicum inuentum dignum pretium, sanguinem Domini nostri Iesu Christi, quem pro nobis omnibus effudit.
units.tr: Basil holds the same view, as Theophylact reports on Hebrews 9. For he writes thus in the Exhortation to Baptism: "All of us who believe have been redeemed from sins by the grace of God, which is through his only-begotten Son, who said, 'This is my blood, the blood of the New Testament, which is poured out for many for the remission of sins.'" This explanation is repeated twice in the following sermon on Baptism: "'For many,' that is, for believers, Christ's blood was shed." Meanwhile, considering the sufficiency of the merit, what he says elsewhere on Psalm 48 is true: "For all men together, one unique and sufficient price has been found, the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, which he poured out for us all."

units.la: Cyrillus in Ioh. lib.11.cap. 19. repugnantiæ speciem conciliàs inter verba Christi, non oro pro mundo: & verba Iohannis, propitiatio est totius mundi, ad hunc modum sententiæ nostræ suffragatur: Beatus Iohannes, inquit, quia erat Iudæus, ne pro Iudæis tantum paracletus esse Dominus apud patrem videretur, necessario adiecit eum propitiationem esse totius mundi, id est, inquit, pro omnibus qui per fidem vocati ad iustitiam & sanctificationem peruenerunt. Do-
units.tr: Cyril, on John, book 11, chapter 19, resolves the appearance of contradiction between the words of Christ, "I do not pray for the world," and John's words, "he is the propitiation of the whole world," and supports our view in this way: "Blessed John," he says, "since he was a Jew, lest the Lord should seem to be an advocate before the Father only for the Jews, was necessarily led to add that he is the propitiation of the whole world, that is," he says, "for all who through faith have been called and have attained to righteousness and sanctification. Do-

units.la: Dd minus autem Iesus suos non a suis separâri, pro eis, inquit, tantummodo, qui verba mea seruant, & iugum meum accipiunt rogo. Nam quorum Mediator atque Pontifex est, ipsis tantummodo mediationis bonum non iniuria tribuit. In eandé sententiam ibidem enarrat dictum Pauli: Deus erat in Christo mundum sibi reconcilians: hoc est, inquit, Christus vt Mediator recipiens omnes qui per fidem ad Deum concurrunt, & per se ipsum patri offerens, Deo mundum reconciliat.
units.tr: "But the Lord Jesus would not have his own separated from their own: 'I pray,' he says, 'only for those who keep my words and take up my yoke.' For it is not unjust to grant the benefit of mediation only to those whose Mediator and High Priest he is." In the same place he explains Paul's saying in the same sense: "God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself." That is, he says, Christ, as <bl>Mediator</bl>, receiving all who draw near to God through faith and offering them to the Father through himself, reconciles the world to God.

units.la: Sed ad Latinos reuertamur, inter quos Prosper Aquitanicus ad capitula Gallorum respondens cap. 9. diserte approbat phrasin hanc, Christum mortuum tantum pro saluandis; quam aduersarij nostri vt blasphemam & Saracenicam exagitant. Verba eius sunt: Cum itaque rectè dicatur Saluator pro totius mundi redemtione crucifixus, propter veram naturæ humanæ susceptionem, & propter communē in primo homine perditionē: potest tamen dici pro his tantum crucifixus, quibus mors ipsius profuit: Dicit enim Euangelista Ioh. 11. Quia Iesus moriturus erat pro gente, nec tantum pro
units.tr: But let us return to the Latin writers. Among them Prosper of Aquitaine, replying to the Chapters of the Gauls, chapter 9, clearly approves this phrase, "Christ died only for those to be saved," which our opponents rail against as blasphemous and Saracenic. His words are: "Since it is rightly said that the Saviour was crucified for the redemption of the whole world, on account of his true assumption of human nature and the common perdition in the first man, yet he can be said to have been crucified only for those to whom his death profited. For the Evangelist says, John 11: 'Because Jesus was about to die for the nation, and not only for the nation,

units.la: Nota, Id Aug. su pra intel. ligebat per commu nem causam. pro Gente, sed etiam vt filios Dei congregaret in vnum.
units.tr: Note: Augustine, above, understood this through a common cause. ...but also that he might gather the children of God into one.

units.la: Idem, aut quisquis tandem autor est operis De vocatione Gentium li.1.cap. 3. negat dictum Apostoli ad Ephes.1.de reconciliatione omnium in Christo, sic accipiendum, quasi nemo exsors reconciliationis huius intelligi debeat. Et paulo post regulam tradit, quæ Cynosuræ instar in tota hac cotrouersia spectanda est: nimirum, in electis & præscitis, atque ab omnium generalitate discretis, speciale quandam censeri vniuersalitatem, & plenitudinem populi Dei, vt de toto mundo totus mundus liberatus, & de omnibus hominibus omnes homines videantur assumti. Frequentissime enim in sacris pro parte terræ omnem terram, pro parte mundi, totum mundum, & pro parte hominum omnes homines nominari. Ad quam normam postea lib. 2.cap.1. exigit verba Iohannis: Ipse est propitiatio pro peccatis totius mundi, eaque exponit de plenitudine fidelium, & non de omnium hominum generalitate, vt faciant aduersarij.
units.tr: The same writer, or whoever is the author of the work On the Calling of the Gentiles, book 1, chapter 3, denies that the Apostle's words to the Ephesians, chapter 1, about the reconciliation of all things in Christ, are to be taken as if no one were to be understood as excluded from this reconciliation. A little later he gives a rule, which must be kept in view throughout this controversy as a guiding star: namely, that among the elect and the foreknown, and distinguished from the generality of all, a certain special universality and fullness of the people of God is to be reckoned, so that from the whole world the whole world is seen to be freed, and from all men all men are seen to be taken up. For in Scripture the whole earth is very often named for part of the earth, the whole world for part of the world, and all men for some men. Applying this rule later, book 2, chapter 1, he takes John's words, "He is the propitiation for the sins of the whole world," and explains them of the fullness of believers, not of the generality of all men, as our opponents do.

units.la: Porrò Primasius re tota complectitur
units.tr: Moreover, Primasius takes up the whole matter

units.la: Com.ad Heb.2.in illud,gustauit mortem pro omnibus. Verba eius sunt: quòd dicit, pro omnibus illum gustasse mortem, quidam doctores ita absoluté intelligunt, vt dicatur, pro omnibus, pro quibus gustauit: id est, pro electis, ad vitam æternam prædestinatis. En restrictionem ad vniuersitatem electo-rum.Sed pergit: Quidam vero ita generaliter accipiunt, vt dicatur pro omnibus mor-tuus, licet omnes non saluentur. Nam etsi non omnes credunt, ille tamen quod suum erat, fecit. Et adducit simile Prosperi, quo & August. vsus fuit ante Prosperum, de poculo immortalitatis, quod quidem in se habet vt omnibus prosit,licet non prosit re ipsa, nisi his qui ex eo bibunt. Ita & Christus, inquit, quantum in ipso fuit,pro omnibus mortuus est;quanquam non prosit passio eius, nisi solummodò iis qui in eum credunt.
units.tr: in his Commentary on Hebrews 2, on the words "he tasted death for all." His words are: "When he says that he tasted death for all, some teachers understand it so absolutely that 'for all' means 'for those for whom he tasted,' that is, for the elect, predestined to eternal life. Here is a restriction to the universality of the elect. But others take it so generally that he is said to have died for all, although not all are saved. For even if not all believe, he nevertheless did what was his own to do." He also adduces a likeness, that of the cup of immortality, which Prosper later used and which Augustine used before him: the cup has in itself that it benefits all, although in fact it benefits only those who drink from it. "So also Christ," he says, "as far as lay in him, died for all, although his passion profits only those who believe in him."

units.la: Memorabile etiam hîc est, quod de vocat. gentiû lib.1. cap. vltimo habetur: Eadem natura in omnibus hominibus ante recôciliationem mala,in omnibus misera,non in omnibus iustificatur,&à percuntibus quadam sui parte discernitur, ab eo, qui venit quaquaerere & saluare quod perierat.
units.tr: Also worth noting here is what is found in On the Calling of the Gentiles, book 1, last chapter: "The same nature, evil before reconciliation, miserable in all men, is not justified in all, and is distinguished from those who perish by a certain part of itself, by him who came to seek and save what had perished."

units.la: Leo Papa Sermone septimi mensis scribit: Effusio sanguinis iusti pro iniustis, tam potens fuit ad priuilegium, tam dives ad pretium, ut si vniuersitas captiuorum in redemtorem crederet, nullum tyrannica vincula detinerent.
units.tr: Pope Leo, in his sermon for the seventh month, writes: "The shedding of the blood of the righteous for the unrighteous was so powerful for a privilege, so rich for a price, that if the whole multitude of captives believed in the Redeemer, tyrannical chains would hold none of them."

units.la: Gregorius Magnus Hom. 2. super Ezechielem: Pro Electorum vita vsque ad mortem tradidit se autor vita.
units.tr: Gregory the Great, Homily 2 on Ezekiel: "For the life of the elect the author of life gave himself up even to death."

units.la: Beda in illud euangelicum, Venit filius hominis ut daret animam suam in redemtionem pro multis. Non dixit, inquit, pro omnibus, sed pro multis, id est qui credere voluerint. Et sic Origenes, nec non Hieron. Comm. in Matth. id ipsum exponunt.
units.tr: Bede, on the Gospel words, "The Son of Man came to give his life as a ransom for many." He did not say, he notes, "for all," but "for many," that is, for those who were willing to believe. Origen likewise, and Jerome in his Commentary on Matthew, expound the same thing.

units.la: Porro Bernhardus Serm. 10. de verf. 9. Psal. Qui habitat, &c. Christus, inquit, secundum tempus quidem pro impiis mortuus est, secundum praedestinationem autem pro fratribus & amicis. Ex horum autem numero nequaquam sunt damnandi: quibus dicetur, nunquam noui vos.
units.tr: Bernard, Sermon 10, on verse 9 of the psalm "Qui habitat": "Christ," he says, "indeed died for the impious according to time, but according to predestination for brothers and friends. Those who belong to this number are by no means to be condemned, to whom it will be said, 'I never knew you.'"

units.la: His addantur, quae supra ad locum Apocal. 1. & 5. retulimus ex Ruperto TuiTuitienfi, qui Bernhardi συνχρον fuit: cuius & hoc dictum est, libro 12. Commentar. in Ioh. Va mundo gaudeti, orante pro suis, id est, moriente & in ara crucis sacrificium se offerente Christo, unigenito filio Dei. Quia pro eis quos dedisti mihi rogo, non pro mundo. Mundus hic accipiuntur dilectores mundi, tam diuersi ab ys pro quibus Christus rogat crucifixus, quam diuersi apud Deum erant Aegyptij filiis Israel, sacro sanguine agni postes suos signantibus. Va igitur tali mundo, quia quod rogat Christus verus agnus Dei, nihil illi proficit, solis illis quos pater filio dedit, per crucem & sanguinem eius euadentius.
units.tr: Add to these what we cited above on Apoc. 1 and 5 from Rupert of Deutz, who was Bernard's [συγχρονος] contemporary. He also said this, in book 12 of his Commentary on John: "Woe to the world rejoicing, while praying for his own," that is, while Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, dying and offering the sacrifice of himself on the altar of the cross. "For I pray for those whom you have given me, not for the world." By "world" are understood the lovers of the world, as different from those for whom the crucified Christ prays as the Egyptians were different in God's sight from the sons of Israel, who marked their doorposts with the sacred blood of the lamb. Woe, then, to such a world, because what Christ, the true Lamb of God, prays for profits it nothing; only those whom the Father gave to the Son escape through his cross and blood.

units.la: Haec ille. Ex quibus omnibus iam luce clarius est, sententiam, quam nos tuemur, minime nouam atque inauditam esse: sed omnibus seculis in populo Dei receptam, optimorumque scriptorum testimoniis, iudiciis atque interpretationibus abunde comprobatam. Quare modestius agere dicant aduersarij, nec tanquam inauditum in populo Dei & Saracenicum illico damnent, quod a sua forte opinione dissentire vident, aut si quo coeperunt pede perrexerint, cognoscet omnes, qua scientia vel conscientia, disputatores eiusmodi, nimium profecto confidentes & ceforij, in patrum lectione versati sint.
units.tr: Thus he. From all of these it is now clearer than light that the opinion we defend is by no means new or unheard of, but has been received in the people of God in every age and is amply confirmed by the testimonies, judgments and interpretations of the best writers. Let our opponents therefore act with more restraint, and not condemn at once as unheard of and outlandish among the people of God what they see differs from their own opinion. Or, if they have set out on some path, let them go on, and everyone will see with what knowledge or conscience such disputants, surely far too confident and headstrong, have been versed in the reading of the Fathers.

units.la: Non me latet quandoque apud patres legi pro omnium redemtione Christum venisse: descendisse pro omnibus, ut cuctis peccatu remitteret & libertate daret vniuersis, & similia. Talia vero, quemadmodum ex propriis ipsorum interpretationibus iam allegatis videre est, intelligut, non quantum ad effectum incarnationis & passionis Dominicae in omnibus. Sed primu, quantum ad sufficientiam, magnitudinem, ac dignitatem pretij atque meriti Christi. Secundo, quantum ad communem causam generis humani attinet. Tertio, etiam efficaciam meritorum Christi respicientes, phrasibus istis vti solent more Scripturae, propter vniuersalitatem fidelium & plenitudinem populi Dei, vt lib.2. cap.12. dixi fusius. Ite quia Omnes homines omnes genus hominum vsitate intelligi volunt. Hinc Ambrosius Serm.55. Dominus
units.tr: I am not unaware that in the Fathers one sometimes reads that Christ came for the redemption of all, came down for all, that he might remit sin to all and give freedom to all, and similar things. But such statements, as can be seen from the very interpretations of theirs already cited, are to be understood not with regard to the effect of the incarnation and the Lord's passion on all, but: first, with regard to the sufficiency, greatness and dignity of the price and merit of Christ; second, with regard to the common cause of the human race; third, looking also to the efficacy of Christ's merits, they are accustomed to use these phrases, in the manner of Scripture, on account of the universality of believers and the fullness of the people of God, as I explained more fully in book 2, chapter 12. Likewise all men, every kind of men are commonly understood in this way. Hence Ambrose, Serm. 55: "The Lord

units.la: Dd iij pepependit in cruce, vt omne genus hominum de mundi naufragio liberaret. Et ferm.53. Cum dixisset, Christum resurgendo resurrectionem praestitisse vniuersis, mox se ipsum declarat de omnibus Christianis, & qui membra Christi sunt. Sic de fuga seculi cap.3. Christus inquit omnibus se infundit spiritu & plenitudine diuinitatis suae. Siquidem de eius plenitudine omnes accepimus, vt sciamus supereminentem caritatem eius. Qui omnes? nonne Christiani omnes? Et alibi, de iis qui initiantur cap.4. In piscina Hierosolymis vnus curabatur quotannis, nunc omnes sanantur, aut certe vnus solus populus Christianus. Talia infinita sunt in scriptis patrum & communi hominum sermone.
units.tr: Dd iij hung on the cross, so that he might free every kind of men from the shipwreck of the world. And in Serm. 53: when he had said that Christ by rising had bestowed resurrection on all, he immediately declares who these are: all Christians, and those who are members of Christ. So in On Flight from the World, chap. 3: Christ, he says, pours himself into all with his Spirit and the fullness of his divinity. For we have all received of his fullness, that we may know his surpassing love. "Who are all? Are not all Christians?" And elsewhere, on those who are being initiated, chap. 4: at the pool of Jerusalem one man was healed each year; now all are healed, or rather only the one Christian people. There are countless such things in the writings of the Fathers and in common human speech.

units.la: CAPVT IX.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX.

units.la: Testimonia scholasticorum aliorumque recentiorum Theologorum.
units.tr: Testimonies of the Schoolmen and other more recent theologians.

units.la: SED vt narrationem testium perteramus, ad Scholasticos quos vocant, progrediamur, qui acceptam à maioribus dodoctrinam hac in parte & ipsi propagarunt.
units.tr: But, to run through the testimony of witnesses, let us move on to the so-called Scholastics, who also themselves handed on the doctrine they had received from their elders on this point.

units.la: Petrus Lombardus, Magister dictus sententiarum, lib. 3. distinctione 18. de sua & aliorum sententia refert, Christum membris suis meruisse redemtionem à peccato & Diabolo, reseratione nemq; regni cœlestis, vt amota ignea romphæa liberè pateret introitus. Eadem distinctione circa finem: meruit nobis per mortis ac passionis tolerantiam aditum Paradisi, & redemtionem à peccato & Diabolo. Ipse enim moriendo factus est hostia nostrae liberationis.
units.tr: Peter Lombard, called the Master of the Sentences, in book 3, distinction 18, reports his own view and that of others: Christ merited for his members redemption from sin and the Devil, and the opening of the kingdom of heaven, so that with the fiery sword removed the entrance lay open freely. In the same distinction, near the end: he merited for us, through his endurance of death and passion, access to Paradise and redemption from sin and the Devil. For by dying he himself became the sacrifice of our deliverance.

units.la: Sed totum hoc redemtionis beneficiū ad eos qui Christi sunt restringens, paulo post subdit: si Adami superbia omnium exstitit ruina, multo magis Christi humilitas, qua mortem gustauit, ingressum regni cœlestis, omnibus suis impleto Dei decreto aperire valuit. Idem distinctione sequenti: Dicimur per mortem Christi iustificari: Quia per fidem in mortem iustificamur: atque vt olim aspicientes serpentem æneum in ligno erectum, à morsibus serpentum sana-
units.tr: But restricting this whole benefit of redemption to those who belong to Christ, he adds shortly after: if Adam's pride brought ruin on all, much more did Christ's humility, by which he tasted death, have power to open the way into the kingdom of heaven for all his own, once God's decree was fulfilled. Likewise in the following distinction: we are said to be justified by the death of Christ, because through faith we are justified into death; and just as those who once looked upon the bronze serpent raised on the wood were healed from the bites of serpents, so if with a right gaze of faith we look upon him who hung for us on the wood, we are loosed from the chains of the Devil, that is, from sins.

units.la: Dd v ban—bantur, ita si recto fidei intuitu, in illum re- spicimus qui pro nobis pependit in ligno, à vin- culis Diaboli soluimur, id est, à peccatis. Alijsq; verbis copiose ibidē docet, libe-rationem àDiabolo eorum demum ef-se qui in Christum credunt.
units.tr: He teaches at length in the same place, in other words, that deliverance from the Devil belongs only to those who believe in Christ.

units.la: Innocentius III. lib. 2. de officio Mis-sa cap. 41. sic distinguit: sanguinem Christi pro solis prædestinatis effusum quantum ad efficientiam: pro cunctis vero hominibus, quantum ad sufficientiam, adducitq; verba Leonis ante à nobis recitata.
units.tr: Innocent III, in book 2, On the Office of the Mass, chapter 41, draws the distinction thus: the blood of Christ was shed for the predestined alone as to its efficacy; but for all men as to its sufficiency, and he cites the words of Leo quoted earlier by us.

units.la: Et hac distinctione nihil tritius apud scholasticos. Hinc Thomas in 1. ad Tim. 2. inquit: Christus propitiatio est pro peccatis nostris: pro aliquibus efficaciter: sed pro omnibus sufficienter: quia pretium sanguinis eius sufficiens est ad salutem omnium; sed non habet efficaciam nisi in electis, propter impedimentum.
units.tr: Nothing is more commonplace among the Schoolmen than this distinction. Hence Thomas, on 1 Timothy 2, says: Christ is the propitiation for our sins: for some effectively, but for all sufficiently, because the price of his blood is sufficient for the salvation of all; but it has no efficacy except in the elect, on account of the obstacle.

units.la: Et clarius super cap. 5. Apocal. De passione Domini, inquit, loqui est dupliciter. Aut secundum sufficientiam, & sic passio redemit omnes: omnibus enim redimendis & salvandis sufficiens est, etsi plures essent mundi, ut dicit Anselmus lib. 2. Cur Deus &c. homo c. 14. Aut
units.tr: And more clearly, on Revelation chapter 5, concerning the passion of the Lord, he says that speaking is twofold. Either according to sufficiency, and so the passion redeemed all: for it is sufficient for all who are to be redeemed and saved, even if the world were more numerous, as Anselm says in book 2 of Cur Deus homo, chapter 14. Or

units.la: Efficiētia. / sufficiētia. Aut secundum efficientiam, & sic non omnes redempti sunt per passionem, quia non omnes adhærent redemptori, & ideo non omnes habent efficaciam redemptionis.
units.tr: according to efficacy, and so not all have been redeemed by the passion, because not all cleave to the Redeemer, and therefore not all have the efficacy of redemption.

units.la: Idem summa de veritate, materia 26. quæst.7. Meritum Christi quantum ad sufficientiam, æqualiter se habet ad omnes: non autem quantum ad efficaciam: quod accidit partim ex libero arbitrio, partim ex diuina electione, per quam quibusdam misericorditer effectus meritorum Christi confertur, quibusdam vero iusto Dei iudicio subtrahitur.
units.tr: The same in the Summa de veritate, matter 26, question 7: The merit of Christ, as to sufficiency, stands equally toward all; but not as to efficacy, which happens partly from free will, partly from divine election, through which the effect of Christ's merits is mercifully conferred on some, while from others it is withheld by the just judgment of God.

units.la: Contra Gentiles lib.4. cap.55. hanc affert causam propositæ distinctionis inter sufficientiam & efficientiā. Mors Christi, inquit, est quasi quædam vniuersalis causa salutis, sicut peccatum primi hominis fuit quasi vniuersalis causa damnationis. Oportet autem vniuersalem causam applicari ad vnum quemque specialiter, vt effectum vniuersalis causæ percipiat. Effectus peccati primi pertinet ad vnumquemque per carnis originem. Effectus autem mortis Christi pertingit ad vnumquemque per spiritualem regenerationem, per quam „ quâ homo Christo quodammodo con- „ iungitur & incorporatur. Alia ex hoc autore testimonia suprà adduximus.
units.tr: In Against the Gentiles, book 4, chapter 55, he gives the cause of the distinction proposed between sufficiency and efficacy. "The death of Christ," he says, "is as it were a universal cause of salvation, just as the sin of the first man was a universal cause of condemnation. But a universal cause must be applied to each single person, so that he may receive its effect. The effect of the first sin reaches each person through origin in the flesh. But the effect of Christ's death reaches each person through spiritual regeneration, by which a man is in some way joined and incorporated with Christ." I have already cited other testimonies from this author above.

units.la: Eandem sequutus distinctionem Petrus Galatinus, homo doctissimus, de arcanis Catholicæ veritatis lib. 8. cap. 14. ad hunc modum scribit: Licet passio Christi ad delenda omnium peccata sufficiens esse debebat: non tamen omnium peccata deletura erat, sed eorum duntaxat, qui in eum credituri essent, & pœnitentiam acturi: Eam ob rem dicit Propheta: ipse peccata multorum tulit.
units.tr: Following the same distinction, Peter Galatinus, a most learned man, writes in this manner in On the Secrets of Catholic Truth, book 8, chapter 14: Although the passion of Christ ought to have been sufficient to blot out the sins of all, yet it was not going to blot out the sins of all, but only of those who were going to believe in him and repent. For this reason the Prophet says: he bore the sins of many.

units.la: Item Stapulensis in 5. ad Rom. Christus habet quidem apud se omnium redemtionem, non solum nobis, sed innumeris etiam mundis redimendis sufficientem: sed propria quadam peruersitate non omnes eius fiunt participes: sicut Lux per se potis est omnium propulsare tenebras, licet non omnium oculi illuminentur.
units.tr: Likewise Stapulensis, on Romans 5: Christ indeed has with himself the redemption of all, sufficient not only for us but also for countless worlds to be redeemed; but by a certain peculiar perversity not all become partakers of him, just as light by itself is able to drive away the darkness of all, though not all eyes are illuminated.

units.la: E nostris Martyr, Caluinus, Zanchius, & alij, eandem admittunt & sequuntur distinctionem, prout lib. 1. cap. 11. pluribus annotauimus. Similiter libro seq. cap. 12. satis opinor euicimus, celcceleberrimos & doctissimos Theologos Heluetiæ, Zuinglium, Musculum, Bullingerum, Gvvaltherum, Wolfium, Simlerum, Lauaterum & alios, re ipsa de vniuersalitate gratiæ idem sensisse, quod nos defendimus.
units.tr: Among our own, Martyr, Calvin, Zanchius and others admit and follow the same distinction, as we have noted at length in book 1, chapter 11. Similarly, in the following book, chapter 12, I think we have sufficiently shown that the most celebrated and learned theologians of Helvetia, namely Zwingli, Musculus, Bullinger, Gwalther, Wolf, Simler, Lavater and others, in fact held the same view about the universality of grace that we defend.

units.la: His & Lutherum adiungamus tomo 3. in Ies. 53. Tanta est, inquit, iustitia Christi, vt infinitos mundos possit iustificare: & offert Christus iustitiam suam omnibus, sed consequuntur ea omnes qui in ipsum credunt, iuxta illud, Qui crediderit & baptizatus fuerit,seruabitur. Alij manent sub peccato & ira.
units.tr: Let us add Luther to these, volume 3, on Isaiah 53: So great is the righteousness of Christ that it could justify infinite worlds; and Christ offers his righteousness to all, but those obtain it who believe in him, according to that saying: whoever believes and is baptized will be saved. Others remain under sin and wrath.

units.la: Ibidem Iustitia Christiana, ait, non accipitur, nisi ante cognoscatur Christus. Item, iustitia Christiana secundum substantiam nihil aliud est, quam noticia Christi, hoc est, fides qua apprehenditur Christus in corde, quod dederit se ἀντίλυτρον pro nobis, & peccatis nostris, sicut Paulus dicit 1. Tim. 2. Verbum quidem offert & prædicat omnibus Christum, tanquam victimam pro nostris peccatis: nisi autem Spiritus sanctus corda illuminet, huic verbo assentiri nemo potest. Assentimur autem cum apprehendimus promissionem, quod in Christo sit benedictio gentium, atque hæc gloria gloria est Christiani, scire quod sua iustitia sit credere in Christum. Idem, vt supra vidimus, dicta illa, vult omnes homines salvos fieri: Nolo mortem peccatoris, quibus male intellectis opinio aduersariorum innititur, longe aliter atque ipsi, edisserit; de voluntate videlicet in verbo Dei revelata, quam ab occulta illa & tremenda discernit, a qua sola dicit pendere omnia, qui accepturi sint verbum, qui non; qui liberandi a peccato, qui occasiendi, qui damnandi, qui iustificandi.
units.tr: In the same place he says: Christian righteousness is not received unless Christ is first known. Likewise: Christian righteousness in its substance is nothing other than the knowledge of Christ, that is, the faith by which Christ is apprehended in the heart, that he gave himself as a ransom [ἀντίλυτρον] for us and for our sins, as Paul says in 1 Timothy 2. The Word indeed offers and proclaims Christ to all as the victim for our sins; but unless the Holy Spirit illumines the heart, no one can assent to this word. We assent, however, when we grasp the promise, that in Christ is the blessing of the nations; and this glory is the Christian's glory, to know that his righteousness is to believe in Christ. The same author, as we saw above, explains those sayings, he wills all men to be saved and I do not desire the death of the sinner, which the adversaries' opinion rests upon when misunderstood, but in a way quite different from theirs: namely, of the will revealed in the Word of God, which he distinguishes from that hidden and terrible will, on which alone he says all depends, who are going to receive the Word and who not; who are to be freed from sin and who to perish, who to be condemned and who justified.

units.la: Neque aliter Brentius, Explic. Catech. docet de vniuersalitate redemtionis Christianæ: omnia nempe peccata propter Christum remitti omnibus: quales quales fuerint, Iudæi siue Ethnici, siue reges siue priuati, siue liberi siue serui: dum modo ad Ecclesiam Christi accedant & credant in ipsum. Quisquis enim, inquit, in Christum credit, & baptizatur in nomen eius, accipit remissionem peccatorum, & ius cœlestis hereditatis. Ac diserte inculcat beneficium hoc non accipi nisi fide &c. Summa, eius viri iudicio, remissio peccatorum rum, receptio in gratiam atque in numerum sanctorum, adoptio item & ius hæreditatis cœlestis (in quibus omnibus redemtio sita intelligitur) propria Ecclesiæ sanctorum & vere credetium dona sunt, & tam late patent quàm late ipsa patet Ecclesia Christi; omniumque nihilominis recte dicuntur, quatenus nemo cuiuscunque ordinis & conditionis ab iis prohibetur, dummodo credat.
units.tr: Brentius, in his Explanation of the Catechism, teaches in no other way about the universality of Christian redemption: that indeed all sins are remitted to all on account of Christ, whatever they may be, whether Jews or Gentiles, whether kings or private persons, whether free or slaves, provided only that they come to the Church of Christ and believe in him. For whoever, he says, believes in Christ and is baptized into his name receives the remission of sins and the right of the heavenly inheritance. He also clearly insists that this benefit is not received except by faith. In sum, by this man's judgment, the remission of sins, reception into grace and into the number of the saints, adoption likewise and the right of the heavenly inheritance (in all of which redemption is understood to consist) are the proper gifts of the Church of the saints and of those who truly believe, and they extend as widely as the Church of Christ itself extends; and they are nonetheless rightly said to be for all, inasmuch as no one of any rank or condition is excluded from them, provided he believes.

units.la: Quò pertinet & explicatio illa, cuius supra quoque ad locum Matth.1. meminimus: Quibus Iesus est Iesus, hoc est, Saluator a peccatis ipsorum? Euangelista dicit, Saluum faciet populum suum. Non facit filuos alienos, sed s v v M populum. Alieni sunt, quotquot non credunt in ipsum. Sui autem sunt, quotquot agnoscunt & amplectuntur eum fide, sive Iudaei sive gentes &c. Hæc disputatores Tubingenses concilient, si possunt, cum figmento cerebri sui, quod simul omnes, sive per fidem ad Christum accedant sive non, ab omni peccato & condemnatione liberati, in gratiam recepti, iustificati, viuificati, & in
units.tr: To this belongs also that explanation which we have mentioned above on Matthew 1: To whom is Jesus Jesus, that is, Saviour from their sins? The Evangelist says: He shall save his people. He does not make alien sons, but his own people. Those are aliens who do not believe in him. Those are his own who acknowledge and embrace him by faith, whether Jews or Gentiles, etc. Let the Tübingen disputants, if they can, reconcile these things with the figment of their own brain, that all together, whether they come to Christ through faith or not, are freed from all sin and condemnation, received into grace, justified, quickened, and in

units.la: {thef.6s} & 116. in numerū sanctorū relati sint: quodq; adeovniucrsi, nemine excepto, sint populus ille Christi, de quo dicitur, Serua-bit populum suum ex peccatis ipsorum.
units.tr: ...and have been reckoned in the number of the saints; and that all, without exception, are that people of Christ of whom it is said, He will save his people from their sins.

units.la: Sed & alium amicum suum audiant pronunciantem, Christum pro omnibus mortuum, quod per ipsum non tantum Iudaei, sed etiam omnes electi Dei, vbi-que gentium, qui ab oriente & occide-te ad Abrahamum patrem suum colli-guntur, seruari debebant. Idem, meri-tum Christi, inquit, longissime totius mundi peccata superare in iudicio Dei repertum est, sicque Christus & omnia eius membra (non membra & vasa diaboli) iustus pronunciatus est. Et addit, ideo potissimum ad tempus mortis Christi referri victoriam Christi contra Sata-nam, quod tum merito mortis acquisi-tus sit thesaurus ille victoriarum, qui alio-qui omnibus temporibus credentibus dis-tribuatur. Et mox: discrimen hic est in-ter potentiam & actum, seu acquisitio-nem & applicationem, seu ius & possessionem. Merito, acquisitioneq; iuris aut potentia, Satan ex omnibus homi-nibus
units.tr: But let them also hear their other friend declaring that Christ died for all, which means that through him not only the Jews but all the elect of God, from every part of the Gentile world, who are gathered from east and west to Abraham their father, ought to be saved. The same author says that the merit of Christ has been found, in the judgment of God, to exceed the sins of the whole world by far, and so Christ and all his members (not members and vessels of the devil) has been pronounced righteous. He adds that the victory of Christ over Satan is assigned especially to the time of Christ's death, because it was then that the treasury of victories was acquired by the merit of his death, which is otherwise distributed to believers at all times. And soon after: here is the difference between power and act, or between acquisition and application, or between right and possession. Rightly, by the acquisition of the right or the power, Satan was cast out from all men, and so from the whole world, at the time of the passion; but he is cast out by application or act only from believers, at all times.

units.la: Illyr. in Ioh. 11.v. 31.
units.tr: Illyr. in Ioh. 11.v. 31.

units.la: In 12. cap. Ioh. 7. 31. nibus,atque ita toto mundo, tempore passionis eiectus est : sed applicatione aut actu tantum ex credentibus eijci-tur,omni tempore.
units.tr: In 12. cap. Ioh. 7. 31. ...and so throughout the whole world, at the time of the passion, he was cast out; but by application or act he is cast out only from believers, at all times.

units.la: Bene notetur distinctio illa potentiæ & actus, seu sufficientiæ & efficaciæ, sicut autor plenius seipsum explanat, cum in verba Ioh.1.Epist.2. arcecaussæ aduersa-riorum, hisce verbis scribit: Cum dicit, pro peccatis nostris, intelligit credentes, qui-bus re ipsa prodest passio Christi. Quod addit, totius mundi, intelligit de potentia, quod omnibus beneficia meritumque Christi pateant, omnesque plenissime per eius satisfactionem saluari queant (tam prestans, sufficiens ac preciosum, esse eius meritum) si modo id appre-hendere dignentur fide.
units.tr: Let that distinction between power and act, or sufficiency and efficacy be carefully noted, as the author explains himself more fully when, writing on the words of 1 John 2, against the cause of his opponents, he says: when he says for our sins, he means believers, to whom the passion of Christ is in fact of benefit. What he adds, of the whole world, he means in power: that the benefits and merit of Christ lie open to all, and all can be most fully saved through his satisfaction (so excellent, sufficient and precious is his merit), if only they deign to apprehend it by faith.

units.la: Longū esset singula recensere. Haud tamen prætereundum videtur, quod nunc dicturus sum; de Synodo Argentina habita Anno M. D. XXXIII. Ibi disputatione instituta cum Melchiore quodam Hofmanno, impostore Anabaptistico & Pelagiano, inter alios eius errores & hic damnatus fuit, quod Ee sta„ statueret omnes electos esse & redem- „ tos omnes per Christū, prorsus vt Hub. „ nō tantum redemtione & meritū Christi, verum etiam electionem in ipso, „ omnibus post lapsum hominibus pro- „ miscue communem esse vult. Contrā „ vero Synodus ex verbo Dei pronun- „ ciauit: Deū, postquam ab æterno præ- „ sciuisset, humanum genus per lapsum „ primorum parentum, æternæ morti „ obnoxium futurum, ex mera miseri- „ cordia, ante iacta mundi fundamenta, „ sibi aliquos ex genere humano, aliis „ præteritis, ad vitam æternam elegisse, „ præsciuisse ac prædestinasse: & pro ho- „ rum peccatis mortem Christi esse pro- „ pitiationem. Itaque neque electionem „ neque redemtionem Christi omnibus „ hominibus esse communem, velut ad „ implicandas miseras conscientias & la- „ nam doctrinam corrumpendam som- „ niaret Hofmannus. Verum propterea „ meritum Christi toti mūdo commune „ dici & prædicari, quòd post Christi glo- „ rificationem, non tantum Iudæi, sed „ omnes aliæ Gentes debuerint eius participes & compotes fieri, quotquot nimirum ex iis electi sunt. Et hoc sensu dicta Synodus exponit Scripturae testimonia ab Hofmanno obiecta: In semine tuo benedicetur omnes Gentes: sicut in Adam omnes moriuntur, ita in Christo omnes vivificantur: cum fuero exaltatus traham omnia ad me: Deus vult omnes salvos fieri, & ad cognitionem veritatis venire. Item, Iesus Christus propitiatio est pro peccatis totius mundi: agnus tollens peccata mundi: aliaque id genus. Neque enim existimandum, ubi posita sint illa vocabula omnes, item omnis mundus: Totus mundus, ibi contestim omnes homines, nemine excepto, intelligendos esse: quippe tales loquutiones non ubique eandem habere significationem.
units.tr: It would be too long to go through each point. Yet what I am about to say should not be passed over: concerning the Synod of Strasbourg held in the year 1533. There, when a disputation had been arranged with a certain Melchior Hofmann, an Anabaptist impostor and Pelagian, among his other errors this too was condemned: that he held that all the elect are, and all are redeemed through Christ, and that he wanted election in him too to be common to all men without distinction after the fall, not only the redemption and merit of Christ. On the contrary, the Synod pronounced from the word of God: that God, having foreknown from eternity that the human race would be liable to eternal death through the fall of the first parents, from pure mercy, before the foundations of the world were laid, chose for himself some from the human race, passing over others, for eternal life, foreknew and predestined them; and that the death of Christ is the propitiation for their sins. Therefore neither election nor the redemption of Christ is common to all men, as Hofmann dreamed, to entangle wretched consciences and corrupt sound doctrine. But the merit of Christ is said and preached to be common to the whole world because, after the glorification of Christ, not only the Jews but all other Gentiles ought to become partakers and sharers of it, namely as many of them as are elect. And in this sense the Synod expounds the testimonies of Scripture objected by Hofmann: In your seed shall all the nations be blessed; as in Adam all die, so in Christ all are made alive; when I am lifted up I will draw all things to me; God wills all to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. Likewise, Jesus Christ is the propitiation for the sins of the whole world; the Lamb taking away the sins of the world, and others of that kind. For it is not to be thought that, wherever the words all and whole world are put, all men without exception are straightway to be understood; for such expressions do not have the same meaning everywhere: all, likewise every world, the whole world.

units.la: Haec qui penitius nosse desiderat, consulat Hieronymum Zanchium piae memoriae, praeceptorem meum revera rendum, quem honoris & debitae observantiae ergo nomino: lib. 3. miscell. pag. 79. ac in primis Acta disputationis Hofmannicae per Martinum Bucerum, quae suo & collegarum nomine edidit im-
units.tr: Whoever desires to know these things more deeply, let him consult Hieronymus Zanchius of blessed memory, my teacher, truly to be revered, whom I name out of honour and due respect: book 3 of the Miscellanies, p. 79; and above all the Acts of the Hofmannite disputation published by Martin Bucer in his own name and that of his colleagues.

units.la: Ee ij prefprefla Argentinæ per Matthiam Apia- rium, anno 1533.
units.tr: Printed at Strasbourg by Matthias Apiarius, in the year 1533.

units.la: Totam vero hanc doctrinam, quam in ea contra Hofmannum disputatio- ne M. Bucerus defendit, vniuersus senatus Argentinenfis vt sanam pro- bauit, & fideliter in ea vrbe doceri at- que prædicari voluit, nec quicquam li- cere cuiquam, quod ei doctrinæ aduer- fetur, siue in angulis siue in propatulo effundere & calumniari, nedum ab ea alios abstrahere, vt testatur libellus, qui inscribitur Ordinatio & ceremoniæ pro mi- nistris Ecclesiæ Argentinensis & ad eam per- tinentibus. Cap. 4. pag. 4.
units.tr: The whole senate of Strasbourg approved this entire doctrine, which M. Bucer defended in that disputation against Hofmann, as sound, and wished it to be faithfully taught and preached in that city; nor was it to be permitted to anyone to do anything contrary to that doctrine, to pour out and slander it either in corners or in public, much less to draw others away from it, as the little book testifies which is entitled Ordinance and ceremonies for the ministers of the Church of Strasbourg and those pertaining to it, chap. 4, p. 4.

units.la: Quæ cum ita sint, qua fronte, quo pudore, aduersarius palam scribere au- det, nullo vnquam tempore nostram de redemtione sententiam auditam in populo Dei, ad tempora vsque colloquij Mompelgardici? O proflitutam calumniandi audaciam, & extremæ te- stem inscitiæ, fi non malitiæ!
units.tr: Since these things are so, with what brow and what shame does the adversary dare to write openly that our doctrine of redemption was never heard among the people of God at any time until the time of the colloquy at Montbéliard? O the prostituted audacity of slander, and the witness of extreme ignorance, if not of malice!

units.la: CAPVT VLTIMVM.
units.tr: The Last Chapter.

units.la: Quo origo & maiores panduntur sententiae aduersariorum.
units.tr: In which the origin and the chief opinions of our opponents are laid open.

units.la: VERVM enim uero qui dicit quae vult, quae non vult, audiet, vt vetus habet dictum. Quando igitur hactenus ostensum est, sententiam quam nos tuemur, abunde in verbo Dei traditam, atque in Ecclesia omnibus temporibus receptam, & ad haec vsque tempora fideliter propagatam fuisse, praeterire nec possum nec debeo, quin hic e contrario repetam originem sententiae aduersariorum. Affero itaque & profiteor, non Spiritum Dei, aut eius oracula, in genuino sensu intellecta: sed Spiritum Pelagianae impietatis ortus sui parentem habere.
units.tr: Indeed, as the old saying goes, whoever says what he pleases will hear what he does not please. Since it has been shown so far that the doctrine we uphold is abundantly delivered in the Word of God, has been received in the Church in every age, and has been faithfully handed down to our own times, I can neither pass over nor ought I to pass over the opposite side: here I shall in turn trace the origin of our opponents' opinion. I therefore affirm and profess that this opinion does not proceed from the Spirit of God, or from his oracles understood in their genuine sense, but has as the parent of its birth the spirit of Pelagian impiety.

units.la: Quod ne fine autore protulisse videar, Prosper Aquitanicus, Epistola ad Augustinum, de reliquiis Pelagianae haereseos, inter alios prauitatis istius errores de gratia & libero arbitrio & praedestinatione, etiam hunc assignat, quod videlicet asseverarent, pro vniuerso humano ...
units.tr: Lest I seem to have put this forward without an author, Prosper of Aquitaine, in his Letter to Augustine on the remnants of the Pelagian heresy, among the other errors of that perversity concerning grace, free will and predestination, also records this one: namely, that they asserted that our Lord Jesus Christ died for the whole human race ...

units.la: Ee iij genegenere mortuum esse Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, & neminem prorsus à redemtione sanguinis eius exceptum, etiamsi omnem hanc vitam alienissima ab eo mente pertranseat (hoc est etiamsi in infidelitate perseueret & damnandus sit) quia ad omnes homines pertineat diuinae misericordiae sacramentum (promissio nempe gratiae, vt hodie loquuntur) Itaque quatenus ad Deum pertinet, paratam omnibus vitam aeternam: quantum autem ad arbitrij libertatem, ab his ea appre-hendi, qui Deo sponte crediderint. Et subiungit, ad talis gratiae praedicationem eos delapsos, quod refugerent confiteri Deum secundum propositum & consilium voluntatis suae, occulto quidem iudicio sed opere manifesto, aliud vas condere in honorem, aliud in contumeliam, nec acquiescerent, praedestinatum electorum numerum nec augeri, nec minui posse.
units.tr: ...and that no one whatever is excluded from the redemption of his blood, even if he spends his whole life in a mind utterly alien to him (that is, even if he persists in unbelief and is to be damned), because the sacrament of divine mercy (that is, the promise of grace, as they now say) pertains to all men. Therefore, so far as concerns God, eternal life is prepared for all; but so far as concerns the freedom of the will, it is laid hold of only by those who have freely believed God. And he adds that, having fallen into the preaching of such grace, they shrank from confessing that God, according to the purpose and counsel of his will, by a hidden judgement but a manifest work, fashions one vessel to honour and another to dishonour, and they would not accept that the predestined number of the elect can neither be increased nor diminished.

units.la: Haec ille; euidenter sane & viuis coloribus non tam Pelagianae haereseos ea aetate reliquias, quam renascentem no-stra stra hac ætate in aduersariis nostris Pelagianisimum depingens.
units.tr: So he wrote. Clearly and in vivid colours he portrays not so much the remnants of the Pelagian heresy of that age as the Pelagianism that is now being reborn among our opponents in our own age.

units.la: Iam Hofmannus ille patrum nostrorum memoria, cuius nuper metionem fecimus, quid nisi monstrum fuit secis Pelagianæ aliarumq; hæreseon? Eum vero Huberus ita refert, quantum ad præsens institutum, vt non omnium ouo sit similius. Etenim is omnes statuebat esse electos, omnes per Christum redemtos, sine cuiusquam exceptione. Quorum vtrumque Hub. thesi 1001. his verbis expressum voluit, omnes homines post lapsum Adami fuisse in Christo electos & ingratia receptos propter benedictum semen, in quo omnium hominum peccata expianda erant. Neque id tantum, verum etiam, ne quid imitationi deesset, iisdem pro-diit Scripturarum locis atque testimoniis male detortis, instructus, quibus Hofmannus etiam, vt superius breuiter indicauimus, errorem suum palliabat.
units.tr: Now that Hofmann of whom we spoke recently, within the memory of our fathers, what else was he but a monster drawn from Pelagianism and other heresies? Huber reports him in such a way, so far as the present purpose goes, that he is hardly different from anyone else. For he taught that all are elect, all redeemed through Christ, without any exception. Huber expressed both points in his thesis 1001 in these words: "all men after the fall of Adam were elect in Christ and received into grace, on account of the blessed Seed, in whom the sins of all men were to be expiated." Nor is that all: equipped with the same passages and testimonies of Scripture, badly twisted, so that nothing might be lacking to his imitation, he also put them forward, with which Hofmann, as we briefly indicated above, also covered over his error.

units.la: Accedit, quod nostra hac tempesta-te, Pacuuius quidam, Pelagianam non obscure præse ferens impietatem, non
units.tr: To this must be added that in our own time a certain Pacuvius, plainly displaying a Pelagian impiety, not

units.la: Ee iiij mo-

modò côtendit, Christum pariter om- nium & singulorum hominum, vt con- ditorem ita & redemtorem esse, om- nésque nasci in statu salutis & gratiæ, ac proinde felices, modò nó accersant si- bi exitium infidelitate: Electionem ité & gratiam esse generalem &c. Verum etiam aperte profitetur & gloriatur, VVirtembergenses Theologos, Lu- theri successores, sed multùm de doctrina Lutheri in hac parte remit- tentes, secum in rei summa consen- tire.
units.tr: only contends that Christ, as Creator, is likewise the Redeemer of all and of each man, and that all are born in a state of salvation and grace, and therefore happy, provided they do not bring ruin upon themselves by unbelief; that election and grace are general, etc. He also openly professes and boasts that the Württemberg theologians, the successors of Luther, though departing much from Luther's doctrine on this point, agree with him in the substance of the matter.

units.la: Sed habeant sibi Pacuuios, & Hof- mannos, & Pelagianos simul omnes, veteres & nouos: nos Prophetas & Apostolos Domini autores habemus, & cóspirantem probatissimorum quo- rumque omnibus seculis scriptorum consensum.
units.tr: But let them keep their Pacuvii, and Hofmanns, and all the Pelagians together, old and new. We have the Prophets and Apostles of the Lord as our authors, and the agreement, in harmony, of the most approved writers of all ages.

units.la: Hæc est, Christiane lectòr, vera, sim- plex & orthodoxa, eaq; minimè acer- ba, aut maledica, sed placida exposi- tio doctrinæ de redemtione generis humani per Christum, propositum nobis à patre propitiatorem & aduocacatum per fidem, ad remissionem peccatorum nostrorum in sanguine eius: quam ita tradiderunt prophetæ, prædicarunt Apostoli, confirmaruntque sanctí Dei homines. Hanc igitur retineamus & nos, in eaque constanter perseueremus, omissis oppositionibus falsò nominatæ scientiæ & verborum pugnis, ex quibus nascitur inuidia, lis, maledicentiæ, suspiciones malæ, perversæ exercitationes hominum mente corruptorum, & qui priuati sunt veritate, & quæstui habent pietatem. In primis autem cum sine fide impossibile sit Deo placere, id operam demus, vt cum vero corde & perfuasione fidei ad thronum gratiæ accedamus, quo consequamur misericordiam, & gratiam adipiscamur ad opportunum auxilium; atque etiam prælucente vera in Iesum Christum fide, vniuersam vitam nostram ita instituamus, id semper agamus & meditemur omnes, vt communi Redemtori nostro, cuius
units.tr: This, Christian reader, is a true, simple and orthodox exposition of the doctrine of the redemption of the human race through Christ, who was set forth by the Father as propitiator and advocate through faith, for the remission of our sins in his blood. This is how the prophets handed it down, the Apostles preached it, and the holy men of God confirmed it. Let us therefore hold to it as well, and persevere in it steadfastly, setting aside the oppositions of falsely named knowledge and the wrangling of words, from which spring envy, strife, slander, evil suspicions, and perverse disputes of men whose minds are corrupted, who are deprived of the truth and regard godliness as a source of gain. Above all, since it is impossible to please God without faith, let us take care to approach the throne of grace with a true heart and the assurance of faith, so that we may obtain mercy and find grace for timely help; and, with true faith in Jesus Christ shining before us, let us all so order our whole life, and always so act and meditate, that we may be found pleasing to our common Redeemer, to whose glory we ought to be wholly dedicated and consecrated, in holiness and righteousness before him, all the days of our life. To him be honour, and glory, and blessing, for ever and ever. Amen, Amen.

units.la: Eev glogloriæ toti dicati confecratiq; esse debemus, grati reperiamur, cum sanctitate & iustitia in ipsius conspectu, cunctis diebus vitæ nostræ. Ei sit honor, & gloria, & benedictio in secula seculorum. Amen, Amen.
units.tr: that we ought to be wholly dedicated and consecrated to the glory of God, and be found acceptable, with holiness and righteousness in his sight, all the days of our life. To him be honour, and glory, and blessing for ever and ever. Amen, Amen.

units.la: FINIS.
units.tr: FINIS.

units.la: LIBER DE PRAEDESTINATIONE DIVINA,
units.tr: BOOK ON THE DIVINE PREDESTINATION,

units.la: CAPVT I.
units.tr: CHAPTER I.

units.la: Proœmium, & partitio doctrinæ suscepta.
units.tr: Preface, and the division of the doctrine undertaken.

units.la: DISPVTATIO per se magna atque ardua est de prædestinatione, & ob humani curiositatem audaciamq; ingenij non parum insuper perplexa atq; adeo periculosa, dum in diuinorum iudiciorum, & sapientiæ penetralia sese ingerens humana ratio, aut rimatur veritatem, aut contemnit & ludibrijs suis impetit quæ nō percipit, & ne potest quidem percipere : quoniam stultitia ei sunt, & spiritualiter, vt ait Apostolus, dijudicantur. Quis enim nouit mentem
units.tr: This disputation about predestination is in itself great and difficult, and because of human curiosity and the boldness of the mind it is not a little more perplexing and therefore dangerous. Human reason, thrusting itself into the inner sanctuaries of God's judgements and wisdom, either pries into the truth or, failing to grasp what it does not perceive (and indeed cannot perceive), scorns it and assails it with its mockery. For, as the Apostle says, "they are foolishness to it, and they are judged spiritually."

units.la: tem {*}fem Domini, vt instruat eum? nos autem mentem Christi habemus, qui in sinu æterni patris existens, omne Dei consilium, quantum nostra ad salutem scire interest, in hac parte, vt in alijs, clementer nobis in verbo suo patefecit.
units.tr: "For who has known the mind of the Lord, that he should instruct him? But we have the mind of Christ," who, existing in the bosom of the eternal Father, has clearly revealed to us in his word, as far as our salvation requires us to know it, the whole counsel of God in this matter, as in others.

units.la: Hanc igitur veritatis & iustitiæ normam sequentes, nec obtrectatorum quicquam reformidantes maledicentiam, adiuuante Domino, in cuius manu sumus tum nos tum sermones nostri, de prædestinatione considerabimus: I. Quid sit prædestinatio. II. Quæ eius sint causæ. III. Quæ effecta. IV. An sit infallibilis atq; immutabilis. V. An & quomodo certi esse queamus de nostri ad vitam æternam prædestinatione. VI. Et postremò aliquid de viu huius doctrinæ agemus, contra eos qui licet vera essent quæ docemus, tamen non promenda, sed silentio premenda ea exiexistimant, tanquam ædificationi aduersa. Proderit autem horum omnium consideratio, tùm ad alios vsus suo loco dicendos, tùm ad maiorem eorum quæ de gratiæ & redemtionis vniuersalitate hactenus exposuimus, certitudinem. Etenim Pelagianorum olim reliquiæ, vt & hodie, neminem prorsus à redemtione sanguinis Christi exceptum perhibentes, & quantũ ad Deum attinet, paratam omnibus vitam æternam contendentes, ad talis gratiæ prædicationẽ idcirco delapsæ sunt, quòd refugerent confiteri, Deum secundum propositũ & cõsilium voluntatis suæ, iudicio qui-dem occulto, sed opere manifesto, aliud vas condere in honorem, aliud in contumeliam, nec acquiescerent prædestinatorum numerũ nec augeri nec minui posse.
units.tr: Following this rule of truth and righteousness, and fearing nothing from the slander of those who find fault, with the Lord's help (in whose hand both we and our words are), we will consider predestination under these heads: I. What predestination is. II. What its causes are. III. What its effects are. IV. Whether it is infallible and immutable. V. Whether and how we can be certain of our own predestination to eternal life. VI. And finally we will say something about the use of this doctrine, against those who think that, although what we teach is true, it should not be published but kept silent, as being unfit for edification. The consideration of all these things will be useful both for other uses to be discussed in their place and for greater certainty about what we have so far set out concerning the universality of grace and redemption. For the remnants of the Pelagians, both formerly and today, who maintain that no one at all is excluded from the redemption of Christ's blood, and who contend that, so far as God is concerned, eternal life is set before everyone, have fallen into preaching such grace for this reason: they shrink from confessing that God, according to the purpose and counsel of his will, by a judgement indeed hidden but a work manifest, makes one vessel unto honour and another unto dishonour, and they do not accept that the number of the predestined can be neither increased nor diminished.

units.la: CAPVT II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: Quid sit prædestinatio: vbi varia nominis & rei definitiones, & comparatio vocum quarundam in hac materia vsitatarum, atque idem fermè significantium.
units.tr: What predestination is: the various definitions of the name and of the thing, and a comparison of certain words commonly used on this subject which mean almost the same.

units.la: PRINCIPIO, quod Latinis est prædestinare, vnde prædestinatio, Græci dicunt προορίζειν vnde προορισμός. Est autem προορίζειν, determinare, decernere, & constituere aliquid antequam illud agas. ὁρίζω enim terminum & finem denotat, modum præterea & regulam, & quasi præscriptum, quo actiones temperantur: atque ὁρίζειν etiam pro constituere & destinare Græcis accipitur. Sic Latinis destinare significat designare, decernere, constituere, vt apud Cæsarem: infectis iis quæ agere destinárat, id est, constituerat. Et apud Ciceronem in officijs de Damone & Pythia Pythagoreis: cum eorum alteri Dionysius diem necis destinassFet, & is qui morti addictus esset, postulasset, &c. Et lib. 1. De diuinatione inquit, sunt benefici Dij, generi humani hominum amici,
units.tr: First, the Latin word praedestinare, whence praedestinatio, is in Greek προορίζειν [proorizein], whence προορισμός [proorismos]. Now προορίζειν means to determine, decree, and establish something before you do it. For ὁρίζω [horizō] signifies a boundary and an end, and besides a measure and a rule, and as it were a prescribed pattern by which actions are regulated; and ὁρίζειν [horizein] is also taken by the Greeks to mean to appoint and designate. So among the Latins destinare means to designate, decree, or establish, as in Caesar: having abandoned the things which he had destined to do, that is, had determined. And in Cicero's De officiis, concerning Damon and Phintias the Pythagoreans: when Dionysius had appointed the day of death for one of them, and he who was condemned to die had asked for a delay, etc. And in book 1 of De divinatione he says: the gods are beneficent, friends of the human race.

units.la: Act 4. v. 28. Rom. 8. v. 29. Eph. 1. v. 5. neq; ignorant ea quæ ab ipsis constituta, & de-signata sunt, id est destinata, προωρισμένα, ἀποτετραγμένα, teste Budæo pag. 710.
units.tr: Acts 4:28; Rom. 8:29; Eph. 1:5. Nor are they ignorant of those things which have been constituted and designated by them, that is, destined, προωρισμένα [prōrismena], ἀποτετραγμένα [apotetragmena], as Budaeus says, p. 710.

units.la: Quoniam autem quæ Deus apud se constituta & designata habet, ab æterno constituit & designauit (nota siquidem ipsi sunt ab æterno omnia opera eius) vox illa προσφίλην, cum de Deo vsurpatur, idem significat quod προκαταβολὴν τῶν ἀιωνίων ὁρίσμων. Quemadmodum etiam expressè est apud Apostolum 1. Cor. 2. Loquimur sapientiam illam occultam, ἣν προώρισεν ὁ Θεὸς πρὸ τῶν αἰωνων, id est, quam ab æterno decreuit seu destinauit, reuelare nobis ad gloriam nostram.
units.tr: Since, however, what God has constituted and designated with himself, he has constituted and designated from eternity (for all his works are indeed known to him from eternity), the word προσφίλην, when it is used of God, means the same as προκαταβολὴν τῶν ἀιωνίων ὁρίσμων [prokatabolēn tōn aiōnion horismōn], the foreordaining of eternal decrees. Just as the Apostle also says expressly in 1 Cor. 2: We speak the hidden wisdom, which God predestined (ἣν προώρισεν ὁ Θεὸς πρὸ τῶν αἰωνων [hēn prōrisen ho Theos pro tōn aiōnōn]) before the ages, that is, which he decreed or destined from eternity to reveal to us for our glory.

units.la: Idcirco si Grammatica significatio verbi spectetur, potest hoc nomen prædestinatio generatim extendi ad vniuersa quæ sunt & fiunt in mundo, definiturque æternum Dei de rerum omnium gubernatione decretum, quod prouidentiam diuinam appellare solemus. Nihil enim temere aut fortuito, sed pa-terno Dei consilio & voluntate omnia eueniunt, vt ne passerculus quidem sine eo in terram cadere posset. Hinc Daniel, iuxta voluntatem suam facit in exercitu cæli & habitatoribus terræ, nec est qui dicat ei, quid facis? Et Sapientia inquit, Non est alius Deus præter te, qui curam habes omnium, & iustus cum sis, iuste gubernas omnia.
units.tr: Therefore, if the grammatical meaning of the verb is considered, this name predestination can be extended generally to all the things that are and happen in the world, and it may be defined as God's eternal decree concerning the governance of all things, which we are accustomed to call divine providence. For nothing happens by chance or accident, but all things come about by the fatherly counsel and will of God, so that not even a little sparrow could fall to the earth without him. Hence Daniel: He does according to his will among the host of heaven and the inhabitants of the earth, and there is none who can say to him, What are you doing? And Wisdom says: There is no other God besides you, who have care of all things; and since you are just, you govern all things justly.

units.la: Minimè autem dubium est, cum voluntate Dei omnia regantur, quin omnia agat secundum æternum propositum voluntatis suæ. Quicquid enim vult, ab æterno vult.
units.tr: Nor is there any doubt that, since all things are governed by the will of God, he does all things according to the eternal purpose of his will. For whatever he wills, he wills from eternity.

units.la: Sic generaliter de prædestinatione scribit Damascenus lib. 2. Orthodoxæ fidei, cap.30. Et Anselmus, lib. de concordia præscientiæ & prædestinationis. Autor item opusculi de prædestinatione Dei apud Augustinum pag. 1296. eandem secutus appellationis generalitatem, dicere non veretur, prædestinasse Deum, ut cælum volueretur, terra autem immobilis circumuoluenti cælo, loco centri haberetur: Sol & Luna diei noctisq; præessent, dies & nox certis temporibus vicissim succederet. Tale etiam est, quod ait Ambrosius, prædestinato tempore fore diem iudicij. E recentioribus Philippus Melanchthon ad eundem modum de prædestinatione locutus est in prioribus locis. Postremò, inquit, libertatem homini adimit diuina prædestinatio: eueniunt enim omnia iuxta diuinam prædestinationem; tùm externa opera, tùm interna cogitationes, in omnibus creaturis.
units.tr: Thus in general terms Damascene writes of predestination in book 2 of De fide orthodoxa, chapter 30; and Anselm in his book on the agreement of foreknowledge and predestination. The author also of the little work on the predestination of God, found among the works of Augustine (p. 1296), following the same general use of the term, does not hesitate to say that God predestined that the heaven should revolve, and the earth, immovable, should be held at the centre while the heaven turns around it; that the Sun and Moon should preside over day and night, and that day and night should succeed each other in fixed times. Similar is what Ambrose says: that the day of judgment will come at a predestined time. Among more recent writers, Philip Melanchthon spoke of predestination in the same way in the earlier places (Loci). Finally, he says, divine predestination takes away freedom from man: for all things happen according to divine predestination, both external works and internal thoughts, in all creatures.

units.la: In sacris literis vnicus est locus Act. 4. qui ad eam significationem vtcunq; accommodari posse videtur: conuenerút aduersus sanctum filium tuum Iesum, quem vnxisti, Herodes & Pilatus, cum gentibus & populo Israël ad faciendum quacunque manus tua & consilium tuum προώρισε γενέσθαι, hoc est prædestinauit vt fierent. Quapropter etiam omissa generalissima hac significatione, restrictiùs fere autores de prædestinatione sentiunt & loquùtur.
units.tr: In Holy Scripture there is only one passage, Acts 4, which seems to be applicable to this meaning in any way: Herod and Pontius Pilate, with the Gentiles and the people of Israel, gathered together against your holy Son Jesus, whom you anointed, to do whatever your hand and your counsel προώρισε γενέσθαι [prōrisen genesthai], that is, predestined to come to pass. Therefore, even leaving aside this most general meaning, writers and speakers on predestination mostly take it in a narrower sense.

units.la: Secundò igitur prædestinatio à quibusdam considerari solet, quatenus in genere circa creaturas rationales, saluandas vel damnandas, spectatur, puta angelos & homines. Nam & angelorum alios electos, alios reprobos esse constat. 1. Tim. 5. v. 21. & Matth. 25. v. 41. vbi diabolo & angelis eius, spiritibus reprobis, ignis æternus dicitur
units.tr: Secondly, then, predestination is customarily considered by some as it is viewed generally with respect to rational creatures to be saved or condemned, for instance angels and men. For it is clear that among the angels some are elect and others reprobate: 1 Tim. 5:21, and Matt. 25:41, where eternal fire is said to be prepared for the devil and his angels, reprobate spirits.
