units.la: II. Significatio. tur paratus, vtique à iactis mundi fundamentis, sicut de regno electis parato ibidem exprimitur. Erit autem praedestinatio eo modo nihil aliud, quàm praeordinatio creaturę rationalis, vel ad salutem, vel ad interitum æternum. Praedestinari, scribit Thomas part.1.q.23.art.1. convenit angelis sicut & hominibus: licet nunquam fuerint miseri. Nihil enim refert ad rationem praedestinationis, vtrū aliquis praedestinetur ad vitam æternam à statu miseriæ vel non: sicut nihil refert ad rationem dealbationis, vtrum ille qui dealbatur fuerit niger aut pallidus, vel rubeus.
units.tr: II. Signification. Prepared, certainly, from the foundation of the world, just as the kingdom is expressed there as prepared for the elect. Predestination in this way will be nothing other than the foreordination of a rational creature either to salvation or to eternal destruction. Thomas, in part 1, q. 23, art. 1, writes: To be predestined belongs to angels just as to men, even though they were never miserable. For it makes no difference to the notion of predestination whether someone is predestined to eternal life from a state of misery or not; just as it makes no difference to the notion of whitening whether the one who is whitened was black, or pale, or red.

units.la: Tertiò, de hominum duntaxat praedestinatione loquendo, duplex quoq; vocis istius esse vsus consueuit. Alias enim vocabulum praedestinationis ad vtrosque, electos & reprobos accommodatur, & tàm hi quàm illi dicūtur praedestinati: sed hi vt sint vasa irę coagmetata ad interitum: isti vt sint vasa misericordię, diuinitus praeparata ad gloriam.
units.tr: Thirdly, when speaking only of the predestination of men, there is customarily a twofold use of this term. For at one time the word predestination is applied to both the elect and the reprobate, and both these and those are called predestined; but the latter are fitted together as vessels of wrath for destruction, the former as vessels of mercy, divinely prepared for glory.

units.la: Sic Augustinus Enchir. ad Laur. c.100. manifeste vocem praedestinationis vsurpat, cum inquit: Deum bene vti etiam malis, tanquam summe bonum, ad eorum damnationem, quos iuste prædestinauit ad pœnam, & ad eorum salutem, quos benignè prædestinauit ad gratiam. Idem tract. 110: in Ioh. Est mundus damnandorum, de quo scriptum est, Ne cum mundo hoc damnemur. Pro ipso mundo non rogat Christus: neq; enim quò prædestinatus sit ignorat: ad æternum nempe supplicium subeundum cum diabolo, vt idem scribit alibi.
units.tr: Thus Augustine, in Enchiridion ad Laurentium, chapter 100, plainly uses the word predestination when he says: God makes good use even of evils, as one who is supremely good, for the damnation of those whom he justly predestined to punishment, and for the salvation of those whom he graciously predestined to grace. The same, in tractate 110 on John: There is the world of the damned, of which it is written, Lest we be condemned with this world. Christ does not pray for this world: for he does not fail to know for what it is predestined, namely to undergo eternal punishment with the devil, as he writes elsewhere.

units.la: In primis autem Fulgentius ad Monimum lib.1. multis disserit de duplici prædestinatione, vna bonorum ad gloriā, altera malorum ad pœnam. Vnde & initio lib.2. prædestinationem sic definit: Prædestinatio Dei, ait, nihil aliud est, quàm præparatio operum eius, quæ in æterna sua dispositione, aut misericorditer se facturum prescuit, aut iuste. Hoc est: prædestinatio est æternum Dei decretum, quo alios ex genere humano ex mera gratia per Christum seruare, alios iusto suo iudicio ab eadem gratia reijcere, & æternū propter peccata sua damnare constituit. Ita & electionem & reprobationem prædestinatio complectetur.
units.tr: Above all, Fulgentius, in Ad Monimum*, book 1, discusses at length the twofold predestination: one of the good to glory, the other of the wicked to punishment. Hence also at the beginning of book 2 he defines predestination thus: The predestination of God, he says, is nothing other than the preparation of his works, which in his eternal disposition he foreknew he would do either mercifully or justly. That is: predestination is God's eternal decree by which he determined that some from the human race should be saved through Christ by pure grace, and others, by his just judgment, should be rejected from that same grace and eternally condemned on account of their sins. Thus predestination will embrace both election and reprobation.

units.la: Alias verò nomen prædestinationis tantùm pro electione vsurpatur, cuiper antithesin reprobatio opponitur. Atqj hoc modo scriptura vbiqj fere loquitur de praedestinatione. Quos praescivit, ait Apostolus Rom. 8. eosdem praedestinauit: quos praedestinauit, eos vocauit: & quos vocauit, eos iustificauit: quos iustificauit, eos glorificauit. & addit, Quis intentabit crimina aduersus electos Dei? Vbi iam expresse electos nominat, quos vocarat praedestinatos. Idem ad Ephes. 1: Elegit nos in ipso antequam iacerentur mundi fundamenta, & praedestinauit nos, quos adoptaret in filios per Christum Iesum in sese.
units.tr: At other times, however, the name predestination is used only for election, to which reprobation is opposed as its antithesis. And in this way Scripture almost everywhere speaks of predestination. Those whom he foreknew, says the Apostle in Rom. 8, he also predestined; those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified. And he adds: Who will bring any charge against God's elect? Here he now expressly names the elect, whom he had called predestined. Likewise in Eph. 1: He chose us in him before the foundation of the world, and predestined us to be adopted as sons through Jesus Christ in himself.

units.la: Augustinus etiam plerunque de praedestinatione hoc sensu loquitur, sumendo eam pro aeterna & gratuita Dei electione, quam interdum distinctionis ergo vocat praedestinationem quae in bono est, & praedestinationem sanctorum. Sed sepissime & vbiqj fermè, quoties de electione & electis loquitur, praedestinatorum & praedestinationis simpliciter meminit. Apud scholasticos quoque Theologos, licet sub eodem praedestinationis nomine, cùm electionem seruanuandorum, tùm reprobationem damnandorum tradent, vix tamen prædestinationis & prædestinatorum vocabula aliter atq; pro electione & electis vsurpari inuenias.
units.tr: Augustine too very often speaks of predestination in this sense, taking it for God's eternal and gratuitous election, which he sometimes, for the sake of distinction, calls the predestination which is in the good, and the predestination of the saints. But very often, and almost everywhere, whenever he speaks of election and the elect, he simply mentions the predestined and predestination. Among the scholastic theologians too, although under the same name of predestination they teach both the election of those to be saved and the reprobation of those to be condemned, you will scarcely find the words predestination and predestined used in any other sense than for election and the elect.

units.la: Appellatione autem ad hunc modum, qui omniũ, vt diximus, receptissimus est, accepta, prædestinationem cum Augustino definiemus, quòd sit gratiæ præparatio. Hoc enim tantum interest, inquit, inter gratiam & prædestinationem, quòd prædestinatio est gratiæ præparatio: gratia verò iam ipsa donatio. Quapropter etiam de fide ad Petrum Diaconum cap. 35. prædestinationem definit, quòd sit gratuitæ donationis præparatio. Per gratiam autē intelligit, tàm gloriam futuram, quàm omnia beneficia Dei in præsenti, quibus tanquā medijs ad finem istum dirigitur & deducuntur prędestinati, seu electi. Hinc de bono perseuerantię cap. 14. ita definit: Prædestinatio sanctorum nihil aliud est, quàm præscientia scilicet & præparatio beneficiorũ Dei, quibus certissimè liberătur, quicunq; liberantur, cæteris in massa perditionis iusto
units.tr: Taking the word in this sense, which is the most widely accepted of all, as we have said, I will define predestination with Augustine as the preparation of grace. For, he says, the only difference between grace and predestination is that predestination is the preparation of grace, while grace is already the gift itself. So too in De fide ad Petrum Diaconum, ch. 35, he defines predestination as the preparation of a freely given gift. By grace he means both the future glory and all of God's benefits in the present, by which, as by means, the predestined, or elect, are directed and led to that end. Hence in De bono perseverantiae ch. 14 he defines it thus: The predestination of the saints is nothing other than the foreknowledge and preparation of God's benefits, by which certainly whoever are delivered are delivered, the rest being left in the mass of perdition by the just

units.la: De prædest. sanctorum cap. 10. Dei iudicio relictis. Eodem recidit quòd alibi prædestinationem interpretatur propositum miserendi: iuxta illud, miserebor, cuius misertus fuero, & commiserabor quem commiseratus fuero.
units.tr: De praedest. sanctorum ch. 10. judgment of God. To the same effect, he elsewhere interprets predestination as the purpose of showing mercy, in line with the words: I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show compassion to whom I have shown compassion.

units.la: Porrò sanctorum ista prædestinatio plerunque in diuinis scripturis electio vocatur. Multi vocati, pauci vero electi, inquit Dominus, Matth.20. Et Paulus ad Eph.1. testatur de electione fidelium in Christo ante iacta mundi fundamenta.
units.tr: Moreover, this predestination of the saints is usually called election in the divine Scriptures. Many are called, but few are chosen, says the Lord, Matt. 20. And Paul, in Eph. 1, testifies to the election of the faithful in Christ before the foundation of the world was laid.

units.la: Haud ignorandum tamen est, varias esse electiones Dei, quarum sacræ litteræ meminerunt. Quædam enim sunt ad certum munus obeundum, ciuile vel Ecclesiasticum, puta regium, sacerdotale, Propheticum, Apostolicum. Sic Aaron fuit comprobatus electus Dei sacerdos, miraculo virgæ germinantis. Eademq; ratione posteri eius, penes quos sacerdotium erat in Israël, electi dicuntur à Domino. Similiter Saul regni vocatur electus Domini. Itemque ex filiis Isai præter Dauidem nemo electus fuit à Domino, nempe ad regnum. De Apostolis quoque que in Euangelio dictum legimus. Nõne ego duodecim vos elegi, & vnus ex vobis est diabolus? de quo etiam vide Luc. 6. ver. 13. Actor. 1. ver. 2.
units.tr: It should not be overlooked, however, that there are various elections of God, of which the sacred letters speak. Some are for discharging a certain office, civil or ecclesiastical, such as the royal, priestly, prophetic, or apostolic office. Thus Aaron was approved as God's chosen priest by the miracle of the budding rod. For the same reason his descendants, in whose hands the priesthood lay in Israel, are called chosen by the Lord. Similarly, Saul is called the Lord's chosen for the kingdom. And among the sons of Isai, none except David was chosen by the Lord, namely for the kingdom. We also read in the Gospel what was said of the apostles: Did I not choose you twelve, and one of you is a devil? On this see also Luke 6:13 and Acts 1:2.

units.la: Accipitur deinde electio Dei, pro electione ad salutem, idque bifariam, vel quæ ab æterno facta est, vel quæ in tempore fit, quæ quidem ex priore ista in mente Dei latente, manat, eiusq; effectus atque executio est; cum videlicet actu iam aliquis e mundo eligitur & Christo inseritur, ac regeneratur ad vitam æternam. De talibus Christus dicit Iohan. 15. Vos e mundo non estis, sed ego elegi vos ex mundo: propterea odit vos mundus. De gemina ista electione ita Augustinus, Electi sumus ante mundi constitutionem ea praedestinatione, in qua Deus sua futura facta præscivit: de mundo autem electi sumus ea vocatione, qua Deus id quod prædestinauit, impleuit.
units.tr: Next, God's election is taken for election to salvation, and this in two ways: either that which was made from eternity, or that which takes place in time. The latter flows from the former, which lies hidden in the mind of God, and is its effect and execution; namely, when someone is actually now chosen out of the world, engrafted into Christ, and regenerated to eternal life. Of such people Christ says in John 15: You are not of the world, but I have chosen you out of the world; therefore the world hates you. Augustine speaks thus of this twofold election: We were chosen before the foundation of the world by that predestination in which God foreknew his future deeds; but we were chosen out of the world by that calling by which God fulfilled what he had predestined.

units.la: Est præterea & hic vocabuli vsus, vt electi in genere dicantur, quicunque externa vocatione ad populum Dei pertinent. Sic Deut. 4. v 37. Et cap. 7. v. 6. Item cap. 14. v. 2. totus Israël dicitur ele-
units.tr: There is also this further use of the word, that those are called elect in a general sense who by external calling belong to the people of God. So Deut. 4:37; ch. 7:6; and likewise ch. 14:2, where all Israel is said

units.la: De præd. Ianct. 17. electus fuisse à Domino, vt nempe ex omnibus populis toto terrarum orbe, esset populus sanctus & peculiaris Domino Deo suo. Quomodo etiam apud Petrum electi vocantur, quicunque ad corpus ecclesiæ vocati sunt, & fideles celentur. Et 1.Cor.1.ait Apostolus Paulus: videtis fratres vocationem vestram, quod non multi sapientes secundum carnem, non multi potentes, nō multi nobiles, supple, vocati estis, sed quæ stulta & infirma sunt in mundo & ignobilia elegit Deus: vbi videmus ad societatem Ecclesiæ vocatos atque electos, pro eodem sumi. Nam vt dicit Augustinus de correpter. & gratia cap.7.&9. quis neget electos, qui credunt & baptizantur? Plane dicuntur electi, sed à nescientibus quid futuri sint, non ab illo, qui illos nouit, Deo. Sunt enim filij Dei, qui nondum sunt nobis, & sunt iam Deo: & sunt rursus quidam, qui filij Dei propter suscep tam vel temporalem gratiam dicuntur à nobis, nec sunt tamen Deo, de quibus ait Iohannes: Exierunt ex nobis sed non erant ex nobis. Nam si fuissent ex nobis, vtiq; permansissent nobiscum. Idipsum & Ambrosius confirmat mat in cap. octauum ad Rom. & Apo- stolus ipsemet, dum cap.11. eius episto- læ discernit inter populum Dei ita in genere nominatum, ratione vocatio- nis & professionis, & inter reliquias in communi cœtu & quasi corpore po- puli istius, quæ saluæ fiunt secundum electionem gratiæ, reliquis pereunti- bus.
units.tr: to have been chosen by the Lord, that out of all the peoples throughout the whole earth it should be a holy people and his own special possession. So too in Peter, all who have been called to the body of the Church and are named faithful are called elect. And in 1 Cor. 1 the Apostle Paul says: Brothers, consider your calling: not many wise according to the flesh, not many powerful, not many noble, are called; but God has chosen the foolish things of the world, and the weak and base things. Here we see that being called to the fellowship of the Church and being chosen are taken to be the same thing. For, as Augustine says in De correptione et gratia, chs. 7 and 9: Who would deny that those who believe and are baptized are elect? Plainly they are called elect, but by those who do not know what they will be, not by God, who knows them. For there are sons of God who are not yet ours, yet are already God's; and there are again some who are called sons of God by us, because of grace received, even if temporary, yet are not God's; of whom John says: They went out from us, but they were not of us. For if they had been of us, they would surely have remained with us. Ambrose confirms the same in his commentary on Romans ch. 8, and the Apostle himself, when in ch. 11 of that letter he distinguishes between the people of God so named in general, by reason of calling and profession, and the remnant in the common assembly and, as it were, the body of that people, who are saved according to the election of grace, the rest perishing.

units.la: Et de ea quidem electione seruan- dorum, & ad vitam æternam ab omni æternitate prædestinatorum, nunc no- bis sermo est. Estq; re ipsa, vt dixi, eadé cum prædestinatione sanctorum, nisi quòd respectu quodam differt. Præde- stinatio enim denotat æternum ac fir- mum in Deo propositum conferendi gratiam & gloriam iis quibus vult: Ele- ctio autem aliquid addit, in quantum videlicet vitam æternam aliquibus præ aliis vult, cum quosdam reprobet: vt bene Thomas 1.quæst.23. art.4. & post eum alij quoque scholastici annotarunt.
units.tr: Now it is of that election of those who are saved, the ones predestined to eternal life from all eternity, that we are speaking. In fact, as I said, it is the same as the predestination of the saints, except that it differs in a certain respect. For predestination denotes God's eternal and firm purpose to confer grace and glory on those whom he wills; election adds something more, namely that he wills eternal life for some rather than others, since he reprobates some. Thomas noted this well in 1 q. 23 a. 4, and other scholastics after him have noted it too.

units.la: Dicitur etiam dilectio : secundum illud Rom.9. Iacob dilexi, Esau autem odio habui. Diligit quidem Deus omnes homines. Omnia enim quæ sunt in natura, diligit, ac nihil eorum, quorum ipse effector est, abominatur: omniumque miseretur, & parcit omnibus, vt habetur Sap. 11. sed gradus sunt dilectionis. Etenim alios diligit, vt creaturas suas: alios, vt membra filij sui, queadmodum copiose explicat Augustinus tract. 110. super Iohan. Et dextre Thomas loco citato art. 3. Deus omnes homines diligit, imo omnes creaturas, in quantum omnibus vult aliquod bonum. Non tamen quodcunque bonum vult omnibus. In quantum igitur quibusdam non vult hoc bonum, quod est vita æterna, dicitur eos odio habere, & reprobare.
units.tr: It is also called love, according to Rom. 9: Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated. God indeed loves all men. For he loves all things that exist in nature, and abhors none of those things of which he himself is the maker; and he has mercy on all and spares all, as is said in Wisdom 11. But there are degrees of love. For he loves some as his creatures, and others as members of his Son, as Augustine explains at length in tractate 110 on John. And Thomas rightly says in the place cited, art. 3: God loves all men, indeed all creatures, insofar as he wills some good for all. Yet he does not will every good for all. Insofar therefore as he does not will this good, which is eternal life, for some, he is said to hate them and to reprobate them.

units.la: Differentiam autem inter electionem & dilectionem Dei, quæ ratione tatum differunt, realiter idem sunt in Deo, assignat art. 4. Prædestinatio, inquit, aliquorum in salutem æternam, præsupponit, quod Deus eorum salutem velit; & ad eam pertinet electio & dilectio: dilectio quidem, in quantum vult eis hoc bonum salutis æternæ. Nam diligere est velle alicui bonum. Electio autem, in quantum hoc bonum aliquibus præ aliis vult, cum quosdam reprobet. Hæc ibi: & repetit eandem distinctione in 9.ad Rom. in illud, Iacob dilexi. Si ergo omnes vellet saluos efficere, diceretur quidem propositum & prædestinatio, & dilectio; sed non electio.
units.tr: The difference between God's election and his love, which differ only in our way of conceiving them, though they are really the same in God, he sets out in art. 4: The predestination of some to eternal salvation presupposes that God wills their salvation; and to this belong election and love: love, insofar as he wills for them this good of eternal salvation, for to love is to will good to someone; election, insofar as he wills this good for some rather than others, since he reprobates some. Thus far Thomas there; and he repeats the same distinction on Rom. 9, on the words Jacob I loved. So if he willed to save all, it would be called purpose, predestination, and love, but not election.

units.la: Sed & hoc obseruandum est cum Augustino, electionem seu prædestinationem quæ in bono est, aliquando significari etiam nomine præscientiæ: sicut ait Apostolus ad Rom. 8. Quos præsciuit eosdem & prædestinauit, vt conformes siant imaginis filij. & cap. 11. non repulit Deus plebem suam quam præsciuit, id est, quam prædestinauit: quod circumstantia textus ostendit. Loquitur enim de reliquijs Iudæorum, quæ saluæ fiebant secundum electionem gratiæ, cæteris pereuntibus. De quibus etiam subiunxit ibidem, quod requirit Israël, id non est assecutus: sed electi assecuti sunt, reliqui vero obcaluerunt.
units.tr: But this too must be observed with Augustine: election or predestination that is for good is sometimes also signified by the name of foreknowledge. So the Apostle says in Rom. 8: Those whom he foreknew, these he also predestined, to be conformed to the image of his Son. And in ch. 11: God has not rejected his people, whom he foreknew, that is, whom he predestined, as the context of the passage shows. For he is speaking of the remnant of the Jews, who were saved according to the election of grace, the rest perishing. Of them he added in the same place: What Israel sought, it has not obtained; but the elect have obtained it, and the rest were hardened.

units.la: Ad eundem modum prisci quoq; patres præscientiam pro prædestinatione accepisse videtur, teste ibidé Augustino. Cuius rei rationem ille hanc affert, quod verbum hoc & facilius intelligatur, & non repugnet, imo congruat veriveritati, quæ de prædestinatione gratiæ prædicatur.
units.tr: In the same way the early Fathers also seem to have taken foreknowledge for predestination, as Augustine testifies in the same place. He gives this reason for it: that the word is more easily understood in this sense, and does not conflict with, but indeed agrees with, the truth that is proclaimed about the predestination of grace.

units.la: Quantum tamen ad proprietatem vocum istarum attinet, generalius est præscire quàm prædestinare. Prædestinatio siquidem sine præscietia non potest esse: potest autem esse sine prædestinatione præscientia. Prædestinatione quippe Deus ea præsciuit quæ fuerat ipse factypus: præscire autem potis est etiam quæ ipse non facit, sicut peccata quæcunque. Nam etsi sunt quædam quæ ita peccata sunt, ut pœnæ etiam sint peccatorum: unde dictum est, tradidit illos in reprobum sensum, vt faciant quæ non conueniunt: tamen non ibi peccatum Dei est, sed iudicium, vt fuse ista Augustinus noster docet, de prædest. sanct. cap. 10. Non male Origines, exponens illud Pauli, Quos præsciuit, hos etiam prædestinauit, vt conformes fiat imagini filij sui, ait, præscientiam non posse accipi pro nuda & simplici notitia, cum Deus etiam impios præscientia sua complectatur, quos tamen non prædestinat, vt conformes fiant imagini filij sui. Ait ergo
units.tr: As far as the proper meaning of these words is concerned, however, to foreknow is more general than to predestine. For predestination cannot exist without foreknowledge, but foreknowledge can exist without predestination. God foreknew by predestination those things of which he himself was the author; but he is able also to foreknow things that he does not himself effect, such as all sins. For although there are certain sins which are also punishments of sins, whence it has been said, "He gave them up to a reprobate mind, so that they do what is not fitting" (Rom. 1), yet there is no sin of God in this, but judgment, as our Augustine teaches at length in On the Predestination of the Saints, chapter 10. Origen, expounding that saying of Paul, "Those whom he foreknew, these he also predestined, that they might be conformed to the image of his Son," rightly says that foreknowledge cannot be taken as bare and simple knowledge, since God also embraces the impious with his foreknowledge, whom nevertheless he does not predestine to be conformed to the image of his Son. He therefore says

units.la: Rom. 1.
units.tr: Rom. 1.

units.la: ergo notitiam illam significare affectu & caritatem, qua Deus aliquos complectatur, sicut ad Timoth. ait Paulus: Novit Dominus qui sint sui.
units.tr: that this knowledge signifies an affection and love by which God embraces certain persons, just as Paul says to Timothy, "The Lord knows those who are his" (2 Tim. 2).

units.la: Quod autem in scholastica Theologia per praescitos reprobi fermè intelligendi veniunt, abusus est vocis contra morem scripturarum, quæ electos, ut dictum est, prædestinatos atq; præscitos nominare solet, non item reprobos & maledictioni affines, instar terræ quæ profert spinas & tribulos.
units.tr: But the fact that in scholastic theology the "foreknown" are generally understood to be the reprobate is an abuse of the word, contrary to the custom of Scripture, which, as has been said, is accustomed to call the elect predestined and foreknown, but not the reprobate and those akin to a curse, like the earth that brings forth thorns and thistles.

units.la: Est autem reprobatio, ut eam scholastici definiunt, præscientia iniquitatis quorundam, & præparatio damnationis eorundem: hoc est, reprobatio est æterna in Deo voluntas quorundam in genere humano, ubi cum aliis in peccatum & damnationem lapsi essent, iusto suo iudicio non miserendi, sed reijciendi eos à salutis in Christo communione, & abijciendi in poenas peccato debitas.
units.tr: Reprobation, as the scholastics define it, is the foreknowledge of certain people's wickedness and the preparation of their damnation. That is, reprobation is the eternal will of God concerning certain persons in the human race who, since they had fallen into sin and damnation along with the others, are by his just judgment not to be pitied, but rejected from communion with salvation in Christ, and cast off to the punishments owed to sin.

units.la: Ut hæc definitio facilius intelligatur: cogitandum est, una eademq; massa damnationis & offensionis nos omnes inuolui
units.tr: So that this definition may be understood more easily, we must consider that we all are wrapped up in one and the same mass of damnation and offence, and that, with the grace of God removed, all men belong to one mass sprinkled with sins and impieties.

units.la: uolui, & remota gratia Dei ad vnam pertinere omnes conspersionem peccatorum & impiorum. Ab ea mafla perditionis, quos gratia & prædestinatione sua Deus discernit, hi sunt electi, & fecundum propositum Dei feruandi: Quos vero in eadem damnabili massa iusto suo iudicio relinquit, ij sunt quos reprobos & damnandos vocamus. Ac damnatis quidem debita redditur pœna: liberatis indebita confertur gratia, vt nec illi fe indignos queratur, nec dignos isti fe glorientur: sed liberatus de non liberato discat, quod etiam sibi supplicium conueniret, nisi gratia subueniret.
units.tr: From that mass of perdition, those whom God distinguishes by his grace and his predestination are the elect, and those who are to be preserved according to God's purpose. But those whom he leaves in that same damnable mass by his just judgment are the ones we call reprobate and condemned. To the condemned the punishment they owe is paid out; to the liberated undeserved grace is given, so that neither the former may complain that they are unworthy, nor the latter boast that they are worthy; but the liberated man, learning from the unliberated, should recognise that the same punishment would have fallen on himself, had grace not come to his aid.

units.la: CAPVT III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: Confirmatio superiorum, quod videlicet ali-qui electi, aliqui reprobati sint à Deo ab æterno: contra errorem quorundam, dicentium omnes homines esse electos in Christo.
units.tr: Confirmation of the above: that some are elected and some reprobated by God from eternity, against the error of certain people who say that all men are elect in Christ.

units.la: NEGARI non potest, Deum præfinito & certo consilio agere omnia, & quidem ab æterno: quoniam nihil tem-pora-
units.tr: It cannot be denied that God does all things by a predetermined and certain counsel, and indeed from eternity, since nothing temporal is in God.

units.la: Sic, Deum proporale est in Deo: alioquin esset mutabilis: vt recte autor De vocat.gentium scripsit lib.2.c. 10. In Deo non est accidens, motus, aut noua voluntas, aut temporale consilium, nec cogitatio eius cum rerum mutabilitate inaequalitate variatur, sed cunctia pariter tempora ac temporalia, sempiterno ac stabili intuitu comprehendit. Quoniam igitur hominum alios seruat, alios damnat Deus, & quidem volens (neque enim ipso simpliciter nolente, & inuito quicquam fieri potest) necessario fatendum est, vtrumque fieri secundum aeternum Dei propositum. Hoc autem nihil aliud est, quam quod Deus alios elegerit, alios reprobarit ab aeterno.
units.tr: Otherwise he would be mutable, as the author of De vocatione gentium rightly wrote in book 2, chapter 10: In God there is no accident, no motion, no new will, no temporal counsel; nor does his thought vary with the mutability and inequality of things, but he comprehends all times and temporal things alike with one eternal and stable gaze. Since, therefore, God saves some of mankind and condemns others, and does so willingly (for nothing can happen if he simply is unwilling and opposed), it must necessarily be confessed that both happen according to God's eternal purpose. This is nothing other than to say that God chose some and reprobated others from eternity.

units.la: Non dissimile est Augustini argumentum a gratia ad praedestinationem. Quibus dona sua gratis data, fidem inquam, bona opera, perseuerantiam in fide & caritate, & alia id genus donat, etiam donaturū se praescuit, & in praescientia sua dispositū ab omni aeternitate. Sed dona illa gratis data, aliis donantur, aliis non donantur ab ipso. Ergo etiam aliis donaturum, aliis non donaturum. rü se ea,ab æterno præsciuit, & in præ- scientia sua disposuit. Id verò hoc ipsum est quod defendimus: Deum vi- delicet alios præ alijs ad gratiam præ- destinasse.
units.tr: Augustine's argument from grace to predestination is no different. To those to whom he gives his gifts freely given (faith, I mean, good works, perseverance in faith and love, and others of this kind), he foreknew that he would give them, and he disposed them in his foreknowledge from all eternity. But those gifts freely given are given by him to some and not given to others. Therefore he foreknew that he would give them to some and not to others, and disposed it in his foreknowledge. This is precisely what we defend: that God predestined some before others to grace.

units.la: » Augustini verba sunt hæc, de bono per- seuerantiâ: Qui, inquit, ita norunt Deum dare sidem, confessionem, obedientiam, perse- uerantiam &c. vt nó ignorent eum daturum se esse præsciuisse, & quibus daturus esset non potuisse nescire, procul dubio norunt prædesti- nationem. Nam in sua quæ falli, mutariq; non potest præscientia, opera sua futura disponere, id omninò nec aliud quicquam est, nisi prædestinatio. Et mox, loquès de gratia fidei & perseuerantiæ vsque in finem, contra Semipelagianos quosdà istorum tem- porum, ait: an forte nec ista dicunt prædesti- nata? Ergo nec dantur à Deo, aut ea se datu- rum esse nesciuit. Quod si etiam dantur, & daturum se ea esse præsciuit, professo prædestinauit. Ibidem cap.2. Orat Ecclesia vt in- credulì credant, & credétes perseuerent. Deus ergo conuertit ad fidem, idemq; perseuerantiâ donat vsque in finem. Hoc Deus futurum esse præsciuit. Ipsa est prædestinatio sanctorum, quos quos elegit in Christo ante constitutionem mundi, ut essent sancti & immaculati &c.
units.tr: These are Augustine's words, from De bono perseverantiae: Those who know that God gives faith, confession, obedience, perseverance, and so on, so as not to be ignorant that he foreknew he would give them, and who cannot fail to know to whom he would give them, undoubtedly know predestination. For to dispose future things by his foreknowledge, which cannot be deceived or changed, is nothing else at all than predestination. And soon after, speaking of the grace of faith and of perseverance to the end, against certain Semipelagians of our own times, he says: Or perhaps they do not say that these things are predestined? Then they are not given by God, or he did not know that he would give them. But if they are given, and he foreknew that he would give them, he has by his own admission predestined them. In the same place, chapter 2: The Church prays that unbelievers may believe, and that believers may persevere. God therefore converts them to faith, and also grants them perseverance to the end. God foreknew that this would be. This is the very predestination of the saints, whom he chose in Christ before the foundation of the world, that they should be holy and without blemish, and so on.

units.la: Tertiò, ex voce electionis firmum est argumentum: aut nullam esse electionem, aut si electio aliqua sit ad vitam æternam, eam esse aliquorum dū taxat, non omnium. Nam si omnibus vita æterna esset parata, seu destinata, quantum ad Deum, diceretur quidem propositum, & prædestinatio, & dilectio, sed non electio, secundum differentiam vocum istarum antea traditam.
units.tr: Thirdly, a strong argument arises from the word election: either there is no election at all, or, if there is some election to eternal life, it belongs to some only and not to all. For if eternal life were prepared or destined for all, as far as God is concerned, there would indeed be talk of purpose, predestination and love, but not of election, according to the distinction between these terms set out earlier.

units.la: Præterea perpende obsecro, Christiane lector, quorsum euadat opinio contraria. Dicit Hub. omnes esse electos, & pariter à patre dilectos in Christo, atque ad vitam æternam destinatos. Attamen cùm certum sit nō omnes seruari, generali electioni alteram specialem adiungit, quæ specialis sit, non quod ad Deū, quasi peculiare consilium pro aliquibus ceperit, sed quod ad homines ipsos qui vniuersalem gratiam Dei sibi applicent: Deum enim elegisse cum conditione fidei, ut qui credunt in Christum salui fiant: qui non credunt, condemnentur.
units.tr: Moreover, Christian reader, I beg you to consider where the contrary opinion leads. Hub. says that all are elect, and equally loved by the Father in Christ, and destined to eternal life. Yet since it is certain that not all are saved, he adds to the general election another, special one. This is special not because God has taken some peculiar counsel for certain people, as though he had chosen them apart, but because of men themselves, who apply to themselves God's universal grace. For God chose on the condition of faith: those who believe in Christ are saved; those who do not believe are condemned.

units.la: Quid hinc aliud colligere est, quàm de fide aliis dada, aliis nō danda, Deum quidem apud se nihil constituisse, nec dare eam quibusdam peculiariter, sed in hominum viribus reliquisse, vt credant Euangelio, aut non credant? Nam si fidem aliquibus dat, profecto peculiare de iis consilium cepit, reliquis praetermissis. Si autem fidem aliquibus peculiariter non dat, actum est de gratia Dei qua seruamur, & vicerint Pelagiani. Deinde, qui ita vt dictum est, de electione imaginantur, verbo electionem Dei fatentes, re ipsa tollunt omnem electionem: quippe, si ita esset, nō Deus nos, sed nosipsū eligeremus, oblatam eius gratiam recipiendo, & essemus electionis Dei figuli. Item, sic eligeremur quia credimus, cum e contrario eligamur vt credamus. Electio siquidem non inuenit, sed facit fideles, teste Augustino.
units.tr: What else can be gathered from this than that God, with regard to faith being given to some and not to others, has settled nothing in himself, nor gives faith peculiarly to certain people, but has left it to the powers of men to believe the Gospel or not? For if he gives faith to some, surely he has taken a peculiar counsel concerning them, the rest being passed over. But if he does not give faith peculiarly to some, then the grace by which we are saved is undone, and the Pelagians have won. Further, those who imagine election in the way described, while professing God's election in words, in fact remove all election. For if it were so, it would not be God who elects us, but we ourselves, by receiving the grace he offers; and we would be the makers of God's election. Likewise we would be elected because we believe, whereas on the contrary we are elected so that we may believe. For, as Augustine testifies, election does not find believers but makes them.

units.la: Verum ne argumentis solum niti vi-deamur, plurima eaq; valde illustria in sacris literis habemus testimonia, probandæ & electioni & reprobationi aliquorum, prout Deus ab aeterno voluit illoillorum misereri, vel non miseretí.
units.tr: But lest we seem to rest only on arguments, we have very many and very clear testimonies in the Holy Scriptures to prove both the election and the reprobation of some, according as God from eternity willed to have mercy on those or not to have mercy on them.

units.la: Christus Matth.11. ait: Gratias tibi ago pater, quòd abscondéris hæc à sapientibus & intelligentibus, & revelàris ea parvulis: Etiá pater, quia sic placuit tibi.
units.tr: Christ says in Matthew 11: I thank you, Father, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding, and revealed them to little ones. Yes, Father, for so it pleased you.

units.la: Matth.13. Vobis datum est nosse mysteria regni cælorum: Illis autem non est datum: sed completur in ipsis prophetia Esaiæ, Auditu audietis & non intelligetis, videntes videbitis & non cernetis. Matth.20. Sedere ad dextram & sinistram meam, dabitur quibus paratum est à patre meo. Et cap.22. Multi sunt vocati, pauci verò electi. Non igitur omnes electi, quibus Euangelium annunciatur: multò minus quibus id non annunciatur; quorum infinitus hodie est numerus, & fuit, prisicis præsertim ætatibus, cùm gentes omnes suis ipsorum viis incedere sinerentur.
units.tr: Matthew 13: To you it is given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it is not given. But the prophecy of Isaiah is fulfilled in them: By hearing you shall hear and not understand; seeing you shall see and not perceive. Matthew 20: To sit at my right hand and at my left will be given to those for whom it is prepared by my Father. And chapter 22: Many are called, but few are chosen. Therefore not all are elect, even among those to whom the Gospel is announced, much less among those to whom it is not announced. Their number is infinite today, and has been so, especially in earlier ages, when all nations were allowed to walk in their own ways.

units.la: Matth.24. Nisi contraherentur dies illi, periret omnis caro, sed propter electos contrahentur. Ibidem: Surgent PseudoChristi & Pseudoprophetæ, & edent signa atque miracula, ita ut seducát, si fieri possit, etiam electos. Si igitur omnes essent electi, nemo seduci aut perire posset, contra quam
units.tr: Matthew 24: Unless those days were shortened, no flesh would be saved; but for the sake of the elect those days will be shortened. Also: False Christs and false prophets will arise and will show signs and wonders, so as to deceive, if it were possible, even the elect. If therefore all were elect, no one could be deceived or perish, which is contrary to what

units.la: Gg ij ibi-
units.tr: Gg ij there-

units.la: ibidem dicitur de duobus in agro, alterum assumtum, alterum relictum iri. Matth.25. Filius hominis statuet oues suas ad dextram suam: hædos autem ad sinistram, & dicet iis qui ad dextram erunt: Venite benedicti patris mei, possidete regnum paratum vobis ab iactis mundi fundamentis. Iis autem qui ad sinistram erunt dicet: Abite maledicti in ignem, qui paratus est diabolo & angelis eius.
units.tr: there is said in the same place, of two men in the field, one to be taken and the other left. Matthew 25: The Son of Man will set his sheep at his right hand, and the goats at his left, and he will say to those at the right: Come, you blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. But to those at the left he will say: Depart from me, cursed, into the fire prepared for the devil and his angels.

units.la: Iohan.10. ad Iudæos in obstinatione permanentes dixit Dominus: Vos non creditis: non enim estis ex ovibus meis: oves mea vocem meam audiunt, & ego agnosco eas, & sequuntur me, & ego vitam æternam do eis, nec peribunt in æternum, nec rapiet eas quisquam e manu mea.
units.tr: In John 10, the Lord said to the Jews who remained obstinate: You do not believe, for you are not of my sheep. My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me; and I give them eternal life, and they shall never perish, nor shall anyone snatch them out of my hand.

units.la: Ioh.17. Dominus suos a non suis separans ait; Non pro mundo rogo te pater, sed pro iis quos dedisti mihi: & hos dicit diligi a patre, & nomen eius se ipsis manifestare, & sanctificari ac seruari eos ad vitam æternam: Quorum nihil in mundum illum competit, pro quo non rogat. Discrimen igitur statuitur manifestum, inter electos & reprobos. Hinc AuAugustinus tract.107. Mundum, pro quo non rogat, vult intelligi, qui non sunt in ea forte gratia, ut eligantur e mundo. Rogat autem pro eis, quos ipsi dedit pater. Per hoc enim quod eos iam illi pater dedit, factum est, ut non pertineant ad eum mundum pro quo non rogat; mundum videlicet damnandorum, ut idem testatur tract.110. pro quo dicit se non orare, quia quo praedestinatus sit non ignorat.
units.tr: In John 17, separating his own from those who are not his, the Lord says: I do not pray for the world, Father, but for those whom you have given me; and these, he says, are loved by the Father, and he manifests his name to them, and they are sanctified and kept to eternal life. None of this applies to that world for which he does not pray. A clear distinction is therefore drawn between the elect and the reprobate. Hence Augustine, tract. 107: 'The world for which he does not pray is meant to be those who are not in that grace by which they are chosen out of the world. But he prays for those whom the Father has given him. For by the fact that the Father has already given them to him, it comes about that they do not belong to that world for which he does not pray, namely the world of the damned,' as he also testifies in tract. 110, where he says that he does not pray for the world, because he does not know that it has been predestined.

units.la: Ibidem 17. Ioh. Iudas dicitur periisse, utpote filius perditionis: ceteri cum Christo permanserunt in ipsius tentationibus, & non perierunt, utpote electi & dati ipsi a patre, ut daret eis vitam aeternam. Quod autem Iudas quoque referatur inter eos, quos pater filio dederat, vel hominum dictum est opinione, ut quibusdam placet: vel accipiendum est, respectu duntaxat Apostolatus, quemadmodum Augustinus exponit tract.106.
units.tr: Ibidem, on John 17: Judas is said to have perished, as the son of perdition; the others remained with Christ in his temptations and did not perish, as chosen and given to him by the Father, that he might give them eternal life. That Judas too is counted among those whom the Father had given to the Son is said either by the opinion of men, as some are pleased to hold, or it must be understood only with respect to the apostleship, as Augustine explains in tractate 106.

units.la: Porro cum scribit Lucas Act.13. Credidisse quotquot erat ordinati ad vitam aeternam: dubitationi locum nullum reliquit, quin hominum alij sint, alij non sint praeordinati seu praedestinati ad vitam.
units.tr: Moreover, when Luke writes in Acts 13, "As many as were ordained to eternal life believed," he leaves no room for doubt that some men are foreordained or predestined to life and others are not.

units.la: Quid vero Paulus, instrumentū electum, qui raptus in paradisum audiuit verba ineffabilia? Quoties prædestinationis veritatem inculcat? Ad Rom.8. ait: Quos præscciuit, eosdem & prædestinauit, vt conformes fiant imaginisilij sui. Quos autem prædestinauit, eos & vocauit: & quos vocauit, eos iustificauit, & quos iustificauit, eos etiam glorificauit.
units.tr: What of Paul, the chosen instrument, who was caught up into paradise and heard unspeakable words? How often does he impress upon us the truth of predestination? In Romans 8 he says: "Whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son. Whom he predestined, them he also called; and whom he called, them he also justified; and whom he justified, them he also glorified."

units.la: Sequentia porrò capita 9.10.11. quid continent, nisi luculentissimam expositionem præsentis doctrinæ de aliorū atque aliorum electione & reprobatione, secundum propositum Dei æternum? Vt ex Apostoli disputatione pauca duntaxat excerpamus, cap.9. de Iacob & Esau gemellis, vno conceptis cōcubitu, inquit: nondum natis pueris, cum nihil fecissent boni vel mali, vt propositum Dei maneret, quod est secundum ipsius electionem, non ex operibus sed ex vocante dictum esse Rebecca: Maior seruiet minori. Et citat locum Malachiæ: Iacob dilexi: Esau odio habui. Et mox, adducto testimonio quodā, & exemplo Pharaonis ex Mosè, concludit his verbis: Itaq; cuius vult mi-
units.tr: What do the following chapters, 9, 10 and 11, contain, if not a most lucid exposition of this doctrine concerning the election and reprobation of some and others, according to the eternal purpose of God? To take only a few points from the Apostle's argument: in chapter 9, concerning Jacob and Esau, twins conceived of one intercourse, he says: "The children not yet being born, and having done nothing good or evil, so that the purpose of God according to election might stand, not of works but of him who calls, it was said to Rebekah: The elder shall serve the younger." And he cites the passage of Malachi: "Jacob I loved, Esau I hated." And soon after, having adduced a certain testimony and the example of Pharaoh from Moses, he concludes with these words:

units.la: Malac.i. feretur; quem autem vult indurat. Item, an-non habet figulus potestatem in lutum, vt ex eadem massa faciat aliud vas ad decus, aliud ad dedecus? & subiungit statim de vasis irae coagmentatis ad interitum, & de vasis misericordiae, quae dicit praeparata a Deo ad gloriam.
units.tr: Malachi 1. "...is carried; but whom he wills he hardens." Likewise: "Has not the potter power over the clay, to make from the same lump one vessel to honour and another to dishonour?" And he immediately adds concerning the vessels of wrath fitted for destruction, and the vessels of mercy, which he says were prepared by God for glory.

units.la: Capite 11. testatur, in multitudine pereuntium Deum semper habere quasdam reliquias seruandorum, secundum electionem gratiae: de quibus etiam dicit: Electi assecuti sunt, reliqui vero obcaluerunt, sicut scriptum est: Dedit eis Deus spiritum soporis, oculos vt non videant, & aures vt non audiant.
units.tr: In chapter 11 he testifies that, in the multitude of those who perish, God always has certain remnants to be saved, according to the election of grace; of whom he also says: "The elect obtained it, but the rest were hardened, as it is written: God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that they should not see, and ears that they should not hear."

units.la: Perinsignis etiam est locus ad Eph.1. Benedictus Deus, qui benedixit nobis omni benedictione spirituali in coelis, in Christo Iesu: sicut elegit nos in ipso, antequam iacerentur mundi fundamenta, vt essemus sancti & inculpati coram ipso per caritatem: praedestinans nos quos adoptaret in filios per Iesum Christum in se, pro beneuolo affectu voluntatis suae, ad laudem gloriosae suae gratiae &c.
units.tr: There is also a most remarkable passage in Ephesians 1: "Blessed be God, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus; as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him in love; predestining us to be adopted as sons through Jesus Christ to himself, according to the good pleasure of his will, to the praise of the glory of his grace, etc."

units.la: Ad Philipp. 2. Deus est qui efficit in nobis velle & perficere, pro bona voluntate: sua vtique,non tua, vt modò vidimus in verbis ad Ephes.
units.tr: In Philippians 2: "It is God who works in us both to will and to perform, according to his good pleasure": his, that is, and not yours, as we have just seen in the words to the Ephesians.

units.la: Poster.ad Theff. 2. eis qui pereunt, & puniuntur efficacia deceptionis, vt credant mendacio,opponit Apostolus dilectos& electos Dei, qui gratia ipsius (pro qua idcirco ibidem gratias Deo agit) vocantur per Euangelium, ad obtinendam gloriam Domini nostri Iesu Christi.
units.tr: In the second letter to the Thessalonians 2, the Apostle sets against "those who perish and are punished, the working of deception, so that they believe a lie," the beloved and chosen of God, who (for which reason he gives thanks to God there) "are called through the Gospel, to obtain the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ."

units.la: De hac eadem vocatione & electione inquit 2.ad Tim.1.vocauit nos Deus vocatione sancta, non ex operibus nostris, sed ex suo proposito & gratia, quae data est nobis in Christo ante tempora secularia: manifestatur autem nunc per apparitionem Iesu Christi. Et cap.2.eiusd.Epist. Firmum,inquit,stat fundamentum Dei, habens sigillum hoc, Novit Dominus qui sint sui. Caterum in magna domo non tantum sunt vasa aurea & argentea, sed etiam lignea & testacea, & alia quidem ad decus,alia ad dedecus.
units.tr: Concerning this same calling and election he says in 2 Timothy 1: "God called us with a holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace, which was given to us in Christ before the secular times, and is now made manifest through the appearing of Jesus Christ." And in chapter 2 of the same letter: "The firm foundation of God stands, having this seal: The Lord knows those who are his. But in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and earthenware, and some indeed to honour, others to dishonour."

units.la: Apocal. 13. & 17. de bestia dicitur, quod eam adoraturi & admiraturi essent omnes incolae terrae, quorum nomina scripta non sunt in libro vitae a iactis mundi fundamentis. Periphrasis est reproborum & percunctorum euntium, quibus opponuntur electi, quorum nomina scripta sunt in libro vitæ ante mundi constitutionem, quoniq; ita tuetur diuina clementia, vt seduci non possint, saltem finaliter.
units.tr: In Revelation 13 and 17 it is said of the beast that all the inhabitants of the earth, whose names are not written in the book of life from the foundation of the world, would worship and marvel at it. This is a periphrasis for the reprobate and the perishing, to whom the elect are opposed, whose names are written in the book of life before the constitution of the world; and the divine mercy so guards these that they cannot be seduced, at least finally.

units.la: Testatur & Iudas in sua Epist. seductores ἀσεβεῖς προγεγραμμένοι εἰς τοῦτο τὸ κρίμα: quod Glossa & Aquinas (ne quis nostros talium glossarum criminetur artifices) exponunt, ab æterno Dei præscientia præuisos in hoc iudicium reprobationis præsentis, vt fordescant, & alios in sordes præcipitent.
units.tr: Jude also testifies in his letter that the seducers are "ungodly, who were long ago marked out [προγεγραμμένοι] for this judgement" (which the Gloss and Aquinas, lest anyone accuse our people of being makers of such glosses, explain as foreseen from the eternal foreknowledge of God for this present judgement of reprobation, that they may grow foul, and push others into filth).

units.la: Veteris Testamenti literis eandem doctrinam proditam legimus. Nam Mosi dicit Dominus Exod. 33. Miserebor, cuius misertus fuero, & commiserabor, quem commiseratus fuero. Et de Pharaone dicit Scriptura Exod. 9. Ad hoc ipsum excitaui te, vt ostendam in te potentiam meam, & vt nomen meum annuncietur in vniuersa terra. Commemorantur & alia eiusmodi testimonia in disputatione ad Rom. Quibus adde quod Prouerb. 16. habetur: Omnia fecit Deus propter semetipsum, etiam impium ad diem malum. lum. Et 1. Sam. 2. de filijs Eli dicitur, quod vocem patris sui non audierint, quia Dominus voluerit eos occidere. Item 2. Paralip. 25.v.16. Prophetæ verba sunt ad regem Amasiam: Noui quod cogitauerit Deus perdere te, quia non paruisti verbo meo.
units.tr: We read the same doctrine set forth in the letters of the Old Testament. For the Lord says to Moses in Exodus 33: "I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy, and I will show compassion on whom I will show compassion." And Scripture says of Pharaoh in Exodus 9: "For this very purpose I have raised you up, that I may show my power in you, and that my name may be proclaimed in all the earth." Other testimonies of this kind are recalled in the disputation on Romans. To these add that Proverbs 16 says: "God made all things for himself, even the wicked for the evil day." And 1 Samuel 2 says of the sons of Eli that they did not heed the voice of their father, because the Lord was willing to kill them. Likewise 2 Chronicles 25:16: these are the words of the prophet to King Amaziah: "I know that God has purposed to destroy you, because you have not obeyed my word."

units.la: Ex his & similibus sententijs sacrarum literarum intelligunt omnes, qui veritatis quàm contentionis amantiores sunt, electionem non totum genus humanum complecti, sed alios in eo esse electos ad salutem, alios ab eadé reiectos secundum æternum Dei consilium atq; beneplacitum. Intelligunt etiam ijdem insufficientem esse definitionem prædestinationis quæ à quibusdam affertur, quasi prædestinatio sanctorum seu electio, nihil aliud sit, quàm decretum Dei de modo salutis consequendæ per Christum: Et reprobatio nihil aliud, quàm decretu eius de damnandis infidelibus & extra Christum manentibus. Quin hæc Deus ita decreuerit & seruet, dubium non est: sed probationes & testimonia allata, præterea euincunt, Deum etiam decreuisse
units.tr: From these and similar sayings of Sacred Scripture, all who are more lovers of truth than of contention understand that election does not embrace the whole human race, but that some in it are chosen to salvation and others are rejected by the same, according to the eternal counsel and good pleasure of God. The same people also understand that the definition of predestination which some put forward is insufficient, as if the predestination or election of the saints were nothing other than God's decree concerning the mode of obtaining salvation through Christ, and reprobation nothing other than his decree concerning the damning of unbelievers and those who remain outside Christ. Indeed, that God has so decreed and preserves these things is not in doubt; but the proofs and testimonies adduced furthermore demonstrate that God has also decreed

units.la: sase,quibusnam daturus,aut non daturus essetfidem, qua Christo inserimur ad salutem,in ipso & per ipsum.
units.tr: whom he would or would not give faith, by which we are grafted into Christ for salvation, in him and through him.

units.la: CAPVT IV. Confutatio obiectionum quarundam.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV. Refutation of certain objections.

units.la: QVID vero aduersarij ad ista? Deus inquiunt vult omnes homines saluos fieri,& ad agnitionem veritatis venire.
units.tr: But what do our opponents say to this? God, they say, wills that all men be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth.

units.la: Quantum igitur ad Deum, parata est omnibus vita æterna,nec perit quisquam quòd Deus nullam gratiam ei conferre velit,sed quod acceptam gratiam repudiârit. In hac sententia erant Pelagianorū reliquiæ illæ apud Prosperum,de quibus in eius Epist.ad Augustt.
units.tr: So far as God is concerned, eternal life is prepared for everyone, and no one perishes because God is unwilling to confer grace on him, but because he has rejected the grace he received. This was the view of those remnants of the Pelagians that Prosper mentions, concerning whom see his letter to Augustine.

units.la: Respondeo, non dicit Apostolus, quòd velit omnes saluos facere, sed omnes saluos fieri,σωθῆναι: omnium nepe inuitatione ad salutem & veritatis cognitionem: Itemq;,approbatione conuersionis omnium. Sed non vult in omnibus & singulis efficere,vt credant & seruentur. Hoc enim si vellet,impleretur omninò eius voluntas, & nemo damnaretur. Iam autem miseretur quorum rum vult, & indurat quos vvlt, ordinauitque consilio suo quos & quales prædicatæ & oblatæ misericordiæ participes esse velit, vt totidem verbis inculcat Lutherus in feruo arbitrio: vbi istum & similes locos, Nolo mortem peccatoris: Ierusalem quoties volui te cogregare, &c. eo plane modo explicat. Augustinus Enchirid.ad Laur. cap. 103. docet etiam sic recte intelligi dictum Apostoli: vult omnes homines saluos fieri, id est, omne genus hominum, per quafcunq; differentias distributum, reges, potentes, pauperes, humiles &c. Ide alibi exponit: Vult omnes homines saluos fieri, vt intelligantur omnes prædestinati: quia omne genus hominum in ijs est. Sed de hoc loco tulius egimus supra lib.2. cap.3.
units.tr: I answer: the Apostle does not say that God wills to save all, but that all should be saved, σωθῆναι [sōthēnai]: that is, that all are invited to salvation and to the knowledge of the truth, and likewise that the conversion of all is approved. But God does not will to bring about in all and each that they believe and are saved. For if he willed this, his will would be wholly fulfilled and no one would be condemned. As it is, he has mercy on whom he wills, and hardens whom he wills, and by his counsel he has ordained whom and what sort of people he wills to share in the mercy that is preached and offered. Luther, in The Bondage of the Will, urges this very point in the same words, and there he explains in just this way such passages as I do not desire the death of a sinner and Jerusalem, how often would I have gathered you, and so on. Augustine, in the Enchiridion to Laurentius, chapter 103, also teaches that the Apostle's words are rightly understood in this way: he wills all men to be saved, that is, every kind of men, distributed by all their differences: kings, the powerful, the poor, the humble, and so on. The same author explains it elsewhere: He wills all men to be saved, so that all the predestined may be understood, because every kind of man is among them. But we have treated this passage more fully above, in book 2, chapter 3.

units.la: Non dissimilis est locus 2. Pet. 3. Haud tardat Dominus quà promisit, quemadmodum nonnulli tarditatem existimant: verum patiens est erga nos, non volens vllos perire, sed omnes ad pœnitentiam tendere. Si neminem vult perire, falsum est quod in æterno consilio suo decreuerit, atque ideo velit, vt aliqui, imò plurimi percant.
units.tr: The passage in 2 Peter 3 is not dissimilar: The Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness; but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance. If he wills that no one perish, it is false that in his eternal counsel he has decreed, and therefore wills, that some, indeed very many, should perish.

units.la: sap.107. (marginal reference)
units.tr: Wisd. 107. (marginal reference)

units.la: sap.107. (marginal reference) cant. Item, si vult vt omnes pœnitentiâ agant, falsum erit, nolle Deum, vt omnes per pœnitentiam Christo adducantur & viuant.
units.tr: Wisd. 107. cant. Likewise, if he wills that all should repent, it will be false that God is unwilling that all should be brought to Christ through repentance and live.

units.la: His mirificè oblectat se Huberus: sed frustra, quamdiu Psalmographi illud stat, Noster Deus in cœlo est, omnia quæ vult facit: & Apostoli illud, cuius vult miseretur, & quem vult indurat.
units.tr: Huber takes great delight in this, but in vain, as long as that saying of the psalmist stands: Our God is in heaven; he does whatever he pleases, and that of the Apostle: he has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens.

units.la: Sed ne scripturas aduersa quasi fróte committere videamur, pro conciliatione sciendum est, dictum Petri à viris doctis non abs re de electorum vniuersalitate exponi, non tantum quia frequens est eiusmodi restrictio in similibus locutionibus sacrarum literarum, sed etiam quia res ipsa exigere eam hîc videtur. Quid enim, an mundi finis propter reprobos differtur, & non potius propter electos Dei? Cum credidérint qui destinati sunt in vitam æternam, ad resurrectionem peruenietur,» inquit Ambrosius: quod quàm verè dictum sit, testatur responsum Apocaly. 6. vers. 11.
units.tr: But lest we seem to set Scripture against itself, for reconciliation we must know that the words of Peter have been rightly explained by learned men as referring to the universality of the elect. This is not only because such restriction is frequent in similar expressions of Holy Scripture, but also because the matter itself seems to require it here. For is the end of the world delayed on account of the reprobate, and not rather on account of God's elect? When those destined for eternal life have believed, the resurrection will come, says Ambrose; and how truly this was said is attested by the answer in Apocalypse 6, verse 11.

units.la: Manendo tamen in generalitate omomnium hominum, sensus erit quem Thomas & alij assignant, quòd non velit vllos perire voluntate signi, vt loquuntur, quatenus omnes præceptis, minis, præmiis, atque etiam tolerantia & longanimitate sua ad pœnitentiam inuitat: sicut scriptum est: An diuitias clementiæ & longanimitatis eius contemnis? Ignoras quòd benignitas Dei ad pœnitentiam te inuitet? Sed hoc quæritur, an non fides & pœnitentia dona Dei sint, quæ aliis det, aliis non det, idque secundum consilium voluntatis suæ imperuestigabile? Id certè clarius est, quàm vt à quoquam non Pelagiano negari queat. Igitur rectè dicitur, Deum velle vt omnes pœnitetiam agat; hoc est, vocat & inuitat omnes ad pœnitentiam: sed nō efficit eam in omnibus, & ne vult quidem: quoniam misereatur quorum vult, & quos vult indurat.
units.tr: Yet, remaining within the generality of all men, the sense will be what Thomas and others assign: that he wills that no one perish by the will of sign, as they call it, insofar as he invites all to repentance by precepts, threats, rewards, and also by his forbearance and longsuffering: as it is written, Do you despise the riches of his kindness and longsuffering? Do you not know that the goodness of God leads you to repentance? But the question is this: are faith and repentance not gifts of God, which he gives to some and not to others, and that according to the unsearchable counsel of his will? That is surely clearer than anything that no one who is not a Pelagian could deny. Therefore it is rightly said that God wills all to repent; that is, he calls and invites all to repentance, but he does not bring it about in all, and indeed he does not even will to do so, since he has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens.

units.la: Hoc pacto & Lutherus distinguit de seruo arbitrio: Non vult mortem peccatoris, verbo scilicet; quia verbo salutis ad omnes venit: vult autem illam voluntate illa imimperscrutabili. Ac multis ibide discer- nit, inter voluntatem Dei occultam ac praedicatam: non quòd proprie sit diuersa voluntas quæ in Deo est, sed locutio diuersa est de voluntate, quia nomen hoc diuersimodè accipitur. Prædicata seu reuelata Dei voluntas est, quicquid ab initio mundi, vel per ipsum Deum immediatè, vel per eius ministros, oblatum est hominibus, præcipiendo, exhortando, minando, benefaciendo. Occulta autem est arcanum illud in Deo consilium de rerum euentu: puta quos & quales, fide donatos speciali gratia, prædicatæ & oblatæ misericordiæ participes esse velit. Secundus est eandem distinctionem etiam Brentius in I. Sam. 2. edisserens locum de filiis Eli: & expl. Catechismi, in illud: Fiat voluntas tua.
units.tr: In this way Luther too distinguishes in The Bondage of the Will: He does not will the death of a sinner, by the word, that is; because he comes to all by the word of salvation; but he wills it by that unsearchable will. And in many places there he distinguishes between the hidden and the preached will of God: not that the will which is in God is properly different, but the way of speaking about the will is different, because this term is taken in different senses. The preached or revealed will of God is whatever has been offered to men from the beginning of the world, either by God himself immediately or through his ministers, by commanding, exhorting, threatening, and doing good. The hidden will, however, is that secret counsel in God concerning the outcome of things: namely, whom and what sort of people, given faith by special grace, he wills to share in the mercy that is preached and offered. Brenz too makes the same distinction, expounding in On 1 Samuel 2 the passage about the sons of Eli, and in his explanation of the Catechism on the words Thy will be done.

units.la: Id æquus lector obseruet cótra quorundam clamores, qui cùm genuina Lutheri atque Brentij soboles audire velint, cauillando tamè & sophisticádo odiosam reddere conantur receptam distinctione & fundatam in verbo Dei. Nam quemadmodum scriptum legimus: quòd velit omnes homines saluos fieri, quòd nolens patiens sit erga nos nolens vllos perire, sed ad pœnitentiam tendere: & quòd voluntas Dei sit sanctificatio nostra. Item, quoties volui congregare filios tuos & noluisti? Ita audimus & in diuinis scripturis legimus: Consilium meum stabit, & voluntatem meam faciam inquit Dominus. Omnia quæcunque voluit, fecit. Miseretur cuius vult, & indurat quem vult: Item, voluntati eius quis resistet? In quibus & similibus magna erit repugnantia, nisi distinctio adhibeatur, secundum quam intelligamus fieri aliquid contra Dei voluntatem, id est, contra præceptum aut prohibitionem, quod tamen nō fit præter & contra voluntatem quæ ipse est. Nam magna opera Domini, & exquisita voluntas eius in omnes, ut miro & ineffabili modo non fiat præter eius voluntatem; quod tamē fit contra eius voluntatē, quia non fieret si non sineret, nec vtiq; nolens sed volēs finit, nec sineret bonus fieri male, nisi omnipotens demalo posset facere bene, inquit AuAugustad Laur. cap. 100. Vide etiam lib.1. Sententiarum dist. 45. & sequentibus: vbi multa Magister de duplici Dei voluntate, beneplaciti & signi, vt scholastici appellant. Si cui lubet, consulat etiam Chrysostomum hom. 18. ad Heb.
units.tr: A fair reader should note this against the outcry of certain people who, though they wish to hear the genuine offspring of Luther and Brenz, try by quibbling and sophistry to make odious the distinction that has been received and is grounded in the Word of God. For as we read in Scripture: that he wills all men to be saved; that he is longsuffering toward us, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance; and that the will of God is our sanctification. Likewise, how often would I have gathered your children, and you would not? So we hear and read in the divine Scriptures: My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure, says the Lord. Whatever he willed, he did. He has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens. Likewise, who has resisted his will? In these and similar passages there will be great contradiction unless a distinction is applied, by which we understand that something is done against the will of God, that is, against his precept or prohibition, which nevertheless does not happen apart from and against that will which he himself is. For the great works of the Lord, and his exquisite will, are such that, in a marvellous and inexpressible way, nothing happens apart from his will; yet something does happen against his will, because it would not happen if he did not permit it, and he permits it not unwillingly but willingly. Nor would the good God permit evil to be done unless the almighty could bring good out of evil, as Augustine says in To Laurentius, chapter 100. See also book 1 of the Sentences, distinction 45 and following, where the Master says much about the twofold will of God, of good pleasure and of sign, as the Schoolmen call them. If anyone wishes, let him also consult Chrysostom, homily 18 on Hebrews.

units.la: Secundo obijcitur, Promissionem gratiæ esse viuersalem; proinde neminem gratia reiectum seu reprobatum, quantum ad Deum attinet.
units.tr: Second, it is objected that the promise of grace is universal; therefore, so far as God is concerned, no one is rejected or reprobated by grace.

units.la: Respondeo: Promissio gratiæ vniuersalis est, quantu ad credentes, quatenus videlicet nemo cuiuscunque gentis aut conditionis, a salute excluditur, dummodo in Christum vere crediderit. Contra, infideles cuiuscunque gentis aut conditionis, expresse excluduntur a fructu promissionum, secundum dicta: Qui crediderit & baptizatus fuerit, seruabitur, &c. Omnis qui credit in filium, non pereat. Hæc est voluntas patris, vt omnis qui credit in filium, habeat vitam æternam. In hoc omnis qui credit iustificatur. Iustitia Dei in omnes & super omnes qui credunt. Non enim est distinctio. Et passim in hunc modum inculcatur promissio vitæ & salutis fa-
units.tr: I answer: the promise of grace is universal as regards believers, insofar as, to be clear, no one of any nation or condition is excluded from salvation, provided he has truly believed in Christ. On the contrary, unbelievers of any nation or condition are expressly excluded from the fruit of the promises, according to the sayings: He who believes and is baptized will be saved, and so on. Whoever believes in the Son shall not perish. This is the will of the Father, that everyone who believes in the Son should have eternal life. In this, everyone who believes is justified. The righteousness of God is upon all and over all who believe; for there is no distinction. And throughout Scripture the promise of life and salvation is pressed in this way, to every believer, with unbelievers excluded on the other side. Promise

units.la: Matth. 16. Ioh. 3. Ioh. 6. Act. 13. Rom. 3. őta cuiuis credenti, exclusis è contrario incredulis. Promissio enim fidem requirit; quæ quia non omnium, sed electorum est, teste Paulo, idcirco promissionum efficacia penes electos demum residet, sicut Apostolus quoq; ad Rom. "docet: Promissiones Dei pertinere ad veros Israëlitas, ad spirituale semen: quod electum est à Deo, non ex operibus, sed ex gratia vocantis.
units.tr: Matt. 16; John 3; John 6; Acts 13; Rom. 3. requires faith; and since faith belongs not to all but to the elect, as Paul testifies, the efficacy of the promises rests in the end with the elect. So the Apostle also teaches in Romans that the promises of God pertain to the true Israelites, to the spiritual seed, which was chosen by God, not from works, but from the grace of him who calls.

units.la: Admonendi tamen hic sumus, licet promissio credentium & electorum propria sit, quantum ad efficaciam: prædicari tamen eam oportere indiscriminatim in aures omnium, fidelium & infidelium, electorum & reproborum. Atq; hoc sensu etiam concedimus, promissiones esse universales, quantum nempe ad prædicationem externam: quia verbi minister non potest aut debet electos à reprobis discernere. Interim gratiam prædicatam atq; oblatam omnibus, non omnes assequuntur: sed electi assequuntur, cæteri non item; atq; ita, vt verbis vtar Lutheri, à prædestinatione pendent omnia, &c.
units.tr: We must nevertheless be reminded here that, although the promise belongs to believers and the elect as far as its efficacy is concerned, it must still be preached indiscriminately to the ears of all, faithful and unfaithful, elect and reprobate. In this sense we also grant that the promises are universal, as far as external preaching goes, because a minister of the Word cannot, and ought not, distinguish the elect from the reprobate. Yet not all obtain the grace that is preached and offered to all: the elect obtain it, the rest do not. And so, to use Luther's words, all things depend on predestination, and so on.

units.la: Tertia obiectio. Quicunq; ad Ecclesiam pertinent, appellantur electi. Ad Ecclesiam vero tam mali quàm boni pertinent. Ergo tam mali quàm boni sunt electi, nemine prorsus præterito.
units.tr: Third objection. Whoever belongs to the Church is called elect. Both bad and good belong to the Church. Therefore both bad and good are elect, without exception.

units.la: Sed obiectio isthæc duo peccat. I. Moris quidem est scripturarum, vt quicunq; ad Ecclesiæ cœtum pertinentes appellentur electi: sed non omnes idcirco ad vitam æternam à Deo electi sunt secundum ipsius propositū. Multi enim sunt electi nobis, secundum iudicium caritatis, & non sunt Deo: & contrà: secundum homonymiam vocabuli prius traditam.
units.tr: But this objection errs in two ways. First, it is indeed the usage of Scripture to call elect all who belong to the assembly of the Church. But not all of them are for that reason elected by God to eternal life according to his own purpose. For there are many who are elect to us, according to the judgment of charity, and are not elect to God; and conversely, according to the ambiguity of the term explained earlier.

units.la: II. Plus est in conclusione quàm in præmissis. Neq; enim valet consecutio: In complexu Ecclesiæ & electorum sunt tam mali quàm boni (eo quo dictum est sensu) Ergo omnes homines sunt electi. Perinde id est ac si dicas: In Ecclesia Christi sunt boni ac mali: Item in hac vel illa ciuitate, verbi gratia, Heidelbergensi, Tubingensi, aut quauis alia, sunt boni & mali. Ergo Ecclesia Christiana, aut hæc illaue ciuitas omnes nes homines complectitur, nemine præterito. Bella consequentia: quasi indefinitè boni & mali homines, atque omnes homines, inter sese æqui pollentia sint.
units.tr: Second, the conclusion contains more than the premises. The inference does not hold: "In the whole body of the Church and the elect there are both bad and good (in the sense already stated); therefore all men are elect." That is just as if you were to say: "In the Church of Christ there are good and bad; likewise in this or that city, for example Heidelberg, Tübingen, or any other, there are good and bad. Therefore the Christian Church, or this or that city, embraces all men without exception." A fine inference, as if indefinitely good and bad men and all men were equal in weight!

units.la: Quarta obiectio: Ad iustitiam in distributionibus pertinet, vt æqualibus non dentur inæqualia: Ergo Deus, cum iustissimis sit, ex massa perditionis in qua considerati omnes æqualiter nos habemus, non vnum eligit & alterum reprobat.
units.tr: Fourth objection: It belongs to justice in distributions that unequal things not be given to equals. Therefore God, since he is most just, does not choose one and reprobate another out of the mass of perdition, in which we all stand equally considered.

units.la: Responsio: Antecedens locum habet in his quę distribuuntur ex debito: non autem in ijs quæ spōte ac ex gratia quis distribuit, vbi prout vult & quibus vult, potest dare plus vel minus absque iniustitia: dummodo debitum nemini subtrahat. Puta, si duos habeas debitores, atq; vni dimittas debitum, alteri non; illi quidem misericors es, huic tamen minimè iniquus. Optimè Augustinus, eo ipso simili adhibito, inquit, de prædest. & grat. cap. 3. Quod Deus aliis gratuita vocatione conuersis, misericordiam largitur indebitam, non ad dispensatoris iniustitiam,
units.tr: Reply: The antecedent holds only for things distributed as a debt; not for things that someone distributes freely and out of grace, where he may give more or less, as he wills and to whom he wills, without injustice, provided that he withholds the debt from no one. Suppose you have two debtors, and you forgive one his debt but not the other: you are merciful to the one, yet not unjust to the other. Augustine, using this very same comparison, rightly says in On Predestination and Grace, chapter 3: That God bestows undeserved mercy on others who are converted by a free calling is to be attributed not to the injustice of the steward but to the most merciful goodness of the giver.

units.la: simile. tiam, sed ad donantis misericordissimam bonitatem referendum est. An audebit debitor creditorem iniquitatis arguere, si alteri donans, ab eo quod debebit exegerit? Si ergo inter contractus hominum ita est, quis in tantam insaniam profana vocis irrumpat, ut iniustitia Deum arguat, si uni indebitam donarit gratiam, alteri debitam reddiderit poenam?
units.tr: Will a debtor dare to accuse his creditor of unfairness if the creditor, forgiving another, exacts what is owed from him? If, then, this is so in the contracts of men, who is so mad as to burst out with profane speech, accusing God of injustice because he has given undeserved grace to one and paid the punishment that is owed to another?

units.la: Eadem est objectio, verbis solum mutatis: Æqualibus dans inæqualia, acceptor est personarum. Ergo cum in massa perditionis consideratí omnes simus æquales, nisi æqualiter & eodem modo Deus erga omnes se habeat, acceptor erit personarum.
units.tr: The objection is the same, with only the words changed: "By giving unequal things to equals, he is a respecter of persons. Therefore, since we are all considered equal in the mass of perdition, unless God stands towards all equally and in the same way, he will be a respecter of persons."

units.la: Sed aliud est acceptio personarum, aliud exceptio, sive delectus hominum apud Deum. Quid enim? multiplices illæ hominum differentiæ, quod alij potentes, alij subditi: alij nobiles, alij ignobiles, alij divites, alij pauperes, visuntur: alijque ingeniosi, alij tardi corde & stolidi nascuntur, homines denique hominibus tot tantisq; rebus præstant; unde nisi à Domino proficiscuntur? Audi sapientem: Quare dies diem praecellit, cum omnis lux dierum anni a sole proficiscatur? Iudicio Domini distincti sunt, qui vicissitudines temporum festorumq; dierum disposuit. Is alios dies extulit ac consecraait, alios in ordinem redegit. Similiter omnes homines e terra orti sunt, Adamq; e terra creatus est: sed Dominus multiplici scientia distinxit eos, & vias eorum diuersas fecit. Alios fortunat atq; euehit, propinquosq; sibi facit: alios execrabiles habet, & deprimit. En vt alios alijs in genere humano multipliciter Deus praeferat. Nam, inquit Sapiens, vt lutum in manu figuli est, quod pro suo tractet arbitrio, ita homines sunt in manu Dei creatoris sui, quibus pro suo iudicio, id est, libera voluntate sua, singulis reddat. Acceptio igitur personarum, vtpote quae in Deum non cadit, toto genere differt ab electione, seu delectu aliorum praealijs, qui maxime Deo competit, atque adeo competit, vt spoliatus virtute & sapientia eligendi, in idolum Fortunae transformaretur, cuius numine omnia temere fierent.
units.tr: But respect of persons is one thing, and election or choosing among men by God is another. For what of those manifold differences among men, that some are powerful and others subject, some noble and others ignoble, some rich and others poor, and that some are born clever while others are slow of heart and dull? In short, men excel other men in so many and such great respects; whence do these come, unless from the Lord? Hear the wise man: Why does one day surpass another, when all the light of the days of the year comes from the sun?
