By the judgment of the Lord they have been distinguished, he who arranged the changes of the seasons and the festival days. He exalted some days and consecrated them, and reduced others to the ordinary order. Likewise all men have arisen from the earth, and Adam was created from the earth; but the Lord with manifold knowledge has distinguished them, and made their ways different. Some he blesses and lifts up, and makes near to himself; others he holds accursed, and casts down. See how God, in the human race, prefers some to others in many ways. For, says the Wise Man, as the clay is in the potter's hand, which he shapes at his own pleasure, so men are in the hand of God their Creator, whom he rewards according to his own judgment, that is, by his free will, each one. Respect of persons, then, since it does not fall upon God, differs entirely in kind from election, or the choosing of some before others, which belongs most of all to God. Indeed it so belongs to him that, if he were stripped of the power and wisdom of choosing, he would be turned into an idol of Fortune, by whose power all things would happen at random.

units.la: Acceptio autem personarum, vt erudite
units.tr: Respect of persons, however, as the ancient writers explain learnedly,

units.la: Eccl. 33.
units.tr: Ecclus 33.

units.la: dite veteres explicant, ibi recte dicitur, vbi ille qui iudicat, relinquens causæ meritum de qua iudicat, alteri contra alterum suffragatur, inueniens aliquid in persona quod honore vel misericordia sit dignum. Si autem quispiam duos habeat debitores, & alteri velit debitum dimittere, ab altero exigere: cui vult donat, sed neminem fraudat: nec acceptio personarum dicenda est, quia iniquitas nulla est. Alioquin eis qui parum intelligunt, poterit acceptio personarum videri, vbi vineæ Dominus operarios æquales fecit in mercede, quorum tàm magna distantia fuerat in labore. Sed quid respondit de hac velut acceptione personarum murmurantibus? Amice, non facio tibi iniuriam. Tolle quod tuum est, & abi, Volo autem huic vltimo dare quemadmodum & tibi. An non licet mihi quod volo facere in meis? an oculus tuus malus est, quia ego bonus sum? Nempe, hic tota iustitia est: hoc volo: tibi, inquit, reddidi, huic donaui, neque vt huic donarem tibi aliquid abstuli, aut quod debebam vel minui vel negaui. Sicut ergo hîc nulla est acceptio personarū quia sic alius gratis honoratur, vt alius debito non fraudetur : sic cùm secundum propositum Dei vocatur alius, alius non vocatur, vocato datur gratuitum bonum, non vocato redditur debitum malum; quia omnes rei sunt per vnum.
units.tr: is rightly spoken of where the judge, leaving aside the merit of the case he is judging, favours one party against the other, finding in a person something worthy of honour or of mercy. But if someone has two debtors, and wishes to remit the debt to one and to exact it from the other, he gives to whom he wishes but defrauds no one; nor is this to be called respect of persons, because there is no injustice. Otherwise, to those who understand little, respect of persons may seem to appear where the lord of the vineyard made the workers equal in wages, though their labour had been so very unequal. But what did he answer to those who grumbled at this supposed respect of persons? Friend, I do you no wrong. Take what is yours and go. But I wish to give to this last man just as to you. Is it not lawful for me to do what I wish with my own things? Or is your eye evil because I am good? Surely here is the whole of justice: this is what I wish. To you, he says, I have given what was yours; to this man I have given a gift; and I have taken nothing from you in order to give to him, nor have I diminished or denied what I owed. Therefore, just as there is no respect of persons here, because one man is honoured freely and the other is not defrauded of his due, so when, according to God's purpose, one is called and another is not called, the one who is called receives a free good, and the one who is not called is repaid the evil that is his due, because all are guilty in one.

units.la: Quinto cauillantur aduersarij quòd ex nostra positione Deus dicendus sit maiorem partem generis humani ad hoc creare, vt illam perdat in æternum. Obiectum hoc & Augustino fuit, vt videre est Tom. 7, ad articulos falsò ipsi im-positos artic. 3.
units.tr: Fifthly, our opponents carp that, on our position, God must be said to create the greater part of the human race for this very purpose: that he may destroy them for ever. This objection was also raised against Augustine, as can be seen in vol. 7, on the articles falsely imposed upon him, article 3.

units.la: Respondemus igitur verbis Augustini: Deum quidem omnium hominum esse creatorem, sed neminem ab eo ideo creari vt pereat, quia alia causa est nascendi, & alia pereundi. Vt enim nascantur homines, est beneficium: vt autem pereant, prævaricatoris est vitium. In Adam quippe, in quo omnium hominum præformata est natura, omnes peccauerunt, eadémque sententia qua ille obstricti sunt. Nimis igitur impius pius & indoctus est, ait ille, qui vitium naturæ non discernit ab autore naturæ, a quo prorsus alienum est, quicquid in vnoquoque damnandum est. Creat enim vt sint homines, nec multiplican- dis generationum successionibus opi- ficium suum subtrahit: secundum con- filium bonæ voluntatis suæ retractatu- rus in multis quod ipse fecit, puniturus in multis quod ipse non fecit. Quo etiam spectat, quod scribit Epist. 105. ad Xixtum presbyterum: Quamuis Deus faciat vasa iræ in perditionem, vt often- dat iram, & demonstret potentiam suam, qua bene etiam malis vtitur, & vt notas faciat diuitias gloriæ suæ in vasa miseri- cordiæ, quæ facit in honorem: tamen in iisdem iræ vasis, propter meritum mal- sæ in cotumeliam debitam factis, id est, hominibus propter naturæ quidè bo- num creatis, sed propter vitia supplicio destinatis, iniquitatem damnare nouit ipse, non facere. Hæc Augustinus.
units.tr: We therefore answer in the words of Augustine: God is indeed the creator of all men, but he creates no one in order that he may perish, because the cause of being born is one thing and the cause of perishing is another. For that men are born is a benefit; that they perish is the fault of the transgressor. In Adam, in whom the nature of all men was pre-formed, all sinned, and they are bound by the same sentence by which he was bound. Therefore he is too impious and too unlearned, says Augustine, who does not distinguish the fault of nature from the author of nature, from whom whatever in anyone is to be condemned is wholly alien. For God creates so that men may exist, and does not withdraw his workmanship by multiplying the successions of generations, while in accordance with the counsel of his good will he will in many cases revoke what he himself made, and punish in many cases what he himself did not make. To this also pertains what he writes in Letter 105 to Sixtus the presbyter: Although God makes vessels of wrath for destruction, in order to display his wrath and to show his power, by which he also makes good use even of evil things, and in order to make known the riches of his glory in vessels of mercy, which he makes for honour: nevertheless, in the same vessels of wrath, which are made for dishonour deserved on account of sin, that is, men created indeed with a good nature but destined for punishment on account of their vices, he himself knows how to condemn iniquity, not to create it. So Augustine.

units.la: Creantur ergo damnandi propter bonum naturæ, & supplicio destinatur ac damnantur propter vitia, idque non quasi in hunc vltimum finem, vt scili- cet ipsi æternum crucientur, sed cùm propter salutem electorum, tùm in primis propter gloriam Dei secundù triplicem modum ab Augustino breuiter assignatum verbis Apostoli. Quade re alibi etiam scriptum reliquit, quòd aliorum perditione ad salutem vtatur aliorum, & periturorúm interitû prædestinatis à se vasis misericordiæ,salutis voluerit esse argumentum. Item, cur gratia nō datur omnibus? Respondeo: quoniam Deus iustus iudex est, proptere a & gratis ab eo datur gratia, & iusto eius in aliis iudicio demōstratur, quòd eis quibus datur,conferat gratia, adeóque gratius suam gratiam in vasis misericordiæ commendat Deus.
units.tr: The damned, then, are created on account of the good of nature, and they are destined for punishment and condemned on account of their vices. This is not as if their eternal torment were the ultimate end. Rather, it serves both the salvation of the elect and, above all, the glory of God, in the threefold manner that Augustine briefly set out in the words of the Apostle. For this reason he also left it written elsewhere that God uses the perdition of some for the salvation of others, and that the ruin of those who perish was meant to be a proof of salvation for the vessels of mercy that he had predestined. Likewise, why is grace not given to all? I answer: because God is a just judge, and grace is given by him freely; and in his just judgment on others it is shown that he bestows grace on those to whom he gives it. And so God commends his grace more fully in the vessels of mercy.

units.la: Postremò si quem mouet, quomodo Deus ab æterno elegerit vel reprobarit nondum existētes: is cogitet Deo vniuersa esse præsentia: quippe cuncta pariter tempora & temporaria,æterno ac stabili comprehendit intuitu. Antequam ergo faceret nos, præscuit nos, & in ipsa præscientia, cùm nondum fecisset, cisset, elegit nos ante mundi constitu- tionem. Intra mundum facti sumus, & ante mūdum electi sumus: quippe præ- scientia sua immutabiliter permanen- te præsciuit nos, quos suo tempore ad imaginem & similitudinem crearet, quosque ab illa dignitate in peccati & mortis foueam, se permittente, lapsos, vel liberaret indebita misericordiæ largitate, vel damnaret debita iudicij veritate.
units.tr: Finally, if anyone is troubled by how God elected or reprobated from eternity those who did not yet exist, let him consider that all things are present to God. He comprehends all times and temporal things together in one eternal and unchanging gaze. Before he made us, then, he foreknew us, and in that foreknowledge, when he had not yet made us, he chose us before the foundation of the world. We were made within the world, and we were chosen before the world. For in his unchangingly abiding foreknowledge he foreknew those whom he would create in his own time in his image and likeness, and whom, having fallen from that dignity into the pit of sin and death, he would either deliver by the undeserved largesse of his mercy, or condemn by the due truth of his judgment, as he permitted them to fall.

units.la: CAPVT V. De causis prædestinationis.
units.tr: CHAPTER V. On the causes of predestination.

units.la: Atque hæc de prima quæstione. Veniamus ad alteram, in qua de causis quæritur prædestinationis. Et materialis quidem causa sunt homines ipsi, & ea quæ Deus prædestinatis facere decreuit; vt sunt gratia in præsenti, fides, bona opera, & perseuerantia in bono &c. & gloria in futurum, quantum ad electos, & pœna, quatum ad reprobos.
units.tr: So much for the first question. Let us come to the second, in which the causes of predestination are asked about. The material cause, indeed, is the human beings themselves, and those things which God has decreed to bestow on the predestined: such as grace in the present, faith, good works, and perseverance in good, etc., and glory in the future, as far as the elect are concerned, and punishment, as far as the reprobate are concerned.

units.la: Formam porrò definitiones ostendunt, quas prius attulimus. Finalis etiam causa, cum electionis tum reprobationis, non obscure a Paulo tradita est, cum testatur ad Rom. 9. quod Deus velit ostendere iram, & notam facere potentiam suam in vasis irae, coaptatis ad interitum: In vasis vero quae praeparauit ad misericordiam, velit notas facere diuitias gloriae suae. Quo & illud de Pharaone spectat: Ad hoc ipsum excitaui te, vt ostendam potentiam meam, & annuncietur nomen meum in vniuersa terra. Et de electis Eph. 1. ait: Praedestinauit nos quos adoptaret in filios, in laudem gloriosae suae gratiae.
units.tr: Moreover, the definitions we set out earlier show the formal cause. The final cause, both of election and of reprobation, has been set forth by Paul not obscurely, when he testifies in Romans 9 that God "willed to show his wrath and to make known his power in vessels of wrath, fitted for destruction; but in the vessels which he prepared for mercy, he willed to make known the riches of his glory." To this also belongs what is said of Pharaoh: "For this very purpose have I raised you up, that I might show my power, and that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth." And of the elect, Paul says in Ephesians 1: "He predestined us whom he would adopt as sons, to the praise of the glory of his grace."

units.la: In summa, electionis & reprobationis vltimus finis est gloria Dei: quemadmodum & Sapiens docet Prou. 16. Omnia fecit propter semetipsum, etiam impium ad diem malum. Sed in electorum salute misericordiam, in supplicio caeterorum iram peculiariter manifestare voluit: bonitatem tamen & iustitiam in omnibus. Quoniam, teste Augustino, bonum est cum debitum redditur, & iustum est cum debitum sine cuiusquam fraude donatur.
units.tr: In sum, the ultimate end of election and reprobation is the glory of God, just as the Wise Man also teaches in Proverbs 16: "The Lord made all things for himself, even the wicked for the day of evil." But in the salvation of the elect he willed especially to manifest mercy, and in the punishment of the rest, wrath; yet goodness and justice in all. For, as Augustine testifies, it is good when what is owed is repaid, and it is just when what is owed is given without fraud to anyone.

units.la: Caeterum quaestio potissimum vertitur titur de causa impulsiua electionis & reprobationis, quæ ad genus causarum efficientium refertur: Possitne aliqua, assignari causa, quæ Deum ad eligen-dum & reprobandum mouerit?
units.tr: Moreover, the question turns chiefly on the impulsive cause of election and reprobation, which is referred to the class of efficient causes: Can any cause be assigned which moved God to elect and to reprobate?

units.la: Ad cuius quæstionis intellectum di-stinguendum est. Vel enim in thesi quæstio accipi potest, cur alios elege-rit, alios reiecerit? vel in hypothesi, de cuiusq; electione & reprobatione: quare hos elegerit, & illos reprobarit? Ver-bi gratia, cur Iacobum præ Esau, Mo-sen præ Pharaone, Petrum præ Iuda elegerit?
units.tr: To understand this question, a distinction must be made. For the question can be taken either in thesi, why he chose some and rejected others; or in hypothesi, concerning the election and reprobation of each individual: why he chose these and reprobated those? For example, why did he choose Jacob before Esau, Moses before Pharaoh, Peter before Judas?

units.la: Et primæ quidem quæstionis ratio-nem reddere est ex ijs quæ ante de fine prædestinationis dicta sunt. Etenim fi-nis, vel consideratur vt est in ipsis rebus, vtq; actionem consequitur, & sic pro-prie dicitur finis: vel vt mente & desi-derio comprehensus mouet agentem, & sic rationem habet causæ impulsiuæ. Quoniam igitur in seruandis, finis vlti-mus propositus est Deo, misericordiæ manifestatio, iustitiæ, in damnandis: & vero finis, quatenus ad agendum mo-uet,
units.tr: To the first question the answer is to be given from what was said earlier about the end of predestination. For an end is considered either as it exists in the things themselves and follows upon the action, and thus is properly called an end; or as it is grasped in the mind and desire and moves the agent, and thus has the character of an impulsive cause. Since, therefore, in saving, the ultimate end proposed to God is the manifestation of mercy, and in condemning, the manifestation of justice; and the end, insofar as it moves to acting,

units.la: uet,rationem habet causæ efficientis: idcirco hæc tùm misericordiæ,tùm iustitiæ,id est,bonitatis & gloriæ Dei manifestatio,efficiens quodammodo causa est,& electionis & reprobationis aliquorum.
units.tr: has the character of an efficient cause: for this reason, this manifestation of mercy and of justice, that is, of the goodness and glory of God, is in a certain way an efficient cause both of the election and of the reprobation of some.

units.la: At quare hos elegerit,illos reprobarit, eius rei nullam aliam possumus afferre rationem, præter meram, eamq; liberrimam & æquissimam Dei voluntatem & beneplacitum.
units.tr: But as to why he chose these and reprobated those, we can give no other reason for this than God's mere, yet most free and most equitable, will and good pleasure.

units.la: Quomodo quidè in rerum vniuersitate assignari ratio potest,cur materiæ primæ,cùm in fe tota vniformis fit,partem alteram sub forma ignis, alteram sub forma terræ, Deus in principio condiderit, vt sic videlicet effet diuersitas specierum in rebus naturalibus : Sed quare hæc pars sub ista, alia sub alia forma existat, id à simplici demum creatoris voluntate pendere necesse est.Sic etiam,vt alio vtamur simili à rebus artificialibus; fi quis multis congregatis lapidibus similibus & æqualibus,ædificare instituat,ratio facilime reddi potest, respectu finis, cur lapidû alios in sum-mo, mo, alios in imo ponat: quia videlicet ad perfectionem domus requiritur, & fundamentum quod habeat lapides in imo, & cacumen parietis, quod habeat lapides in summo. Sed cur æqualium lapidum hos in summo, illos in imo ponat, nō habet aliam rationem, nisi quia artifex ita vult.
units.tr: Just as in the whole universe a reason can be assigned why God, in the beginning, established the first matter, which is wholly uniform in itself, partly under the form of fire and partly under the form of earth, so that there would be diversity of species in natural things; but why this part exists under that form and another under another, it must necessarily depend upon the simple will of the Creator. So also, to use another likeness from artificial things: if someone, having gathered many similar and equal stones, plans to build, a reason can very easily be given, with respect to the end, why he places some stones at the top and others at the bottom: namely, because the perfection of the house requires a foundation which has stones at the bottom, and a gable of the wall, which has stones at the top. But why he places these equal stones at the top and those at the bottom has no other reason, except that the builder wills it so.

units.la: Ita prorsus & hic se rem habere fatendum est, & docet exprese Apostolus: quorum vult miseretur: quos autem vult indurat. Et ad Ephes. 1. ait: prædestinatos nos ab eo κατ' ἐυδοκίαν τῆς θελήματος αὐτοῦ. Elegantėr etiam Siracides cap. 33. cuius & supra memini: Quare dies diem præcellit, cum omnis lux dierum à sole proficiscatur? Iudicio Domini distincti sunt, qui vicissitudines temporum festorum, disposuit. Is alios dies extulit & consecrauit, alios in ordinem redegit. Similiter omnes homines e terra orti sunt, Adam quoque e terra creatus est: Sed Dominus multiplici scientia distinxit eos, & vias eorum diversas fecit. Alios fortunauit, euexit, consecrauit, sibi propinquos fecit: alios execrabiles habet, & depressit. Sicut lutum in manu fi-guli est, ita homines sunt in manu Dei creato-ris. ris sui, quibus pro iudicio suo singulis reddat. Plana haec & perspicua sunt. Quoniam tamen res ardua est, & variis orthodoxorum & haereticorum disputationibus iactata, latius agendum videtur.
units.tr: Just so, and in this matter too, it must be confessed that the case is thus, and the Apostle teaches it expressly: "He has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens." And in Ephesians 1 he says that we were predestined by him "according to the good pleasure of his will" [κατ' εὐδοκίαν τῆς θελήματος αὐτοῦ]. Elegantly also Ecclesiasticus, chapter 33, of which I have also spoken above: "Why does one day surpass another, when all the light of the days comes from the sun? By the judgment of the Lord they are distinguished, who arranged the changes of the seasons and festal days. He exalted and hallowed some days, and reduced others to the ordinary. Likewise all men are from the earth, and Adam too was created from the earth; but the Lord with manifold knowledge distinguished them, and made their ways diverse. Some he has blessed, exalted, hallowed, and made near to himself; others he has cursed and brought low. As the clay is in the hand of the potter, so men are in the hand of God their Creator, to whom he renders according to his judgment, each one." These things are plain and clear. Since, however, the matter is difficult and has been tossed about in the various disputations of the orthodox and the heretics, it seems that it should be treated at greater length.

units.la: CAPVT VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: Afferuntur varia sententia de causa electionis & reprobationis.
units.tr: Various opinions on the cause of election and reprobation are set out.

units.la: Ac primum Origenes, in libris suis περὶ ἀρχῶν qui erroribus undique scatet, fabulas secutus gentilium Philosophorum, Platonis atque Pythagorae, somniauit, Deum ab initio creaturas duntaxat spirituales condidisse, easque omnes aequales: postea autem diversitate & inaequalitatem subsecuta esse creaturarum, ex diversitate meritorum. Nam illarum creaturarum spiritualium, quasdam per amorem Deo adhaesisse plus vel minus, ac secundum hoc distinctos esse ordines angelorum: quasdam vero auersas a Deo, plus vel minus peccasse, & secundum hoc diversos sortiri status, demersas in corpora nobilia bilia, vel ignobilia, vt sunt corpora cœ-lestia, dæmonum, hominum, &c.
units.tr: First, Origen, in his book On First Principles [περὶ ἀρχῶν], which is full of errors everywhere, following the fables of the pagan philosophers Plato and Pythagoras, dreamed that God at the beginning created only spiritual creatures, and that all of them were equal. Afterwards, he says, diversity and inequality of creatures followed, according to the diversity of their merits. For some of those spiritual creatures, through love, clung to God more or less, and according to this the orders of angels were distinguished. Others turned away from God and sinned more or less, and according to this they obtained different states, being plunged into bodies, noble or ignoble, such as the heavenly bodies, demons, humans, and so on.

units.la: Ita finxit secundū bona vel mala opera animarum simul creatarū & in cœlesti Hierusalem, etiam ante mundi fabricam, præexistentium, Deum ante mundi constitutionem alios elegisse, vt haberent adoptionem in Christo, alios pœnis perpetuis destinasse. Meminerunt fabulæ istius Hieron. in 1. caput ad Ephes. nec non quæst. 10. ad Hedibiam. August. contra duas Epist. Pelagianorum, lib. 2. cap. 6. Aquinas & alij.
units.tr: So he imagined that, according to the good or evil works of souls created together and already existing in the heavenly Jerusalem, even before the fabric of the world, God before the foundation of the world chose some to have adoption in Christ and destined others to eternal punishments. Mention of this fable is made by Jerome on Ephesians, chapter 1, and in question 10 to Hedibia. Augustine against the two letters of the Pelagians, book 2, chapter 6. Aquinas and others.

units.la: Verùm, delirium hoc stultum & impium, merito iam olim explosum est, quia totum quod garrit de animarum præexistentia, & meritis ante corpora, & inde subsecuta diuersitate, contrariū est dicto Apostoli de Iacob & Esau: quod nondum natis pueris dictum sit: maior seruiet minori, vt nempe propositum Dei quod est secundum electionem, non ex operibus, sed ex vocante, firmum maneret. Quo etiam pertinet quod apud Iobum legitur: Vbi eras, quando fundabam terram, cum me laudarent lucida sidera, & iubilarent omnes
units.tr: But this foolish and impious delirium has long since been rightly exploded, because everything it babbles about the pre-existence of souls, and about merits before bodies, and the diversity that follows from that, is contrary to the Apostle's word about Jacob and Esau: that it was said when the boys were not yet born, the elder shall serve the younger, so that the purpose of God according to election, not of works but of him who calls, might remain firm. To this also belongs what is read in Job: "Where were you when I founded the earth, when the morning stars praised me and all the sons of God shouted for joy?"

units.la: Iob. 38. nes filii Dei? Si Origenis vera esset fabula, Iob respondere potuisset: eram inter ipsos filios Dei iubilantes. Adhaec (vt Hieronymus etiam vrget) qui dicit animas electas esse propter sanctitatem, contradicit Apostolo, testanti nos electos ad hoc ipsum, vt simus sancti & inculpati coram Deo, non autem quia tales eramus. Pluribus errorem istum refellit Thomas contra Gentiles, lib.2. cap.44.
units.tr: Job 38. Had Origen's fable been true, Job could have answered: I was among the very sons of God who were rejoicing. Besides, as Jerome also urges, whoever says that the souls were chosen because of their holiness contradicts the Apostle, who testifies that we were chosen for this very purpose, that we should be holy and blameless before God, and not because we were already such. Thomas refutes this error at greater length in Against the Gentiles, book 2, chapter 44.

units.la: Secuti sunt Pelagiani, Augustini aetate, cum is iam in Episcopatu esset, exorti. Hi contendebant, hominem solius naturae seu liberi arbitrij viribus, seruare & implere posse mandata Domini, etiam absque gratia, difficilius tamen quam si gratiae accederet adiutorium. Neque id tantum; verum etiam impietatem impietate cumulantes, & contra gratiam furentes, statuebant, gratiam Dei secundum merita dari. Qua ingrata Deo sententia, & gratuitis ipsius beneficijs, quibus liberamur, omnino inimica, gratiam re ipsa tollebant: quoniam si ex meritis, iam non est ex gratia.
units.tr: The Pelagians arose in the time of Augustine, when he was already a bishop. They contended that man, by the powers of nature or free will alone, could keep and fulfil the commandments of the Lord, even without grace, though with more difficulty than if the help of grace were added. Nor was this all: heaping impiety upon impiety and raging against grace, they maintained that grace of God was given according to merits. This opinion is ungrateful to God and wholly hostile to his free benefits by which we are delivered; in fact they abolished grace, since if it is from merits, it is no longer from grace.

units.la: Ceterum, quod ad causam electionis & reprobationis, eam ad præuisa opera bona vel mala referebant: vnumquemq; vel ad vitam vel ad mortem à Deo prædestinatum, prout bene vel male victurum præsciuisset.
units.tr: As for the cause of election and reprobation, they referred it to foreseen good or evil works: that each person was predestined by God to life or to death, according as he had foreseen he would live well or badly.

units.la: Sed contra est quod Paulus electionem testatur esse gratiæ. Quod si autem per gratiam, iam non ex operibus, alioquin gratia non esset gratia. Sin ex operibus, iam non ex gratia, alioquin opus non esset opus. Adhæc satis constat ipsamet bona opera effectus esse electionis: Ergo nequeunt esse causa electionis: quia non potest idem esse causa & effectus sui ipsius. Nam vt docet Apostolus, electi sumus non quia eramus, sed ad hoc vt essemus sancti & inculpati coram Deo per caritatem. Et ipse est qui efficit in nobis velle & perficere pro beneplacito. Vocantis est ergo gratia; percipientis vero gratiam consequenter sunt opera bona, non quæ gratiam pariant, sed gratia pariantur. Non enim ideo bene currit rota vt rotunda sit, sed quia rotunda est. Sic nemo
units.tr: But against this stands the fact that Paul testifies that election is of grace. "But if by grace, then it is no longer of works; otherwise grace would not be grace. But if of works, then it is no longer of grace; otherwise work would not be work." Moreover, it is quite clear that the good works themselves are effects of election. Therefore they cannot be the cause of election, because one and the same thing cannot be the cause and effect of itself. For, as the Apostle teaches, we were chosen not because we were, but that we should be holy and blameless before God in love. And it is he who works in us both to will and to do according to his good pleasure. Therefore grace belongs to the one who calls, and good works follow for the one who receives grace; they do not produce grace, but are produced by grace. For a wheel does not run well because it is round, but it is round because it runs well. Thus no one works well in order to receive grace, but because he has received it;

units.la: Ephes. I.
units.tr: Ephes. 1.

units.la: Philip. I. „ nemo propterea bene operatur, vt ac- „ cipiat gratiam, sed quia accepit: ideoq; „ nec præuidit Deus bona cuiusquam o- „ pera, nisi quæ dare iam constitutum „ apud se habebat.
units.tr: Phil. 1. and so God does not foresee the good works of anyone, except those which he had already decided to give and kept with himself.

units.la: Sed enim defensa olim fide catholi- ca contra Pelagianos, & expugnato eo- rum errore ab orthodoxis Episcopis, præsertim Augustino, insigni patrono fidei, vt ab Hilario iure laudatus est; emerserunt alij nonnulli clari atque egregij in omni virtutum studio viri, nisi quòd spiritus Pelagianæ impietatis iis illusit; Semipelagiani idcirco appel- „ lati. Horum definitio ac professio erat, „ omnes quidem homines Adamo pec- „ cante peccasse, & neminem per opera „ sua, sed per Dei gratiam regeneratio- ne saluari: vnicuique tamen tantum re- liquum esse gratiæ naturalis, vt ad istam saluantem gratiam, initialis gratiæ ope „ queat peruenire, si velit. Itaque quan- „ tum ad Deum pertinet, omnibus para- „ tam vitam æternam: quantum autem ad „ arbitrij libertatem, ab his eam appre- „ hendi, qui Deo sponte, tanquam ex se, crecrediderint, atque auxilii gratiæ me-rito fidei acceperint. Seu, vt dicam clarius: Defendebant quidem illi contra Pelagianos, hominem quidè non posse ex seipso resurgere & bene operari: voluntatem tamen resurgendi, quæ tantum medicum quærat, nó autem quicquam ipsa iam valeat, cuilibet homini inesse putabat, nec vllam ita extinctam vel depravatam esse dicebat naturam, vt non debeat vel possit se velle sanari: ac proinde, cum prostratis & nunquam suis viribus surrecturis annunciatur obtinendæ salutis occasio, eo merito quo voluerint & crediderint à suo morbo se posse sanari, & fidei augmentum, & totum sanctitatis suæ effectum, eos consequi. Ceterum ad nullum opus vel incipiendum, nedum perficiendum, quenquam sibi sufficere posse consentiebant. Distinguebant enim inter opera & fidé, cuius si non augmentum, saltem principiû, tametsi tenue, in hominis situm potestate volebat intelligi, vt initium salutis ex eo qui saluatur, nó ex eo qui saluat, esse crederetur, & vo-
units.tr: But the Catholic faith was defended long ago against the Pelagians, and their error was overthrown by the orthodox bishops, above all Augustine, the outstanding champion of the faith, as Hilary rightly praised him. Yet there arose some other famous and eminent men, distinguished in every pursuit of virtue, except that the spirit of Pelagian impiety deceived them. For this reason they were called Semipelagians. Their definition and profession was this: that indeed all men sinned when Adam sinned, and that no one is saved by his own works but by the grace of God through regeneration. Yet to each person there remains so much natural grace that, by the aid of initial grace, he can come to that saving grace, if he wills. Thus, as far as God is concerned, eternal life is prepared for all; but as far as freedom of the will is concerned, it is laid hold of by those who believe God of their own accord, as though from themselves, and have received by the merit of faith the help of grace. Or, to put it more clearly: they defended against the Pelagians that man cannot rise by himself and do good; yet they thought that a will to rise, which seeks only a physician but cannot itself accomplish anything, is present in every man, and they said that no nature is so extinguished or depraved that it ought not, or cannot, will to be healed. Therefore, when the opportunity of obtaining salvation is announced to those who are prostrate and will never rise by their own strength, they held that by the merit of willing and believing that they can be healed of their disease, they obtain both an increase of faith and the whole effect of their holiness. Moreover, they agreed that no one is sufficient for himself for any work, still less for its completion. For they distinguished between works and faith; and if not the increase of faith, at least its beginning, however slight, was to be understood as within man's power, so that the start of salvation would be believed to come from the one being saved and not from the one saving, and the will of man would be thought to obtain for itself the help of divine grace, and that the

units.la: lunlutas hominis diuinæ gratiæ sibi parere opem, non gratia voluntatem sibi subiicere existimaretur.
units.tr: will of man would obtain divine help for itself, and that grace would not be thought to subject the will to itself.

units.la: Atque hoc posito; talem omnibus superesse voluntatem, qua vel cötemnere vel ampleéti quis valeat oblatam salutem, de compendio rationem putabat reddi electorum vel reiectorum: Deum videlicet ante mundi constitutionem præscIuisse, qui crediturii, quiue in ea fide, quæ deinceps per ipsius gratiam effet iuuanda, mansuri essent, vel non: & secundum præscientiam istam, vel elegisse credituros, vel reprobaffe non credituros, vel saltem quos præsciuerit non perseueraturos. Vnde prædestinatio ipsis nihil aliud erat quàm propositum diuinum eligendi credituros.
units.tr: And this being laid down, they thought that the reason for the election or rejection of individuals could be briefly stated: namely, that God foresaw before the foundation of the world who would believe, and who would remain in that faith, which would afterwards be aided by his grace, and who would not; and according to that foreknowledge he chose those he foresaw would believe, or rejected those who would not believe, or at least those whom he foresaw would not persevere. Hence predestination meant for them nothing other than God's purpose to elect those who would believe.

units.la: Hæc Semipelagianorum fuit sententia de his articulis longè maximis: de libero arbitrio, inquam, de gratia & prædestinatione. Et fuit Augustinus ipsemet in eadem sententia initio ante Episcopatum, vt apparet ex libro expositionum eius in Epist. ad Rom. & ex Epist. Hilarij ad August. Verba eius sunt(quæ etiam pro opinione sua obij- ciebant reliquiæ istæ prauitatis Pelagianæ) quod Deus præscientia eligat creditu- ros, & damnet incredulos, nec illos ex operibus eligens, nec ipsos ex operibus damnans, sed & illorum fidei præstans ut bene operentur, & illorum impietatem obdurans, ut male operentur. Et iterum ait: Non quidem Deus in præscientia opera cuiusquam eligit, quæ ipse largitur: sed tamen fidem eligit in præscientia, ut quem creditypum esse præsciuerit, ipsum elegerit &c. Hæc tum Augustinus.
units.tr: This was the opinion of the Semipelagians on these most important articles: on free will, I mean, on grace and predestination. And Augustine himself held the same opinion at first, before he became a bishop, as appears from his book of Expositions on the Epistle to the Romans and from Hilary's letter to Augustine. His words (which those remnants of Pelagian depravity also cited in support of their view) are: that God, by foreknowledge, chooses those who will believe and condemns the unbelieving, choosing them not from works, nor condemning them from works, but both granting their faith that they act well, and hardening their impiety that they act badly. And again he says: God indeed does not, in foreknowledge, choose anyone's works, which he himself bestows; yet he chooses faith in foreknowledge, so that whom he foreknew would believe, he chose, etc. Thus Augustine.

units.la: Similiter errarunt multi alij viri doc- ti, nondum nata hæresi Pelagiana minus assueti, minusq; sine hoste soliciti, ut alicubi de Ticonio Augustt. loquitur. Hinc & Commentarij ad Rom. qui in tomis Hieron. leguntur, scriptum habent, fidei merito apud Deum separatos fuisse Iacobum & Esau, antequam nascerentur. Item, illius miserebor quem præsciui posse misericordia promereri. Et Hieron. ipse ad Hedibiam quæst. 10. eo inclinare videtur, inquies, non homines ipsos, sed eorum voluntates eligi. Quanquam rectius Hieron. sentit in scriptis contra Pelagianos, quibus de Augustino honorificentissime loquitur, atq; in eius contra Pelagianos disputationibus acquiescere se testatur. Chrysostomus vero expofit. in 9. ad Rom. aperte scribit, Deum prout vnuquemq; gratia sua dignum vel indignum praeuiderit, ita vel elegisse vel reprobasse.
units.tr: Similarly many other learned men went astray, being less accustomed to the Pelagian heresy, which had not yet arisen, and less anxiously on guard against an enemy, as Augustine says somewhere of Ticonius. Hence also the Commentaries on Romans which are read among the works of Jerome state that Jacob and Esau were separated by God on account of the merit of their faith before they were born. Likewise: "I will have mercy on him whom I foreknew could merit mercy." And Jerome himself, in his Questions to Hedibia, question 10, seems to incline to this, you will say, that not the men themselves but their wills are chosen. Yet Jerome judges more rightly in his writings against the Pelagians, in which he speaks of Augustine in the most honourable terms, and he testifies that he himself rests in Augustine's disputations against the Pelagians. Chrysostom, however, in his exposition on Romans 9, writes plainly that God, according as he foresaw each man to be worthy or unworthy of his grace, so either chose or rejected him.

units.la: E recentioribus Erasmus in Diatribe & Hyperaspiste, pro eadem opinione pugnat. Nec abesse multum ab ea videntur qui totidem verbis scribunt: fidem esse causam electionis: nec tamen Pelagiani esse volunt. Sint ergo Semipelagiani. Quale etiam est, quod alius eiusgem farinae scribit, Deum praescium ab aeterno, qui sint recepturi gratiam & permansuri, qui non electioni sua substrauisse hypothesin seu conditionem istam, ut qui credunt in Christum salui sint. Quid obsecro differt haec sententia a definitione Semipelagianorum, praedestinationem seu electionem dicentium propositum eligendi crediturosٙ? Aut si hoc distare ab ijs se putant, quòd fidem non naturæ, sed Spiritus sancti opus agnoscunt, an non vident se nodum astringere, non soluere? Hoc ipsum enim quæritur, cur diuinitus alijs inspiretur, alijs non inspiretur viua & constans fides ad salutem?
units.tr: Among more recent writers Erasmus fights for the same opinion in his Diatribe and Hyperaspistes. Nor are those far from it who write in so many words: "faith is the cause of election," and yet they do not wish to be Pelagians. Let them then be Semipelagians. Also what another of the same kind writes is of the same sort: "God, knowing from eternity who would receive grace and persevere, did not make his election depend upon this hypothesis or condition, that those who believe in Christ are saved." What, I beg you, does this opinion differ from the definition of the Semipelagians, who say that predestination or election is the purpose to choose those who will believe? Or if they think they differ from them in this, that they acknowledge faith to be the work of the Holy Spirit and not of nature, do they not see that they are tying a knot rather than loosening it? For this very question is being asked: why is living and steadfast faith unto salvation inspired by God in some and not in others?

units.la: Sed ad rem. Siue operum, siue fidei præscientia ponatur esse causa electionis, error est minime ferendus. Etenim sacris literis euidenter docemur, non bona solum opera, sed & ipsam fidem, vnde omnis iustitia sumit initium, atq; ipsum adeo initium fidei & voluntatę credendi, esse ex mera gratia, & non tanquam ex nobis. Sicut scriptum est, Quid habes quod non accepisti? Si autem accepisti, quare gloriaris ac si non acceperis? Item: Sine me nihil potestis facere, ait veri- tas. Et aperte Paulus ad Philipp. Vobis inquit, datum est non solum credere in Christum, sed & affligi pro eo.
units.tr: But to the matter. Whether the foreknowledge of works or of faith be posited as the cause of election, the error is by no means to be tolerated. For we are clearly taught by the sacred letters that not only good works but faith itself, from which all righteousness takes its beginning, and the very beginning of faith and the will to believe, are from pure grace and not as from ourselves. As it is written: "What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?" Again: "Without me you can do nothing," says the Truth. And Paul plainly to the Philippians: "To you," he says, "it has been given not only to believe in Christ, but also to suffer for him."

units.la: His & similibus testimoniis diuinarum scripturarum conuictus Augustinus, errorem suum hac in parte ingenuè agnouit, retractauitq; : de prædest. sanct.cap.3. & passim eo libro. Ad Simplicia. cianum, Sancti Ambrosii successorem apud Mediolanenses, lib. 1. quaest. 2. contra duas Epist. Pelag. lib. 2. cap. 8. Retract. lib. 1. cap. 23. & lib. 2. cap. 1. Labi enim & errare humanum est: sed scientem prudentem in errore perseuerare, diabolicum est: nec debet quisquam tam esse iniustus aut inuidus, vt vel nolit proficere, vel proficere cupientes prohibeat.
units.tr: Augustine, convicted by these and similar testimonies of the divine Scriptures, frankly acknowledged his error on this point and retracted it: On the Predestination of the Saints, chapter 3, and throughout that book. To Simplicianus, successor of Saint Ambrose at Milan, book 1, question 2; Against Two Letters of the Pelagians, book 2, chapter 8; Retractions, book 1, chapter 23, and book 2, chapter 1. For to err is human, but for a man who knows and understands to persevere in error is diabolical; nor ought anyone to be so unjust or envious as either to be unwilling to make progress, or to hinder those who desire to make progress.

units.la: Quarto, alij causam quidem electionis ad vitam aeternam, agnoscunt in solo Deo esse, gratiam videlicet & beneplacitum ipsius: verum causam reprobationis, non minus quam superiores, in ipsis hominibus esse arbitratur: praeuisum nempe abusum liberi arbitrij ad infidelitatem, aliaque mala opera. Verentur enim ne iniquitas sit apud Deum, si aliqui dicantur ab ipso reiecti citra omnem operum respectum. Itaque vt iustitiam eius tueantur scilicet, scribunt propter finale peccatum praeuisum reprobatos quicunque reprobati sint. E scholasticis Scotus eiusque discipuli hanc opinionem sectantur. Hinc quidam eiusdem farinae definiuit reprobatiobationem, quod sit æterna præcognitio malivsus liberi arbitrij, ratione cuius Deus decreuerit hominem aliquem priuare gratia in præsenti, & in futuro punire pœna æterna.
units.tr: Fourthly, others acknowledge that the cause of election to eternal life lies in God alone, namely his grace and good pleasure; but they judge that the cause of reprobation, no less than in the former view, lies in men themselves, namely the foreseen abuse of free will to unbelief and other evil works. For they fear that there would be iniquity with God if some were said to be rejected by him without any regard to works. So, to defend his justice, they write that all who are reprobated are reprobated on account of foreseen final sin. Among the Schoolmen Scotus and his disciples follow this opinion. Hence a certain man of the same kind defined reprobation as the eternal foreknowledge of the wickedness of free will, by reason of which God has decreed to deprive a man of grace in the present life and to punish him with eternal punishment in the future.

units.la: Sed vti recte censet Augustinus ad Simplic.si daremus reprobationem ex præuisis malis operibus pendere, omnino sequeretur ex contrario, electionem etiam ex præuisis bonis operibus nasci. Quod si verum est, falsum est quod non ex operibus.
units.tr: But as Augustine rightly judges in his letter to Simplicianus: if we were to grant that reprobation depends on foreseen evil works, it would altogether follow by contrast that election also arises from foreseen good works. And if that is true, then it is false that it is not from works.

units.la: Quinta igitur,eaq; vera sententia est: Sicut præuisa seruandorum opera,aut fides,causa minime sunt electionis ipsorum: sic neq; damnandorum infidelitatem aut alia peccata præuisa, caulam esse eorundem reprobationis: sed & illos ex mera misericordia in Christo electos, & hos iuste ab eadem misericordia reiectos, secundum propositum voluntatis Dei, vt liberrimæ ita iustissimæ,adeoq; omnis recti ac iusti regulæ.
units.tr: The fifth, therefore, and this is the true opinion: just as the foreseen works or faith of those to be saved are by no means the cause of their election, so neither is the foreseen unbelief or other sins of those to be damned the cause of their reprobation; but those elected from pure mercy in Christ, and those justly rejected by the same mercy, according to the purpose of the will of God, which is most free and at the same time most just, and therefore the rule of all that is right and just.

units.la: CAP.
units.tr: CHAPTER.

units.la: CAPUT VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.

units.la: Assertio electionis gratuitæ ex mero Dei beneplacito.
units.tr: The free election asserted from God's mere good pleasure.

units.la: Pro hac veritate defendenda, & opinionibus contrarijs plenius refellendis, argumenta & testimonia scriptura-rum varia, eaq; clarissima & luculentis-sima, suppetunt, ex quibus aliqua duntaxat in medium proferemus.
units.tr: To defend this truth and refute the contrary opinions more fully, there are various arguments and testimonies of Scripture, very clear and luminous, of which we shall bring forward only some.

units.la: I. Causa non est posterior effectu. Sed opera & fides in nobis, & ipsa credendi voluntas atq; cupiditas, & quicunq; vsus bonus liberi arbitrij in nobis, posteriora sunt electione. Isthæc enim omnia temporalia sunt, cùm electio æterna sit: secundum dicta: Elegit nos ante mundi constitutionem. Venite benedicti patris mei, possidete regnum vobis paratum ante iacta mundi fundamenta. Vocavit nos vocatione sancta, ex suo proposito & gratia, quæ nobis data est in Christo Iesu ante tempora secularia.
units.tr: I. A cause is not posterior to its effect. But works and faith in us, and the very will and desire to believe, and every good use of free choice in us, are posterior to election. For all these are temporal, whereas election is eternal, according to the words: He chose us before the foundation of the world. Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you before the foundation of the world. He called us with a holy calling, according to his own purpose and grace, which was given us in Christ Jesus before the secular times.

units.la: Si excipiant, opera nostra, non ut facta, sed ut facienda & præuisa à Deo, æque æterna esse: respondemus, Deum nihil in nobis præuidisse boni operis vel voluntatis, quod non statuerit in nobis efficere, quodq; prædestinando nobis non præparauerit, sicut dicitur ad Eph. 1. Ipsius sumus opus conditi in Christo Iesu ad bona opera, quæ præparauit Deus vt in iis versaremur. Et cap. 1. eiusdem Epist. Elegit nos ante mundi fundamenta, vt simus sancti & inculpati coram eo. Vnde intelligitur, cum ex eo quod diuinitus ad vitam sumus prædestinati, fiat, vt bona operemur, & credamus, vel sic præcognitionem futuræ in nobis fidei, & eorum quæ benefacturi eramus, electione posteriorem esse, saltem ordine.
units.tr: If they object that our works, not as done but as to be done and foreseen by God, are equally eternal, we reply that God foresaw in us no good work or good will which he had not decided to effect in us, and which he had not prepared for us by predestining, as it is said in Eph. 1: We are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand that we should walk in them. And in chapter 1 of the same epistle: He chose us before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him. Hence it is understood that, since we are predestined to life by God, it comes about that we do good works and believe. So foreknowledge of the future faith in us, and of the good deeds we were going to do, is posterior to election, at least in order.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Eodem recidit, si ad hunc modum argumentemur: Bona opera, similiter fides, & quicunq; liberi arbitrij vsus ad operandum aut ad credendum, aut etiam cogitandi aliquid boni, ex mera Dei gratia manant, tanquam effectus diuinæ electionis, vt pluribus infra oftenderur. Ergo neq; vt facta, neq; vt facienda & præuisa à Deo, considerari ista possunt tanquam causæ electionis. Nihil enim simul esse potest causa & effectus. fedus,respedu eiusdem. Opera, inquit Augustinus, non gratiam pariunt, sed gratia pariuntur. Non ut feruēat calefacit ignis, sed quia feruet. Nec ideo bene currit rota, ut rotunda sit, sed quia rotunda est. Sic nemo propterea bene operatur, ut accipiat gratiam, sed quia accepit.
units.tr: The same conclusion follows if we argue in this way: good works, likewise faith, and every use of free choice for acting or believing, or even for thinking anything good, flow from God's mere grace, as effects of divine election, as will be shown below. Therefore these things cannot be considered as causes of election, neither as done nor as to be done and foreseen by God. For nothing can be both cause and effect in the same respect. Augustine says: works do not produce grace, but are produced by grace. Fire does not heat so that it may be hot, but because it is hot. Nor does a wheel run well so that it may be round, but because it is round. So no one works well in order to receive grace, but because he has received it.

units.la: III. Si praeuisa nostra bona opera essent causa praedestinationis ad salutem aeternam, causa quoq; forent vocationis & iustificationis nostri. Falsum est posterius. Ergo & prius.
units.tr: III. If our foreseen good works were the cause of predestination to eternal salvation, they would also be the cause of our calling and justification. The latter is false; therefore the former is too.

units.la: Maior probatur regula: Quod est causa causae, etiam causa est causati, ut loquuntur: hoc est, effectus. Praedestinatio autem causa est vocationis & iustificationis, dicente Apostolo: quos praedestinauit, eos vocauit: quos vocauit, eos & iustificauit: quos iustificauit, eos & glorificauit.
units.tr: The major premise is proved by the rule: what is the cause of a cause is also the cause of what is caused, as they say; that is, of the effect. But predestination is the cause of calling and justification, as the Apostle says: Whom he predestined, them he also called; whom he called, them he also justified; whom he justified, them he also glorified.

units.la: Minor etiam facilime probatur, cum expresse testetur Spiritus sanctus, seruari nos a Deo, & vocari vocatione sancta, non ex operibus nostris, sed ex ipsius propositio & gratia, data nobis in Christo ante tempora secularia. Similiter de iustificatione omnibus modis gratuita, Paulus noster fusissime disserit, ad Rom. & Galatas.
units.tr: The minor premise is also very easily proved, since the Holy Spirit expressly testifies that we are saved by God and called with a holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace, given us in Christ before the secular times. Likewise our Paul argues at great length that justification is in every way gratuitous, in Romans and Galatians.

units.la: Fidem quidem requirit tanquam medium, quo oblatam Euangelio iustitiam & salutem nobis applicemus: sed non tanquam ex nobis. Dei enim donū est. Ac proinde si vel praescientia fidei, tanquam ex nobis, causa statuatur electionis, consequens erit, ut nec iustificatio omni modo gratuita sit. Alioquin stat, fide nos iustificari, tanquam medio, nec tamen fidem esse causam praedestinationis vice versa. Nam ut recte docet Aquinas, si effecta praedestinationis inter se coferantur, nihil vetat unum esse causam alterius: praecedens nimirum sequetis. Sic vocatio per verbum, causa est fidei: quia fides ex auditu: fides, causa iustificationis: iustificatio, bonorum operum, & gloriæ in vita cœlesti. Eadem tamen effecta praedestinationis, neque disiunctim, neque coniunctim considerata, queunt esse principium praedestinationis, cum idem non possit esse causa & effectus.
units.tr: Faith is indeed required as the means by which we apply to ourselves the righteousness and salvation offered in the gospel, but not as coming from us, for it is the gift of God. Therefore, if foreknowledge of faith, as coming from us, is set as the cause of election, it will follow that justification is not in every way gratuitous. Otherwise it stands that we are justified by faith as a means, and yet faith is not the cause of predestination, and vice versa. For, as Aquinas rightly teaches, if the effects of predestination are compared with one another, nothing prevents one being the cause of another, the preceding being the cause of the following. Thus calling through the word is the cause of faith, because faith comes from hearing; faith is the cause of justification; justification is the cause of good works and of glory in the heavenly life. Yet these same effects of predestination, considered neither separately nor together, cannot be the principle of predestination, since the same thing cannot be both cause and effect.

units.la: IV. In
units.tr: IV.

units.la: IV.
units.tr: IV.

units.la: In toto opere salutis id præcipuè spectatur, vt excludatur gloriatio omnis humana, vt sicut scriptum est, qui gloriatur glorietur in Domino. Quis enim te discernit? quid habes quod non accepisti? quod si autem accepisti, quid gloriaris, quasi non acceperis? Quod beatus Cyprianus imitari solebat, inquiens, In nullo gloriandum est, quia nihil nostrum est.
units.tr: In the whole work of salvation this is chiefly aimed at: that all human boasting be excluded, as it is written: He who boasts, let him boast in the Lord. For who makes you to differ? What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast, as if you had not received it? This blessed Cyprian used to imitate, saying: We must boast in nothing, because nothing is ours.

units.la: At gloriatio humana non omnis excluderetur, nisi electio, quæ principiū & fundamentum salutis est, à gratuita Dei voluntate & proposito penderet, citra vllius qualitatis nostræ respectum. Puta, si Deus quidem parem cunctis gratiam offerre, & vniuersos vocare dicatur: in hominis autem voluntate positum esse credatur, vt vocationi obtemperet; iam certè obtemperans à reluctante, fidelis ob impio seipsum discreuerit, nec poterit ei dici, quid gloriaris? Quis te discernit? quid habes quod non acceperis? Poslet enim dicere homo inflatus aduersus alterum, discernit me fides mea, iustitia mea, liberi arbitrij mei bonus vsus, vel siquid aliud.
units.tr: But human boasting would not be wholly excluded unless election, which is the principle and foundation of salvation, depended on God's free will and purpose, without regard to any quality in us. Suppose God is said to offer grace equally to all and to call everyone, but it is believed to lie in the man's own will whether he obeys the calling. Then one who obeys, when another resists, has by his own faithfulness distinguished himself from the impious, and it cannot be said to him: why do you boast? Who makes you differ? What do you have that you did not receive? For the puffed-up man could say against the other: my faith distinguishes me, my righteousness, the good use of my free choice, or whatever else.

units.la: V. Infirma & valdè incerta ess[?] et electio, ac proinde salus nostra, si à proposito voluntatis nostræ penderet. Instabilis enim hominum voluntas huc illuc flectitur, instar arundinis quam ventus agitat. E contrario, firma atque inconcussa stat electio in Dei beneplacito, proposito, ac voluntate gratuita erga nos in Christo Iesu: quemadmodum multis ostendit Apost. ad Rom. 8. inquiens: His qui Deum diligunt, cooperantur omnia in bonum: ijs videlicet, qui ex proposito ipsius vocati sunt. Nam quos præscivit, eosdem & prædestinavit, vt conformes fiant imagini filij sui. Quos vero prædestinavit, eos & vocavit, iustificavit, glorificavit. Et mox: quis nos separabit à caritate Christi? num oppressio? num angustia? num persecutio? num fames? num nuditas? nū gladius? Imò in his omnibus plus quàm victores sumus per eum, qui dilexit nos. Mihi persuasum est, quod neque mors neque vita, neque ulla res creata, possit nos separare à caritate Dei, quæ est in Christo Iesu. Homines igitur cùm simus, non inni- tamur nostræ infirmitati, sed firmiori quàm infirmiori; Deo qua nobis, fidè, spem,
units.tr: V. Election, and so our salvation, would be weak and very uncertain if it depended on the purpose of our will. For the unstable human will is bent this way and that, like a reed the wind shakes. On the contrary, election stands firm and unshaken in God's good pleasure, purpose and gratuitous will toward us in Christ Jesus, as the Apostle shows at length in Romans 8, saying: All things work together for good for those who love God, namely for those who are called according to his purpose. For whom he foreknew, these he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son. And whom he predestined, these he also called, justified and glorified. And soon after: Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation? Distress? Persecution? Famine? Nakedness? The sword? No, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us. For I am persuaded that neither death nor life, nor any created thing, can separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus. Therefore, since we are human, let us not lean on our weakness, but on what is firmer than the weak; let us rather commit our faith and hope to God,

units.la: K k spem, vitam & salutem nostram potius committamus, profitetes quod res est, ab ipsius vniuersa depedere proposito.
units.tr: life and salvation, professing, as is the truth, that all depends on his purpose.

units.la: VI. Referendum huc est & ipsius Iesu mediatoris, ac capitis nostri exemplum, quod Augustinus de praedest. sanct. cap. 15. & de bono perf. cap. 24. non potest satis commendare. I. conceptus est è Spiritu S. natus ex Maria virgine, conceptione & generatione singulari, & sine omni peccato. II. Humana, id est, nostra natura in Christo vnita est cum diuina in vnitatem persōnæ: verbo, vt loquitur Augustinus, singulariter eam suscipiente, & in vnicum filium Dei sublimante, ita vt qui suscepit, & quod suscepit, vna sit in trinitate persona. Quæ naturæ humanæ tanta & tam celsa subuectio est, vt quò attolleretur altius, non haberet, sicut pro nobis ipsa diuinitas quo vsque se deprimeret humilius, nō habuit, quàm quod suscepit naturam hominis cum infirmitate eius ad mortem vsque crucis.
units.tr: VI. This should also be referred to the example of Jesus himself, the Mediator and our head, which Augustine (On the Predestination of the Saints, ch. 15, and On the Gift of Perseverance, ch. 24) cannot sufficiently commend. I. He was conceived of the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary, by a singular conception and generation, and without any sin. II. Human nature, that is, our nature, was united in Christ with the divine nature in the unity of person: the Word, as Augustine puts it, taking it up in a singular way and exalting it into the one Son of God, so that he who took up and what was taken up are one person in the Trinity. Such is the elevation of human nature, so great and so lofty, that it could not be raised higher, just as divinity itself, for our sake, could not humble itself lower than by taking up the nature of man with its weakness, even to the death of the cross.

units.la: Ista autem omnia in Christo singulariter accepit natura humana, hoc est nostra natura,nullis suis meritis, sed ex sola Dei gratia. Ergo & nos nō ex operibus nostris,sed ex Dei prædestinantis proposito & gratia ad vitam æternam prædestinati fumus. Eadem enim ratio est capitis & membrorum: sed hoc interest,quòd ille prædestinatus est vnus, vt caput nostrum eflet, nos multi prædestinati fumus, vt membra ipsius efle-mus. Ac proinde in capite est fons gratiæ, & inde fecundum vniuscuiusque mensuram se per cuncta eius membra diffundit.
units.tr: Human nature received all these things in Christ alone, that is, our nature, not through any merits of its own but from the sheer grace of God. Therefore we too have not been predestined to eternal life on account of our works, but by the purpose and grace of God who predestines. For the reason is the same for head and members; but there is this difference: that one was predestined to be our head, while we, many, have been predestined to be his members. And so grace has its source in the head and from there flows through all his members, according to the measure of each one.

units.la: VII. Omnis hæc ratio, qua defendimus gratuitam prædestinationem ex Dei proposito, magnopere confirmatur exemplo paruulorum : quo vnò omnes contradicentiū & humana merita asserentium vires frangantur necesse est. Argumentum id tale est. Paruuli nostri etiam infantili ætate moriētes, promissionem habent regni cœlorum. Sunt igitur ad regnum prædestinati. Idque vel ex operibus vel ex gratia:non ex operibus,quia in tātilla ætate locum opera non habent, & ne præscientia quidem operum. Quæ enim neclsunt nec futurasunt, non possunt dici præscita, nisi vt non futura sunt. Ergo ex gratia, & per consequens aliorum quoque prædestinatio talis est, tanquam ex proposito Dei, & non ex operibus.
units.tr: VII. This whole line of reasoning, by which we defend predestination as free, flowing from God's purpose, is greatly strengthened by the example of infants; by this alone all who oppose it and who assert the powers of human merit must necessarily be broken. The argument runs thus. Our little children who die in infancy have the promise of the kingdom of heaven. They are therefore predestined to the kingdom. And this is either from works or from grace. Not from works, because at so tender an age works have no place, nor even foreseen works; for what neither is nor will be cannot be called foreknown, except as not going to be. Therefore it is from grace, and consequently the predestination of others too is of this kind, flowing from the purpose of God and not from works.

units.la: Pelagiani quomodo aut quorsum cuaderent, his coarctati angustiis, nescicbant. Postmodum tamen Semipelagiani rimam excogitantes elabendi, nouo absurditatis genere contenderunt, infantes ad vitam vel mortem prædestinatos pro suis futuris meritis, quæ fecissent si vixissent. Commentum hoc, non tam callidum quam temerarium & stolidum, diligentissimè atque optimè Augusst. refellit, tum alibi, tum lib. de bono perf. cap. 12. & 13. Inter alia opponit dictum Apost. Rom. 14. Omnes stabimus ante tribunal Christi, vt referat vnusquisque secundum ea quæ per corpus gessit, sive bonum sive malù: hoc est, secundum ea quæ gessit eo tempore quo in corpore fuit. Alioquin enim multa facit sola anima, & non per corpus aut corris membrum, ad poenam nihilominus vel praemium spectantia. Dixit autem, gesśit, non adiunxit, vel gesturus fuit. Unde etiam Sap. 4. de iusto legimus, qui per immaturam mortem tentationum subtrahitur incerto: Raptus est ne malitia mutaret intellectum eius. Ita firmum stat argumentum ab exemplo infantum, ut quod in illis negare non possumus de praedestinatione gratiae, in adultis quoque fateri & tueri debeamus: siquidem una eademque praedestinationis omnium ratio est.
units.tr: The Pelagians, hemmed in by these narrow straits, did not know how or where to turn. Later, however, the Semipelagians, devising a crack through which to escape, contended with a new kind of absurdity that infants are predestined to life or death on account of their future merits, that is, what they would have done had they lived. This fiction, not so much clever as rash and foolish, Augustine refuted most diligently and admirably, both elsewhere and in the book On the Good of Perseverance, chapters 12 and 13. Among other things he sets against it the saying of the Apostle, Rom. 14: We shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ, that each one may receive according to what he has done through the body, whether good or evil: that is, according to what he did during the time he was in the body. For otherwise the soul alone does many things, not through the body or any member of the body, which nonetheless pertain to punishment or reward. He said, has done; he did not add, or was going to do. Hence also we read in Wisdom 4 of the righteous man who is snatched away by untimely death from the uncertainty of temptations: He was taken away, lest wickedness should change his understanding. So the argument from the example of infants stands firm, so that what we cannot deny in them concerning the predestination of grace, we ought also to confess and defend in adults; for there is one and the same reason of predestination for all.

units.la: CAPVT VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: Idem testimoniis sacrarum literarum probatur.
units.tr: The same is proved by the testimonies of the sacred letters.

units.la: SED ad manifestiora veniamus. B. Moses Deut. 17. dicit ad populum Israëliticum: Populus sanctus es Domino Deo tuo, te elegit Dominus Deus tuus, ut sis ipsi populus peculiaris ex omnibus populis qui sunt in superficie terrae. Audimus Israëlis electionem, de cuius causa statim subdit: Non quia plures estis prae omnibus populis, amauit vos Dominus, & elegit vos: Etenim eratis vos pauciores omnibus populis: sed quia dilexit vos Dominus, & custodire voluit iuramentum, quod iurauerat patribus vestris, eduxit vos manu forti. En propositum Dei gratuitum, electionis istius causam.
units.tr: But let us come to plainer passages. Moses, in Deut. 17., says to the people of Israel: You are a holy people to the Lord your God; the Lord your God has chosen you, that you should be to him a peculiar people out of all the peoples that are upon the face of the earth. We hear of the election of Israel, and he at once adds its cause: Not because you were more in number than all peoples did the Lord set his love upon you and choose you, for you were fewer than all peoples; but because the Lord loved you, and wished to keep the oath which he had sworn to your fathers, he brought you out with a mighty hand. Here is God's free purpose, the cause of that election.

units.la: Idem, cap. 8. Caue ne dicas in corde tuo, fortitudo & potentia manus meæ fecit mihi opes has, sed memineris Domini Dei tui, quia ipse dat tibi potentiam, vt confirmet pactum quod iurauit patribus. Et in sequentibus; Ne dicas in corde tuo, cum propulsauerit Dominus gentes istas a facie tua: propter iustitiam meam introduxit me Dominus, vt terram istam possideam, & propter impietatem gentium istarum Dominus expulit eas a facie tua. Non propter iustitiam tuam & rectitudinem cordis tui ingrederis ad possidendam terram eorum: quanquam propter iniustitiam gentium istarum Dominus Deus tuus expellet eas a facie tua, sed vt stabiliat Dominus verbum, quod promiserat patribus tuis, Abrahamo, Isaaco & Iacobo. Nec sufficit Moßi, quod dixerat, non propter meritam ipsorum hæreditatem terræ illius Israë-
units.tr: Again, in chapter 8: Beware lest you say in your heart, My strength and the might of my hand have gotten me this wealth; but remember the Lord your God, for it is he who gives you power to establish the covenant which he swore to your fathers. And in what follows: Do not say in your heart, when the Lord has thrust out those nations from before you, It is for my righteousness that the Lord has brought me in to possess this land; and because of the wickedness of those nations the Lord drives them out from before you. It is not for your righteousness or the uprightness of your heart that you go in to possess their land; but because of the wickedness of those nations the Lord your God drives them out from before you, and so that the Lord may establish the word which he promised to your fathers, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. Nor was it enough for Moses to have said that the inheritance of that land was not granted to the Israelite people on account of their merits; he also adds this:

units.la: Deuter. 8. Israelitico populo fuisse concessam, nisi etiam adderet, scilicet quod non propter iustitiam tuam Dominus dat tibi terram istam optimam hereditate possidendam, quoniam populus dura cervicis es. Quo omni bono indignos eos declarabat.
units.tr: Deut. 8. Namely, that not for your righteousness does the Lord give you this excellent land to possess as an inheritance, since you are a stiff-necked people. By this he declared them unworthy of every good.

units.la: Ecce igitur antiquissimum dogma gratiæ, atque electionis secundum gratiam, in ipsis Israelitici populi exordiis Spiritus sancti voce firmatum. Clare siquidem bonitatem & seueritatem Dei Propheta ostendit in uno eodemque scripturæ loco, dicens, non propter iustitiam populi sed gratia tantum miserentis donari illis terra hereditatem: gentes autem pelli eadem terra propter iniustitiam suam.
units.tr: Here, then, is the most ancient doctrine of grace and of election according to grace, affirmed by the voice of the Holy Spirit at the very beginnings of the Israelite people. For the Prophet shows clearly both the goodness and the severity of God in one and the same passage of Scripture, saying that the land was given to them as an inheritance not on account of the righteousness of the people but by grace alone, of him who shows mercy; while the nations were driven out of that same land on account of their wickedness.

units.la: Quia tamen Israelitis cum Cananeis atque Amorrœis communis erat iniustitia, liquet eo magis, nihil boni in illis vidisse Deum, vt eam gentem præ omnibus aliis nationibus extolleret. Ac pulcre Ezech. describit, quod Dominus ex mera misericordia populum illum ab initio respexerit, vt puellam nudam, fœdatam, & contaminatam vndique. Et quoties obsecro Dominu ten-
units.tr: Yet since the Israelites shared their wickedness with the Canaanites and the Amorites, it is all the more plain that God saw nothing good in them by which he should exalt that nation above all other nations. And Ezekiel describes beautifully how the Lord, out of pure mercy, looked upon that people from the beginning, like a naked, foul and filthy girl, defiled all over. And how often, I beg you, did they tempt the Lord

units.la: tentauerunt in deserto? quoties saluauit eos propter misericordiam & patientiam suam? Quando non Spiritui sancto restiterunt? Ergo manifestum est elegisse Deum quos voluit, ex mera gratia.
units.tr: in the wilderness? How often did he save them because of his mercy and patience? When did they not resist the Holy Spirit? It is therefore manifest that God chose whom he willed, out of pure grace.

units.la: At Moses ibi agit de electione temporali Israelitarum, vt essent Dei populus; & de beneficiis temporalibus eam electionem consecutis: vt erant, liberatio ex Ægypto, introductio in terram Canaan, &c.
units.tr: But Moses there is speaking of the temporal election of the Israelites, that they should be God's people, and of the temporal benefits that followed that election: such as their liberation from Egypt, their introduction into the land of Canaan, and so on.

units.la: Respondeo: I. temporalis illa electio etiam includebat æterna: etsi non quod ad totum corpus populi, tamen quod ad aliquos in eo corpore. Nam in cœtu vocatorum semper sunt aliqui electi, dolii vita æterna. Et speciatim de illo populo id Apostolus attestatur ad Rō. II.
units.tr: I answer: I. That temporal election also included the eternal; not indeed as regards the whole body of the people, but as regards some within that body. For in the company of the called there are always some elect, who are destined for eternal life. And the Apostle bears witness to this about that very people in Rom. 11.

units.la: II. à liberatione ex Ægypto, & introductione in terram Canaan, valet consequentia, tanquam à typis ad rem significatam, etiam redemtionem à peccato, & vitam æternam Deũ gratis atque ex mera dilectione dare, quibus vult & voluit ab æterno.
units.tr: II. From the liberation out of Egypt and the introduction into the land of Canaan, the inference holds, as from types to the thing signified, that God also gives freely, and from pure love, redemption from sin and eternal life to whom he wills and has willed from eternity.

units.la: III. militat hîc generalis ratio: si externa illa à nullis Israëlitarû meritis, sed à solo miserentis proposito pendebant, multò magis ab eodem pendere electionem ad regni cœlestis hæreditatem.
units.tr: III. A general argument also bears on this: if those external benefits depended not on any merits of the Israelites but on the purpose of the merciful God alone, much more does election to the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom depend on the same.

units.la: Est & locus ille Eccles. 33. non contemnendus, tametsi liber iste non sit pari autoritate cum scripturis canonicis: ut dies iedem præcellat iudicio Domini, ita multiplici scientia eius distingui homines, & extolli vel deprimi. Quoniam ut lutum in manu figuli est, quod pro suo tractat arbitrio, ita homines sunt in manu Dei creatoris sui, quibus pro suo iudicio singulis reddat. Vt contrarium malo bonum, contrariaq; morti vita est: sic oppositus peccatori pius est, & pio peccator. Ita in omnibus operibus altissimi bina videas, quorum unum repugnet alteri.
units.tr: There is also that passage in Eccles. 33, not to be despised, although that book does not have the same authority as the canonical Scriptures: As one day is distinguished from another by the Lord's judgement, so by his manifold knowledge are men distinguished and exalted or cast down. For as clay is in the potter's hand, which he shapes at his pleasure, so men are in the hand of God their Creator, to whom he renders to each according to his judgement. As good is set against evil, and life against death, so the sinner is opposed to the godly, and the godly to the sinner. So in all the works of the Most High you may see two things, one of which is opposed to the other.

units.la: I. Admonemur hîc, omnes homines pares esse natura & origine: sicut natura pares sunt dies: paria item vasa ex eodem formata luto, quantum ad materiam & originem. Sumus sane & nos omnes ex eodem luto, sive ex una eademque massa: omnes quippe é terra ortum trahimus. Inde Adamus Protoplastus, & ex Adamo vniuersi nos. Neq; tantùm origo eadem est omnibus mortalibus, sed eadem quoq; nascendi conditio; quoniam cunċti cum pecca- to nascimur ex Adamo, postquam ille à primæua defecit origine.
units.tr: I. We are reminded here that all men are equal in nature and origin, just as days are equal in nature; likewise vessels formed from the same clay are equal as regards their material and origin. We are indeed all from the same clay, or from one and the same mass: for we all draw our origin from the earth. Hence Adam, the first-formed, and from Adam all of us. Nor is the origin only the same for all mortals, but the condition of birth is the same too, since we all are born with sin from Adam, after he fell from his original state.

units.la: II. docemur verbis propositis, quas- cunque & qualescunque hominum differentias existere à Deo, alios eu- hṛente,alios deprimente, alios benedi- stos,alios execrabiles habente.
units.tr: II. We are taught by the words set forth that whatever and whatever kind of differences among men exist, they exist from God, who exalts some, humbles others, blesses some, and holds others accursed.

units.la: III. distinctionis istius nulla alia cau- sa affertur, præterquam dispositio, ar- bitrium, sapientia, & iudicium altis- mi; qui cùm omnium creator sit, in o- mnia quoque opera sua summum at- que irrefragabile ius obtinet,multò ma- gis quàm figulus ex eodem fingens lu- to quicquid animus tulerit.
units.tr: III. For this distinction no other cause is given except the disposition, will, wisdom and judgement of the Most High; who, since he is the Creator of all, holds the highest and irresistible right over all his works, much more than the potter, who from the same clay fashions whatever his mind has decided.

units.la: Ad Paulum progredior, qui tanquā scriba doctissimus in regno cœlorum, è thesauro suo protulit noua & veteraad doctrinæ huius confirmationem. Is ca- pite 9. ad Rom. diluere volens scanda- lum ex perfidia Iudæorum,quo ea æta- te multorum animi grauiter tentaban- tur,
units.tr: I come to Paul, who, like a most learned scribe in the kingdom of heaven, brought forth from his treasure things both new and old for the confirmation of this doctrine. In chapter 9 of Romans, wishing to dispel the scandal arising from the unbelief of the Jews, by which in that age the minds of many were sorely troubled,

units.la: Scopus ad Rom.9. tur, quasi aut excideret sermo Dei, & irrita redderetur promissio, aut Iesus Nazarenus non esset promissus à Deo Seruator (alterutrum enim horum sequi videbatur, eò quòd Israelitarum erant fœdera, cultus & promissiones) multis ostendit verum semen Abrahæ, verosque Israelitas, ad quos promissa in Christo benedictio & salus pertineant, solos esse electos: filios videlicet promissionis, non carnis, ex Iudæis pariter & gentibus. Atque ita ingreditur Apostolus amplam & profundam de prædestinatione doctrinam: in qua, vt de re quæ nunc agitur, loquamur, aliis omissis, perspicuè docet, quod ad causam prædestinationis attinet; Deū, vtpote liberrimum, eligere quos velit ex mera gratia, & iusto, licet occulto, consilio voluntatis suæ reprobare quos velit.
units.tr: (the scope of Rom. 9.) as if the word of God had failed and its promise had become void, or as if Jesus of Nazareth had not been promised by God as Saviour (for it seemed that one of these two must follow, since the covenants, worship and promises belonged to the Israelites), he shows to many that the true seed of Abraham, and the true Israelites, to whom the blessing and salvation promised in Christ pertain, are alone the elect: namely, the children of the promise, not of the flesh, from Jews and Gentiles alike. And so the Apostle enters upon an ample and profound doctrine of predestination. In it, to speak of the matter now under discussion, setting other things aside, he teaches plainly, as far as the cause of predestination is concerned, that God, as most free, chooses whom he wills out of pure grace, and by a just, though hidden, counsel of his will rejects whom he wills.

units.la: 1. Docet id exemplo Iacobi & Esau, quorum ille huic prælatus est mero Dei fauore: quia cum essent ambo per omnia pares, ex eodem concepti concubitu, nondum natis pueris, cum nihil hil fecissent boni vel mali, oraculum redditum est eorum matri Rebeccæ: Maior seruiet minori. Non igitur est electio ex operibus, sed ex gratia.
