Frustra autem confugietur hic ad cauillatio-nem de præuilione boni alicuius in Iacobo: quia Paulus remouere voluit omne diferimen à duobus istis fratribus, vt prorsus intelligamus fuisse pares, quantum ad ipsos.
units.tr: 1. He teaches this by the example of Jacob and Esau, of whom the one was preferred to the other by the mere favour of God: for although the two were in every way equal, conceived of the same union, and before the boys were born, when they had done neither good nor evil, an oracle was given to their mother Rebekah: The elder shall serve the younger. Election, therefore, is not from works but from grace. Nor is it useful here to take refuge in the quibble about some foreseen good in Jacob, because Paul wished to remove every difference between those two brothers, so that we understand they were altogether equal as far as they themselves were concerned.

units.la: II. Apostolus expressè causam discretionis inter Iacob & Efau, & horum exemplo in genere inter electos & reprobos, reuocat ad Dei προθεσιν propo-situm & beneplacitum, quo nimirum elegit & præterijt, quos voluit, & quia ita voluit. Hæc enim est ὁ κατ' ἐκλογὴν τὴν θεοῦ προθεσιν.
units.tr: II. The Apostle expressly refers the cause of the distinction between Jacob and Esau, and by their example, in general between the elect and the reprobate, to God's purpose [πρόθεσιν] and good pleasure, by which he assuredly chose and passed over whom he willed, and because he so willed. For this is "the purpose [πρόθεσις] of God according to election" [ὁ κατ' ἐκλογὴν τῆς θεοῦ πρόθεσις].

units.la: III. Subiunxit Apoft. maioris explicationis causa: Non ex operibus, sed ex vocante. Quæ verba alij construunt cum præcedenti, vt fit descriptio electionis gratuitæ & non ex operibus: alij referunt ad sequens verbum, ἐρρέθη dictum est: quam lectionem & Augufl.sequitur ad Laur. cap. 98. Quicquid fit, apparet, & cleelectionem, & vocatione, quæ illius effectu est, esse ex gratia, & no ex operib. Simpliciter autem quemcunque operu remouet intuitum, ut sine vllis bonorum malorumue operu meritis, vnum Deus diligat, oderitq; alterum. Nam si futura opera, vel bona huius, vel mala illius, quæ Deus præuidebat, vellet intelligi, nequaquam diceret, non ex operibus:sed diceret, ex futuris operibus, eoque modo iltam soluaret quæstionem: vti notat Augustinus Enchir. ad Laur. cap. 98. & ad Simplic. lib. 1. quæst. 2.
units.tr: III. The Apostle added, for the sake of fuller explanation: Not of works, but of him who calls. Some construe these words with what precedes, so that they describe free election, which is not from works. Others refer them to the following verb, "it was said" (ἐρρέθη), and Augustine also follows this reading in his letter to Laurentius, chapter 98. Whichever reading is adopted, it is clear that both election and the calling that follows from it are of grace and not of works. He simply sets aside every consideration of works, so that God loves one and hates another without any regard to good or evil deeds. For if he wanted it understood that he looked to future works, whether good in the one or evil in the other, which God foresaw, he would never have said not of works. He would have said of future works, and in that way would have resolved the question. Augustine notes this in the Enchiridion to Laurentius, chapter 98, and in his books to Simplicianus, book 1, question 2.

units.la: iv. Facit huc propheticum illud, Iacob dilexi: Esau vero odio habui. Dei igitur electio discernit inter electos & reprobos. Ea vero in hoc est, teste Johanne, non quod ipsum nos dilexerimus, sed quod ipse dilexerit nos. Nec obstat quod Deum scimus diligere omnia opera sua, nec quicquam odisse eorum quæ fecit: siquidem, vt supra quoque dictum est, gradus sunt dilectionis Dei: & quia non omnibus vult hoc bonum, quod est vita æterna, ideo dicitur quosdam diligere, quosdam odisse.
units.tr: IV. The prophetic saying also bears on this: Jacob I have loved, but Esau I have hated. God's election therefore distinguishes between the elect and the reprobate. According to John, this election consists not in our having loved him, but in his having loved us. Nor is it an objection that we know God loves all his works and hates nothing that he has made. As was said above, there are degrees of God's love, and because he does not will this good, which is eternal life, for all, he is said to love some and to hate others.

units.la: v. Ex præoccupatione idem appa-ret: Num igitur iniustitia apud Deum? Nam quæstio hæc ne locum quidem haberet, nisi id vellet Apostolus, electionem nimirum non esse ex vllis operibus, factis vel futuris, sed ex solo Dei beneplacito. Si enim quisquam electus vel reprobatus est à Deo, prout quemque male vel bene vsurum libero arbitrio præuidit, ipsa ratio humana fatebitur hoc esse æquissimum. Sed quod audit, vbi omnia sunt paria, Deum tamé pro sua voluntate vnum eligere, alterum reprobare, atque ita æqualibus tribuere inæqualia, hinc ille fremitus rationis humanæ contra iustitiam Dei.
units.tr: V. The same appears from the objection the Apostle anticipates: Is there then unrighteousness with God? This question would have no place at all unless the Apostle meant that election is not from any works, past or future, but from God's good pleasure alone. For if God elected or rejected anyone according to how well or badly he foresaw each would use his free will, human reason itself would admit that this is most just. But when human reason hears that, where all are equal, God nonetheless chooses one by his own will and rejects another, and so assigns unequal things to equals, it rages against the justice of God.

units.la: vi. Ni ita esset, Apostolus soluens obiectionem allatam, non reijceret eam cum stomacho, inquiens, ἀλλ᾽ γένοιτο sed sic soluerct quæstionem, Deum vnumquemque ex suis meritis, saltem præuisis, pœnæ vel præmio destinatum, non posse videri iniustum. Fuisset hæc apertissima & facilima diuinæ iustitiæ defensio.
units.tr: VI. If this were not so, the Apostle, answering the objection raised, would not have rejected it with indignation, saying God forbid (ἀλλὰ γένοιτο). He would have answered the question by saying that God, appointing each man to punishment or reward according to his merits, at least foreseen merits, cannot be thought unjust. This would have been the plainest and easiest defence of divine justice.

units.la: vii. Longè alia vtitur solutione, qua
units.tr: VII. He uses a quite different solution, one that seems less to resolve the question than to tighten it, when he says:

units.la: {a} Aug. ad Laur. cap. 3. qua non tam soluere, quàm adstringere videtur quæstionem, cùm inquit, Mosi dicit miserebor cuius misertus fuero, & commiserabor quem commiseratus fuero. Qua sententia docemur, Deum, licet generatim loquendo misericordiam suam nulli subtrahat, secundum quendam tamen misericordiæ modum, horum constituisse misereri, horum non: idque ideo, quia ita velit. Sic enim libertam quandam potestatem significare volentes dicere solemus, faciam quod facturus sum.
units.tr: {a} Augustine, to Laurentius, chapter 3. It is the answer that seems less to resolve the question than to bind it fast, when he says: To Moses he says, I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show compassion on whom I have compassion. By this statement we are taught that God, although speaking generally he withholds his mercy from no one, nevertheless, according to a certain measure of mercy, has determined to show mercy to some and not to others, and this because he so wills. For when we wish to express a certain freedom of power, we commonly say, I will do what I am going to do.

units.la: VIII.
units.tr: VIII.

units.la: Vnde etiam Apostolus ex oraculo illo sic infert: Ergo non est currentis nec volentis, sed miserentis Dei. Si autem principium salutis à nobis esset, sicut fingunt ij, qui ex bonis nostris operibus, aut voluntate bona præuisa, electionem proficisci statuunt, iam certè contra Apostoli sententiam esset volentis & currentis.
units.tr: Hence the Apostle also draws this conclusion from that oracle: So then it is not of him who wills nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy. If, however, the beginning of salvation came from us, as those maintain who hold that election proceeds from our good works or from a foreseen good will, then surely it would be against the Apostle's teaching that it is of him who wills and runs.

units.la: Nec est quod Semipelagianus aliquis dicat, voluntati ad bonum persequendum infirmæ, ad id tamen propensæ, gratiam opitulari: & propterea dictum, non non volentis nec currentis, sed miserentis est Dei, tanquam diceretur: Non sufficit sola voluntas hominis, si non sit etiam misericordia Dei. Etenim cum Augustino respondemus: si eo quod voluntas hominis sola non implet salutem, recte dictum est, non volentis est hominis, sed miserentis Dei: etiam e converso, si misericordia Dei eam sola non implet, recte diceretur: non miserentis est Dei, sed volentis est hominis: quod piae aures non ferunt. Restat ergo propterea dici: non volentis nec currentis est hominis, ut totum Deo detur, qui hominis voluntatem bonam & praeparat adiuuandam, & adiuuat praeparatam. Nam ut scriptum est: Misericordia eius praevenit nos, & misericordia eius subsequitur nos. Nolentes praevenit ut velimus, volentes subsequitur, ne frustra velimus.
units.tr: Nor should anyone say, as some Semipelagian might, that grace comes to the aid of the human will, which is weak for pursuing the good but nonetheless inclined to it, and that therefore it is said that salvation is not of him who wills nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy, as if it were said: the will of man alone is not enough, unless the mercy of God is there too. For with Augustine we reply: if it is rightly said, because the will of man alone does not accomplish salvation, that it is not of the man who wills, but of God who shows mercy, then conversely, if the mercy of God alone does not accomplish it, it would rightly be said: it is not of God who shows mercy, but of the man who wills, which pious ears cannot bear. It remains, then, to say that it is not of him who wills nor of him who runs, so that the whole is given to God, who both prepares the good will of man to be helped and helps it when prepared. For as it is written: His mercy goes before us, and his mercy follows us. He goes before the unwilling so that we may will, and follows the willing so that our willing is not in vain.

units.la: 1 x. Apostolus ad utrumque concludens, id est ad misericordiam & iudicium, inquit: Itaque cuius vult miseretur, quem autem vult indurat. Miseretur scilicet magna bonitate: & obdurat nulla iniquitate: quoniam in quo non fit misericorsericordia, in eo non fit iniquitas, sed iudicium. Vrrumque autem, miseratio inquam & iudicium, cur illum potius quàm illū liberet aut non liberet, diuinæ tribuitur voluntati, quæ sola discernit liberandos à non liberandis, cum communis causa vniuersos perditionis massæ inuoluat.
units.tr: X. The Apostle, drawing his conclusion on both points, that is, on mercy and judgement, says: So then he has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills. He shows mercy, to be sure, out of great goodness, and hardens out of no iniquity, since where there is no mercy there is no iniquity, but judgement. Both, I say, both the showing of mercy and the judgement, why he sets free this one rather than that one, or does not set free, is ascribed to the divine will, which alone distinguishes those to be set free from those not to be set free, since the common cause involves all of the lump of perdition.

units.la: x. Ad rem nostram facit, quod de figulo & vasorum diuersitate adducit Paulus. Figulus enim non considerans luti meritum, pro suo tantum arbitrio ex eodem luto format cuiuscunq; generis vasa, ad honorem & ignominiam. Ergo multo magis Deus, non hominū merita, sed suam duntaxat voluntatem, in eligendo & reprobando sequi dicendus est, incolumi tamen eius iustitia, de qua postea. Eleganter Sapiens: Sicut lutum, ait, in manu figuli est, quod pro suo tractet arbitrio: ita homines sunt in manu Dei creatoris sui, quibus pro suo singulis iudicio, seu arbitrio, reddat. Similiter Apostolus: An non potestatem habet figulus in lutum, ut ex eadem massa faciat aliud quidem vas ad decus, aliud ad dedecus? Et subijcit de utrisque vtriusque vasis, irae & misericordiae: illa coagmentata ad interitum, haec praeparata a Deo ad gloriam. Quod si Deo eligenti aut reijcienti opera ipsectanda essent, potestas illa nulla esset, & plus posset figulus aliquis quam Deus.
units.tr: X. What Paul brings in about the potter and the diversity of vessels bears on our case. For the potter, without considering the merit of the clay, forms out of the same clay, at his own pleasure alone, vessels of whatever kind, some for honour and some for dishonour. Therefore, much more, God must be said to follow not the merits of men but his own will alone, in choosing and rejecting, yet with his justice left intact, which we shall discuss later. The Wise Man says it well: As the clay is in the potter's hand, to be handled at his pleasure, so men are in the hand of God their creator, to be rendered to each according to his own judgement or will. Likewise the Apostle: Has not the potter power over the clay, to make out of the same lump one vessel for honour and another for dishonour? And he adds, concerning both kinds of vessel, of wrath and of mercy: those fitted together for destruction, these prepared by God for glory. But if works had to be considered by God in choosing or rejecting, that power would be nothing, and some potter would have more power than God.

units.la: Etsi autem in antithesi vasorum duplicis generis, diuersis verbis non exprimitur, a quonam irae vasa ad interitum coagmentata dicantur: attamen similitudo a Paulo adhibita scrupulum iustum facile eximit. Figulus utique ex eodem luto vasa pro suo format arbitrio, adhonorem vel cotumeliam. Quapropter aut non quadrabit hoc simile figuli, aut fatendum erit ingenue, utraque vasa praeparata a Deo, & destinata suis vsibus, pro ipsius proposito. Hinc aperte Augustus lib.2. de nuptiis & concupisc. ad Valerium cap.16. Nonne vasa irae sub diabolo? An vero quia sub diabolo sunt, alius ea quam ille facit, qui vasa misericordiae facit? aut aliunde & non ex eadem massa facit? Nec tamen Deus Diabolo vasa facit, sed sibi, vt qui sciat eis vti ad opera sua iusta & bona, sicut ipse vtitur Diabolo. Idem ad Simpl. lib.i.quæst.2. Ex numero impiorum, quos Deus non iustificat, facit vasa in contumeliam, nec in eis odit Deus quod ipse facit, creando vel ordinando, in quantum videlicet homines sunt, & in quantum vasa sunt: Sed tamen, quod vasa eos facit perditionis, ad vsum aliquem facit, vt per eorum ordinatas pœnas, vasa quæ fiunt in honorem, proficiant. Additque ibidem, quod ex conspersione impiorum fiant vasa perditionis, opus esse ordinationis diuinæ. Vas enim irae esse, vt alibi explicat, esse hominem qui propter naturam bonum creatur, propter vitia supplicio destinatum esse. Idcirco diuinæ ordinationis esse, cui licet ambigere? Sic Fulgentius ad Monimum lib. 1. ait: In hoc vasa irae Deus aptauit, in quod prædestinauit: hoc est, inquit, in interitum, non in peccata. Hæc notent quos locutio offendit, de vasis irae à Deo apparatis ad interitum. Ideo autem offendit, quia perperam intelligunt, tanquam de vitio ipso, & non de supplicio propter vitium. Quo sensu nec nos inficiamur Deum vasa irae non facere, sed reperire potius.
units.tr: Although, in the contrast between the two kinds of vessel, the words do not state in different terms by whom the vessels of wrath are said to be fitted together for destruction, yet the comparison Paul uses easily removes a just scruple. The potter, certainly, forms vessels from the same clay at his own discretion, for honour or for dishonour. Therefore either this comparison of the potter does not fit, or it must be frankly admitted that both kinds of vessel were prepared by God and destined for their uses according to his purpose. Hence Augustine states plainly in book 2 of On Marriage and Concupiscence, to Valerius, chapter 16: Are not the vessels of wrath under the devil? Or is it that, because they are under the devil, another makes them than he who makes the vessels of mercy? Or does he make them from another lump, and not from the same? Yet God does not make vessels for the devil, but for himself, so that he may know how to use them for his just and good works, just as he uses the devil. The same in his book 1, question 2, to Simplicianus: From the number of the impious, whom God does not justify, he makes vessels for dishonour, and God does not hate in them what he himself makes, by creating or ordaining them, insofar as they are men, and insofar as they are vessels. But in that he makes them vessels of destruction, he makes them for some use, so that through their appointed punishments the vessels which are made for honour may profit. He adds in the same place that the vessels of destruction are formed from the mass of the impious by a divine ordinance. For to be a vessel of wrath, as he explains elsewhere, is to be a man who is created good by nature but is destined for punishment on account of his vices. Who could doubt, then, that this is by divine ordinance? So Fulgentius, in his letter to Monimus, book 1, says: God fitted the vessels of wrath for that purpose for which he predestined them: that is, he says, for destruction, not for sins. Let those note this who are offended by the expression, about vessels of wrath prepared by God for destruction. They are offended because they understand it wrongly, as if it referred to the vice itself, and not to the punishment on account of the vice. In this sense we too do not deny that God does not make vessels of wrath, but rather finds them.

units.la: CAPVT IX.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX.

units.la: Exceptionum quarundam solutiones.
units.tr: Solutions of certain objections.

units.la: POssent ifthæc, quantum ad hunc locu attinet, sufficere pro tuenda gratuita Dei electione, qua ex genere humano libere, & pro potestate sua ad vitam æternam alios eligit, alios præterit, nullo operum aut dignitatis indignitatisue in ipsis hominibus respectu. Sed quia lubricus animus, & qui veritatem fugit, nec tamen effugit, multa diuerticula & effugia quærit, ad exceptiones quasdam respondendum est, antequâ ad alias probationes ex alijs scripturarum locis pergamus.
units.tr: These points, as far as this passage is concerned, might be enough to defend God's free election, by which from the human race he chooses some to eternal life and passes over others, freely and by his own power, with no regard to works or to worth or unworthiness in the men themselves. But because a slippery mind, which flees the truth yet does not escape it, seeks many side-paths and escapes, certain objections must be answered before we go on to other proofs from other passages of Scripture.

units.la: Erasmus in libro quem edidit de libero arbitrio, cui Lutherus se acriter oppositu, videns disputationem Apostoli contra se stare de Iacob & Esau, excipiebat oraculum Genes. 25. Maior seruiet minori, non pertinere ad salutem hominis, verum ad rem temporariam: posse autem Deum pro sua libera voluntate decernere, ut homo seruus sit & pauper, velit nolit, nec tamen reiciatur ciatur ab æterna salute. Illud vero Mala chiæ, quod Paulus attexit, Iacob dilexi, Esau odio habui, eadem industria torque-bat: Prophetā nō videri loqui de odio, quo quis damnetur in æternum, sed de temporaria duntaxat afflictione poste-rorum Esau, quòd regio ipsorum esset vastata, nec spes esset reædificationis. Huc autem exceptiones istæ spectant, quasi Paulus mala fide (quod absit) scri-pturas citauerit, aut etiam attulerit pro testimonijs, quæ parum ad propo-situm facerent. Quemadmodum Era-smū non potuit huc referre, quod ni-mis profecto superciliosè, & parū Chri-stiane, imo profane, scribit alicubi Hie-ronymus, ea pugnare apud Paulum, quæ suis locis non pugnent. Quod si verum est, abusus est Apostolus simpli-citate imperitorum, vt impius calu-mniabatur Porphyrius.
units.tr: Erasmus, in his book on free will, which Luther opposed fiercely, saw that the Apostle's argument about Jacob and Esau stood against him. So he explained away the oracle of Genesis 25, The elder shall serve the younger, as not concerning man's salvation but a temporary matter. He said that God could decree by his free will that a man be a servant and poor, whether he wished it or not, and yet not be cast off from eternal salvation. As for the words of Malachi that Paul added, Jacob have I loved, Esau have I hated, he twisted them with the same diligence: the prophet, he said, does not seem to speak of a hatred by which someone is condemned forever, but only of a temporary affliction of the posterity of Esau, because their land was laid waste and there was no hope of rebuilding. These evasions aim at making it seem that Paul, with bad faith (God forbid), cited Scripture or brought forward as proofs passages that hardly suited his purpose. Erasmus could not apply to this what Jerome, rather haughtily and not very Christianly, indeed profanely, writes somewhere: that in Paul things fight with one another which do not fight in their own places. If that is true, the Apostle abused the simplicity of the unlearned, as the impious Porphyry slandered him.

units.la: Sed ad rem. Primo respondetur per concessionem. Etsi testimonia prophe-tica tantùm de rebus corporalibus lo-querentur, quod verum non est; nihil id Pauli vel nostro instituto officeret.
units.tr: But to the matter. First, we answer by concession: even if the prophetic testimonies spoke only of bodily things, which is not true, that would not harm Paul's argument or ours.

units.la: Pondus enim argumenti est in hoc, quòd sola vocantis gratia Iacob peruenerit, quò Esau non peruenit, nec huius vel illius meritis factum sit, vt alter alteri præferretur, ac dominio vel seruituti, dilectioni vel odio, deputaretur. Hic non valde interest de dominio & seruitute spirituali, vel corporali, verba oraculi accipiamus. Quod de dilectione & odio similiter valet. Si de dominio & seruitute temporali dictum intelligere placet, quatenus Idumæi, qui ab Esau erant oriundi, tempore Dauidis & Salomonis Judæis paruerunt: quamquam sensus is tenuis admodum est, firmum tamen erit argumentum animori hoc modo: Si quod posteri Iacob dominium habuerūt in posteros Esau, factum est non propter horum vel illorum merita, sed quia sic voluit Deus; quanto magis aliorum præ aliis ad verū dominium & regnum cœlestę vocationem, ex sola gratia vocantis, & non ex operibus æstimare oportet?
units.tr: For the weight of the argument lies in this, that Jacob obtained by the grace of the one calling alone what Esau did not obtain, and that it was not by the merits of this one or that one that the one was preferred to the other and assigned to lordship or servitude, to love or hatred. Here it does not much matter whether we take the words of the oracle of spiritual or bodily lordship and servitude. The same holds for love and hatred. If one wishes to understand it of temporal lordship and servitude, in so far as the Edomites, who were descended from Esau, obeyed the Jews in the time of David and Solomon, although that sense is rather thin, the argument will still be firm in this form: if the posterity of Jacob had lordship over the posterity of Esau, and this came about not because of the merits of these or those but because God so willed, how much more must we judge that some are preferred to others for true lordship and the heavenly kingdom, and for the calling, by the grace of the one calling alone and not from works?

units.la: Secundò, non de temporarijs solùm agi dicto illo prophetico: Maior seruiet minori, minori, conuincitur ex ipso textu. Sic enim habet oraculum Genes. 25. Duo populi ex utero tuo dividentur, populusque populum superabit, & maior serviet minori.
units.tr: Second, that the prophetic saying The elder shall serve the younger does not concern temporal matters only is proved from the text itself. For the oracle in Genesis 25 reads: Two peoples shall be divided from your womb, and one people shall overcome the other, and the elder shall serve the younger.

units.la: Hic manifeste duo populi discernuntur: alter in gratiam Dei recipitur, licet minor, ut sit populus Dei, sicut evictu ipso comprobatum fuit: alter a gratia illa repellitur. Suscipi vero in populum Dei, aut non suscipi, non pertinet ad temporalia bona vel mala tantum, sed ad omnia. Neque enim Deus noster tantum temporalium Deus est, sed omnium. Unde Psalmographus beatum celebrat populum, cui Iehoua Deus est. Atque is fuit sensus prophetiae, Jacobi non Esaui posteritatem electam a Domino, in qua esset Ecclesia, & verus Dei cultus, verbum, benedictio, Spiritus, promissio Christi, & regnum æternum: id quod etiam latius postea Scriptura confirmat, vbi Iacob benedici & promissiones & regnum accipere describit. Huc enim tendit benedictio Isaaci in Iacobum prolata, Genes. 27. non ut sanctus Patriarcha
units.tr: Here two peoples are clearly distinguished: one is received into the grace of God, though it is the lesser, so that it may be the people of God, as the outcome itself proved; the other is repelled from that grace. Now to be received into the people of God, or not received, concerns not only temporal good or evil but all things. For our God is not the God of temporal things only but of all. Hence the Psalmist celebrates the blessed people whose God is Jehovah. This was the sense of the prophecy: that the posterity of Jacob, not of Esau, was chosen by the Lord, in which there would be the Church, the true worship of God, the word, the blessing, the Spirit, the promise of Christ, and the eternal kingdom. Scripture later confirms this more fully, where it describes Jacob receiving the blessing, the promises and the kingdom. For the blessing of Isaac spoken over Jacob, Genesis 27, aims at this, not that the holy patriarch should

units.la: Psal.144. — Benedictio Iacob {a}spem filij in mundo includat, quo spreto meliorem ipse patriam, coelestem nimirum, exspectabat; sed vt beneuolentiam Dei in omnibus ipsi testetur, & Principem illum constituat & caput sancti atque electi populi. Quæ omnia Paulus breuiter indicat, nos ad Mosen remittens latius hæc tractantem; vt dicere possimus, testimonia quæ Paulus citat fortius pugnare locis suis quàm apud ipsum.
units.tr: Psalm 144. — the blessing of Jacob should bound the son's hope in the world, the son who, scorning it, looked for a better country, namely the heavenly one; but that it should bear witness to God's goodwill towards him in all things, and appoint him prince and head of the holy and chosen people. Paul briefly indicates all these things, and sends us to Moses, who treats them at greater length; so that we may say that the testimonies Paul cites fight more strongly in their own places than in his letter.

units.la: Eodem pertinet dictum Malachiæ, quod Paulus cum priore coniungens, satis testatur vnam in vtroque mentem quærendam. Ait ergo: Iacob dilexi, Esau vero odio habui. Quibus significatur, Deum gratuito suo amore ita discreuisse Jacobum ab Esau, vt in illius posteritate conseruaretur ac propagaretur Ecclesia: & hanc dilectione suam erga Israelitas Deum etiam testatam fecisse terræ optimæ donatione, populumque in eandem restitutione e captiuitate Babylonica, cum nihil tale contigerit posteris Esau. Conferantur cum his quæ de electione & dilectione Israëlis inculcat Moses Deut: 7. v.6. Quod
units.tr: To the same point belongs the saying of Malachi, which Paul joins to the earlier one, showing well enough that one mind is to be sought in both. He says: Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated. By these words it is signified that God, by his free love, so separated Jacob from Esau that the Church was preserved and propagated in Jacob's posterity; and that God also bore witness to this love towards Israel by giving them the best land and by restoring the same people from the Babylonian captivity, whereas nothing of the kind happened to the posterity of Esau. Let these be compared with what Moses urges about the election and love of Israel in Deuteronomy 7:6. What

units.la: {a} Iacob dilexi.
units.tr: {a} Jacob have I loved.

units.la: Quod autē dicimus: Jacobi semen elē‑ctum fuisse, vt esset Ecclesia, reiectis ab ista dignitate Idumæis alijsq; gentibus: intelligendum est pro tempore veteris Test. & quidem indefinitè, tanquam de corpore populi, &non de singulis ex posteritate Esau, aut alijs gentibus, oriundis. Quod dum non obseruat Hu‑berus, sædè hîc impingit in torquendis Bezæ quibusdam dictis, quasi nemo nisi carnaliter ex Jacobo propagatus, seruari olim potuerit, aut etiamnum possit. Quæ isthæc importunitas? Quæ calumniandi libido? Cur non & Paulo idem affingit? Ait enim Gentes quondam extrâneas fuisse à pactis promissionis, spem non habentes absque Christo Dei expertes.
units.tr: When we say that the seed of Jacob was chosen so that there might be the Church, with the Edomites and other nations rejected from that dignity, this must be understood as applying to the time of the Old Testament, and indefinitely, as concerning the body of the people, and not concerning single persons from the posterity of Esau or from other nations. Huber, who does not observe this, stumbles shamefully here in twisting certain words of Beza, as though no one but one born carnally from Jacob could formerly be saved, or still can be. What is this importunity? What lust for calumny? Why does he not attribute the same to Paul as well? For Paul says: The Gentiles were once strangers from the covenants of promise, having no hope and without Christ, strangers to God.

units.la: Ceterùm vtraque solutio iam allata Lutheri est Erasmum refellentis, vt mirum fit sub Lutheri nomine inueni‑ri, qui potius quàm veritati cedant, E‑rafmi diuerticula & effugia sectentur, necLutheri solidis pro veritate respon‑sionibus acquiescant. Is certè cuius modo mentio facta est, æstuat, laborat‑que quonam pacto ostendat, quod Lu‑thero thero tcfte,verum non cft, Iacobi dominium,dilectionem,benedictionem, ad corporalia & temporalia, non ad spiritualia & æterna pertinere.
units.tr: Moreover, both solutions already given are Luther's, refuting Erasmus; so it is a wonder that they are found under Luther's name, when Erasmus's evasions and escapes are followed instead of yielding to the truth, and Luther's solid answers, given for the truth, are not accepted. The man just mentioned is certainly sweating and labouring to show how, against Luther's testimony, it is not true that Jacob's lordship, love and blessing pertain to bodily and temporal things rather than to spiritual and eternal ones.

units.la: Idem vrget & hoc, vt Erafmi industriam in quærendis fubterfugijs non modo æquarę, sed superare videatur, Efauum & Iacobum non opponi tanquam singulares duas personas,sed collectiue horum amborum posteros notari. Neque id tantum, verum etiam appellatione Efau complectitur omnes gentes,& sic exponit: Efau odio habui,id est, gentes: Iacob dilexi, id est, Iudæos: vt sensus fit: libera & iusta Dei voluntate Israelitas quondam gentibus præteritis,dilectos& electos fuisse,vt eifent populus Dei: sicut e contrario, tempore Noui Teft. gentes ad hoc electæ sint, reiectis Iudæis. Ex quo inferre nititur, Paulum non agere de præcisa electione vel reprobatione ad vitam vel mortem æternam.
units.tr: He also presses this, that Erasmus's diligence in seeking subterfuges seems not merely to equal but even to surpass his own: that Esau and Jacob are not set against each other as two single persons, but that the posterity of both is collectively meant. And not only that, but under the name Esau he also embraces all nations, and explains it thus: Esau have I hated, that is, the Gentiles: Jacob have I loved, that is, the Jews: so that the sense is that by the free and just will of God the Israelites were once loved and chosen, the Gentiles having been passed over, so that they might be the people of God; just as, conversely, in the time of the New Testament the Gentiles were chosen and the Jews rejected. From this he strives to infer that Paul is not treating of the precise election or reprobation to eternal life or death.

units.la: Respondeo: Quantum ad antecedens, facile damus nomine Iacobi & Efaui vtriusque posteritatem intelligendam.
units.tr: I answer: as to the antecedent, we readily grant that the posterity of both Jacob and Esau is to be understood by the names.

units.la: Neque id dissimulant nostri scriptores: vt nihil necesse fuerit collu&#x0league;atorem 5o ferme thesibus occupari circa hoc quod κεχυμένον no est. Verum eo posito, consequentiam negamus. Id enim vult, & eo spectat Apostolus, quod non obstante perfidia & abiectione maioris partis Judæorum, Deus populū suum quem præcognouit, non abijciat, sed feruet fecundum electionem gratuitā, quemadmodum cap.11.claris verbis distinctio illa exprimitur. Ita duplicem confiderat electionem Israelis; vnam generalem & externam, qua totus Israel carnalis ab alijs populis segregatus, in peculium Dei consecratus erat, de qua electione habemus Deut.7.&aliàs sæpè. Omnes enim Israelitas pariter eisdem gratiæ fuç teftimonijsverbo nepe & sacramentis dignabatur. Alteram specialem & arcanam, in generali inclusam ; ex numero filiorum Israelis, qui erat vt arena maris, Deo ex mera gratia fecundum arcanum consilium voluntatis suæ sibi deligente & referuante ad salutem, quos visum est.
units.tr: Our writers do not deny this either, so that it was hardly necessary for an opponent to be occupied with nearly fifty theses about what is not in question [κεχυμένον]. But granted that, we deny the consequence. For this is what the Apostle means and aims at: that, despite the unbelief and rejection of the greater part of the Jews, God does not cast off his people whom he foreknew, but preserves a remnant according to gracious election, as that distinction is expressed in clear words in chapter 11. Thus he considers a twofold election of Israel: one general and external, by which the whole carnal Israel was set apart from other peoples and consecrated as God's own possession, concerning which election we have Deuteronomy 7 and often elsewhere. For God gave all the Israelites alike the same testimonies of grace, that is, the word and the sacraments. The other is special and secret, contained within the general one: out of the number of the sons of Israel, who were like the sand of the sea, God chose by pure grace, according to his secret counsel of will, those whom it pleased him to keep for salvation.

units.la: Hæc
units.tr: These things

units.la: Cap. 9.
units.tr: Chap. 9.

units.la: Hæc plana sunt ex serie disputationis Paulinæ, & ex distinctione initio posita, filiorum nimirum carnis & promissionis. Non enim omnes, inquit, qui sunt ex patre Israël, sunt Israël, neque quia sunt semen Abrahæ, ideo omnes sunt filij, sed in Isaac vocabitur tibi semen: id est, non qui filij carnis, ij filij Dei, sed qui sunt filij promissionis, censentur in semine. Filios carnis appellat secundum carnis successionem Abrahamo descendentes, quorum eximia iam prærogatiua erat præ aliis populis & tribubus, ob gratiam fœderis in eo populo. Filios autem promissionis vocat, qui Abrahamo per promissionem & fidem donabantur, in quibus longè eminentior dignitas atque gratia Dei viget. Et eiusmodi quidem sunt ex Judæis & gentibus: sed nunc peculiariter de Iudæis sermo est.
units.tr: These things are plain from the course of Paul's argument, and from the distinction laid down at the outset, namely between the children of the flesh and the children of the promise. For not all who are of Israel are Israel, nor are they all children because they are Abraham's seed; but in Isaac shall your seed be called: that is, it is not the children of the flesh who are children of God, but the children of the promise are reckoned as the seed. He calls the children of the flesh those descended from Abraham by natural succession, who already had an outstanding prerogative over other peoples and tribes because of the grace of the covenant in that people. He calls the children of the promise those who were given to Abraham through promise and faith, in whom a much more eminent dignity and the grace of God flourish. Such children are found both among the Jews and among the Gentiles, but now the discussion is specifically about the Jews.

units.la: At spiritualis ista electio non videtur probari posse per testimonia de generali electione Israëlis, & generali reiectione Ismaëlitarum, Idumæorum, aliarumque gentium. Resp. Potest sane, licet non eo modo, vt nullo discrimine vnam pro altera sumamus. Verum sic procedit argumentum Apostoli: cum gratuita promissione Isaac fuerit prælatus Ismaeli, itemque Iacob Esau ut ab ipsis flueret electa Abrahami progenies, & Ecclesia Dei in terris, Ismael autem & Esau suam quoque gentem singuli haberent, sed extraneam ab Ecclesia: mirum non esse, si Deus ex ipso Israële, suo arbitrio sibi deligat seruandos quos visum est. Deinde respondent aliqui, quamuis testimonia Prophetica proprie intelligenda sint de posteris Iacobi & Esau, ea qua dictum est ratione: attamen alienum non esse, si in ipsis etiam personis Iacob & Esau, tanquam in capitibus duplicis istius posteritatis, dicamus propositum fuisse specimen particularis cum electionis, tum reprobationis. Certe Augustinus acerrimi iudicij scriptor, & in hac materia verissimus, sentit Esau um à salutis gratia reiectum, ad quam Iacob electus fuerit. Verba eius sunt ad Simpl. lib. 1. Misericordiam per quam bonus factus est Iacob, defuisse Esau, ut etiam ipse per illam
units.tr: But this spiritual election does not seem capable of being proved by the testimonies concerning the general election of Israel and the general rejection of the Ishmaelites, the Edomites and the other nations. I answer: it certainly can, though not in such a way that we take one for the other without distinction. The Apostle's argument proceeds thus: since Isaac was preferred to Ishmael by gratuitous promise, and likewise Jacob to Esau, so that from them flowed the chosen progeny of Abraham and the Church of God on earth, while Ishmael and Esau each had their own nation, but one foreign to the Church, it is no wonder if God, from Israel itself, chooses by his own judgment whom he wills to save. Next, some reply that although the prophetic testimonies are properly to be understood of the posterity of Jacob and Esau, for the reason already given, yet it is not out of place to say that in the very persons of Jacob and Esau, as heads of that twofold posterity, there was set forth an example both of particular election and of particular reprobation. Certainly Augustine, a writer of most acute judgment and most true in this matter, holds that Esau was rejected from the grace of salvation, to which Jacob was elected. His words, in the book to Simplicianus, book 1, are: the mercy through which Jacob was made good was lacking in Esau, so that he too might be made good through it

units.la: Ioan. 1. illam effet bonus. Et mox: Misericordia hæc subtracta est ab Esau, inquit, vt non sic vocaretur, vt vocato inspiraretur fides, & credens bene operaretur. Quid? quòd ipse autor ad Heb.12. animose satis de Esau iudicasse videtur? Sed de eius salute vel exitu nihil attinet scrupulosius indagare, cùm veritas prædestinationis etiam sine hoc defendi possit.
units.tr: John 1. that he might be good. And soon after: This mercy, he says, was withdrawn from Esau, so that he was not called in such a way that faith might be breathed into the one called, and believing, he might work well. What of it? Does the author of Hebrews 12 not also seem to have judged Esau rather boldly? But there is no need to inquire more scrupulously into his salvation or his end, since the truth of predestination can be defended even without this.

units.la: CAPVT X.
units.tr: CAPVT X.

units.la: Alia probationes gratuitæ electionis.
units.tr: Other proofs of gratuitous election.

units.la: His ad hunc modum expositis ad euitandas strophas aduersariorum, pergamus ad alia scripturarum testimonia, quibus probatur gratuita seruandorum electio pro liberrima voluntate eligentis.
units.tr: Having set out these matters in this way, and in order to avoid the cavils of our opponents, let us go on to other testimonies of Scripture, by which it is proved that the election of those who are to be saved is gratuitous, arising from the most free will of the one who elects.

units.la: Rom. 11. locus est manifestissimus. Dicit Apostolus, Deum non abiecisse populum suum, quem præcognouit: id est, prædestinauit: ad distinctionem carnalis Israël, qui & ipse populus Dei erat externa vocatione. Videbatur enim absurdum illud sequi, si Iudæi ob increpaincredulitatem reiicerentur, Deum videri abiicere suum ipsius populum. Hic Paulus distinguit inter populum Dei vocatum & electum, seu vt ipse vocat, praescitum; intelligendo de notitia quæ coniuncta est cum approbatione, secundum quam dicuntur præcogniti ij, quos Deus suscipit, quoisque vt suos & seruandos seperauit à reliqua hominum turba. Alioquin, si de simplici notitia phrasis intelligatur, inanis erit ea restrictio, cum & damnandi cognitionem Dei non effugiant. Atque vt ostenderet, quos vocat præscitos, adiunxit, exemplo temporum Eliæ, in populo incredulo & obstinato reseruationem quandam factam secundum electionem.
units.tr: Romans 11 is a most manifest passage. The Apostle says that God has not cast off his people, whom he foreknew, that is, predestined, in contrast to the carnal Israel, who were also God's people by external calling. For it would seem absurd to conclude, if the Jews were rejected on account of their unbelief, that God was casting off his own people. Here Paul distinguishes between the people of God called and the people elected, or, as he himself calls them, foreknown; he means foreknowledge joined with approval, by which those are said to be foreknown whom God takes up and sets apart from the rest of the crowd of men as his own and to be saved. Otherwise, if "foreknown" is understood as bare knowledge, the restriction will be empty, since they do not escape God's knowledge even when he condemns them. And to show whom he calls foreknown, he added the example of the time of Elijah, when in a stubborn and unbelieving people a certain remnant was reserved according to election.

units.la: Et mox, quod requirit Israël, inquit, hoc non est assecutus: Electio autem assecuta est: cæteri vero obcaluerunt. In hac ergo electione, & in ista reseruatione, quæ per electionem gratiæ facta est, voluit intelligi populum, quem propterea Deus non repulit, quia præscuit, vt pluribus Aug. explicat de bono perseu. cap. 18. Quid autem dicit porro de ista electione? quam
units.tr: And soon after, "What Israel seeks, that it has not obtained: but the election has obtained it, and the rest were hardened." In this election, and in this remnant which was made by the election of grace, he wanted us to understand the people whom God therefore did not reject, because he foreknew them, as Augustine explains at length in De bono perseverantiae, chapter 18. But what does he go on to say about this election? What cause does he assign for it, apart from the sheer grace of the one who elects? For he says: "So also at this present time there is a remnant according to the election of grace," that is, a grace freely given, in the Hebrew manner of speaking. "But if it is by grace, then it is no longer of works: otherwise grace is no more grace. But if it is of works, then it is no longer of grace: otherwise work is no more work." Nothing could have been said more neatly to exclude every regard to works in human beings.

units.la: Populus præscitus. eius causam assignat, praeter meram gratiam eligentis? Ait enim: Ita & hoc tempore feruatio facta est secundum electionem gratia, hoc est, gratuita, phrasi Hebraica. Quod si autem per gratiam, non iam ex operibus: alioquin gratia non est gratia: Si ex operibus, iam non ex gratia, alioquin opus non esset opus. Nihil potuit dici rotundius ad excludendum quemuis operum in hominibus respectum.
units.tr: The people foreknown. "So also at this present time there is a remnant according to the election of grace," that is, a grace freely given, in the Hebrew manner of speaking. "But if it is by grace, then it is no longer of works: otherwise grace is no more grace. But if it is of works, then it is no longer of grace: otherwise work is no more work." Nothing could have been said more neatly to exclude every regard to works in human beings.

units.la: Sequitur nunc locus praeclarissimus ad Eph.1. Benedictus Deus pater Domini nostri Iesu Christi, qui benedixit nobis omni benedictione in coelis, in Christo, sicut nos elegit in ipso antequam iacerentur fundamenta mundi, ut simus sancti & inculpati coram eo per caritatem. Qui praedestinauit nos quos adoptaret in filios per Iesum Christum in se, pro beneuolo affectu voluntatis suae ad laudem gloriosae suae gratiae, qua nos gratis effecit sibi gratos in illo dilecto.
units.tr: Now follows a most remarkable passage, Eph. 1. "Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ; as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame before him in love. He predestined us to be adopted as sons through Jesus Christ to himself, according to the good pleasure of his will, to the praise of the glory of his grace, by which he has made us freely acceptable to himself in the Beloved."

units.la: Principio manifestum est, quod nihil potest poni vt causa praedestinationis, quod est praedestinationis effectus; ne quidem prout est in Dei praescientia. At, Paulo teste, quicquid est volun-tatis ratis vel operis boni in homine, est esse-ctus prædestinationis. Non enim elegit nos quia aut eramus, aut futuri esse-mus sancti, sed vt sancti & immaculati essemus coram ipso. Nihil igitur boni in homine, etiamsi accipiatur prout est in præscietia Dei, potest esse causa prædestinationis, seu electionis ad vitam æternam.
units.tr: In the first place, it is clear that nothing can be put forward as the cause of predestination which is an effect of predestination, not even as it exists in God's foreknowledge. But, on Paul's testimony, whatever good will or good work there is in a human being is an effect of predestination. For he did not choose us because we were, or would be, holy; rather, that we should be holy and without blemish before him. Therefore nothing good in a human being, even if it is taken as it exists in God's foreknowledge, can be the cause of predestination, or of election to eternal life.

units.la: Præter hoc argumentum, quod palmare est ex isto loco, cócurrunt & alia. Alterum igitur esto argumetum ex eo, quod testatur Apostolus, nos electos in Christo. Qui in Christo eliguntur, ij certè non ex suis operibus, aut propter vllum dignitatis proprie intuitum eliguntur. Sic enim dicendi essent electi n se, non in Christo.
units.tr: Besides this argument, which is plain from this passage, others also converge. Let the second argument be drawn from the Apostle's testimony that we are chosen in Christ. Those who are chosen in Christ are certainly not chosen on account of their own works or from any regard to some personal worth. For otherwise they would be said to be chosen in themselves, not in Christ.

units.la: III. Electi sumus nondum nati, imò ante mundi constitutionem, quando neque boni neque mali quicquam feceramus. Nec locum habet tergiuersatio de præuisione alicuius boni in nobis, quia vt supra quoque memoři, & præcedentia Apostoli verba confirmabant, nihil boni præuideri poterat in nobis, nisi præparatum à Deo per gratiam prædestinationis.
units.tr: III. We were chosen before we were born, indeed before the foundation of the world, when we had done neither good nor evil. Nor does the evasion about foreseeing some good in us find room, because, as I have also noted above, and as the preceding words of the Apostle confirm, no good could be foreseen in us except what had been prepared by God through the grace of predestination.

units.la: iv. Vltimus electionis nostræ finis est, agnitio & celebratio gloriosæ gratiæ Dei, qua nos gratis sibi gratos efficit in illo dilecto. Hūc autem finem Deus nō assequeretur, nisi electio esset omni modo gratuita. Scite enim & vere August. Gratia non est vllo modo si non est gratuita omni modo.
units.tr: IV. The ultimate end of our election is the acknowledgement and celebration of the glorious grace of God, by which he makes us graciously acceptable to himself in the beloved. But God would not attain this end unless election were wholly gratuitous. For Augustine rightly and well says: "Grace is not grace in any way if it is not gratuitous in every way."

units.la: v. Expressè causam prædestinationis nostræ assignat Paulus, cum ait: Prædestinauit nos secundum beneplacitum suum, non ait, secundum propositum voluntatis nostræ, quasi Deus spectarit futura nostra bona opera, aut voluntatis nostræ consensum in oblatam gratiam, seu bonum vsum liberi nostri arbitrij, aut simile quid in nobis ipsis. Græce est valde significanter, κατὰ τὴν εὐδοκίαν τῆς θελήματος αὐτοῦ. Proinde interrogantibus, cur Deus hos elegerit, illos non elegerit, verissime & optime respondetur: quia sic ipsi placuit. Quomodo & Christus non aliam affert causam Euangelij absconditi à sapientibus, & reuelati par-
units.tr: V. Paul expressly assigns the cause of our predestination when he says: "He predestined us according to the good pleasure of his will." He does not say "according to the purpose of our will," as if God had looked to our future good works, or to our consent to the offered grace, or to the good use of our free choice, or to something similar in ourselves. The Greek is very significant: [κατὰ τὴν εὐδοκίαν τῆς θελήματος αὐτοῦ]. Therefore, to those who ask why God has chosen these and not those, the most true and best answer is: because it so pleased him. In the same way Christ also gives no other cause why the gospel was hidden from the wise and revealed to little ones,

units.la: Matth. ii. paruulis, nisi <bl>εὐδοκίαν</bl> patris.
units.tr: Matthew 11: except the good pleasure [εὐδοκία] of the Father.

units.la: Et sane, si diligenter spectemus in scripturis, quæ de causa prædestinationis tradutur, videbimus ea recidere ad ista fermè capita: videlicet, ad beneplacitum & voluntatem Dei, quæ ambæ voces ad Ephes. coniunguntur: ad propositum ipsius quod est secundum electionem, ad Rom.9. Ad potentiam item, dicente Apostolo: Nonne potestatem habet figulus? Denique ad misericordiam & dilectionem Dei: cum ait: Non est volentis neque currentis, sed miserentis Dei. Et, Iacob dilexi: Esau vero odio habui. De operibus autem factis vel faciendis, ne verbum quidem facit scriptura in hoc negocio, nisi ut semper ea excludat, sicut à vocatione & iustificatione, ita etiam ab electione.
units.tr: And indeed, if we carefully look into the Scriptures, which are handed down concerning the cause of predestination, we will see that they come back almost to these heads: namely, to the good pleasure and will of God, which two expressions are joined in Ephesians; to the purpose of God, which is according to election (Romans 9); also to the power of God, the Apostle saying: "Has not the potter power over the clay?"; and finally to the mercy and love of God, when he says: "It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy," and: "Jacob I have loved, but Esau I have hated." But concerning works done or to be done, Scripture says not even a word in this matter, except always to exclude them, just as from vocation and justification, so also from election.

units.la: Huc præterea facit, quod Joh. 15. ait Dominus: Non vos me elegistis, sed ego elegi vos. Elegissemus autem nos ipsum, si secundum nostram fidem, vel voluntate bonam, esset electio. Quod si, inquit Augustinus eligeremur à Deo, eo quod præsciuerit nos credituros, non autem quod ipse facturus fuerit credentes, procul dubio nos ipsi
units.tr: In addition, this bears on the point that the Lord says in John 15: "You did not choose me, but I chose you." Now we would have chosen him ourselves if the election were according to our faith or good will. "But if," says Augustine, "we were chosen by God because he foresaw that we would believe, and not because he himself would make us believers, then without doubt we ourselves

units.la: De præd. sanƈt.c.17. ipsi eum prius eligeremus credendo in eum, ut elegi mererentur ab eo. Aufert id omnino qui dicit: Non vos me elegistis, sed ego vos.
units.tr: (On the Predestination of the Saints, ch. 17) would have chosen him first by believing in him, so that we might deserve to be chosen by him. He wholly removes this who says: 'You did not choose me, but I chose you.'"

units.la: CAPUT XI. De causa reprobationis.
units.tr: CHAPTER XI. On the cause of reprobation.

units.la: SATIS ergo liquet tot probationibus in medium allatis, Deum sanctos suos elegisse in Christo ad vitam aeternam, non ex viris operibus, aut praescientia fidei ipsorum; sed secundum propositum voluntatis suae, ex mera gratia, quae non invenit electos, sed facit, ut vetus habet dictum. Etsi vero eadem opera quid de reprobationis causa tenendum sit, non obscure attigisse videmur: tamen ut res sit clarior, lubet seorsum ostendere, causam reprobationis non consistere in futura reproborum infidelitate, aut aliis peccatis quae Deus praevidit, sed in ipsius Dei voluntate, electionis quos voluit, & reprobantis quos voluit, voluntate quidem a nostris sensibus remota, attamen rectissima, & adoranda potius quam scrutanda. Etenim sipecsi peccata essent ratio reprobationis, omnes fuissemus reprobati ; quando- quidem omnes sumus sub peccato, filij iræ & mortis æternæ, vt quales reprobat abdicatio, tales adoptet electio. Ac licet gratia mediatoris Euangelio nobis offeratur, tamen vt fidem incipiamus habere, & eandem ad finem retineamus, Dei donū est. Quid enim habes quod non accepisti? Cur igitur mi- sericordia hæc subtrahitur à reprobis, vt fides eis non inspiretur? an quia nolunt?Minimè.Sic enim è conuerso electi ideo crederent, quia volunt: atque ita nō eis Deus donaret fidem, sed eam sibi ipsi volendo præstarent, & haberet aliquid,quod non accepissent.
units.tr: It is therefore sufficiently clear from the many proofs we have set out that God chose his saints in Christ to eternal life, not on account of their works or of foreseen faith in them, but according to the purpose of his will, from mere grace, which does not find the elect but makes them, as the old saying goes. Although our earlier discussion seems to have touched clearly enough on what must be held about the cause of reprobation, still, to make the matter plainer, we think it worth showing separately that the cause of reprobation does not lie in the future unbelief of the reprobate or in other sins which God foresaw, but in the will of God himself, who elects whom he wills and reprobates whom he wills. This will is indeed remote from our senses, yet most right, and to be adored rather than searched into. For if foreseen sins were the reason for reprobation, we would all have been reprobated, since we are all under sin, children of wrath and of eternal death; so that election adopts such as rejection casts off. And although the grace of the Mediator is offered to us in the Gospel, yet that we begin to have faith and keep it to the end is the gift of God. "For what do you have that you did not receive?" (1 Cor. 4.7). Why, then, is this mercy withheld from the reprobate, so that faith is not breathed into them? Is it because they are unwilling? By no means. For in that case the elect would believe because they are willing, and God would not give them faith, but they would supply it to themselves by their own willing, and would have something they had not received.

units.la: Deinde, si consideremus reprobationem manare ex infidelitate, aut ex malitia præuisa : necessario sequetur electionem pendere à fide vel operibus præscitis. Argumentum hoc Augustini est ad Simpl. nisi quod in hypothesi de Jacob & Esau loquitur: Si, inquit,concedimus, Esauum non nisi iniustitia merito odio fuisse, incipit & Iacob iustitia merito diligi. Item: si quia praesciebat Deus futura mala opera Esau, propterea eum praedestinauit, ut seruiret minori; & Iacob propterea praedestinarit Deus, ut ei maior seruiret, quia futura eius opera praesciebat.
units.tr: Next, if we consider that reprobation springs from unbelief, or from foreseen wickedness, it will necessarily follow that election depends on foreseen faith or works. This is the argument of Augustine to Simplicianus, except that he speaks in the case of Jacob and Esau: "If," he says, "we grant that Esau was hated only for the merit of injustice, then Jacob too begins to be loved for the merit of justice." Likewise: if God predestined Esau so that he should serve the younger because God foresaw Esau's future evil works, and predestined Jacob so that the older should serve him because God foresaw Jacob's future works.

units.la: ii. Paulus aeque pronunciat de utroque: Nondum natis pueris cum nihil fecissent boni vel mali, ut propositum Dei secundum electionem firmum maneret, non ex operibus, sed ex vocante dictum esse: maior seruiet minori. Haec verba expendens Augustinus, expresse scribit, loco iam citato: nullo merito Esauum improbatum fuisse: quia & ipse nondum natus, & nihil operatus erat, ac ne praescientia quidem futura mala voluntatis eius: quia sic & Iacob approbatus fuisset praescientia futura bona sua voluntatis, & frustra diceretur, non ex operibus. Eadem scribit ad Laur. cap. 98.
units.tr: Second, Paul pronounces the same about both: "Before the children were born, when they had done neither good nor evil, in order that God's purpose according to election might stand, not by works but by him who calls, it was said: the elder shall serve the younger." Weighing these words, Augustine writes expressly in the passage already cited: "Esau was rejected for no merit, since he was not yet born and had done nothing, nor even on account of foreseen future evil of his will; for in that case Jacob would have been approved on account of the foreseen future good of his will, and it would be said in vain, not by works." He writes the same in his letter to Laurentius, chapter 98.

units.la: iii. Obiectio, quam mouet Apostolus: Num igitur iniquitas apud Deum? & solutio obiectionis iustius, atque etiam parabola figuli, pro potestate & arbitrio suo fingentis vasa ad decus, & vasa ad ignominiam, sententiam nostram abunde confirmant; quod sicut electionis nis horum, ita reiectionis aliorum nullam aliam possimus assignare rationem, nisi quoniam Deo ira placet, ad misericordiæ vel iudicij sui manifestationem.
units.tr: Third, the objection which the Apostle raises: "Is there then unrighteousness with God?" and his answer to it, and also the parable of the potter who, by his power and will, shapes some vessels for honour and some for dishonour, abundantly confirm our view. Just as we can assign no other reason for the election of some, so we can assign no other reason for the rejection of others, except that God is pleased with wrath, for the manifestation of his mercy or of his judgment.

units.la: v. Accedit causa innumerabilium paruulorum extra Ecclesiam, qui morte præueniuntur, antequam rationis vtantur iudicio, & de neglectu opitulatis gratiæ iuste argui nō possint. De his si rogentur dissentientes, an nullos eorum perire existiment, non audebunt puto diffiteri: Si pereunt, numerantur inter eos quos Deus reprobauit. Nullum tamen contemtum gratiæ in illis potuit præuidere, cum habituri illum non fuerint, imo præscuit potius illos gratiam non contemturos. Nec quicquam iuuat commentum, Deum vidisse quid facturi fuerint si superuixissent. Deus enim in puniendo & condonando non spectat quid aliquis facturus fuerit: sed quid boni vel mali in corpore fecerit. Ita constat reprobationem impiorum non minus quàm electionem sanctorum, ex sola Dei voluntate, nonautem ex praeuisis hominum voluntatibus, bonis vel malis pendere.
units.tr: Fifth, there is the case of the countless little children outside the Church, who are taken by death before they come to the use of reason, and cannot justly be charged with neglecting the help of grace. If those who dissent are asked whether they think none of these perish, I suppose they will not dare to deny it. If they perish, they are counted among those whom God reprobated. Yet God could not have foreseen any contempt of grace in them, since they would not have had it; rather, he foresaw that they would not despise grace. Nor does the invention help, that God saw what they would have done had they lived on. For God, in punishing and pardoning, does not look at what someone would have done, but at what good or evil he has done in the body. Thus it is clear that the reprobation of the wicked, no less than the election of the saints, depends on the will of God alone, and not on the foreseen wills of men, good or bad.

units.la: Nec est quod huius vel illius nomine doctrinam hanc quidam sugillent atque odiosam reddere conentur. Scripturarum ea est, & secundum scripturas, vt videmus, constanter ab Augustino defensa. Quemadmodum etiam ab Hilario, Prospero, Primasio, & alijs, quibus antiquitus perspecta fuit praui-tas Spiritus Pelagiani. Prosperi verba sunt ex Epist. ad Aug. de reliquijs Pelagianæ haer. Secundum propositu Dei ante mundum natum, discretione factam eligendorum & reijciendorum, & secundum quod placuit creatori alios vasa honoris, alios vasa, contumelia creatos. Et rursus ait, Deu secundum propositum & consilium voluntatis sua, occulto iudicio, opere autem manifesto, aliud vas coderein honorem, aliud in contumeliam: cum nemo nisi per gratiam iustificetur, & nemo nisi in praevaricatione nascatur. Et hoc, inquit, necessario concedunt, qui confitentur a gratia omnia bona merita praeueniri, & ab ipsa, vt possint esse, donari. Nec alia est doctri-
units.tr: Nor should anyone under this or that name disparage this doctrine or try to make it hateful. It is the doctrine of Scripture, and, as we see, it was steadfastly defended by Augustine according to Scripture, as also by Hilary, Prosper, Primasius and others, to whom the perversity of the Pelagian spirit was clearly known long ago. These are the words of Prosper, from his letter to Augustine on the remains of the Pelagian heresy: "According to the purpose of God before the world was made, a distinction was made between those to be chosen and those to be rejected; and according to what pleased the Creator, some were made vessels of honour, others vessels of dishonour." And again he says: "God, according to the purpose and counsel of his will, by a hidden judgment, though manifest in its working, made one vessel for honour and another for dishonour, since no one is justified except by grace, and no one is born except in transgression. And this, he says, those necessarily concede who confess that all good merits are anticipated by grace, and are given by grace so that they may exist."

units.la: ctristrina Magistri sententiarū, quę vocat, lib.1.dist.41. Ait enim: Elegit quos voluit gratuita misericordia, non quia fideles futuri erant, sed vt fideles essent. Ita etiam reprobauit quos voluit, non propter futura merita quæ præuideret: veritate tamen rectissima, & sensibus nostris remota. Eandem sententiam Thomas Aquinas & alij inter scholasticos non obscuri nominis se-quuntur, validisque comprobat ratio-nibus.
units.tr: The teaching of the Master of the Sentences is no different; he is cited in book 1, distinction 41. For he says: "Freely given mercy elected whom it willed, not because they were going to be faithful, but so that they might be faithful. Likewise it reprobated whom it willed, not on account of future merits which it foresaw; yet this is most right in truth, though remote from our senses." The scholastics of no mean name, such as Thomas Aquinas and others, follow the same opinion, and they confirm it with strong reasons.

units.la: Consulatur & Lutherus de seruo ar-bitrio: vbi ad locū Malachiæ intrepidè scribit in hæc verba: Æternus & immutabilis est amor Dei, æternum odium Dei erga homines, antequam mundus fieret, non solum ante meritum & opus liberi arbitrij. Et pa-lam reijcit figmentum, vt nondum na-tos odisse Deus dicatur, quia præscierit illos gesturos odio digna. Nec obstat inquit, quòd Iudæos merito incredu-litatis excisos legimus de olea: gentes fide insertas. Scimus fide inseri, infide-litate excindi homines, eosque exhor-tandos esse vt credant, ne excidantur. Sed nos non disputamus quid sequatur
units.tr: Let Luther also be consulted in On the Bondage of the Will, where, on the passage of Malachi, he writes fearlessly in these words: "The love of God is eternal and unchangeable, and the hatred of God towards men is eternal, not only before merit and work of free will, but before the world was made." And he plainly rejects the fiction that God is said to hate those not yet born because he foresaw that they would do things worthy of hatred. Nor, he says, does it stand in the way that we read the Jews were cut off from the olive tree on account of the merit of unbelief, and the Gentiles were grafted in through faith. We know that men are grafted in by faith and cut off by unbelief, and that they must be exhorted to believe, lest they be cut off. But we do not dispute what follows

units.la: credentes aut incredulos: sed quo merito, qua ope perueniant homines ad fidem qua inseruntur, aut ad infidelitatem qua excidunt. Hoc meritum nobis describens Paulus docet, quod nullo nostro opere; sed solo Dei amore & odio Dei contingit. Hæc omnia Lutherus.
units.tr: for believers or unbelievers, but by what merit, by what work men come to the faith by which they are grafted in, or to the unbelief by which they are cut off. Describing this merit for us, Paul teaches that it comes about "by no work of ours, but by the love and hatred of God alone." All this is Luther's.

units.la: Idem postea ad similc de figulo & luto, diluens cauillum, quòd figulus hic (vt Diatribe interpretabatur) faciat vas in contumeliam ex meritis præcedentibus, sicut Judæos reiecerit ob infidelitatem, gentes receperit ob fidem: Si sic, inquit, operatur Deus, cur illi murmurant & expostulant? cur dieunt, quid queritur? quis voluntati eius resistet? quid opus Paulo illos compescere? Deinde vbi manet potestas faciendi quod vult, si meritis & legibus subiectus non finitur facere quod vult? Pugnat enim respectus meritorum cum potestate & libertate faciendi quod vult, &c.
units.tr: Again, later, on a similar point about the potter and the clay, refuting the quibble that this potter (as the Diatribe explained it) makes a vessel for dishonour from prior merits, just as he rejected the Jews for unbelief and received the Gentiles for faith, Luther says: If God works in this way, why do they murmur and complain? Why do they say, "What is he finding fault with? Who resists his will?" What need was there for Paul to silence them? Then where does the power of doing what he wills remain, if he is bound by merits and laws and is not allowed to do what he wills? For the regard for merits is at odds with the power and freedom of doing what one wills, and so on.

units.la: Quæ ergo importunitas est? quæve aduerlus veritatem inuidia, Caluini, smu nobis exprobrantium? quod asserimus, neciuftitiam nec malitiam ho- minum esse causam, sed occultam Dei voluntatem, quare ex communi exitio, cui omnes natura fumus obnoxij, alios gratia eripiat, alios non eripiat? Si Caluinifticu id est, quid Luthero fiet, vt de antiquis nihil dicam?
units.tr: What, then, is this shamelessness? And what is this hostility against the truth, this odium that they cast at us, the Calvinists, as if we were... What we assert is that neither the injustice nor the wickedness of men is the cause, but the hidden will of God, why he should snatch some from the common ruin to which all of us by nature are liable, and not snatch others. If this is Calvinism, what will become of Luther, to say nothing of the ancients?

units.la: Obseruandum tamen est, nos non afferere, sicut aduersarij malitiose de nobis fingunt: Propter peccata aut incredulitatem, tanquam causam προχειρ- ταξτικω,neminem damnari. Cotrarium nos docemus, & semper docuerut no- ftri vnanimi consensu, de nemine sumturum Deum poenas, neminemque ab ipso damnatum iri, nisi ob peccatum. Poena enim non habet locum nisi respectu peccati.
units.tr: We must observe, however, that we do not assert what our opponents maliciously make up about us: that no one is condemned on account of sins or unbelief, as if these were the cause [προχειροταξτικῶς]. We teach the opposite, and our churches have always taught with one voice, that God will inflict punishment on no one and that no one will be condemned by him except on account of sin. For punishment has no place except in relation to sin.

units.la: Deinde & hoc verum est: sicut Deus non damnat nisi peccatores, & damnationem ob peccata merentes, sic etiam non nisi propter peccatu damnare decreuisse. Nam quicquid suo tempore facit Deus, id etiam ab aeterno facere constituit, eo quo fit modo. Quoniam igitur reprobos damnat, & damnaturus turus est propter peccata: proculdubio constituit quoque ab æterno eos damnare propter peccata.
units.tr: Next, this also is true: just as God condemns only sinners, and only those who deserve condemnation for their sins, so he has decreed to condemn no one except on account of sin. For whatever God does in its time, he has also determined from eternity to do, and in the same manner in which it is done. Since, then, he condemns the reprobate and will condemn them on account of their sins, he has without doubt also determined from eternity to condemn them on account of their sins.

units.la: Atque hinc rursum apparet doctrinæ nostræ depravatio per aduersarios, cum fingunt nos docere, Deũ sine respectu peccati, sola & absoluta sua voluntate & decreto alquos damnationi addixisse. Imò decretũ est Dei de danandis tantum peccatoribus, & quidem propter peccata. Verum enim cum omnes peccatores simus & damnatione digni, cur hos ad gloriam gratis dandã, illos ad pœnam iusto iudicio propter peccata infligendam prædestinarit, huius nullam habemus assignare rationem, præter vnicam eamque liberam & iustam Dei voluntatem.
units.tr: Here again appears the distortion of our teaching by our opponents, who pretend that we teach that God, without regard to sin, by his sole and absolute will and decree, has assigned some to damnation. Rather, God's decree concerns only the condemnation of sinners, and indeed on account of their sins. For since we are all sinners and worthy of damnation, why he has predestined these to be given to glory freely and those to be punished for their sins by a just judgment, we have no reason to assign, apart from the one and free and just will of God.

units.la: Id ipsum sibi vult quorundam distinctio inter decretum prædestinationis, cuius nulla sit causa nisi voluntas Dei: & executionem decreti, cuius causa sint peccata damnandorum. A cuius distinctionis sensu non discrepat quod Thomas scribit: præscientiam peccatorum posse dici aliquam rationem reprobationis ex parte
units.tr: This is what the distinction of certain men between the decree of predestination, which has no cause except the will of God, and the execution of the decree, whose cause is the sins of those to be condemned, means. Thomas's statement does not differ in sense from this distinction: the foreknowledge of sins can be said to be some reason of reprobation on the part

units.la: Expos. in s. ad Rom. parte pœnæ, quæ præparatur reprobis, in quan-tum scilicet Deus proponit se puniturum ma-los propter peccata, quæ à seipsis habent, non à Deo. Et secundum Richardum, referente Ec-kio, hominis demerita sunt ratio reprobatio-nis, quantum ad connotatum, quod est temporalis obduratio, & futura damnatio: non autem ipsius præordinationis, inquit, ad eam damnationem est aliqua ratio: in homine vi-delicet.
units.tr: (Expos. in ep. ad Rom.) of the punishment which is prepared for the reprobate, namely insofar as God declares that he will punish the wicked on account of sins which they have from themselves, not from God. And according to Richard, as reported by Eck, the demerits of man are the reason of reprobation as regards the connoted matter, which is temporal hardening and future damnation; but not, he says, is there any reason for the predetermination itself to that damnation: namely, in man.

units.la: Calvinus id ipsum respiciens, concedit propinquam causam reprobationis esse, quod sumus omnes in Adam maledicti, natiua vitiositate, quæ per totum genus humanum diffusa est, ad damnationem sufficiente. Sicut Esau, inquit, merito reiectus fuit, quia naturaliter erat filius iræ: nec tamen vllius culpæ aut vitij respectu eius quam fratris fuisse deteriore conditionem Paulus contendit, ut discamus in nudo ac simplici Dei beneplacito acquiescere. Quid multa? Quos Deus reprobauit, ideo reprobauit, quia voluit. Reprobauit autem, id est, præordinauit ad pœnam iustam luendam propter peccatum.
units.tr: Calvin, having this very point in view, grants that the proximate cause of reprobation is that we are all cursed in Adam, by our native corruption, which is spread through the whole human race and is sufficient for damnation. Just as Esau, he says, was rightly rejected because he was by nature a child of wrath, yet Paul contends that his condition was no worse than that of his brother with respect to any fault or vice, so that we may learn to rest in the bare and simple good pleasure of God. Why say more? Those whom God reprobated, he reprobated because he willed to. He reprobated them, that is, predetermined them to pay a just penalty for sin.

units.la: Quo modo etiam Auguft. illud rectè intelligitur, Deum facere alios vasa irae secundum meritum (naturaliter enim omnes sumus filij irae) alios autem vasa misericordiae secundum gratiam.
units.tr: In this way also that saying of Augustine is rightly understood: that God makes some vessels of wrath according to merit (for by nature we are all children of wrath), and others vessels of mercy according to grace.

units.la: CAPVT XII. Refutatio obiectionum quarundam contra expositam doctrinam de causa electionis & reprobationis.
units.tr: CHAPTER XII. Refutation of certain objections against the doctrine set forth concerning the cause of election and reprobation.

units.la: CETERVM magnitudo quaestionis quā tractamus, obturbat sensus hominum de voluntate Dei superbè nimium disputantium: quo fit, vt multi multa obiiciant contra hanc altitudinem misericordiae & iudicij divini, qua inter homines ipsos nulla existete diuersitate, nulla meritorum distinctione, iste praedestinatur, vt ex massa perditionis discernatur & eligatur, fiatque vas in honorem: alius vero reprobatur, vt sit vas in contumeliam.
units.tr: Moreover, the magnitude of the question we are treating confuses the minds of men who dispute too arrogantly about the will of God. Hence many raise many objections against this depth of mercy and of divine judgment, by which, with no difference existing among men and no distinction of merits, one man is predestined so that he may be discerned and chosen out of the mass of perdition and become a vessel unto honour, while another is reprobated so that he may be a vessel unto dishonour.

units.la: Primùm, repugnare videtur ipsum nomen electionis. Electio enim maximè fit respectu qualitatis, qua alius alij praestat, aut praestare videtur. Sic elegantia deformib. accommoda incommodis, & magis vtilia mi- nus vtilibus præferre eligendo solemus. Ergo dicendum videtur, Deum quoque aliquid in ele-ctis spectasse, cuius gratia aliis eos præstulerit.
units.tr: First, the very name of election seems to be inconsistent. For election is made chiefly with respect to some quality by which one person excels, or seems to excel, another. Thus in choosing we are accustomed to prefer the elegant to the deformed, and the more useful to the less useful. Therefore it seems necessary to say that God too looked upon something in the elect, on account of which he preferred them to others.

units.la: Resp. Cogitationes Dei non sunt vt cogitationes hominum, nec viæ ipsius vt viæ nostræ, ait Dominus. Nos homines quidem eligere solemus qua dictu est ratione: sed longe aliter electio & dilectio sese habent in Deo atque in hominibus. Voluntas enim hominis mouetur ad amandum intuitu alicuius boni in re amata, & boni alicuius respectu, vt dictum est, veri, vel apparetis, rem quā eligit, alteri præfert & caram habet. Sed voluntas Dei causa est omnis boni in creatura: atque ideo nō propter aliquod bonum quod in homine eligat, Deus eum diligit, sed potius eo, quòd ipsum diligit, præfert eū aliis eligendo: voledo nimirum ei bonū quod non vult aliis. Nā diligere est bonū alicui velle.
units.tr: Answer: The thoughts of God are not as the thoughts of men, nor his ways as our ways, says the Lord. We men indeed are accustomed to choose for the reason just stated, but election and love stand quite differently in God than in men. For the will of man is moved to love by regard for some good in the thing loved, and by regard for some good, as has been said, true or apparent, it prefers the thing it chooses to another and holds it dear. But the will of God is the cause of all good in creatures. Therefore God does not love someone on account of some good he finds in that man; rather, because he loves him, he prefers him to others by choosing him, willing for him, to be sure, a good that he does not will for others. For to love is to will good to someone.

units.la: Secundò, ait Apost. 2. Tim. 2. In magna domo non tantum sunt vasa aurea & argentea, sed etiā lignea ac testacea: & alia quæ ad decus, ad alia dedec. Si quis igitur seipsum expurgarit ab his, erit erit vas ad decus, sanctificatum ac commodum vsibus Domini, &c. Ergo vt simus vasa in honorem vel contumeliam, electi vel reprobi, a nobis ipsis pendet.
units.tr: Second, the Apostle says in 2 Tim. 2: "In a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and earthenware; some are for honour, others for dishonour. If anyone therefore purges himself from these, he will be a vessel for honour, sanctified and useful for the Lord's purposes," and so on. Therefore, that we may be vessels unto honour or dishonour, elect or reprobate, depends on ourselves.

units.la: Verum enimuero, qui ita loco isto abutuntur, necesse est prius cum sophistis quoque & inimicis gratiae statuant, in viribus liberi arbitrij posita hominis emundatione. Quatenus enim ea gratiae beneficiu est, effectus manet electionis qua fiunt vasa ad honore, nec vllo modo causa eius esse potest. Deinde negatur consequentia: quia eo loci von agitur de causa praedestinationis, sicut ad Rom. 9. sed tantum nota traditur, ex qua dignoscere possimus electos & sanctos. Ea est sincera & constans confessio nominis diuini, & studium iustitiae. Etenim occurrit Apostolus offendiculo ex apostasia Hymenaei & Phileti, hominum quantiuis precij, vt habiti fuerant: ac ostendit ad fidelium consolationem, electos perire non posse, sed illos Deo, non nobis notos esse, nisi ab effectis & a posteriore, vt loquimur, secundum regulam, discedat ab iniustitia omnis qui inuocat nomen Domini. Nostrum igitur est perseuerare in vera confessione, iustitiam colere, nec commisceri errorum magistris aliisque improbis, vt simus, hoc est, re ipsa testemur nos esse vasa honoris.
