units.tr: Truly, those who abuse that passage in this way must first, together with the sophists and enemies of grace, hold that a man's cleansing lies in the powers of free will. For insofar as that cleansing is a benefit of grace, the effect of election remains, by which men are made vessels unto honour, and in no way can it be the cause of that election. Next, the inference is denied, because the passage is not dealing with the cause of predestination, as in Rom. 9, but only gives a mark by which we may recognize the elect and holy. That mark is a sincere and steadfast confession of the divine name and zeal for righteousness. For the Apostle, to remove a stumbling block arising from the apostasy of Hymenaeus and Philetus, men of whatever worth they had been held to be, meets the difficulty and shows, for the comfort of the faithful, that the elect cannot perish, but that they are known to God and not to us, except from their effects and from what follows, as we say, according to the rule: "Let everyone who calls on the name of the Lord depart from iniquity." It is therefore our task to persevere in true confession, to cultivate righteousness, and not to associate with teachers of error and other wicked men, so that we may be, that is, so that by the very fact we bear witness that we are vessels of honour.

units.la: Tertia Obiect. Iubemur 2. Petri 1. vocationem & electionem nostram firmam facere: per bona nempe opera, vt quidam Græci & Latini codices additum habent, & sensus per se flagitat. Argumentum tale erit:
units.tr: Third objection: In 2 Pet. 1 we are bidden to make our calling and election firm, namely by good works, as some Greek and Latin codices have added, and as the sense itself requires. The argument will be this:

units.la: Per quod electio firma efficitur, id causa eius est.
units.tr: Whatever makes election firm is its cause.

units.la: Atqui electio firma efficitur per bona opera.
units.tr: But election is made firm by good works.

units.la: Ergo opera bona sunt causa electionis.
units.tr: Therefore good works are the cause of election.

units.la: Respondetur, quantum ad Deum, electio firma est in sese, seu in proposito Dei eligentis; quia, teste Apostolo, firmum stat fundamentum Dei, & propositum secundum electionem manet, non ex operibus sed ex vocante. Sed quantum ad nos, firma redditur electio per bona opera, tanquam per effecta. Nam quia electi sumus, vt sancti simus & inculpati, non immeritò vitæ sanctimonia electionis spe= specimen, & testificatio habetur. Atque is verborum Petri lenfus est. Vnde solutio patet ad maiorem argumenti per distinctionem: per quod electio firma efficitur, quantum ad Deum nempe, id causam esse electionis. Sed per bona nostra opera electio efficitur firma, non Dei, sed nostri respectu: tanquam per effectum & lignum, vt dictu est. Sic fides, sic iustificatio, sic hæredi-tas vitæ æternæ firma nobis redduntur, per promtum, & minime fimulatu studium bonorum operum. Nec tamen bona opera idcirco causa sunt fidei, & iustificationis, sed effectus eorundem, & lignum vitæ æternæ gratis dandæ per & propter Christum. Et generatim non quicquid alterum confirmat, flatim causa eius conseri debet.
units.tr: The answer: as far as God is concerned, election is firm in itself, or in the purpose of the electing God, because, as the Apostle witnesses, "the firm foundation of God stands, and the purpose according to election remains, not from works but from the one who calls." But as far as we are concerned, election is made firm through good works, as through effects. For since we are elect so that we may be holy and blameless, a holy life is rightly held to be a sign and testimony of the hope of election. This is the sense of Peter's words. Hence the solution to the major premise is clear by distinction: whatever makes election firm, as far as God is concerned, that is the cause of election. But election is made firm through our good works not with respect to God but with respect to us, as through an effect and a sign, as has been said. So faith, justification, and the inheritance of eternal life are made firm to us through the prompt and by no means feigned zeal for good works. Nor are good works on that account the cause of faith and justification; rather they are its effects, and the sign of eternal life given freely through and for the sake of Christ. And generally, whatever confirms another thing must not at once be counted its cause.

units.la: Quarta obiectio. Expressè dicimur electi secundum præscientiam Dei patris. 1. Pet. 1.
units.tr: The fourth objection. We are expressly said to be elect according to the foreknowledge of God the Father. 1 Pet. 1.

units.la: Recte: sed non fecundum præscientiam nostræ fidei, siue operum, aut alicuius in nobis hærentis. Verum præscius ille omnium rerum Deus, ab æterno, no, cum nondum essemus, elegit nos secundum præscientiam suam, quia su- tura opera sua nota habet atque dispo-suit ab æterno.
units.tr: Rightly so, but not according to the foreknowledge of our faith, or of our works, or of anything inhering in us. Rather, God, who foreknows all things, elected us from eternity, before we existed, according to his foreknowledge, because he has known from eternity his own future works and has disposed them.

units.la: Quinta obiect. Electi sumus in Christo ait Apostolus ad Ephes. 1. Ergo non eligimur absoluto aliquo decreto, aut misericordia Dei absoluta, sed in Christo limitata atque descripta.
units.tr: Fifth objection. We are elect in Christ, says the Apostle in Ephesians 1. Therefore we are not elected by some absolute decree or absolute mercy of God, but by a mercy limited and defined in Christ.

units.la: Respondeo, Insidiæ sunt in voce absolu-ta. Decretum & misericordia Dei, se-cundum quam aliquos ex genere hu-mano eligit certò liberandos, absoluta vocari possunt quod ad causam, quate-nus nihil in electis ipsis hærens, potest esse causa istius, sive decreti, sive mise-ricordiæ: contra quam Pelagianorum, & Semipelagianorum statuebat opi-nio, de præuisione operum, aut etiam fidei vel incredulitatis: sed respectu mediorum, per quæ electos misericor-diter seruare statuit, omnino miseri-cordia illa limitata est in Christo me-diatore, per quem Deus decreuit ser-uare quicunque seruantur. Sensus igi- tur est: Elegit nos in Christo, non tanquam in illo existentes; aut futuros tanquam ex nobis; sed vt essemus in illo, perquè eum seruaremur. Et sic Paulus ipse explicat: prædestinauit nos quos adoptaret in filios, per Iesum Christum, idque secundum beneplacitum voluntatis suæ. Atque id ipsum de reprobatione etiam valet: quod Deus nec perdat, nec perdere statuerit reprobos absoluta iustitia, citra neiupe ipsorum meritum; sed quos perdit, propter peccata perdit & perdere constituit ab æterno.
units.tr: Answer: Respondeo, There is a trap in the word absoluta. The decree and mercy of God, by which he chooses certainly to deliver some from the human race, can be called absolute with respect to the cause, insofar as nothing inhering in the elect themselves can be the cause of that decree or mercy. This is against the opinion of the Pelagians and Semipelagians, who held that God foresaw works, or even faith or unbelief. But with respect to the means by which he decided to preserve the elect in mercy, that mercy is wholly limited to Christ the mediator, through whom God decreed to save all who are saved. The sense, therefore, is this: He elected us in Christ, not as though we existed in him, or would exist as from ourselves, but so that we would be in him and be saved through him. And Paul himself explains it thus: he predestinated us, whom he would adopt as sons, through Jesus Christ, and that according to the good pleasure of his will. The same holds of reprobation: that God neither destroys, nor has decreed to destroy the reprobate by an absolute justice apart from any merit of theirs; but those whom he destroys, he destroys on account of their sins, and has determined from eternity to destroy.

units.la: Sexta obiect.: Eadem electionis, quæ iustificationis causa est: & reprobationis, quæ damnationis. At causa iustificationis est fides cum misericordia Dei concurrens, eamque apprehendens; causa autem damnationis, infidelitas, aspernans gratiam Dei in Christo oblatam, aliaque peccata, Ergo &c.
units.tr: Sixth objection: The cause of election is the same as the cause of justification, and the cause of reprobation the same as the cause of damnation. But the cause of justification is faith, concurring with the mercy of God and laying hold of it; the cause of damnation, however, is unbelief, spurning the grace of God offered in Christ, and other sins. Therefore etc.

units.la: Respondeo: vitium est in maiore. Iidè quidem sunt electi & qui iustificantur, vt à posteriore iudicando statuere possimus, haud dubiè electos esse, qui misericordiam propter Christum promissam fide apprehendunt, nec abiiciùt eam fiduciam usque ad extremum.
units.tr: Answer: The fault lies in the major premise. Indeed, those who are justified are elect, so that judging from the latter we may determine beyond doubt that those are elect who lay hold by faith of the mercy promised for Christ's sake and do not cast away that confidence to the end.

units.la: Verum eandem esse iustificationis & electionis causam proximam (qualis in negotio iustificationis est fides) concedi neque debet, neque potest. Nam iustificatio effectus est electionis, quemadmodum & ipsa fides, qua iustificamur: secundum illud, quos prædestinauit, eos vocauit: quos vocauit, eos etiam iustificauit. Item, crediderunt quotquot erant prædestinati ad vitam æternam. Iam vero constat, causam causæ, puta electionem, etiam causam esse effectus, seu causati, vt loquuntur, nimirum iustificationis, sed non contrà: quoniam idem esset causa sui ipsius. Propterea ipsa quidem effecta electionis ita ordinari possunt, vt unum sit causa alterius; sicut fides iustificationis, iustificatio glorificationis; sed nullum effectum electionis potest considerari vt eius causa: & per consequens fides, cum effectum sit electionis, eius perinde ac iustificationis, causa conferri nequaquam potest. Idem est iudicium de infidelitate, aliisque peccatis, quæ etsi proprie non dicenda sunt effecta reprobationis, tamen effectum eius est diuina desertio, quam infidelitas caeteraque peccata sequuntur. Confirmatur haec tota responsio iis quae supra cap. ii. ex Luthero recitata sunt de Iudaeis, incredulitate sua excisis de olea, & gentibus fide in eandem insitis.
units.tr: But the same proximate cause of justification and election (such as faith is in the matter of justification) ought not to be granted, and cannot be. For justification is an effect of election, just as faith itself, by which we are justified, is: according to the words, whom he predestinated, them he also called; whom he called, them he also justified. Likewise, as many as were predestinated to eternal life believed. Now it is established that the cause of a cause, namely election, is also the cause of the effect, or of what is caused, namely justification, but not the reverse, since then the same thing would be the cause of itself. Therefore the effects of election can be so ordered that one is the cause of another, as faith is of justification and justification of glorification; but no effect of election can be considered as its cause. And consequently faith, since it is an effect of election, just as justification is, cannot in any way be made the cause of it. The same judgement holds concerning unbelief and the other sins, which, although they cannot properly be called effects of reprobation, nevertheless the effect of reprobation is divine desertion, which unbelief and the other sins follow. This whole response is confirmed by what was cited above in chapter ii from Luther concerning the Jews, cut off from the olive tree by their unbelief, and the Gentiles grafted into it by faith.

units.la: Affinis est obiectio septima. Depraedestinatione nec ex ratione, nec ex lege, sed ex Euangelio iudicandum est. Euangelium autem testatur in gratiam recipi & seruari, eos, electos esse credentes: & contra damnari, eos, reprobatos esse incredulos & permanentes in peccatis. Electio igitur & reprobatio ab hominum fide, vel incredulitate dependent.
units.tr: The seventh objection is related. Concerning predestination we must judge neither from reason nor from the law, but from the Gospel. The Gospel, however, testifies that those who believe are received into grace and preserved, and are elect; and on the contrary, that those who are unbelieving and persist in sins are condemned and are reprobate. Election and reprobation therefore depend on men's faith or unbelief.

units.la: Sed plus est inconclusione. Minor siquidem nihil affirmat de causa praedestinationis, sed hoc tantum vult, ex nota fidei vel incredulitatis finalis, dignosci electos vel reprobos. Unde hoc tantum sequitur: secundum hoc Euangelij testimonium nobis quoque iudicandum, qui electi sint, qui reiecti. Interim Euangelium non negat, sed manifeste affirmat, fidem, obedientiam, perseuerantiam, dona Dei esse gratuita, eaque eáque donari, aut non donari ab ipso, quibus Deo visum est, fecundum beneplacitum ipsius. Matth.11.v.25. Et capite,13. v.11.Ioh.6.v.44. 45.& 65. Et apud eundem cap.10.v.26. ad Ephes.1.v.8. & ibidem v.15.& sequentibus 2.Tim.1.v.9. Ad Heb.8.verf.10.Ierem.31.&c.
units.tr: But this is more than the conclusion allows. The minor premise affirms nothing about the cause of predestination, but only means that the elect or the reprobate are known from the mark of faith or of final unbelief. Hence only this follows: according to this testimony of the Gospel we too must judge who are elect and who are rejected. Meanwhile the Gospel does not deny, but clearly affirms, that faith, obedience and perseverance are gifts of God, freely given, and that they are granted or not granted by him to whom it pleases God, according to his good pleasure. Matth. 11.25. And chap. 13.11. John 6.44, 45 and 65. And in the same place chap. 10.26. Eph. 1.8, and in the same place v. 15 and following. 2 Tim. 1.9. Heb. 8.10. Jer. 31, etc.

units.la: Hinc secundum Euangelium iudicando, colligemus: sicut Euangelium docet hominem seruari, aut non seruari, ita Deus seruare aut non seruare eū ab æterno destinauit. Sed Euangelium non solum docet fide hominem seruari, infidelitate perire: verum etiam tradit fidem ipsam, aliaque beneficia, quibus tanquam medijs ad salutem peruenitur, illis dari, his non dari à Deo, prout ipsi placet. Ergo etiam fidem & id genus beneficia ad salutem, Deus quibusdam dare, quibusdam non dare ab æterno destinauit, prout ipsi placuit.
units.tr: Hence, judging according to the Gospel, we shall conclude: just as the Gospel teaches that a man is saved or not saved, so God from eternity determined to save him or not to save him. But the Gospel not only teaches that a man is saved by faith and perishes by unbelief, but also hands down that faith itself and the other benefits, by which as means we come to salvation, are given by God to some and not given to others, as it pleases him. Therefore God also determined from eternity to give faith and that kind of benefit to salvation to some and not to give it to others, as it pleased him.

units.la: CAPVT XIII.
units.tr: CAPVT XIII.

units.la: Oculus nequam perperam suspectum Deum habet iniquitatis.
units.tr: The wicked eye wrongly suspects God of injustice.

units.la: SEQVITVR nunc illa obiectio, quae a temeritate, ne dicam impietate rationis humanae emergeS, maxime animos simplicium perturbat. Ea vero est, quod oculus nequam humani ingenij Deum suspectum habet de iniquitate, si sine vllis bonorum malorumue meritis, vnum eligat, alterum reprobet, merito arbitrio suo. Iniustum enim videtur in distributionibus, si inaequaliter aequalibus distribuatur. Homines autem remota differentia meritorum sunt aequales. Si ergo absque differentia meritorum Deus inaequaliter distribuit, vnum eligens, et alterum reprobas, videtur quod sit apud eum iniquitas.
units.tr: Now comes that objection, which arises from the rashness, not to say the impiety, of human reason, and which most of all disturbs the minds of simple people. It is this: the wicked eye of the human mind suspects God of injustice if, without any merit of good or evil, he chooses one and rejects another by his own will alone. For it seems unjust in distributions if equals are distributed unequally. But men, apart from any difference in merits, are equal. So if God, without any difference in merits, distributes unequally, choosing one and rejecting another, it seems that there is injustice in him.

units.la: Deinde, quomodo iustitiam Dei defendemus, si mera voluntate sua tot hominum millia nullo ipsorum merito, nullo opere motus, ad aeternos cruciatus praedestinauit? Hoc iniquum, hoc crudele, hoc intolerabile visum est de Deo sentire, et hoc offensi sunt tot et tanti viri tot seculis, et quis non offenderetur? inquit quit Lutherus de seruo arbitrio, vbi hanc ipsam obiectionem multis dissoluit.
units.tr: Next, how shall we defend the justice of God if, moved by his mere will, with no merit or work of theirs as the motive, he predestined so many thousands of men to eternal torments? To think this of God has seemed unjust, cruel and intolerable, and so many great men have been offended by it over so many centuries. And who would not be offended? says Luther in On the Bondage of the Will, where he resolves this very objection in many ways.

units.la: De inæqualitate iam ante quoque respondi, in his quæ ex debito distribuuntur, pertinere ad iustitiam, vt æqualibus non distribuantur inæqualia: non autē in iis quæ sponte & ex gratia quis distribuit sine alterius iniuria. Sicut paterfamilias ille redarguebat murmurantes: Amice, non facio tibi iniuriam: tolle quod tuum est, & abi: Volo autem huic vltimo dare vt & tibi. An non licet mihi de meis facere quod volo? An oculus tuus nequam est, quia ego bonus sum? Discant itaque compescere oculum illum nequam, qui aduersus Deum murmurant, tanquam iniustum, & acceptorem personarum. Sed iniustum est, inquiunt, in vna eademque mala causa hunc liberari, illum puniri: quia iustum est vtrumque puniri.
units.tr: I have already answered the question of inequality earlier: in things that are distributed as a matter of debt, justice requires that unequals not be given equal shares; but not in things that someone distributes freely and by grace, without injury to another. So the householder rebuked those who grumbled: Friend, I am doing you no wrong. Take what is yours and go. But I wish to give to this last man as much as to you. Is it not lawful for me to do what I will with what is mine? Or is your eye evil because I am good? Let those who murmur against God, as if he were unjust and a respecter of persons, learn to restrain that wicked eye. But they say it is unjust that one man in the same bad case be freed and another punished, because it is just that both be punished.

units.la: Imò vtrumque iustum est, siue debitum creditor exigat, siue donet debitori, dummodò sine cuiusquam fraude: iniustum vero demum, exigere non debitum. Nempe igitur, vt pie monet
units.tr: Indeed, both are just: whether the creditor demands what is owed or forgives the debtor, provided no one is defrauded. Only to demand what is not owed would be unjust. Accordingly, as Augustine piously advises:

units.la: Augustinus. Gratias agamus Saluatori, dū nobis redditum non cernimus, quod in damnatione similium & nobis debitum fuisse cognoscimus: nec simus ingrati quod secundum beneplacitum suum in laudem gloriæ gratiæ suæ tam multos liberet Deus misericors, de tam debita perditione, vt si inde neminem liberaret, non esset iniustus.
units.tr: Augustine. Let us give thanks to the Saviour, since we see that the redemption of others is not owed to us, though we know that we too deserved condemnation like theirs. Let us not be ungrateful that God, merciful according to his good pleasure, frees so many for the praise of the glory of his grace from a perdition so deserved that, even if he freed no one from it, he would not be unjust.

units.la: Quod porrò ad multitudinem perentium attinet, respondeo, nec illorum respectu vllam apud Deum esse iniquitatem. Nam in quibus non fit misericordia, in ijs iudicium fit, non iniquitas. Et sicut indebita gratia datur liberatis: ita non nisi debita pœna datur damnatis, vt nec dignos se illi gloriari, nec isti se indignos queri possint.
units.tr: As for the multitude of those who perish, I answer that there is no injustice with God even with respect to them. For where there is no mercy, there is judgement, not injustice. Just as undeserved grace is given to the redeemed, so only deserved punishment is given to the damned, so that the one cannot boast of being worthy and the other cannot complain of being unworthy.

units.la: Nam quia vniuersa massa merito damnata est, contumeliam debitam reddit iustitia, honorem debitum donat gratia, non meriti prærogatiua, non fati necessitate, non temeritate fortunæ, sed altitudine diuitiarum sapientiæ & scientiæ Dei. Si ergo in remittendo debitum bonitas, in exigendo æquitas intel-
units.tr: For since the whole mass is justly condemned, justice repays the deserved disgrace, and grace gives the undeserved honour; not through any prerogative of merit, nor by the necessity of fate, nor by the chance of fortune, but by the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God. If therefore in forgiving the debt goodness is understood, and in exacting it equity,

units.la: Epist. 105 intelligitur, nusquam apud Deum ini-quitas inuenitur. Laudat misericor-diam qui liberatur, nec culpet iudici-um qui punitur.
units.tr: Epist. 105. then nowhere is there injustice to be found with God. Let the one who is freed praise mercy, and let the one who is punished not blame judgement.

units.la: Dicam amplius quid cum Augusti-no. Si humanum genus quod creatum primitus constat ex nihilo, non cum debita mortis & peccatis origine nasceretur, & tamen ex eis creator omnipotens in æternum nonnullos damnare vellet ad interitum: quis omnipoteti creatori diceret, quare fecisti sic? Qui enim cum non essent, esse donauerat, quo fine essent, habuit potestate. Nec dicerent caeteri, cur paribus omnium meritis diuinum discrepare arbitriu, quia potestate habet figulus luti. Nunc autem cum damnatis poena iusta reddatur, saluatis autem gratia donetur indebita, quis humanæ conditionis oblitus, diuini sensus arcana discutiat?
units.tr: I will say more, with Augustine. If the human race, which was originally created out of nothing, were born without the debt of death and the origin of sin, and yet the almighty Creator willed from among them to condemn some to destruction forever, who would say to the almighty Creator, "Why have you made them so?" For he who gave being to those who were not had the power to determine for what end they should be. Nor would the others say, "Why does the divine will differ among those whose merits are equal?" because the potter has power over the clay. But now, since to the condemned a just punishment is rendered, and to the saved an undeserved grace is given, who, forgetting the human condition, would search into the hidden things of the divine mind?

units.la: Sed inquiet aliquis: cur in eadem causa me potius, quam illum puniet, aut illum potius quam me liberabit? Respondeo, id in arbitrio Dei esse, non nostro, sicut non in eorū qui debitores sunt, sed in eius cui debetur arbitrio fi-tum est, vt vel exigat, vel donet debitū. Hinc Augustus. In Adamo omnes mori-mur, & vna quaedam missa summus peccati, supplicium debens divina summaque iusti-tia, quod sive exigatur, sive donetur, nulla est iniquitas. Aquibus autem exigendum, & quibus donandum sit, superbe iudicant debi-tores. Dei est exigere a quo placet: donare, cui placet; qui nequaquam exigit indebitum, ne-quaquam donat alienum. Idem alibi: Qua-re huic ita, & huic non ita Deus facit, inue-stigabiles sunt viae eius, & inscrutabilia iudi-cia eius: quorum tam magnum profundum adorare potius, quam scrutari debemus, ut caveamus praecipitium.
units.tr: But someone will say: why does he punish me rather than him in the same cause, or free him rather than me? I answer that this lies in the will of God, not ours, just as it is not in the will of debtors but in the will of him to whom the debt is owed to decide whether to exact or to forgive the debt. Hence Augustine: In Adam we all die, and by one common lump of sin we owe punishment to divine and supreme justice; whether it is exacted or forgiven, there is no injustice. But the proud debtors judge as to whom it should be exacted from and to whom forgiven. It is for God to exact from whom he pleases, and to forgive whom he pleases; he who never exacts what is not owed, and never forgives what is not his own. Again elsewhere: That God deals thus with this one and not thus with that one: his ways are unsearchable and his judgements inscrutable. We ought to adore rather than scrutinise this great deep, lest we fall into the precipice.

units.la: Itaque huius impudentiam quęstio-nis retundentes dicamus cum Apostolo: o altitudo sapientia & scientia eius, quam inscrutabilia eius iudicia, quam imperuestigabiles sunt viae eius? Item, O homo, tu quis es qui respondeas Deo? num figmentum dicit figulo, cur sic me fecisti? Annon habet potesta-tem figulus in lutum?
units.tr: Therefore, in checking the impudence of this question, let us say with the Apostle: O the depth of the wisdom and knowledge of God, how inscrutable are his judgements and how unsearchable are his ways! Likewise: O man, who are you to answer back to God? Will the thing formed say to him who formed it, "Why have you made me thus?" Has not the potter power over the clay?

units.la: Neque vero nos pigeat oblatran-tium ora sic obstruere. Nam si illos non pu-
units.tr: Nor should we be ashamed to silence the mouths of the barkers in this way. For if they are not ashamed

units.la: Ad Simpl. lib. 1. q. 2. pudet, non nobis, sed Paulo contradicere: cur nos pigeat eis hoc idem atq; identidem dicere, quod dixit Apostolus? Præclare Augustinus Paulum secutus: Tu homo, inquit, expectas à me responsum, Et ego sum homo. Itaque ambo audiamus dicentem: ô homo tu quis es? Melior est fidelis ignorantia, quàm temeraria scientia. Quære merita, non invenies nisi pœnam. ô altitudo. Petrus negat, latro credit. ô altitudo. Quæris tu rationem? Ego expavescam altitudinem. Tu ratiocinare, ego mirabor: Tu disputa, ego credam. Altitudinem video, ad profundum non pervenio. Requiescit Paulus, quia admirationem invenit. Vocat ille inscrutabilia iudicia, & tu scrutari venisti? Rursum, Fateor, Dei consilium sicut homo, explicare non possum. Novi enim cum Paulo ἀποστόλω expavescere, ô altitudo sapientiæ, & scientiæ eius! Nobis consideratio, admiratio, tremor, exclamatio; quia nulla penetratio. Ipsi autem quid? Gloria in sæcula sæculorum, sive de vasis in honorem, sive de vasis in contumeliam.
units.tr: Ad Simpl. lib. 1, q. 2. to contradict not us but Paul, why should we be ashamed to say to them the same thing, again and again, that the Apostle said? Augustine, following Paul, puts it splendidly: You, man, he says, expect an answer from me. And I am a man. So let us both hear him saying: O man, who are you? Faithful ignorance is better than rash knowledge. Seek merits, you will find nothing but punishment. O the depth! Peter denies, the thief believes. O the depth! Do you seek a reason? I shall be struck with dread at the depth. You reason, I shall marvel; you dispute, I shall believe. I see the height; I do not reach the bottom. Paul rests, because he has found something to admire. He calls the judgements inscrutable, and have you come to scrutinise them? Again: I confess that I cannot explain God's counsel as a man. For I know, with Paul, to be astonished [ἀποστόλω] at O the depth of the wisdom and knowledge of God! For us there is consideration, admiration, trembling, exclamation, because there is no penetration. But as for them, what then? Glory for ever and ever, whether concerning the vessels of honour or the vessels of dishonour.

units.la: Hoc vero loco contra stultos quosdam, quos etiam sæpè memoratus autor perstringit, putantes Apostolum in responsione...
units.tr: But at this point, against certain fools whom our author often also rebukes, who think that the Apostle, in his reply...

units.la: {a} De verbis Apost. Serm. 20. responsione defecisse, & inopia reddēdæ rationis repressisse contradictoris audaciam, admoniti esse debemus, re ipsa magnam esse redditionem rationis in ijs quæ sunt dicta. Ad nostræ enim capacitatis considerationem reuocamur, verbo quidem breui, sed magnū de exaggeratione nominum pondus inijciente, cum dicit: o homo tu quis es, qui respondeas Deo? homo videlicet Deo, lutum figulo. Similiter quod expauescens exclamat, o altitudo, quam inscrutabilia sunt iudicia Dei! latis declarat, occulta hæc opera Dei esse posse, iniusta esse non posse: quia iudicia sunt eius, qui iustus est, & orbem iudicat, cuiusque adeo voluntas summa est iustitiæ regula, ut quicquid vult & facit, eo ipso quod facit iustum habendum sit. Neque enim de diuina iustitia secundum humanam iustitiam, aut potius nominē iustitiæ plane superbiam, disputare fas est. Nam, ut scite probat Lutherus de seruo arb. circa finem: si talis esset iustitia Dei, quæ humano captu posset iudicari esse iusta, plane non esset diuina. na,& nihil differret ab humana iustitia. Adhæc,cum Deus totus incomprehe- sibilis & inaccessibilis sit humana ra- tione (quid enim est homo compara- tus Deo?quid nostra potentia,scientia, substantia? quid denique omnia nostra ad Deum?)par est;imo necessarium est, vt& iustitia ipsius incomprehensibilis sit. Quocirco non immerito Augustus de prædest.& gratia, Quis ita,inquit, desipiat,aut potius quis ita blasphemet,vt dicat de iustitia Dei,lege humana iustitia disputandum? quæ profecto iustitia Dei aduersatur,iniusta est. Ab illo qui summe iustus est, omne quod qualitercunque iustum est, manare manifestum est. Quis ergo erit, qui immutabiliter manentem,& omnia quæ sunt, condentem, regentem atque seruantem Dei sapientiam pendat humanæ sapientiæ arbitrio? Non est ergo de illa maiestate diuinæ sapientiæ, humanæ vanitatis arbitrio disputandum. Adorandus Deus est,non iudicandus,ait Tertull. grauiter increpans diuinitatis censores, dicentes: sic non debuit Deus: & sic magis debuit. Sed stultum Dei, sapientius est hominibus. Et tunc maxime magnus est, cum homini pusillus, & maxime iustus, cum homini iniustus, ait ille.
units.tr: {a} De verbis Apost. Serm. 20. ...gave up in his answer, and by lack of an argument to give back checked the audacity of the objector, we ought to be warned that in fact there is a great deal of reasoning in what has been said. For we are called back to a consideration of our own capacity, by a brief word which nevertheless lays a great weight upon the amplification of the names, when he says: O man, who are you, who answer back to God? Man, that is, to God; clay to the potter. Likewise, when in astonishment he exclaims, O the depth, how inscrutable are the judgements of God! he makes it plain that these works of God may be hidden, but cannot be unjust, because they are the judgements of him who is just and judges the world, and whose will is so much the supreme rule of justice that whatever he wills and does must be held just by the very fact that he does it. Indeed it is not right to dispute about divine justice according to human justice, or rather, to dispute by the name of justice at all is plainly pride. For, as Luther rightly proves in On the Bondage of the Will, near the end: if the justice of God were such that it could be judged just by human comprehension, it would plainly not be divine, and it would differ in nothing from human justice. Besides, since God is wholly incomprehensible and inaccessible to human reason (for what is man compared with God? what is our power, our knowledge, our substance? what, in short, are all our things in relation to God?), it is fitting, indeed necessary, that his justice too be incomprehensible. Wherefore Augustine, in On Predestination and Grace, not without reason says: Who would be so foolish, or rather who would so blaspheme, as to say that the justice of God must be disputed by the standard of human justice? That justice would certainly be opposed to the justice of God, and would be unjust. It is clear that whatever is just in any way proceeds from him who is supremely just. Who, then, will be one who weighs the immutably abiding wisdom of God, which creates, rules and preserves all that exists, by the judgement of human wisdom? Therefore the majesty of divine wisdom is not to be disputed by the judgement of human vanity. God is to be adored, not judged, says Tertullian, severely rebuking the censors of the divine nature, who say: God ought not to have done so; he ought rather to have done so. But the foolishness of God is wiser than men. And he is then greatest when he is least in the eyes of men, and most just when he seems unjust to men, as he says.

units.la: At inquiunt, vera haec omnia sunt & sufficientia ad defendendam iustitiam divinae electionis, & reprobationis, si consideremus quid nobiscum agat Deus ex praesuppositione lapsus generis humani. Cum enim omnes damnatione aeterna obstricti teneantur, quod illos misericorditer inde liberet, illos iuste puniat, prout ipsi visum est, nullius insimulari potest iniustitiae, quia potest misereri quorum vult, & pro arbitrio punire quos vult. Verum in hanc ipsam corruptionem, in quam Adam posteros suos praecipites secum egit, sine Dei voluntate non decidisse mus.
units.tr: But they say that all these things are true and sufficient to defend the justice of divine election and reprobation, if we consider what God does with us from the presupposition of the fall of the human race. For since all are held bound by eternal damnation, it is no charge of injustice against God that he mercifully frees some from it and justly punishes others, as seemed good to him, because he may have mercy on whom he wills and punish at his pleasure whom he wills.

units.la: Quid igitur adhuc irascitur? cur hominibus vitio imputat, in iisque plectit, quorum necessitatem ordinatione sua imposuit? Nam voluntati eius quis resistat? Sic caro concludit, ut se excusat, & in Deum culpam deriuet. Nec mirum, Adamo iam corrupto, ad cuius imaginem sumus geniti, idem factitate in paradiso.
units.tr: Why, then, is he still angry? Why does he impute the fault to men and punish those whom he has placed under necessity by his own ordinance? For who can resist his will? So the flesh reasons, excusing itself and shifting the blame onto God. This is no wonder, since Adam was already corrupt, to whose image we were born, and he did the same thing in paradise.

units.la: Sed fides & spiritus longè aliter iudicant. 1. Est quod & hîc retorquea-mus illud Apostoli: ô homo tu quis es qui respondeas Deo? Num dicit figmentum figulo, cur me sic fecisti?
units.tr: But faith and the Spirit judge far otherwise. (1) We may turn back on them that saying of the Apostle: O man, who are you to answer back to God? Does the thing formed say to the one who formed it, Why have you made me thus?

units.la: 11. Apud Christianos omnes in confesso est, ob lapsum primorum nostrorū paretum in paradiso, peccatum & mortem non solum temporariam, verùm etiam multo magis æternam, in omnes iuste transiisse. Aduersus improborum verò profanitatem Dominus ipse iustitiam suam satis tuebitur αυτοκατακρίτως eos reddendo. Quorsum ergo iis de iniquitate, vbi iustitia in confesso est?
units.tr: (2) Among Christians it is agreed by all that, because of the fall of our first parents in paradise, sin and death, not only temporal but much more eternal, have passed justly upon all. As for the profanity of the wicked, the Lord himself will sufficiently defend his justice by making them self-condemned [αὐτοκατακρίτως]. Why then complain to them of iniquity, when justice is agreed upon?

units.la: 111. Homo vtique sua, non Dei culpa cecidit. Quod quidam explicare volètes, ad distinctionem confugiunt, voluntatis & permissionis: quasi genus hu-manum in Adamo ceciderit, nude tantum permittente, non autem aliqua ratione, etiam volente Deo, sine cuius tamen voluntate ne passerculus quidem cadit in terram. Vocem ipsam permissionis non reiicio, qua & scriptura vtitur: tur: sed explicationem reprehendo: quoniam non nolens, sed volens Deus permittit, quicquid permittit. Alia igitur ratione, eaque vera & solida Augustinus ostendit, quomodo sua, non Dei culpa, homo ceciderit. Nimirum Deus qui condidit omnia valde bona, dederat homini voluntatem bonam, in qua cum fecerat rectum, & ad imaginem suam. Dederat etiam adiutorium, quo posset in ea manere, si vellet. Ut autem hoc vellet, aut nollet, in eius permisit arbitrio. In ipso igitur homine & diabolo causa extitit, ut fieret deterior. In diabolo, quia suasit: In homine, quia voluntate libera consensit; atque ita per liberum arbitrium Deum deserens, iu-stum iudicium Dei expertus est, ut cum tota sua stirpe, quae in illo adhuc posita, tota peccaverat, damnaretur.
units.tr: (3) Man fell, of course, by his own fault, not by God's. Some who want to explain this take refuge in a distinction between will and permission, as if the human race had fallen in Adam with God merely permitting it, without any reason, and not also willing it, although not even a sparrow falls to the ground without his will. I do not reject the word permission itself, which Scripture also uses, but I find fault with that explanation, since God does not permit whatever he permits unwillingly, but willingly. Augustine therefore shows, by another reasoning, one that is true and solid, how man fell by his own fault and not God's. Namely, God, who made all things very good, had given man a good will, in which he had made him upright and according to his own image. He had also given him help by which he could remain in that state, if he wished. But whether he would wish it or not he left to man's own choice. Thus the cause of his becoming worse lay in the man himself and in the devil: in the devil, because he persuaded; in the man, because with free will he consented. And so, by abandoning God through free choice, he experienced God's just judgment, so that he was condemned together with his whole stock, which, still contained in him, had sinned entirely.

units.la: Quod autem ei datum non fuit, ut in statu illo recto & sine vitio perseveraret, vtiq; ideo datum non est, quia Deus noluit: melius iudicans de malis bene facere, quam mala nulla esse permittere, vt ait Augustinus. Quod ipsum alibi lu-
units.tr: Now the reason he was not given to persevere in that upright state without fault is certainly that God was unwilling to give it. For God judged it better to bring good out of evil than to permit that no evils exist, as Augustine says. He explains this very clearly elsewhere,

units.la: {a} Quare Deus fuerit Adamus labi. bi luculenter explicans,scribit: Saluberrimè confitemur, quod rectissimè credimus, Deum, Dominumque rerum omnium, qui creauit omnia bona valde, & mala ex bonis exortura esse prasciuit, & sciuit magis ad suam omnipotetissimam bonitatem pertinere, etiam de malis benefacere, quàm mala esse non sine-resic ordinasse Angelorum & hominum vitam, ut in ea prius offenderet, quid posset eorum liberum arbitrium: deinde quid posset sua gratia beneficium, iustitiaque iudicium. De hoc vide etiam Tertull. lib.2. contra Marcionem: & 2.Sent.dist.23. quare Deus permiserit hominem tentari, sciens eum esse casurum. Et erudite lib.1. dist. 45. explicatur, quomodo & quatenus permissio Dei ad voluntatem ipsius referenda sit; secundum illud Augusti. Non fit aliquid, nisi Omnipotens fieri velit, velij-nendo ut fiat, vel ipse faciendo. Vbi includit, & bona & mala omnia quæ fiunt, sed cum discrimine, ut mala intelligatur velle, sinendo fieri; bona autem, ipse faciendo. Nam finit vtique non nolens, sed volens, vt idem ait Ench.ad Laur.c. 100. Et de prædestit. & grat. ca.15.dicit,
units.tr: {a} Why God allowed Adam to fall. Clearly explaining, he writes: We most wholesomely confess, what we most rightly believe, that God, the Lord of all things, who created all things very good, and foreknew that evils would arise from goods, and knew that it pertained more to his almighty goodness to bring good even out of evils than to allow evils not to exist, so ordered the life of angels and men that in it he might first test what their free will could do, and then what his grace could bestow as a benefit, and his justice as a judgment. On this see also Tertullian, book 2 against Marcion, and 2 Sentences, dist. 23: why God permitted man to be tempted, knowing that he would fall. And book 1, dist. 45, explains learnedly how and how far God's permission is to be referred to his will, according to that saying of Augustine: Nothing happens unless the Almighty wills it to happen, either by willing it to be done by allowing it, or by doing it himself. Here he includes both all the good and all the evil that happen, but with a distinction: evil is understood to be willed by allowing it to happen, but good by his doing it himself. For he indeed allows it, not unwillingly but willingly, as the same author says in the Enchiridion to Laurentius, chapter 100. And in On Predestination and Grace, chapter 15, he says,

units.la: Oo ij Om-
units.tr: Oo ij Om-

units.la: cap.27 De Corr. & grat.ca. 18.
units.tr: Chapter 27; On Correction and Grace, chapter 18.

units.la: Enchir.
units.tr: Enchiridion.

units.la: Cap. 13
units.tr: Chapter 13

units.la: Omnia vel adiuuante Domino perfici, vel deferente permitti, ut nouerimus tamen nolete Domino nihil prorsus admitti. Certe si quid fit, quod Deus simpliciter omni modo factum nolit, vel non fit, quod facta velit, periclitatur ipsum fidei nostrae initium, quo nos in Deum Omnipotentem credere confitemur, & aliquis de Epicuri schola Deus inducitur. Noster enim Deus in caelo & in terra facit quaecunque vult.
units.tr: All things are either brought about with the Lord's help or permitted by his allowing, yet so that we know nothing at all is admitted by the Lord against his will. Certainly, if anything happens that God wholly does not will to happen, or if something does not happen that he wills to happen, then the very beginning of our faith is endangered, the faith by which we confess that we believe in God Almighty, and a god from Epicurus' school is introduced. For our God in heaven and on earth does whatever he wills.

units.la: Lutherus de re tota sic pronunciat: Iis qui quaerunt, cur permisit Adam ruere, cum potuisset illum seruare, dicitur, Deus est, cuius voluntatis nulla est causa, nec ratio. Vide ut permissione sub voluntate includat. Unde & cap. 197. scribit: sive sinat, sive inclinet Deus, ipsum sinere, vel inclinare, non fit nisi volente Deo, quia voluntas hominis non potest effugere actionem Omnipotentis Dei.
units.tr: Luther pronounces on the whole matter thus: To those who ask why Adam was allowed to fall, when he could have preserved him, the answer is: God is, and his will has no cause or reason. See how he places permission under the will. Hence also in chapter 197 he writes: Whether God allows or inclines, the allowing or inclining itself does not happen except with God willing, because the will of man cannot escape the action of Almighty God.

units.la: CAPUT XIV. De effectis electionis.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIV. On the effects of election.

units.la: Deinceps de effectis, cum electionis, ctionis, tum reprobationis, dicendum est. Quoniam vero prædestinatio illa Sanctorum, quam electionem vocamus, præparatio est gratiæ, id est, gloriæ in futuro, & beneficiorum in præsenti, quibus tanquam mediis ad destinatam sibi gloriam ducuntur electi: vtraque, & finis & media, effecta sunt electionis.
units.tr: Next we must speak of the effects both of election and of reprobation. Since that predestination of the saints, which we call election, is the preparation of grace (that is, of glory in the future and of benefits in the present), by which the elect are led as by means to the glory appointed for them, both the end and the means are effects of election.

units.la: Per finem intelligimus salutem & gloriam electorum. Nam ipsorum respectu is electionis finis est, licet quod ad Deum alius & superior quidam sit: demonstratio nempe diuitis ipsius gratiæ in vasis misericordiæ ad gloriam ipsius.
units.tr: By the end we understand the salvation and glory of the elect. For with respect to them this is the end of election, although with respect to God it is another and higher end: namely, the demonstration of the rich grace of God in the vessels of mercy to his own glory.

units.la: Media vero fini isti subordinata, sunt quæcunque beneficia, quibus certissime liberantur quicunque liberantur, vt ait Augustus. Sunt quoque ea duplicis omnino generis: quædam omnibus pariter seruandis, adultis & infantibus necessaria sunt. Verbi gratia, meritum Christi, iustificatio, & regeneratio per Spiritum sanctum. Quædam adultos tantum consequuntur ob defectum discretionis boni ac mali in paruulis: vt est
units.tr: The means subordinate to this end are all the benefits by which all who are delivered are most certainly delivered, as Augustine says. These are of two kinds. Some are equally necessary for all who are to be saved, both adults and infants: for example, the merit of Christ, justification, and regeneration through the Holy Spirit. Others belong only to adults, because infants lack the discernment of good and evil: such as

units.la: Oo iij cocognitio Christi, vera in ipsum fiducia, studium bonorum operum, perseuerantia in tentationibus, & id genus alia.
units.tr: the knowledge of Christ, true trust in him, zeal for good works, perseverance in temptations, and other things of that kind.

units.la: Licet autem multi & varij sint effectus electionis: principaliores tamen, ad quos alij ferme reducuntur, sunt quatuor: nimirum Christus, tanquam mediator & Pontifex cum toto opere suae humiliationis & gloriae: tum vocatio efficax ad Christum, iustificatio item, & glorificatio. Hinc Apostoli illa catena vere aurea: quos Deus praedestinauit, eos etiam vocari, & quos vocat (intellige de vocatione quae est secundum propositum Dei) eos etiam iustificari, quos autem iustificat, eos etiam glorificari. Ac de Christo, extra quem nemo seruari potest, subiungit statim: Quid igitur dicemus ad haec? Si Deus pro nobis, quis contra nos? is quidem qui proprio filio non pepercit, sed pro nobis omnibus tradidit eum. Quis intentabit crimina aduersus electos Dei? quis est qui condemnet? Christus is est, qui mortuus est, imo qui & excitatus est, qui etiam est ad dextram Dei, qui etiam postulat pro nobis. Vt ergo de his aliquid dicamus, exor- fi à Mediatore,& capite electorum, Domino nostro Iesu Christo: is sane nostri cum Deo coniunctionis, ideoque omnis nostræ beatitudinis vnicum fundamentum est: liquidem tantæ gloriæ,ad quam electi fumus capaces non fuissemus, nisi cœlestis pater à nostra indignitate in Christum oculis conuersis, in illo dilecto nos sibi gratos effecisset. Propterea Paulus testatur, nos in Christo electos ante iacta mundi fundamenta: hoc est, vt ipsemet interpretatur, nos prædestinatos ad adoptionem in filios, aliaque cœlestia bona, per & propter Christum consequenda. Quo sensu etiam ad Timoth. scribit: gratiam nobis datam in Christo Iesu ante tempora sæcularia: quasi dicat, Deum ab æterno constituisse nobis dare gratiam qua feruamur,sed in Christo,fonte gratiæ.Sic igitur statuamus: Deum, cum aliquorum vellet misereri, vt notas faceret diuitias gloriæ suæ erga vasa misericordiæ,ad hoc autem Mediatore idoneo opus effet, qui sua morte & satisfactione,placata ira Dei,iustitiam & vitam amissam ijs acquireret, partamque salutem tueretur ac conseruaret, ordinasse æterno, & vere paterno consilio suo, vt filius patri cosubstantialis & coæternus, assumta in plenitudine temporis natura vere humana, pro peccatis nostris moreretur, & resurgens a mortuis ad dextram Dei regnaret, atque interpellaret pro nobis. Ita Christus, qua Mediator, primum & principale effectum est diuinę prædestinationis, à quo alia omnia dimanant: sicut Petrus etiam testatur de agno illo immaculato & incontaminato, cuius precioso sanguine sumus redemti, patefactum quidem fuisse vltimis temporibus propter credentes, præordinatum vero ante iacta fundamenta mundi. Scite Aug. Ille vnus prædestinatus est, vt caput nostrum esset, nos multi prædestinati sumus, vt membra eius essemus.
units.tr: Although the effects of election are many and various, the principal ones, to which the rest are for the most part reduced, are four: namely, Christ as mediator and high priest, with the whole work of his humiliation and glory; then effectual calling to Christ; likewise justification; and glorification. Hence that truly golden chain of the Apostle: whom God predestined, these he also called; and whom he called (understand the calling that is according to God's purpose), these he also justified; and whom he justified, these he also glorified. And concerning Christ, outside of whom no one can be saved, he immediately adds: What then shall we say to these things? If God is for us, who is against us? He who did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how will he not also with him freely give us all things? Who shall bring a charge against God's elect? It is God who justifies. Who is he who condemns? Christ Jesus is the one who died, yes, who was also raised, who is also at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us. So, to say something about these things, let us begin with the Mediator and head of the elect, our Lord Jesus Christ. Certainly he is the one foundation of our union with God and therefore of all our blessedness. For we would not have been able to receive so great a glory, for which we have been chosen, unless the heavenly Father, with his eyes turned from our unworthiness to Christ, had made us acceptable to himself in that Beloved. Therefore Paul testifies that we were chosen in Christ before the foundation of the world: that is, as he himself explains, we were predestined to adoption as sons, and to the other heavenly goods to be obtained through and on account of Christ. In the same sense he also writes to Timothy: the grace given to us in Christ Jesus before the ages of time: as if he said that God had decided from eternity to give us the grace by which we are saved, but in Christ, the fountain of grace. Thus, then, let us hold: God, wishing to show mercy to some, so that he might make known the riches of his glory toward the vessels of mercy, and since for this a suitable Mediator was needed, who by his death and satisfaction, the wrath of God being appeased, would win back for them the justice and life that were lost, and would preserve and maintain the salvation thus obtained, ordained by his eternal and truly fatherly counsel that the Son, consubstantial and coeternal with the Father, having assumed a truly human nature in the fullness of time, should die for our sins, and rising from the dead should reign at the right hand of God and intercede for us. Thus Christ, as Mediator, is the first and principal effect of divine predestination, from whom all the others flow; just as Peter also testifies of that spotless and unblemished Lamb, by whose precious blood we have been redeemed, that he was indeed made manifest in the last times for the sake of believers, but foreordained before the foundation of the world. Augustine rightly says: He alone was predestined to be our head; we, many, were predestined to be his members.

units.la: Ex hoc etiam apparet, propriam causam missionis & passionis filij Dei, fuisse salutem electorum, ac proinde, quantum ad propositum Dei, & effectum missionis, ac passionis Christi attinet, illum pro-
units.tr: From this it also appears that the proper cause of the sending and passion of the Son of God was the salvation of the elect; and therefore, as far as God's purpose and the effect of the sending and passion of Christ are concerned, he was sent and suffered

units.la: {a} De præd. sanct. c.15. proprie missum & pasjum duntaxat pro electis. Nisi enim electis ordinatus fuisset mediator, non erat cur in carne veniret, nedum cur morti omnium ignominiosissimæ se ipsum exponeret.
units.tr: {a} On the predestination of the saints, ch. 15. only for the elect. For unless the Mediator had been appointed for the elect, there would have been no reason for him to come in the flesh, much less to expose himself to the most shameful of deaths.

units.la: Alterum electionis effectum, vti didicebamus, est vocatio, quia iam prædestinatio hominis impleri & manifestari incipit. Nam quos prædestinauit, vocat, ait Paulus. Et alibi: Vocauit nos vocatione sancta, non ex operibus nostris, sed ex suo proposito & gratia, quæ data est nobis in Christo, ante tempora sæcularia. Vbi vocationem non obscure ponit effectum donationis gratiæ ab æterno, id est prædestinationis.
units.tr: The second effect of election, as we have learned, is calling, because the predestination of the man now begins to be fulfilled and made manifest. For whom he predestined, these he also calls, says Paul. And elsewhere: He called us with a holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace, which was given to us in Christ before the ages of time. Here he clearly places the calling as the effect of the bestowal of grace from eternity, that is, of predestination.

units.la: Vt autem intelligatur, quænam & qualis sit ea vocatio, distinguendum est inter vocationem externam, & internam. Exterior rursum est, vel naturalis vel supernaturalis.
units.tr: So that we may understand what this calling is, and of what kind, we must distinguish between external and internal calling. The external calling is in turn either natural or supernatural.

units.la: De priore accipiendum est, quod canit Psalmes: Cœli enarrant gloriam Dei, & opus manuum eius annunciat firmamentum. Non est lingua nec loquela, ubi non audiatur vox eorum. Et Paulus ad Rom. scribit: inuisibilia Dei, æternam videlicet tum potentiam, tum diuinitatem, ex creatione mundi perspici, ad hoc vt reddantur homines inexcusabiles. Et alibi, non sine testimonio semetipsum reliquit, benefaciens, dans cælitus tempora fructifera.
units.tr: It is of the former that the Psalmist sings: The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the work of his hands. There is no speech nor language where their voice is not heard. And Paul writes to the Romans that the invisible things of God, namely his eternal power and divinity, are perceived from the creation of the world, so that men are rendered without excuse. And elsewhere: he did not leave himself without witness, doing good and giving from heaven rains and fruitful seasons.

units.la: Hoc naturæ testimonium nunquam de Domini bonitate ac potestate conticescit, sed prædicatione perpetua maiestatem loquitur sui autoris. Quia tamen ad vocem naturæ obsurduerunt aures nostræ, quo minus quæ monemur vtiliter audiamus, accessit doctrina legis ac Euangelij, & instituti sunt ministri verbi & gratiæ, per quos opportune, importune, fides & resipiscentia, cuncti s, prout contigerit, prædicentur, electis ac reprobis; siquidem inter se commixti sunt, nec hominum iudicio discerni possunt nec debent. De hac vocatione inquit Dominus: multi sunt vocati, pauci vero electi. Non enim omnes auscultant Euangelio, qui audiunt. Esaias enim dicit, Domine quis credidit sermoni nostro? toto die expandi manus meas ad populum rebellem & contradicentem.
units.tr: This testimony of nature never falls silent about the goodness and power of the Lord, but by perpetual proclamation it speaks of the majesty of its author. Yet because our ears have grown deaf to the voice of nature, so that we do not hear profitably what we are admonished, the teaching of the law and of the Gospel has been added, and ministers of the Word and of grace have been appointed, through whom faith and repentance are proclaimed, opportunely and inopportunely, to all as occasion arises, to the elect and the reprobate alike; for they are mixed together, and cannot and ought not to be distinguished by human judgment. Of this calling the Lord says: Many are called, but few are chosen. For not all who hear the Gospel listen to it. Isaiah indeed says: Lord, who has believed our report? All day long I have stretched out my hands to a rebellious and contradictory people.

units.la: Superest igitur, interior eademque efficax adChriftum vocatio, electorum propria: quam Paulus appellat vocationem secundum propositum Dei. Nouimus, inquit, ijs qui Deum diligunt, omnia conferre ad bonum, ijs videlicet, qui secundum propositum vocati sunt.
units.tr: There remains, therefore, the inward and at the same time effectual calling to Christ, which is proper to the elect: this Paul calls the calling according to God's purpose. We know, he says, that for those who love God all things work together for good, namely for those who are called according to his purpose.

units.la: Est autem vocatio ista nihil aliud quàm diuinus quidã gratiæ instinctus, quo mouetur homo ad assentiendum & obtemperandum Euangelio, hoc est, ad fidem & conuersionem. Et hæc vocatio fit, partim verbo, partim & principaliter afflatu Spiritus sancti, corda intus illuminantis & mouentis. Nec eodem omnes tempore vocantur, sed alij prima luce, alij vndecima hora diei; prout visum Deo est, suam in illis gratiam dispensare.
units.tr: This calling, however, is nothing other than a certain divine impulse of grace, by which a man is moved to assent to and obey the Gospel, that is, to faith and conversion. And this calling takes place partly by the Word, but chiefly by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, who illuminates and moves the hearts within. Nor are all called at the same time: some at the first light, others at the eleventh hour of the day, as it has seemed good to God to dispense his grace to them.

units.la: Propositam descriptionem Augustinus confirmat de prædestinatione: Sanct. vbi fuse materiam hanc persequitur. Illa, inquit vocatio secundum propositum Dei, non omnium est qui vocantur, sed tantum electorum. Hos Deus vocat, vt faciat eos membra filij sui, non ea vocatione qua vocati sunt, qui noluerunt runt venire ad nuptias, sed qua vocatione fit credens. Ad quam vocationem qui pertinent, omnes sunt docibiles Dei, nec potest eorum quisquam dicere: credidi ut sic vocarer: prae-uenit eum quippe misericordia Dei, qua sic vocatus est, ut crederet. Omnes enim docibiles Dei veniunt ad filium, quoniam audierunt, & didicerunt a patre. Valde remota est a sen-sibus carnis haec schola, in qua pater auditur & docet, ut veniatur ad filium: nec agit cum carnis aure, sed cordis.
units.tr: Augustine confirms the description proposed, in his work on predestination, where he pursues this matter at length: That calling according to God's purpose, he says, is not of all who are called, but only of the elect. God calls these so that he may make them members of his Son, not by that calling by which those were called who refused to come to the marriage feast, but by that calling by which the believer is made. All who belong to this calling are taught by God, and none of them can say: I believed so that I might be called; for the mercy of God has gone before him, by which he was so called that he might believe. For all who are taught by God come to the Son, because they have heard and learned from the Father. This school, in which the Father is heard and teaches so that one may come to the Son, is far removed from the senses of the flesh; it does not work through the outer ear of the body, but of the heart.

units.la: Hinc sane cum Euangelium praedicatur, quidam credunt, quidam non credunt, imo contradicunt. Nam qui credunt praedicatore foris secus sonante, intus a patre audiunt & discunt: qui autem non credunt, foris audiunt, intus non audiunt, neque discunt: hoc est illis datur ut credant, illis non datur; quia nemo, inquit, venit ad me, nisi pater, qui misit me, traxerit eum. Quod apertius postea dicitur: Nemo venit ad me, nisi fuerit ei datum a patre. Ergo trahi a patre ad Christum, sicut & audire & discere a patre, ut quis ad Christum veniat, nihil aliud est, quam donum acci-
units.tr: Hence, when the gospel is preached, some believe and some do not; indeed they contradict it. For those who believe hear and learn from the Father inwardly, though the preacher sounds outwardly in a different way. Those who do not believe hear outwardly but do not hear or learn inwardly. So it is given to some to believe and not given to others, because, he says, no one comes to me unless the Father who sent me draws him. This is stated more plainly afterwards: no one comes to me unless it has been given him by the Father. Therefore to be drawn to Christ by the Father, just as to hear and learn from the Father, so that someone comes to Christ, is nothing other than to receive a gift from the Father by which he believes in Christ.

units.la: Ibidem Augustin. : Iohan. 6. : Trahi a patre. accipere à patre, quo credat in Christum. Hæc patrum orthodoxorum princeps ille Augustt.
units.tr: Ibid., Augustine, on John 6: "To be drawn by the Father." "To receive from the Father, by which he believes in Christ." This is what Augustine, that prince of the orthodox Fathers, says.

units.la: Quadruplex autem error hic cauendus est: in primis Pelagianorum, quo aduersus gratiam sese extollentes, atque os suum in cælum ponentes dicebant; hominem iis valere viribus, vt tanquam ex se ipso credere & bene operari possit, dum modò voluntas Dei prædicetur, & ad hoc tantum iuuetur à Deo per legem & doctrinam Euangelij, vt discat quæ facere & sperare debeat. Ita secundum eos vocatio Dei tantum esset, quæ verbo extrinsecus fit.
units.tr: Here a fourfold error must be guarded against. First is that of the Pelagians, who, lifting themselves up against grace and setting their mouths against heaven, said that man has such strength that he can believe and do good works, as it were from himself, provided only that the will of God is proclaimed and he is helped by God, through the law and the teaching of the gospel, only so far as to learn what he ought to do and hope for. Thus, according to them, the calling of God would be only that which comes outwardly by the word.

units.la: Quasi vero audientes Euangelium a non audientibus, & non potius credentes a non credentibus discreuerit, qui dixit: Nemo venit ad me nisi fuerit ei datum a patre. Et passim docet scriptura, fidem & conuersionem, & quicquid boni operis habemus, a Deo manare. Conuerte nos Domine ad te, & conuertemur, ait Ierem. promittitur-que apud Prophetas, fore vt Deus inscriscribat legem cordibus suorum, det illis cor nouum, cor carneum, ablato lapideo: indat spiritum nouum, & timorem fui, in cordibus ipforu, deniq; faciat vt in praeceptis eius ambulemus. In Euangelioetiam Dominus de fructu iustitiae loquens testatur, nos fine ipso nihil posse facere. Item, Non vos me elegistis, sed ego elegi vos, & constitui vos vt fructum afferatis, & fructus vester maneat. Et Paulus inquit: Quid habes quod non accepisti? quod si autem accepisti, quid gloriaris quasi non acceperis? Ac diserte idem refipiscentiam perhibet Dei donum esse, 2. Tim. 2. Quemadmodum etiam fidem, omniaque bona opera fructus censet spiritus. Conditos etiam nos testatur in Christo Iesu ad opera bona, quae praeparavit Deus, vt in iis versaremur. Et ne qua maneat dubitatio, diserte scribit, nos electos ante iacta mundi fundamenta, vt essemus sancti & inculpati. Idcirco etiam orationes Ecclesia facit, cum pro infidelibus, & doctrinae Euangelij resistentibus, vt conuertantur ad Deum; tum profidelibus, vt proficiant in fide, & perseuerent in ea. Non enim poscerentur à Deo quæ præcepit fieri, nisi ab illo etiam donaretur vt fierent.
units.tr: As if he who said, "No one comes to me unless it has been given him by the Father," had not distinguished between those who hear the gospel and those who do not, and rather between those who believe and those who do not believe! Scripture teaches everywhere that faith and conversion, and whatever good work we have, flow from God. "Convert us, O Lord, to yourself, and we shall be converted," says Jeremiah. It is promised also by the Prophets that God will write his law on the hearts of his people, give them a new heart, a heart of flesh, taking away the stony heart; he will put in their hearts a new spirit and fear of himself, and finally make us walk in his precepts. In the Gospel, too, the Lord, speaking of the fruit of righteousness, testifies that we can do nothing without him. Likewise: "You did not choose me, but I chose you, and appointed you that you should bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain." And Paul says: "What do you have that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you glory as if you had not received it?" The same apostle plainly says that repentance too is a gift of God (2 Tim. 2.), just as he judges faith and all good works to be the fruit of the Spirit. He also testifies that we have been created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God has prepared, that we should walk in them. And lest any doubt remain, he writes plainly that we were chosen before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless. For this reason the Church also offers prayers, both for unbelievers who resist the teaching of the gospel, that they may be converted to God, and for believers, that they may advance in faith and persevere in it. For things which he has commanded to be done would not be asked of God unless it were also granted by him that they be done.

units.la: Alij, licet bona opera, atque ipsam quoque fidem, secundum incrementum, faterentur esse à Deo: Fidei tamen initium, ex nobis esse volebant: tanquam fidês non à Deo donetur nobis, sed ab ipso tantum augeatur, in nobis, merito nostrae credulitatis, siue bonae voluntatis: atque ita bona voluntas hominis, diuinae causa sit gratiae, non gratia causa voluntatis.
units.tr: Others, although they admit that good works and faith itself, as to its increase, are from God, nevertheless wanted the beginning of faith to be from us, as if faith is not given to us by God, but only increased in us by God, on account of our own credulity or good will. And so the good will of man would be the cause of divine grace, and not grace the cause of the will.

units.la: Hanc sententiam Prosper & Hilarius Semipelagianis, seu reliquiis (vt ipsi vocant) hæreticos Pelagianæ attribuunt. Et fuit aliquando in hoc errore ipsemet Augustus, velut cum ait: quod credimus nostrum est: quod autem bonum operamur, illius est, qui credentibus dat Spiritum sanctum. Et paulo post: Nostrum est credere & velle: illius autem dare credentibus & volentibus facultatem bene operandi per Spiritum sanctum. Sed errorem istum agnouit postea & emendauit libro I. retractat. cap. Cap.23. Et copiosissime lib. de prædest. Sanct. Vbi fusissime demonstrat, non solum auctam, verum etiam incoatam in nobis fidem, Dei donum esse, gratia vocatis præueniente voluntate nostram, vt velimus: secundum dicta, Quus prior dedit illi, & retribuet ei? quoniam ex ipso, & per ipsum, & in ipso sunt omnia. Vobis datum est non solum vt credatis in eum, sed etiam vt patiamini pro eo. Simpliciter ait: vt credatis, non, vt perfectius credatis. Quale & illud est ad Rom. Vnicuique Deus partitus est mensuram fidei. Item ad Ephes. Gratia salui facti estis per fidem, & hoc non ex vobis, Dei donum est: id est; & quod dixi per fidem, non ex vobis sed Dei donum est. Idem Apostolus 2.Corin.3. Non sumus idonei cogitare aliquid, tanquam ex nobis ipsis. Nec credere igitur: quoniam credere nihil aliud est, quam cum assensione cogitare. Item ca.4. prioris Epistolæ: Quid habes quod non accepisti? quod si autem accepisti, quare gloriaris quasi non acceperis? Expresse etiam de voluntate dicitur, deum operari in nobis, & vt velimus, & vt efficiamus pro bona voluntate, sua vtique non nostra.
units.tr: Prosper and Hilary attribute this opinion to the Semipelagians, or to the remnants (as they call them) of the Pelagian heresy. And at one time Augustine himself was in this error, as when he said: "What we believe is ours; but that we do good works belongs to him who gives the Holy Spirit to those who believe." And a little later: "To believe and to will is ours; but to give to those who believe and will the power of doing good through the Holy Spirit is his." But he afterwards recognised this error and corrected it, in Retractations, book 1, chapter 23, and very fully in the book On the Predestination of the Saints, where he demonstrates at great length that not only the increase of faith in us, but even its beginning, is a gift of God, the will being anticipated by grace in those who are called, so that we may will it, according to the words: "Who has first given to him, and it shall be repaid to him? For from him, and through him, and in him are all things." "To you it has been given not only to believe in him, but also to suffer for him." He says simply: "that you believe," not "that you may believe more perfectly." Such also is that in Romans: "God has apportioned to each one a measure of faith." Likewise in Ephesians: "By grace you have been saved through faith, and this not of yourselves; it is the gift of God," that is: and what I said, through faith, is not of yourselves but the gift of God. The same apostle, in 2 Corinthians 3: "We are not sufficient to think anything as of ourselves." Nor therefore to believe, since to believe is nothing other than to think with assent. Likewise in chapter 4 of the first letter: "What do you have that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you glory as if you had not received it?" It is also said expressly of the will: "God works in us both to will and to work for his good pleasure," certainly his, not ours.

units.la: Philip.2. nostra. Fixum igitur manet, voluntatem à Deo præueniri, & ab illo instillari nobis vt credamus.
units.tr: Philip. 2. Therefore it remains fixed that the will is anticipated by God, and that he instils in us that we may believe.

units.la: At inquies, dona Dei dantur orantibus: oratio autem præsupponit fidem. Ergo homo à se ipso assert fidem, saltem initium eius, vt capax sit gratiæ, & donorum Dei. Sed maior particularis est, cum alia det Deus etiam non orantibus, vt initium fidei; alia non nisi orantibus. Et Sic Augustinus modum istum soluit cap. 16. de bono pers. & aliis in locis.
units.tr: But you will object: God's gifts are given to those who pray, and prayer presupposes faith. Therefore man himself supplies faith, at least its beginning, so that he may be capable of grace and the gifts of God. But the answer is a distinction: God gives some things even to those who do not pray, such as the beginning of faith, and other things only to those who pray. Augustine resolves this objection in chapter 16 of On the Gift of Perseverance, and in other places.

units.la: Tertio, inuenta sunt à quibusdam opera, nescio quæ, moraliter bona, qui-bus homo ante fidem & conuersionem seipsum ad gratiam præparet, imò gratiam promereatur de congruo, vt loquuntur. Atque id Cornelij exemplo probare volunt, qui, Domino precęs & eleemosynas eius respiciente, cognitione Christi donatus est.
units.tr: Thirdly, some have devised certain works, I know not what, morally good, by which man, before faith and conversion, prepares himself for grace, and even merits grace de congruo, as they put it. And they wish to prove this from the example of Cornelius, who, when the Lord regarded his prayers and alms, was granted the knowledge of Christ.

units.la: Ex horum vero opinione non recedit ab ingrata Deo sententia, quam Pelagius ipse in Episcopali iudicio Pa-lastino, damnauit, licet fi&to corde, nempe gratiam Dei secundum merita nostra dari. Præterea cũ Apostolus dicat,quis te discernit? quid habesquod nõ accepisti? secundum hos licebit dicere: discernit me opus meum, conatus & meritum meum. Quid? quod scriptura docet, nos omnes in offensis & peccatis esse mortuos ante fidë, & sine hac impossibile esse nos, vel nostra opera, Deo placere? Dic mihi obsecro, quid boni Paulus volebat, ac non potius magna mala, quod spirans cædem pergebat ad vastandos horrenda mentis cæcitate ac furore Christianos? Quibus meritis bonæ voluntatis, qua operum præparatione Deus illum ab his malis ad fidem conuertit? Similiter quàm multi inimici Christi quotidie, occulta Dei gratia, subito trahuntur ad Christum? Denique clamat Apostolus: Non ex operibus iustitiæ quæ nos fecimus, sed secundum misericordiam suam saluos nos fecit. Quare valeat præparationes huiusmodi, quibus homines ad gratiam se putentur disponere, quo Christo inserantur.
units.tr: Indeed, the opinion of these men does not differ from the view, which Pelagius himself condemned at the Palestinian episcopal judgement, though with a dissembling heart, namely that grace is given according to our merits, which is hateful to God. Moreover, since the Apostle says: "Who makes you to differ? What do you have that you did not receive?" according to these men it would be permissible to say: "My own work, endeavour and merit make me to differ." What? Does not Scripture teach that we are all dead in offences and sins before faith, and that without this it is impossible for us, or our works, to please God? Tell me, I beg you, what good did Paul intend, rather than great evils, when he went on breathing slaughter to lay waste the Christians with a dreadful blindness and fury of mind? By what merits of good will, or by what preparation of works, did God convert him from these evils to faith? Similarly, how many enemies of Christ are every day suddenly drawn to Christ by the hidden grace of God? Finally the Apostle cries out: "Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us." Therefore such preparations, by which men are thought to dispose themselves for grace, are of no value for being grafted into Christ.

units.la: August. de prædest. Sanƈt. cap. 6. errorem istum non obscurè reiicit, taxans vulgi sermonem, quo dici solet, hic aut ille ideo credere meruit, quia bonus erat antequam crederet. Quod ad exemplum Cornelij, ibidem respondet, eum fide non prorsus caruisse. Nam quomodo invocasset, in quem non crediderat? quomodo preces & eleemosynæ sine fide acceptæ fuissent coram Deo? Postea tamen Petri demum ministerio credidit in Christum, videlicet ut iam incarnatum Dei filium sciret, & sacramentum regenerationis acciperet.
units.tr: Augustine, in On the Predestination of the Saints, ch. 6, plainly rejects this error, censuring the common saying: "This man or that one deserved to believe because he was good before he believed." As for the example of Cornelius, he answers in the same place that Cornelius was by no means without faith. For how could he have called on one in whom he had not believed? How could his prayers and alms have been accepted before God without faith? Yet he came at last to believe in Christ through the ministry of Peter, namely so that he might know the Son of God as already incarnate and receive the sacrament of regeneration.

units.la: Postremus circa vocationem, de qua loquimur, error est quorundam efficaciam eius extenuantium, quasi effectus eius sit in hominis potestate, ut si nolit, frustra Deus vocet.
units.tr: The last error concerning the calling we are discussing is that of certain men who diminish its efficacy, as if its effect lay in man's power, so that if he is unwilling, God calls in vain.

units.la: Imò si nolit homo, & oblatæ gratiæ relucta ri pergat, nihil certius est, quàm vocationis huius necdum esse participe. Etenim efficacissimam esse hanc vocationem, Christus testatur: Omnis qui audiuit à patre meo & didicit, venit ad me.
units.tr: Indeed, if a man is unwilling, and keeps resisting the grace offered, it is most certain that he has not yet become a partaker of this calling. For Christ testifies that this calling is most efficacious: "Everyone who has heard from my Father and learned, comes to me."

units.la: Quæ verba Augustinus considerans, inquit, si omnis qui audiuit à patre & didicit, venit: profecto omnis qui non
units.tr: Augustine, considering these words, says: if everyone who has heard from the Father and learned comes, then surely everyone who does not come has not heard nor learned.

units.la: „ venit, non audiuit nec didicit. Nam si au- „ diuisset & didicisset, veniret. Neque enim „ vllus audiit & didicit, & non venit: sed „ omnis, vt ait veritas, qui audiuit, & di- „ dicit, venit. Haec itaque gratia, quae oc- „ culte humanis cordibus diuina largi- „ tate tribuitur, a nullo duro corde re- „ spuitur: ideo quippe tribuitur, vt cor- „ dis duritia primitus auferatur, secundum „ illud: tollam cor lapideum, & dabo vobis cor „ carneum. Vide eundem ad Simpl. lib. I. quaest. 2. Non potest, inquit, effectus misericordiae Dei esse in hominis potestate, vt frustra ille miseretur si homo nolit: quia si vellet etiam reluctantium misereri, posset ita vocare, quomodo illis aptum esset, vt moverentur, & intelligerent & sequerentur. Nam etsi multos vocat, eorum tamen miseretur, quos ita vocat, quomodo ijs vocari aptum est, vt sequantur: nec vllius frustra miseretur. Illi ergo electi, qui sic vocati, vt vocantem non respuunt: Ceteri non electi, quia non secuti, quantumuis vocati. Eandem doctrinam de vocatio- nis huius efficacia praeclare Lutherus de seruo arb. confirmat, cap. 45.
units.tr: comes, does not hear nor learn. For if he had heard and learned, he would come. Indeed, no one hears and learns and does not come, but everyone, as the Truth says, who hears and learns, comes. This grace, which is secretly bestowed on human hearts by divine bounty, is spurned by no hard heart. It is given, of course, so that the hardness of the heart may first be taken away, according to that: I will take away the stony heart, and give you a heart of flesh. See the same author to Simplicianus, book 1, question 2: The effect of God's mercy cannot be in man's power, so that he would have mercy in vain if the man were unwilling. For if he were willing even to have mercy on those who resist, he could call them in such a way as would be fitting for them to be moved, and to understand and to follow. For although he calls many, he has mercy only on those whom he calls in such a way as is fitting for them to be called so that they follow; and he has mercy on no one in vain. Therefore those are the elect who are called in such a way that they do not spurn the one calling; the others are not elect, because they do not follow, however many are called. Luther, in his book On the Bondage of the Will, chapter 45, admirably confirms this same doctrine of the efficacy of this calling.

units.la: quaest. 1. tis idem verbum audientibus, non omnes ita vocemur, vt vocatorū obedientia cōsequatur: parum appositè responderetur à nonnullis, quia ipsi nolūt. Nam si fideles ideò credunt, quia volunt, non eis fidem Deus donauit, sed eam sibi ipsi volendo præstiterunt. Nemo quidem potest credere, nisi volens: qui enim crederet inuitus? sed ex nolente volentem facit is, quo trahete ad Christum venimus. Trahuntur ergo miris modis electi, vt velint, ab illo qui nouit intus in ipsis hominum cordibus operari, non vt homines (quod fieri non potest) nolentes credant, sed vt volentes ex nolentibus fiant.
units.tr: Question 1. When the same word is heard by many, and not all are called in such a way that obedience follows from those who are called, some answer rather inappositely that they themselves are unwilling.
