For if the faithful believe because they are willing, God has not given them faith; rather they have produced it for themselves by willing it. No one indeed can believe unless he is willing; for who would believe against his will? But he who draws us to Christ makes the willing out of the unwilling. The elect are therefore drawn in wonderful ways, so that they become willing, by him who knows how to work within the very hearts of men; not so that men, being unwilling (which cannot happen), believe, but so that the willing arise out of the unwilling.

units.la: Sed cur non omnes ita trahit? Quia miseretur quorum vult, & indurat quos vult: iudicio vtique iustissimo, quoniā apud Deum nulla est iniquitas. Nam qui credit ex vno omnes illos in condemnationem, sine dubio iustissimam, intelligit nullam Dei fore iustam repre hensionem, etiamsi nullus inde liberaretur, & idcirco magnam esse gratiam, quòd plurimi liberentur, & quid sibi dedeberetur, in eis qui non liberantur, agnoscant: vt qui gloriatur, non in suis meritis, quæ paria videntesse damna-tis, sed in Domino glorientur.
units.tr: But why does He not draw everyone in this way? Because He has mercy on whom He wills, and hardens whom He wills: by a judgment surely most just, since with God there is no iniquity. For he who believes that all are condemned in one man, a condemnation undoubtedly most just, understands that there will be no just reproach of God even if no one were freed from it; and therefore he recognises that grace is great because very many are freed, and what was owed to them is due to those who are not freed; so that he who glories may glory not in his own merits, which appear equal to those who are condemned, but in the Lord.

units.la: Quare autem hunc trahat, illum nō trahat, inscrutabilia sunt iudicia eius, & imperuestigabiles viæ eius. Ideò noli hoc velle iudicare, si non vis errare, ait alicubi August. super Ioh.
units.tr: Why He draws this one and does not draw that one, His judgments are inscrutable and His ways past tracing out. Therefore do not wish to judge this, if you do not wish to err, as Augustine says somewhere on John.

units.la: CAPVT XV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XV.

units.la: Alÿ effectus electionis, Iustificatio & glorificatio, vbi & de electorum perseuerantia.
units.tr: Other effects of election: justification and glorification, and also the perseverance of the elect.

units.la: Sed de vocatione satis. Venio ad tertium effectum principalem electionis, nempe iustificationem. Nam Paulo teste, quos vocat, eos etiam iustificat.
units.tr: But that is enough about calling. I come now to the third principal effect of election, namely justification. For, as Paul testifies, "those whom he calls, he also justifies."

units.la: Quàm vero beneficium hoc necessarium sit electis ad destinatum sibi finé vitæ & gloriæ cœlestis consequendum, cuiuis liquet. Cùm enim omnes simus sub peccato, & propter peccatū rei irę, & damnationis æternę, regnum cœlorum videre nequimus, nisi à peccatis eatis absoluamur, & coram Deo iusti reputemur, per eorundem gratuitam condonationem.
units.tr: How necessary this benefit is to the elect, if they are to attain the end appointed for them, which is life and heavenly glory, is plain to anyone. For since we are all under sin, and because of sin we are liable to the wrath and eternal damnation, we cannot see the kingdom of heaven unless we are absolved from our sins and reckoned righteous before God, through their free forgiveness.

units.la: Id vero nihil aliud est, quàm iustificari, prout vox ea hic sumitur. Sic Paulus, ad Rom. 4. Iustificationem definit, per iustitiæ imputationem: atque hanc si-tam docet in remissione peccatorum, adducto ad id testimonio Dauidis Psal. 32. Beati quorum remissæ sunt iniquitates, & quorum obtecta sunt peccata: beatus vir, cui non imputauit Dominus peccatum. Varie alioquin verbum iustificandis in scripturis sumitur. Alias enim significat, eum qui bonus & iustus est, tale agnosci & prædicari: vt quod Deus iustificari dicitur in sermonib. suis: Et narrante Luca, plebs Christo audito, Deû iustificauit: Et sapientiâ Christus pronúciat iustificari à filijs suis. Alias idé est, quod donari iusti tia inhærete, per infusionem nouarum qualitatum & bona opera. Quomodo Apocal. 22. scribitur: qui nocet, noceat adhuc: & qui iustus est, iustificetur adhuc. Tertiò, ex idiotismo Hebræorum vsitatissima est sacris literis verbi significatio tio forensis, vt sic dicam, nempe vt iustificari idem sit, quod à reatu absolui, vocabulo accepto relatiue, non autem vt qualitatem aliquam notet. Ita vsurpatur Prouerb.17.v.15.Iesa.5.v.23.
units.tr: This is nothing other than being justified, as that word is taken here. So Paul, in Romans 4, defines justification as the imputation of righteousness, and teaches that this consists in the forgiveness of sins, citing the testimony of David in Psalm 32: Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered: blessed is the man to whom the Lord does not impute sin. Otherwise the word "to justify" is used in the Scriptures in various ways. In one sense it means to recognise and declare someone to be good and righteous, as when God is said in his sayings to be justified; and when Luke relates that the people, having heard Christ, justified God; and when Christ declares that wisdom is justified by her children. In another sense it means the same as to be given righteousness inherent in us, through the infusion of new qualities and good works, as is written in Revelation 22: "He who does harm, let him do harm still; and he who is righteous, let him be justified still." Thirdly, according to the Hebrew idiom, the forensic sense of the word, so to speak, is most common in the sacred letters, so that to be justified means to be absolved from guilt, the term being taken in a relative sense and not indicating some quality. It is used in this way in Proverbs 17:15 and Isaiah 5:23.

units.la: Atque hæc significatio præsenti negotio quadrat, cùm de hominis peccatoris iustificatione coram Deo quæritur. Nempe igitur iustificamur ab ipso, cùm qui in nobis ipsis gehennæ rei sumus coram tribunali Dei, nihilominus gratiâ ipsius ab omni reatu absoluimur, vt aduersarius condemnare amplius non possit: ipso videlicet nos iustos reputante gratis per redemtionē in Christo Iesu, per fidem in sanguine ipsius, & non ex operibus. Tametsi enim in iustificatione impij simul donatur Spiritus sanctus, qui cor renouat, & nouas qualitates infundit, quibus excitamur ad operum bonorum studium: tamen per nouitatem istam non deletur reatus præcedentium peccatorum: nec propter opera demum accepti fimus, sed necesse est, vt ante fimus accepti, quo opera nostra, vt pote imperfecta, & coinquinata, ipsi placere possint. Sed de his nihil nunc attinet speciali ùsagere. Illud insuper notandum, quod Apostolus hoc gratuitæ iustificationis donum ex prædestinatione oriri docet, propriúqj facit electorum, postquam diuinæ vocationis iam participes euaserunt. Nã ait, quos prædestinauit, vocauit: &quos vocauit, τούτους καὶ ἐδικαίωσεν. Non dicit, sicut spiritus imaginatur erroris, omnes reprobos pariter & electos, vocatos & nō vocatos, quotquot scilicet ex Adamo peccatores nascuntur, etiam in Christo iustificari, & ab omni peccato iudicioque Dei liberatos in gratiam recipi. Et ne qua dubitatio maneat, se ipsum explanans, subiunxit Paulus: Quid igitur dicemus ad hæc? Si Deus pro nobis, quis contra nos? qui filio proprio non pepercit: sed pro nobis omnibus tradidit eum. Quis accusabit electos Dei? Deus is est qui iustificat. Quis condemnet? nempe electos Dei. Christus is est, qui mortuus est, imo qui etiam excitatus. Audimus electos, horum esse iustificationem: pro his omnibus Christum in mortem traditum. Simul etiam refellitur sententia, & è reproborum numero aliquos iustificari dicentium, verum irritam in ijs reddi reconciliationem. Rectius Augustinus ad Apostolici dicti mentem: Qui in numero prædestinatorum non sunt, iuxta neminem adducit Deus ad pœnitentiam salutem & spiritualem, qua homo in Christo reconciliatur Deo. Similia habentur apud eundem in Soliloquijs, cap. 28.
units.tr: This meaning fits the present matter, when we ask about the justification of a sinful man before God. We are therefore justified by him, since we who in ourselves deserve hell are before the judgement seat of God, nevertheless by his grace we are absolved from all guilt, so that the adversary can no longer condemn us; God himself, that is, reckons us righteous freely, through redemption in Christ Jesus, through faith in his blood, and not from works. For although in justification the godless are at the same time given the Holy Spirit, who renews the heart and infuses new qualities by which we are stirred to the study of good works, nevertheless this newness does not wipe out the guilt of previous sins; nor are we accepted at last on account of works, but it is necessary that we be accepted beforehand, so that our works, being imperfect and tainted, may be able to please him. But there is no need now to speak specially of these things. It should further be noted that the Apostle teaches that this gift of gratuitous justification arises from predestination, and makes it peculiar to the elect, after they have already become partakers of the divine calling. For he says: "Whom he predestined, these he also called; and whom he called, these τούτους καὶ ἐδικαίωσεν [these he also justified]." He does not say, as the spirit of error imagines, that all the reprobate and the elect alike, the called and the uncalled, however many are born sinners from Adam, are also justified in Christ, and are received into grace freed from all sin and from the judgement of God. And lest any doubt should remain, Paul, explaining himself, added: "What then shall we say to these things? If God is for us, who is against us? He who did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all. Who shall accuse the elect of God? It is God who justifies. Who shall condemn? Namely the elect of God. It is Christ who died, yes, rather who was also raised." We hear that the justification of these is for the elect, and that Christ was delivered to death for all of them. At the same time the opinion is refuted of those who say that some of the number of the reprobate are justified, but that the reconciliation in them is void. Augustine rightly, in line with the meaning of the apostolic saying: "God brings to repentance and to spiritual salvation, by which a man is reconciled to God in Christ, no one who is not in the number of the predestined." Similar things are found in the same author in the Soliloquies, chapter 28.

units.la: Sequitur quartus effectus prædestinationis electorum, Glorificatio. Nam quos vocat & iustificat, eos etiam glorificat, ait Apostolus. Vtitur enim verbis in præterito, pro præsenti, phraři Hebraeorum. Glorificatio autem designat regnum sanctorum in vita cœlesti: simulque completitur aut præsupponit donum perseuerantiæ usque in finem, de qua dicitur: qui perseuerauerit usque in finem, is saluus erit. Similes sunt promissiones Ioh. 6. Quicquid dat mihi pater, ad me venit: & eum qui venit ad me, non eiciam foras. Et statim: Hæc est voluntas eius qui misit me, patris, ut quicquid dederit mihi non perdam ex eo quicquam, sed suscitem illud die nouissimo. nouissimo. Item, nemo venit ad me, nisi pater traxerit eum: Ego vero suscitabo illum vl-timo illo die.
units.tr: There follows the fourth effect of the predestination of the elect, glorification. For, as the Apostle says, "whom he calls and justifies, these he also glorifies." For he uses the verbs in the past tense for the present, a Hebrew idiom. Glorification denotes the reign of the saints in the heavenly life; and at the same time the gift of perseverance to the end is either fulfilled in it or presupposed, of which it is said: "He who perseveres to the end, he will be saved." Similar are the promises in John 6: "Whatever the Father gives me comes to me; and him who comes to me I will not cast out." And soon after: "This is the will of him who sent me, the Father, that of all that he has given me I should lose nothing, but raise it up on the last day." Likewise: "No one comes to me unless the Father draws him; and I will raise him up on the last day."

units.la: Plana est demonstratio : Quisquis patre trahente venit ad Christum, ab eo suscitabitur ad resurrectionem vitæ. Veniunt autem omnes, qui Christo dati, hoc est, in ipso prædestinati sunt. Ij igitur omnes suscitabuntur ab eo ad resurrectionem vitæ, hoc est, glorificabuntur.
units.tr: The demonstration is plain: whoever comes to Christ when the Father draws him is raised by him to the resurrection of life. Now all come who have been given to Christ, that is, who have been predestined in him. Therefore all of these will be raised by him to the resurrection of life, that is, they will be glorified.

units.la: Perseuerantia vero, cuius memini, est tentationibus non superari: &, vt Paulus copiosissimè describit, neque oppressione, neque angustia, neque vlla re creata separari à caritate Dei, sed in omnibus plus quàm victorem esse, per eum qui dilexit nos.
units.tr: The perseverance of which I have spoken is not being overcome by temptations; and, as Paul describes at length, neither by oppression, nor by distress, nor by any created thing, is one separated from the love of God, but in all things one is more than a conqueror, through him who loved us.

units.la: Notandumque hoc loco est, de magno isto perseuerantiæ bono; cum quod electi omnes id habeant, tum quod non ex se, verùm aliunde, nempe ex gratiæ diuinæ largitate habeant.
units.tr: And in this place it must be noted concerning this great good of perseverance, both that all the elect have it, and that they have it not from themselves but from elsewhere, namely from the bounty of divine grace.

units.la: Quod ad prius, aperta sunt testimonia, Matth. 24. Rom. 8. Item, 2. Tim. 2. firmum stat fundamentum Dei. Adhæc cum SpiSpiritus Dei testetur perseuerantibus salutem, vincentibus coronam vitæ repositam: necessariò perseuerant, qui ad regnandum cum Christo electi sunt.
units.tr: As to the former, there are clear testimonies: Matthew 24; Romans 8; likewise 2 Timothy 2: "the firm foundation of God stands." Moreover, since the Spirit of God testifies that salvation is laid up for those who persevere, and the crown of life for those who conquer, necessarily those persevere who are elect to reign with Christ.

units.la: Accedit, quod Christus vniuersaliter pro electis suis orauit & exauditus est, non minus quàm pro Petro legitur rogasse, ne deficeret fides ipsius. Quo quid aliud rogauit, nisi vt haberet in hac de, liberrimam, fortissimam, inuictissimam, perseuerantissimam voluntate?
units.tr: Add to this that Christ prayed universally for his elect and was heard, just as we read that he asked for Peter, that his faith should not fail. What else did he ask for in this, except that they should have the most free, most strong, most invincible and most persevering will?

units.la: Pro electis ergo orante Christo, ne deficiat fides eorum, perseuerabit vtique in finem, nec eam nisi manentem vitæ huius inueniet finis: vt exemplo Petri colligit Augustinus de corr. & grat.cap. 11. & 12.
units.tr: Therefore, since Christ prays for the elect that their faith should not fail, they will certainly persevere to the end, and the end of this life will find it remaining in them; as Augustine infers from the example of Peter, in On Correction and Grace, chapters 11 and 12.

units.la: Iam verò perseuerantiam diuini esse muneris, confiteri nos cogunt, & propriæ infirmitatis sensus, & multitudo tentationum quibus cum assiduè contra Diabolum, mundum, & propriam nostram carnem, luctandum nobis est, in præsenti seculo nequam. Quis inter tot insidias, & gladios, diaboli, nisi manu Dei sustentante, tutus esse queat?
units.tr: Now indeed the feeling of our own weakness and the multitude of temptations, with which we must continually struggle against the devil, the world and our own flesh in this evil age, compel us to confess that perseverance is a gift of God. Who, amid so many snares and swords of the devil, could be safe, unless he were sustained by the hand of God?

units.la: Secundò, testimonia ad hoc mani- festissima sunt inscriptis propheticis atque Euangelicis. Ierem.32. ait Domi-nus: timorem mei dabo in cor eorum, vt à me non recedant. Quod quid est aliud, quàm talis, & tantus erit timor mei, quem dabo in cor eorum, vt mihi perseueranter adhæreant?
units.tr: Secondly, the testimonies to this are most manifest in the prophetic and evangelical writings. In Jeremiah 32 the Lord says: "I will put my fear in their heart, that they may not depart from me." What else is this but that my fear, which I will put in their heart, will be of such a kind and so great that they will cling to me persistently?

units.la: Hose. 2. Desponsabo te mihi in perpetuum, in iustitia & fide &c. Desponsauit autem sibi omnes verè credentes. Joh. 10. Ego omnibus meis do vitam æternam, nec peribunt in æternum, neque rapiet eas quisquam è manu mea. Pater meus, qui dedit mihi, maior est omnibus. Phil.1. Qui incepit in vobis opus bonum, perficiet vsque in finem.
units.tr: Hosea 2: "I will betroth you to me for ever, in righteousness and faith, etc." Now he has betrothed to himself all who truly believe. John 10: "I give to all my own eternal life, and they shall never perish, nor shall anyone snatch them out of my hand. My Father, who gave them to me, is greater than all." Philippians 1: "He who began a good work in you will complete it until the end."

units.la: Tertiò, perseuerantiam omnes sancti à Deo poscunt, & tota fermè oratione Dominica, quando oratur à sanctis, nihil pene aliud quàm perseueran-tiam posci intelligitur, præsertim cùm dicimus: Ne nos inducas in tentationem, sed libera nos à malo. Frustra autem petere-tur à Deo perseuerantia, si non daretur ab ipso. Mera enim irrisio est, à Deo pete-
units.tr: Thirdly, all the saints ask God for perseverance, and almost the whole of the Lord's Prayer, when it is prayed by the saints, is understood to ask for nothing else than perseverance, especially when we say: "Do not lead us into temptation, but deliver us from evil." Yet perseverance would be sought from God in vain if it were not given by him. For it is pure mockery to ask God for what you suppose he will not give, and which, since he does not grant it, lies in the power of man.

units.la: August. de bono perseu. cap. 2. petere quod statuas eum non dare, sed ipso non donante in hominis esse potestate. Argumentum hoc Augustinus est de bono perseverantiae cap. 2.
units.tr: Augustine, On the Gift of Perseverance, chapter 2. Augustine makes this argument in On the Gift of Perseverance, chapter 2.

units.la: Obiicitur contra perseverantiam sanctorum, quod sacris literis et experientia testantibus multi a fide deficiant, naufragiumque eius faciant. Argumentum tale est: Quicunque credentes fuerint electi, quia Paulo teste, fides electorum est. Aliqui autem credentes deficiunt. Ergo aliqui electi deficiunt.
units.tr: It is objected against the perseverance of the saints that, as the Holy Scriptures and experience bear witness, many fall away from the faith and suffer shipwreck of it. The argument runs thus: "Whoever have been believers are elect, since, by the witness of Paul, the faith is that of the elect. But some believers fall away. Therefore some elect fall away."

units.la: Resp. Maior vera demum est de fide iustificante ac saluifica. Ea vero in fundamento posita, neminem perire permittit. Multi autem deficiunt a fide historica nempe, et temporaria, ut vocamus: dum Euangelium amplexi, postmodum ab eo relabuntur, et doctrinis adhaeret Daemoniorum sub nomine Christiani praetextu. Sic Chrysostomus et Theophylactus testimonia Paulina edisserunt.
units.tr: I answer: the major premise is true only of justifying and saving faith. Such faith, once laid as a foundation, permits no one to perish. Many, however, fall away from historical faith, that is, temporary faith, as we call it: they embrace the Gospel but afterwards fall back from it and cling to the teachings of demons under the name and pretext of Christianity. So Chrysostom and Theophylact expound the Pauline testimonies.

units.la: At, Apostatas eiusmodi scriptura electos Dei appellat ante defectionem.
units.tr: But Scripture calls such apostates the elect of God before their defection.

units.la: Ad Ephes. 1. v. 4. Et 1. Pet. 1. v. 1. Itemque cap. 3. verf. 9. · Hæc instantia dissoluitur ambiguitate vocabuli obseruata, de qua initio monui: per electos videlicet alias strictè vocari prædestinatos ad vitam æternam: alias in genere, quicunque ad populum Dei pertinent externa vocatione. Quis enim neget, eos electos, quos eandem fidem, & conuersionem Christianam nobiscum cernimus profiteri? plane dicuntur & habentur electi iudicio caritatis, a nescientibus quid futuri sint, ait Augustus. non ab illo qui eos noluit non habere perseuerantiam, quæ ad beatam vitam ducit electos. Hinc Johannes unus ex numero prædestinatorum, qui de pectore Domini biberat hoc secretum, de talibus pronunciat: E nobis egressi sunt, sed non erant ex nobis. Nam si fuissent ex nobis, mansissent. Quid est quæso, non erant ex nobis? Nonne utrique a Deo creati? utrique ex Adam nati? nonne utrique vocati, & sacramentorum participatione Ecclesiæ membra? vera sunt hæc: secundum hæc omnia ex nobis erant. Veruntamen secundum aliam quadam discretionem, non
units.tr: See Ephesians 1:4, 1 Peter 1:1, and likewise 1 Peter 3:9. This objection is resolved by observing the ambiguity of the word, which I warned about at the beginning: namely, that "the elect" is sometimes taken strictly for those predestined to eternal life, and at other times in a general sense, for all who belong to the people of God by external calling. For who would deny that those are elect whom we see professing the same faith and Christian conversion as ourselves? They are rightly called and regarded as elect by the judgement of charity, as Augustine says, by those who do not know what they will become; not by him who did not wish them to lack the perseverance that leads the elect to blessed life. Hence John, one of the number of the predestined, who had drunk this secret from the Lord's breast, pronounces of such people: "They went out from us, but they were not of us. For if they had been of us, they would have remained." What, I ask, does "they were not of us" mean? Were they not both created by God? Were they not both born of Adam? Were not both called, and members of the Church by participation in the sacraments? These things are true: according to all of these they were of us. Nevertheless, according to another distinction they were not of us,

units.la: De Cont. & grat. cap. 7. non erant ex nobis, quia non erant secundum propositum Dei vocati: non erant in Christo electi ante constitutionem mundi: non erant in eo lortem consecuti: non erant praedestinati, secundum propositum eius qui omnia operatur. Nam si hoc essent, ex illis essent, & cum illis sine dubitatione manssissent. Ceterum numero sanctorum suorum ideo Deus quosdam miscet nō vere sanctos nec perseveraturos, ne simus securi. Non enim expedit electis in huius vitae tentatione securitas: sed qui videtur stare, videat ne cadat.
units.tr: On Rebuke and Grace, chapter 7: they were not of us, because they were not called according to the purpose of God; they were not chosen in Christ before the foundation of the world; they had not obtained a lot in him; they were not predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things. For if they had been these things, they would have been of those, and would without doubt have remained with them. Otherwise, God mingles some who are not truly holy and will not persevere among his saints, so that we may not be secure. For security is not expedient for the elect in the temptation of this life: "let him who seems to stand take heed lest he fall."

units.la: Deinde respondetur ad Minorem argumenti: etiam vere credentes & pios, & per consequens electos, graviter quandoque labi a cofessione & vita Christiana. Sed partim fidesipsorum couerfione ne sopitur potius quam extinguitur eiusmodi lapsibus: partim eadem reparatur antequam vita ista finiatur, & deleta, quae inter currerat iniquitate, usque in finem perseverantia deputatur: sicut exempla ostendunt Dauidis & Petri. Et hoc est quod canit Psaltes: Iustus sicsi ceciderit, non collidetur, quoniam Dominus suscipentat manum eius.
units.tr: Next, the minor premise of the argument is answered: even those who truly believe and are pious, and consequently elect, sometimes fall grievously from the confession and the Christian life. But such falls are partly not so much extinguished as put to sleep by the conversion of their faith; and partly that same faith is restored before this life ends, and the iniquity that intervened is blotted out, and perseverance is reckoned as lasting to the end. So the examples of David and Peter show. And this is what the psalmist sings: "Though the righteous fall, he shall not be cast down, for the Lord upholds his hand."

units.la: Obiiciuntur praeterea exhortationes sacris literis familiares, quae specie habent minarum, quales sunt: Tene quod habes, ne alius accipiat coronam tuam. Qui sibi videtur stare, videat ne cadat. Insitus es in populum Dei? time, nam si non permanseris, et tu extinderis. Haec & similia in incerto videntur ponere perseverantiam eorum ad quos dicuntur. Dicuntur autem ad omnes, etiam electos & pios.
units.tr: Moreover, exhortations familiar to Holy Scripture are objected to, which have the appearance of threats, such as: "Hold fast what you have, lest another take your crown." "Let him who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall." "Are you grafted into the people of God? Fear; for if you do not remain, you too will be cut off." These and similar sayings seem to make the perseverance of those to whom they are addressed uncertain. Yet they are addressed to all, the elect and the pious included.

units.la: Respondeo, tales exhortationes sacris literis visitatas esse, cum quia in coetu vocatorum multi sunt non perseveraturi: tum quia Deo visum est electos suos talibus adminiculis excitare & corroborare ad perseverandum, contra carnis securitatem. Sed longior hic non ero, quoniam infra de immutabilitate electionis plura de hoc agemus.
units.tr: I answer that such exhortations are customary in Holy Scripture, both because among the company of the called there are many who will not persevere, and because it has pleased God to rouse and strengthen his elect by such aids to persevere, against the security of the flesh. But I will not be longer here, since below we shall treat more of this in the discussion of the immutability of election.

units.la: CAPVT XVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVI.

units.la: De effectibus reprobationis.
units.tr: On the effects of reprobation.

units.la: Ceterum, sicut electionis effectus ństus est nō solum gratia illa qua in præ-senti iustificamur, atque ad recte viue-dum & in bono perseuerandum, adiu-uamur, verum etiam qua in futurum glorificabimur: Ita etiam reprobatio-nis Dei, qua ab æterno quosdam non e-ligedo reprobauit, effectus secundum duo consideratur: quorum alterum hic reprobis adhæret, alterû subsequetur eos in futuro. Sunt autem hæc, æterna danatio, & desertio, quæ & induratio & excæcatio, quibus iniustos iustus Deus vlciscitur. Hinc Fulgentius ait lib. 1. ad Monimū, circa finem: Bene malis interi-tus à Deo redditur, qui nunc iuste deserùtur, & post modum iuste torquebuntur. In talibus enim Deus iudicium suum desertione incoat, cruciatione consummat.
units.tr: Just as the effect of election is not only that grace by which we are justified in the present and helped to live rightly and persevere in good, but also that by which we shall be glorified in the future, so the effects of God's reprobation, by which from eternity he reprobated certain people by not choosing them, are considered in two respects. One of these clings to the reprobate here; the other will follow them into the future. These are eternal damnation and desertion, which is also hardening and blinding, by which the just God takes vengeance on the unjust. Hence Fulgentius says in book 1 to Monimus, near the end: It is well that death is rendered by God to the wicked, who are now justly forsaken and afterwards will be justly tormented. For in such people God begins his judgment with desertion and completes it with torment.

units.la: Sed scripturarum de his testificatio-nem audiamus. Matth. 25. manifeste o-stenditur à Deo non solum paratum regnum vbi lætentur boni, sed & igne æternum vbi crucientur mali. Bonis enim dicturus est, Venite benedicti patris mei, possidete regnũ vobis paratum ab æterno. Malis autem, abite maledicti in ignem æteræternum, qui paratus est Diabolo & angelis eius.
units.tr: But let us hear the testimony of Scripture on these matters. Matthew 25 clearly shows that God has prepared not only a kingdom where the good rejoice, but also eternal fire where the wicked are tormented. For he will say to the good, Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from eternity. But to the wicked, Depart, accursed, into the eternal fire, which is prepared for the devil and his angels.

units.la: Et capite 10. apud eundem Euangelistam: Nolite metuere qui occidunt corpus, animam autem non possunt occidere. Magis autem eum timete qui corpus & animam potest perdere in gehenna. 2.Pet.2. Novit Dominus pios e tentatione eripere: iniustos autem in diem iudicij puniendos seruare. Si igitur Dei opus est damnatio gehennæ, etiam quibus eam infligturus esset, ab æterno præscuit: hoc est, prædestina- uit. Prædestinatio enim eius præparatio est operum eius, quæ in æterna sua dispositione aut misericorditer aut iuste facturum se præscuit.
units.tr: And in chapter 10 of the same evangelist: Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Rather fear him who can destroy both body and soul in hell. 2 Peter 2: The Lord knows how to rescue the godly from temptation, and to keep the unjust for punishment on the day of judgment. If therefore the damnation of hell is the work of God, he foreknew from eternity also those whom he would inflict it on; that is, he predestined them. For his predestination is the preparation of his works, which in his eternal disposition he foreknew he would do either mercifully or justly.

units.la: Apocal. 20. libri aperti sunt, & iudicatum est de singulis secundum opera ipsorum: & qui non inuentus est in libro vitæ scriptus, coniectus est in stagnum ignis. Quid, quod reprobi vasa iræ dicuntur, & quidem coagmentata ad interitum? Vas enim iræ esse, ut explicat Augustinus, homi- nem qui propter bonum naturæ creatur, propter vitia supplicio destinatum esse. Et dicente Fulgentio, in hoc vasa iræ
units.tr: Revelation 20: The books were opened, and judgment was given on each one according to their works; and whoever was not found written in the book of life was cast into the lake of fire. What of the fact that the reprobate are called vessels of wrath, and indeed fitted together for destruction? For a vessel of wrath, as Augustine explains, is a man who is created on account of natural good but destined for punishment on account of his vices. And as Fulgentius says, in this

units.la: Fulgent. lib.1. & 2. ad Monimum.
units.tr: Fulgentius, books 1 and 2, to Monimus.

units.la: Epist. 105. irae Deus aptauit, ad quod praedestina-uit: hoc est, non ad peccatum, sed ad interitum propter peccatum. Interitus ergo pereuntium opus est Dei reprobantis, ac reprobationis proinde effectus.
units.tr: Letter 105. God fitted for wrath, for which he predestined: that is, not to sin, but to destruction on account of sin. The destruction of those who perish is therefore the work of God reprobating, and so an effect of reprobation.

units.la: At inquis: Perditio ipsis qui pereunt adscribenda est, sicut Hosea ait, Perditio tua ex te Israel, sed tantum in me auxilium tuum.
units.tr: But you say: the perdition is to be ascribed to those who perish, as Hosea says: Your destruction is from you, Israel; but your help is in me alone.

units.la: Verum id est, de culpa non de poena loquendo. Culpam enim perditionis in seipsis habent qui damnantur, sed poenam inferre eius est qui mundum iudicat, qui iniquitatem damnare nouit, non facere. Atque hic sensus est Prophetae, Deum non punire nisi propter peccata quae homines a seipsis habent: liberationem autem ab ipso manare gratis, non propter opera. Sicut & Paulus dicit: Stipendium peccati mors: donum autem Dei est vita aeterna in Christo Iesu Domino nostro.
units.tr: That is true, but it speaks of fault, not of punishment. For those who are condemned have the fault of their perdition in themselves; but to inflict punishment belongs to him who judges the world, who knows how to condemn iniquity, not to make it. And this is the sense of the prophet: that God punishes only on account of the sins which men have from themselves, while deliverance flows freely from him and not on account of works. As Paul also says: The wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.

units.la: Solent etiam opponi dicta, Mortem Deus non fecit: Invidia diaboli mors intrauit in mundum. Item, nolo mortem morientis. &c.
units.tr: The following sayings are also commonly raised as objections: God did not make death; through the envy of the devil death entered the world. Likewise, I do not desire the death of the dying, etc.

units.la: Sed hïc surda aure prætereundum non est, quod alibi mortem & vitam, bona & mala à Deo esse legimus. Quæ repugnantiæ spècies vt tollatur, sciendum est, mortem sicut & vitam, non tantum dupliciter, sed etiam tripliciter intelligi poîse. In primo namque homine & animam & carnem Deus creauit immortalem. At dum homo peccauit, anima obijt, & mors ista animæ, peccatum nempe, principium est & causa duplicis alterius mortis, corporalis, & infernalis. Primam & secundam sacræ literæ appellant. Mortem igitur animæ Deus non fecit, quia peccatum non fecit: sed autor eius est Diabolus per suggestionem peccati: & per consequens autor quoq; est aliarum mortis specierum, quæ ex peccato ortæ sunt, ratione nempe fomitis, non autem per potentiam retributionis, quemadmodum Deus. Distinctè Augustinus contra Iulian. lib. 7. cap. 7. Deceptor hominis causa mortis est Diabolus: quam non vt primus autor, sed vt peccati vltor, intulit Deus. Locum Ezechielis de animæ illa mor-
units.tr: But here we must not pass over with a deaf ear the fact that elsewhere we read that death and life, good and evil, come from God. To remove this kind of contradiction, it must be understood that death, like life, can be taken not only in two ways but even in three. For in the first man God created both soul and flesh immortal. But when man sinned, the soul died; and that death of the soul, namely sin, is the beginning and cause of the twofold other death, bodily and infernal. Sacred letters call the first and second death. Therefore God did not make the death of the soul, because he did not make sin; its author is the devil, through the suggestion of sin, and consequently he is also the author of the other kinds of death which arose from sin, namely by reason of the fomes, but not by the power of retribution, as God is. Augustine makes this distinction clearly: Against Julian, book 7, chapter 7: The deceiver is the cause of man's death, the devil; which death God brought in, not as its first author, but as the avenger of sin. Concerning that death of the soul in Ezekiel

units.la: te quidam accipiunt, vt Fulgentius: alij tamen ad poenam peccati referunt, adhibita distinctione voluntatis Dei, secretae & reuelatae. Sic Lutherus de seruo arbitrio cap. 109. Non vult mortem peccatoris, verbo scilicet: dum verbo salutis ad omnes venit, & sic omnes homines vult salvos fieri. Vult autem illam voluntate illa imperscrutabili. Quae voluntas, inquit ibidem ca. 107, non requirenda, sed cum reuerentia adoranda est, vt secretum diuina maiestatis longe remotissimum. Item, non vult morte morientis per se, & quatenus destructio est; sed quatenus poena est: quoniam perditione viuorum non delectatur Dominus, vt scriptum est. Vltor autem est praeuaricatorum.
units.tr: some take it, as Fulgentius does; others, however, refer it to the punishment of sin, with a distinction between God's secret will and his revealed will. So Luther, On the Bondage of the Will, ch. 109: He does not will the death of a sinner, that is, in word: while by the word of salvation he comes to all, and so wills all men to be saved. But he wills it by that inscrutable will. He says in the same place, ch. 107: This will is not to be inquired into, but adored with reverence, as the most remote secret of the divine majesty. Likewise, God does not will the death of the dying as such, insofar as it is destruction; but insofar as it is punishment, since the Lord takes no pleasure in the destruction of the living, as it is written. But he is the avenger of transgressors.

units.la: Iam ad desertionis, excaecationis, indurationis negocium quod attinet: vt pauca e multis testimonia proferam, legimus in sacris: quorum vult miseretur, & quos vult indurat. Electi assecuti sunt: reliqui autem occaluerunt, sicut scriptum est: Dedit eis Deus spiritum soporis, oculos vt non videant, & aures vt non audiant. Vide Prophetiam Iesaia 29. verf. 10. & cap. 6. Vade, & dic
units.tr: As for the matter of desertion, blinding and hardening, to bring forward a few of the many testimonies, we read in the sacred writings: He has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens. The elect obtained it, but the rest were hardened, as it is written: God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that they should not see, and ears that they should not hear. See the prophecy of Isaiah 29, verse 10, and chapter 6: Go, and say

units.la: Rom. 9. & 11. & dic filijs Israël: audiendo audietis, & non intelligetis, & videntes videbitis & non cernetis, obstina cor populi huius & aures eius aggrana, & oculos eius obline, ne forte videant oculis suis, & audiant auribus suis, & corde intelligant, quo conuertantur & sanem eos.
units.tr: Romans 9 and 11: and say to the children of Israel: Hearing you shall hear and shall not understand, and seeing you shall see and not perceive. Harden the heart of this people, make their ears heavy and shut their eyes, lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and be converted, and I heal them.

units.la: Quam Prophetiam adducens Iohannes, asserit Iudæos, licet signis multis conspectis, in Dominum non credidisse, & ne potuisse quidem credere: quòd excæcasset oculos eorum, & obdurasset corda eorum. Iisdem infidelibus Iudæis Dominus dicebat: Vos non creditis: non enim estis ex ouibus meis. Oues meæ vocem meam audiunt, & ego agnosco eas & sequuntur me. Idem discipulis suis, Vobis, inquit, datum est nosse mysteria regni cœlorum: aliis non est datum: propterea per parabolas loquor eis.
units.tr: Quoting this prophecy, John asserts that the Jews, although they had seen many signs, did not believe in the Lord, and could not even believe, because God had blinded their eyes and hardened their hearts. To these same unbelieving Jews the Lord said: You do not believe, for you are not of my sheep. My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me. To his disciples he said: To you, he says, it is given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven; to others it is not given; therefore I speak to them in parables.

units.la: Nec temere factum est, quod tot seculorum lapsu ante Christi manifestationem, gentibus salutiferæ doctrinæ lux non innotuit: sed Paulo teste Deus ille viuus, qui fecit cœlum & terram, præteritis ætatibus siuit gentes omnes suis ipsarum viis incedere: donec nimirum aduenien te tempore gratiæ,inuc- tus est ab iis,qui ipsum non quærebant. In Israële autem completum fuit quod idem Propheta ait: toto die expandi ma- num ad populum rebellem & contradicen- tem.
units.tr: Nor was it by chance that, through so many ages before the manifestation of Christ, the light of saving doctrine did not become known to the Gentiles. Rather, as Paul testifies, that living God who made heaven and earth allowed all the nations in past ages to walk in their own ways, until, the time of grace arriving, he was found by those who did not seek him. In Israel, however, was fulfilled what the same prophet says: All day long I have stretched out my hand to a rebellious and contradicting people.

units.la: Ex his perspicuum est, qui ad vitam ordinati non sunt, etiam à gratia fidei & conuersionis reijci,& in contumacia propria relinquì : dum vel audiendi verbi facultate priuatur, vel si audiant, non sic vocantur, quomodo eis aptum est vt sequantur. Loquimur autem nunc de totali,vt sic vocem,excæcatio- ne, quæ finalem impœnitentiam coniunctam habet: non autem de quauis particulari,quæ in prædestinatos etiam cadit, quos Deus subinde ante & post conuersione, permittit cadere in pec- cata, sic tamen vt omnia cooperentur ijs in salutem. Vius horum est, vt intelligamus quantæ agendæ sint gratiæ misericor- diæ Dei,qui in aliorum pœna quid alijs donet ostendit.
units.tr: From these things it is clear that those who are not ordained to life are also rejected from the grace of faith and conversion, and are left in their own obstinacy, either because they are deprived of the opportunity of hearing the word, or, if they hear, they are not called in such a way as would be fitting for them to follow. But we are now speaking of total blindness, as I may call it, which has final impenitence joined to it, and not of any particular blindness, which also falls upon the predestined, whom God from time to time, before and after conversion, permits to fall into sins, yet so that all things work together for their salvation. The use of this is that we understand how great thanks must be rendered to the mercy of God, who shows in the punishment of others what he grants to others.

units.la: CAPVT XVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVII.

units.la: Quomodo Deus dicatur indurare, excæcare.
units.tr: How God is said to harden and to blind.

units.la: RESTAT nunc vt videamus, qualiter Deo tribuatur excæcatio atque induratio impiorum. Nam nisi recte hoc intelligatur, Deus videbitur accusari iniustitiæ, & peccantes contrà excusari, secundū illud, quid adhuc succensset? Nam voluntati eius quis resistet?
units.tr: IT remains now that we see in what sense hardening and blinding of the wicked are attributed to God. For unless this is rightly understood, God will seem to be accused of injustice, and sinners on the other hand will be excused, according to that saying: "Why does he still find fault? For who resists his will?"

units.la: Nonnulli, vt scopulos istos declinent, interpretatur Deum indurare, permittendo duntaxat, videnturque non vno modo omnes permissionem istam accipere: alijs ad tolerantiam & lenitatê Dei eam referentibus: vt indurare dicatur, cùm non statim castigat peccantes; misereri autem cùm mox per afflictiones ad pœnitentiam inuitat: Alijs permissionem declarantibus hoc loco, gratiæ priuationem: vt indurare idem sit quod non mollire per gratiam.
units.tr: Some, to avoid these rocks, interpret God's hardening as merely permitting it. They seem to take this permission in more than one way. Some refer it to God's forbearance and gentleness, so that he is said to harden when he does not punish sinners at once, but to show mercy when he soon calls them to repentance through afflictions. Others understand permission here as the withdrawal of grace, so that to harden means the same as not to soften through grace.

units.la: Prior expositio ad Originem & Hieronymum ronymum ab Erasmo refertur. Sed validissimis argumetis confutatur Seruo arbitrio Lutheri cap. 139. & sequentibus. Illuc enim redit licentia ista interpretandi, vt noua & inaudita Grammatica confundantur omnia, vt cum Deus dicit, Ego indurabo cor Pharaonis, mutatis personis sic accipias, Pharao indurat se mea lenitate. Deus indurat cor nostrum, id est, nos ipsi induramus nos, Deo poenas differente. Ita Deum misereri iam non significat donare gratiam, remittere peccata, iustificare aut a malis liberare: sed contra significat inferre malum & castigare. Hoc nihil aliud est, quam ex misericordia iram facere, ex ira misericordiam, peruerso penitus loquendi visu. Quod si tum dicendus est Deus indurare cum benefacit & tolerat, misereri vero cum affligit & castigat: iam non Pharaonem Deus induraßi, sed contra miserrus esse eius dicendus erit. Quid enim omisit in affligendo, castigando, vocando ad poenitentiam Pharaone? Haec & alia multa ibi Lutherus. Augustinus etiam Iulianum Pelag. erroris arguit hoc nomine, quod indu-rationem ad patientiam Dei solummodo, non ad eius potentiam pertinere arbitraretur, quasi Deus non induret nisi patientem bonitatem præbendo, cum mala fiant. Quidefi inquit, quod quotidie dicimus: Ne nos inferas in tentationem? nisi vt no tradamur concupiscentiis nostris? An forte hoc a Deo petimus, vt non sit erga nos patiens benitas eius? Quis ista sapiat sanus? quia sic non eius inuocaremus misericordiam, sed potius iracundiam provocaremus.
units.tr: The former explanation is traced by Erasmus back to Origen and Jerome. But Luther refutes it with the strongest arguments in De servo arbitrio, cap. 139 and following. For this licence of interpretation leads to a new and unheard-of grammar in which everything is confused. Thus when God says, "I will harden the heart of Pharaoh," you change the persons and take it as, "Pharaoh hardens himself through my gentleness." God hardens our heart, that is, we harden ourselves while God defers his punishments. So God's showing mercy no longer means bestowing grace, forgiving sins, justifying, or freeing from evils; on the contrary, it means inflicting evil and chastising. This is nothing else than making wrath out of mercy and mercy out of wrath, in a wholly perverse way of speaking. But if God is to be said to harden when he does good and tolerates, and to show mercy when he afflicts and chastises, then God will not be said to have hardened Pharaoh, but rather to have been merciless toward him. For what did he leave undone in afflicting, chastising, and calling Pharaoh to repentance? Luther says these and many other things there. Augustine too accuses Julian the Pelagian of error on this point, because Julian thought hardening pertains only to God's patience and not to his power, as if God hardens only by offering patient goodness while evils are done. "What, then, is it," he says, "that we say daily: 'Lead us not into temptation'? Is it not that we not be given over to our lusts? Or do we perhaps ask God that his patient goodness toward us may not be? Who in his right mind would think this? For then we would not be invoking his mercy, but rather provoking his anger."

units.la: Plenius quiddam sentiunt, qui licet promissionis & ipsi hac in re meminerint, indurationem tamen accipiunt pro subtractione seu priuatione gratiæ. Et hoc est quod apud Aug. legitur: Indurare, excæcare, repellere Deus dicitur eum, quem mollire, illuminare, vocare noluerit. Nec enim obdurat Deus impertiendo malitiam, sed non impertiendo misericordiam. Item ad Simpl. lib. 1. cap. 2. Obduratio eius est nolle misereri, vt non ab illo irrogetur aliquid quo homo fit deterior, sed tantum quo melior melior sit, no irrogetur. Et mox, quibusdam peccantibus misericordiam iustificationis sua non largitur, & ob hoc dicitur peccantes quodam indurare: quia eorum no miseretur; non quia impellit ut peccent. In hanc sententiā de induratione etiam loquuntur Lomb. &
units.tr: Those who think more fully about the matter, though they too recall the promise in this regard, nevertheless take hardening to mean the withdrawal or privation of grace. This is what is read in Augustine: "God is said to harden, to blind, and to reject the one whom he has been unwilling to soften, enlighten, and call. For God does not harden by bestowing wickedness, but by not bestowing mercy." Likewise, to Simplicianus, book 1, chapter 2: "His hardening is his unwillingness to show mercy, so that nothing is inflicted by him by which a man becomes worse, but only that by which he might become better is not inflicted." And soon after: "To some sinners he does not grant the mercy of his justification, and for this reason they are said in a certain sense to be hardened: because he does not have mercy on them, not because he impels them to sin." Lombard and others speak of hardening in this same sense.

units.la: Etsi autem expositio isthæc tolerabilis est, idem tamen Aquinas exp.in 9. ad Rom. in dictum, quem vult indurat: ingenuè profitetur, aliquid amplius in hoc esse intelligendum; & addit, instinctu quodam homines moveri à Deo ad bonum vel malum: sed differenter. Ad bonum enim instigari hominē à Deo, directe & per se, tanquam ab autore boni; ad malum autem occasionaliter. Conferri possunt quę hac de re habet Lutherus de ser. arb. c.150. & 154. Et Brent. in 1. Sam.2. de filiis Eli, scribit in hæc verba: ut pro meritorum suorum dignitate punirentur, occulta sua potentia Dominus effecit, ut ad patris monitionem non respicerent, & perirent: nimirum intus operans, quod foris verbo suo prohibet. Atque hoc non est. si autorem sui causam esse malitiæ, sed est iustum inferre supplicium propter malitiam, &c. Hæc ille.
units.tr: Although this explanation is tolerable, Aquinas, in his exposition of Romans 9 on the words "whom he wills he hardens," frankly confesses that something more must be understood here. He adds that men are moved by God by a certain impulse to good or to evil, but in different ways: to good, God urges a man directly and through himself, as the author of good; to evil, only occasionally. What Luther says on this matter in De servo arbitrio, chapters 150 and 154, may be compared. Brenz, on 1 Samuel 2, on the sons of Eli, writes in these words: "That they might be punished in accordance with the dignity of their deeds, the Lord by his hidden power brought it about that they did not heed their father's admonition and perished, working inwardly what he forbids outwardly by his word. And this does not make him the author of their malice; it is just to inflict punishment for malice, and so on." So he writes.

units.la: In primis autem Aug. de grat. & lib. arb. cap. 21. multis probat ac declarat Deum in cordibus etiam malorum hominum agore sicut vult, reddendo eis secundum merita ipsorum. Sic Deus operatus est inquit, in corde Amasiæ (cui iuste vtique irascebatur propter Idololatriam) vt admonitionem salubrem non audiret, sed ea contempta iret in bellum, vbi cum suo exercitu caderet. Et in Psalmis de Ægyptiis dicitur, quid eis Deus fecerit. Conuertit cor eorum, vt odissent populum eius, & dolum machinarentur seruis eius. Ex his & talibus testimoniis diuinorum elogiorum, concludit postea, operari Deum in cordibus hominum ad inclinandas eorum voluntates quocunque voluerit, siue ad bonum, pro sua misericordia, siue ad malum, pro meritis eorum, iudicio vtique suo, aliquando aperto, aliquando occulto, semper autem iusto.
units.tr: Above all, Augustine in De gratia et libero arbitrio, chapter 21, proves and declares at length that God works in the hearts even of wicked men as he wills, repaying them according to their merits. Thus God, he says, worked in the heart of Amaziah (with whom he was justly angry because of idolatry), so that he would not hear a salutary admonition, but, scorning it, went to war, where he fell with his army. And in the Psalms it is said of the Egyptians what God did to them: "He turned their heart to hate his people, and to plot deceit against his servants." From these and similar testimonies of the divine sayings, Augustine afterwards concludes that God works in the hearts of men to incline their wills wherever he wills, whether to good, out of his mercy, or to evil, according to their merits, by his judgment, which is sometimes open, sometimes hidden, but always just.

units.la: Similiter contra Iulianum 5. cap. 5.
units.tr: Similarly, against Julian, book 5, chapter 5.

units.la: Multa, inquit,commemorare possemus, qui-bus liquidò appareat, occulto iudicio Dei fieri peruersitatem cordis ut verum no audiatur, & inde peccetur, in praecedentis poenam pec-cati. Commemorat autem haec inter alia: Ad Rom. 1. propter hoc (nem pein compensationem erroris ipsorum) tra-didit eos Deus in passiones ignominiae, & in mentem reprobam, ut facerent quae minime conueniebat, oppleti omni iniustitia, fornica-tione, improbitate, auaritia, &c. 2. ad Thes. 2. propterea quod dilectionem veritatis non receperunt, ut salui fierent, mittit illis Deus efficaciam erroris, ut credant mendacio. Isa. 19. Miscuit eis spiritum erroris, & seduxe-runt Aegyptum. Et cap. 65. Quid errare fecisti nos Domine a via tua? obtudisti corda nostra, ut non timeremus te? 1. Reg. 22. Iussu & iudicio Dei exit spiritus mendax ad se-ducendum Achab um per Pseudoprophetas.
units.tr: "We could recall many things," he says, "by which it clearly appears that through God's hidden judgment a perversity of heart comes about, so that the truth is not heard, and from this men sin, as punishment for a preceding sin." Among other things he recalls this: Romans 1: "For this reason (namely, as recompense for their error) God gave them up to shameful passions, and to a reprobate mind, to do what was not fitting, filled with all injustice, fornication, wickedness, greed," and so on. 2 Thessalonians 2: "Because they did not receive the love of the truth so as to be saved, God sends them the working of error, so that they believe a lie." Isaiah 19: "He has mingled a spirit of error among them, and they have led Egypt astray." And chapter 65: "Why, Lord, have you made us err from your way? You have hardened our hearts, so that we do not fear you?" 1 Kings 22: "By the command and judgment of God a lying spirit went out to seduce Ahab through the false prophets."

units.la: Facit haec miris & ineffabilibus mo-dis, inquit Augustinus, qui nouit iusta iudi-cia sua non solum in corporibus homi-num, sed etiam in ipsis cordibus opera-ri; qui non facit voluntates malas, sed vi-tur eis prout voluerit, cum aliquid mali iniquè velle non possit.
units.tr: "He who knows that his just judgments work not only in the bodies of men but also in their very hearts, does these things in wonderful and ineffable ways," says Augustine, "he who does not make evil wills, but uses them as he pleases, since he cannot unjustly will anything evil."

units.la: Cyprianus etiam serm.de Orat.Domin. in illud: Ne inducas nos in tentationem: seu, vt ipse legit: ne patiaris vos induci in tentationem, scribit aduersarium nihil conitra nos posse, nisi Deus antea permiserit, & potestas ipsi inde tribuatur: tribui autem potestatem malo aduersus nos dupliciter: vel ad poenam cum delinquimus, vel ad gloriam, cum probamur. Quod ipsum totidem penè verbis Augusti. noster expressit, de serm.Domini in monte lib. 2. Fiunt tentationes, inquit, per Satanam, non potestate eius, sed permissu Dei, ad homines aut pro suis peccatis puniendos, aut pro Domini misericordia probandos & exercendos.
units.tr: Cyprian too, in his sermon on the Lord's Prayer, on the words "Lead us not into temptation", or as he himself reads it, "Suffer not yourselves to be led into temptation," writes that the adversary can do nothing against us unless God has first permitted it and power has been granted to him. Power is granted to the evil one against us in two ways: either for punishment when we sin, or for glory when we are tested. Our Augustine expressed nearly the same thing in almost the same words, in On the Sermon of the Lord on the Mount, book 2: "Temptations come about through Satan, not by his power but by God's permission, either to punish men for their sins or to test and exercise them for the Lord's mercy."

units.la: Ex his ergo omnibus vtcunque cernere est, indurationē, cum Deo inscriptus tribuitur, non solum permissionem, sed diuinae quoque irae operationem significare: siquidem vt res externas taceam, quae ad indurationem reproborum faciunt, Satan ipse, qui efficax est in filiis cōtumaciae, ita est in potestate Dei, vt nō nisi eius imperio agat. Illud autem diligenter notandum, siue deferendo, siue alio quocunque explicabili vel inexplicabili modo, Deus summe bonus & ineffabiliter iustus, huiusmodi iudicia exerceat, non autorem sed vltorem esse criminum, dum peccatis peccata punit. Quaerimus namque meritum misericordiæ, reflexe Augustus nec inuenimus: quia nullu est, ne gratia euacuetur, si non gratis donatur sed meritis redditur. Quaerimus autem meritum obduratonis, & inuenimus. Merito namque peccati vniuersa massa damnata est originaliter: & crescente aetate crescit iniuper malitia per propriam voluntatem, eoque & damnatio. Ideo traditionem in desideria mala, efficaciamque erroris, & alia id genus, scripturæ commemorant tanquam flagella iræ diuinæ, & iustam mercedis retributionem.
units.tr: From all these things, then, it can be discerned in some measure that hardening, when it is ascribed to God, signifies not only permission but also an operation of divine wrath. For, to say nothing of external things that contribute to the hardening of the reprobate, Satan himself, who is effective in the sons of disobedience, is so much in God's power that he acts only by God's command. But it must be carefully noted that whether God executes such judgments by permitting, or by some other explicable or inexplicable manner, he, being supremely good and ineffably just, is not the author but the avenger of crimes, punishing sins with sins. "For we seek the merit of mercy, as Augustine reflects, and we do not find it: because there is none, lest grace be emptied if it is not given freely but repaid as merit. But we seek the merit of hardening, and we find it." For by the merit of sin the whole mass was condemned in its origin, and as age grows, malice grows besides through one's own will, and with it damnation. Therefore Scripture recalls the handing over to evil desires, the efficacy of error, and other things of that kind, as scourges of divine wrath and a just repayment of wages.

units.la: Dat, duritiam cordis Deus operatur, inquis. Duritia autem cordis peccatum est: quid enim aliud est, quam resistere Dei, mandato, vt Stephanus Iudæis exprobrabat? Ergo Deus peccatum operatur.
units.tr: Granted, you say, that God works hardness of heart. But hardness of heart is sin: what else is it than to resist the command of God, as Stephen reproached the Jews? Therefore God works sin.

units.la: Resp. 1. Duritiem, cordis, vt dictu est, Deus non operatur malitiam instil-lando, sed deferendo, ac tradendo de-sideriis cordis, adeoque ipsi Satanæ.
units.tr: Answer, first: as has been said, God does not work hardness of heart by instilling malice, but by abandoning and handing over the heart to its own desires, and so to Satan himself.

units.la: II. Fallacia est accidentis in Mi-nore. Etenim, vt docet Auguft. contra Iul. Pelag. duritia cordis, vt multa alia, trifariam considerari potest: nimirum quatenus peccatum; quatenus præce-dentium peccatorum pœna: & quate-nus causa peccatorum sequetium, cum videlicet cæci cordis errore mali ali-quid committitur. Atque hi diuersi re-spectus in vno eodémque opere con-currunt per accidens. Quatenus ergo peccatu est durities de qua loquimur, hominis & diaboli opus est: Dei autem non nisi qua pœna est. Autor enim est omnis pœnæ peccati, quæcunq; illa sit: quia omnis pœna peccati, qua talis, bona est, quoniam iusta. Peccati autem autor Deus non est, quia malum est. Deus autem summe bonus & iustus, mali & iniusti autor esse nequit, sicut scriptum est: Non Deus volens iniquita-tem tu es. Et Clemens Alexandrinus lib.5. Stromatum ex poeta citat: Iupiter
units.tr: Second, the minor premise commits the fallacy of accident. For, as Augustine teaches against Julian the Pelagian, hardness of heart, like many other things, can be considered in three ways: (1) as sin; (2) as the punishment of earlier sins; and (3) as the cause of later sins, namely when, through the blind error of the heart, some wrong is committed. These different respects come together accidentally in one and the same work. Insofar, then, as the hardness we are speaking of is a sin, it is the work of man and of the devil; it is God's work only insofar as it is a punishment. For God is the author of every punishment of sin, whatever it may be, because every punishment of sin, as such, is good, since it is just. But God is not the author of sin, because sin is evil. Now God, who is supremely good and just, cannot be the author of evil and injustice, as it is written: For you are not a God who wills iniquity. And Clement of Alexandria, in the fifth book of the Stromata, cites a poet: Jupiter, ruler of the gods, who looks on all things, is not the cause of evils for mortals.

units.la: Rr regnator superum qui omnia aspicit, non est mortalibus causa malorum.
units.tr: Jupiter, ruler of the gods, who looks on all things, is not the cause of evils for mortals.

units.la: Hinc & alterius pendet solutio objecta: quod Deo homines indurante, ij qui peccant reddi videantur excusabiles. Voluntati enim eius quis resistet?
units.tr: The solution of the other objection also hangs on this: it is said that when God hardens men, those who sin seem to be made excusable. For who can resist his will?

units.la: Sed duplici de causa nullus defensionis aut tergiuersationis locus relinquitur induratis. 1. Quia meritum indurationis in ipsis haeret, vt vidimus. 11. Ipsimet scientes ac volentes, contra praeceptum Dei cor suum obfirmant, & seipsos indurant: quemadmodum de Pharaone non solum scribitur quod Deus eum induraret, sed etiam quod ipse cor suum aggrauauerit. Et Sapiens testatur, errare improbos, quod propria malitia eos excaecet. Quippe prae malitia oculos sibimetipsis claudunt ne videant, aureisque obturant ne audiat, instar aspidis surdae, quae aurem suam obturat, ne audiat vocem incantantium.
units.tr: But for two reasons no room for defence or evasion is left to the hardened. First, because the merit of the hardening clings to them themselves, as we have seen. Second, knowing and willing it themselves, they harden their own heart against the command of God and harden themselves; just as it is written of Pharaoh that not only did God harden him, but also that he himself made his heart heavy. And the Wise Man testifies that the wicked err because their own malice blinds them. Indeed, through malice they shut their eyes so that they will not see, and stop their ears so that they will not hear, like the deaf adder, which stops its ear so that it does not hear the voice of the charmers.

units.la: CAPVT XVIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVIII.

units.la: An etiam reproborum infidelitatem, & peccata in genere Deus prædestinarit.
units.tr: Whether God also predestined the unbelief and sins of the reprobate in general.

units.la: ATQVE hæc de effectibus reprobationis. Quæri autem præterea hîc soletnum reprobi, sicut ad damnationem pro peccatis luendam prædestinati dicuntur, ita etiam ad ipsa peccata, infidelitate & alia, quibus damnationem sibi attrahunt, prædestinati sint, nec ne? Et generatim, an quemquâ ad peccandum Deus prædestinauerit?
units.tr: And so much for the effects of reprobation. But here it is customarily asked further whether the reprobate, just as they are predestined to pay the penalty of damnation for their sins, are also predestined to the sins themselves, such as unbelief and the others by which they draw damnation upon themselves, or not. And more generally, whether God has predestined anyone to sin.

units.la: Nonnulli sanè non verentur id affirmare, tanquam veritati non repugnâs nec inconueniens. Cuius sententiæ est Anselmus Episc. Cătuariensis, qui claruit anno 1060. Is enim lib. de Concord. grat. & lib. arb. indubitanter statuit, prædestinationem non solùm bonorum esse, sed malorum etiâ posse dici quadantenus: eò quòd mala non fiant nisi Deus permittat. Vnde hoc modo, inquit, non est inconueniens Deum prædestinasse mala, dum malos & eorum opera mala non corrigit, sed bona specialiter præscire & prædestinare. nare dicitur, quia in illis facit quod sunt, & quod bona sunt: in malis autem non nisi quod sunt essentialiter, non autem quod mala sunt.
units.tr: Some indeed do not hesitate to affirm this, as though it were neither contrary to truth nor unfitting. Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury, who flourished in 1060, holds this opinion. In his book On the Agreement of Grace and Free Will, he confidently states that predestination can be called, in a certain sense, not only of good things but also of evil things, because evil things do not come about unless God permits them. "In this way," he says, "it is not unfitting that God has predestined evil things, since he does not correct evil men and their evil deeds, but specifically foreknows and predestines good things. He is said to predestine them because in them he makes what they are and that they are good; but in evil things he does only what they are in essence, not that they are evil."

units.la: Contra Fulgentius lib. 1. ad Monim (vbi copiose & ex professo quæstionem hanc tractat) definit, Deum bonum & iustum præscius esse quidem peccata hominum, quia nihil eum latere potuit futurorum, non tamen quemquam prædestinasse ad peccandum. Sententiam hanc ex definitione prædestinationis confirmat, quæ secundum ipsum nil aliud est quam præparatio operum Dei: seu futuri divini operis dispositio, misericors & iusta. Cùm igitur ad opus Dei non pertineat iniquitas, quam punire ille nouit, non facere; sequetur ex definitione iam allata, hominem à Deo non prædestinatum ad patranda peccata. Affert & hanc rationem: quòd peccatores iniuste à Deo punirentur, si voluntate ipsius peccarent, tanquam ad peccandum ab ipso prædestinati. Ad hæc Augustinum & Prosperum citat eiusdem sententiæ.
units.tr: On the other side, Fulgentius (in the first book To Monimus, where he treats this question fully and expressly) declares that God, being good and just, indeed foreknows the sins of men, since nothing of future things could escape him, but has not predestined anyone to sin. He confirms this view from the definition of predestination, which according to him is nothing other than the preparation of God's works, or the merciful and just arrangement of the future divine work. Since iniquity, which God knows how to punish, is not part of God's work but rather its absence, it follows from the definition just given that man has not been predestined by God to commit sins. He also adduces this argument: if sinners were to sin by God's will, as if they had been predestined by him to sin, they would be punished unjustly by God. To these points he also cites Augustine and Prosper as holding the same opinion.

units.la: August. enim luculentissimo illo opere, quod scripsit de prædest. sanct-cap.10. inter Dei præscientiam & prædestinationē distinguens, inquit: Prædestinatio sine præscientia esse non potest: esse autem potest sine prædestinatione præscientia. Prædestinatione quippe Deus ea præscivit, quæ fuerat ipse facturus: Præscire autem potens est etiam quæ ipse non facit: sicut quæcunque peccata. Nam etsi quædam ita peccata sunt, ut pœnæ etiam sint peccatorum: hic tamen non peccatum Dei est, sed iudicium. Idem ad articulos sibi falsò impositos, art.7.8.9.& quibusdam sequentibus, cum Pelagiani doctrinam Prædestinationis odiosè traducerent, quasi Deum constitueret autorem criminum; detestandā & abominandam illam blasphemiam multis refellens, sic scribit: Prædestinatio Domini nunquam extra bonitatem, nunquam extra iustitiam est: universa enim via Domini misericordia & veritas. Adulteria autem matronarum, & corruptelas virginum, non instruere novit sancta diuinitas, sed damnare: nec disponere, sed punire. Ibidem, non catus ruentium, nec malignitatem iniquorum, neque iniquitates peccantium prædestinatio Dei Dei aut excitauit, aut suasit, aut impulit, sed plane praedestinauit iudicium suum, quo vnicuique retributurus est prout gesserit, siue bonum siue malum: quod iudicium futurum non esset, si homines Dei voluntate peccarent. Item, ad praevaricationem legis & perpetrationem qualiscunque peccati nulla est praedestinatio Dei. Scire sufficit, & ab illo esse quod statur, & non esse ab illo quod ruitur: nec est consequens, sicut putant qui talia obiicium, vt Deus quibus poenitentiam non dederit, resipiscentiam abstulerit; & quos non leuauerit, alliserit: cum aliud sit insontem in crimen cadere, quod alienum est a Deo; aliud criminoso veniam non dedisse, quod de peccatoris est merito. Rursum Hypog. 6. Inconcusse tenenda est huius disputationis regula, quae diuinis testimoniis claret, peccatores in malis propriis praescitos esse tantum; poenam autem iis esse praedestinatam. His Prosper vir eruditus & sanctus suffragatur, ad 14. obiect. Gallorum: infidelitas non credentium Euangelio, nequaquam ex Dei praedestinatione generatur. Bonorum enim Deus autor est, non malorum. Et respons. ad obiect. 15. Praescies tantummodo, non etiam praedestinauit Deus, quæ non ex ipso erant causam operationis habitura. In eandem sententiam definiit Conc. Arauf. can. vlt.
units.tr: For Augustine, in that most lucid work which he wrote On the Predestination of the Saints, distinguishing between God's foreknowledge and predestination in chapter 10, says: "Predestination cannot exist without foreknowledge, but foreknowledge can exist without predestination. For by predestination God foreknew those things which he himself was going to do; but he is able also to foreknow things which he does not himself do, such as all sins. For although some sins are such that they are also punishments of sins, nevertheless this is not God's sin but his judgment." The same Augustine, in answering the articles falsely imposed on him (articles 7, 8, 9 and some that follow), when the Pelagians slanderously represented the doctrine of predestination as though it made God the author of crimes, refuting that detestable and abominable blasphemy in many ways, writes thus: "The predestination of the Lord is never outside goodness, never outside justice: for all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth. But the adulteries of matrons and the corruptions of virgins holy divinity knows not how to instigate but to condemn, not to arrange but to punish." In the same place: "The predestination of God has neither stirred up, nor persuaded, nor impelled the falling of those who fall, the malice of the wicked, or the iniquities of sinners; but he has plainly predestined his judgment, by which he will repay each one according as he has acted, whether good or evil. That judgment would not be future if men sinned by the will of God." Likewise: "There is no predestination of God to the transgression of the law and to the commission of any kind of sin. It is enough to know that what stands is from him, and that what falls is not from him. Nor does it follow, as those who raise such objections think, that God, having not given repentance to some, has taken away their repentance, and that he has cast down those whom he has not raised up; since it is one thing for an innocent man to fall into crime, which is alien to God, and another for God not to have granted pardon to a criminal, which is due to the sinner's merit." Again, in the Hypognosticon, book 6: "The rule of this discussion must be held without wavering, a rule which is made clear by divine testimonies: that sinners are only foreknown in their own evils; but the punishment for them is predestined." Prosper, a learned and holy man, supports these points in answer to the fourteenth objection of the Gauls: "The unbelief of those who do not believe the Gospel is in no way produced by the predestination of God. For God is the author of good things, not of evil ones." And in his answer to the fifteenth objection: "God has only foreknown, and has not also predestined, those things which were not going to have their cause of operation from himself." The Council of Orange, in its last canon, defined in the same sense.

units.la: Ad Anselmum vero quod attinet, is non tam sensu quam verbis discrepat ab his quæ patres illi scribunt & sentiunt: quandoquidem voce prædestinationis generaliore significatione vsus est, pro præordinatione: vt prædestinare idem sit, quod statuere futurū esse. Iam autem nolente Domino nihil prorsus admittitur: sic tamen vt bona nouerimus fieri ipso adiuuante atque operante, mala permitti ipso deserente atque ordinante & dirigente ea in fines bonos, in quos ipsi visum est. Et hoc est quod etiam scribit Fulgetius, Deum autorem sane non esse malarum cogitationum, ordinatorem tamen esse malarum voluntatum, nec de malo opere cuiuslibet mali desinere bene facere.
units.tr: As for Anselm, he differs from those Fathers in what they write and think more in words than in sense, since he used the word predestination in a more general meaning, for pre-ordination, so that to predestine means the same as to decree that something will be. Now nothing at all is admitted apart from the will of the Lord; yet we must recognise that good things come about with his help and action, while evil things are permitted by his desertion and ordering, and he directs them to good ends, to which it has seemed good to him. This is also what Fulgentius writes: "God is certainly not the author of evil thoughts, yet he is the orderer of evil wills, and from an evil deed of any kind of evil man he does not cease to do good."

units.la: Dicet aliquis, electos prædestinatos non tantum ad gloriam, sed etiam ad iustitiam; ad fidem nempe, & bona opera. Ergo etiam reprobos prædestinatos videri tum ad culpam, tum ad pœnam.
units.tr: Someone will say that the elect are predestined not only to glory but also to righteousness, namely to faith and good works. Therefore the reprobate also seem to be predestined both to guilt and to punishment.

units.la: Resp. Electio & reprobatio conue-niunt quidem secùdum hoc, quòd sic-ut electio est præparatio gloriæ, ita re-probatio est præparatio pœnæ: diffe-rùt autem, quod electio importat præ-parationé fidei & operum bonorum, quibus peruenitur ad gloriam: sed re-probatio nō importat præparationem peccatorum, quibus peruenitur ad pœ-nam. Quare hoc tantum sequitur, cùm electi prædestinati sint ad fidem & con-uersionem, vt sancti sint & inculpati coram Deo; reprobos ad eam gratiam non esse prædestinatos.
units.tr: Answer: Election and reprobation agree indeed in this, that just as election is the preparation of glory, so reprobation is the preparation of punishment. But they differ in that election implies the preparation of faith and good works, by which one attains glory; whereas reprobation does not imply the preparation of sins, by which one attains punishment. Hence only this follows: since the elect are predestined to faith and conversion, so that they may be holy and blameless before God, the reprobate are not predestined to that grace.

units.la: At, obduratio reproborum diuini-tus prædestinata est. Ea autem pecca-tum est. Ergo aliquod peccatum præ-destinatum est diuinitus.
units.tr: But the hardening of the reprobate has been predestined by God. Yet this hardening is a sin. Therefore some sin has been predestined by God.

units.la: Ad hanc obiectionem respondeo iam liquet ex superioribus. Reproborum quippe induratio ita peccatum est, vt simul etiam sit pœna peccati: & eatc-nus, ad prædestinationem Dei perti-net, quia ab operatione eius non alie-na est. Quæ enim sic peccata sunt, vt si-mul etiam pœnæ sint peccatorum, in iis non peccatum, sed iudicium Dei prædestinationis diuinæ est, vt ex Augustino retuli.
units.tr: I answer this objection, as is already clear from what has gone before. The hardening of the reprobate is indeed a sin in such a way that it is at the same time also a punishment of sin; and so far it pertains to the predestination of God, because it is not alien from his operation. For those things which are sins in such a way that they are at the same time also punishments of sins, in them it is not sin but the judgment of God; and this is the divine predestination, as I have related from Augustine.

units.la: CAPVT XIX. Quod stabilis atque immota sit prædestinatio.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIX. That predestination is stable and unchangeable.

units.la: QVARTVM membrum totius huius tractationis, secundum partitionem inuitio propositam, est de prædestinationis immutabilitate. Vbi sane tenendum est, electionem & reprobationem, decretum videlicet Dei de hominibus aut misericorditer seruandis aut iuste puniendis, mutari haud posse, ita vt ex numero electorum quisquam pereat, aut contra aliquis seruetur ex parte reproborum: sed tam vni infallibiliter seruantur, quam alteri infallibiliter damnantur.
units.tr: The fourth part of this whole treatment, according to the division proposed above, concerns the immutability of predestination. Here it must certainly be held that election and reprobation, that is, God's decree concerning men either to be saved in mercy or to be justly punished, cannot be changed. So none of the number of the elect perishes, and conversely none of the reprobate is saved. Rather, the one group is infallibly saved and the other is infallibly condemned.

units.la: Hæc sententia multis confirmari potest, ac in primis sacrarum literarum testimonijs. Ioh. 6. ait Dominus: omne quod dat mihi pater, ad me veniet, & omnem qui venit ad me, non eiciam foras. Et
units.tr: This view can be confirmed by many arguments, and first of all by the testimonies of Holy Scripture. In John 6 the Lord says: All that the Father gives me will come to me, and whoever comes to me I will not cast out. And

units.la: Rr v cap.10.Oues mea vocem mea audiunt, & ego agnosco eas, & vita aeterna do eis, nec peribunt in aeternum, neq; rapiet eas quisquam e manu mea. Pater meus qui dedit mihi, maior omnibus est, neq; quisquam potest rapere eas ex manu patris mei. 1.Ioh. 2. E nobis egressi sunt, sed non erant ex nobis. Nam si fuissent, permansissent utique nobiscum. 2.Tim.2. Firmum stat fundamentum Dei, habens sigillum hoc, novit Dominus qui sint sui &c. Quomodo etiam Apocal.7. refertur de sigillo Dei viui, & certo numero obsignatorum in frontibus suis: seruorum, inquam, Dei quos ipsius gratia inter medias calamitatum procellas terra marique grassantes, illaesos atque intactos praestat. Sic postea eodem libro cap.13. & 17. Draconi & bestiae datur potestas seducendi vniuersam terram, exceptis tamen electis, quorum nomina scripta sunt in libro vitae a iactis mundi fundamentis. Electi ergo seduci nequeunt, saltem finaliter. Quemadmodum & Matth.24. dicitur: Surgent Pseudochristi & Pseudoprophetae, & edent signa magna & miracula, ita ut seducant si fieri possit, etiam electos. Quid voxilla Pauli ad Rom.8. Nouimus ijs qui diligunt Deum omnia cooperari in bonum, qui videlicet ex proposito vocati sunt? Omnia inquit, etiam mala, etiam peccata ipsa, teste Augustino. Et luculentissime id ipsum confirmans Apostolus subdit: Nam quos præsciuit, eos etiam prædestinauit conformes fieri imagini filij. Quos prædesti-nauit, eos etiam iustificauit: quos iustifica-uit, eos etiam glorificauit. Quid igitur dice-mus ad hæc? Si Deus pro nobis, quis contra nos? is quidè qui proprio filio non pepercit, sed pro nobis omnib. tradidit eum, qui non omnia nobis cum eo gratificabitur? Quis accusabit electos Dei? quis condemnabit? quis nos separabit a caritate Christi? Neque mors, neque vita &c. Idem cap.9. eiusdem Epistolæ: Fieri non potest vt excidat sermo Dei. Cuius vult miseretur, & quem vult indurat. Voluntati eius quis resistet? Et cap. II.
