Non abiecit Deus populum suum quem præcognouit: id quod ibidem exemplo temporum Eliæ & suæ ætatis Iudæorum ostendit: inter quos licet admodum degeneres & Euangelio aduersantes, Deus tamen reliquias secundum electionem gratiæ sibi reseruabat. Et subiungit sententiā memorabilem: quod requirit Israël, hoc non est consecutus, sed electi ād̄ecuti sunt, reliqui vero obcaluerunt. Et aliquanto post: Itaque quod ad Euangelium attinet, sunt inimici propter vos: quod ad electionem autem, diliguntur propter patres. Sine enim pœnitentia sunt dona & vocatio Dei: id est sine mutatione stabiliter fixa sunt, vt explicat Augustinus, qui etiam monet dictum hoc intelligendum, non de vocatione illa qua dictum est: Multi vocati &c. sed de illa qua vocantur electi.
units.tr: cap.10. My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, nor will anyone snatch them out of my hand. My Father, who gave them to me, is greater than all, and no one can snatch them out of my Father's hand. In 1 John 2: They went out from us, but they were not of us. For if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us. In 2 Timothy 2: The firm foundation of God stands, having this seal: The Lord knows those who are his, etc. Likewise in Revelation 7 mention is made of the seal of the living God and of a certain number sealed on their foreheads, namely the servants of God whom his grace preserves unharmed and untouched amid the storms of calamities that rage over land and sea. So later in the same book, in chapters 13 and 17, power is given to the dragon and the beast to seduce the whole earth, except for the elect, whose names are written in the book of life from the foundation of the world. Therefore the elect cannot be seduced, at least not finally. Just as in Matthew 24: False Christs and false prophets will arise, and will show great signs and wonders, so as to deceive, if it were possible, even the elect. What of Paul's words in Romans 8: We know that for those who love God all things work together for good, namely for those who have been called according to his purpose? All things, he says, even evil things, even sins themselves, as Augustine testifies. And the Apostle, confirming this very thing most clearly, adds: For whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son. Whom he predestined, these he also justified; whom he justified, these he also glorified. What then shall we say to these things? If God is for us, who is against us? He who did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how will he not also with him freely give us all things? Who will accuse God's elect? Who will condemn? Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Neither death nor life, etc. The same in chapter 9 of the same Epistle: It is not possible that the word of God should fail. He has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills. Who can resist his will? And in chapter 11: God has not cast away his people whom he foreknew. This he shows in the same place by the example of the times of Elijah and of the Jews of his own age, among whom, although very degenerate and opposed to the Gospel, God nevertheless kept a remnant for himself according to the election of grace. And he adds a memorable sentence: What Israel seeks, that it has not obtained, but the elect have obtained it, and the rest were hardened. And a little later: So, as far as the Gospel is concerned, they are enemies for your sake; but as far as election is concerned, they are beloved for the sake of the fathers. For the gifts and calling of God are without repentance, that is, they are fixed firmly without change, as Augustine explains. Augustine also warns that this saying must be understood not of that calling by which it is said: Many are called, etc., but of that by which the elect are called.

units.la: Secundo sententia propolita rationibus nititur efficacissimis. Nam quæ Deus ab æterno præscit, certò & infallibiliter eueniant necesse est, prout ab illo præsciuntur. Præscientia enim est cognitio rei futuræ: Quod autem futurum est, non potest non fieri. Iam vero in confesso est, Deum præscire qui seruandi, & qui damnandi sint. Ergo &c.
units.tr: Second, the proposition stated above rests on very strong arguments. For those things which God foreknows from eternity must necessarily come to pass with certainty and infallibility, just as they are foreknown by him. For foreknowledge is knowledge of a future thing, and what is future cannot fail to happen. Now it is agreed that God foreknows who are to be saved and who are to be condemned. Therefore, etc.

units.la: Præterea, decreta Dei immutabilia sunt. Electio autem & reprobatio, vt dictum est, sunt decreta Dei, misericorditer videlicet seruandi quos vult, iusteiusteque damnandi quos vult. Fieri igitur nequit, quin cum electio tum reprobatio firma sit atq; immutabilis, ita vt nec electi perire, nec reprobi seruari possint. De immutabilitate enim decretorum Dei dicitur: Triumphator in Israel non parcit, & poenitudine non flectitur. Neque enim homo est, vt poenitentia ducatur. Item, non est Deus quasi homo, vt mutetur, nec vt filius hominis, vt mutetur: dixit, & non faceret? locutus est, & non impleret? Et apud Ief. Dominus exercituum decreuit, & quis potest dissoluere? Manus Dei extenta est, & quis auertet eam? Et cofilium meum stabit, ac omnem voluntatem meam faciam.
units.tr: Moreover, the decrees of God are unchangeable. But election and reprobation, as has been said, are decrees of God: namely, that he will save in mercy whom he wills, and condemn justly whom he wills. It cannot therefore be that either election or reprobation is not firm and unchangeable, so that neither can the elect perish nor the reprobate be saved. For concerning the immutability of God's decrees it is said: The Triumphant One in Israel does not spare, and he is not turned by repentance; for he is not a man, that he should be moved to repent. Likewise: God is not like a man, that he should change, nor like a son of man, that he should change. Has he said and not done it? Has he spoken and not fulfilled it? And in Isaiah: The Lord of hosts has decreed, and who can annul it? His hand is stretched out, and who will turn it back? And my counsel will stand, and I will do all my pleasure.

units.la: Quod autem subinde quædam Deus denunciat & minatur, quæ tamen post ea non facit, exemplo Niniuitarum & Ezechiæ: sciendum est, in ijs scriptura loqui quantum ad naturam secundarum causarum attinet, vel alioquin cum conditione respiscentiæ & precum tacite subintellecta, vt Ierem. 18. eiusmodi explicantur: non autem quatum ad simplex & absolutum Dei decretum attinet. Quo sensu scite à Gregorio
units.tr: As for the fact that God sometimes announces and threatens certain things which he afterwards does not do, as in the example of the Ninevites and of Hezekiah, it must be understood that Scripture there speaks with respect to the nature of secondary causes, or else with the condition of repentance and tacit prayer understood; as Jeremiah 18 explains such passages. It is not to be understood with respect to the simple and absolute decree of God. In this sense Gregory has aptly said:

units.la: 1. Sam. 15. Num. 23. Ierem. 18. Item c. 4 5. gorio dictum est: Nouit Dominus mutare sententiam suam: sed nunquam nouit mutare consilium. Et ab Augustino: Deus nouit mutare sententiam, si nos mutemus vitam.
units.tr: 1 Sam. 15; Num. 23; Jer. 18; likewise chapters 4 and 5: as Gregory said: The Lord knows how to change his sentence, but never knows how to change his counsel. And Augustine: God knows how to change his sentence if we change our life.

units.la: Tertiò: Infallibilitatem prædestinationis exempla manifeste euincunt. Pharao, Sichon, & reges Cananæorum vna cum subditis, exitio destinati erat. Quid fit? indurantur corda eorum, vt pugnantes contra Israelem perirent propter peccata sua. Et expresse scribitur: a Domino fuit hoc vt induraret cor eorum in occursum belli cum Israel, quo disperderet eos. Sic filii Eli non audierunt vocem patris sui, quia Dominus destinârat eos occidere. Roboam non exaudiit populum, quia Domino visum erat ea ratione regnum scindere, & auferre posteritate à Salomonis. Absalon & omnis vir Israel spreto Achitophelis consilio bono, audierunt Husai: quia Dominus volebat destruere consilium Achitophel, vt plecteretur Absalon. Similiter de sermone Domini contra domum Achab, non cecidit quicquam super terram, fecitque Deus, quemadmodum modum locutus erat per seruum suum Eliam.
units.tr: Third, examples clearly prove the infallibility of predestination. Pharaoh, Sihon, and the kings of the Canaanites together with their subjects were destined for destruction. What happens? Their hearts are hardened, so that, fighting against Israel, they perish on account of their sins. And it is expressly written: It was from the Lord that he hardened their hearts to meet Israel in battle, so that he might destroy them. So the sons of Eli did not heed the voice of their father, because the Lord had determined to kill them. Rehoboam did not listen to the people, because it seemed good to the Lord in this way to split the kingdom and take it away from Solomon's posterity. Absalom and all the men of Israel, rejecting the good counsel of Ahithophel, listened to Hushai, because the Lord willed to overthrow the counsel of Ahithophel, so that Absalom would be punished. Similarly, concerning the word of the Lord against the house of Ahab, not one thing fell to the ground, and God did as he had spoken through his servant Elijah.

units.la: Ex altera parte, quàm mirabiliter Ioseph vs, fratribus exitium ipsi machinantibus in Ægyptum missus, & ad regni gubernationem euectus est, quò consilium Domini impleretur? Quid item coram hominibus insperatius regno Davidis? Ex omnibus tamen persecutionibus suis ad regni fastigiū emersit, & rexit populum prudentia manuum suarum, vt consilium Domini staret, dissipatis cogitationibus & consiliis populorum. Clara hæc sunt: sed illud sublimius quod de ipso Christo legimus. Aduersus eum Herodes & Pontius Pilatus, cum gentibus & populo Israël coacti fuere, vt facerent, quæcunque manus & consilium Domini prius definierant facienda. Cumque definito consilio & prouidentia Dei deditum accepissent, manibus sceleratis cruci affixum interemerunt, perfecerunntque omnia, quæ de eo scripserat Prophetæ, quantumuis aliud interim agentes. Quid Apostolus & doctor
units.tr: On the other hand, how wonderfully was Joseph, sent into Egypt when his brothers plotted his destruction, and raised to the government of the kingdom, so that the counsel of the Lord might be fulfilled! Likewise, what could be more unexpected in the eyes of men than the kingdom of David? Yet out of all his persecutions he rose to the summit of the kingdom, and ruled the people with the prudence of his hands, so that the counsel of the Lord might stand, the thoughts and counsels of the peoples being scattered. These things are clear; but more sublime is what we read of Christ himself. Herod and Pontius Pilate, together with the Gentiles and the people of Israel, were gathered against him, so that they might do whatever the hand and counsel of the Lord had determined beforehand should be done. And when they had received him, delivered up by the set counsel and foreknowledge of God, they killed him by fastening him to the cross with wicked hands, and they fulfilled everything that the prophets had written about him, although in the meantime they were doing something else. What of the Apostle and teacher of the Gentiles, who before he was called to the Gospel was a blasphemer, a persecutor and an insolent man, yet was called powerfully and miraculously, when it pleased God, who had set him apart from his mother's womb?

units.la: Ibid. ctor gentium? qui blasphemus prius erat & persecutor, & iniuriosus, quàm potenter & miraculose ad Euangelium vocatus fuit, quando placuit Deo, qui segregauerat eum ab utero matris? Et ut exemplis non tàm personarū, quàm populorum vtar, gentes quæ non sequabantur iustitiam, apprehenderunt eam, Dominusque inuentus est ab iis qui non quærebant eum, & conspicuus factus est iis, qui ipsum non interrogabant: Israël autem contradixit, & propriam studens iustitiam constituere, iustitiæ Dei subiectus non fuit. Nam electi assequuntur, reliqui indurantur, sicut scriptum est: Dedit eis spiritum sopo-ris, oculos ut non videant, & aures ut non audiant.
units.tr: Ibid. The teacher of the Gentiles? He was a blasphemer and persecutor, and an insolent man, before he was called to the Gospel, powerfully and miraculously, when it pleased God, who had set him apart from his mother's womb. And, to use examples not so much of persons as of peoples: the Gentiles, who did not pursue righteousness, laid hold of it; the Lord was found by those who did not seek him, and was made manifest to those who did not ask for him. But Israel, though it pursued the law of righteousness, did not attain to that law. Why? Because it pursued it not by faith but as if by works, and it stumbled at the stumbling stone. Yet Israel was not subject to the righteousness of God, because it wished to establish its own righteousness. For the elect obtain it, and the rest are hardened, as it is written: God has given them a spirit of stupor, eyes that they should not see, and ears that they should not hear.

units.la: Quarto, eadem doctrina de incommutabilitate diuinæ prædestinationis, passim ab Augustino in culcatur: ut de corrept. & grat. cap. 7. Electi rusi quisquam perit, fallitur Deus, & vitio humano vincitur; sed nemo eorum perit, quia non fallitur nec vlla re vincitur Deus. Loquitur autem de electis ad regnandum cum Christo.
units.tr: Fourthly, the same teaching about the immutability of divine predestination is inculcated everywhere by Augustine, in On Correction and Grace, chapter 7: None of the elect perishes; God is not deceived, nor is he overcome by human fault; but none of them perishes, because God is not deceived and is overcome by nothing. He is speaking, however, of the elect who are to reign with Christ.

units.la: Rom. 11. Christo, non quomodo electus erat Iudas ad opus cui congruebat. Et Re-sponf.ad artic.falsò impositos: Prædestinatio Dei,etsi apud nos incerta est, apud illum tamen qui fecit quæ futura sunt, incommutabilis permanet: nec quæ illuminat, excæcat, nec quæ ædificat, destruit, nec quæ plantauit, euellit. Sine enim pœnitentia sunt dona & vocatio Dei, & firmum stat fundamentum Dei, habens signaculum hoc, nouit Dominus qui sunt eius.
units.tr: Rom. 11. with Christ, not in the way that Judas was chosen for the work to which he was suited. And in the Response to Articles Falsely Imposed: The predestination of God, although it is uncertain to us, remains immutable with him who has made what is to come: it neither blinds those whom it enlightens, nor destroys those whom it builds up, nor uproots those whom it has planted. For the gifts and calling of God are without repentance, and the firm foundation of God stands, having this seal: the Lord knows those who are his.

units.la: Et pulcerrimè in Soliloquijs cap. 28. Omnes nos quasi panus menstruata, de massa corrupta & immunda venientes: mundas autem de nobis filijs hominum, tu qui solus es mundus eos, in quibus tibi complacuit habitare, quos sine eorum meritis prædestinasti ante mundum, & tibi elegisti in templum sanctum tuum, quorum nomina numerumque tu nosti, qui nequaquam possunt perire: quibus omnia cooperantur in bonum, etiam ipsa peccata. Cum enim cadunt, non collabuntur, quia tu supponis manum tuam, custodies omnia ossa eorum, ut unum ex eis non conteratur. Attamen mors peccatorum pessima; eorum, inquam, quos antequam faceres cœlum &c. & terram, secundum abyssum multam iudi-ciorum tuorum occultorum, semper autem iu-storum, praesciuisti ad mortem aeternam, quo-rum dinumeratio nominum & meritorum est apud te, qui numerum arena maris dinu-merasti, & dimensus es profundum abyssi: quos reliquisti in immunditiis suis, quibus omnia cooperantur in malum, & ipsa etiam oratio vertitur in peccatum, vt si vsque ad coelos etiam ascenderint, & inter sidera coeli collocauerint nidu suum, quasi sterquilinium in fine perdantur.
units.tr: And most beautifully, in the Soliloquies, chapter 28: We all come like a menstruous rag, from a corrupt and unclean mass; but the clean among us, the sons of men, you alone are clean, you who make clean those in whom it has pleased you to dwell, whom you predestined before the world without their merits, and chose for yourself as your holy temple, whose names and number you know, who can by no means perish; for whom all things work together for good, even their sins. For when they fall, they are not overthrown, because you put your hand under them, and you keep all their bones, so that not one of them is broken. Yet the death of sinners is most wretched, I mean of those whom you foreknew to eternal death, before you made heaven and earth, according to the deep abyss of your hidden judgments, which are always just; whose number and merits are recorded with you, who have numbered the sand of the sea and measured the depth of the abyss; whom you left in their uncleanness, for whom all things work together for evil, and even prayer itself is turned into sin, so that, even if they should climb up to the heavens and set their nest among the stars of heaven, they are destroyed at last like a dunghill.

units.la: Similiter autor de vocat. gent. lib. 2, c. 10. ait: Omnes adoptionis filij, non solum in eo tempore, quo iam existentes, vocati sunt, sed etiam priusquam mundus conderetur, electi sunt: in qua electione, quicquid hominum in Christo praecognitum non est, nulla eidem ratione sociabitur. Et mox: De plenitudine membrorum corporis Christi, praescientia Dei nihil perdit, & nullo detrimento minui potest summa praecognita, atque in Christo ante saecula aeterna praelecta.
units.tr: In a similar way the author, in On the Calling of the Gentiles, book 2, chapter 10, says: All the sons of adoption were chosen not only at the time when, already existing, they were called, but even before the world was founded. In that election, whatever of men is not foreknown in Christ shall have no part in it by any reason. And soon after: Of the fullness of the members of the body of Christ, the foreknowledge of God loses nothing, and the sum foreknown, and chosen beforehand in Christ before the eternal ages, can be diminished by no loss.

units.la: Lutheri hanc eandem esse doctrinam dubitare nemo potest, qui librum de seruo arb. legit, vbi inculcat, electos ververbo ædificari & meliores reddi, reprobos offendi & deteriores fieri: illos vitam suam corrigere per Spiritum Sanctum, hos incorrectos perire: & si errore aliquo teneantur electi, tamen ante mortem eos redire in viam: hoc necessarium esse, nec posse eos scandalizari finaliter. Et præf. ad Rom. scribit, stabilem esse sententiam atque immotam necessitatem divinæ prædestinationis: & hanc necessitatem dicit summe necessariam ad nostram salutem & consolationem; quoniam tam imbecilles simus in nobis, ut si in nostris manibus salus sita esset, paucissimi, aut nulli salvarentur. Diabolus enim omnes vincleret. Nunc vero cum hæc stabilis & certissima Dei sententia mutari non possit, nec ab ulla creatura cogi, spes nobis reliqua est tandem vincedi peccatum, quantumvis nunc in carne sæviat. Hæc ibi.
units.tr: No one who reads Luther's book On the Bondage of the Will can doubt that his teaching is the same, where he inculcates that the elect are built up and made better by the Word, while the reprobate are offended and made worse; that the former correct their life through the Holy Spirit, while the latter, uncorrected, perish; and that if the elect are held by some error, nevertheless before death they return to the way; this is necessary, and they cannot finally be scandalized. And in his preface to Romans he writes that the sentence of the necessity of divine predestination is stable and immovable; and he says that this necessity is supremely necessary for our salvation and consolation, since we are so feeble in ourselves that, if our salvation lay in our own hands, very few, or none, would be saved. For the devil would overcome all. But now, since this stable and most certain sentence of God cannot be changed, nor compelled by any creature, there remains for us the hope that sin will at last be conquered, however much it now rages in the flesh. Thus far there.

units.la: Ceterum ut catholicum est sentire quod prædestinatus electorum numerus nec augeri nec minui possit: ita in eo non acquiescere Pelagianum est, tenante Prospero. Quod & Hilarius Sf ij con-
units.tr: Just as it is Catholic to hold that the predestined number of the elect can neither be increased nor diminished, so not to rest content with this is Pelagian, as Prosper maintains.

units.la: cap. 4. cap. 5. cap. 11. confirmat, referens molestè tulisse Pe-lagianorum reliquias, quod ab ortho-doxis sic prædicarentur homines præ-destinati ad vtramque partè, vt ab aliisad alios nullos possit accedere.
units.tr: Hilary also confirms this (chap. 4, chap. 5, chap. 11), reporting that the remnants of the Pelagians took it badly that the orthodox preached men as predestined to both outcomes in such a way that no one could pass from some to others.

units.la: Ex his ergò liquet, ad vitam æternam prædestinatos non perire, ac ne posse quidem: ídque ob consilium volunta-tis Dei, quod à nulla creatura infringi retardarive potest. Liquet etiam, certum ac definitum esse saluădorum nu-merum apud Dominum, qui suos novit, & dinumerat arenam maris. Vnde August. de Corr. & grat. cap. 13. Prædestina-torum in regnum Dei ita certus est numerus, vt nec addatur eis quicquam, nec minuatur ex illis. Item ad Laur. cap. 29. Beatorum numerus, siue qui est, siue qui futurus est, in contemplatione eius est artificis, qui vocat ea quae non sunt, tanquam ea quae sunt, atque in mensura & numero & pondere cuncta disponit.
units.tr: From these things it is clear that those predestined to eternal life do not perish, and cannot even perish, and this because of the counsel of God's will, which no creature can break or hinder. It is also clear that the number of those to be saved is certain and fixed with the Lord, who knows his own and counts the sand of the sea. Whence Augustine, De correptione et gratia, chap. 13: The number of those predestined to the kingdom of God is so certain that nothing is added to them, nor is anything taken away from them. Likewise, in the letter to Laurentius, chap. 29: The number of the blessed, whether it already is or is yet to be, lies in the contemplation of that craftsman who calls things that are not as though they were, and arranges all things in measure and number and weight.

units.la: Quòd autem à nonnullis existimatur, numerus electorum tantus præcisè, quantus Dæmonum est, qui à societate angelica lapsi sunt, curiosum saneest. Melius Augustinus loco nunc citato: qui licet agnoscat hominum electos lapsis Angelis succedere ad restaurādam ciuitatem Dei, de numeri tamē æqualitate nihil pronunciat, imò in dubio reliquit, tanquam secretum Deo cognitum. Quid enim attinet cum periculo affirmare, quod sine periculo nescitur?
units.tr: But that some think the number of the elect is exactly as great as the number of the demons who fell from the angelic fellowship is certainly a curious notion. Augustine, in the place just cited, is better: although he acknowledges that the elect of men succeed the fallen angels for the restoration of the city of God, he pronounces nothing about the equality of the numbers, and indeed leaves it in doubt, as a secret known to God. For what good is it to affirm with danger what is not known without danger?

units.la: CAPVT XX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XX.

units.la: Eorum quæ contra immutabilitatem prædestinationis obyci solent, solutiones.
units.tr: Solutions of the objections commonly raised against the immutability of predestination.

units.la: Occurritur autem nobis hoc loco à nonnullis, quasi partes constituendo, quibus nec adiiciendū sit aliquid nec detrahendum, fenestra ad impietatem aperiatur: & fatalis necessitas inducatur: liberum hominis arbitrium negatur: verbi minissterium & preces tollātur: peccantes excusentur: &(quod absit) Deus tanquam peccati autor accusetur: hominesque ad desperationem solicitentur: & quæ huius generis sunt alia, quibus per aperta se iactât calumniatores astuti, & iactabant se olim Pelagia-
units.tr: But here we meet some people who, as if laying down premises from which nothing may be added or taken away, claim that a window is opened to impiety, that a fatal necessity is introduced, that the free choice of man is denied, that the ministry of the Word and prayer are done away with, that sinners are excused, and (God forbid) that God is accused as the author of sin, and that men are driven to despair; and whatever else of this kind there is, by which these cunning slanderers openly boast, as the Pelagians once boasted, according to Prosper and Hilary.

units.la: Sf iij lagialagiani, referentibus Prospero & Hilario. Deinde praeter consequentias istas rationis humanae male detortas, obiiciuntur & loca quaedam scripturae : sed frustra, vt videbimus.
units.tr: Besides these consequences, which are wrongly drawn from human reasoning, certain passages of Scripture are also objected. But they are in vain, as we shall see.

units.la: Principio ergo cauillantur, fenestram aperiri flagitiis, quia homines sic cogitent : Oportet fieri quod Deus praedestinauit; Ergo siue bene siue male egero, si ad regnum prædestinatus sum, seruabor; si non sum, damnabor.
units.tr: First, then, they carp that a window is opened to wickedness, because men reason thus: It must come to pass what God has predestined. Therefore, whether I act well or badly, if I am predestined to the kingdom, I shall be saved; if I am not, I shall be damned.

units.la: Respondeo. Quid homines imperiti, ne dicam Epicurei, cogitent aut non cogitent, nihil ad nos. Nam & doctrina gratiae multi abutuntur, vt cogitet, quia gratis iustificamur, peccatis indulgendum, vt gratia abundantior fiat: quorum iudicium iustum est, ait Paulus. Enimuero id abusui imputandum est, non ipsi doctrinae. Primum siquidem nostrum non est de occultis Dei ferre sententiam, sed sequenda est voluntas Dei in verbo reuelata. Ea autem iubet audire filium, agere poenitentiam, & credere Euangelio, vt seruemur. Sic Luther rus sceleratas istas voces retūdit, in Gen. 26. & alibi. Perinde enim est ac si quis didicat: Oportet fieri quod Deus constituit: igitur incerta & inanis est omnis cura animarum, omnisque labor noster.
units.tr: I answer. What foolish men, not to say Epicureans, think or do not think is nothing to us. For many also abuse the doctrine of grace, reasoning that since we are justified freely, sins are to be indulged so that grace may abound more; their condemnation is just, says Paul. Indeed, this abuse must be charged to the abusers, not to the doctrine itself. For, first, it is not for us to pass judgment on the secret things of God, but the will of God revealed in the Word must be followed. That will commands us to hear the Son, to repent, and to believe the Gospel, so that we may be saved. Thus Luther blunted those wicked words in Gen. 26 and elsewhere. For it is just as if someone were to learn: What God has decreed must come to pass; therefore all care of souls is uncertain and vain, and all our labour too.

units.la: Secundò, Prædestinatio non tantùm est finis, sed etiam mediorum ad finem: dicente Apostolo, quos prædestinauit, eos etiam vocauit, & quos vocauit, iustificauit, quos iustificauit, glorificauit: Item, elegit nos in ipso, vt essemus sancti & inculpati coram eo. Quocirca implicatio est contradictionis, qui prædestinatus sit, eum male posse velle & agere finaliter.
units.tr: Secondly, predestination is not only the end but also the means to the end, as the Apostle says: Whom he predestined, them he also called; and whom he called, them he also justified; and whom he justified, them he also glorified. Likewise: He chose us in him, that we should be holy and blameless before him. Hence it is a contradiction to say that someone who is predestined can will and act wickedly to the end.

units.la: Quin potius, vt scribit Augustt. qui ex numero electorum & prædestinatorum sunt, etiamsi pessimam ducant vitam ad tempus, tamen per Dei benignitatem ad pœnitentiam adducuntur, nec subtrahuntur huic vitæ in ipsa scelerum perpetratione: siquidem prædestinatio præparatio beneficiorum Dei est, quibus certissime liberatur quicunque liberatur. Nō ergo nos impedit ignaua illa ratio quæ dicitur, cui si pareamus nihil est omnino quod in vita agamus.
units.tr: Rather, as Augustine writes, those who are of the number of the elect and predestined, even if for a time they lead the worst of lives, are nevertheless brought by God's goodness to repentance, and are not taken from this life in the very commission of their sins; for predestination is the preparation of God's benefits, by which surely whoever is delivered is delivered. Therefore that idle reasoning, which is called the "lazy argument," does not hinder us; if we obeyed it, there would be nothing at all that we would do in life.

units.la: Enimvero, qui ita prædestinationē introducunt, vt media à fine seeparent, in eos torqueatur obiectio. Talis fuit quondam Prædestinatorum hæresis, qui, teste Sigeberto in Chron. sub Honorio Imp. & Zosimo Papa exorti, sic à doctrina vocabantur: quia prædestinationem & gratiam male intelligentes afferebant, nec pie viuentibus prodesse bonorum operum laborem, si à Deo ad mortem prædestinati foret, nec impiis obesse, quòd improbè viuant, si à Deo prædestinati fuerint ad vitā. Qua assertione & bonos à bonis auocabant, & malos ad mala prouocabant.
units.tr: Indeed, those who introduce predestination in such a way as to separate the means from the end, let the objection fall upon themselves. Such was once the heresy of the Predestinarians, who arose, as Sigebert reports in his Chronicle, under the emperor Honorius and Pope Zosimus, and were called by this name from their teaching: because, misunderstanding predestination and grace, they asserted that the labour of good works profits nothing for the godly living if they were predestined by God to death, nor does the wicked life of the impious harm them if they were predestined by God to life. By this assertion they both drew the good away from good and provoked the wicked to evil.

units.la: Altera Obiect. erat, Fatum induci, si ex stabili & immota prædestinationis sententia pendeant omnia, puta qui accepturi sint verbum, qui non: qui credituri, qui non credituri, eoque qui saluandi, qui damnandi.
units.tr: The second objection was: Fate is introduced if all things depend upon the stable and unmoved decree of predestination, namely who will receive the Word and who will not, who will believe and who will not, and so who are to be saved and who damned.

units.la: Resp. Non fatum, sed gratiæ diuinæ altitudinem prædicamus, qua electorum à massa perditionis discretio facta est, reliquis in eadem massa iusto iudicio Dei derelictis. Quòd autem ordo ille gratiæ & iudicij diuini immotus est, id nihil ad fatum: nisi forte, vt fatum tum à fando dictum intelligamus, id est, àloquendo. Non enim abnuere possumus semel locutum esse Deum, id est, immobiliter & incommutabiliter decreuisse quæ facturus est, sicut nouit incommutabiliter omnia quæ futura sunt. Qua ratione, vt scribit Augustinus de ciuit. Dei lib. 5. cap. 9. possumus à fando fatum appellare. Sed nomen hoc in alia re consueuit intelligi. Nam vsitata loquendi consuetudine per fatum intelligunt vim positionis siderū, sicut est cum quidam nascitur, vel concipitur, vel incoatur: & hoc est fatum Mathematicum. Multis etiam scriptoribus dicuntur ea fatalia, quæ præter Dei & hominum voluntatem cuiusdam ordinis necessitate contingunt; quemadmodum versiculus ille indicat: Quod fore paratum est: summum id excedit.
units.tr: Answer. We do not preach fate, but the height of divine grace, by which the election of some from the mass of perdition has been made, the rest being left in that same mass by the just judgment of God. That this order of grace and divine judgment is unmoved has nothing to do with fate, unless perhaps we understand fate as so called from fando, that is, from speaking. For we cannot deny that God has spoken once, that is, has decreed immovably and unchangeably what he will do, just as he knows unchangeably all things that are to come. In this sense, as Augustine writes in De civitate Dei, book 5, chapter 9, we may call it fate from fando. But this name is customarily understood in another sense. For in common usage by fate they mean the force of the positions of the stars, as when someone is born, or conceived, or begun; and this is mathematical fate. Among many writers also those things are called fatal which happen by a certain necessity of order, apart from the will of God and of men, as that verse indicates: What is destined to come about, the highest power surpasses.

units.la: Iouem. Et apud poetarum principem Homerum lamentatur Iupiter, quod carum sibi filiū Sarpedona, quem fata cogebant mori, è morte eripere non poterit. Similiter Neptunus, quòd reditum Vlyssis in patriam impedire non posset, vt Cyclopem filium vlciscere-tur: quoniam fatis decretum erat, vt Vlysses rediret in Ithacam. Et apud O-uidium idem Iupiter:
units.tr: Jupiter. And in the chief of the poets, Homer, Jupiter laments that he could not snatch from death his dear son Sarpedon, whom the fates compelled to die. Similarly Neptune, because he could not prevent the return of Ulysses to his homeland, so that he might avenge his son the Cyclops, since it had been decreed by the fates that Ulysses should return to Ithaca. And in Ovid the same Jupiter:

units.la: Tu sola insuperabile fatum,
units.tr: Do you think that you alone, a daughter, can move

units.la: Nata mouere putas? Et postea:
units.tr: the unconquerable fate? And afterwards:

units.la: Qua neq; concursum cœli, nec fulminis iram,
units.tr: Those things which neither the collision of heaven nor the wrath of the thunderbolt,

units.la: Nec metuunt vllas tuta atq; æterna ruinas.
units.tr: nor any ruins, safe and eternal, fear.

units.la: Stoicis quoque Philosophis fere opinio ita tribuitur: quanquam August. sententiam istorum mitigat, quod a Io-ue, quem summum Deum putabant, connexionem dixerint pendere fato-. Enimuero apud Aulum Gellium lib. 6. ca. 2. extat definitio fati Chrysippea, quod sit φυσικὴ ςυντάξις ἡ ἀπαραβάτος ςυμ-πλοκὴ τῶν ὅλων ἐξ ἀιδίου, τῶν ἑτέρων τοῖς ἑτέ-ροις ἑπακολουθούντων: sempiterna atque in-declinabilis rerum series, & quidem naturalis. Quomodo & Cicero opinio-nem assignat dicentium, omnia natu-rali colligatione conserte contexteque fieri.
units.tr: The opinion is also commonly ascribed to the Stoic philosophers, although Augustine softens their view, since they said that the connection of things depends on fate and on Jove, whom they thought the supreme God. Indeed, in Aulus Gellius, book 6, chapter 2, there is the Chrysippean definition of fate, that it is a natural arrangement, or an unbreakable interweaving of all things from eternity, one thing following upon another [φυσικὴ σύνταξις ἡ ἀπαράβατος συμπλοκὴ τῶν ὅλων ἐξ ἀϊδίου, τῶν ἑτέρων τοῖς ἑτέροις ἐπακολουθούντων]: an everlasting and unalterable series of things, and that a natural one. In the same way Cicero also ascribes to them the opinion that all things come about by a natural connection, woven together and interlaced.

units.la: Hæc deliria non modo Ecclesia, sed etiam Philosophia sanior reiicit atque dam-
units.tr: These follies are rejected and condemned not only by the Church but also by sounder philosophy,

units.la: Fatum Stoicum. De ciuit. Dei lib. 5. cap. 9.
units.tr: Stoic fate. De civitate Dei, book 5, chapter 9.

units.la: Cicer. de fato. damnat: tùm quia Deo suam libertatem ac omnipotentiam adimunt, tum quia ordinem & modum agedi in causis secundis diuina sapientia instituti abolent. Quippe causarum secundarum aliæ ad effectus certos ac definitos à Deo ordinatæ sunt, aliæ non sunt, sed suapte natura indifferenter sese habet ad hunc vel illum effectum progenerandum.
units.tr: Cicero, On Fate. both because they take away from God his liberty and omnipotence, and because they abolish the order and manner of acting in secondary causes, which divine wisdom has instituted. For some secondary causes are ordained by God to certain and defined effects, while others are not, but by their own nature stand indifferently towards producing this or that effect.

units.la: Alij fati nomine appellant omnium connexionem seriemque causarum à Dei pendentem voluntate: quam nos prouidentiam diuinā dicere solemus. Sic Anneus Seneca lib. Epist. 18. Ducunt volentem fata, nolentem trahunt, euidentissimè fata nominauit, quam ibidem dixerat summi patris voluntatem. Et Apuleius in dogmate Platonis, diuinam legem esse ait fatum, per quod ineuitabiles cogitationes Dei atque incepta compleantur. Ad eundem modum Boëthius multa de fato disseruit. Vult enim ordinem fatalem ex prouidentiæ diuinæ simplicitate pendere: vt prouidentia quidem sit diuina ratio cuncta dispodisponens, fatum vero, inhærens rebus mobilibus dispositio: hoc est, æternæ illius in Deo prouidentiæ executio. Ac cum ab immobilis prouidentiæ exor- dijs fatum proficiscatur, hinc fieri scri- bit, vt ipsum quoque immutabile sit.
units.tr: Others use the name of fate for the whole connection and series of causes, depending on the will of God, which we are accustomed to call divine providence. Thus Annaeus Seneca, in his letters, book 18: Fate leads the willing, and drags the unwilling, very clearly named fate what he had just called the will of the highest Father. And Apuleius in the doctrine of Plato says that fate is the divine law, through which the unavoidable thoughts and undertakings of God are fulfilled. In the same way Boethius discussed fate at length. For he holds that the order of fate depends on the simplicity of divine providence: so that providence is indeed the divine reason disposing all things, while fate is the disposition inhering in mobile things, that is, the execution of that eternal providence in God. And since fate proceeds from the unmoved origins of providence, he writes that from this it follows that fate itself is also unchangeable.

units.la: Cum talibus, si Augustino credimus, de verbi controuersia non magnopere laborandum atque certandū est: quandoquidem ipsum causarum ordinem, quo fit omne quod fit, summi Dei voluntati & potestati tribuunt, qui optime & veracissimè creditur, & cuncta scire antequam fiant, & nihil inordinatum relinquere, suntque ab eo omnes potestates, quamuis ab illo nō sint omnes voluntates. Malæ quippe voluntates ab illo non sunt, quoniam contra naturam sunt, quæ ab illo est.
units.tr: With such people, if we believe Augustine, there is no great need to labour and contend over the word, since they attribute the very order of causes, by which everything that happens comes about, to the will and power of the supreme God, who is rightly and most truly believed to know all things before they come to pass and to leave nothing disordered, and all powers are from him, although not all wills are from him. For evil wills are not from him, since they are contrary to the nature which is from him.

units.la: Quoniam tamen de diuinis ad regulam pietatis loquendū est, præstat nos à fati nomine abstinere, sicut pulcrè Augustinus ibidem monet cap.1. Prorsus diuina prouidentia regna constituuntur humana; quæ si propter ea fato quisquam tribuit, buit,quia ipsam Dei voluntatem velpotesta-tem fati nomine appellat, sententiam teneat, linguam corrigat.
units.tr: Since, however, we must speak of divine matters by the rule of piety, it is better for us to abstain from the word "fate", as Augustine rightly warns in the same place, chapter 1: Human kingdoms are indeed established by divine providence; if anyone on that account attributes them to fate, because he calls the will or power of God by the name of fate, let him keep his opinion but correct his tongue.

units.la: Id verò impium atque sacrilegum est, quod ordinem illum causarum sibi hærentium, qui præscieti & disponenti Deo certus est, redarguere nonnulli conantur: qui eò tandem delabantur necesse est, vt & Dei præscientiam, & omnem Prophetiam luce clariorem, negent, exemplo Ciceronis 2. de Diuinat. Nam si præscita sunt omnia futura, hoc ordine euenient, quo futura esse præscita sunt. Et si hoc ordine eueniét, certus est ordo rerum præscienti Deo. Si autem certus est ordo rerum, certus etiam est ordo causarum. Non enim aliquid fieri potest, quod non aliqua causa efficiens præcesserit.
units.tr: It is impious and sacrilegious indeed that some try to refute that chain of connected causes, which is certain to God who foreknows and disposes all things; and they must in the end come to deny both God's foreknowledge and all prophecy, which is clearer than light, following the example of Cicero, De divinatione book 2. For if all future things are foreknown, they will come about in the order in which they have been foreknown to be future. And if they will come about in this order, the order of things is certain to God who foreknows. But if the order of things is certain, the order of causes is also certain. For nothing can happen that was not preceded by some efficient cause.

units.la: Sed in hac hærentium sibi serie cau-arum, est ne vlla liberi nostri arbitrij libertas? An ipsos quoque humanorum motus animorum prædestinationis catena constringit?
units.tr: But in this unbroken chain of causes, is there any liberty of our free choice at all? Or does the chain of predestination also bind the very motions of human minds?

units.la: Respondeo, triplex est libertas, secundum vulgatam distinctionem: li-berbertas à coactione, à peccato, & à miseria. Ex his tribus, libertas à coactione inamissibilis voluntatis est proprietas, vt ait Bernhardus: vt videlicet quicquid vult, siue bonum, per gratiam Dei: siue malum, per naturam suam, id semper libere, hoc est, spontaneo motu, & minime coacta velit. Agimus quidem multa inuiti & coacti: at ipsa tamen volutas nihil vellevel eligere potest inuita & coacta; quoniam si coacta vellet, nolens vellet: quod implicat contradictionem. Ceteroquin libero arbitrio, vt est apud Augustinum male vtens homo, & se perdidit, ac ipsum, ac per hoc ad peccandum liber est, qui peccati seruus est: ad iuste autem faciendum liber non est, nisi à peccato liberatus, seruus ceperit esse iustitiae.
units.tr: I answer: there is a threefold liberty, according to the common distinction: liberty from coercion, from sin, and from misery. Of these three, liberty from coercion is a property of the unlosable will, as Bernard says: namely, that whatever it wills, whether good through the grace of God or evil through its own nature, it always wills freely, that is, by spontaneous motion, and not at all under compulsion. We indeed do many things unwillingly and under compulsion; but the will itself can will or choose nothing unwillingly and under compulsion, since if it willed under compulsion, it would be willing while unwilling, which implies a contradiction. Otherwise, as Augustine says, man, misusing free choice, has lost both himself and it, and so he is free to sin, though he is the slave of sin; but he is not free to do what is right unless, set free from sin, he has begun to be a slave of righteousness.

units.la: Adhæc, si liberum intelligitur quod nulli subiicitur, nec aliunde dependet aut determinatum est, eo sensu haud dubitandum est, nullam esse posse humanae voluntatis libertatem, sed omnia fieri necessitate, prout Deus præscuit, & agit consilio & virtute infallibili: bili; sicut Lutherus cap. 160. de feruo arb. & paßim eo libro inculcat. Nam vt cæteræ res, ita electiones voluntatum; angelorum & hominum, prouidentiæ Dei subduntur, in quo viuimus, sumus, & mouemur: quisque cor regis quocunque vult inclinat.
units.tr: Besides, if that is understood as free which is subject to no one, depends on nothing else, and is not determined, then in that sense there is no doubt that there can be no freedom of the human will at all, but everything happens by necessity, as God foreknew, and he acts by counsel and infallible power; as Luther insists in chapter 160 of De servo arbitrio and throughout that book. For, like other things, the choices of the wills of angels and men are subject to the providence of God, in whom we live, move, and have our being; he inclines the heart of the king wherever he wills.

units.la: Dicit quidem Gregorius Nyssenus, libro quem de homine fecit: Prouidentiam esse eorum quæ non sunt in nobis: Et Damascenus lib.2. Orth. fidei scribit, quod ea quæ in nobis sunt, Deus præscit tantum, non prædeterminet. Verum ista periculose dicuntur; nec nisi magna cautione admitti debent aut possunt: quemadmodum & Thomas admonet contra gentiles lib. 2. cap. 90. Augustinus melius: Omnia Dei voluntati subdita sunt, etiam voluntates omnes, quia non habent potestatem, nisi quam ille concedit.
units.tr: Gregory of Nyssa indeed says, in the book he wrote on man: "Providence is of those things which are not in us." And Damascene writes in book 2 of De orthodoxa fide that "God foreknows, but does not predetermine, the things which are in us." But these statements are dangerous, and they ought not to be admitted, nor can they be, except with great caution; as Thomas also warns in Contra gentiles book 2, chapter 90. Augustine puts it better: "All things are subject to the will of God, even all wills, because they have no power except what he grants."

units.la: At inquies, quod à Deo determinatum est, necessario ita euenit vt determinatum est. Actiones autem & motus animorum humanorum à Deo determinati sunt. Necessario igitur ita eueniunt: & vi consequentis nulla in ijs est arbitrij nostri libertas.
units.tr: But you will object: "What has been determined by God necessarily happens as it has been determined. The actions and motions of human minds have been determined by God. Therefore they necessarily happen so, and by force of the consequence there is no liberty of our choice in them."

units.la: Syllogismo hoc concesso negatur illatio. Discernendum enim est inter necessitatem coactionis & immutabilitatis. Illa externo tantum principio violenter mouet: hæc necessitatem quidem causis secundis, vt hoc aut illud efficiant, eoque & effectis vt ita eueniant, imponit; attamen naturas rerum non tollit, sed confirmat potius. Proinde, licet Dei respectu omnia infallibiliter præuidentis, & immutabiliter præordinatis, necessario, i. infallibiliter & incommutabiliter, omnia eueniat: respectu tamen secundarum causarum, earum videlicet quæ sua natura ad certos effectus definitæ non sunt, vt sunt quælibet angelorum & hominum voluntates, multa fiunt contingenter & per electionem. Ac notandum, cum effectus a causis proximis appellationes sortiantur, eiusmodi effectus rectè contingentes nominari: sicut qui ex causis secundis necessario agentibus existunt, vt motus cœli, calor ignis, necessarij sunt & dicuntur, licet interim respectu Dei, ordinem naturæ quoties visum est immutantis, etiam in talibus concontingentia locum habeat.
units.tr: Granting this syllogism, the inference is denied. For we must distinguish between the necessity of coercion and the necessity of immutability. The former moves by an external principle, forcibly; the latter does indeed impose necessity on secondary causes, so that they bring about this or that, and so on their effects, so that they come about in this way, yet it does not abolish the natures of things but rather confirms them. Therefore, although with respect to God, who foresees all things infallibly and has preordained them immutably, everything happens necessarily, that is, infallibly and unchangeably, nevertheless with respect to secondary causes, namely those which by their nature are not fixed to particular effects, such as the wills of angels and men, many things happen contingently and by choice. And it should be noted that, since effects take their names from their proximate causes, effects of this kind are rightly called contingent; just as those which arise from secondary causes acting by necessity, such as the motion of the heavens or the heat of fire, are and are called necessary, although in the meantime, with respect to God, who changes the order of nature whenever he sees fit, contingency has a place even in such things.

units.la: Hanc responsionem exempla confirmant. Verbi gratia: oportuit Christum pati & occidi: attamen sponte passus & mortuus est, sicut scriptum est: Ego pono animam meam, ut eam rursus assumam. Nemo tollit eam à me: potestatem habeo ponendi, & potestatem habeo rursus assumendi eam. Item, oportuit omnia impleri quæ de ipso scripta erant. Quid tamen magis contingens, spectatis naturis causarum secundarum, quàm quòd milites sortiti sunt vestes Christi? quòd eos non fregerunt? & alia id genus. In angelis quoque & spiritibus perfectorum in cœlis, tàm potens est gratiæ regnum, ut necessariò non peccent. Ideóne arbitrij libertate eos priuabimus? Quid Deus ipse incommutabiliter bonus, quem necesse est semper viuere & cuncta præscire? Absit tamen ut vitam & præscientiam Dei sub necessitate ponamus: sicut nec potestas eius minuitur, cùm dicitur mori salliique non posse. Quo exemplo & Augustinus vtitur de Ciuit. Dei lib. 5. cap. 10. Vbi propositam quæstionem distinctione illa duplicis necessitatis similiter dissoluit. Et cap. 9. scribit, non esse consequens, vt si Deo certum sit ordo causarum, ideo nihil sit immostræ voluntatis arbitrio, cum in ipso causarum ordine, & voluntates nostræ habeantur. Plu-ribus hac de re Anselmus, de concordia præscientiæ & prædest. Dei cum libero arbitrio.
units.tr: Examples confirm this answer. For instance: it was necessary for Christ to suffer and be killed; yet he suffered and died of his own accord, as it is written: "I lay down my life, that I may take it again. No one takes it from me; I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again" (John 10:17–18). Likewise, it was necessary that all things written concerning him should be fulfilled. Yet what could be more contingent, looking at the natures of secondary causes, than that the soldiers cast lots for Christ's garments, and that they did not break his legs, and other things of that kind? Also in angels and in the spirits of the perfected in heaven, the kingdom of grace is so powerful that they cannot sin of necessity. Shall we therefore deprive them of freedom of choice? What of God himself, who is unchangeably good, whom it is necessary to live always and to foreknow all things? Yet far be it from us to place God's life and foreknowledge under necessity; just as his power is not diminished when it is said that he cannot die or be deceived. Augustine also uses this example in De civitate Dei book 5, chapter 10, where he similarly resolves the question proposed by that distinction between two kinds of necessity. And in chapter 9 he writes that it does not follow that, if the order of causes is certain to God, therefore nothing is left to the choice of our will, since our wills are included in that very order of causes. Anselm treats this matter more fully in De concordia praescientiae et praedestinationis Dei cum libero arbitrio.

units.la: CAPVT XXI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXI.

units.la: Ceterarum obiectionum solutiones.
units.tr: The solutions of the remaining objections.

units.la: Sed aiunt, doctrina de incommutabili prædestinatione Dei euerti & tolli funditus ministerium verbi; omnes videlicet præceptiones, exhortationes, correptiones, consolationes, doctrinam denique omnem, tum publicè, tum priuatim. Etenim quæ immutabiliter à Deo prædestinata sunt fieri, ÿs frustra adhibentur media. Talis autem est salus hominum. Ergo frustra adhibentur eiuscemodi media.
units.tr: They say, however: the doctrine of the unchangeable predestination of God overturns and utterly destroys the ministry of the Word, namely all precepts, exhortations, rebukes, consolations, and indeed all teaching, both public and private. For means are used in vain for things that God has immutably predestined to happen. But such is the salvation of men. Therefore such means are used in vain.

units.la: Verum error est in Maiore, quæ tantum vera est de mediis à Deo non ordinatis, seu, sine quibus euentus illos immutabiles eum effecturum esse co-stat. stat. Non autem valet de mediis, quibus & ipse vti vult ad fines à se destinatos, atque nos etiam vti iussit. Huiusmodi sunt media, quæ in obiectione commemorantur. Scriptum enim est: Attende exhortationi, & lectioni: hæc exerce, in his esto; attende tibi ipsi & doctrinæ, persiste in ipsis. Id enim si feceris, & te ipsum seruabis, & eos qui te audiunt. Item, insta sermoni, tempestiue, intempestiue; argue, obiurga, exhortare cum omni veritate & doctrina, vigila in omnibus. Et Dominus ipse ait: Si peccauerit in te frater tuus, veni & argue eum, &c. Si te audierit, lucratus es fratrem. Et passim iubemur pigros hortari, delinquentes corripere, vt conuertantur.
units.tr: The error lies in the major premise, which is true only of means that God has not ordained, or without which he will bring about those immutable events. It does not hold for the means which he himself wishes to use for the ends he has set, and which he has also commanded us to use. The means mentioned in the objection are of this kind. For it is written: Attend to exhortation and reading; devote yourself to these things, and be in them; attend to yourself and to the teaching, and persist in them. For if you do this, you will save both yourself and those who hear you. Likewise: Be urgent in the word, in season and out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all patience and teaching; watch in all things. And the Lord himself says: If your brother sins against you, go and rebuke him, etc. If he listens to you, you have gained your brother. And everywhere we are commanded to exhort the idle and to rebuke offenders so that they may be converted.

units.la: Ad hæc certum est, prædestinationē non tantum esse finis, puta, salutis prædestinatorum, sed & mediorum ad eū finem; verbo Dei & experientia attestantibus, paucissimis esse donatum, vt nullo sibi homine prædicante, per ipsum Dominum, vel per angelos doctrinam salutis acciperent; multis vero id esse donatū, vt Deo per homines cre-
units.tr: Moreover, it is certain that predestination is not only the end, namely the salvation of the predestined, but also the means to that end. Scripture and experience attest that very few have been granted to receive the doctrine of salvation without any human preacher, through the Lord himself or through angels; but to many it has been granted that they should believe God through men.

units.la: Tt ij dederent. Etenim seruat Deus hunc ordinem vulgò erga electos suos, vt quos gratiæ largitate à damnatione discreuit, iis & audiendum procuret Euangelium, & audientibus inspiret vt credat, atque in fide, quæ per dilectionem operatur, vsque in finem perseuerent: & si quado exorbitarint, correpti emendentur. Nonnullos etiam, etsi ab hominibus non corripiantur, in viam, quam reliquerant, reducit.
units.tr: For God generally keeps this order toward his elect. Those whom by the abundance of his grace he has set apart from damnation, he also brings it about that they hear the Gospel, and inspires in those who hear that they believe, and that they persevere in the faith which works through love to the end. And if at any time they go astray, they are corrected and amended. Some also, even if they are not corrected by men, he brings back to the path they had left.

units.la: Cæterū in filiis perditionis fit quod scriptum est, vt audientes non audiant: audientes videlicet corporis sensu, non audiant cordis aliensu. Interim cū nos nescimus, qui ad prædestinatorū numerum pertineant, qui non, sic affici debemus caritatis affectu, vt omnes velimus salvos fieri, cunctos & singulos pro re nata, cum lenitate monedo, corripiendoque, si quando eis det Deus, vt agnoscant veritatem, & elapsi è diaboli laqueo, à quo captiui tenentur, metis sanitatem recipiant. Nos igitur, quod nostrum est faciamus, omnibus, ne pereant vel perdat alios, fraternam adhiadhibentes correptionem. Dei autem est, illis eam facere utilem, quos ipse præscivit, ac prædestinavit, conformes imagini filij sui. Ac licet non omnibus utilem eam faciat (multi enim sunt filij perditionis) nobis tamen satis est, quod dum nostra culpa illi non pereunt, animas nostras liberamus. Sicut ad Ezech.ait Dominus: Cum dixero impio, moriendo morieris, & non monueris eum, nec locutus fueris, ut recedat impius a via sua impia, ut viuat, ipse impius morietur: verum sanguinem eius de manu tua requiram. Sin autem monueris eum, & non fuerit conuersus ab impietate sua, ipse morietur in iniquitate sua, sed tu animam tuam liberasti. Et Paulo teste, Christi bona fragrantia sumus Deo in iis qui seruantur, & in iis qui pereunt.
units.tr: But in the sons of perdition what is written comes to pass: that, hearing, they do not hear. That is, they hear with the sense of the body, but do not hear with the understanding of the heart. Meanwhile, since we do not know who belongs to the number of the predestined and who does not, we ought to be moved by such affection of love that we wish all to be saved, and we should admonish and rebuke each and every one, as occasion arises, with gentleness, whenever God grants them to recognise the truth, and, having escaped the snare of the devil by which they are held captive, they recover soundness of mind. So let us do what is ours, offering fraternal correction to all, lest they perish or destroy others. But it is God's part to make it profitable to those whom he foreknew and predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son. And although he does not make it profitable to all (for there are many sons of perdition), it is enough for us that, while they do not perish through our fault, we have freed our own souls. As the Lord says to Ezekiel: When I say to the wicked, "You shall surely die," and you do not warn him, nor speak so that the wicked turns from his wicked way and lives, the wicked man shall die in his iniquity; but his blood I will require at your hand. But if you warn the wicked and he is not turned from his wickedness, he shall die in his iniquity, but you have delivered your soul. And by the testimony of Paul: We are the good fragrance of Christ to God among those who are saved, and among those who perish.

units.la: Redduntur etiam impij inexcusabiles, audiendo quod oportet: ne dicant, si sciissem, feciissem: ideo non feci, quia nesciui.
units.tr: The wicked are also made inexcusable by hearing what they ought to hear, so that they cannot say: "If I had known, I would have done it; I did not do it because I did not know."

units.la: Eadem est precium ratio, quas nihilo magis otiosas reddit incommutabilitas diuinæ prædestinationis, ac propositi, sicut nonnullis perperam videtur. tur. Nam etsi precibus diuina núquam mutatur prædestinatio, ad prædestinationis tamen, cum effecta multa, tum finem ipsum consequendum, illis, tanquam mediis quibusdam ad hoc àDeo ordinatis, iuuamur: secundum promissionem, Omnis qui nomen Domini inuocauerit, saluabitur. Et in Euangelio, Petite & dabitur vobis: Quisquis enim petit, accipit. Et mox: quanto magis pater vester cœlestis dabit Spiritum Sanctum petentibus?
units.tr: The same is true of the reasoning about prayers, which the unchangeableness of divine predestination and purpose does not make any the more idle, as some wrongly think. For although predestination is never changed by prayers, yet we are helped by prayers toward the effects of predestination, and toward the very end to be attained, as means ordained by God for this purpose, according to the promise: Whoever calls on the name of the Lord shall be saved. And in the Gospel: Ask, and it will be given to you; for whoever asks receives. And soon after: How much more will your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask?

units.la: Sed hic tenendum, quæ sancti viri orando efficiunt, ita prædestinata esse, vt precibus obtineantur, vt recte Gregorius dixit. In quam sententiam, & Augustinus ait, preces plurimum valere ad ea impetranda, quæ precantibus concedi Deus præsciuit.
units.tr: But here it must be held that what holy men accomplish by praying is so predestined that it is obtained by prayers, as Gregory rightly said. To this effect Augustine also says: prayers avail greatly to obtain those things which God foreknew would be granted to those who pray.

units.la: Duplex ita excluditur error. Vnus est superstitiosorum quorundam, quasi decretum Dei, de homine aliquo factum, puta de eo damnando, mutari posse sacrificijs ac precibus; quemadmodum de Traiano Imp. fabulantur, cum esset in inferno, loco reprobורum, liberatum inde fuisse orationibus Gregorij.
units.tr: In this way a twofold error is excluded. One is that of certain superstitious people, who think that God's decree made concerning some man, for example to condemn him, can be changed by sacrifices and prayers. So they fable about the Emperor Trajan, that when he was in hell, the place of the reprobate, he was freed from there by the prayers of Gregory.

units.la: Luc. 11. gorij. Alter error in contrarium pec-cat, quasi res tam salutaris, tamque ne-cessaria, oratio videlicet, vnicum inter Deum & homines commercium, vt ait Boëthius, nihil virium habere videa-tur, eo quod indeflexe apud Deum co-stitutum sit, quos seruare, quos damnare velit: quorum illud ad misericor-diam, hoc ad iudicium ipsius pertinet.
units.tr: Luke 11. The other error sins in the opposite direction, supposing that prayer, a thing so salutary and so necessary (the sole commerce between God and men, as Boethius says), has no power, because it is fixed unalterably with God whom he wishes to save and whom to condemn. Of these, the former belongs to his mercy, the latter to his judgment.

units.la: Minime autem ferre, audireque oportet, homines aut nequa & ignaros, & nocentes & audaces, qui cum delin-quunt, & secure peccatis indulgent, per-fugiunt ad prædestinationis necessitate, tanquam in aliquod fani asylum, & quæ peßime faciunt, prædestinationi attri-buenda esse dicunt. Quo pacto & se extra culpam videri, & Deum in culpa haberi volunt, tanquam peccatorum autorem, sicut ad Rom. 9. tales dicunt: Quid adhuc succenset? Nam voluntati illius quis resistet? Sed recte istos qui de Deo se conantur excusare, Iacobus increpat. Nemo cum tentatur, dicat se a Deo tentari: sed unusquisque tentatur, cum a propria cupiditate abstrahitur. Deinde cupidi-tas, tas, postequam concepit, parit peccatum. Et liber Ecclesiasticus geminam impietatem vna eademque responsione dissipat, cap. 15. Ne dicas, deliqui impulsu Domini: nam quae odit ille, tu non debes facere. Ne dicas, ipse me induxit in errorem: neque enim opus ei est viro improbo. Omne nefas odit Dominus, nec probatur iis, qui eum timent. Ipse hominem creauit ab initio, eumque permisit arbitrio consilij sui. Si volueris, mandata seruabis.
units.tr: By no means should one tolerate or listen to men who are negligent, ignorant, harmful and bold, who when they sin and indulge their sins with impunity, flee to the necessity of predestination as to some sanctuary of a temple, and say that what they do most wickedly must be ascribed to predestination. By this they wish both to appear free of guilt and to have God held guilty, as the author of sins; such men say, as in Rom. 9: Why does he still find fault? For who resists his will? But Iacobus rightly rebukes those who try to excuse themselves by blaming God: Let no one, when tempted, say that he is tempted by God; but each one is tempted when he is drawn away by his own desire. Then desire, when it has conceived, gives birth to sin. And the book of Ecclesiasticus dispels a double impiety with one and the same answer, ch. 15: Do not say, "I fell through the impulse of the Lord"; for what he hates you ought not to do. Do not say, "He himself led me into error"; for he has no need of a wicked man. The Lord hates every abomination, and it is not approved by those who fear him. He created man from the beginning and left him in the hand of his own counsel. If you will, you will keep the commandments.

units.la: Nempe hi sunt fontes peccatorum, propria peccantium cupiditas, & libertum ipsorum arbitrium: siquidem ad perpetranda peccata homo nequaquâ cogitur, sed sponte illa facit, & maximè probat atque vult ea, quemadmodum & hæc dicta scripturarum testantur. Noluit intelligere, vt bene faceret. Et, noluerunt accipere disciplinam, & plura talia in libris diuinorum eloquiorum. Dei autem prædestinatio neutiquam peccatorum fons existimari debet. Eius si- quidem opera, vt pulcre Augustinus scri-ptum reliquit, multos scimus retentos, ne laberentur; nullos autem vt laberentur im-pul-
units.tr: Indeed, these are the sources of sins: the sinners' own desire and their free will. For a man is by no means compelled to commit sins, but does them of his own accord, and especially approves and wills them, as the sayings of Scripture also testify: He was unwilling to understand, so as to do good. And: They were unwilling to receive discipline; and many such things in the books of the divine oracles. But the predestination of God ought by no means to be regarded as a fount of sins. For by his work, as Augustine finely wrote, we know that many are held back lest they fall; but none are pushed so that they fall

units.la: Ad artic. falso imp. pulsos, ac per hoc prædestinatio Dei multis est causa standi, nemini causa labendi. Ideoque ait, detestanda opinio est, quæ Deum cuius- quam male voluntatis, aut male actionis cre- dit auctorem. Peccata autem homines cum admittunt, suis concupiscentijs & cupiditati- bus seruiunt: cum autem declinant a malo & faciunt bonum, a Domino gressus hominis di- riguntur, vt viam eius velit. Et alibi Hy- pognft. 6. Qui absque prædestinationis gra- tia sunt, id est, alieni a proposito Dei, & perdu- rant in operibus malis, non nos eos dicimus, vt vos putatis, ita a Deo omnium opifice ordi- natos vt perirent, tanquam ipse illis mores mala vita creauerit, ipse ad omne opus mor- tis inuitos præcipitauerit. Absit a diuino proposito. Nec dicimus, vt fingitis, & si crede- re velint, & bonis vacare operibus, hac Deum illis nolle præstare, cum huiusmodi velle Dei sit donum &c. Hæc pater illeSpiritui bla- sphemiarum veritatem per Pelagianos calumnianti, opposuit. Sed perseuerat idem Spiritus etiam nunc in aduersa-rijs, qui fingunt, quod nos minime sen- timus, quasi Deus impellat reprobos, vt delinquant, & ruat, rapiat, obterat eos, etiam causa indicta. ô blasphemiam!
units.tr: pushed, and so the predestination of God is a cause of standing for many, and a cause of falling for no one. Therefore he says, the opinion is to be detested which believes God to be the author of any evil will or evil action. But men, when they commit sins, serve their own concupiscences and cupidities; but when they turn from evil and do good, the steps of man are directed by the Lord, so that he wills his way. And elsewhere, in the Hypognosticon, book 6: Those who are without the grace of predestination, that is, alien to God's purpose, and persist in evil works, we do not say, as you suppose, that they are so ordained by God the maker of all that they perish, as if he himself had created their morals and evil life, and himself hurled them, unwilling, into every deed of death. Far be that from the divine purpose. Nor do we say, as you fabricate, that even if they wish to believe and devote themselves to good works, God is unwilling to grant this to them, since such willing is itself a gift of God, etc. That father opposed this to the spirit of blasphemies, who calumniates the truth through the Pelagians. But the same spirit persists even now in our adversaries, who feign what we least of all think: as if God impels the reprobate to sin, and rushes upon, snatches, and crushes them, even without any cause given. O blasphemy!

units.la: Sed excipiunt, Peccatores extra culpam videri, quod non obediant Deo, quòd ipsa obedientia munus eius sit. Hanc, inquiunt, non accipimus: quid igitur corripimur, quasi nos eam dare nobis possimus, & nostro arbitrio dare nolimus? Argumentum tale est:
units.tr: But they object that sinners are not to blame for failing to obey God, since obedience itself is his gift. "We do not receive it," they say, "so why are we rebuked, as if we could give it to ourselves and are unwilling to give it by our own choice?" The argument runs like this:

units.la: Qui non accipiunt fidem & conuersionem a Deo, videntur excusabiles: siquidem fidem & conuersionem Deo non donante, habere non possumus.
units.tr: Those who do not receive faith and conversion from God seem excusable, since without God granting faith and conversion we cannot have them.

units.la: Tales autem sunt omnes non resipiscentes. Ergo.
units.tr: All who do not repent are such people. Therefore...

units.la: Hic maior falsa est, etsi speciosa videatur humanæ rationi: quia fecit Dominus hominem rectum ab initio, & ad imaginem sui condidit eum: homo autem ex rectitudine, in qua primitus factus est, sua malitia & impulsore Diabolo decidens, prauus effectus est. An verò quia nos acceptam gratiam amisimus, Deus debitor nobis est, vt restituat? Aut non licebit propterea ei quod suum est, à nobis repetere? Habet, bet,habet potestatem exigendi : habet etiam remittendi. A quibus autem exigendum, quibus remittendum sit, Domini, non debitorum est iudicare.
units.tr: The major premise is false, although it may seem plausible to human reason. The Lord made man upright from the beginning and created him in his own image. But man, having fallen from the uprightness in which he was first made, through his own malice and at the instigation of the devil, became depraved. Does God then owe us, because we have lost the grace we received, to restore it? Or may he not, for that reason, demand back from us what is his own? He has the power to exact and also the power to remit. It is for the Lord, not for debtors, to judge from whom it is to be exacted and to whom it is to be remitted.

units.la: Aiunt inquiunt, reprobi, De ipsos deserente & indurante, peccata euitare non possunt. Iniustum autem videtur, si Deus hominem puniat, propter ea quae vitare non potest.
units.tr: "The reprobate," they say, "cannot avoid sins, since God forsakes and hardens them. But it seems unjust for God to punish a man for things he cannot avoid."

units.la: Resp. Scio quidem id Alberto Pighio, aliisque sophistis, quorum Deus infatuauit sapientiam, visum fuisse iniustum, sed qua iniuste, patet: quia si illa valeret ratio, non posset Deus sine nota crudelitatis & iniustitiae punire peccatum originis, quod certe nemo hominum nascendo potest euitare.
units.tr: Reply: I know that this seemed unjust to Albert Pighius and other sophists, whom God has struck with foolishness. But how it is unjust is plain. For if that argument held, God could not punish original sin without the mark of cruelty and injustice, and yet no one can avoid it by being born.

units.la: Obiiciunt & hoc: Qui peccatum praevidet, nec impedit cum possit, culpa non vacat. Deus praevidet peccata, & cum nullo negotio posset impedire, non tamen impedit. Ergo, &c.
units.tr: They also raise this objection: "He who foresees sin and does not prevent it, when he could, is not free of guilt. God foresees sins, and though he could prevent them without any trouble, he does not. Therefore..."

units.la: Ad hoc quidam respondent, Deum non auertere peccata; quia vult creaturam rationalem retinere suam libertatem, & electionem boni & mali, quā alioalioquin amitteret. Sed si ea ratio valeret, aut destrueretur gratia Dei, quapij & electi peccata declinat, aut dicedi illi esset carere electione boni & mali. Pro veriore igitur solutione & hic meminisse oportet, non esse disputandum de iustitia Dei lege iustitiæ humanæ. Maior de hominibus valet, non de Deo. Quippe homines & naturæ societate, & Dei lege obligati sunt sibi inuicem, vt alter alterius salutem procuret, in-teritumque impediat. Deus autem nemini obligatus est, & de creatura potest facere quicquid vult, sine iniuria creaturæ: tamquam vniuersorum dominus, & habens plenum dominium in re sua. Adhæc, pro Omnipotentissima bonitate & sapientia sua, etiam de malis nouit bene facere: quod homines non norunt.
units.tr: Some answer this by saying that God does not turn sins away, because he wishes the rational creature to keep its freedom and its choice between good and evil, which otherwise it would lose. But if that reasoning held, either the grace of God would be destroyed, by which he turns away sins even from the elect, or it would follow that God's elect lacked the choice between good and evil. For a truer solution, we must remember here that we ought not to dispute about God's justice by the law of human justice. The major premise holds for men, not for God. Men are bound to one another both by the fellowship of nature and by the law of God, so that each should promote the other's salvation and prevent his ruin. But God is bound to no one, and he may do with his creature whatever he wills without wronging it, as the Lord of all things, having full dominion over what is his. Moreover, by his almighty goodness and wisdom he knows how to bring good even out of evils, which men do not know.

units.la: Quæ cum ita sint, nemo causetur Deum in corde suo, qui vnicuiq; redditurus est secundum opera sua: sed sibi imputet quisque cum peccat, & dicat cum damnatur: Iustus es Domine in omnibus quæ fecisti nobis, & omnia iudicia tua.
units.tr: Since this is so, let no one accuse God in his heart, for he will render to each according to his works. Rather, let each man impute to himself when he sins, and say when he is condemned: "You are just, O Lord, in all that you have done to us, and all your judgements are true."

units.la: Psal. 102. tua vera. Et dicet quicunque liberatur, Misericors & miserator Dominus. Non se-cundum peccata nostra retribuit nobis.
units.tr: Psal. 102. "Your judgements are true." And whoever is set free will say: "The Lord is merciful and gracious. He has not dealt with us according to our sins."

units.la: Quod addebatur de desperatione, hominum animis eam ingenerari; doctrinâ de firma & incommutabili tum electionis, tum reprobationis diuinæ propositio: mera item calunia est. Imò verò hoc est verissimum omnis consolationis, & salutis fundamentum, & velut basis, quòd scimus Deum suos, qui vera fide Christum amplectuntur, in ipso ante iacta mundi fundamenta elegisse, & praedestinasse ad adoptionem, pro beneuolo affectu voluntatis suæ: atque hoc propositū electionis & praedestinationis gratuitæ, tam esse firmū, vt neque à creatura vlla mutari possit, neque ipsum Deum donorum & vocationis suæ vnquam poeniteat. Id loca scripturæ passim confirmant quibus de praedestinatione agitur: vt quod ait Apostolus: Firmum stat fundamentum Dei, habens sigillum hoc: Nouit Dominus qui sint sui. Certè ad consolationem nostram hoc dicit scriptura, ne turbemur ob quoquorundam ab Euangelio defectione, aliaue scandala. Et plenius ad Rom.8. Nouimus iis, qui Deum diligunt, omnia simul conferre in bonum, iis videlicet, qui ex propo-sito vocati sunt. Nam quos praesciuit, eos & praedestinauit, vt conformes fiant imaginis-suae, &c. Et concludit his verbis: perfua-sus sum, neque mortE, neque vitam, neque angelos, neque vllam creaturam posse nos separare a cari-tate Dei, quae est in Christo Iesu. Videmus, vt Apostolus aduersus omnes tentatio-nes huius mundi muniat nos ea per-suasione, quod firma & stabilis sit elec-tio, qua ad aeternam vitam gratis, atque ex mera caritate in Christo electi sumus: quemadmodum & Dominus in Euangelio nos eo consolatur, quod electi
units.tr: As for the objection that the doctrine of the firm and unchangeable election and reprobation of God breeds despair in men's minds, that too is a mere calumny. Indeed, this is the most certain foundation and, as it were, the basis of all comfort and salvation: that we know God chose in Christ before the foundations of the world those who embrace Christ with true faith, and predestined them to adoption, out of the kindly purpose of his will. This purpose of free election and predestination is so firm that it can be changed by no creature, nor will God himself ever repent of his gifts and calling. The passages of Scripture that treat of predestination confirm this throughout, as when the Apostle says: "The firm foundation of God stands, having this seal: The Lord knows those who are his." Surely Scripture says this for our consolation, so that we may not be troubled by the defection of some from the Gospel or by other stumbling-blocks. And more fully in Romans 8: "We know that for those who love God all things work together for good, namely for those who have been called according to his purpose. For those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, etc." And he concludes with these words: "I am persuaded that neither death nor life, nor angels, nor any creature, can separate us from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus." We see that the Apostle fortifies us against all the temptations of this world with this persuasion, that the election by which we are chosen freely, and out of pure love, to eternal life in Christ is firm and stable. In the same way the Lord in the Gospel comforts us by this, that the elect

units.la: Matth. 24. seduci nequeunt: quod oues suas non patitur sibi rapi e manu sua: quod nomina nostra scripta sunt in caelis. Item, ne time parue grex, quia patri visum est vobis dare regnum. Et apud Ioh. ne credentes incredulorum contumacia offenderentur; quicquid, inquit, dat mihi pater, ad me venit, & qui venit ad me, eum non eiciam foras, quia descendi de caelo, vt faciam voluntatem eius qui misit me.
units.tr: Matth. 24. cannot be led astray; that he does not allow his sheep to be snatched out of his hand; that our names are written in heaven. Likewise: "Fear not, little flock, for it has pleased your Father to give you the kingdom." And in John, so that believers should not be offended by the obstinacy of unbelievers: "Whatever the Father gives me comes to me, and whoever comes to me I will not cast out, because I have come down from heaven to do the will of him who sent me."

units.la: Apparet ergo inspectis scripturarum sententiis, doctrinam de soliditate diuinæ electionis, ad hoc nobis patefactam esse, vt esset totius fundamentum certitudinis, aduersus omne genus tentationum, quæ vel nostræ infirmitatis inter tot pericula piorum, vel aliorum incredulitatis, aut etiam à fide naufragij, aliarumve rerum respectu existunt.
units.tr: It is clear, then, from the sayings of Scripture, that the doctrine of the certainty of divine election has been revealed to us for this purpose: to be the foundation of all assurance against every kind of temptation, whether it arises from our own weakness amid the many dangers that beset the godly, or from the unbelief of others, or from shipwreck of faith, or from other circumstances.

units.la: De hoc præclarè Lutherus præf. ad Rom. Vbi cum aliquando ita: [?] stabilem atque immotam esse sententiam prædestinationis, subnectit, hanc necessitate summè necessariam ad salutem & consolationem. Rationem assignat, quòd in nobis tam imbecilles sumus, vt, si in nostris viribus sita esset salus nostra, paucissimi, aut nulli saluarentur: Diabolus enim omnes vinceret.
