Nunc vero, inquit, cum stabilis, & certissima Dei sententia mutari non possit ab vlla creatura, spes nobis est tandem vincendi peccatum. Pluribus idem docet, atque exaggerat consideratione tot periculorum, & dæmonum quotidie nos impugnantium, defer. arb. cap. 244.
units.tr: Luther has spoken admirably on this in his preface to Romans. There, after saying that the sentence of predestination is stable and immovable, he adds that this doctrine is of the greatest necessity for salvation and consolation. He gives the reason: we are so feeble in ourselves that, if our salvation rested on our own strength, very few or none would be saved, for the devil would overcome all. But now, he says, since the stable and most certain sentence of God cannot be changed by any creature, we have hope at last of overcoming sin. He teaches the same more fully and enlarges on it by considering the many dangers and the demons who assail us daily. De servo arbitrio, cap. 244.

units.la: Et sanè mirandum est, inter tot difficultates, quibus vita nostra obsidetur, quemquam infirmitati suæ se malle committere, quàm firmitati promissionis & gratiæ Dei.
units.tr: And indeed it is remarkable that, amid so many difficulties by which our life is beset, anyone would prefer to entrust himself to his own weakness rather than to the firmness of God's promise and grace.

units.la: Sed incerta est mihi ipsi, inquis, de me ipso voluntas Dei. Atque hoc ipsum est quod anxium me habet, quod cùm certus & obsignatus sit prædestinatorum numerus, qui augeri & minui nequit, incertus sum an ad numerum illum pertineam: id si scirem, in solido illo fundamento acquiescerem.
units.tr: "But the will of God concerning me personally is uncertain to me, you say. And this is just what troubles me: since the number of the predestined is fixed and sealed and can be neither increased nor diminished, I am uncertain whether I belong to that number. If I knew this, I would rest in that solid foundation."

units.la: Resp. Alia hæc quæstio est, unde scire queamus nos esse electos, de qua post: alia, utrum desperationi, an consolationi potius seruiat firmitas electionis. Deinde, concesso nunc (quanquam concedi non debet) incertam nobis esse voluntatem Dei, de salute nostra, tuâne tibi de te ipso voluntas certa est? Qui videtur stare, videat ne cadat.
units.tr: Reply: This is one question, how we can know that we are elect, which I will treat later. It is another question whether the firmness of election serves despair or rather consolation. Next, even granting now (though it ought not to be granted) that the will of God concerning our salvation is uncertain to us, is your own will about yourself certain to you? "He who seems to stand, let him see that he does not fall."

units.la: Cùm igitur utraque & Dei & tua voluntas, id est, conatus & perseuerantia tua tanquam ex te, incerta sit: cur non homo firmiori quàm infirmiori, fidem, spem, caritatemque committat? Atque hæc dicta sunto, contra obiectiones prioris generis, consequentias videlicet rationis humanæ.
units.tr: Since, then, both the will of God and your will, that is, your effort and perseverance as if from yourself, are uncertain, why should a man not entrust his faith, hope and love to the firmer rather than the weaker? These things are said against objections of the former kind, namely the consequences of human reason.

units.la: CAPVT XXII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXII.

units.la: Ad loca quædam scripturæ, quæ objici solent, contra firmitatem prædestinationis.
units.tr: Concerning certain passages of Scripture which are commonly objected against the firmness of predestination.

units.la: SED enim qui communem omnibus electionis gratiam faciunt, eamq; ingratitudine postmodum a multis irritam reddi volunt, e sacris literis hæc fere obiiciunt. Primum, Pharisæi & legis periti dicuntur reiecisse consilium Dei adversus sese, Luc. 7. v. 30. Ergo electionem quam cum aliis communem habuerunt, sibi ipsi irritam reddiderunt.
units.tr: But those who make the grace of election common to all, and who afterwards want it made void by the ingratitude of many, usually object the following from the sacred letters. First, the Pharisees and the lawyers are said to have rejected the counsel of God against themselves, Luke 7:30. Therefore they made void for themselves the election which they had in common with others.

units.la: Resp. per consilium Dei eo loci non intelligitur electio, seu ordinatio Pharisæorum ad vitam æternam. Si enim ad eam ordinati fuissent, utique crediderint. Sed denotatur voluntas Dei revelata, per ministerium nempe Baptistæ, ut cupientes servari, & fugere iram venturam, baptizarentur baptismo re-
units.tr: Answer: by the counsel of God in that place election, or the ordination of the Pharisees to eternal life, is not meant. For if they had been ordained to it, they would certainly have believed. Rather, the revealed will of God is meant, namely through the ministry of the Baptist, so that those who wished to be saved and to flee the coming wrath would be baptized with a baptism of re-

units.la: Vu sipisipiscentiæ & in eum qui post ipsum venturus erat, hoc est, in Iesum Christum crederent. Hoc igitur vult Euangelista, plebem & publicanos doctrinæ Iohannis paruisse ad salutem: Pharisæos & scribas non paruisse, magno suo malo, vt pote propriam iustitiam studentes constituere. Ad hunc modum & Paulus, ad exprimendam fidelitatem in ministerio, quod acceperat ad testificandum Euangelium gratiæ Dei, ait, se nihil subterfugisse, quo minus annunciaret Ephesiis omne Dei consilium: id est, fidem & conuersionem, secundum declarationem, quem textus ibi habet.
units.tr: pentance, and would believe in him who was to come after him, that is, in Jesus Christ. The evangelist therefore means that the common people and the tax collectors submitted to the teaching of John for salvation, while the Pharisees and scribes did not submit, to their great harm, since they, as men seeking to establish their own righteousness, did not. In this way Paul also, to express his faithfulness in the ministry which he had received to testify to the gospel of the grace of God, says that he shrank from nothing that would keep him from declaring to the Ephesians the whole counsel of God: that is, faith and conversion, according to the explanation which the text there gives.

units.la: II. obiectio: Quibus Epistolæ aliquot Apostolicæ inscriptæ sunt, erant sancti & electi. In iis tamen multi à fide relapsi sunt & perierunt. Ergo aliqui electi pereunt. Respondetur ad maiorem: Erant illi sancti & electi, sed non omnes: quia multi semper sunt hypocritæ in cœtu Ecclesiæ visibilis. Ideo argumentum est ex puris particularibus. Deinde appellatio electorum non vno modo in scri-ptupturis vsurpatur. Præter significatio-nem specialem, qua electi intelligun-tur ad vitam æternam præordinati, est & hic vocabuli visus, vt in genere (lo-quendo secundum canonem caritatis, non autem fidei) electi dicantur, qui-cunque externa vocatione populo Dei accensentur, siue reuera iam sint fide-les, & sanctificati, & electi apud Deum, siue non: & secundum generalem istã significationem conceditur totum ar-gumentum.
units.tr: Second objection: those to whom some apostolic epistles are addressed were saints and elect. Yet many among them fell away from the faith and perished. Therefore some of the elect perish. To the major premise it is answered: they were saints and elect, but not all of them, because there are always many hypocrites in the visible assembly of the Church. So the argument rests on particular instances only. Moreover, the title "elect" is not used in one way only in the Scriptures. Besides the special sense, in which the elect are understood as those foreordained to eternal life, there is also another sense of the word, in which (speaking according to the rule of charity, not of faith) those are called elect who are reckoned among the people of God by external calling, whether they are in truth already believers and sanctified and elect before God or not. And according to this general sense the whole argument is granted.

units.la: III. Obiectio difficilior est de libro vitæ, dicente Dauide, Psal. 69. Delean-tur de libro viuentium, & cum iustis nõ scri-bantur. Quomodo etiam Moses, interce-dens pro populo, precatus est, Exod. 32. Aut remitte peccata eorum, aut sinon, dele me de libro, quem scripsisti. Cui Dominus: qui peccauerit in me, delebo illum de libro vi-tæ.
units.tr: Third, the objection is more difficult, concerning the book of life, where David says, Psalm 69: Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and let them not be written with the righteous. Likewise Moses, interceding for the people, prayed, Exodus 32: Either forgive their sin, or else blot me out of the book which you have written. To him the Lord replied: Whoever has sinned against me, I will blot him out of my book of life.

units.la: Ergo aliqui scripti in libro vitæ de-leri inde possunt, & per consequens, aliqui ad vitam prædestinati pereunt, quia prædestinatio sanctorum, & liber vitæ, idem sunt; saltem re, licet ratio-ne nonnihil differant. Prædestinatio enim est ipsa ordinatio sanctorum ad vitam æternam. Liber autem vitæ μεταφρασις nihil aliud est, quàm prædestinatorum notitia in mente diuina, vt Thomas in 4. cap.ad Philipp.& alij explicant.
units.tr: Therefore some who are written in the book of life can be blotted out from it, and consequently some who are predestined to life perish, because the predestination of the saints and the book of life are the same, at least in reality, though they differ somewhat in reasoning. For predestination is the very ordination of the saints to eternal life. But the book of life is, by metonymy [μετωνυμία], nothing other than the knowledge of the predestined in the divine mind, as Thomas, on the fourth chapter to the Philippians, and others explain.

units.la: Resp. Nodū istum Augustinus, locum illū Psalmi enarrans, in hanc sententiam dissoluit, quod qui re ipsa scripti sunt in libro vitæ, eorum nemo deleatur : sed deletio ad eos duntaxat pertineat, qui non secundum rei veritatem, sed tantùm secundum suam vel aliorum hominum opinionem ibi scripti sunt: quódque tales dicantur deleri, quando in hoc vel futuro seculo manifestum fit, eos non fuisse in numero prædestinatorum. Quidam sic distinguunt, librum vitæ sumi bifariam, vel pro catalogo electorum ad vitam æternam, vel pro catalogo eorum qui profitentur fidem Christi, & inter Ecclesiæ membra habentur, quorum multi sanè delentur. Sic Ezechiel. 13. dicitur de Pseudoprophetis; In cætu populi mei non erunt, & in scriptura, hoc est libro, domus Israël. Israël non scribentur. Significat, quamuis Pseudoprophetæ videri vellent populus & Ecclesia Dei, imò columnæ eius, adeò non debere censeri in illo gradu, vt prorsus extranei essent habendi à populo Dei. Res eodem recidit.
units.tr: Answer: Augustine, expounding that passage of the Psalm, resolved this knot to this effect: that none of those who are truly written in the book of life is blotted out; the blotting out applies only to those who are written there not according to the truth of the matter, but only according to their own opinion or the opinion of other men. And such people are said to be blotted out when it becomes manifest, in this age or the age to come, that they were not in the number of the predestined. Some distinguish thus: the book of life is taken in two ways, either for the catalogue of the elect to eternal life, or for the catalogue of those who profess faith in Christ and are counted among the members of the Church, of whom many are indeed blotted out. So in Ezekiel 13 it is said of the false prophets: They shall not be in the assembly of my people, nor shall they be written in the scripture, that is, in the book, of the house of Israel; they shall not be written in the land of Israel. It signifies that although the false prophets wished to seem to be the people and Church of God, indeed its pillars, they ought not to be counted in that rank, so that they were to be held entirely as strangers to the people of God. The matter comes to the same thing.

units.la: Dictam expositionem confirmat Augustinus, partim eo quod sequitur in verbis Dauidis: & cum iustis non scribantur: unde colligit, tales, quantum ad Dei iudicium, nondum inscriptos libro viuentium: partim aliis scripturæ locis de libro vitæ, vt quod in Apocal. ait spiritus Dei, adoraturos bestiam omnes quorum nomina non sunt scripta in libro vitæ. Proinde, inquit Augustinus, non erant adoraturi, qui scripti sunt. Huc accedit quod prophetia apud Dauidem tota directa est contra Iudam prodito-rem, aliosque obstinatos Christi hostes, à gratia electionis alienos & reprobos, ac filios perditionis, quemadmodum ex Pauli interpretatione planum est. Sic enim ait: Quod requirit Israël, id non est consecutus, sed electi assecuti sunt, reliqui vero obcaluerunt, sicut scriptum est est: Fiat mensa ipsorum pro laqueo: obtene- brentur oculi ipsorum &c. Hæc iam iunt ipsissima Dauidis verba ex præsenti Psalmo: quæ cum spiritus Dei exponat de Iudæis reprobis, & minime ad electionem pertinentibus, apparet eorundem in libro vitæ scriptionem non posse aliter accipi, quàm quatenus Ecclesiæ titulo aliquantisper gloriabantur, donec delerentur, id est, declararentur abdicati, & nullo modo ad Ecclesiæ corpus pertinentes.
units.tr: Augustine confirms this exposition, partly by what follows in David's words, and let them not be written with the righteous, from which he gathers that such people, as far as God's judgment goes, are not yet written in the book of the living; partly by other passages of Scripture about the book of life, as when the Spirit of God says in the Apocalypse that all whose names are not written in the book of life shall worship the beast. Hence, says Augustine, those who are written were not going to worship it. To this may be added that the whole prophecy in David is directed against Judas the traitor and other obstinate enemies of Christ, who are strangers to the grace of election, reprobate, and sons of perdition, as is plain from the interpretation of Paul. For he says: What Israel seeks, that it has not obtained; but the elect have obtained it, and the rest were blinded, as it is written: let their table become a snare for them, let their eyes be darkened, and so on. These are the very words of David from this same Psalm. Since the Spirit of God expounds them of the reprobate Jews, who have nothing to do with election, it is clear that their being written in the book of life cannot be understood otherwise than insofar as they gloried for a while in the title of the Church, until they were blotted out, that is, declared rejected and in no way belonging to the body of the Church.

units.la: At Moses erat inter prædestinatos Dei filios, & verè scriptus erat in libro viuentiū, Ergo aliqui verè in libro vitæ saripti ex ea delentur, aut deleri possunt.
units.tr: But Moses was among the predestined sons of God, and was truly written in the book of the living. Therefore some who were truly written in the book of life are, or can be, blotted out of it.

units.la: Nego cons. quia maior quæ omittitur in argumento falsa est: Mosen videlicet deletum, aut potuisse deleri è libro viuentium. Optauit quidem inde deleri ob peccatum Israëlis, potius quàm Dei nomen inter gentes blasphemaretur: sed non quia optauit, factum est, aut fieri poterat. Nec mirari debemus, Mosen, quod fieri non potuit optasse, cùm hoc non infrequens sit in sanctorum votis, vt impetu quodam caritatis Dei vel proximi rapiatur eorū voluntas etiam ad ea quę fieri non possūt Documēto est quod in hoc ipso voto Moses pœnā & damnatione transgressorū in se potiusderiuare cupiebat, si Deus præuaricationi ipsorum omnino nollet ignoscere. Neque enim iustitia Dei patitur, vt innocentem plectat pro nocentibus, sed anima quæ peccauit plectetur. Quemadmodum & hic Mosi tale quid optanti respōsum fuit à iudice mundi: qui peccauerit in me deleboillum è libro quem scripsi. Ita & Dauid orauit: Quis mihi det vt moriar pro te fili Absalon, cūm tamen fieri non posset, vt pro Absolomo moreretur. Christus etiam satis sciebat, oportere se bibere calicem; attamen dixit: Pater, si possibile est, transeat à me calix iste. Atque vt exēplo vtamur simili mo, Paulus optabat esse anathema à Christo pro fratribus suis Israëlitis; nempe, præ Christi amore, si fieri ita potuisset, regni cœlestis iacturam pati, & gehennam adire paratus erat: vt passim locum illum exponit Chrysost.
units.tr: I deny the conclusion, because the major premise omitted in the argument is false: namely that Moses was blotted out, or could have been blotted out, from the book of the living. He indeed wished to be blotted out from it on account of the sin of Israel, rather than that the name of God should be blasphemed among the nations; but it did not happen because he wished it, nor could it have happened. Nor ought we to wonder that Moses wished for what could not be done, since this is not uncommon in the prayers of the saints: their will is carried by a certain impulse of love for God or neighbour even toward things that cannot be done. The evidence is that in this very prayer Moses was rather desiring that the punishment and damnation of the transgressors should fall upon himself, if God were altogether unwilling to pardon their transgression. For the justice of God does not allow the innocent to be punished for the guilty, but the soul that has sinned shall be punished. In the same way the Judge of the world gave Moses, who prayed for something of the kind, this answer: Whoever has sinned against me, I will blot out of the book which I have written. So too David prayed: Would God I might die for you, my son Absalom, although it could not come about that he should die for Absalom. Christ too knew well enough that he had to drink the cup; yet he said: Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me. And to use a similar example: Paul wished to be anathema from Christ for his brethren the Israelites; that is, out of love for Christ, if it could have been done in that way, he was ready to suffer the loss of the heavenly kingdom and to go to hell. Chrysostom expounds that passage in this way in many places.

units.la: Vu iiij
units.tr: Vu iiij

units.la: Cæterùm, quod ad responsionem Domini ad Mosen, cùm ait, se delet- rum è libro suo qui in se peccauerint: eadem est solutio quæ prius ad locum Psalmi, quam & Ambrosius in cap. 9. ad Roman. calculo suo apertè comprobat, & subscribit eidem è recentioribus D. Heer- brandus, disputat. de electione & prædest. di- uina, thesi 11. Eos igitur consulat Hube- rus, potius quàm veritatè & eius aman- tes irrideat, & per Sarcasmum doctores vocet æquiuocos, cùm ipse disputatorem verius agat æquiuocum, vocum æquiuocationibus ludens ad decipien- dum alios.
units.tr: As for the Lord's answer to Moses, when he says that he will blot out of his book those who have sinned against him, the solution is the same as before for the passage of the Psalm, which Ambrose, in his comment on Romans 9, plainly confirms, and which among the more recent writers Heerbrand also subscribes to in his disputation on divine election and predestination, thesis 11. Let Huber therefore consult them, rather than mock the truth and its lovers, and call the doctors equivocators by sarcasm, when he himself is rather the equivocating disputant, playing with the equivocations of words to deceive others.

units.la: Obiicitur præterea ex Epist.ad Heb. 12. Accessistis ad montem Sion, & ciuitatem Dei viui, Ierusalem cœlestem, & myriadas angelorum, conuentum & concionem primogenitorum &c. Videte ne aspernemini eum qui loquitur. Nam si illi non effugerunt, qui aspernabantur eum qui loquebatur Dei nomine in terra: multo magis nos, si eum qui de cælis est, auersemur.
units.tr: The objection is also raised from the Epistle to the Hebrews 12: "You have come to Mount Sion, and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to myriads of angels, the assembly and congregation of the firstborn, etc. See that you do not refuse him who speaks. For if those did not escape who refused him who spoke on earth in God's name, much more shall we not escape if we turn away from him who is from heaven."

units.la: Aliqui horum de quibus sermo iste est, excidunt, atque pereunt æternum: quia terret eos poenis æternis, si verbo reluctentur. Ii autem de quibus sermo est, sunt conscripti in cælis. Ergo talium nonnulli pereunt.
units.tr: Some of those of whom this speech is spoken fall away and perish eternally, because he terrifies them with eternal punishments if they resist the word. But those of whom the speech is spoken are written in heaven. Therefore some such people perish.

units.la: Respondeo, ex puris particularibus nihil concludi. Certè minor particularis tantum est: quia de primogenitis illis dicitur, quod scripti sint in cælis, non de aliis quibuscunque ad eorum & Ecclesiæ societatem pertinentibus: inter quos multos esse hypocritas suo tempore iudicandos à Domino, minimè dubium est.
units.tr: I answer: nothing follows from purely particular premises. Certainly the minor premise is only particular, because it is said of those firstborn that they are written in heaven, not of any others whatever who belong to their fellowship and that of the Church. That among these there are many hypocrites, to be judged by the Lord in his time, is by no means doubtful.

units.la: Sed, inquiunt, scriptum est: Tene quod habes ut nemo accipiat coronam tuam. Qui stat, videat ne cadat. Si Deus naturalibus rami non pepercit, vide ne tibi quoque non parcat. In timore & tremore operamini salutem vestram.
units.tr: But, they say, it is written: "Hold fast what you have, so that no one takes your crown. Let him who stands see that he does not fall. If God did not spare the natural branches, see that he does not spare you either. Work out your salvation with fear and trembling."

units.la: Hæ & similes exhortationes comminationesque ad omnes pertinent, etiam ad electos Dei. Ergo electi non sunt extra periculum amittendæ salutis.
units.tr: These and similar exhortations and threats pertain to all, even to the elect of God. Therefore the elect are not beyond the danger of losing salvation.

units.la: Respondeo. Fallacia est à non causa ut causa. Nam quod eiusmodi exhortationes & comminationes in scripturis obuiæ sunt, non ideò fit quod salus Vu v eleelectorum non sit in tuto posita, quantum ad gratiam eligentis; sed cùm electi multiplices infirmitates circumferant in se, & varias patiantur tentationes à mundo, visum est spiritui sancto iis mediis vigilantiam, atque perseverantiam in ipsis operari ad salutem. Sed quid dicemus ad illud Apostoli, Contundo corpus meum, & in servitutem redigo, ne quo modo cum aliis praedicauerim, reprobus fiam. Paulus sine dubio erat electus, attamen laborabat ne reprobus fieret.
units.tr: I answer: this is the fallacy of taking a non-cause for a cause. For the fact that such exhortations and threats are found in Scripture does not happen because the salvation of the elect is not secure, as far as the grace of the electing God is concerned. Rather, since the elect carry about many infirmities in themselves and suffer various temptations from the world, the Holy Spirit has seen fit to work vigilance and perseverance in them for their salvation by these means. "But what shall we say to that saying of the Apostle: I beat my body and bring it into subjection, lest perhaps after preaching to others I myself should become reprobate? Paul was without doubt elect, yet he laboured lest he become reprobate."

units.la: <bl>Resp.</bl> Nodum istum Grammatica expedit. Reprobus enim opponitur hic probato, & sensus est, se aliis exemplo praeire, ne non faciendo quod diceret, in contemtum se ipsum induceret. Sic argentum reprobum dicitur, Ierem. 6. v. 30. Et aliquoties recurrit haec significatio 2. Corint. vlt. v. 6. & 7. Secundò, ut maximè daremus, reprobum hic sumi pro aeterna morte damnando; quae ista est consequentia? Paulus aliique ad vitam electi, carnem suam castigant, aliaque adhibent exercitia fidei & poenitentiae ne pereant. Ergo aliqui ex electis âdis gratia excidunt. Imò idcirco non excidunt, quia lapsus solicitè cauent, & mediis ad salutem vtuntur.
units.tr: Answer: grammar unties this knot. For "reprobate" is here opposed to "approved", and the sense is that he goes before others as an example, lest by not doing what he preached he bring contempt upon himself. Thus silver is called reprobate, Ierem. 6. v. 30. This meaning recurs several times, as in 2. Corint. vlt. v. 6. & 7. Second, even if we grant, for the sake of argument, that "reprobate" is here taken for condemnation to eternal death, what kind of consequence is this? Paul and the others who are elect to life chastise their flesh and use other exercises of faith and repentance so that they may not perish. Therefore some of the elect fall from grace. Nay, rather, they do not fall for this very reason: they carefully guard against lapses and make use of the means to salvation.

units.la: AN ET QVOMODO CERTI ESSE QVEAMVS DE NOSTRI in Christo electione. CAPUT XXIII. De salutis & proinde electionis certitudine, contra Papistas.
units.tr: Whether and how we may be certain of our election in Christ. CHAPTER XXIII. On the certainty of salvation, and therefore of election, against the Papists.

units.la: EXIMIA, vt vidimus, prærogatiua & dignitate pollet electi Dei, quos nulla creatura separare potest à caritate ipsius in Christo Iesu, in quo, nec dum iactis mundi fundamentis, ad æternam gloriam immutabiliter prædestinati sunt. Verùm vt huius consolationis participes esse valeamus, expendendum est, an & quomodo certi esse possimus, de nostri in Christo electione: Vbi etiam, quid de fratribus nostris in Christo, & proximo nostro in genere, hac in parte iudicandum nobis sit, attingemus.
units.tr: As we have seen, the chosen of God enjoy an outstanding privilege and dignity: no creature can separate them from the love of God in Christ Jesus, in whom they were immutably predestined to eternal glory before the foundations of the world were laid. But if we are to share in this consolation, we must consider whether and how we can be certain of our election in Christ. We shall also touch on what we ought to judge in this matter concerning our brothers in Christ and our neighbours in general.

units.la: Harum trium quæstionum prima inter nos & Pontificios disceptari so-let. Etsi enim ij nobiscum defendunt firmitatem & certitudinem diuinæ ele-ctionis,in sese:nobis tamen,quantisper in hac mortalitate viuitur, an simus in numero electorum atque seruandorum, imò an in præsenti in gratia simus apud Deum, incertum esse volunt, nec sciri id posse autumant absque singulari pa-tefactione,qualem Paulo & paucis aliis tribuunt.Hinc Conc. Trident. sub Paulo, III. celebratum, sessione 6.cap.12. in hunc modum definiuit: Nemo quam-diu in hac mortalitate viuitur, de arcano di-uinæ prædestinationis mysterio, vsque adeo præsumere debet, vt certò statuat, se omnino esse in numero prædestinatorum, quasi ve-rum esset, quod iustificatus aut amplius pec-care non possit, aut si peccarit, certam sibi resi-piscentiam promittere debeat. Nam nisi ex speciali revelatione sciri non potest, quos Deus sibi elegerit. Et eadem sessione inter Ca-nones,quibus dubitationem de remis- peccatorum & gratia Dei patres Tri-dentini stabiliunt, anathema pronuncia-tur si quis dixerit, hominem renatum & iustificatum teneri ex fide ad credendum, se cer- to esse ex numero prædestinatorum.
units.tr: Of these three questions, the first is commonly disputed between us and the Papists. For although they agree with us in defending the firmness and certainty of divine election in itself, they hold that for us, as long as we live in this mortal life, it is uncertain whether we are among the number of the elect and those to be saved, indeed whether we are now in grace before God. They maintain that this cannot be known without a special revelation, such as they grant to Paul and a few others. Hence the Council of Trent, held under Paul III, in session 6, chapter 12, defined as follows: No one, as long as he lives in this mortality, ought to presume so far concerning the secret mystery of divine predestination as to determine with certainty that he is altogether among the number of the predestined, as if it were true that one who is justified cannot sin any more, or, if he sins, must promise himself certain repentance. For, unless by special revelation, it cannot be known whom God has chosen for himself. And in the same session, among the canons by which the Fathers of Trent establish the doubt concerning the remission of sins and the grace of God, anathema is pronounced if anyone says that a man reborn and justified is bound by faith to believe that he is certainly of the number of the predestined.

units.la: Hæc Papatus est doctrina, nec mirū, cum iustitiæ Dei non sint subiecti, stu- dentes propriam iustitiā erigere digni- tatis & meritorum humanorum. Cum enim in misericordia Dei per & propter Christum gratis remittentis pec- cata cuiuis credenti minime acquie- scant, sed propriam quoque dispositio- nem, dignitatem, satisfactiones atque merita ad iustificationem spectent, mi- nus adhuc quàm decebat faciūt, quod de acceptione sui in gratiam, seu iusti- ficatione tatum dubitant. Paulus enim remota omni dubitatione categorice pronunciat, se nullius rei sibi conscium, sed per hoc non iustificatum. Et ad Gal. Ecce ego Paulus dico vobis, sacti estis inanes Christi, quicunque per legem iustificamini, & a gratia excidistis. Nam quotquot ex operibus legis sunt, sub execratione sunt.
units.tr: This is the doctrine of the papacy, and no wonder, since they are not subject to the righteousness of God, but strive to raise up their own righteousness of dignity and human merits. For since they do not rest in the mercy of God, who forgives sins freely through and for Christ, to every believer, but also refer their own disposition, dignity, satisfactions and merits to justification, they do even less than they should in doubting whether they are accepted into grace at all. Paul, by contrast, removing all doubt, categorically declares that he is conscious of nothing against himself, yet is not thereby justified. And to the Galatians: Behold, I, Paul, say to you: you are severed from Christ, whoever of you are justified by the law; you have fallen from grace. For as many as are of the works of the law are under the curse.

units.la: Verum enimuerò doctrina istæ dubitationis de gratia Dei in præsenti si- ue in futuro, toto cœlo aberrat à scopo diuinarum scripturarum. Nam di-
units.tr: Indeed, this teaching of doubt about the grace of God, whether in the present or in the future, wanders far from the aim of the divine Scriptures. For the Apostle

units.la: dicit Apostolus, qua scripta sunt, ad nostram doctrinam scripta sunt, ut per patientiam & consolationem spem habeamus.
units.tr: says, whatever things were written, were written for our instruction, that through patience and comfort of the Scriptures we might have hope.

units.la: Spes autem excludit dubitationem: quia spes, vel ipsis Pontificijs confitentibus & definientibus, virtus est, qua spiritualia & aeterna cum fiducia expectantur: seu quod idem est: Spes est certa expectatio futurae beatitudinis ex gratia & veritate Dei veniens. Addunt ipsi & meritis praecedentibus, eo, quod sine meritis aliquid sperare, non spes sed praesumtio dicenda sit. Quasi vero non praesumtionis potius sit, merita contra gratiam erigere. Nam si ex operibus, iam non ex gratia, inquit Apostolus: Sin ex gratia, non ex operibus.
units.tr: Hope, however, excludes doubt. For hope, as the Papists themselves confess and define, is a virtue by which spiritual and eternal things are awaited with confidence; or, what is the same, hope is the certain expectation of future blessedness coming from the grace and truth of God. They add and preceding merits, on the ground that to hope for anything without merits would be not hope but presumption. As if it were not rather presumption to raise up merits against grace! For, as the Apostle says: if it is by works, then it is no longer by grace; but if by grace, then it is not by works.

units.la: Deinde, firmissimum argumentum contra pontificiam dubitationem, sumitur ex eo, quod in scripturis iubemur credere remissionem peccatorum & vitam aeternam, idque non tantum historice, & in genere, sed etiam cum applicatione promissionis gratiae ad nos: sicut etiam ubique scripturae sanctae. stæ flagitant. Vt credamus in Christum, mortuum pro peccatis nostris, vt nobis amissam gratiam Dei, iustitiam & vitam æternam restituerët. Iam autem manifeste pugnant inter se, credere & dubitare, quemadmodum videre est Iacobi 1. Quod si vestrum cuiquam defit sapientia, postulet à Deo, sed cum fiducia, nihil disceptans: quod Græcè est, μηδὲν διακρινόμενος [?]: id est, nihil addubitans, aut vacillans huc illuc, instar fluctuum maris, qui vento agitantur. Et confirmant idipsum voces sacris literis vsitatæ ad fidei vim & naturam exprimendam: vt quod fidei tribuitur πληροφορία, ὑπόστασις, ἐλεγχος, πεποίθησις, παῤῥησία. quæ certe non hæsitationem animi, sed firmam certamque fiduciam significant. Quo igitur directa est doctrina & officina dubitationis apud Papistas, nisi ad euertendam prorsus fidem, & inuertendum nobis vsum scripturæ? ideo à sanctis Dei hominibus traditæ, vt credamus Iesum esse Christum, & credentes vitam habeamus per nomen eius?
units.tr: Next, the strongest argument against the Papist doubt is drawn from the fact that in the Scriptures we are commanded to believe the remission of sins and eternal life, and this not only historically and in general, but also with the application of the promise of grace to ourselves, as all the holy Scriptures everywhere demand: that we believe in Christ, who died for our sins, so that he might restore to us the lost grace of God, righteousness and eternal life. Now believing and doubting plainly contend with each other, as may be seen in James 1: But if any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask of God, but in faith, nothing doubting [μηδὲν διακρινόμενος], that is, not wavering or going hither and thither like the waves of the sea that are driven by the wind. The words customarily used in Holy Scripture to express the power and nature of faith confirm this: what is attributed to faith as fullness of assurance [πληροφορία], substance [ὑπόστασις], conviction [ἔλεγχος], confidence [πεποίθησις] and boldness [παρρησία]. These surely signify not a hesitation of mind but a firm and certain confidence. To what end, then, is the teaching and workshop of doubt among the Papists directed, except to overthrow faith altogether and to turn our use of Scripture upside down? Yet the holy men of God handed it down so that we might believe that Jesus is the Christ, and believing might have life through his name.

units.la: Accedunt expressa scripturæ dicta:
units.tr: To these are added the express sayings of Scripture.

units.la: Matth.8. Confide fili, remittentur tibi peccata tua. Luc.7. Remissa sunt tibi peccata tua mulier. Fides tua saluam te fecit, vade in pace. Confugiunt quidem hic ad speciale revelationem: verum vt nos eam non inficiamur, ita dicimus speciales illas revelationes inniti fundamento generali, promissioni nempe gratiae credentibus factae in Euangelio:qui crediderit & baptizatus fuerit, saluabitur; qui non crediderit, condemnabitur.
units.tr: Matth.8. Take heart, son, your sins are forgiven you. Luc.7. Your sins are forgiven you. Woman, your faith has saved you; go in peace. Admittedly, they here take refuge in special revelation. But although we do not deny such revelation, we say that those special revelations rest on a general foundation, namely the promise of grace made to believers in the Gospel: he who believes and is baptized will be saved; he who does not believe will be condemned.

units.la: Quid Pauli illa testimonia? Noui cui credidi, & mihi persuasum est, eum posse seruare depositum meum in illum diem. Item, certamen praeclarum decertaui, fidem seruaui: quod superest, reposita mihi est iustitiae corona, quam reddet Dominus illo die, iustus iudex: non solum autem mihi, sed omnibus qui diligunt aduentum eius. Item, persuasum mihi est, neque mortem: neque vitam, neque angelos, neque principatus, neque vlla aliam rem creatam posse nos separare a dilectione Dei, quae est in Christo Iesu erga nos.
units.tr: What of those testimonies of Paul? I know whom I have believed, and I am persuaded that he is able to keep what I have committed to him until that day. Likewise: I have fought the good fight, I have kept the faith; for the rest, there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will give me on that day; and not to me only, but to all who love his appearing. Likewise: I am persuaded that neither death nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor any other created thing can separate us from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus toward us.

units.la: Frustra hic excipiunt, Paulum ijs locis tantum de sua certitudine, quam ex singulari revelatione habuerit, loqui. Nam loquitur iñ plurali de se & aliis vera fide Christo insitis, & aduentum eius diligentibus.
units.tr: It is in vain that they object here that Paul speaks in these places only of his own certainty, which he had from a special revelation. For he speaks in the plural, of himself and of others who are implanted in Christ by true faith and who love his coming.

units.la: Sic alibi Apostolus in genere testatur: Iustificati fide pacem habemus erga Deum, & gloriamur in spe gloriæ Dei per Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum. Iustificati enim sanguine eius, nunc multo magis seruabimur per eum ab ira. Et ad Ephesios. Postquam credidistis, obsignati estis spiritu promissionis sancto, qui est arrhabo hæreditatis, in diem videlicet redemptionis.
units.tr: So the Apostle elsewhere bears witness in general: Justified by faith, we have peace with God, and we glory in the hope of the glory of God through our Lord Jesus Christ. For being justified by his blood, we shall now much more be saved through him from wrath. And to the Ephesians: After you believed, you were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise, who is the pledge of our inheritance, until the day of redemption.

units.la: Attestatur & Iohannes: Scimus nos translatos à morte ad vitam. Et per hoc cognoscimus nos in eo habitare, & ipsum in nobis, quod de Spiritu suo dederit nobis.
units.tr: John also bears witness: We know that we have passed from death to life. And by this we know that we abide in him and he in us, because he has given us of his Spirit.

units.la: Hæc & similia testimonia palam euincunt, hominem fidelem posse & debere certò statuere, quod Deum habeat & habiturus sit propitium ad vitam æternam.
units.tr: These and similar testimonies plainly prove that a believing man can and ought to determine with certainty that he has God, and will have him gracious unto eternal life.

units.la: Hoc promisit Deus, inquit Augustus. hoc dixit Deus: si parum est, iurauit Deus. Quia ergo non secundum merita nostra, sed secundum illius misericordiam, firma est promissio, nemo debet cum trepidatione prædicare, unde non potest dubitare. Probè id non tantum contra Papistas, qui quoniam iustificationem ex suis operibus, si non in totum, saltem ex parte pendere volunt, ut supra dictum est, & ipsi non dissimulant, nunquam hanc gratiae certitudinem statuere possunt. Sed vt praeclare apud Bernardum est, serm. 68. super Cant. de meritis quid solicita sit Ecclesia, vbi de propositio & misericordia Dei firmior suppetit, securiorque gloriandi materia? Et alibi serm. 3. de septem fragm. Tria considero, in quibus tota spes mea consistit: Caritatem adoptionis, veritatem promissionis, potestatem redditionis. Murmuret iam quantum voluerit insipiens cogitatio mea, dicens: quis es tu? aut quanta est illa gloria? quibusve meritis hanc obtinere speras? Ego fiducialiter respondeo, scio cui credidi, & certus sum, quia in caritate nimia adoptavit me, quia verax est in promissione, quia potens est in exhibitione. Hic est funiculus triplex, qui difficulter rumpitur, è patria caelesti in hunc carcerem ad nos missus, hunc firmiter tenea-mus.
units.tr: God has promised this, says Augustine. God has said this; if it is too little, God has sworn. Since, therefore, the promise is firm not according to our merits but according to his mercy, no one should proclaim with trembling what he cannot doubt. Rightly so, and not only against the Papists, who, since they want justification to depend on their own works, if not wholly then at least in part, as has been said above, and as they themselves do not conceal, can never establish this certainty of grace. But as Bernard admirably says in sermon 68 on the Song of Songs: what is the Church anxious about in regard to merits, where there is a firmer foundation in the proposal and mercy of God, and a securer matter for glorying? And elsewhere, in sermon 3 on the seven fragments: I consider three things in which my whole hope rests: the charity of adoption, the truth of the promise, the power of restitution. Let my foolish thought murmur as much as it will, saying: who are you? or how great is that glory? or by what merits do you hope to obtain it? I answer confidently: I know whom I have believed, and I am certain that in his exceeding charity he adopted me, that he is true in his promise, that he is powerful in fulfilling it. This is the threefold cord, which is hardly broken, sent to us from the heavenly homeland into this prison; let us hold it firmly.

units.la: Suffragatur & Ambrosius, in cap.1.
units.tr: Ambrose also supports this, in cap. 1.

units.la: Luc. Nō omnis qui iustus est ante hominem, iustus est ante Deum. Beatus plane qui in conspectu Dei iustus est. Beatus ille de quo Dominus dignatur dicere: Ecce verus Israëlita. Verus Israëlita Deum videt, & videri se nouit à Deo, & ipsi exhibet cordis occulta.
units.tr: Luke. Not everyone who is just before men is just before God. Plainly blessed is he who is just in the sight of God. Blessed is he of whom the Lord deigns to say: Behold a true Israelite. A true Israelite sees God, and knows himself to be seen by God, and God shows him the secrets of his heart.

units.la: Contra hæc aduersarij, qui iubent conscientias dubitare, an consequamur remissionem peccatorū, loca quædam scripturæ obiiciunt de imperfectione bonorum operum in hoc seculo, etiam in sanctissimis quibusq;, quorum est confessio ista, delicta quis intelligit? etiam ab occultis munda me Domine. Item, nihil mihi conscius sum, veruntamen in hoc non sum iustificatus.
units.tr: On the contrary, the adversaries, who bid consciences to doubt whether they obtain remission of sins, object certain passages of Scripture about the imperfection of good works in this age, even in the holiest people. Their confession is this: who understands his errors? cleanse me from hidden faults, O Lord. Likewise: I am conscious of nothing against myself, yet I am not justified by this.

units.la: Verùm perperam hæc contra nos allegantur: qui iustificationem hominis coram Deo non nostra dignitate & operibus, sed solius Christi morte & satisfactione æstimamus. Huic enim omnes Prophetæ & Apostoli testimonium dant, remissionem peccatorum accipere per nomen eius quemuis qui crediderit in eum.
units.tr: But these passages are wrongly alleged against us, who judge that a man is justified before God not by his own dignity and works, but by the death and satisfaction of Christ alone. For all the Prophets and Apostles bear witness to this: that whoever believes in him receives remission of sins through his name.

units.la: Sed nihil vulgatius pro Papistarum opi-
units.tr: But nothing is more widely cited in support of the Papists'

units.la: opinione illo Salomonis in Ecclesiaste: Nescit homo utrum amore, non odio dignus sit, sed omnia in futurum seruantur incerta: quomodo vetus habet versio; quod secundum Hebraicam veritatem est, etiam amorem, etiam odium nescit homo: omnia confusim militer omnibus eueniunt, iusto & impio euentus vnus est &c.
units.tr: opinion than that saying of Solomon in Ecclesiastes: man does not know whether he is worthy of love or of hatred, but all things are kept uncertain for the future, as the old version has it. According to the Hebrew truth it reads: man knows not even love, not even hatred; all things happen confusedly to all alike, one outcome for the righteous and the wicked, etc.

units.la: Sed praesidium hoc ficulneum est. Quid enim? obscurumne est in doctrina Ecclesiae, an qui in Christo sunt, & secundum spiritum viuunt, Deo placeant? & contrà eidem displiceant fures, scortatores, adulteri, ebriosi, idololatrae, & similes, de quibus tam euidenter Apostolus pronunciat, tales regnum Dei haud possessuros? Quantum autem ad sententiam Salomonis, ex Hebraeis Aben, Ezra, amore & odio ad homines refert actiuè: quae homines amant vel oderunt, res nimirum secundas vel aduersas sibi euenturas, neminem esse qui sciat. Planior tamen est sensus, quem etiam Olympiodorus super Ecclesiasten assignat; ex euentibus externis huius vitae sciri non posse, an
units.tr: But this prop is a fig-leaf. For what? Is it obscure in the teaching of the Church whether those who are in Christ and live according to the Spirit please God? And, on the other hand, whether thieves, fornicators, adulterers, drunkards, idolaters and the like displease him, of whom the Apostle so plainly declares that such people will not possess the kingdom of God? As for Solomon's sentence, Aben Ezra and Ezra among the Hebrews refer love and hatred actively to men: that men love or hate, namely that pleasant or adverse things will befall them, and that no one knows this. The sense is plainer, however, which Olympiodorus also gives in his commentary on Ecclesiastes: that from the external events of this life it cannot be known

units.la: 1. Cor. 6. Gal. 5. an quis in amore vel odio sit apud Deū. Quem sensum plane confirmat, quod rationis loco additum est, omnibus similiter omnia euenire, iusto & impio, colenti & contemnenti Deum. Hoc animaduerso Alphonsus ingenuè fatetur, testimonium hoc, quod sibi vt plerisque aliis in Papatu, apertissimum prius visum fuisset, parum aut nihil in hac causa probare.
units.tr: (1 Cor. 6; Gal. 5) whether anyone is in the love or the hatred of God. This sense is plainly confirmed by what is added as the reason: all things happen alike to all, to the righteous and the wicked, to him who worships God and to him who despises him. Noticing this, Alphonsus frankly admits that this testimony, which had seemed to him, as to many others in the Papacy, most evident at first, proves little or nothing in this matter.

units.la: Obiicitur etiā ex Ioelis 2. quod Propheta exhortans Dei populum, vt se conuertat toto corde ad Dominum, ait: quis scit si conuertatur Dominus & ignoscat, & relinquat post se benedictionem? Quomodo & Niniuitarum rex populo pœnitentiam suadens, dicebat, Ionæ 3. quis scit si conuertatur, & pœniteat eum, vt non pereamus? Et apud Amos cap. 5. legimus: odio habete malum, & diligite bonum: forte miserebitur Deus exercituum reliquiis Ioseph. Tale etiam est, quod Petrus dicebat Simoni Mago. Act. 8. Resipisce & roga Deum, si forte remittatur tibi cogitatio cordis tui. Hæc omnia aduersari videntur certitudini gratiæ. Sed enim admodum inconsideraté faciunt Pontificij talia adducentes, nisi negare velint ex toto corde resipiscentibus Deù peccata dimittere, quod sex centis scripturæ locis facilè probatur: adeóque illę ipsæ conciones, ex quibus dubitationis illa species oritur, manifeste idem comprobant, dicente Domino apud Amos: quærite me, & viuetis, & erit Iehoua Deus vester vobiscum. Sicut & Ioël testatur, si resipiscant, fore vt Dominus zelo commotus parcat populo suo; vtpote benignus, & clemens, & multæ misericordiæ.
units.tr: It is also objected from Joel 2, where the Prophet, exhorting God's people to turn to the Lord with their whole heart, says: "Who knows whether the Lord will turn and forgive, and leave a blessing behind him?" Likewise the king of the Ninevites, urging repentance on the people, said (Jonah 3): "Who knows whether he will turn and repent, so that we do not perish?" And in Amos 5 we read: "Hate evil and love good; perhaps the God of hosts will have mercy on the remnant of Joseph." Similar is what Peter said to Simon Magus (Acts 8): "Repent and pray to God, if perhaps the thought of your heart may be forgiven you." All these seem to oppose the certainty of grace. But the Papists, in bringing such passages forward, act very thoughtlessly, unless they wish to deny that God forgives sins to those who repent with their whole heart, which is easily proved from six hundred passages of Scripture. Indeed those very sermons from which this appearance of doubt arises clearly confirm the same thing, the Lord saying in Amos: "Seek me, and you shall live, and the Lord God of hosts will be with you." As Joel also testifies, if they repent, the Lord, moved by zeal, will spare his people, being kind, and merciful, and abounding in mercy.

units.la: Quorsum ergo Spiritus Dei aliquoties per Prophetas & Apostolos dubitanter loquitur de spe veniæ? Primùm, etsi culpam Deus remittit vere pœnitentibus, non tamen semper calamitatem corporalem auertit, vt patet Dauidis exemplo, nisi quod pœna resipiscentibus in castigationem paternam convertitur. Secundò, monent docti interpretes, dubitationem, qua scriptura hominum more de Deo loquens, nonnunquam vtitur, non esse ex parte Dei, sed ex parte hominum, quoniam de ijs incertum sit, an pœnitentiam acturi sint. Tertiò, in grauitate criminum salubris instar medicinæ est difficultate proponere veniæ, ut qui peccarunt, initio gustum aliquem habeant gratiæ Dei, & paulatim colligant animos, atque interea non statim assurgant ad securitatem, sed solicitè veniant ad Deum, cum multa agnitione & deprecatione culpæ. Sic medicus non statim leniet dolorem, sed videbit quid magis expediat, forte magis augebit dolorem, quia necessaria videt acriore purgatiorem.
units.tr: Why then does the Spirit of God at times speak doubtfully through the Prophets and Apostles about the hope of pardon? First, although God truly remits guilt to those who repent, he does not always avert bodily calamity, as the example of David shows; except that the punishment of those who repent is turned into fatherly chastisement. Second, learned interpreters point out that the doubt which Scripture sometimes uses, speaking of God in the manner of men, is not on God's side but on men's, since it is uncertain whether they will repent. Third, in the gravity of crimes it is a healthy remedy, like medicine, to propose forgiveness with difficulty, so that those who have sinned may at first have some taste of the grace of God, and gradually gather their spirits; meanwhile they should not at once rise to security, but come anxiously to God with much acknowledgment and entreaty of their fault. So a physician does not at once ease the pain, but sees what is more expedient; he may even increase the pain, because he sees that a sharper purging is necessary.

units.la: Quarto, Ambrosius verba Petri ad Simonē expendes contra Nouatia nos ijs abuti solitos, multis exemplis docet, eam consuetudinem esse scripturæ, vt locutionibus eiusmodi, quibus species aliqua inest dubitationis, etiam citra dubitationem vtatur, simplicitate quadam elocutionis.
units.tr: Fourth, Ambrose, weighing Peter's words to Simon, shows by many examples against the Novatians, who are accustomed to abuse them, that it is the custom of Scripture to use expressions of this kind, which have some appearance of doubt, even where there is no doubt, by a certain simplicity of speech.

units.la: Porrò quod causantur aduersarij, certitudinem gratiæ, si de ea hominibus constaret, ansam & causam fore magnæ licentiæ & Epicureæ securitatis, tis, mera est inscitia & calumnia. Fieri enim non potest, quin sensus caritatis Dei erga nos, qua multitudo peccatorum nostrorū clementer obtegitur, vicissim amorem nouæ obedientiæ cordibus nostris magis magisque ingeneret: sicut scriptum est, Apud te est propitiatio vt timearis. Item, diligā te Iehoua fortitudo mea, arx mea, & cornu salutis mea.
units.tr: As for the adversaries' claim that certainty of grace, if it were established for men, would be the occasion and cause of great licence and Epicurean security, this is sheer ignorance and calumny. For it cannot happen that the sense of God's love towards us, by which the multitude of our sins is kindly covered, should not in turn kindle in our hearts a love of new obedience more and more; as it is written: "With you there is forgiveness, that you may be feared." Likewise: "I will love you, O Lord, my strength, my fortress, and the horn of my salvation."

units.la: Quid, quod aduersarij ipsimet confitentur, specialem patefactionem concedi aliquibus de certitudine suæ salutis? Sequetur ergo secundum ipsos, Deum tales obiicere periculo profanitatis & securitatis Epicureæ.
units.tr: What of the fact that the adversaries themselves confess that special revelation is granted to some concerning the certainty of their salvation? It follows, then, by their own account, that God exposes such people to the danger of profanity and Epicurean security.

units.la: Nec vero quicquam certitudini salutis detrahit, quòd iubemur esse pauidi in cauendis lapsibus, non efferri animo, nec altum sapere, sed timere, vt qui videtur stare, non cadat. His enim & similibus, securitas carnis, non fides damnatur, & requiritur vsus mediorum saluti subordinatorum. Sic Paulus, licet per Angelum certior factus de sua & secum nauigantium incolumitate, & credēs Deo ita futurum quemadmoadmodum locutus erat ipsi, non passus tamen est nautas e naui elabi, sed dixit: nisi isti in naui manserint, vos seruari non poteritis. Ita optime concordant, fiducia salutis, & solicitudo pia vtendi mediis, & non tentandi Dominum.
units.tr: Nor does it in any way detract from the certainty of salvation that we are commanded to be fearful in guarding against falls, not to be puffed up in mind or to be wise above measure, but to fear, lest one who seems to stand should fall. For by these and similar admonitions the security of the flesh is condemned, not faith, and the use of means subordinate to salvation is required. So Paul, though made certain by an Angel of his own safety and that of his fellow sailors, and believing God that it would be just as he had been told, nevertheless did not allow the sailors to slip out of the ship, but said: "Unless these remain in the ship, you cannot be saved." Thus confidence of salvation, pious care in using the means, and not tempting the Lord agree very well together.

units.la: Solet etiam praesumtionis obiectione doctrinam nostram grauare, sed frustra. Credimus enim promittenti Deo. Quo- circa non praesumtione propria, sed ipsius promissione, fiducia & certitudo nostra nititur, vt scite Augustinus diffinitur, tract. 22. super Iohan.
units.tr: Our doctrine is also burdened by the objection of presumption, but in vain. For we believe God who promises. Therefore our confidence and certainty rest not on our own presumption but on his promise, as Augustine rightly defines in tract. 22 on John.

units.la: Tandem pro se torquent, quod nostri scriptores aperte fatentur ipsimet, neminem in hoc seculo omnem sem- per dubitationem de salute sua, & cura sui quam Deus gerit, posse excludere. Qui, inquiunt, de salute sua dubitat, de ea non est certus. Dubitant autem omnes. Ergo nemo de ea est certus. Verum insidias istas facile declinamus hac cautione, siue distinctione. Qui dubitat, non est certus, nempe pro eo tempore quo est in dubitatione, & loquendo de idea quadam certitudinis. Iam autem piorum animis mis ob carnis infirmitatem, & luctam aduersus Spiritum, subinde dubitatio oboritur, non semper, atque eluctan- tur rursum virtute eius ad quem cla- mant cum lacrymis: credo Domine, succurre incredulitati meæ. Etsi vero satis hoc est impedimenti, quominus ideam cer titudinis fidei, qua omnis hæ ratio tre- pidatioque excluditur, pijs tribuere possimus: non satis tamen causæ est, omni certitudine gratiæ & salutis eos priuandi, nisi pari argumento statuere quis velit, & sanctos Dei homines, Ieremiam, Habacuc, Asaphum & alios, de Dei prouidentia & iusta rerum omnium gubernatione incertos fuisse, propter carnis quasdam ea de re dubitationes, Ierem.12. Hab.1. & præsertim Psal.73.
units.tr: Finally, they twist to their own purpose what our own writers openly confess, that no one in this age can exclude all doubt about his salvation, and about the care God takes of him. "He who doubts of his salvation," they say, "is not certain of it. But all doubt. Therefore no one is certain of it." But we easily avoid these snares by this caution, or distinction: he who doubts is not certain, namely for the time in which he is in doubt, and speaking of a certain idea of certainty. Now, however, in the minds of the pious, because of the weakness of the flesh and the struggle against the Spirit, doubt arises from time to time, not always, and they struggle free again by the power of him to whom they cry out with tears: "I believe, Lord; help my unbelief." Although this is indeed enough of an obstacle to prevent us from attributing to the godly the idea of the certainty of faith, by which all such trembling and fear is excluded, nevertheless there is not enough reason to deprive them of all certainty of grace and salvation, unless someone wishes to establish by the same argument that the holy men of God, Jeremiah, Habakkuk, Asaph and others, were uncertain about God's providence and the just governance of all things because of certain doubts of the flesh on that matter: Jer. 12; Hab. 1; and especially Ps. 73.

units.la: Fixum igitur maneat, dum in hac mortalitate, & tanquam exilio huius seculi viuitur, viam & rationem nobis non deesse, qua ad nostri consolationè de salute nostra fiamus certiores. Hoc vero stante, necessario consequitur, quod electionem quoque nostri ad vitam æternam cognitam exploratam- queque habere possimus. Nam cum salus tantum electorum sit, eius profecto certitudo constare nequit sine certitudine diuinæ electionis, quæ salutisfons, origo & fundamentum est.
units.tr: It must therefore stand firm that, while we live in this mortal state, and as it were in exile from this age, we are not without a way and means by which we may be made more certain of our salvation, for the comfort of our own consciences. This being granted, it necessarily follows that we can also know and ascertain our own election to eternal life. For since salvation belongs only to the elect, its certainty cannot stand without the certainty of divine election, which is the fountain, origin and foundation of salvation.

units.la: CAPVT XXIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIV.

units.la: Vnde & qua ratione certi reddamur de nostri in Christo electione.
units.tr: How and by what reasoning we are made certain of our election in Christ.

units.la: MODVS porro quo quis certus fieri possit de sui ad vitam æternam electione, pendet à reuelatione, non carnis & sanguinis, verum ipsius Dei eligentis. Quis enim cognouit mentem Domini, aut quis ei fuit à consilio? Aut quis hominum nouit ea quæ sunt hominis, nisi spiritus hominis, qui est in eo? Ita etiam nemo nouit ea, quæ sunt Dei, nisi spiritus Dei. Nos vero, ait Apostolus, non spiritum mundi accepimus, sed spiritum qui est ex Deo, vt sciamus quæ Deus nobis est gratificatus. Cum ergo consilia Dei sciri nequeant citra patefactionem diuinam, quid mirum si tantum arcanum, prædestinationem inquam nostri ad [illegible, ~1 word] & ad vitā æternam, aliter introspicere nequeamus?
units.tr: The way in which anyone can become certain of his election to eternal life depends on revelation, not of flesh and blood but of God himself who elects. For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counsellor? Or who among men knows the things of a man, except the spirit of the man which is in him? So also no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God. But we, says the Apostle, have received not the spirit of the world, but the Spirit which is from God, that we may know the things that have been freely given us by God. Since therefore the counsels of God cannot be known apart from divine disclosure, what wonder is it that we cannot look into this great secret, namely the predestination of ourselves to [illegible] and to eternal life, by any other means?

units.la: Quod si speculatiue, & a priore vt loquuntur, ad æternum Dei consilium de salute nostra penetrare tentemus, abyssus abripiet nos, & scrutator maiestatis opprimetur a gloria.
units.tr: But if we try to penetrate speculatively, and from the cause prior, as they say, to the eternal counsel of God concerning our salvation, the abyss will sweep us away, and the searcher of majesty will be overwhelmed by glory.

units.la: Est autem triplex fere electionis revelatio; nimirum per effecta ipsius electionis certissima, per verbu promissionis, & per oblignationem spiritus sancti.
units.tr: There are, moreover, roughly three revelations of election: namely, through the most certain effects of election itself, through the word of promise, and through the sealing of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Primus itaque modus, vt dixi, est per effecta electionis, cuiusmodi sunt, vera ac viua in Christum fides, & per fidem in Christum insitio, & iustificatio, regeneratio item spiritus, per vitæ nouitatem, & iustitiæ ac bonorum operum studium sese exerens magis magisque. Ex his a posteriore iudicium fit de electione, tanquam propria iustorum causa. Nam sicut a causa ad effectum, ita vicissim ab effectu ad causam, firma ducuntur argumenta, vt notum est ex Dialecticorum regulis.
units.tr: The first way, as I have said, is through the effects of election. These are a true and living faith in Christ, engrafting into Christ through faith, justification, likewise regeneration of the spirit, shown in newness of life and in a zeal for righteousness and good works that shows itself more and more. From these, judgment about election is made a posteriori, as the proper cause of the righteous. For just as firm arguments are drawn from cause to effect, so conversely from effect to cause, as is known from the rules of the dialecticians.

units.la: Minorem huius argumenti, quòd nempe fides, iustificatio, couerfio, &c. ab electione tanquam causa propria proficiscantur, supra multis confirma-ui-
units.tr: I have confirmed the minor premise of this argument, namely that faith, justification, conversion, and so on proceed from election as their proper cause, by many arguments above.

units.la: Prouer. xj.
units.tr: Proverbs 11.

units.la: Qux & qualis ea fit, uimus, cùm de prædestinationis effectibus ageretur: hîc sólum in conspectu habeantur dicta quædam scriptu-ræ. Act. 13. crediderunt quotquot ordinati erant ad vitam æternam. AdRom. 8. Quos præsciuit, eos & prædestinauit conformes fieri imagini filij sui. Quos autem prædestinauit, eos vocauit, quos vocauit, eos iustificauit, & quos iustificauit, eos glorificauit. AdRom. 11. Electio assecuta est, reliqui occalluerunt. Ad Ephes. 1. Elegit nos in ipso antequam iacerentur mundi fundamenta, vt simus sancti & inculpati coram eo per caritatem, & prædestinauit nos quos adoptaret in filios per Iesum Christum &c. Ibidem cap. 2. Ipsius sumus opus, conditi in Christo Iesu ad opera bona, quæ præparauit Deus vt in iis versaremur. Quò etiam pertinet, quod fides, teste Apostolo, non est omnium, sed electorum Dei. Intellige autem fidem veram atque efficacem per dilectionem: fidem non dæmonis, sed Christiani, quæ in fundamento posita neminem perire permittit, secundum Aug. de fide & operibus. Ioh. 6. Quicquid dat mihi pater, venit ad me, & eum qui venit ad me non eiciam foras.
units.tr: What kind of faith this is we have said when we treated the effects of predestination; here let only some words of Scripture be kept in view. Acts 13: As many as were ordained to eternal life believed. Romans 8: Whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son. Whom he predestined, these he also called; whom he called, these he also justified; and whom he justified, these he also glorified. Romans 11: The election obtained it, the rest were hardened. Ephesians 1: He chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him in love, and he predestined us to adoption as sons through Jesus Christ, etc. The same chapter, chapter 2: We are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand that we should walk in them. To this also belongs the fact that faith, as the Apostle testifies, is not of all, but of the elect of God. But understand faith to be true and effective, working through love: not the faith of demons but the faith of a Christian, which, once laid on the foundation, does not allow anyone to perish, according to Augustine On Faith and Works. John 6: Whatever the Father gives me will come to me, and him who comes to me I will not cast out.

units.la: 2. Thess. 1. Tit. 1.
units.tr: 2 Thessalonians 1; Titus 1.

units.la: cap. 11. ràs. Nemo venit ad me, nisi pater, qui misit me, eum traxerit, & ego suscitabo eum in novissimo die. Est scriptum in prophetis, & erunt omnes docti à Deo (vtique omnes regni illius homines, ait Augustinus.) Quisquis ergo audiuit à patre, & didicit, venit ad me.
units.tr: Chapter 11. Nobody comes to me unless the Father who sent me draws him, and I will raise him up on the last day. It is written in the prophets, and they shall all be taught by God (certainly all the men of that kingdom, says Augustine). Everyone therefore who has heard from the Father and has learned comes to me.

units.la: Ioh.10. Vos non creditis. Nam non estis ex ouibus meis, sicut dixi vobis, oues mea vocem meam audiunt, & ego agnosco eas, & sequuntur me, & ego do eis vitam aeternam, & non peribunt.
units.tr: John 10: You do not believe, for you are not of my sheep, as I have told you. My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me, and I give them eternal life, and they shall not perish.

units.la: His docemur veram fidem & conuersionem dona esse electorum propria, eaque manare ex aeterno Dei de electis suis decreto, vt merito in quaerenda electionis nostrae certitudine oculos huc referamus. Vnde beatus Petrus quoq; admonet, vt per opera bona vocationem & electione nostri firmam efficiamus: adijciendo fidei virtutem, virtuti scientiam, scientiae temperantiam, tolerantiam, pietatem, caritatem infratres &c. Ita futurum est, vt copiose subministretur nobis introitus in aeternum regnu Domini nostri Iesu Christi. Eodem sensu Paulus ad
units.tr: From these passages we are taught that true faith and conversion are the proper gifts of the elect, and that they flow from God's eternal decree concerning his elect. Therefore we rightly turn our eyes here when we seek certainty of our election. Hence blessed Peter also admonishes us to make our calling and election firm by good works, adding to faith virtue, to virtue knowledge, to knowledge temperance, to temperance patience, to patience godliness, to godliness brotherly love, and so on. In this way it will come about that an entrance into the eternal kingdom of our Lord Jesus Christ will be richly supplied to us. In the same sense Paul to Timothy, when he had testified of the firmness of his own election, that the firm foundation of God stands, Having this seal, The Lord knows those who are his, immediately adds another seal, as far as we are concerned: Let everyone who calls on the name of the Lord depart from iniquity. And he adds: If anyone therefore cleanses himself from these things, he will be a vessel for honour.

units.la: 2. Pet. 1. ad Tim. cum testatus esset de firmitate electionis in se, firmum stare fundamentum Dei, habes sigillum hoc, Novit Dominus qui sunt eius: statim subdit alterum sigillum, quantum ad nos: Discedat ab iniquitate, omnis qui invocat nomen Domini. Et addit: Si quis igitur se ipsum ab his expurgauerit, erit vos ad decus. Quibus omnibus significat, in cognoscenda nostri electione, optimam esse rationem sanctimoniæ studiū. Adhæc, idem Paulus de Thessalonicensium & aliorum fidelium electione statuens, non aliunde quam ex fide, caritate, spe alijsque fructibus ipsorum vocationis ad Christū, & participationis in Euangelio, eam æstimabat.
units.tr: By all these things he signifies that in recognising our election the best method is zeal for holiness. Moreover, the same Paul, when he judged the election of the Thessalonians and of other faithful people, estimated it from nothing other than their faith, love, hope and other fruits of their calling to Christ and their participation in the gospel.

units.la: At, si̊ siem & iudicium hoc Pauli in aliquibus haud dubie fefellit, aut superauit exitus. Ergo fides, caritas, spes &c. non sunt certa electionis signa ad vitam æternam. Ad hoc respondeo, caritatem quidem ex eiusmodi signis de proximi electione statuentem, nonnunquam falli: verū causam erroris non esse, quod fides & caritas non sint certa electionis documenta ta in fe'fe,sed quod de proximi fide non simulata & caritate ex puro corde, non perinde ac de nostra iplorum certi efle queamus. De quo diícrimine plenius in sequentibus agetur, vbi quæ huius loci sunt, executi fuerimus.
units.tr: But if this judgment of Paul has in some cases undoubtedly been deceived, or the outcome has surpassed it. Therefore faith, love, hope, etc. are not certain signs of election to eternal life. To this I answer that love, indeed, when it judges the election of a neighbour from such signs, sometimes errs; but the cause of the error is not that faith and love are not in themselves certain evidences of election, but that concerning a neighbour's faith, which is not feigned, and love from a pure heart, we cannot be certain in the same way as we can be about our own. This difference will be treated more fully in what follows, when we have dealt with what belongs to this place.

units.la: Secundus igitur modus quo quis certus fieri possit de sui ad vitā præde- stinatione, est verbum promissionis. Etsi enim singulari promissione tibi aut mihi non dicit Deus: tu es electus, & seruaberis ad vitam æternam: tamen generalis est promissio in verbo, eaque fida & digna omnibus modis quā am- plectamur: quòd quisquis in filium Dei crediderit, habeat vitam æternam, & nin condemnationem non sit veturus, sed suscitandus ad gloriam regni cœlorum, ideoq; ad regnū hoc electus sit: quia re- gnū hoc patris nō dabitur, nisi quibus paratū est ante mundi constitutionem.
units.tr: The second way, therefore, by which anyone can become certain of his predestination to eternal life is the word of promise. For although God does not say to you or me by a particular promise, You are elect and will be saved to eternal life, nevertheless there is a general promise in the Word, and it is faithful and worthy in every way to be embraced: that whoever believes in the Son of God has eternal life, and will not come into condemnation, but will be raised up to the glory of the kingdom of heaven; and therefore he is elect to this kingdom, because this kingdom of the Father will not be given except to those for whom it has been prepared before the foundation of the world.

units.la: Sub hac promissione vniuersali as- sumat in animo quisquis doni Dei par- ticeps est: Ego sum fidelis; & porrò concludat: Ergo seruabor, & per con- sequens sum electus.
units.tr: Under this universal promise, let whoever is a partaker of God's gift take to heart: I am faithful; and let him further conclude: Therefore I shall be saved, and consequently I am elect.

units.la: Pro argumenti huius confirmatione sciendum est, maiorem loqui tantùm de fide salvifica seu iustificante, & per dilectionem agente : hæc enim fides neminem perire permittit: non autem de fide historica, aut temporaria, qualis est multorum, verbum quidem excipientium cum gaudio (gratulantur enim sibi gustum & intellectum aliquem veritatis contra errores, quibus immersi fuerant) sed orta oppressione vel persecutione propter sermonem, statim deficientium; quia non habent radicem in sese, sed πρόσκαιροι sunt.
units.tr: To confirm this argument it must be noted that the major premise speaks only of saving or justifying faith, which works through love; for this faith does not allow anyone to perish. It does not speak of historical or temporary faith, such as that of many who receive the word with joy (for they rejoice that they have some taste and understanding of the truth, against the errors in which they had been immersed), but which immediately fails when affliction or persecution arises on account of the word; because they have no root in themselves, but are temporary [πρόσκαιροι].

units.la: Si autem infirmæ cogitationi succurrat, num qui credit certus esse quea-t, se vera in Christum fide esse prædi-tum? audiatur Apostolus 2. Cor. ulti-mo: Vos ipsos tentate an sitis in fide, vos ipsos probate. An non vos ipsos agnoscitis? videlicet Iesum Christum esse in vobis? Et sanè alterutrum necessarium est, ut aut credens sciat se credere, aut si nesciat, de iustificatione quoque incertus sit, cùm persidem sit iustificatio. Dicimus igitur cum Augustino, quòd suam qui-
units.tr: But if a weak thought comes to mind, whether one who believes can be certain that he is endowed with true faith in Christ, let us hear the Apostle in 2 Corinthians, last chapter: Test yourselves whether you are in the faith; prove yourselves. Do you not recognise yourselves, that Jesus Christ is in you? And indeed one of the two alternatives must be the case: either the believer knows that he believes, or, if he does not know it, he is also uncertain about his justification, since justification is by faith. We therefore say with Augustine that each one should see his own faith within himself and...

units.la: Yy que fidem apud se ipsum videat & noritiam praesertim cum fidei natiua indoles nō ea sit, vt quasi obruta delitescat: sed per vitae nouitatem & per fructus bonorum operum in dies magis magisq; sese aperiat.
units.tr: Let each person look for faith within himself and recognise it, especially since the native character of faith is not such that it lies hidden as if buried. Rather, through the newness of life and the fruits of good works it reveals itself more and more from day to day.

units.la: At apud me ipsum, inquies, reperio magnam fidei infirmitatem, multas & graues dubitationes, quibus fides mea cocutitur. Recte. Verum quaDominus clementia est, infirmum in fide non abiicit sed assumit, nec linum fumigas extinguit, aut calamum quassatum confringit. Et, vt Paulo respondit, potentia eius per infirmitatem perficitur. Tatum infirmitate tuam deplora, & gratia Spiritus sancti assidue implora.
units.tr: "But," you will say, "I find within myself great weakness of faith and many serious doubts by which my faith is shaken." Quite so. But since the Lord is merciful, he does not cast off the one who is weak in faith but takes him up. He does not quench the smoking flax or break the bruised reed. And as was answered to Paul, his power is made perfect in weakness. Only lament your weakness, and constantly implore the grace of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: At anxius sum de finali perseuerantia. Na qui credit, scilicet perseueranter ad finem usque, seruabitur. Si quis autem subduxerit se, non probat eu animus meus, ait Dominus.
units.tr: "But I am anxious about final perseverance." For the one who believes, that is, who perseveres to the end, will be saved. "If anyone shrinks back, my soul has no pleasure in him," says the Lord.

units.la: Ad hanc exceptionem de finali perseuerantia quod attinet, opponi debet perspicuae & indubitatae Dei promissiones non solum de gratia eius in praesenti, sed etiam de finali perseuerantia in eadem, omnium vere fidelium: cuiusmodi sunt, Eum qui ad me venit (veniunt autem credentes) non eiciam foras. Item, hæc est voluntas eius qui misit me, vt omnis qui videt filium & credit in eum habeat vitam æternam. Ego vero suscitabo eum nouissimo die. Item Ioh. 10. Noui oues meas, nec peribunt in æternum, nec rapiet eas quisquam e manu mea. Oues autem Christi sunt, audientes vocem eius: hoc est, vere credentes. Item Ioh. 14. Ego rogabo patrem, & alium paracletum dabit vobis, vt maneat vobiscum in æternum. Et rogaui pro te Simon Petre, ne deficiat fides tua. Rogauit autem pro omnibus suis iam tum credetibus, & credituris. Et apud Paulum: Iis qui Deum diligunt omnia cooperantur in bonum. In omnibus plus quam victores sumus per eu qui dilexit nos. Fidelis Deus, qui non sinit vos tentari supra id quod potestis, sed præstabit vna cum tentatione etiam exitum, vt sufferre possitis. Persuasum habeo, quod qui cœpit in vobis opus bonum, etiam perficiet ad diem usque Iesu Christi. Quis hic, (vt cum Cypriano loquar) anxietatis & solicitudinis locus est? Quis inter hæc trepidus & mœstus est, nisi cui spes & fides deest? Si iustus es & fide vi-uis, si verè in Deum credis, cur non de Domini pollicitatione securus ample-śteris? Deus tibi perseuerantiam polli-cetur, & tu dubitas & fluctuas?
units.tr: As regards this objection about final perseverance, there ought to be set against it the clear and indubitable promises of God, not only concerning his grace in the present but also concerning final perseverance in that grace, for all who truly believe. Of this kind are: The one who comes to me (and believers do come) I will by no means cast out. Likewise: This is the will of him who sent me, that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him should have eternal life. And I will raise him up on the last day. Likewise John 10: I know my sheep, and they will never perish, nor will anyone snatch them out of my hand. Christ's sheep are those who hear his voice, that is, those who truly believe. Likewise John 14: I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, that he may be with you forever. And: I have prayed for you, Simon Peter, that your faith may not fail. He prayed for all his people, who already believed and who would believe. And in Paul: All things work together for good for those who love God. In all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us. God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you can bear, but with the temptation will also provide the way out, so that you may be able to endure it. I am persuaded that he who began a good work in you will also complete it until the day of Jesus Christ. What place is there here for anxiety and worry (to speak with Cyprian)? Who is trembling and sorrowful amid these things, except one who lacks hope and faith? If you are righteous and live by faith, if you truly believe in God, why do you not, secure in the Lord's promise, lay hold of it? God promises you perseverance, and do you doubt and waver?

units.la: Quod loca quædam Scripturæ, & exempla apostatarum, qui fidem habuisse commemorantur, in contrarium afferri solent: ad ea responsum est alias, ne actum agamus.
units.tr: As for the fact that certain passages of Scripture, and the examples of apostates who are said to have had faith, are commonly brought forward to the contrary, a reply to these has been given elsewhere, so that we do not do the same work twice.

units.la: Restat tertius modus, quo electione sanctis suis Deus reuelat, per obsignationem nempe Spiritus sancti in cordibus nostris: secundum dicta Eph. 1. Postquam credidistis, obsignati estis Spiritu il-lo promissionis sancto, qui est arrhabo hereditatis nostræ, dum vindicemur in libertatem &c. Et cap. 4.
